# Isaiah 13-28

### CHAPTER 13

**V. 1.** *{The burden of Babylon*} Here begin prophecies concerning foreign states: all that went before, being concerning God's people, Judah and Israel: save what is by the way occasionally interlaced, concerning the two kings of Syria and Assyria, Rezin and Sennacherib, ch. 7.8. & 8.4. & 10.5–19,33,34. the foreign states, whose ruin is in these prophecies foretold, were such specially, as God's people either had in former times been; at present were, or, in future times should be, much vexed and oppressed by; or, such as they had overmuch rested and relied on. Of the former sort, Babylon stands in the front, whose kings, besides what they had formerly done, were to be principal instruments of the utter subversion of the Jewish estate.

*{the burden*} In this verse, is the inscription of a sermon, or prophecy, against Babylon, contained in this whole chapter, and the next, four last verses of the latter, only excepted: and it is styled as our English renders it, *a burden*. The word in his tropical use, as it is applied unto matter of instruction, or prediction, seems to be more general, and to import only *a lesson*, *a speech taken up*, as we say, by some, or *taken from* some other. As of Balaam it is said, that *God put a word in Balaam's mouth*; and that, *he then took up his parable*. Numb. 23.5,7. And so the Greeks render it; and the Greek writers on Scripture expound it; as implying, *documents*, or *instructions, received* from God, by the prophets. Thus it would be rendered, in the title of King Lemuel's instructions, given him, by his mother; not *the prophecy*: (for there is nothing prophetical in it) but *the lesson, wherewith his mother schooled him*; as also, Lam. 2.14. It seems to include *sermons, preachings*, or *predictions*, in general; where it is said of the fawning false prophets, that they preached unto the people, *sermons*, rather, than *burdens*, (for burdensome lessons, neither the people liked; nor they listed to preach) *of vanity*. But of that see further, on the place. Besides, it is alleged to this purpose, that this title is sometime prefixed before some prophecies, or sermons, that contain no heavy, but joyful and lightsome matter, concerning the people concerned in them; as Zach. 12.1. *The burden*, as it is rendered, *of the word of the Lord*; or, *a lesson of the word of the Lord, concerning Israel*; or, *in Israel's behalf*. Howbeit, since that the word, in his first and proper notion, signifies *a burden*; and it is, in a manner, generally prefixed before such sermons, or prophecies, as contain matter of heavy, and sad occurrents, to betide those, whom they concern; it may not amiss in most places be rendered, *a burden*; or, *burdensome prophecy*: and so here, the subject matter of this prophecy, as touching Babylon, being altogether of that nature: that which is also confirmed, by that which we find in Jeremy, concerning the people's mocking of God's prophets; with the frequent use of this word, in their messages, and God's answer thereunto; Jer. 23.33,36. of which see on the place. The notion of the word is found, in that speech of Jehu, concerning Joram, 2 King. 9.25. *the Lord lifted up*, or *laid this burden* (that is, uttered this sentence, passed this heavy doom) *upon him*.

*{of Babylon*} Heb. *Babel*: Concerning the original of the name; we find, Gen. 11.9. that when upon the vain and presumptuous attempt of people, after the flood, to build a tower, of such an unheard of height, as might secure them against a second deluge; God by dividing their tongues, had bred a confusion among them, and so dissipated their design, the place that they had begun to build, was thereupon, from the Hebrew word *Balal*, that signifies, *to confound*, termed *Babel*: not as some of the Rabbins, and some of ours following them; as compounded of *Ba*, and *Bel*, and so signifying, *confusion comes*: as Leah said, when she named the child her husband had by her servant Zilpah, *Gad, bagad, a troop comes*. For though she used those words, (of the signification whereof also some question is:) yet she gave him not that name; but rather, as others, with more plainness and probability: (for such manner of compositions, are not so common in Hebrew:) *Babel*, simply, without composition; for *Balbel, confusion*, of *Balal*: (as *Golgotha*, in the Greek, and *Gugtalha* in the Syriac, Matth. 27.33. for *Golgoltha, a skull*, of *Galal*) and from thence, with the Greeks, *Babylon*. Now this Babel, or Babylon, became afterwards a prime seat of Nimrod, that great tyrant, who began to settle his principality in Chaldea; from whence he pierced into Assyria, where he built Nineveh, Gen. 10.10,11. the head city of the Assyrian monarchy, at the time of this prophecy, chap. 37.37. Babylon being both then, and for some time after, held by an inferior prince, from the Assyrian monarch: as appears by the story of Manasses; 2 Chron. 33.11. who afterwards, having with some other, shaken off the Assyrian yoke, grew great by the fall of that state; and so settled a new monarchy, called the Chaldean, or Babylonian monarchy. Now by this monarchy, under Nebuchadnezzar, was the Jewish state to be suppressed, Jerusalem surprised, and sacked, the temple destroyed, and the people of the land carried away to Babylon, there to remain in captivity, for a long time: against the terror and trouble whereof, to forearm the faithful, and to support such of them, as might survive the ruin of their country; and remain in that servile condition, with an hopeful expectation of their deliverance from thence, and their return, after some time, into their own country again, the prophet in this prophecy, foreshows the downfall of that state; and the delivery of his people, by means thereof, out of that bondage, which under it they had endured. See of the same argument, Jer. 50. and 51. As for the special occasion of delivering, and divulging this prophecy against Babylon; some suppose it to be, in regard of those grievous calamities, which were foretold should befall the Jewish state, in the latter part of the first, and sixth chapters of this book; which were, say they, to be inflicted by the Chaldeans and Babylonians. But that to me seems not so likely: because there is no mention of Chaldeans, or Babylonians, at all, there: I should rather deem, that it was revealed to the prophet, and by him published, sometime, after that sad message that he brought to King Ezekiah, upon his showing of all his treasure and gallantry, to the Babylonian ambassadors; concerning the evils, that his people, and posterity, in the age following, should from Babylon sustain, chap. 39.6,7. I am not ignorant, that a learned man of great note, would have this prophecy to be understood, not of the destruction of Babylon by Cyrus, but of a former and nearer at hand, between the times of Sennacherib, and Nebuchadnezzar, by Deioces, and the Medes, of whom by a cunning contrivement he had made himself king. But, besides that I find no clear footing of any such conquest of Babylon, in any profane author; nor any footstep at all of it, in holy writ, there are two main arguments, which the prophecy itself affords, for the removal of this groundless conceit. The one is, that the destruction of Babylon, here denounced, is said to be executed on her, for the deliverance of God's people; and the procurement of their liberty, to return again into their own country; chapter 14.1,3. nor is there mention, of any, deportation of them to Babylon, before the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. The other is, that such a ruin of Babylon is foretold, as should be irrecoverable, chap. 13.19,20. & 14.22,23. But if in the interval, between these two terms of time, Babylon had been by the Medes sacked and ruined, as this author would have it, the prophet's words, of her irrecoverable ruin, could not be true; were not then, at least fulfilled: for it is apparent that under Nebuchadnezzar, she was in a most flourishing and magnificent condition, Dan. 2.37,38. & 4.30. This prophecy therefore cannot be understood of any other overthrow of Babylon, save that alone, whereupon followed immediately, the release of God's people, 2 Chr. 36.22,23.

*{which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see}* See the notes on ch. 1.1. & 2.1.

**V. 2.** *{Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain}* At the entrance into this prophecy, there is a solemn proclamation made, as in God's name, for the calling together of those people, that were by his appointment, to be employed against Babylon. So Jeremy begins with somewhat the like, Jer. 50.2.

*{Lift up a banner*} To summon men to appear, to call in people, that may be set apart and enrolled for this service. To which purpose kings are wont to set up their standard, when they intend some expedition, that those of their subjects, who by virtue of their places, or tenures, are obliged to such service, and such others as are willing to be that way employed, may know whither to resort. Of this use of an ensign, or banner, see also ch. 5.26.

*{upon the high mountain*} Some render the particle, not *upon*, but *against*. By *the mountain*, here mentioned, understanding Babylon, so termed not from her situation; (for she stood in a low ground) but for her high towers and stately buildings: in regard whereof also it is by Jeremy so styled, Jer. 51.25. and the epithet here given it, some of them interpret, *quiet*, and *secure*, such as Laish is said to have been, Judg. 18.27. deriving it from a Chaldee word, so used in the Talmud. Others, *plain*, as Jerusalem is called *the mountain in the field* and *the rock of the plain*, Jer. 17.3. & 21.13. fetching it from a Syriac word, in that version oft used: other of them again, *dark*, and *gloomy*, whom the old Latin follows, deducing it (but with no very good analogy) from the Hebrew word, that signifies the *evening*. But the greater number of interpreters render the whole branch, as our English has it, *upon an high mountain*. For so I suppose it would be a little better, and more suitable to the original, wherein no article is expressed, as not pointing to some one special place; but intending an high, or eminent place, from whence such a signal may be farthest descried: such as are usually made choice of for the erecting of beacons, and displaying of banners, for that purpose set up. See chap. 18.3. and 30.17. Nor need we make doubt of rendering it an *high hill*; since that we find the word so frequently used in that sense, Numb. 23.3. chap. 41.18. & 49.9. Jer. 3.2,21. & 4.11. & 7.29. & 12.12. & 14.6. notwithstanding that a late learned annotator contends strongly, to have it both here, and in all those places, to signify *a plain*, because the like word in Syriac signifies *a plain*, Luk. 3.5. His reason here is, because soldiers are wont to be mustered, not on the hill, but in the plain. But the use of the banner here erected, is to call those together, that may be mustered afterward, in the plain.

*{exalt thy voice unto them*} Cry aloud unto, or call aloud upon, those that are to be employed against Babylon; that you may be heard of them, as far as may be. So ch. 40.9. Jer. 22.20.

*{shake the hand*} Beckon with the hand, unto those that are farther off, whom your voice will not reach unto. See on chap. 10.33.

*{That they may go into the gates of the nobles*} Heb. *and they shall go*: as chap. 11.3. That they may march unto Chaldea, and surprise the cities belonging to that empire, (*gates*, for *cities*, as Deut. 16.5.) or, (because it is another word, that is commonly used in that kind of speech; and this for distinction sake, would be rendered, *door*, rather than *gate*, as Ezek. 46.3.) to break into the houses and palaces of the Babylonian princes, ch. 45.1.

*{into*} This particle is not in the text; but it is to be supplied, as Gen. 10.11.

*{the nobles*} The great peers of Babylon, like those of Nineveh, chap. 10.8. equal to princes. The word here used, answers that of the Greek rendered *Benefactors*, Luk. 22.25. and it signifies properly men of *frank*, and *free* disposition, Exod. 35.5,22. such as keep great houses, and are large, and liberal in expense, chap. 32.5,8. that which our English title of *Lord*, is in the old Saxon, said also to import, as intimating, what men of that rank sometime were, ever ought to be. Now unto the houses of such great ones, would the enemy endeavor, especially to make entry, partly, because these were the heads of the state, and their houses most conspicuous, and partly, because both most and best pillage was there to be had, chap. 45.1,3.

**V. 3.** *{I have commanded my sanctified ones*} I have by a secret instinct given in charge, (as chap. 10.6. & 23.11. Jer. 34.22. & 50.21.) to those whom I have prepared and set apart for this service, to wit, the expedition against Babylon. For so is the word *sanctify* used, Jer. 6.4. & 12.3. Joh. 10.36. & 17.19. a metaphor, from the religious rites, that men were to use in way of preparation, when they were to set upon any holy duty, any solemn part of God's service, Exod. 19.10,11. 1 Sam. 16.11. 2 Chr. 30.3,15–19. Job 1.5. Psal. 26.6. and the slaughter to be made by these, of God's enemies, was a service of God, and unto him as a sacrifice, ch. 34.2,6,7. Jer. 48.10. who these *sanctified ones* are, see Jer. 51.27,28. and in part hereafter, ver. 17.

*{I have also called my mighty ones*} The same thing in other terms expressed. For God's *call*, here, is the same with his *charge* before, as ch. 41.2. & 46.4. his *mighty ones* here, with his *sanctified ones*, there. Such, as he has fitted and furnished with might and ability sufficient, to go through stitch with his work, chap. 5.27. and 45.5. and that come armed with his might, chap. 45.1,2. Joel 2.11.

*{for mine anger*} Some refer these words to *mighty ones*, as if the meaning were that therefore, they were mighty, because armed with God's anger: as God is said therewith to arm himself, ch. 59.17. See ch. 10.5. But they depend rather upon the verb, *called, I have called* them, as some, *in mine anger*, or, as ours well render it, *for mine anger*, to execute vengeance for me, upon Babylon. So the Lord made the wicked *for the day of evil*, Prov. 16.4. the genuine sense of that place.

*{even them that rejoice in my highness*} Such, as shall go willingly and gladly about my work: and triumph in those gallant actions, that I shall work by them. So the most, rendering the words much to the same effect, that our version yields. But the Hebrew syntax well considered, may seem to run somewhat a diverse way. The word translated, *them that rejoice*, is not a participle; but a noun substantive; and signifies *exulters*, or *triumphers*, rather, than barely, *rejoicers*, and it is in a ruling form, taking unto it the word following, rendered *highness*, but signifies, as that of near affinity with it, chap. 12.5. sometime *excellency*, or *gallantry*, as Deut. 33.29. sometime, *pride*, or *haughtiness*, as ch. 9.9. & 16.6. so that the term sounds, word for word, *triumphers of gallantry*, or, (if we will take the term in the worse part, which here suits not so well) *of haughtiness*, that is in our language, *gallant triumphers*, such as do gallantly triumph. There rests the pronoun, *my*, which in the ordinary course of construction, is to be annexed rather with the word ruling, than ruled, though in the reading it be annexed to the latter. So chap. 2.20. *his idols of gold*, and *his idols of silver*; not *the idols of his gold*, or *the idols of his silver*; though the pronoun be there also affixed to the latter, and so would it be rendered here, not *the rejoicers*, or, *triumphers of*, or, *in his gallantry*, but, as before, *his sanctified, his valiant*: so here, *his brave*, or *gallant, triumphers*. Those his commanders, and servitors, that shall bravely demean themselves in this service, and gallantly triumph in their victorious successes, v. 15,17.

**V. 4. ***{The noise of the multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people}* Heb. *the voice of a multitude*, or, *of tumult*; or, *tumultuous noise*, (as Psal. 65.7. Amos 5.23.) *is*, or, *is heard upon the mountains*; according *to the likeness*, or *similitude*, (as Ezek. 13.15.) *of the noise of a great* or, *ample*; that is, numerous people. The word, *noise*, should be supplied in the latter branch from the former. See the like, ch. 5.10. There shall be heard upon the mountains such a tumultuous and confused noise as is wont to be in a place, where a great multitude of people are gathered together, Ezek. 1.14. In which words, the prophet, as speaking of a matter in present action, and as if he heard the very noise, that the companies made, either in their muster, or in their march, does in a very lively manner, represent unto us, either the great swarms of people; flocking and thronging together unto God's standard before mentioned, erected on the hills, v. 2. or the warlike troops of the Medes and other their associates, passing over the mountains to break into Chaldea.

*{a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of the nations gathered together*} Heb. *a voice of tumult*: as chap. 16.6. or, *of a streperous*, or, *tumultuous company*: as chap. 17.12. The same thing repeated: implying withal, that Cyrus his vast army, wherewith he marched against Babylon, should consist, not of one nation though one only be named: v. 17. but be gathered out of many kingdoms: See Jer. 25.14. & 27.7. & 50.41. & 51.27,28.

*{the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle*} Heb. *the host of war*; that is, *his warlike host*, as Num. 31.14. A defect of the pronoun as if he had said; No marvel, if the army be so numerous, and made up of people out of so many countries, when the Sovereign Commander of all the creatures, musters up his forces; as princes are wont to do, when they are to set forth, or send out some great army. See ch. 1.9.

**V. 5.** *{They come from a far country*} From Media and Persia, places remote from Babylon. For Assyria, and some other countries intervened them. See on Jer. 51.46. Heb. *from a land of longinquity*. So ch. 46.11.

*{from the end of heaven*} That is, of the land, or country lying under heaven: as Matth. 24.30. So Jer. 50.26. A common phrase used to signify the people; or countries, most remote, of the world commonly known: or with whom any ordinary commerce is, Neh. 1.9. Act. 2.5. Col. 1.23. Nor is it here any hyperbolical speech, as some would have it; it is no more than if he had said, *from the land's end*; which is precisely true of the Persians, the Medes, associates, and both subjects to one king, to wit, Cyrus. For their country is bounded on no small part of it, with the main sea, and the Persian gulf; as is Media also on the one side with the Caspian Sea.

*{even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation*} Or, *instruments of his wrath*. For the word is very general, see ch. 22.24. & 23.7. those that he makes use of, to execute vengeance by, and to punish those, with whom he is wroth, ch. 10.5.

*{to destroy the whole land*} Of Chaldea: whereof Babylon was the head city, Jer. 25.12. or, as some render it, *the whole earth*, that is, the whole world. The Chaldean empire, that had subdued a great part of the world then commonly known in those parts; and whose kings in the height of their pride deemed themselves lords of the whole world, Jer. 27.5–8. Dan. 2.37,38. The whole verse may well thus be rendered, *There are coming from a far country from the land's end, the Lord, and his instruments of wrath, to destroy the whole land*. For the prophet speaks of it, as of a thing present; before; as if he heard the noise of them thronging together, here, as if he saw them, now in their march onward toward Babylon. See the like of the Assyrians' march towards Jerusalem, ch. 28.32.

**V. 6.** *{Howl ye*} The prophet turns his speech, here, to the Babylonians, and as before he called on those people, that were to be employed against Babylon, to meet together, and march thitherward: so now he calls upon the Babylonians, to howl and lament, in regard of the calamities that were coming upon them. So ch. 23.1,6. Jam. 5.1.

*{for the day of the Lord*} God's day, that is, his time of visitation, and vengeance, wherein he will come unto judgment against Babylon. So chap. 2.12. and 10.3. Jer. 46.10,21. and 50.20,27. Zeph. 1.7.

*{is at hand*} It is *near*: because they that are to execute it, are on their way thither, v. 5. so Ezek. 30.3. Joel 1.15. & 2.1. & 3.14. Obad. v. 15. Zeph. 1.7.

*{it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty*} And therefore unavoidable. So Job 31.23. Joel 1.15. There is an elegancy in the sound, of the words, in the original; which our English cannot so fitly express. The title given to God here, is *Shaddai*. Concerning the notation and proper sense thereof, there is some diversity of opinion among the learned. Those that render it, *Almighty*, derive it from a word that signifies *to waste*; and so understand it, to intimate one, that is able, as a mighty conqueror, to lay all waste at his pleasure. That which suits well with the words here, *as devastation, from the devastator*. Others derive it from a word, that signifies, *a teat*, that yields milk; and so it should imply one, that feeds all, and ministers nourishment unto all; that which is frequently given unto God in Scripture, Gen. 48.15. Psal. 23.1. & 104.11,15. 136.25. & 145.15,16. & 147.9. Others, lastly, render it, *All-sufficient*, one that has *all-sufficiency* in himself, and is able to supply and furnish his creatures with all sufficiency needful for them, Psal. 23.1. and 34.9,10. and 84.11. Luk. 22.35. 2 Cor. 9.8. 1 Tim. 6.6,17.

**V. 7.** *{Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every heart shall melt*} An utter discouragement, and failing both of hand and heart, shall upon the report hereof, befall the Chaldeans; and no marvel, when God himself is coming in the head of the host against them, Ps. 76.5–7. Ezek. 22.14. See the same, Ezek. 21.7.

*{all hands*} All their *hands*, to wit, of the Babylonians, and their associates, as v. 22.

*{hands be faint*} Or, *feeble*, as 2 Sam. 4.1. or, *fall down*, or, *hang down*: as they are wont to do when men are so weakened, or tired out, or quashed, upon some sudden affrightment, their spirits being quailed that they are not able to hold them up, or make use of them for their succor or defense, Exod. 17.11. Jer. 6.24. & 50.43. Ezek. 7.17.

*{heart melt*} A metaphor from wax, that melts, when the fire comes near it, Psal. 22.14. & 68.2. or the dew that melts with the heat of the sun, Exod. 16.21. Hos. 6.4. or any such moist and flashy bodies, as upon slight occasions, alteration of air, change of weather, a little rain or wet falling on them, and the like, are prone to melt away, and run to water, Exod. 15.15. Deut. 1.28. Josh. 2.11. & 5.1. & 7.5. & 14.8. 2 Sam. 16.10. Ps. 39.11. & 58.7,8. & 112.10. ch. 10.17. & 19.1. Nah. 2.10.

**V. 8.** *{And they shall be afraid*} As Job 21.6. or, *For they shall be affrighted*: as it is rendered, Jer. 51.32. or, *troubled*, as 1 Sam. 28.21. 2 Sam. 4.1. or, *amazed*, as Exod. 15.15. Judg. 20.41. or, *dismayed*: as ch. 21.3. for the word signifies such a fright, as disturbs, and distracts, or such a sudden fright, as casts women into travail, and makes them to miscarry, Psal. 48.5,6. ch. 21.3.

*{And*} Or, *For*: as Chap. 8.21. & 9.11. for a reason is here rendered, why their hands became so feeble, and their hearts so faint. They were surprised with extreme fear and terror.

*{pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them*} A defect of the pronoun: as ch. 1.3,15. v. 15.

*{they shall be in pain, as a woman that travaileth*} Heb. that is, *bringing forth*. Such pangs and pains shall seize on them, as are wont to do on women in such case. A similitude oft used, to express extremity of distraction and distress. So, besides, the places before pointed to, Chap. 36.17,18. & 37.3. Jer. 6.24. & 22.23. & 30.6. & 49.24. & 50.43. Mic. 4.9,10.

*{they shall be amazed one at another*} Or, *they shall be amazed*, looking *one at*, or, *one another*; as Gen. 43.33. & Jer. 36.16. They shall be dismayed to see others of their own, and those, such as sometime seemed so valorous and courageous, to be now so faint-hearted, Jer. 50.43. or they shall stand like men, amazed and amated, staring one upon another, as being at their wits' end, not knowing what to do; nor having the heart to turn their hand unto aught, whereby to help themselves, or others. So Psal. 107.27. Chap. 19.14–16.

*{one at another*} Heb. *a man at*, or, *on his neighbor*, or *friend*. A familiar phrase in that language, Gen. 11.3. Exod. 11.2. Jer. 7.5. & 9.7. & 22.8. & 23.30. Zach. 8.16,17.

*{their faces shall be as flames,}* Heb. *faces of flames* shall *their faces* be. For the syntax: see Lam. 4.7. Now this, here, some understand of shame. They shall so blush for shame of their cowardice and distraction, that their faces shall look as if they were all on a fire: as Ezek. 7.18. *shame* shall be *upon all faces*. But such fear and faintness, as is here intimated, usually drowns, and destroys shame: at least hinders such blushing. Others expound it of such illness of look, as famine and hardship, and such calamities as attend war, are wont to produce, making men look many times even like unto chimney stocks. So Lam. 4.8. *their visage is blacker than a coal*: and Lam. 5.10. *our skin is black, as an oven, through famine*. And these places indeed, well express the meaning of the phrase, *faces of flames*. Being rather, *faces scorched with the flame*, Ezek. 20.47. such as theirs are wont to be, that work at the forge, and the fire; or such, as men's faces seem to be, when they stand before some kind of fire; that is, pale, wan, swarthy, and discolored; than as some would have it of the same color with flame, but they fail in the ground of such kind of visage here implied. Thus manner of look here mentioned, proceeding not from those evil effects of war; not as yet produced: but from the fear and dreadful expectation of it, as yet only approaching them, and on the way toward them; as Jer. 30.5,6. *a voice of fear, and trembling, every man, with his hands on his loins, and all faces turned into paleness*, Joel 2.6. *before their face, people shall be much pained; all faces shall gather blackness*: and Nahum 2.10. *the heart melteth, the knees smite one against another; much pain is in all loins; and all their faces gather blackness*. Which places, precisely parallel to this, both clear the phrase, here used; and hold out also the ground of such appearance in the face here described, the very same that is here intended, extreme fear. Of the sense of the place, then, there is no doubt; it is clear enough, that they should look pale, or black, in the face; nor need much question be made of the ground or occasion thereof, that it should be out of fear. Howbeit, the phrase seems somewhat harsh, *faces of flames*, for *faces scorched*, or discolored. I incline, therefore, to that, which some of our Jewish authors have, to wit, that by the word here used, is to be understood, not *flames* of fire; but a certain people inhabiting some part of Africa, of the posterity of *Mizraim*, or *Egyptus*, in Scripture sometime termed *Lehabim*, (the word here used) Gen. 10.13. 1 Chr. 1.11. and sometime *Lubim*, 2 Chr. 16.8. *Lehabyans*, or *Lybians*, as we commonly style them, coming nearer to the latter; who are for visage not unlike to the *Ethiopians*, or *blackmoors*, Jer. 13.23. Amos 9.7. on the north of whom they border, being tawny moors at least. And I see not what should hinder this exposition, *their faces*, shall be, as *the faces of Lybians*, *inde facies Livida, Latinis*: defect they shall look like blackmoors, tawny moors, for fear; the defect of the note of similitude, is common, Gen. 49.9. Deut. 33.22. c. 8.

**V. 9.** *{Behold the day of the Lord cometh*} Or, *is come*, as of a thing present: before, he said it was near, vers. 6. he says now, *it is come*. So Ezek. 7.10. *Behold the day, behold it is come, Behold*, as chap. 10.33.

*{cruel*} *cruel* he is, or, *cruel* it is, either he, or the day, or he, in that day; as they dealt cruelly with God's people, Jer. 6.23. Chap. 46.6. So will God then cause the enemy to deal cruelly with them, Jer. 50.42.

*{both with wrath, and fierce anger*} Heb. *and wrath, and heat of nose*, *and* for *both*, as Gen. 36.24. Jer. 17.26. *with wrath*, as, *with thy sword, and with thy hand*, Psal. 17.13,14. compared with v. 7. and *heat*, or *fervor of nose*, or, *visage*, (the word signifies either,) for *fierceness of anger*, as ch. 7.4. vers. 13. because anger then usually discovers itself, Psal. 18.15. & 34.16. So God says of himself, Ezek. 38.18. *heat*, or *fury*, or, *fume shall rise in my nose*, or *my face*.

*{to lay the land desolate*} Heb. *to put the land*, (to wit, of Chaldea, as ver. 5.) *into desolation*, as Jer. 2.15. and 4.7. See vers. 8.

*{and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it*} As Ps. 37.38. & 104.35. See ch. 14.23.

**V. 10.** *{For the stars of heaven, and the constellations thereof, shall not give their light*} A description of extreme horror, without any glimpse or hope of relief, counsel, or comfort. When men are in such an horrid confusion, and forlorn condition, as if the light of heaven were wholly taken away from them; all shall be so full of horror and terror, that the heavenly bodies may seem to have lost their light. So ch. 5.30. & 34.4. Ezek. 32.7,8. Joel 2.10,31. Matth. 24.29. Mar. 15.24. Luk. 21.25. a resemblance taken, as some think, from men in distress at sea, to whom no light from heaven, for direction, appears Act. 27.20.

*{the stars of heaven*} Fixed in the firmament to give light to those upon the earth, Gen. 1.16,17. Psal. 83. & 148.3.

*{the constellations thereof*} The word, *cesil*, whose plural is here used, does signify some particular and special, either star, or constellation, that is, company of stars neighboring and making up one sign or figure; as appears by Job 9.9. & 38.31. Amos 5.8. Where this and some other are reckoned up together. That which crosses the conceit of those, who suppose *Cocab*, and *Cesil* to be distinguished, in Hebrew, as *aster*, and *astron*, in Greek, *Stella*, and *Sidus*, in Latin. The former in each language, to signify a single star, the latter, a compound figure. For to omit, that it might, without much labor, be showed, that in the two latter languages, the words are oft promiscuously used; the places before pointed to, do evidently evince, the word *Cesil*, to signify, not *a constellation*, or *configuration*, in general; but some particular, either signal star, or, such. Some of the Hebrew doctors, suppose it to denote a single star, and that to be *the Scorpion's heart*. The Greeks sometime render it *Hesperus*, or *the evening star*, otherwhere, otherwise. And it is not unlikely, that those three mentioned together in Job, were rather single stars, (and why not some of the wandering ones, as well, as the fixed,) of more eminent luster, of whom more special notice was taken in regard of the times of their appearance, than such configurations, as from our artists we now have, and the Greeks and Latins before us; the greatest number whereof, have their figures and denominations assigned them, from the feigned stories of the old fabulous Greeks, it being very questionable whether any such figures were in Job's time, invented, or no. Howbeit, most writers take it to be, not a single star, but a composure of stars, made up, into some figure; which some guess to be the *Pleiades*, or *seven-stars*, at the *bull's head*, called by the Greeks, also, *Hyades*, because at their rising, they used to bring rain. And this, it seems, they conjecture because some of the Rabbines affirm it to be that constellation, which the Arabians call *Subchin*, or, *Suchelin*, (for the Latins differ) by a term manifestly corrupted from the Latin; *Suculae* a name given to those *seven-stars*, by the old Latins, upon a mistake, supposing the Greek term *Hyades*, to have risen, not from the verb *hyein*, that signifies to rain; but from the noun, *hyes*, that signifies *swine*. But against this is objected, that this knot arises in June; whereas this *Cesil* should rise in the Hebrews' ninth month, answering to our November, in part, which thereof also is deemed to have its name, *cislew*, Zach. 7.1. Others, therefore, (and so both the old Greek, and Latin, sometime) render it rather, *Orion*, a constellation, consisting of many bright stars, and rising in the month before mentioned. Here, and here only, we have it in the plural number, whereof by the Hebrews two reasons are rendered. Some say, because of two stars of the same name near to the two poles: a thing unlikely, that notice should be taken by the Hebrews of such stars as in their hemisphere did never appear. Others suppose, that it is as plural, comprehending all those, that made up such a constellation: one whereof, being of more eminency than the rest, should be termed *Cesil*, and that with the rest of them *Cesilim*, that is to say, *Cesil*, and his companions. I suppose, that it is plural, to denote, by a metaphorical manner of speech, any the brightest stars, or constellations; as if it were said, *no Cesils*, or, (supposing *Orion* to answer *Cesil*,) *no Orions*, shall afford any light. That star, or configuration of stars, being one of the brightest in the sky. So are proper names, very frequently used both in our own and other languages, *Had we so many Pauls and so many Nestors*, and the like: that is, so many comparable, for piety, to the one, and for policy, to the other. The prophet's words then, may thus be rendered, *Neither the stars of heaven, nor the Orions thereof* (the brightest of them, or of the constellations thereof) *shall give their light*, See *Nimrim*, Ch. 15.6.

*{the sun shall be darkened in his going forth*} When he comes forth, as a bridegroom out of his chamber; or sets forth, as a man of might to run a race, Psal. 19.5. he shall no sooner begin to peep out, but he shall clasp in again: or, he shall be eclipsed at his rising: as one stifled in the birth. See Amos 8.9. Act. 2.20.

*{and the moon shall not cause her light to shine*} There shall be no light with them, either by day, or by night, Gen. 1.16. Psal. 136.7–9. And this may seem to have respect, to what is spoken of the Babylonian king, or state, chap. 14.12. where for his goodly, and glorious luster, he is compared to the bright *morning star*, and yet, now said to have no spark or glimpse of light; much less able to afford, or make show of it to any other, sitting in darkness himself, chap. 47.5.

**V. 11.** *{And I will punish the world for their evil; and the wicked for their iniquity}* Heb. *and I will visit upon the world evil, and upon the wicked their iniquity*. That is, I will in my visitation by judgment inflict evil upon the world, (that is, upon the Chaldean land, and state. See on ver. 5.) and upon the wicked, the punishment of their iniquity, as Gen. 4.13. Or, I will punish them, for the evil that they have done; and the wicked among them, (as the *sinners*, before, v. 9.) for the iniquities committed by them: *to visit*, for to *punish*, as chap. 26.14. Jer. 51.44. and *evil*, for their *evils*, a defect of the pronoun, as v. 11. or their *prayers*, Isa. 65.2.

*{and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and lay low the haughtiness of the terrible*} Or, *of the roisters*; or, *tyrants*; such as in a bravery, force and offer violence to others; for so the word properly signifies, chap. 25.4,5. I will pull down the pride of Babel; whose excessive pride and insolency, has been so formidable and burdensome to other people, Jer. 51.55. Pride is one of the sins, that that state is taxed for. See chap. 14.4,6,13,14. Dan. 4.30. & 5.20. and pride, wheresoever it is found, shall be plucked down, Chap. 2.11–17. & 10.12. & 24.10,12. Luk. 14.11. & 18.14. The same thing in divers terms repeated, as vers. 12.

**V. 12.** *{I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir*} This is spoken, to intimate, either the small number of people that should be left, after the Medes had made spoil and havoc of them, in the city, as things that are rare, are wont to be deemed *precious*: 1 Sam. 3.1. Prov. 25.17. See ch. 4.1. or the eagerness the enemy should have, to make slaughter of them that they should not for the best gold that was, were it tendered them, be hired to spare the life of a Babylonian, ver. 17. Yet let it be considered, whether this may not be understood, of the difficulty that should be, for the Babylonian king to retain men with him, to maintain fight against the enemy, and to defend his city; when upon their approach, such a terror should surprise all sorts, even the valiant ones among them; as was before related, vers. 7,8. Surely, the prophet Jeremy foretells, Jer. 50.16. & 51.9. that those which had been called in, from other parts, to assist Babylon, when they perceived, how it was likely to go with him, should begin to withdraw themselves, and leave her to shift for herself: and these, it is likely, would not with gold, or silver, be hired to stay by it, for fear of losing their lives, see ch. 51.6. And this I take to be the true intent of the prophet, in this place. See ver. 14,15.

*{a man*} The words here used are, *Enosh*, and *Adam*: of which, see on Ch. 2.9. They are here used promiscuously: for whereas, some would have the former, here, to signify, a man of price, and worth, the latter a common man: the notation of the former word will not bear it.

*{than fine gold*} An expression oft used; to show the excellency of that wherewith it is compared. Psal. 19.10. & 119.127. Prov. 8.19. The word here used, is *paz*, or *phaz*, which some think so called, because *mupaz*, or, *muphaz*, that is, *fused*, and by fining (the drossy matter, and baser metal, being wrought out of it) made more solid. For whereas it is said of Solomon, 1 King. 10.18. that *he covered his throne*, *with Mupaz gold*: it is said of the same, 2 Chr. 9.17. that he covered it with *pure gold*: yet, others suppose it to be so called, rather, from the name of the place whence it was brought; and from whose some suppose the kingdom of *Phez* in Africa, to retain its name to this day: and so *gold of uphaz*, Dan. 10.5. they conceive to be *gold from uphaz*, as it is, Jer. 10.9. That is, brought from thence; as *gold of Ophir*; that is, gold brought from Ophir: yea they want not, that guess the word *muphaz* in Solomon's story, to be contracted of *meuphaz*, that is, *from Uphaz*. But that is not so probable; and yet the want of that letter in some words, is not unusual: of which see on ver. 20. Some make this the same with Ophir; the rather, because they find mentioned by Ptolomy, a bay, called *Pasi*, and a river, called *Phasis*, in the island of *Taprobane*; which they conceive therefore to be Ophir. I am not ignorant also, that some, and those of no small note, would have this word not to signify *gold*, but some precious *stone*: and that the word *topaz*, is thence derived: the Greek article prefixed to it. But the places of Scripture, where it is found oft used, evince the contrary: as *vessels of paz*, Job 28.17. and *a crown of paz*, Ps. 21.3. But of the several names of gold, in the Hebrew, see on Job 28.15–19.

*{gold of Ophir*} A place of special note for fine gold, 1 Kings 10.11. Job 22.24. Ps. 45.9. The region seems to have been at first so termed, from the posterity of Ophir, one of Sem's issue, who there seated themselves, Gen. 10.29. Some of later times have supposed it, to be *Peru* in America; upon a weak conjecture, from some letters, in either word the same. But those that have made more diligent inquiry into the story, of the discovery of those parts, inform us; that no region there was anciently of that name: but that it came to be so called by the discoverers, upon a mistake, through ignorance of the country language, from an answer returned them, unto a demand made by them, from the natives, which they misunderstood. Nor is it likely, that Solomon's fleet, or Jehoshaphat's, which they manned out for Ophir, ever came near those parts. 1 Kings 9.28. & 22.48. Others therefore seek for, and would seat this Ophir elsewhere. Some in Arabia, near to the Red Sea now termed the *Arabian Gulf*, or in an island situate in the mouth of that sea. Here, the rather in regard of the *gold of Sheba*, mentioned, Ps. 72.15. and the great quantity of gold that the queen of that country brought with her to Solomon: 1 Kings 10.1,2,10. Sheba being held generally to be a region in those parts. But that is too near a place, for a fleet sent out from Ezion gaber, on the coast of that sea, to make a three years' voyage. 1 Kings 9.26,28. & 10.22. Others therefore travel further westward, to find it in Africa: because store of gold, is at this day, found in those parts; and it is almost the only trade for it, that we now have: besides, that *uphaz* famous for fine gold, they suppose to be *Phez*, as was before said. But others run as far eastward to discover it in India, these; most of them, seat it in the kingdom of Siam in Sofala, or Sumatra called by our ancienter geographers, the *golden continent*, and the *golden Chersonesus*, or *Peninsula*, which yet they suppose, to be an entire island, rent off from the continent, as Sicily from Italy. Though some of them lately in *Zeilam*, rather, which they conceive to be that, which was called anciently *Taprobane*, termed, as they conjecture, by the Phenicians, at first, *Taph-par-van*, or, *provan*, that is, the coast of *Parvan*, whereof, 2 Chr. 3.6. And in process of time, *Taprobane*; wherein also they find a port, called *Hipporus*, or *Ipporus*. Pliny, lib. 6. cap. 22. and Solin, c. 4. which they guess to be the same with *Ophir*. In these parts, some suppose it the more probable, that Ophir was situate; because the issue of Sem, whereof *Ophir*, and *Havilah* were two brethren, are said to have seated themselves to the East, Gen. 10.39,40. And of the land of *Havilah*, which in likelihood was not far remote from Ophir, it is said, that it has store of *good gold*. Gen. 2.11,12. Howbeit in these days, there is no report of any great store of gold, that is found in those Indian quarters, where ours trade; we send much thither, receive little thence. Besides, that they are enforced by the site of *Havilah*, Gen. 2.11. to make two *Ophirs*, as well as two *Havilahs*. Gen. 10.7,29. In a matter, therefore, so abstruse and ambiguous, I dare not determine.

**V. 13.** *{Therefore I will shake the heavens; and the earth shall remove out of her place*} *Therefore*, that is, because of their sins, and wickedness, their pride, and cruelty before mentioned, v. 9,11. or, by reason of that extremity, dread, and horror, that shall possess them, upon the approach of the enemy, and their own forces forsaking them; I will cause them to be in such confusion and distraction, as if heaven itself were falling upon their heads, and the earth moving, or removing, from under their feet. A proverbial form, intimating a most horrid confusion. See the like, Psal. 18.7–15. & 76.8. & 77.16–18. & 114.3,4. Chap. 29.6. Jer. 50.46. Joel 2.10. Hag. 2.21. See also Job 9.5,6.

*{in the wrath*} Or, *through the wrath*, by reason of it, as Psal. 18.7. Or *in the day of the wrath*, the word *day*, supplied from the next clause; as Ch. 18.7. & 22.5. & 30.17.

*{of the Lord of hosts*} In my wrath, or through my wrath. For God himself speaks it, the noun for the pronoun, as ch. 6.12. & 8.7. Of the title, see ch. 1.9.

*{and in the day of his fierce anger*} See v. 6,9. Psal. 18.8. ch. 6.4. Jer. 4.8.

**V. 14.** *{And it shall be*} Babylon shall be.

*{as the chased roe*} Or, *as a chased roe*, (for there is no article in the Hebrew) as one of the most timorous sort of creatures, and most unable, save by flight, to shift for itself, among those, that use to be hunted, Prov. 6.5. 1 Chr. 12.9.

*{and as a sheep, that no man taketh up*} Like a straggling sheep, one of the silliest creatures, and less able to defend itself against any ravenous beasts, or by flight to make escape, than the former; and sure therefore to miscarry, in places where such beasts of prey are, if none look after it, Psal. 119.179. she shall be at her wits' end, not knowing whither to betake herself, or where to be in safety. See Jer. 50.17.

*{they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land*} The reason why Babylon shall be in such plight, to wit, she shall be forsaken by her hired forces and confederates, Jer. 50.16. & 51.9.

*{every one*} Heb. *a man*: as ch. 9.20.

*{turn*} Heb. *look back to*, or, *look after*, ch. 8.22. & 53.6.

**V. 15.** *{Every one that is found, shall be thrust through*} The reason why people shall withdraw themselves from her, because they cannot with any likelihood, of safety, without loss of life, stay with her.

*{that is found*} By the Medes, or, simply, that is, or stays in Babylon *to be found*, for, *to be*, or, *abide*. An usual Hebraism, Deut. 19.10. Esth. 1.5. Act. 8.40. A defect of the particle, *therein*, or, *in her*, as Deut. 8.12. ch. 35.9.

*{shall be thrust through*} Slain with the sword, or lance, Jer. 51.4.

*{every one, that is joined unto them*} As an assistant. Heb. *added* to them: as Chap. 29.1. & 30.1. a defect of the pronoun, as ver. 8. Yet some render the word, *decrepit, consumed*, and spent with years and age: and the word sometime signifies, *consumed*, 1 Sam. 26.10. 1 Chron. 21.12. as if the meaning were that the Medes should no more spare old, than young, as of the Chaldees the like is said, 2 Chron. 36.17. Lam. 5.12. and so it should have reference to what follows, ver. 16. But I suppose it rather to have reference to the former part of the verse; and to be rendered by ours there aright.

*{shall fall*} Be slain as ch. 10.34. Jer. 44.12.

*{by the sword*} Or other weapon of the enemy. One of most general use put for all, chapter 1.20. Jer. 47.6. & 50.35–37.

**V. 16.** *{Their children shall be dashed in pieces*} The Babylonians' children, according to that prophetical curse, Psal. 137.9. They shall, through the just judgment of God, in way of requital, be served themselves, as they had beforetime served God's people, 2 Chr. 36.17. Of the like cruelty, see 2 King. 8.12. Hos. 14.1. Nah. 3.10.

*{before their eyes*} To increase their grief. See Chap. 1.7. Deut. 28. 31,32. Jer. 39.6.

*{their houses shall be spoiled*} Or, *rifled*, Zach. 14.2. Jer. 51.56.

*{and their wives ravished*} So had they dealt with God's people before, Lam. 5.11. See this judgment threatened, Deut. 28.30. Amos 7.17. Zach. 14.2.

**V. 17.** *{Behold*} See ver. 9.

*{I will stir up*} Heb. *I am raising up*: or, *Behold me raising up*. I am even now about it. See ch. 3.1. He speaks as of a thing present, in act, and in sight, ch. 43.19.

*{stir up*} Or, *raise up*. ch. 41.2. & 45.13.

*{the Medes*} Heb. *Madai*. A people descended from *Madai*, the son of Japhet, Gen. 10.2. 1 Chr. 1.5. whose country is commonly called *Media*. Of the site whereof, see ver. 5. ch. 41.2. Jer. 50.3. The Medes with the Persians, and other their associates, marching under the conduct of Cyrus and Darius, were those sanctified ones, spoken of, ver. 3. for under the name of the Medes, are the Persians also comprehended; as in some sort, one people, as well for vicinity, as affinity, and acknowledging one king, ch. 21.2. Jer. 51.11. Dan. 5.28. and 9.1.

*{against them*} The Chaldeans, and Babylonians, v. 19.

*{which shall not regard silver, and as for gold, they shall not delight in it*} The like syntax, see ch. 8.13. & 45.9. they shall not regard to spare any for ransom, as Saul did Agag, 1 Sam. 15.10. *the ransom of a man's life are his riches*, says Solomon, Prov. 13.8. but this ransom will not serve in the day either of God's wrath, Prov. 11.4. or of man's rage, Prov. 6.34,35. Ezek. 7.19.

**V. 18.** *{Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces*} Or, *But they shall dash to pieces the youths*, shot thorough *with bows*: *But*. Heb. *And*, the copulative for the adversative: as ch. 11.4,14. *they shall dash to pieces the youths*, shot thorough; that is, when they have shot them through, they shall dash them to pieces: or, they shall shoot them through, and then dash them to pieces. See the like defective construction, ch. 14.12. & 38.14,17,21. *with bows*, a defect of the preposition: as ver. 9. or *with* their *bows*, a defect also of the pronoun: as ver. 7. *hands*, for, their *hands*. They shall be so outrageously affected towards them; and enraged against them, that it shall not suffice them, to have shot them through, and slay them; but they shall batter also their dead bodies to pieces. An expression of extreme cruelty, ch. 3.15. Jer. 50.17. Mic. 3.3.

*{and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eye shall not spare children*} They shall neither give quarter upon any terms, unto any that are able to crave it, nor afford it to young children, and tender infants, that are not able to ask it. They shall show no more pity on them, than themselves did, when time was, to God's people, 2 Chr. 36.17. Psalm 137.8. Jer. 50.15,29. Jam. 2.13.

*{the fruit of the womb*} Children proceeding from the womb, as fruit from a tree, Psal. 127.3. & 132.11. or enclosed yet in the womb, whom they should destroy, by slaughtering the mother going great with them, or ripping them up in inhumane manner, 2 King. 8.12. & 15.16. Amos 1.13.

*{their eye shall not spare children*} The very sight of whose tender estate, might move to commiseration, and their tears and cries much more, Exod. 2.6. no rueful sight shall move them to show mercy on any. See the phrase, Deut. 7.16. & 13.9. & 19.13,21. & 25.12. Ezek. 5.11. & 7.4,9. & 8.18. & 9.5,10. & 16.5. & 20.17.

**V. 19.** *{And Babylon the glory of kingdoms*} Heb. *the beauty*, or, *delicacy of kingdoms*. The most beautiful, and delicate estate and monarchy, that ever was, that *goodly head of gold*, Dan. 2.37,38. that *Lady of kingdoms*. Ch. 47.5. *the praise of the whole earth*, Jer. 51.41. The word contains in it, a resemblance of the roe, before mentioned, ver. 14. a very comely and lovely creature; whom the spouse therefore compares her love unto, Cant. 2.9,17. and 8.14. See Chap. 4.2.

*{The beauty of the Chaldees' excellency*} Or, *the Chaldees' excellent bravery*, as the word is rendered, Chap. 3.18. (the words are both joined together, Chap. 4.2.) So is Babylon styled, because the chief city of Chaldea; and such, as for ornaments, riches, and stately buildings, might compare with any city in the world, Dan. 4.20. and was that therefore, whereof the Chaldees did most vaunt themselves. And the word here signifies, as excellency, and stateliness; so haughtiness also and pride, Job 35.12. & 38.11.

*{the Chaldees*} Heb. *Chasdim*. A people so termed, from *Chesed*, the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, Gen. 22.22. Of whom, they were descended. So Ezr. 5.12. Jer. 34.11. & 37.5. But, sometime, it is used, for magicians, and astrologers; because the Chaldees were much addicted to such studies, Dan. 2.10. and 4.7. and 5.7.

*{shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah*} Heb. *as*, or, *according to* (as Jer. 3.26.) *God's overthrowing*; or, *God's subversion* (as Amos 4.11.) *with Sodom and with Gomorrah*, or, wherewith he overthrew (the verb supplied out of the noun: as Deut. 1.27. Hos. 3.1.) *Sodom, and Gomorrah*. Of which, Gen. 19.24. The same is said of Babylon, Jer. 50.40. An usual expression, importing, a sudden, a total, inevitable, and irrecoverable destruction, Deut. 29.23. Chap. 1.9. Jer. 49.18. Zeph. 2.9. 2 Pet. 2.6. Jud. 7. Howbeit, I cannot approve of what the Rabbines tell us, out of their legends, rather than chronicles; that Darius having slain Baltasar, Dan. 5.30,31. reigned one year in his stead; yet destroyed not Babylon, as is here foretold. But in the year following, it was burnt with fire from heaven, as Sodom and Gomorrah were. To which purpose they abuse a place of Scripture, Jer. 51.46. Of which, when we shall come to it. But this is but a figment of theirs, whereof there is no store wanting in them. The truth is; that this utter devastation of Babylon, was not at once; but began at the conquest of it, by Cyrus and Darius, and in the succeeding ages was consummated.

**V. 20.** *{It shall never be inhabited*} Heb. *It shall not sit for ever*: sit to wit, on a throne, as a queen, or empress: as c. 10.13. or, *inhabit*, that is, be inhabited by any, (as the word is used, Jer. 17.6.) or have place to inhabit, Jer. 51.41. So Zach. 7.7. & 9.5. *Not for ever*, that is never, as Joh. 8.51. & 11.26. to wit, after that it is once thus utterly destroyed. Nor need we, as some would have it, expound the words, with a concealed restriction, until the time set by God, for her restitution and restoration. For the ground they build on, taken from a twofold destruction of that state, whereof the one is imaginary, (see ver. 1.) is but sandy.

*{neither shall it be dwelt in*} Heb. *neither shall it dwell*, Jer. 50.29. It shall neither have throne to sit on, nor place to dwell in: neither regain power to rule; nor rise to be a place, for habitation, again, Jer. 51.26,43,52. or, *it shall neither abide*, (as ch. 11.6. *nor dwell*: have no place of abode, or dwelling; that is, have no being, being utterly abolished: as Job 7.9,10. & 14.10. Psal. 37.36. & 103.16. Jer. 51.64. Rev. 18.21.

*{from generation, to generation*} Heb. *unto generation, and generation*, that is *for many ages* successively, as Joel 2.2. or, *for ever*, as before; and as Psal. 100.5. contrary to that, which, presumptuously, she promised to herself, that she should *sit*, not *as a widow*; but as *a Lady, for ever*, ch. 47.7,8.

*{neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there*} The Arabians are a people, that kept in tents, wherewith they removed from place to place as they met with pasture for their cattle, Jer. 49.29. called *Scenitae* therefore by the Greeks; but in Hebrew they were so termed, either from the *plains*, whereon they lived, Jer. 3.2. (the word so signifying. See Deut. 2.8. & 3.17.) or because their country lay toward the *evening* quarter, the *west*, (see on chap. 59.19.) between the Persian gulf, and the Red Sea; the utmost west of Asia, or, because they were a *mixture*, or medley of divers nations, Jer. 25.24. as the word itself also sometime imports, Exod. 12.38. Neh. 13.3. For I suppose that most unlikely, which yet some hold out that in regard of their hue, they should so be termed from the *raven*, Cant. 5.11. the one having the same radical letters with the other, and because the *Kedarenes* from their *blackness* may seem so termed. See on Chap. 21.16. See also further of *Arabia*, on Chap. 21.13. The word rendered, *pitch tent*, is observed to want a letter, to wit, *Aleph*: the like whereunto is found, Job 35.11. Prov. 17.4. and as some, 1 King. 10.18. See on ver. 12. The meaning is, that the place shall be so waste, that those wandering people shall not sit down there, because they shall not find conveniency of feeding for their flocks. Though some would have it to be, in regard of those harmful creatures, that should roost and harbor in the rubbish and ruins of the city, ver. 21,22.

*{neither shall the shepherds make their folds there*} Heb. *shall not make* (their cattle) *to lie down*, (or, *lodge*) *there*. So Jer. 33.11. See the like defect of the noun after the verb, Cant. 1.7. The same thing is in divers terms expressed. And we may observe a further desolation denounced against Babylon; than is against Nineveh, Zeph. 2.14. for it is said, that *the flocks yet shall lie down* in the one; which is denied here of the other. The reason whereof, see Chap. 14.23. and 17.2.

**V. 21.** *{But wild beasts of the deserts shall lie there*} He had before showed who should not lodge, or abide there: he relates, now, who should.

*{wild beasts of the desert*} Heb. *Tsijim*. Such kind of beasts as are wont to haunt, and abide in *Tsijah*, that is, in *dry* places, or, *wastes*, ch. 41.18. & 53.2. So Chap. 34.14. Jer. 50.39. It is used also sometime for people, that dwell in such regions, Psal. 72.8. compared with Psal. 68.6. Some of the Rabbines say, that they are such, as we call *martens*.

*{and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures*} Heb. *Ochim*, a word nowhere else found. It is by most thought to signify, some such kind of harmful creatures, as by biting, or scratching, put men to pain: as derived from an interjection of a mournful notion, Ezek. 6.11. & 21.9. Some of the Rabbines say, they are such, as astonish men at the sight of them: yet others, again, would have them to be no other than our *ferrets*. Nor want there of the Jewish writers, that suppose the word to signify, not a beast, but a bird: some kind of fowl, so termed of the doleful tune that it has. These, whatsoever they were, should lodge in their houses, being destitute of inhabitants; or in the wastes, where they sometime stood; as Chapter 5.17.

*{and owls shall dwell there*} Heb. *the owls' daughters*: and it is not unworthy the observation, that the name here given the *owl*, is never found in Scripture single, or simply; but instead of *owl*, or *owls*, is constantly said, *the daughter of the owl*, Levit. 11.16. Deut. 14.15. or. *the owls' daughters*, Job 30.29. Chap. 34.13. & 43.20. Jer. 50.39. Mic. 1.8. save once only, Lam. 4.3. where the masculine plural is found alone. Hence one of the Jewish writers gathers, that the *Ochim* before mentioned, are no other than these *owls' daughters*, or young ones which for want of food in those waste places, (wherein owls, in the places pointed to, are noted most to abide) being forsaken by the dam, (as in that place of the Lamentations is implied, that they oft are) do make a very doleful, and hideous noise. But the text seems to relate them, as several sorts of wild creatures: and the generality of the term would imply some other matter. But these among others, were to be as the inhabitants and free-denizens of ruined Babylon. See Rev. 18.2.

*{and satyrs*} The word here used, does most commonly signify *a goat*, Gen. 37.31. Levit. 4.23. So called, because he is very *shaggy*, or *hairy*. For that seems to be the primary notation of the word, Gen. 27.11. Hence it is, that it is here rendered, *Satyrs*. Which were among the ancients, supposed to be monstrous creatures, haunting woods, and waste places, of a mixed composure, having visage, and hands like a man, and going upright, as men do: but horned, and hairy, and cloven-footed like goats; and Jerome tells of an eremite, that should meet with one of them in the wilderness. Some such monsters, it seems, our translators thought here intended. To which purpose, also, one of the Jewish doctors says, that it is a kind of inhuman wild goats. The word is sometime used for *Devils*: such, as the idolatrous people in old time adored. So it is taken, Levit. 17.7. 2 Chr. 11.16. and they seem so termed; either because they appeared in the shape of goats, unto those that adored them, or had dealings with them: as to witches at their meetings, they are reported oft-times to have done; or because by ugly, and dreadful apparitions, they used to strike terror, and horror, into those that beheld them, and make their hair, as we say, stand an end. For the word sometime, signifies *horror*, chap. 28.2. Ezek. 27.35. & 32.10. and *an horrid tempest*, Job 9.17. & 18.20. such, as these also, sometime raise, or appear with, Job 1.19. And this way the Jewish commenters, most of them go, making the *Seirim*, here, the same with the *Shedim*, Deut. 32.17. and Psal. 106.37. In which place of Moses, there is an allusion to the notation of the word here used, in the root, from whence it springs, in that clause, *with whom their fathers were not affrighted*. And this exposition may seem to receive strength, as from that in Matth. 12.43. where the devil dispossessed is said to haunt waste and dry places: so, from that parallel place, Rev. 18.2. where it is said, that Babylon was, upon her fall, become *an habitation of devils, and an hold of every foul spirit*. Nor do I doubt, but that that place has a compliance with this. But that is spoken of spiritual, and mystical; this, of corporal, and material Babel. And I suppose, rather, the word, here, to signify some kind of strange beasts, as used to keep in waste places: from their horrid, and ugly shapes so termed: and the rather, because it is said, chap. 34.13. *the Seir shall cry to his mate*: see further there. There want not, also, that suppose the *Seir* here mentioned, to be a kind of fowl, and that of the rank of *owls*, of a middle size, between the least and the greatest: called by the Greeks, *scops*: whence also, we have our English word, *scoff*: because it is a fowl full of gesticulation, prone to imitate the gestures that others represent it with, and to act, what it sees them do: and is by such means, commonly, taken, as the dotterel is with us. The main reason, I suppose, that induced them to entertain this conceit, was the word of *dancing*, here used. Which, of how small force it is, to infer this new notion, will in the opening of it appear.

*{shall dance there*} So the verb signifies, when applied to man: as 2 Chron. 15.29. Eccl. 3.4. but *to skip*, rather, when referred to beasts, as to rams, and lambs, Psal. 114.4,6. and to calves, and the young of other creatures, sporting, either by themselves, or one with another, Ps. 29.6. unless we shall, with the Rabbines, and the Greek, render it; *and devils shall dance there*. The prophet may seem, the rather, to have used the word, that signifies, as well *to dance* as *to skip*, to comply with the word in the next branch, ver. 22. that signifies as well *to sing*, as *to cry*.

**V. 22.** *{And the wild beasts of the islands*} Heb. *Ijim*. The word signifies primarily *islands*, chap. 11.11. & 40.15. & 42.15. here such wild creatures, as breed, and keep in islands, destitute of inhabitants; or unto which, few or none, have any ordinary access. The Chaldee expounds it, *wildcats*; the Latin, *owls*. The Rabbis, some of them, *Pies*, or, *Jays*. Some of ours translate it, *a terrible*, or, *affrighting wight*: and expound it, a *dragon*. This they build upon two grounds. The former, concerning the translation, is from the form of the verb, which is singular; and they would have the noun also, so to be, as derived from the word *Ajim*, that signifies *terrible*, or *dreadful*; whence the *Emim* had their name, Deut. 2.20. But there is no reason to make *Ijim*, more, than *Tsijim* a singular; and of the syntax more anon. The other ground concerning the exposition, is drawn from the prophet's method. He began, say they, with beasts, the *Tsijim*, and *Ochim*; then passed on to fowls, *Owls*, and *Seirs*, ver. 21. and here he comes to speak of creeping things, or serpents. But this they speak without proof. And I see no good ground therefore, for this new devised notion, and for the exposition, as little. Our English renders it not amiss in the general; the Jewish writers, for the notation, backing them therein; though in the particular designation of the kind, not agreeing among themselves.

*{shall cry*} It is by the Jewish writers observed here, that the noun is plural, the verb singular: the meaning, say they, being, that *each one* of them *shall cry*. Of which kind of syntax, see chap. 2.20. The word here used, signifies properly *to answer*: but it is used for *to sing*, chap. 27.2. Hosh. 2.17. according to which use of the word, some of the Hebrews would have it taken here: but to signify, *crying aloud*, and that, as they suppose, in a doleful tune. See Zeph. 2.14. But the word, when it is applied to singers, and *singing*, does not so much import, simply, *to sing*, as *to sing by course*, one party, as it were, answering another. So Exod. 15.21. Ezra 3.11. And so *the Ijim shall answer* (so the old Latin renders it) or, *cry*: each, to others, chap. 34.14. *the Seir shall call*, or, *cry to his mate*. Those of the Jewish writers, that would render it, *shall dwell*, or *abide*: as derived, from a word, that signifies a place of *mansion*, or *abode*, Psal. 90.1. Nah. 2.13. seem to strain overfar, without example, and that needlessly, having a plain, and obvious sense, at hand.

*{in their desolate houses*} Some of the Rabbines read it, with change of one letter, an R, for an L, *in their palaces*: avouching for it, the like, Ezek. 19.7. and so the Chaldee Paraphrast takes it. But another of them, controls this interpretation, affirming, that these letters are not convertible, and he renders the words *they shall cry*, there, *with their widows*: such of their kind, as have lost their mates; as also our English editions, some of them, represent it there in the margin; and that of Geneva, has it in the text: and it is well known, that the word, is commonly used for *widows*, chap. 10.2. & 54.4. and does properly so signify. But I find none, that herein concur with this Rabbi. Our last, here, renders it. *desolate houses*, as in Ezekiel, *desolate palaces*, as if he had said, widowed ones, as some give it in Latin: which, howsoever, it might well be admitted here in regard of the story; yet that place in Ezekiel, will not so well brook it; for it seems not suitable to the rest of the relation, describing the pranks, that a stirring and potent prince should play, to say, that *he wasted the desolate palaces* of other princes, *and laid waste their cities*. I suppose rather, that both there, and here, it should be rendered, simply, *palaces*, without any such superfluous addition, as our old ancient English versions all had it; nor was the old Latin other; and that, either by the scribe's oversight one letter slipped in for another, (the like whereunto see, Jer. 2.20. & 15.14.) or by a kind of lisping pronunciation, the one came to be sometime used for the other.

*{in their*} Heb. *in his*; to wit, in the palaces of their king, or, of each one of his nobles, also, of whom, before, vers. 2. So Chap. 32.14.

*{and dragons*} To wit, *shall cry*, (to be supplied, as the Rabbine well observes, from the former branch, as Gen. 1.16. vers. 6.) after their manner. The word signifies the greatest sort of fish, such as we call *whales*, Gen. 1.21. See on Lam. 4.3. and likewise the greater sort of *serpents*, or, *snakes*: to wit, of such, as wanting feet (which some serpents, as the crocodile, and others have) glide along by wriggling of their bodies, to and fro, on the ground, as those great fish, whom in shape, also, they resemble, do in the water. So it is taken, Job 30.29. chap. 34.13. & 35.7. & 43.20. Jer. 9.10. & 10.22. & 49.33. & 51.37. and of the greatness of some of them, see *Plinius natural history*, l. 8. c. 11,14.

*{in their pleasant palaces*} Heb. *in the palaces of delicateness*; or, *deliciousness*, or, *voluptuousness*. So Mich. 2.9. *houses of pleasure*, or, *delight*, for, pleasant houses, but, here, rather, in the worse part, for their curious, and delicate, or their voluptuous, their banqueting, and reveling houses, that is, in the places, where such, sometime stood. See ch. 32.13. See the use of the word, Deut. 20.54,56. chap. 47.1. Jer. 6.2. the pronoun is wanting, as ver. 7.

*{and her time is near to come*} As ch. 56.1. Jer. 48.16. Ezek. 36.8. Babylon's time, wherein she is to be destroyed, so ver. 6. where it may be demanded, how this may be made good, when as it was not till about some two hundred years, after this prophecy, that Babylon was surprised and sacked, and the Chaldean empire ruined by Cyrus, and Darius. For this prophecy was delivered above one hundred year, and upward, before the Babylonian captivity, which lasted full seventy years, Jer. 25.11,12. Whereunto (passing by that novel, and groundless conceit of a former destruction of Babylon, of which, on vers. 1.) answer may be returned. First, that what may seem long with man, is short with God, with whom a thousand years are but as yesterday, Psal. 90.4. or, but as tomorrow; for a thousand years, and a day, are all one with him, 2 Pet. 3.8. Secondly, that this is by the prophet thus spoken, as speaking to them, that were in, and under the captivity, (the most of whom, in all likelihood, were as yet unborn) for whose support, and comfort, in that heavy time, this was especially delivered, and for their use left upon record, by him. So Jeremy writing to them, in the very beginning of the captivity; in the reign of Zedekiah, Jer. 51.59. speaks of Babylon's ruin, as of a business approaching, Jer. 50.1,2. & 51.46,56. And lastly; that as to the eye of faith, things future, and afar off, are as present, Joh. 8.56. 2 Cor. 4.17,18. Heb. 10.37,38. So the prophet by the Spirit of prophecy, seeing these things, revealed unto him, as present, or approaching, vers. 5. does accordingly speak of them. See ver. 4,5. & Jam. 5.8,9.

*{and her days shall not be prolonged*} Her *days*; that is, the days of her welfare, of her prosperity, and tranquility (so the Hebrew doctors) shall not last long, or be prolonged any longer, as Job 9.25. Ps. 89.45. Jer. 51.47. Lam. 4.18. & 5.21. Or, the days of her visitation, as Hosh. 9.7. no longer deferred; and so it is the same in effect with the former. The time shall not be long, before this be put in execution. God will hasten to effect it, in his due time. It shall not be protracted beyond that set time, that God has assigned it; See Ezek. 12.25,27,28.

### CHAPTER 14

**V. 1.** *{For the Lord will have mercy upon Jacob*} This chapter is a continuation of the denunciation of the destruction of Babylon. And it begins with a reason rendered of the hastening of it, mentioned, chapter 13.22. God's mercy, and compassion towards his people; the deliverance of whom depended upon Babylon's destruction, Jer. 50.3,4. So Ps. 102.13. Zach. 1.16.

*{Jacob*} See ch. 2.5. & 9.8. Ps. 14.7.

*{and will yet choose Israel*} He will receive them into grace and favor, as if he had made a new choice of them again. So some. Others, he will make it appear, that they are still his chosen people, as at first they were, Deut. 7.6,7. It may be rendered, *I will refine* (as he promised to do, ch. 1.25.) or, *make choice ones* of them; *again*, as the word is used; ch. 48.10. Hagg. 2.23. So the *elect* or, *choice lady*, 2 Joh. 1. And of Paul, *an elect vessel*, or, *instrument*; Act. 9.15. for, *a choice one*; or, *I will select*, or, pick them out again, and gather them out of the places, into which they were scattered, see ch. 11.11. & 27.12,13. So the word is used, 1 Sam. 2.28. & 24.2. Luk. 6.13. Joh. 15.19. So Zach. 1.17. & 2.12. And this interpretation the next branch confirms.

*{yet*} Or, *yet again*, to take away the ambiguity, for the word, here used, does not answer the English, *yet*, for, *notwithstanding*; but as we say, *further yet*; or, *yet again*, as chap. 8.5. So *once*; not for *sometime*; but *once only*, Heb. 9.27,28. compared with vers. 25,26. Jud. 3.

*{Israel*} See chap. 1.4. Some render it here. *in Israel*, that is, say they, not all Israel, but some in Israel; the remnant of elect ones, chap. 10.21,22. Rom. 11.5. And there is indeed a particle in the Hebrew here, that does usually so signify; but, that particle, in the syntax of that language with some verbs, (this here used among other) is either superfluous, or a note of the accusative case only. So here; the main body of the people surviving then, intended, and so, chapter 44.1,2. Deut. 14.2. 1 King. 8.16. & 11.32,34.

*{and set them in their own land*} Deut. 30.3–5. Jer. 24.6. & 32.37. Ezek. 37.14.

*{and the strangers shall be joined with them*} Heb. *the stranger*, or, *the sojourner, shall join himself* (as ch. 56.3. *unto them*, as in the next clause, Gen. 15.13. & 2.3,4. the singular number put collectively, as Exod. 12.48. Lev. 19.33. Deut. 10.18. & 24.17. Many strange people, taking notice of the strange works, that God should then work for his people in this their delivery, Ps. 126.2. shall join themselves unto them, to worship together with them. See the like, Esth. 8.17. Ps. 7.8,9. ch. 44.5. & 56.3. & 60.3. This, no doubt, was in part accomplished, at their return from Babylon; but more exactly, and plentifully fulfilled, in the kingdom of Christ, by the ministry of the gospel, c. 2.3. Zach. 2.10,11. Eph. 2.13.

*{and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob*} As 1 Sam. 26.19. The same, in other terms, with the former. See ch. 2.5.

**V. 2.** *{And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place*} Heb. *Peoples*, people of divers nations, (as ch. 2.3. & 12.4.) shall be helpful to them, in fitting, and furnishing them, with all necessary accommodations for their journey, in their return to their land again, Ezra 1.4,6. & 7.13,16. ch. 11.12. & 66.20.

*{and the house of Israel shall possess them, in the land of the Lord, for servants, and for handmaids*} The converts, or proselytes of other people, shall freely offer themselves, unto the church, to do her any service: they shall of their own accord, be as serviceable to them, as any servants, or bondmen, could be, that had been bought by them. ch. 60.7,10,12. & 61.5. Rom. 16.1,2. 1 Cor. 16.15. 2 Cor. 8.4,5. There is in the words an allusion, to a law; concerning strangers. Lev. 25.44,45.

*{the land of the Lord*} The land of Judea so called, as, in a special manner, his, Lev. 25.23. because he had made choice of it, to place his people in it; Exod. 15.17. in regard whereof, also, it is called *God's sanctuary*: chap. 63.18. as a type of his church.

*{and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were*} Heb. *they shall captive their captivers*: as Psal. 137.3. That which was fulfilled, in such victories as God gave the Jewish nation after their return from Babylon, in the times of the Maccabees, over such people, as had beforetime held them in captivity. Though some expound it, of buying the Babylonians for slaves; as they, also, well might, from the Medes and the Persians, that had surprised them. The meaning is, that the tables now should be turned, and those now made lords over them, whom they had been in subjection and bondage to, before; and those in subjection to them, that had before lorded it over them chap. 26.13. Spiritually, most interpreters understand it, of those people; who by the ministry of the apostles were, out of all nations, subdued, and brought in to the obedience of Christ's scepter, Psal. 45.5. & 68.18. Rom. 15.16,19. 2 Cor. 10.4,5.

*{and they shall rule over their oppressors*} Heb. *their exactors*, as ver. 4. ch. 60.17. The same things repeated in other terms. See chap. 60.14.

**V. 3.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day*} Or, *at that time*: See chap. 2.20. & 3.7,18,24. or simply, *when*: as Gen. 3.17. Ruth 4.5.

*{that the Lord shall give thee rest*} Heb. *of the Lord's making thee to rest*: as Deut. 25.19.

*{from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage, wherein thou wast made to serve*} Heb. *which was served upon thee*, as Deut. 21.3. When you shall be set free from the Babylonian bondage; wherein you endured much sorrow, and hardship, and lived in continual fears. Lev. 26.36. Deut. 28.48,65,66. Luk. 1.74. The prophet, here, turns his speech to the people.

**V. 4.** *{That thou shalt take up*} As Ezek. 21.2. See chap. 13.1.

*{this proverb*} Or, *byword*, or, *taunting speech*: as Ezek. 16.44. so Deut. 28.37. Jer. 24.9. The word signifies not *a parable*, or *similitude*; only; but any quick speech, or sentence of special note, and ordinary use: so called, as the most, from the verb *mashal*, that signifies *to rule*, as being such, as does sway commonly with men; either in their minds, or in their tongues. Though some would by a transposition of letters fetch it, from the word *Shalam*; which say they, signifies *to assimilate*. But neither are such derivations, by transpositions, over-usual in the Hebrew; nor do I find, where the verb *Shallam*, ever so signifies.

*{against the king of Babylon*} Insulting now over him, who before tyrannized over you: *against*, or, *concerning*, as ch. 1.1. By the king of Babylon, some understand some one king; either Nebuchadnezzar, the first monarch of the Chaldean empire, who ruined the Jewish state, 2 Chron. 36. or, Baltasar, the last of that empire, with whom that state fell. But the speech concerns not, so much this, or, that king, as the kingdom, which successively was holden by them. See Dan. 7.17,23.

*{and say, how hath the oppressor ceased*} The byword, and taunting speech concerning him, his state and city; spoken not so much in way of interrogation, as in way of admiration, and derision. So ver. 10,12.

*{the oppressor*} Or, *exactor*: as ch. 60.17.

*{ceased*} ch. 16.4. See ch. 33.8.

*{the golden city ceased*} For, *golden*; which well suits with the *golden head*. Dan. 2.32,38. and *the golden cup*, that Babylon is said to be. Jer. 51.7. Some render it, *gold-thirsty*; some *exactress of gold*; she that stripped other people of their gold; as Assyria had done before her, chap. 10.14. & 39.6. The word is rather, Syriac; (which language the Chaldees used, in those times. Dan. 2.4.) than Hebrew: the prophet would have them, taunt that city by a term of their own language; as another, their idols, by a sentence of the same, Jer. 10.11. The substantive is wanting, but must be supplied, either *city*, or *state*; not *king*: for the word is feminine; or, *the golden one* simply, without any other adjection. See the like defect, Ps. 73.10. ch. 40.10. Ezek. 13.11.

**V. 5.** *{The Lord hath broken the staff of the wicked*} The answer to the question moved, vers. 4. Not Cyrus; but the Lord by Cyrus. chap. 41.2. & 44.48. & 25.1,2. has pulled down the power of the wicked king, and state of Babylon: he has broken the staff, wherewith, the wicked Babylonians did beat God's people. See ch. 9.4. & 10.5. & 47.6.

*{and the sceptre*} Or, *rod*; as the word properly signifies: see ch. 9.4. & 10.5,24. and so it would, here, be rendered, for that which follows, ver. 6.

*{of the rulers*} The Babylonian princes, and great ones: see Ezek. 19.11. the word, whence that for a proverb, comes, ver. 4.

**V. 6.** *{He that smote the people in wrath, with a continual stroke*} Or, *That struck the people, in wrath, with a stroke unavoidable*, or, *irrecoverable*. For the words, *strike*, and *stroke*, in the original, do here, the one answer the other. And some understand it of the *rod*, or *staff's striking*, ver. 5. Others, of *the striker*, the *hand* (so some of the Rabbines) or, the person striking with it. And of these latter, some understand the words on this manner: *he that struck the people in wrath*, his *stroke*, *shall not depart*, or, *be removed*: or, *the stroke of him, that struck the people*; (Heb. *peoples*; as ver. 2.) *in wrath, shall not depart*. He that before, with so much fury, and rage, laid load upon many nations, and struck them, at pleasure; has now received such a stroke, as he was not able to avoid; or has such a blow given him, as he shall not be able to recover. But the former seems the plainer way, and to flow most naturally from the text. However we take the words, there is a reason, therein rendered; why God had broken the rod of Babylon, for the cruelty that had by her, been executed and exercised on other people.
