*{he that ruled the nations in anger is persecuted, and none hindereth*} This reading admitted, would strengthen the latter interpretation of the former branch: for the same thing, questionless, is after this prophet's usual manner, (though in other terms expressed) intended in either: yet most interpreters, (some of them, also, controlling the points in the Hebrew) render it, otherwise; as spoken, wholly, of the Babylonian king's cruelty; not of aught, that had befallen him; thus rendering the words. *He that ruled the nations in anger; that pursued*, or, *persecuted* them, *without hindrance*, or, *none withholding*; or, *that hindered*, or, *restrained; not those that did persecute*; ruled roughly; and restrained not those, that under him did the like. And this version comes near, indeed, to the prophet's purpose, and intendment: but the words will not admit it; I incline therefore, to that, which I meet with in the Jewish commentaries, upon this place; who thus render it: *That ruled the nations in anger, the persecuted without restraint*; or out of the former branch, supplying, what may make the sense more complete, (as Gen. 1.16. ch. 3.25.) *he ruled with anger the persecuted*: that tyrannized over those, whom incessantly, none daring to oppose, or being able to restrain him, he persecuted. See ch. 10.14. This syntax, and sense, the text freely yields, without force.

**V. 7.** *{The whole earth is at rest and is quiet*} The inhabitants of the world, who could have no rest, or ease, ver. 6. while Babylon so reigned, and ruled, as ver. 6. are now at rest, and may sit quietly in the places of their abode, Zach. 1.11. *the earth* for it inhabitants: as Ps. 98.4,9.

*{is at rest, and is quiet*} Heb. *resteth; is quiet*. A quick form of speech, having some emphasis in it. See the like, ch. 24.4. & 52.9. Lam. 2.19.

*{they break forth into singing*} So the same is rendered, chap. 44.23. & 49.13. & 54.1. & 55.12. and with some addition, chap. 52.9. *break out into joy*. For the prophet seems much delighted with this word; in this form and sense; nowhere found in Scripture, out of his writings; save once, Psal. 98.4. where it is rendered, *make a loud noise*; which may seem to be the genuine notion of the word. It is once, only, but in another form, used, for *to break asunder*, Mic. 3.3. and may seem to imply, a widening of the mouth, or a wide opening of the lips, and lungs; the natural instruments of voice, to make the louder noise. The Jewish doctor says, that in the Arabic tongue it signifies *to speak plainly, and clearly*: ch. 32.4. And it may be deemed to imply such a joy (for of no other note is it used) as cannot be contained, or kept in, but must needs break forth; and by singing, and shouting, in acclamation and outcries, express itself, see 1 King. 1.40,45.

*{singing*} So is the word rendered, in the places of this prophet, before quoted; but it is rendered elsewhere, sometimes *joy*, and *rejoicing*, Psalm 30.5. & 98.4. sometime *triumph*. Psal. 47.2. sometime *shouting*, and *shouting for joy*, Psalm 35.17. chap. 12.6. Prov. 11.10. it signifies *a loud cry*, in general; as Prov. 1.20. and, that indifferently; whether an expression of grief, or of joy: of grief, and sorrow, in way of exclamation, and supplication; as Jer. 7.16. Lam. 2.19. of joy, and gladness, in way of acclamation and exultation; so most commonly, and so in this place. It may well be rendered, then *cry aloud* with a joyful *shout*. For there is a defect of the instrumental particle, here, as ch. 5.12. and oft, elsewhere expressed, Ps. 42.4. ch. 48.20. The meaning is, that there should be very great joy everywhere, upon the fall of that great empire, ch. 49.13. & 55.12. Jer. 51.48.

**V. 8.** *{Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon*} He turns his speech, here, to Babylon; telling her, that the very trees themselves, the firs, and cedars, should rejoice at her fall. By *firs*, and *cedars*, (say some of the Jewish writers, and others, following the Chaldee Paraphrast) the prophet understands great princes, and potentates, states, and dominions, compared to, and resembled by, such, ch. 2.13. & 10.33,34. Ezek. 31.3–9,16. Hab. 2.17. Others suppose the meaning to be, that the cruelty of the Babylonians had been such, that the very senseless creatures themselves, might seem to be sensible of it, and to rejoice, therefore, at her ruin, Ezek. 31.16. Jer. 51.48. But the sense is simply, and plainly, this, that these trees, which had from time to time, so frequently, and so in great abundance, been felled, to furnish her with timber, for her shipping, and her buildings, might well be glad, had such creatures sense of what befell them, as hoping to be much spared, over what they had been, by her fall. See Sennacherib's threats, chapter 37.24. This sense, the words ensuing confirm.

*{and the cedars*} A defect of the copulative, as ver. 7. ch. 37.24. Hab. 3.11.

*{saying*} By a figurative form of speech, sense, and speech is given to dumb and senseless creatures, so Judg. 9.8–15. Hab. 2.11,12. But the term implying it, is wanting, here, as Psal. 105.14,15.

*{Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us*} We are not felled so frequently, as we had wont to be, since your fall, since you were felled, Dan. 4.14,23. Ezek. 31.12.

*{art laid down*} Heb. *hast lain down*, the word signifies, properly, *to lie down* to sleep, Job 7.4. but sometime *to lie down*, by death, 2 Sam. 7.12. Job 3.13. & 14.12. because death is as a sleep, Psal. 13.3. Act. 7.60. & 13.36. 1 Cor. 11.30. & 15.6. and the fall of a state is as its death, ver. 15. Ezek. 31.15,16. Howbeit some of the Jewish writers take this clause also, in a figurative sense, expounding it, of the death of Nebuchadnezzar, termed here, say they, the *hewer*, or, *cutter*, (which exactly answers the Hebrew) because he cut down kingdoms, and either slew or enslaved their kings; whereas his successors, made them tributaries only. But this, as has been said, suits not so well with the intendment of the text; for the Chaldean estate fell not with him.

**V. 9.** *{Hell from beneath is moved for thee, to meet thee at thy coming*} After the joyful, and gladsome deportment of the whole world here, upon the fall of Babylon, and of the creatures therein, as well senseless, as endued with sense and reason, rhetorically related; the prophet proceeds, here, in a lofty, and poetical strain, to describe the entertainment, given in the other world, to the king of Babylon, or to the state thereof; personated in the king, by those, who were gone before him.

*{Hell*} Or, *The grave*, the common receptacle of all that depart hence. See on ch. 5.14. So ver. 11,15.

*{is moved*} The word signifies, sometimes; *to tremble*, and *quake* for fear, ver. 3.15. Psal. 4.4. Joel 2.1,13. And so some of the Rabbines would have it taken here, as if the fear, and terror of his tyranny, had possessed even the dead; and put them into a fear, at his coming among them: but this fits not with what follows, vers. 10,11. Sometime, *to rage*, in tumultuous manner, chap. 37.28. Prov. 29.9. but that suits not here: Sometime, *to raise up* one's self, for some employment, chap. 28.21. so rather here. The grave does rouse up itself, as upon apprehension of the approach of so great a state, to give him entertainment, suitable, in some sort, to his greatness.

*{to meet thee*} As men are wont to go forth, to meet persons of note and state, Gen. 46.29. 1 Sam. 13.10. & 18.6. a defect of the pronoun, as ch. 13.8,15.

*{it stirreth up the dead for thee*} So the word is used, Psal. 88.10. Prov. 2.17. & 9.18. chap. 26.14. so called; of a word, that signifies, *to be enfeebled, to faint, to remit, to give over, to cease*. Because men in dying grow *faint*, and *feeble*, being dead, *cease* to act, and to live, Job 14.10. and so most of the Jewish commenters here take it; yet the Chaldee renders it, *mighty ones*, from Ezek. 32.21. or, *giants*: those (say some of ours) that lived before the flood, though that name be not given them, Gen. 6.4. the sons of Anak (say some of the Rabbines) so termed, Deut. 2.11,20. who seem to have been so called, from a people of that name, Gen. 14.5. & 15.20. (who may be deemed to have possessed that valley near Jerusalem, Josh. 15.8. & 18.16.) either because of the posterity of them, or like to them, for stature. But the text here, seems to intend, neither those, nor these; but such puissant princes, as had known, and felt the power of the Chaldean state, being overthrown by it, or living in subjection to it, ver. 10.

*{even all the chief ones of the earth*} Or, *Leaders*, princes, rulers, chieftains, great ones, that go in and out before the people, Numb. 27.16,17. 1 Sam. 18.13. though these places seem to allude, to the manner of shepherds in those parts, going in and out before their flocks, Joh. 10.3,4,10. Heb. *great goats*, such, as lead, and go, before the rest of the flock, ch. 1.11. & 34.6. Jer. 50.8. & 51.40.

*{it hath raised up*} To meet you, as before. Heb. *made to stand up*: as if they had been sitting in state before; so Judg. 5.20. 1 King. 2.19. Jon. 3.6.

*{from their thrones*} He speaks of them, says the Jewish commenter, as if they were living, and sitting on their thrones, that, here, they had: or, as if they had thrones in the other world, as well as in this. Though some of ours, by their *thrones*, understand their sepulchers, or the stately monuments, wherein their corpses lay interred, verse 18. But some of them, it is likely, had no such.

*{all the kings of the nations*} That lived under that state; and were subservient to it, Jer. 25.9. & 27.6–8. Dan. 2.37,38.

**V. 10.** *{All they shall speak, and say unto thee*} The dead are induced, here, speaking; as the place of the dead, before, bestirring itself; and with a tart ironical, and satirical speech, entertaining, and welcoming to them this grand tyrant: not that they should, or could so do, but that such things, might truly, and justly, be then said. See Ezek. 32.21.

*{speak*} Heb. *answer*: as Cant. 2.10. Mat. 11.25. a form very frequent, both in the Old and New Testament.

*{art thou also become weak as we*} Heb. *sick*: as chapter 38.1. and 39.1. The word imports such weakness, as comes by sickness and pain: as we use the word, *infirmity*. Are you pulled down by some mortal disease, who reputed yourself to be immortal? ch. 47.7.

*{art thou become like unto us*} You that thought yourself the only great one; and no other your compeer, ch. 47.8.

**V. 11.** *{Thy pomp is brought down to the grave*} All your state, and bravery, wherein you did pride yourself, (see ch. 13.11.) is laid in the dust, Ps. 7.5. not that it accompanied him unto the grave; but that it perished with him, when he went down to the grave, Ps. 49.14,17. & 73.19,20.

*{and the noise of thy viols*} The melody of your music, which you had of all sorts, Chap. 3.5. & 6.18. Amos 5.23. one sort, put for all. See chapter 5.12. For I suppose them too wide, here, who imagine this passage, to have respect unto such music, as was used either at funerals, or, beside, the deceased, while they lay in the house, laid out; but not carried forth yet to burial, chap. 16.11. Jer. 48.36. Mat. 9.23. for the music here mentioned, is implied, to be ceased, and silenced together with their pomp. See Ezek. 26.13. Yet it may well be deemed to have an eye to that jollity and solemn festival, attended, and graced, no doubt, with much variety of music, at which the city was surprised. See Jer. 51.39,41,57. Dan. 5.1,30. Some would have it, *the noise of thy drums*, or, *thy bagpipes*, instruments of music used in war. But we find no such use of the word in Scripture, nor of such military music in those times. The *trumpet*, or, *cornet*, are all of that kind we find mentioned, Numb. 10.9. Josh. 6.4. The *tabors*, and *harps* mentioned, ch. 30.32. seem to be, not of fight, or conflict; but of triumph after victory: the copulative is wanting, as ver. 6.

*{the worm is spread under thee, and worms cover thee*} Instead of those costly carpets, that you feasted and trod on, and those stately rich, and gorgeous coverings, and other bed-furniture, which you did formerly make use of, worms, and maggots, will now take up their rooms, and supply their place, Job 7.5. & 17.14. & 21.26. & 24.20. and this the rather with you; because you shall not be embalmed, or put up in cerecloth, to preserve your corpse, as kings, and great ones, ordinarily are, Gen. 50.2. 2 Chron. 16.14. but shall be cast out, and thereby exposed to putrefaction. See ver. 19,20. There are two several words in the Hebrew; whereof the one, as some Jewish authors suppose, signifies, properly, a lesser sort of worm, such, as breeds in flesh, or cheese, and such, as the manna bred, Exod. 16.20,24. which we commonly term a *maggot*. The other, either, the greater sort, as the long *earthworm*, where they are, as here, distinguished; or any *worm*, in general, where no such distinction is. The words are both, here, singular; though the verb joined with the latter, plural; because taken collectively, both, and distributively, also, the latter. Of which syntax, see chap. 2.20. The text may be rendered, *The maggot is*, or *maggots are spread*, or, *laid under thee: and the earthworm*, or, each sort of *worms cover thee*. And let it be considered, whether this whole verse, may not be read, by way of interrogation, as well as those: both before, and after. *Is thy pomp thrown down to the grave; and the noise of thy viols? is the maggot spread under thee, and doth the worm* of all sorts, *cover thee*; for the note of interrogation is in Hebrew, oft wanting: as Job 13.15. & 14.8. Prov. 23.5.

*{spread*} The word is applied, as to bedding, most commonly, Psalm 130. 9. 8. Chap. 28.20. so to sackcloth, and ashes, that on days of humiliation, they were wont to lie in, Esth. 4.5. ch. 58.5.

**V. 12.** *{How art thou fallen from heaven O Lucifer*} The following passage, many, both of the ancients, and others, understand to have reference to the fall of the apostate angels. Wherein, one of the learnedest among the former, does, not undeservedly, with a little tartness control them. But it is a continuation of that satirical, and ironical language, wherewith those deceased ones are feigned to entertain the king of Babylon, at his coming among them, ver. 10.

*{fallen from heaven*} From the height of that glorious, and illustrious estate, wherein you shined, so brightly and so conspicuously before, Lam. 2.1. Ezek. 28.16,17. Matth. 11.23. Luk. 10.15,18. Rev. 9.1. & 12.4.

*{O Lucifer*} This name some fondly give, by occasion of this Scripture, unto *the prince of devils*; whom the Jews call *Beelzebub*, Mat. 12.24. Whence, that, byword among us, *as proud as Lucifer*. But the name is nowhere in Scripture given unto him. It is given unto Christ, by the ministry of the gospel, shining into men's souls, 2 Pet. 1.19. Rev. 2.28. 2 Cor. 4.6. The word signifies the *morning star*, one of the seven planets; or wandering stars, commonly called *Venus*, in regard of its beauty, and brightness: and the name here given it, comes of a word, that signifies *so to shine*, Job 25.5. & 31.26. ch. 13.10. It is used to represent the conspicuous estate of the Chaldean king, and empire, that seemed to shine as bright, when it was in its height, as *the day-star*, itself, in the sky: though there want not, that expound it, of Sennacherib, and his fall, ch. 37.38. the rather for what is said, ver. 25. whereof in its place.

*{Son of the morning*} So is that bright, and beautiful star termed; because it appears usually in the morning, somewhat before the sunrising, thereby giving warning of day approaching, 2 Pet. 1.19. as if say some, it were by the morning produced. But the Hebrew phrase is very general, calling everything, almost, the *son* of that, which it has any special relation unto. So, *the son of a year*, for, one of a year, in his reign, 1 Sam. 13.1. *the son of stripes*: one that deserves whipping, Deut. 25.2. *the son of death*, one that is worthy to die, 2 Sam. 12.5. *the son of hell, and of perdition*: one to whom hell, and destruction belongs, Matth. 23.15. Joh. 17.12. *the son of this world*: one that lives in this world; or, that has his portion, here, Ps. 17.14. Luk. 20.34. & 16.8. and so, to pass by all other: *the son of the morning*, here, because, wont then to appear: and not so much, as produced by it; but rather, as ushering it, in, or, bringing it along with it.

*{How art thou*} *How*, is not in the original; but is supplied, as wanting, from the former branch. Yet may it safely be omitted; and the words without it rendered; *thou art cut down*: the rather, because the prophet in this latter clause, passes from one similitude to another; from a star fallen down, to a tree hewn down.

*{cut down to the ground*} Not cut down close to the ground: as is intimated of that tree, that represented Nebuchadnezzar's person, only, Dan. 4.14,23,24. but, *cut down*, and cast *to the ground*, (of which kind of defective speech, see Psal. 7.5. & 31.17. & 89.39,44. chapter 21.9. & 22.18. Jer. 41.17.) as of the tree that resembled the Assyrian empire; Ezek. 31.3–14. as this does the Chaldean, here: importing an utter, and irrevocable ruin of it, as laid along on the ground, never to be reared, or raised up again.

*{which didst weaken the nations*} Some of the Rabbines expound it, *which didst cast lots upon the nations*. Supposing the word here used, to be of the same stock, with one of the same sound, which in their miscellane language they use, for *a lot*: and this, the rather, they would have it, to signify; because of the particle, usually, signifying *upon*, found here, in the text. But neither is the verb, ever used, in Scripture: and the particle is, by other of them observed, to be here redundant, as oft-times it is. The word signifies in Scripture sometime, *to be weak*, or, *to weaken*, Joel 3.10. Sometime, *to discomfit*, or, *overcome*, Exod. 17.13. & 32.18. or, *to overthrow*, or, *lay along*; as some of the Jewish writers expound it, Job 14.10. *man dies, and is cut down*; overthrown; laid along: and so I suppose it would here be rendered, *Thou art cut down*, and cast *to the ground*: laid along on it; *That didst overthrow the nations*: that did cut down, and lay along others; you are served now, as you, sometime, served them. See the Assyrians' purpose, and practice; chapter 10.7. See also of Babylon, Jer. 50.23. & 51.20.

**V. 13.** *{For*} Heb. *And*: as chap. 8.21. & 9.11. as rendering a reason, why the Babylonian monarch should so be cut off, and cast down; to wit, for his extreme insolency against God himself. Others render it, rather, *But*; as ch. 7.17. & 11.14. or, *Yet*: as Jer. 2.32,35. as subjoined in way of opposition to the foregoing denunciation of his fall, ver. 12.

*{thou hast said in thine heart*} Or, *thou saidst in thine heart*: you thought within yourself: as Ps. 14.1. ch. 9.9.

*{I will ascend into heaven*} Not, that he made account to go to heaven, when he died, as the faithful, 2 Cor. 5.1. nor, that he supposed he could, by climbing, get up into the heaven, while he lived. But it is an hyperbolical description of the excessive pride, and insolency of that Babylonian tyrant, in such an height of impiety, invading, and breaking in furiously upon the church of God, compared to heaven, and thereby resembled, Rev. 4.1,2. & 12.1. and the people of God, the saints especially, and those of prime note, and place among them, compared to stars, Rev. 1.20. & 12.1,4. and God's temple, or sanctuary, which was as his throne, or his chair of state, Ps. 99.1. Jer. 17.12. as if he made account to subdue, and dethrone God himself. See ch. 10.10,11. & 37.23,24,29. Dan. 8.10,11. & 11.28,30,36. and of that *sinful man*, 2 Thess. 2.4. And this elegant description, as one of the Jewish commenters observes, does consist of sundry proverbial forms, usual in that language, whereunto, not a few are found, very suitable, both in the Greek, and Latin, used thereby to express a power, or greatness, affected, or advanced, far above all human height. See Deut. 1.28. Psalm 36.5,6. & 139.8. Joh. 3.13. Eph. 4.10.

*{I will exalt my throne above the stars of God*} The stars of God's making, Gen. 1.16. Ps. 148.3,5. or, that give light from the heavens, the place of God's habitation, ch. 57.15. & 66.1. or, *the stars of greatest excellency*; as *the hills of God*, Ps. 36.6. and *the trees of God*, Ps. 104.16. for, the greatest, and highest hills; the fairest, and tallest trees. See Dan. 8.10.

*{I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation*} I will set my throne, on Mount Sion, the place of God's special residence, his palace, to which his people resorted, there to adore, Ps. 20.2. & 68.15,16,17,24,26,29. & 84.7. & 122.1–4. ch. 33.20. & 64.10,11. See Dan. 11.45.

*{of the congregation*} Or, *set*, or, *solemn meeting*. See chap. 1.14. the word comes from a root, that signifies in its first form active, *to set*, or, *appoint*, time, or place. 2 Sam. 20.5. Jer. 47.7. in the passive thereof, at such a set time; or, in such a set place to meet, Josh. 11.5. Neh. 6.2,10. Hence, the word here used, and thence deduced, is sometime put for a set time of meeting in general, 2 Sam. 20.5. Dan. 11.29. more specially, for the set times of meeting, for performance of holy duties, Levit. 23.2,4. Ezek. 46.9,11. sometime, for a place of meeting, or resort in general, Josh. 20.9. and so the grave is called *the appointed meeting-house, for all living wights*, Job 30.23. more specially, for religious exercises, so the tabernacle, is termed *the tent*, or *Tabernacle of convention*; or *set meeting*; because God appointed his people, at certain times there to meet, for such purposes; and had promised to meet them there, Exod. 25.8,21. & 29.42,43. & 33.7. and the synagogues are called, *God's meeting places*, Ps. 74.8. and mount Sion, is called, here, *the mount of convention*, or *meeting*: because thereon stood the temple, which, for that sacred use, succeeded the tabernacle, 2 Sam. 7.6,13. 1 King. 8.4,6,21.

*{in the sides of the North*} Mount Moriah, whereon the temple was built, 2 Chron. 3.1. stood on the northerly side of mount Sion; but reckoned as a part of it, Psal. 48.2. The Rabbi doted, that would have the city of Babylon, here meant, by *the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the North*; so termed, in regard of her strength, and stately buildings, Jer. 51.25. the resort of all people to her, Jer. 51.44. & her northerly situation to the land of Judah, Jer. 1.15. & 4.6. For what needed their king to vaunt, that he would set his throne there, where he had it erected already? Dan. 4.29, 30.

**V. 14.** *{I will ascend above the heights of the clouds*} Heb. *cloud*, or, *thick cloud*, (as the word, properly, signifies and is so rendered, Job 22.14. Psal. 18.11, 12.) but taken, here, collectively, for *clouds* in general: and, *heights of clouds*, for, *the highest clouds*: as *the heights of the hills*, for, *the highest hills* Psal. 95.4. Some think an allusion, in the word, *cloud*, to the cloud, wherein God manifested himself on Mount Sinai, Exod. 19.9. Deut. 4.11, 22. in the tabernacle, Exod. 40.34, 35. and the temple, 1 King. 8.10, 11, 12: but to the first of them especially, as if he would set his throne higher, than God, at that time, seemed to have done, above that place wherein God then appeared.

*{I will be like the most high*} God's peculiar attribute, Psal. 83.18. Eccl. 5.8. It was our first parents' ambitious affectation, and vain hope, to become like God, that stripped them of the true likeness of God which they were possessed of, at first, Gen. 3.5, 6, 22. and it was this proud tyrant's affecting of an equality with God, to sit on even ground with him, yea, to raise his throne higher than his, that proved the means of his fatal, and irrecoverable ruin. So Ezek. 28.2, 3, 6–10.

**V. 15.** *{Yet*} As Psal. 73.1. notwithstanding these your haughty conceits of your power, and presumption of your future greatness. See ch. 10.6.

*{thou shalt be brought down*} Heb. *made to descend* (as ver. 11.) *to hell* or, *the grave*, instead of your presumptuous conceit of *ascending up* into heaven, v. 13.

*{to hell*} As Matth. 11.23. or, *to the grave*: as ver. 9. Psal. 16.10. & 55.15. the words following confirm it. See Ezek. 32.27.

*{to the sides of the pit*} Heb. *thighs of the pit*, for, *sides*, as Exod. 26.23. Joh. 1.6. instead of those stately *sides of the North*, whereon you bragged that you would set your throne, ver. 13. you shall be thrown down, to the sides of some base and loathsome pit. See Ezek. 32.23, 24. *the pit*, for *the grave*, Psal. 30.3, 9. & 88.4. but here, in a larger extent, for any pit, though not made, or intended, for such use, that some vile, and loathsome corpse, might be carelessly cast into, 2 Sam. 18.17. *the thighs of the pit*, the sides, or cheeks of it, on which as on the mouth of it, a stone is wont to be laid, that is borne up by them, as the body of man is by the thighs. See Lam. 3.53. Yet because the word, that properly signifies *a thigh*, in Hebrew, is, sometime, put for the *foot* of a thing, as Exod. 37.17. Levit. 1.11. Hence, some would have it to signify, not the *sides*, but the *bottom* of a pit: some pit of the deepest. See Psal. 88.6. But this seems to strain more than needs.

**V. 16.** *{They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee*} Or, *seeing thee*: or, *when they see thee*: (for it seems to have special reference to those before spoken of, ver. 10.) *shall look wistly upon thee*. The word is used only here: and Psal. 33.14. Cant. 2.9. As for what some of the Rabbins say, in way of exposition of it; they shall *weigh well* how it is with you, and get understanding by you, as Jer. 23.20. is for the living, not for the dead: and indeed, so some understand it, as spoken by men surviving the Babylonian king, and beholding his carcass cast out: see the like, Psal. 53.7. But it seems more probable, that the prophet, as in his former parable, spoke of the dead.

*{and consider thee, saying*} A defect of the copulative, as ver. 7. and of the participle, as ver. 8. Yet this latter may sufficiently be supplied, if it be rendered, *and think*, as it is rendered, Job 31.1. and may well, ch. 43.18. or, *think with themselves* (because the word is in a reciprocal form) *of thee*, or, *concerning thee*. For so the particle is oft used, Gen. 20.2. Psal. 2.7. ch. 33.33.

*{Is this the man that made the earth to tremble*} They speak of the state, as of a man; because the king thereof a man, one in nature, the same with any one mean man, Psal. 82.7. Chapter 2.22.

*{that made the earth to tremble*} *the earth*; for the inhabitants of it: as v. 7. But the figure makes it emphatical, as if out of his pride, and by his power, he had made a general earthquake, throughout the whole world. See Psal. 60.2. ch. 2.19. and for the word, here, used. See ver. 9. see also Ezek. 32.23, 24, &c.

*{that did shake kingdoms*} Or, *that made its kingdoms shake*. A defect of the pronoun: as Chap. 13.22. but to be supplied, as it is, ver. 17. that did so shake them, as to unsettle them, and remove them out of their places. See Chap. 13.13. Hab. 2.21, 22. Heb. 12.26, 27. there is an elegancy, in the sound of the words, in the Hebrew, which, in our English, cannot so well be expressed; yet may we come somewhat near to it, if we render the words, *that made the earth to quake, and made the kingdoms thereof to shake*.

**V. 17.** *{That made the world as a wilderness*} That laid all before him waste; as those locusts, Joel 2.3. See Zeph. 2.13.

*{and destroyed the cities thereof*} Either by consuming their inhabitants or by razing, and burning the cities themselves, 2 King. 25.9, 10, 11. 2 Chr. 36.19, 20. Psal. 137.7.

*{the world*} Properly, *the habitable world*, as the Greeks use to style it: or, *the fertile world*, that that yields aught useful, for food of man, or beast. For from a word that so signifies, it seems to be deduced, Levit. 26.4. Judg. 6.4. which here wants not its emphasis, being opposed, to the *wild* or *waste*.

*{that opened not the house of his prisoners*} Of which reading, see on Chap. 42.7. Or, *that did not loose his prisoners* (as the word is used, Chap. 51.14. Jer. 40.4.) *homeward*. That is, and send them *home*; or let them go *home*. A defective form, such, as ver. 11. that kept his captives in perpetual restraint, and would not suffer them to return to their own country, and the places of their former abode, Jer. 50.33. was not content, in the height of his pride and ambition, to overthrow, and subdue them: but in cruel, merciless, and inhumane manner, after he had subdued them, kept them in perpetual imprisonment, and restraint, Lam. 3.34.

**V. 18.** *{All the kings of the nations*} Other kings and princes, ordinarily, or the most part of them, as ver. 9. So is *all* oft taken, for all in a manner, or the greater number, or most, or many, Exod. 9.6, 20. Jer. 26.7, 8, & 44.12, 27, 28. Mat. 3.5. Joh. 2.10. & 11.48. Rom. 5.18, 19. Phil. 2.21.

*{even all of them lie in glory*} Are laid up in stately tombs and monuments; where they lie; as in their beds. See ver. 8. Chap. 57.2. It is that, that usually great kings obtain; either by the provision of their peers, or the care of their successors, thereby to ingratiate themselves with the people.

*{every one*} Heb. *a man*, as Cant. 3.8. ch. 13.14.

*{in his house*} Or, *in his place*: (as some render the word, 1 Sam. 27.3. 2 Sam. 15.17. Job 8.17. Prov. 8.2.) To wit, of sepulture, or burial: in his sepulcher, in his grave. So some of the Jewish doctors here expound it, following the Chaldee; and alleging that of Solomon; *Man goes to his everlasting house*, or, *his long home*, Eccl. 12.5. But it seems rather to have an eye, to the ancient manner of preparing their sepulchers, and burying them in their own lands, grounds, or possessions, where their ancestors had been laid before them, and which, with kings and potentates, was usually in some part of, or place near unto their palaces. See Judg. 2.9. 1 Sam. 25.1. 1 King. 2.10, 34. 2 King. 12.21.

**V. 19.** *{But thou art cast out of thy grave*} You shall miss of that honor that other kings usually have, to wit, a solemn funeral, an honorable interment. For your corpse shall lie above-ground, unburied. So Josh. 7.26. & 8.29. 2 Sam. 18.17. Jer. 22.18, 19.

*{But*} Heb. *And*; as ch. 13.21.

*{cast out of thy grave*} Heb. *cast out from the grave*. That is, *cast out*, and kept *from thy grave*; as Psal. 79.2, 3. For the meaning is not, that he should be raked, or dragged out of his grave again, after he was buried; as some, of whom anon, fondly feign. But that he should be cast out, and kept from ever coming to be laid up in that tomb, or sepulcher, which he had, in his lifetime, prepared for himself, 2 Sam. 18.17, 18. Chap. 22.16–18. Matth. 27.60. Of the manner of speech, see ver. 27. This some understand of Sennacherib; who should lie at Niniveh unburied, while his two sons that slew him, held that city. But of this there is neither story, nor probability, they two that slew him, being said to have fled upon it, and a third of his own issue immediately (for aught that appears) to have reigned in his room, ch. 37.38. On the other side, the Jewish doctors will have it spoken of Nebuchadnezzar. And some they say have a conceit of him, that whereas he thought, that the palace which he built at Babel, should be, as his sepulcher; that is, he should live a long time in it, as a man does in his grave; Psal. 49.11. Eccl. 12.5. Luk. 12.19, 20. there came an evil spirit, or a malignant blast from God that blew him, or cast him out of his house, and caused him to abide abroad, for some time, among the beasts, Dan. 4.31, 33. So that he could not rest in his house, as other kings do in theirs, ver. 18. Others, and the most of them, tell us, that when Nebuchadnezzar in the time of his distraction, was driven out from his palace; Dan. 4.33. the peers of the kingdom set up his son Evil-merodach Jer. 52.31. And that Nebuchadnezzar after his wits restored again to him, returning to his palace, Dan. 4.34. and finding his son sitting on his throne, committed him to prison, and did not set him at liberty again, so long as he lived. Whereunto they apply what is said, ver. 19. But that, after his decease, when the nobles brought him forth of prison, and would have him take the crown again, he refused it, for fear, lest, his father, being not dead, as the nobles made him believe, should return again, as before he had done, and should then kill him. Whereupon, to give him satisfaction, they should take up his father's corpse again, and either let it lie, and rot above ground; or else caused it to be devoured by beasts; as did those, Psal. 79.2, 3. & 83.10. But these are mere fictions. More likely it is that Baltasar's corpse should be cast out, and lie above ground, being slain in the nighttime, upon the surprisal of the city, Dan. 5.30. when all was in a combustion, and no man had lust, or leisure to look after him or to take order for his interment.

*{like an abominable branch*} Or, *as* (that it may run alike with the rest) *an abhorred* (as 1 Chro. 21.6. Job 15.16.) *sprig*, or, *twig*, Ch. 11.1. Such a spray, as being not regarded by those that cut it off, or pared it away, in pruning their trees, as matter of no worth, or use; not so much as picked up by women, wherewith to kindle, or keep in, their fire, chap. 27.11, is let lie, and lies so long upon the ground, that being now corrupted and rotted, is not only not worth the taking up, but too vile and loathsome to be taken up, nor good for aught, save to make soil of. This some expound of Nebuchadnezzar, supposing an allusion, in the word here used, to the latter part of his name. Some other understanding it of one Darius that should succeed Baltasar, Dan. 5.31. & be slain by Cyrus, not at Babylon, but far from thence, at Borsippe (concerning which, see on Jer. 51.30, 31.) conceive him, therefore, here so termed: as *a bastardly slip*, Wisd. 4.3. because not of the blood royal; but of the Median race, and of mean descent, Dan. 9.1. & 11.1. But whether any such Darius ever were, or any king of Babylon of that name, after Baltasar, save that Darius who is deemed to have come in together with Cyrus, is very uncertain: and I shall leave it to be discussed by those, whose task it shall be to deal with Daniel's oracles.

*{and as the raiment of those that are slain*} Which are wont to be so stained, and polluted with gore blood, that scarce any can endure to touch them. See ch. 9.5. The copulative not found in the Hebrew, might here well have been spared, there following a third branch of the similitude, and either reserved for the last, or wholly omitted, as is usual, where the members are more than twins; as Chapter 1.8.

*{thrust through with a sword*} This is added, because men may be slain otherwise (suppose stifled, or dry-beaten to death) without much effusion of blood. Heb. *Thrust through of a sword*. The word, here used, is nowhere in Scripture read, save here, and Gen. 45.17. where it signifies to *lade*; *Lade your beasts*. But the Rabbins inform us that in the tongue of Kedar, that is the Arabian language, it signifies to *prick, stab*, or *thrust through*; whence also some would have it rendered in that place of Moses; *prick on your beasts*, to make the more speed.

*{that go down to the stones of the pit*} That are, together with their raiment so polluted, cast, unstripped, into any pit, (see ver. 15.) or quarry, that comes next hand, 2 Sam. 18.17. Howbeit, some suppose an allusion to the stone, or rocks, out of which their sepulchers were usually hewn. chap. 22.16, Matth. 27.60. Others, to those heaps of stones that were cast upon the bodies of ignominious persons, either by judiciary course, or otherwise put to death. Josh. 7.26. and 8.29. 2 Sam. 18.17. See Lam. 3.53. Ezek. 32.29, 30.

*{as a carcass trodden under feet*} Like some vile carrion, or a carcass trodden to pieces, and not neglected only; but with misusage, so bruised, battered, broken to pieces, and dismembered, that scarce any well can, much less endure to put hand unto it for the composing, and committing of it to the ground, 2 King. 9.33, 35, 37. Jer. 22.9.

**V. 20.** *{Thou shalt not be joined to them in burial*} Heb. *united with them*; as Gen. 49.6. You shall not lie in grave among them, nor be buried in such solemn and honorable manner as they were, and kings were wont to be, with embalming, and burning odors for them, and attending their corpse with great state to the ground, ver. 18. See Gen. 50.2, 3, 7–10. 2 Chro. 16.14. & 21.19, 20.

*{because thou hast destroyed thy land, and slain thy people*} A defect of the copulative, as ver. 16. You were not content to destroy other nations, but did exercise much cruelty upon your own people, in grievous exactions, and extreme penalties, imposed and inflicted, even to loss of life, many times, either upon slight occasions, or for your own pleasure alone; by means whereof your cities were sometime wasted, and sometime ruined at your command. This the Rabbins apply to Nebuchadnezzar, alleging the bloody sentence given by him against his wise men, when they could not tell him his dream, Dan. 2.12. But that this cannot be meant of Nebuchadnezzar in person, appears by the words following, both in this verse and the next.

*{the seed of evil doers shall never be renowned*} Heb. *shall not be called for ever*. That is, it shall not last always, nor continue for any long time; but be cut off ere long. *To be called*, for, *to be*, *to continue*. See ch. 4.3. Or, *to be called*, for, *to be named*, as the son of such an one: as God to Abraham, Gen. 21.12. *in Isaac shall thy seed be called*. He shall in a more special manner, as heir to your house, bear, and propagate your name. And Jacob, *Let my name be called upon by them*, Gen. 48.16. that is, Let them be called, and accounted as mine. Or, *to be called*, for, *to be of name, and renown*; as Numb. 1.16. Ezek. 23.23. But I suppose the first here intended, for what follows, ver. 21. concerning the cutting off of his issue. *Not for ever*, for, *not at all; never*, as our English well renders it. So Joh. 8.15, 51. & 11.26. A general sentence, of which see Job 18.5, 19. Psal. 21.10. & 37.28. & 109.13. applied here to Baltasar, the last Chaldean king, whose issue perished together with him; and to the former his predecessors, whose line failed with him and his. See Jer. 27.7.

**V. 21.** *{Prepare slaughter for his children*} The prophet here turns his speech to the Medes and Persians, as from God calling upon them, to prepare, and make themselves ready for the doing of execution upon the king of Babylon; Baltasar, and his whole house, children, and nephews also, if he had any; as 1 King. 14.10. & 15.29. & 16.3, 11, 12. 2 King. 9.8, 9, 10. & 10.6, 7, 11. And we need not understand by his *sons*, either the people of Babylon, or his princes; (though they in likelihood, many, or most of them were slain together with him, at the surprisal of the city, Chap. 13.15–18. Jer. 50.27, 35–37. & 51.39, 40.) but his natural issue that was cut off with him, ver. 22. That which with Nebuchadnezzar did not fall out at his death; for his son, and son's son, Evil-merodach and Baltasar, both survived, and succeeded him in the empire, Jer. & 7.27.52.31. Dan. 5.18, 22.

*{for the iniquity of their fathers*} Wherein they imitate them, or partake with them, Jer. 6.11. & 7.18–20. Dan. 5.20, 22, 23. In regard whereof some expound here, *the iniquity of their ancestors*, not done by them, but such as they did, as *the sins of Manasseh*, for such like sins, as Manasseh committed, 2 King. 24.5. But neither is it necessary that that place, should be so interpreted, when it may be taken simply as it sounds. Nor can it well be so here understood, since that it includes the whole race of those kings, as well young as old. (See ver. 22.) Whereof, though some peradventure were not of years, yet, to do much mischief, or had not been yet much in action, yet must they suffer also for their parents' and ancestors' iniquity, Exod. 20.5. & 34.7. Numb. 16.27, 30, 32, 33. Josh. 7.15, 23, 25. 1 King. 15.29, 30. Matth. 23.35. Which course, though man, without God's special command, may not take; the rather, God having inhibited him so to do, Deut. 24.16. 2 King. 14.5, 6. Yet may God justly do it, and cause it to be done, because all persons, as well children as parents, owe a death unto him; for what either has been done by them, or is in them, 1 King. 8.46. Psal. 51.5. & 130.3. & 143.2. Pro. 21.9. Eccl. 7.20. Rom. 3.20, 23. & 5.12. Which he may therefore without any impeachment of justice, take, how, and when, by what means, in what manner, and upon what occasion he pleases, and does, oftentimes, inflict upon children, who for their own personal corruptions, and accesses, stand guilty before him, having an eye therein, not to theirs so much, as to their parents' sin, in inflicting of penal things at that time upon them, that he may punish their parents in them. See 1 King. 14.9–14.

*{that they may not rise nor possess the land*} Heb. *they shall not rise and inherit the earth*: that is, *that they may not rise, to inherit the earth*; as Josh. 24.9. That they may not stand up in their fathers' room, to repossess that land, and raise up again that state which their forefather sometime held; but God's pleasure was now, that it should be irrecoverably ruined, Chap. 13.20. ver. 23. Howbeit, in the text, I should prefer *earth*, before *land*; because *world* follows, and that empire extended itself to lands, and regions, not a few, Jer. 27.5, 6. The final, or finitive particle is wanting in the Hebrew; as Chap. 5.11. & 10.2. Of which see on Ch. 7.25. The future is put for the potential; as ch. 45.3. Mal. 2.7.

*{nor fill the face of the world with cities*} Heb. *and fill*. But either the negative, must be supplied from the former branch; as Psal. 9.18. Or it must be rendered according to the forementioned syntax, *to possess, and to fill the face*, or *surface of the world*, (the upper part of it which people dwell on; as Gen. 6.7. & 7.18, 23.) *with cities*. That they may not rise again; and return to reestablish their state, and replenish the world again, by dispersing themselves into several regions, and enlarging their dominions with great cities built by them, as Nimrod at first did, Gen. 10.9–12. And thus most take the words. Howbeit the Jewish doctors, following the Chaldee, read it, *And fill the world with enemies*; or, *malignants*. And so indeed is the word here used, taken, 1 Sam. 28.16. Psal. 139.20. Dan. 4.19. and as some also, Psal. 9.6. Mic. 5.11, 14. But the former seems to suit better here with the frame of the context; and to sort better with the words beforegoing. There is another exposition of this verse, found in the writings of some of the Rabbins, who supposing this passage to have reference to what was before said of the Babylonian kings, *making the world a wilderness, and destroying the cities thereof*, ver. 17. thus render the words; *They shall not rise again*; or, *Let them not stand up again*; as continuing the charge given to the enemy) *that they may*, or men *may possess the earth*, or *land*, (whence they were before, by them expelled) *and may fill the face of the world* (which they made to be like a wilderness) *with cities*: reedifying those which they had formerly ruined. Of the use of the copulative before: Of the verb indefinite, *that they may possess the earth*, (or, as the word is, *inherit it*, as Psal. 37.11. Matth. 5.5.) *and fill the world*; (Gen. 1.28. & 9.1.) that is, that the earth may be possessed, and the world filled; see on ch. 2.19. The exposition seems neither forced, nor improbable. But I leave it to the consideration, and judgment of the learned. See on ch. 26.14.

**V. 22.** *{For I will rise up against them (saith the Lord of hosts)*} Heb. *And*; as chap. 53.2. The reason why that which is threatened must be executed, and shall be effected: because God, who has all creatures at command, (see chap. 1.9.) will have it done; will have; not him alone, to be cut off; but his whole issue also with him. Yea, he it is that comes against them, and will, by these his selected, and appointed ones, do it. See ch. 13.3.

*{rise up*} Answering to what he had before said, in the charge given to the enemy, v. 21. *I will rise up against his children* to slay them; that they may not *rise up* to repossess their land, or, repair the ruins of their state; or, reedify their cities; as ch. 9.9, 10. Mal. 1.4.

*{and I will cut off from Babylon*} That is, from the king thereof, v. 21.

*{the name, and remnant*} That is, as some, all *memory*, and *remainder*, or *monument* of them; as Exod. 17.14. 1 Sam. 15.5. Psal. 9.5, 6. & 83.4. But by *name*, we may understand *male issue*, 1 King. 14.10. & 21.21. so called in Hebrew, because the memory of the stock is preserved in such. As on the other side the *females*, as most think, (but of that, see ch. 3.12.) because it is lost, and perishes in them, Numb. 27.4. Deut. 25.6. 2 Sam. 14.7. & 18.18. By *remnant*, other issue, or issue in general. Because females, in such cases, are sometimes neglected, and spared, as weak, and unable to make head. See Jer. 39.6. & 41.10. Or as others, *kindred*: for so is the word used, Levit. 18.6, 12, 13. See 1 King. 16.11.

*{and son and nephew*} Or, *even*, (as Ezr. 1.8. & 8.26.) or *both* (as Jer. 6.24.) *son*, (as Gen. 21.23.) *and nephew*: or, *son's son*; for so the Chaldee, and Jewish writers, not as we use the word; the whole race of him, Job 18.19.

*{saith the Lord*} For more certainty repeated.

**V. 23.** *{I will also make it*} To wit, the city of Babylon, or the seat of it, the place where it is now situate. See chap. 13.19, 20. There is in the Hebrew an elegant consonancy, between the first word of the verse, next beforegoing, and this, which our English cannot express.

*{a possession*} Or, as some, *an hereditary possession*, Num. 27.11. Jer. 49.1, 2. Or, as here rather, *a possession acquired* by, or upon *the expulsion*, of the former inhabitants, and possessors. For the word signifies also *to expel*, or *dispossess*; and by *dispossession* to possess. Numb. 21.32, 35. 2 Chro. 20.7. Psalm 44.2. It may well imply either here; both a possessing of it, by these wild creatures, in the room of the inhabitants, either slain in it, or driven out of it, and their so possessing it, not for some term of time; but as an inheritance, or perpetuity to them, and theirs, forever. See ch. 34.11.

*{for the bittern*} Or, *butor*. A kind of waterfowl, that thrusting her bill into the mire, or some broken cane, is wont to make therewith a most hideous noise. And this seems not unlikely, as well for what here next follows, as also for that it is elsewhere joined with another taken commonly for the *cormorant*, chap. 34.11. Zeph. 2.14. Yet some later interpreters suppose it, rather, to be an *osprey*, a kind of eagle that preys upon fish or a *bald buzzard*, which as they affirm) haunt lakes, and pools, and prey upon ducks. And some an *owl*, that uses to abide, and breed in old decayed, and deserted buildings; peradventure because of some fowl of that kind, mention is made, together with this, chap. 34.11. And such are said to dwell in Babylon's ruins, chap. 13.21. Jer. 50.39. But this is not so likely; though one of the Rabbins, contrary to his own exposition here, does, in that other place of this prophet, so expound it. But the most of the Jewish doctors make it not a bird, but a beast. And they take it generally to be a *porcupine*, or a *hedgehog*: with whom also the Chaldee, Greek, and Latin concur; save that one of them calls it, a *tortoise*. For the former they ground their opinion upon this, because, in Arabic, the word so signifies, including as well the *porcupine*, as the *hedgehog*. But these are neither of them such, as keep in or about watery places; the one roosting in hedges; in hilly places the other. The *tortoise* rather may be meant, because one kind of them keeps most, or much, at least in the water. Or, as some other, the *beaver*, that builds (I may well term it a building) on the edge, or brink of lakes and rivers, and feeds on the fish in them. Of whom they understand it, the rather, because the word it comes of, signifies *to cut down*, or *cut asunder*, chap. 38.12. Ezek. 7.25. That which the *beaver* (therein going beyond our *otter*) is wont to do with the trunks, or bodies, even of vast trees, and to shear men's bones asunder. See Pliny in his *natural history*, lib. 8. cap. 30.

*{and pools of water*} That which confirms the creature before mentioned, to be such, as haunts places so conditioned. The reason why it should not be for sheep to lodge in, chap. 13.20. The site of Babylon, of itself moorish, by reason of that great river, Deut. 1.7. & 11.24. to wit, Euphrates on whose banks it stood: (see on Jer. 50.38. & 51.32.) became after the surprisal by Cyrus, and in the times succeeding, much more such; the dams, and sluices being neglected, that should keep the river within its due compass; and the dikes choked that should receive the waters of it, in its accustomed inundations.

*{and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction*} The word here used is an Arabic word: which one of the Jewish doctors acknowledges that he did not understand, until he heard an Arabian chambermaid ask of her mistress *a broom*. But the phrase you may find, 1 King. 14.10. It alludes to the sweeping of a house, wherein all the soil, being swept together, is then cast out of doors. See somewhat the like, Ezek. 26.4.

*{saith the Lord of hosts*} As ver. 22.

**V. 24.** *{The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying*} He has taken a solemn oath upon it, which shows the doom to be irrevocable, Psal. 110.4. & 132.11. He has sworn it; and thereby manifested his will to have it done, his purpose to do it: and he is *the Lord of hosts*: and therefore wants no power to effect, whatsoever he will have done. See ch. 1.9. v. 27.

*{Surely*} Heb. *If not*. A defective form of speech usual in oaths. Of which see ch. 5.9. & 22.19.

*{as I have thought, so shall it come to pass*} Heb. *as I have imagined*, (Num. 33.56. See Chap. 10.7.) *so it shall be*, as Chap. 5.7.

*{and as I have purposed, so shall it stand*} Psal. 33.11. See chap. 7.5–7. ver. 26, 27. the same in other words repeated. That which I have determined concerning the irrecoverable destruction of Babylon, shall never be disannulled, or revoked.

**V. 25.** *{That I will break the Assyrian in my land*} Heb. *To break*, as ch. 23.9. or, *In breaking*: as Exod. 14.11. Deut. 9.18. Some understand this of Sennacherib the king of Assyria, whose forces God destroyed in his land, that is, the land of Judah, so called, because set apart by him, for his own peculiar, as an habitation for his peculiar people, and a seat for his solemn service, Psalm 114.2. and, 132.14. and 135.12. verse 1, 2.) as is recorded, Chapter 37, 38: added here, not only to confirm what had been before delivered, concerning the destruction of that insolent king, chap. 10.33, 34. but to give the stronger assurance thereby of what was here foretold, concerning the ruin of the Chaldean empire. The like whereunto, see Ezek. 31.3–18. Howbeit, it follows not hence what some would infer, that *the fall of Lucifer*, mentioned ver. 12. should respect, not the Babylonian; but the Assyrian king, and state. Yet some understand this of the Babylonian king, who seems to be termed the *king of Assyria*, Neh. 9.32. 2 Chr. 33.11. and of the Assyrians that served under him, as being taken up by him, their country lying between Chaldea, and Judah, in his expedition against Jerusalem; and to have been denounced after the fall of Sennacherib. Concerning which latter branch, as I will not contend, supposing the time of this prophecy to have been later than his fall; and to have been occasioned by that heavy doom passed upon the Jewish state, and the royal issue, that from the Babylonians should befall them, chap. 39.6, 9. otherwise, there was no ground, as yet, to tell this people of the overthrow of Babylon, from whom they had hitherto sustained no damage, nor, save in regard of that prediction, had cause to expect any. So for the turning it away, from Sennacherib, and his forces overthrown in that country, to the ruinating of the Chaldean estate. I cannot concur, since that the text must endure many forced interpretations, ere it will yield to any such diversion. I suppose therefore, that the fall of Sennacherib is here spoken of, as a thing past, and performed already: and here produced, as some other in the like manner, chap. 9.4, 5. & 10.24, 26. for a pregnant example of the certainty of God's predictions, and purposes, to take place, and not fail, which themselves had late proof of, in the strange, and unexpected destruction of the Assyrian forces among them: and for a parallel of the undoubted execution of the doom, forepassed upon Babylon, in its due time to be effected. And to this purpose I should thus read the words, *As in breaking the Assyrian in my land*. Of the use of this particle with the indefinite verb, examples were before given, to which more might be added. See chap. 3.8. & 10.2. Gen. 2.3. & 3.22. & 24.30. Deut. 13.18. & 17.2. & 20.19. 1 Sam. 12.17. Neh. 13.7. And for the defect of the note of similitude it is very usual in Scripture. See Prov. 25.20, 25, 28. & 26.9, 14, 17, 21, 23. & 28.15. It is then, as if the prophet had said; You need not doubt of the performance of this doom passed upon Babylon; for the Lord has taken a solemn oath upon it, that what he has spoken, and purposed, concerning it, shall be effected; as well as that, which was threatened formerly against the Assyrian, chap. 10.12, 16–19, 33, 34. which having been lately done in your own land, your own eyes have been witness of.

*{and upon my mountains tread him under foot*} Or, *and trampling upon him*; or, *when* (as ch. 8.21. & 43.10.) *I trampled on him, upon my mountains*.

*{tread him under foot*} Heb. *and I will trample upon him*. But the future, is oft put for the forepast: as Psal. 18.36, 37, 42, 43. Then God seemed to trample in contempt upon him, as he had trampled upon God's people, chap. 10.5, 6. when by the slaughter of his people, he enforced him, to fly, with shame. So Psal. 44.5. & 60.12. Dan. 7.7. & 8.7, 10. Rom. 16.20. an allusion to that, that has in disgrace, and despite, been sometime done, to persons subdued, and taken, either in war, or otherwise, Josh. 10.24. 2 King. 9.33. See Judg. 20.40. ch. 63.3, 6. Zach. 10.5.

*{upon my mountains*} Not mount Sion, as some, in way of excellency, so termed; as *wisdoms*, for, *wisdom*, Prov. 1.20. & 8.1. because near to it was the slaughter of Sennacherib's host; but the hills rather about Jerusalem, on which it is likely they lodged, while they lay in leaguer about it, Psal. 125.2. or, the mountains of Judah in general, being a mountainous country, Deut. 8.9. Psal. 133.3. Ezek. 6.2, 3. & 39.2, 4, 17. called *his mountains* here; and cap. 65.9. as the *land* before *his*. The mountains where he had placed his people, called *his*, here, as those by which they were to pass, in their return thither from Babylon, ch. 49.11.

*{then shall his yoke depart from off them*} Heb. *And his yoke shall depart* (as chap. 6.1. or, *that his yoke might depart*, (as Chap. 10.19. & 13.2. and so some interpreters of the best note, here render it) *from off them*, to wit, the people of God, the Jews, that had before, with tributes imposed, and hostile invasions, been grievously afflicted by him; See ch. 10.5, 6. & 36.1.

*{and his burden depart from off their shoulders*} See ch. 9.4. & 10.27. The end, for which God destroyed the Assyrian, to give ease, and rest to his people, Chap. 10.24, 25. and 33.20. and 38.6.

**V. 26.** *{This is the purpose, that is purposed*} The conclusion of this whole burdenous prophecy denounced against Babel. Heb. *the counsel that is consulted*: *counsel*, for, *purpose*, or, *determination*; the end, and issue of it, as Chapter 7.5. and 19.12. Jer. 49.20, 30.

*{upon the whole earth*} This great empire, that seems to command the whole world, cap. 13.11. or, *against* (as Jer. 49.20.) *the whole land*, to wit, of Chaldea; whereof Babylon the head city as ch. 13.5, 19.

*{and this is the hand that is stretched out*} See chap. 5.25. & 9.12, 21.

*{upon all the nations*} Or, *against all these nations*, to wit, the Chaldeans, and others subject to it, and serving under it. See ch. 13.14, 15. Jer. 50.21.

**V. 27.** *{For the Lord of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it*} Or, *determined*, or, *resolved* (as ver. 26.) *it, and who can disannul it*? the future in a potential notion: as Job 14.4. & 37.23. & 41.13, 29. Matth. 12.25. with Mar. 3.24. The particle *it*, having reference to God's particular purpose, and resolution concerning Babylon, and those that adhere to her, ver. 26. is wanting in the text: as chap. 9.9. Rev. 11.1. See ver. 24. So Psal. 33.10, 11. Prov. 24.21. & 21.30. Chap. 43.31.

*{and his hand is stretched out*} *and his hand* it is, *that is stretched out*. The hand, that I told you was stretched out against Babylon's adherents, ver. 26. is not some sorry mortal man's hand, that may be restrained, enfeebled, cut short, turned back, or shrunk up. Gen. 31.29. 1 King. 13.4. chap. 13.7. Jer. 50.15, 43. but the hand of God Almighty.

*{and who shall turn it back?*} Or, *can turn it back?* as before. See 2 Chron. 20.6. Job 9.12. & 23.13. Dan. 4.35.

**V. 28.** *{In the year that king Ahaz died*} Here begins another sermon, or prophecy, distinct, as well in time, as in matter, from the former; that being against the Babylonians, this, against the Philistines. In regard whereof also, some have made a several, and entire chapter of it. For the prophet having begun with the Babylonians, the greatest oppressors of God's people, Jer. 50.17. but more remote, Jer. 6.22. & 8.19. he proceeds now to their evil neighbors, that were nearer at hand, and of them sets the Philistines in the front. The time of the delivery hereof, is expressly noted, as of that. chap. 6. the one bearing date, the year of Uzziah's, the other, the year of Ahaz his death. Of which, 2 King. 16.20. This is expressed for a special reason; of which, ver. 29. But hence some take occasion here to begin a new book, supposing that the prophecies here recorded, from Chapter the seventh, unto this latter part of the fourteenth, were all of them, and that against Babylon, among the rest, delivered and published in Ahaz his reign: with whom therein, I cannot accord. See ch. 1.1. & 14.25.

*{was this burden*} This heavy prophecy (see chap. 13.1.) against Palestine, or the Philistines. Of whom see the like. Jer. 47. Ezek. 26.13, 17.

**V. 29.** *{Rejoice not thou whole Palestina*} Heb. *Pelesheth*, or *Palesheth*, Psal. 60.8. ver. 31. as *Serug*, Gen. 11.21. Luk. 3.35. and *Sabaoth*, Rom. 9.29. Jam. 5.4. It is the name of a country, deemed part of Syria, and bordering westward, on the land of Judah. Chap. 2.6. & 9.12. Whence the whole country thereabout, taking in the *holy land*, as they style it, is called Palestine at this day: but in Scripture does design only that particular coast, inhabited by the Philistines people of the posterity of Cham, and Cush, by the Egyptian race, Gen. 10.14. and were constant enemies; and vexers of the Jewish people their neighbors. See ch. 9.22.

*{because the rod of him that smote thee is broken*} By the rod that smote the Philistines, is generally deemed to be meant Uzziah, who prevailed much in his wars with the Philistines, dismantled many of their strong towns, and built others within their borders, to keep theirs under, and raise contribution from them, 2 Chr. 26.6, 7. Yet not him alone; but other kings of Judah before him, that had had the better of them, as David. 2 Sam. 5.20, 21. & 8.1, 12. Ps. 108.9. and the state of Judah, that in the times of those kings, kept them under. Whose, yet, might, and means were so sorely impeached, and and impaired under Ahaz, God, for his sins, suffering other people to break in upon him, and to prevail against him, that their power seemed to be utterly, and irrevocably broken: (as Chap. 9.4.) Now this was to the Philistines, the whole body of them, (as upon the surprisal of Samson, Judg. 16.23–25.) matter of much joy, to see that state so enfeebled, and at so low an ebb. But the prophet bids them, not be overjoyed; for their joy should not last long. It is not unlike David's ironical speech to that country, or, the people thereof, *Palestine triumph thou because of me*, Psal. 60.8. Of which see the note on the place: or, that of Hoshea to Israel, Hos. 9.1. *Rejoice not, O Israel*, in regard of the late successes God has vouchsafed to give you by Jeroboam against the Syrians, 2 King. 14.27, 28. for your joy will not last long, it will be shortened for your sins.

*{for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice*} That is, as most, both Jews and Christians, understand it, one of Uzziah's issue, who did shrewdly bite you, 2 Chr. 26.6, 7. shall arise in his stead; to wit, Ezekiah, whose great-grandfather Uzziah was, 1 Chr. 3.12, 13. that shall bite, and vex you far more grievously, than ever he did: and indeed so he did: for he overran their whole country, so as neither fort, or fenced city could escape him, 2 King. 18.8. Yet one I find, that expounds this whole passage of the kings of Assyria, understanding by the *rod broken*, Sennacherib, Chap. 10.5. & 14.25. by *the serpent*, Tiglath-Pileser, whose successors should be more grievous to the Philistines, than he had been; by *the cockatrice*, Sennacherib; by the *fiery flying serpent*, Nebuchadnezzar; who came from the *north*, ver. 31. but this is nothing probable; nor suits well with the times of those kings. For neither could the Philistines rejoice at the death of Ahaz, in regard of Sennacherib's fall; which was not before the fourteenth year of Ezekiah his successor, 2 King. 18.13. nor did Sennacherib ever rise, and recover strength again after that overthrow, Chap. 37.37, 38. But this to salve, another I light on, that makes the broken *rod*, and the *serpent* Sargon, of whom, ch. 20.1. the *cockatrice*, Salmaneser, the *fiery flying serpent*, Sennacherib. But neither is there story to confirm this; nor is it said upon the death of Sargon, of which, no mention is found; but upon the death of Ahaz, and, consequently, the entrance of Ezekiah, at whose coming to the kingdom, it is not unlikely, that God would have this prophecy delivered, to make him the more gracious in the eyes of his people, as one that should recover that power, and regain that honor (by repressing the malignant attempts of their adversaries, and his good, yea great success against them) which his father had embezzled, and lost by his folly. See Chapter 32.1.

*{Serpent's*} The word is generally for any sort of *serpents*: so called, of their subtlety, Gen. 3.1. so the verb it comes of, is used, Gen. 44.15.

*{root*} For progenitor: as Chap. 11.1. Judg. 5.14. and it is joined with the two sorts here mentioned, as a common term comprehending both, Num. 21.6. Jer. 8.17. but neither was Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar's progenitor, nor Nebuchadnezzar of Sennacherib's issue.

*{a cockatrice*} Or, *basilisk*: though some, *a viper*, that eats out her mother's bowels, say they: but that is a mere fable. Some, *an asp*, that, coming to be seventy years old, turns *cockatrice*; and becomes then so deaf, that she can no more be charmed, Psal. 58.4, 5. but that is a Jewish tale. It is supposed to have its name according to some, by a transposition of letters, from a word, that signifies *to wound*, for it stings grievously, Prov. 23.32. where it is rendered, *an adder*: yet it seems to be a kind of those, that have their venom, not in their tails, as the *scorpion*, Rev. 9.10. but in their teeth; wherewith they are said to bite, Jer. 8.17. they are such as burrow in the ground, chap. 11.8. and bring forth, not young, as does the *viper*, thereof indeed having its name; but eggs, chap. 59.5. The root whence it comes, seems to signify *putting out*, or, *bringing forth*, for thereof come two words; one, that signifies *excrements*, Ezek. 4.15. another, that denotes *issue*, chap. 22.24. where it is joined also with a word, issuing from the verb here used, and of the fecundity of it, a thing common to it, with such creeping things, as lay eggs, it may well have its name. See Exod. 1.7.

*{and his fruit shall be*} *fruit*, for *issue*, either of man, or beast: though properly, and primarily of trees, or plants, Num. 13.26, 23, 27. Chap. 4.2. So Deut. 28.4, 18. Psal. 21.20. & 132.11. *his fruit*, not the *cockatrice's*, as some, supposing it meant of a second descent; but of the *serpent* before mentioned, that should breed a *cockatrice*, yea, worse than so, a *fiery flying serpent*: and I should rather render it, *yea his fruit shall be*: as Neh. 6.10. Psalm 18.10. Chapter 3.9.

*{a fiery flying serpent*} The word, *Saraph*, here used, signifies such a kind of serpent, as with extreme heat, pains and kills. For it comes of a word, that signifies *to burn*. Whereof the Seraphim also, Chap. 6.2. have their name; being the very same with this, used, Num. 21.6. where it is said of them, they bit the people, some of them, even to death: and it is of the Greeks, for the same cause, called *prester*. The word *serpent*, is not here in the text; though it be joined with it, Deut. 8.14. And it is said to *fly*, as here, so chap. 30.6. either because it is winged, as those *Seraphs* were, chap. 6.2. and as some dragons, or serpents, are reported to be, of which kind I have sometime seen one, that had a kind of wing like your flying fish; or, because of their swift motion, whereby suddenly jerking up, they shoot themselves forward, or dart themselves out of trees, on men, or beasts, as they pass by. For of a swift motion is the Hebrew word also used, Psal. 18.10. & 91.5. Chap. 11.14. In regard whereof, some conjecture the serpent, here mentioned, to be that which the Greeks call *Acontias*; and the Latin *Jaculus*, from a *javelin*, or a *dart*. Howbeit, I cannot concur, with those that render it, *a feathered fiery serpent*, for such feathered ones, I suppose to be figments only. Now to such serpents, as are here mentioned, is Ezekiah compared, not for any fierce, fell, or mischievous disposition; but for the hurt, and damage that he should do to the Philistines; and to this latter also, for his swiftness, and celerity, in overrunning, and subduing their country. See Dan. 7.4. & 8.5.

**V. 30.** *{And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the needy shall lie down in safety*} This some suppose added, because by the terms formerly given him, Ezekiah might be deemed to be some cruel tyrant, to show, that though he should be such as is thereby intimated, yet he should be careful of the good, and safety of his own people, whose prosperity and plenty, security, and indemnity he should thereby procure. The scope seems to be, to declare what a vast difference there should shortly be, between the state of the Philistines, who now so much flourished; and the state of the Jewish people, at present, so much impoverished; for whose consolation this prophecy was principally intended. Thus *God strengtheneth the spoil against the strong*, Amos 5.9. For what some would have here intimated of their enlargement, quiet condition, and full feeding, after the Assyrian siege dissolved, Ch. 33.16, 17, 20. & 37.30. seems to be without the verge of this.

*{the firstborn of the poor*} Those that are brought to extreme poverty, as the Jews at that time were. See 2 Chro. 28. The ground of the phrase is, because the firstborn was of chief note and place in the family; and had a special portion above the rest, Deut. 21.17. 1 Chro. 5.1, 2. with Gen. 48.16, 22. Hence those phrases, Exod. 4.22. Ps. 89.27. Rom. 8.29. Col. 1.15, 18. Re. 1.5. That especially, that comes nearest to this here, Job 18.13. *The firstborn of death*: for the cruelest, and most grievous death.

*{shall feed*} Either *shall eat upon thee*: *shall depasture thee*: who before fed upon them, chap. 27.10. Zeph. 2.5, 7. and then there is a defect of the pronoun, as before, ver. 9. Or, *shall* then *feed* to the full, when you shall be starved, Chap. 5.17. & 65.13. Or, shall feed *quietly*, *in safety*, (supplied out of the next branch, as Mal. 1.10.) being rid of such bad neighbors; or freed, at least, from the fear of them who did formerly disturb them, Zeph. 3.13.

*{needy*} *Poor*, and *needy*; as ch. 26.6. See ch. 10.2.

*{lie down*} It is a metaphor, as the former, of *feeding*, taken from beasts or cattle, chap. 17.2. Zeph. 2.14. that use to lie down, when they have fed, ch. 27.10.

*{in safety*} Without fear, of disturbance, or distraction. As cattle, where no ravenous creature is near at hand, to worry, or scare them, Ezek. 34.25. & 39.26.

*{and I will kill thy root with famine*} Or, *but*; as ch. 11.4, 14. because the contrary condition of the Philistines here follows. Heb. *I will make thy root to die*. A metaphor from a stock, or tree, whose, not branches, or body only; but the very root also is dried up, for want of moisture to feed, and maintain it. An intimation of an utter destruction, Ps. 52.5. c. 5.24. Hos. 9.16. Mal. 4.1. See Hos. 2.3. Nor need we make any curious inquiry, what the *root* should mean here; as some that would have to be meant here, by *root*, the nobility, and by *remnant*, in the next clause, the commonalty, as if they sprung from the nobility, as from a root; whereas the nobility rather rises from them. For no more is meant there, than is elsewhere said of Ekron, a prime town of the Philistines, 1 Sam. 6.17. alluding to the name of it: *Ekron shall be rooted up*, or, *rooted out*, Zeph. 2.4.

*{and he shall slay thy remnant*} The same thing is said, save that the person is changed. For what was *root* there, is *remnant* here. He shall slay, that is, Ezekiah, before metaphorically described, ver. 29. as the most interpreters expound it. Or, God rather, as ch. 13.6. that God speaks this, what instruments soever he should use for the effecting of it. For it was not done by any one man, or at any one time: or the verb being taken indefinitely, *thy remnant shall be slain*; as ver. 32. See chap. 2.19. you shall be utterly destroyed. See Zeph. 2.5, 6. a *remnant* of God's people, is still said to be reserved, and saved, chap. 1.9. & 10.21, 22. but the very *remnant* here is threatened to be destroyed; that which was not fulfilled in Ezekiah's day. For how could Jeremy, Ezekiel, and Zephany, then, so long after again, denounce it. See vers. 31.

**V. 31.** *{Howl, O gate, cry, O city*} The prophet, upon this direful prediction of utter destruction, turns his speech again, as before he began it, ver. 29. to Palestine, calling to her cities, to howl, and cry out, as people are wont to do in sudden dangers, and distresses. See the like, chap. 13.6. & 23.1. Jer. 48.20. & 49.3. Joel 1.11, 13. Zach. 11.2. The same thing twice spoken, in divers terms; *gate*, and *city*, all one, as chap. 3.26. Ezek. 21.15. *gate* and *city*, collectively, for *gates*, and *cities*; to wit, of Palestine, whereof, in times past, were seven principal ones, 1 Sam. 6.17. and *gate* or *city*, not as some, the rulers, that sit in the gate; 1 Sam. 19.8. Jer. 38.7. but the people, or inhabitants of the cities in general; as chap. 1.21, 27. See Jer. 47.2.

*{thou whole Palestina art dissolved*} Heb. *melted*, as wax, and metals with fire: or, *mellowed*, and *dissolved*, as earth, and mold with water. For so the word properly signifies, Psalm 46.6. & 65.10. ch. 34.9. Amos 9.5, 13. Nah. 1.5. & 2.6. applied to a multitude, when they drop away one from another, as things do when they melt, either with heat, or with moisture, 1 Sam. 14.16. of particular persons, either when their flesh wastes, chap. 64.7. Job 30.22; or their hearts faint; Exod. 15.15. Josh. 2.9, 24. Psalm 75.3. & 107.26. Jer. 49.23. Ezek. 21.15. It may well be here understood in this latitude, said of Palestine, that it should be, either wholly wasted; or wholly dismayed; or, that the state itself should be dissolved, and it is said, *thou whole Palestina*, in reference to what was before said, *thou whole Palestina* ver. 29. you shall be wasted, dismayed, and dissolved, as you rejoiced all before: your dread, and desolation shall be now, as general, as your joy, and triumph was before.

*{for there shall come from the north a smoke*} *from the north*, that is, say some, from Assyria. Of which, Jer. 51.20. to wit, Sennacherib with his forces: but that was after Ezekiah smote the Philistines, 2 King. 18.8, 13. Nor do we read of any great mischief that he did to the Philistines: and it is not unlikely, that he would rather rescue from the Jews, that were planted, or placed among them, to keep them under, whose peace, and quiet abode in their own land, he came purposely to disturb, and so did; chap. 36.1. contrary to that which is here implied, ver. 30. from Chaldea, say others, to wit, Nebuchadnezzar, with his vast army; which seems to be confirmed, from Jer. 47.2. where the evil threatened the Philistines *from the north*, is generally acknowledged to be meant of Nebuchadnezzar who is oft times said to come *from the north*, Jer. 1.13, 14. & 4.6. & 6.22. but the circumstances here mentioned, will not admit it; that especially, ver. 32. concerning the safety of those, that repaired to Sion for succor. Sion itself being then surprised, and the Jewish state involved in the same calamity with the Philistines. I understand it therefore, with most of the Jewish, and Protestant, yea, some Popish also, writers; of Judea, that stood northeast from Palestine; and Jerusalem, that was likewise situate in regard of Gaza, and the coasts about it, surprised by Ezekiah, 2 King. 18.8. for which having so clear Scripture, and so suitable both to the time of the delivery of this prophecy, and to the subject matter of it, I see no sufficient reason why any should strive to divert it, and to turn it any other way.

*{a smoke*} Some by *smoke*, here understand a cloud of dust, raised by the footing of horses, and men, chariots, and carriages, giving warning of some great army approaching. Others, the noise of the neighing, and prancing of horses, clashing of armor, rushing of chariots, and rumbling of wheels, Jer. 8.16. & 47.3. forerunners of war, as smoke of fire. Others, of the report of the enemies' approach, that should utterly fright and dismay them, Jer. 4.15. & 6.24. Others fetch in here *the boiling pot*, with the mouth northward, Jer. 1.13. and by *smoke*, understand here the steam of it, or the like. I conceive *smoke* to be here taken, not as it is a sign, & forerunner, or forewarner of fire, Judg. 20.40. but as it dims, or darkens the air, or offends and chokes, Prov. 10.26. Ezekiah's forces, wherewith he should invade the Philistines, are compared to a great, thick, and stifling smoke, that should overspread all their country, and either vex, and annoy them, in their dwelling, or expel, and drive them out of the places of their abode: or, that should set all in a combustion with them, make their whole land, as Mount Sinai, sometime, Exod. 19.8. Josh. 8.20, 21. chap. 34.10. and this the rather; for the smoke is said to come with them.

*{and none shall be alone in his appointed times*} Or, *meeting places*, or *assemblies*. See ver. 13. Most interpreters, both Jewish, and Christian, understand this, as spoken of those Jewish forces, that Ezekiah should raise for his expedition, against Palestine, that they should none come alone; but resort by flocks, to him, at his *set times*, for entertainment of them, or *set places*, where they were appointed to meet; so willing, and glad they should be, to be employed against a people, that had so much, and so often molested them. See the like, Psal. 110.3. chap. 13.2–4. Howbeit, one of the Rabbins expounds it of the Philistines, that they should not dare, or endure to stay in their *meeting places*, their palaces, or strongholds, any one of them, when these forces break in upon them; as when a smoke comes, says he, no man, though alone, can endure to stay in his house. Chap. 6.4. Of the latter word, see Psal. 74.8. Of the former, Psal. 102.7. And this seems more suitable to the tenor of the context, if the words will bear it. The smoke, that shall be driven in upon you, from the fire of God's wrath incensed against you, shall in all places so pursue you, and annoy you, that you shall nowhere be in rest. See Deut. 29.20. Psalm 18.8.

**V. 32.** *{What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation*} Heb. *And, what shall he answer*: *And*, for, *then*; as Chap. 8.3, 14. *shall he answer*, that is, Ezekiah, say some, as ver. 30. but rather, *shall be answered*, as ch. 13.9. & 15.5. As also, by *the messengers of the nation*, some understand the Babylonian ambassadors, sent to Ezekiah, chap. 39.1. but the time accords not with the circumstances of things here foretold. See on ver. 29, 31. Some, the Philistines' ambassadors sent, upon unequal terms, to procure a peace: but of this, there is no ground. Others, any messengers sent from any people, to congratulate with the Jews, upon these their successes, as the manner of princes is, upon such occasions to do, 2 Sam. 8.10. and take the word therefore collectively, *nation*, for, *nations*, Deut. 28.49. and others yet more generally, any strangers, that repair to Jerusalem, by occasion of commerce, and business, which though a word thence derived signifies Levit. 11.32. & 16.29. yet I find not the word itself, ever so used. I suppose to be meant any messengers in general, that upon any occasion shall come sent unto them, from foreign parts.

*{that the Lord hath founded Sion*} He has built it, and will so establish it, and protect it, and those that repair to it: and that there is little hope therefore for any to prevail against them, or it, Psal. 87.1. & 102.13–16. chap. 37.32, 33.

*{and the poor of his people shall trust in it*} Or, *shall betake themselves unto it*; as to a place of retreat for surety, and safeguard. So is the word used Judg. 9.15. Psal. 36.7. & 57.1. & 61.4. & 91.4. or, *that they may repair thereunto*; (see chap. 13.2.) as to a place by God set apart, and appointed for such purpose. So the noun hence deduced Job 24.8. Psalm 104.18. Chap. 4.6. & 25.4. & 28.15. & 30.3.

*{the poor of his people*} Of whom before, ver. 30. and for whose comfort this was principally intended, see Psal. 9.9. Joel 2.32. Zeph. 3.12, 13. This answer may be given to the ambassadors of foreign princes, by them to be returned unto those that sent them.

### CHAPTER 15

**V. 1.** *{The burden of Moab*} Of *burden*, see chap. 13.1. *Moab* was the son of Lot, begot on his elder daughter in drink, Gen. 19.33, 37. From him, his posterity, and the country they inhabited, (bordering upon the land of promise, out of which, the Emim were by them expelled, Deut. 2.20, 21.) had their name. These were ever bad neighbors to the Jewish people, and ill affected towards them, Numb. 22.5, 6. Deut. 23.3, 4. Judg. 3.12–14. 2 Kings 13.20. & 24.18. Psalm 83.6, 8. against these therefore, as the constant adversaries of God's people, is this burdensome prophecy of sad menaces denounced, in this chapter, and the next.
