The like whereunto, see Amos 2.1–3. & Jer. 48. in which latter place also, are many passages found, borrowed from this prophet; as in their due places shall be shown.

*{Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste*} The prophet begins this prophecy concerning Moab, with a relation of the devastation, and destruction of some chief cities, and principal parts of that country; which afterwards he does more largely, and particularly prosecute; together with the Moabites' distraction and vain devotions, thereupon flocking unto their idols, who could do them no good.

*{Because*} So the word most usually signifies; and so the most here take it. Yet some render it here, *certainly*: and so it is sometime used; as chapter 5.9. & 7.9, 16.

*{in the night*} That is, suddenly, unexpectedly, as *the day of the Lord* is said to come *as a thief in the night*, 1 Thess. 5.1, 2. So Matth. 25.6. Mar. 13.31–35. Luk. 21.34, 35. Eccl. 9.12. or, *in a night*, for there is no article in the text: that is, within the compass of a night: as of Jonas his *Kikayon*, it is said, that *it came up in a night, and was destroyed in a night*, Jon. 4.10. though that, by a proverbial speech, be spoken of the celerity, both of the growth, and the decay of that plant. So of a famous city in France, burnt down in a night, a heathen author says, that *there was but a night between a notable city, and none at all*. See Jer. 4.20.

*{Ar of Moab*} *Ar*, the chief, or mother city of Moab, Num. 21.28. which seems also to have given the name to the whole region, round about it, and to the greatest part of the Moabites' ancient possession, Deut. 2.9. Some suppose it to be the same with *Aroer*, mentioned, Num. 32.34. Deut. 2.36. & 3.12. Jer. 48.19. but of that there is no certainty, yea, or likelihood.

*{is laid waste*} Or, *spoiled*; or, *sacked*, or, *plundered*: as Psal. 119.61. he speaks in the present tense, as of a thing already done; or in doing; and so all along afterward. The usual guise of prophetical language; implying the certainty of the things foretold, as sure to be done, as if effected already. See Chapter 3.1. 1 Kings 14.14.

*{and brought to silence*} So the old Latin, and so the word may seem to be taken, Jer. 8.14. but that rather from another root. It were better rendered, *is cut off*, for so it is used, Jer. 47.5. Hos. 10.9, 15. Obad. 15. Zeph. 1.11. And if we retain this reading, the copulative, which is wanting in the Hebrew, need not be expressed; but the word without it, rendered, *it is cut off*. See chapter 14.11, 13, 19, 20. and this seems to go beyond the former; not *sacked*, or *plundered* only, but *cut off*, destroyed, ruined, either burnt down, or beaten down.

*{because in the night Kir of Moab is—laid waste, and brought to silence*} *Kir*, a city of special note in the land of Moab; called also *Kir-heres*, and *Kir-hareseth*, chap. 16.7, 11. And *of Moab* here, to distinguish it from another of that name in Media, mentioned, chap. 22.6. 2 King. 16.9. Howbeit the whole verse, is, some other ways, rendered by interpreters: for the old Latin has it, concluding the whole sentence within this verse, thus; *Because Ar is wasted by night, Moab is silenced; because the wall* (he took the city's name for a common term) *is wasted, Moab is silenced*. That is, either is destroyed, and brought to the grave, the place *of silence*, as Psalm 30.17, 18. or, he is become *mute*: all his rejoicing, and shouting is gone, ch. 16.9, 10. Or, all his bragging, and vaunting is ceased, chap. 16.8. Jer. 48.2. Or, he sits *still*, and dares not stir to make any resistance, as Psal. 4.4. Jer. 8.14. Others, of late, have thus rendered it, *Because Moab is wasted, Ar is cut off; because Moab is wasted, Kir of Moab is cut off*: and so carrying the sentence on to the next verse. The reason why they read it thus, taking in the word *Moab*, from the foregoing inscription, is, because the verb of *wasting* is masculine, whereas the names of cities are feminine. But that need not enforce any such supply, since that the genders are not in the Hebrew so commonly observed. So chap. 13.11. where the nouns are both feminine, the verb joined to the one, and the participle to the other both masculine. And the like, ch. 16.3. observed there by the Hebrew critics, and oft elsewhere. See Jer. 2.23, 24. Beside that the unevenness of the composure may be helped by supposing the *inhabitant* to be intended: as indeed it is, *Ar is wasted*, for the inhabitants of *Ar*: and of *Kir* likewise. And *inhabitant*, for *inhabitants*, as chap. 5.3. See chap. 18.2. So chap. 47.11. *evil*, or *adversity shall come upon thee*; for the day of *evil*, or the time of *adversity*: as is more fully expressed, Psalm 27.5. & Jer. 30.19. *Praise*, or, *thanksgiving shall come forth*. That is, the voice of *praise*, or *thanksgiving*: as Psal. 26.7. Jon. 2.9. in all which places, the form of the verb, for the gender of it, agrees not with the noun expressed, but with that understood. But a late writer, of great note, to cut off these difficulties makes the former verb of *waste*, an infinitive, thus rendering the words; *Surely in the night that Ar of Moab was sacked, was he cut off: surely in the night that Kir of Moab was sacked, was he*, (that is, Moab) *cut off*. Moab was destroyed in that night, wherein those his two principal cities were surprised and sacked. And this reading seems very probable. The word *night*, in a regent form, here confirming it. The like syntax, see chap. 30.29. unless a defect of the relative be in either place; as chap. 29.1. Now this destruction, wherewith Moab is here threatened, was inflicted, as some think, by Salmaneser, when he invaded Samaria, 2 King. 17.5. as others, by Sennacherib, when he came against Judea, 2 King. 18.13. Or, as others again, by Nebuchadnezzar, after the surprisal of Jerusalem, 2 King. 25.1, 4. See ch. 16.14.

**V. 2.** *{He is gone up*} Or, *is gone unto*. See Chap. 7.1. and 8.7. *He*, that is, *Moab*, his king and his people, supplied from the latter part of the verse; as chap. 14.30. they run to, and fro, from idol, to idol, from temple, to temple, to seek relief, and succor; but in vain, chap. 16.12.

*{to Bajith*} A city so styled, as an idol's *house*, or *temple*, in way of eminency, above all other in that country: or as if the whole city were all but one idol's *house*, or *temple*; it is called at large, *Beth-baal-Meon*; that is, *The house of Baal's habitation*, Josh. 13.17. more briefly, *Beth-Meon*, Num. 32.38. 1 Chr. 5.8. and yet cut shorter, *Beon*, Num. 32.3. here, by the first word in the name at large, *Bajith*: which yet some here take not for the name, of a city; but for an *house*, or a *temple*; and render the words, *to the house*, or *temple*; to wit, of Chemosh his chief god. See ch. 16.12. Jer. 48.7, 13. But of this, more anon. See ver. 6.

*{and to Dibon*} Another city of Moab, which was sometime together with Ar, and much of his country surprised, and taken from him, by the Amorites, Num. 21.26, 30. By means whereof it came into the Israelites' hands, having subdued the Amorite, Num. 32.3. And was possessed first by the Gadites, Num. 32.34. & 33.45. though it fell afterward to the Reubenites, Josh. 15.17. but was (it seems) again afterward by the Moabites recovered, and by them repossessed, Jer. 48.18, 22. See ver. 9. These two places are deemed to have been unto the Moabites, as Dan and Bethel were unto the idolatrous Israelites, 1 King. 12.28, 29. the principal places of their idolatrous services. See Jer. 48.13.

*{the high places*} Some take these words, as joined by way of apposition, to the names of the two forementioned places; as if it were said, *He is gone to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places*: that is, to those high places that are there. Others take it, for the proper name of a city, situate near to the foot of Pisgah, called sometime Bamoth, Numb. 21.19, 20. sometime *Bamoth-Baal*, or *the high places of Baal*, Josh. 13.17. and they render the words, *and to Bamoth*: supplying the copulative, which they suppose is wanting, as ver. 1. But one of the Jewish writers, whom some of ours also follow, goes a third way; rendering the words to this effect, *He* (to wit, Moab, that is, the king especially, or the people of Moab) *is gone up to the temple*, (to wit, of Chemosh, called *his sanctuary*, chap. 16.12.) *and Dibon*, (that is, the inhabitant, taken collectively, or the inhabitants of Dibon) *to the high parts*. And this I the rather incline to, because the article is prefixed before, both *Bajith*, and *Bamoth*; which in proper names is not so usual; and it suits best with what we find afterward, ch. 16.12. See Num. 21.28.

*{to weep*} Heb. *for weeping*; the noun for the verb: not to sacrifice, as usually, but to *weep*, that is, to lament, and by prayer and supplication to seek to these idols for help, and succor, in their present distresses, *to pray*, ch. 16.12.

*{Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba*} Or, *for Nebo and for Medeba*: as chap. 24.11. Lament. 2.7, 18. two cities also of Moab. *Nebo*, possessed sometime by the Reubenites, Numb. 32.3, 38. so called, as may seem, from the mount near to it, on which Moses deceased, Deut. 32.49, 50. & 34.1; both, as some, from the prophecies, or oracles, that their idols there gave. See chap. 46.1. *Medeba*, a city on the confines of those parts of Moab, which the Amorites sometime took from him, Numb. 21.30. and became afterward a boundary of the Reubenites' portion, Josh. 13.16. for these, *Moab*, that is, the Moabite, *shall howl*; (the ground of their forementioned *weeping*;) because by the enemy surprised, and sacked. See chap. 14.31.

*{on all their heads shall be baldness*} Or, *all their heads shall be bald*. Heb. *on every his head*; or, *on his whole head, shall be baldness*; as having reference to Moab before spoken; but taken collectively. The lamentation shall be general; because the affliction so also, see ch. 1.5.

*{on all heads baldness, and every beard cut off*} Heb. *lopped*: used properly of trees, or the branches of them, Chap. 10.33. & 14.12. Dan. 4.14. This was to come to pass, either by tearing of their hair, through extremity of grief, and impatiency of spirit, Ezra 9.3. See ch. 3.24. or, by cutting, and shaving of head, and beard. An usual practice, anciently in times of mourning, and lamentation, Levit. 19.27, 28. & 21.5. Deut. 14.1. Job 1.20. Jer. 7.29. Ezek. 7.18. Amos 8.10. Mic. 1.16. And the reason of this practice, on such occasion, the Rabbins render, because the hair of head, and beard, is accounted as an ornament to a man's person; and the mangling of it a disgrace; 2 Sam. 10.4. and ornaments in mournings are laid aside; as unseasonable; Exod. 33.4–6. See the same, Jer. 48.37.

**V. 3.** *{In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth*} Heb. *In his*, as before, ver. 2. *streets*, or *outways*, otherwise: *streets* comes in afterward. See [unclear]. When they come abroad, they shall go clad with sackcloth girt to them: the wonted habit of mourners, 2 Sam. 3.31. 1 King. 20.31, 32. & 21.27. 2 King. 6.30. & 19.1, 2. Neh. 9.1. Esth. 4.1–4. Job 16.15. Psal. 30.11. and 35.13. Chap. 3.24. & 20.2. and 22.12. and 37.1, 2. & 55.5. Dan. 9.3. Joel 1.8, 13. Amos 8.10. Rev. 11.3. See Jer. 48.37.

*{on the tops of their houses*} On which being flat, roofed, as terraces, or, open galleries, Deut. 22.8. Josh. 2.6. they used to pray, Act. 10.9. as also to repair thither in danger, and distress, for more security, or to look about for relief. See chapter 22.1. Jer. 7.29.

*{and in their streets*} The usual places of common, and general lamentation, and mourning, Eccl. 12.5. Chap. 24.11. or, as well those, that run to and fro in the streets, as those that are got up to the tops of their houses.

*{everyone shall howl*} There shall be nothing but howling, and weeping, in city and country; both within doors and without, v. 4, 5, 8. See Jer. 48.38.

*{weeping abundantly*} Heb. *descending with weeping*: that is, say some, coming down with weeping, and heavy hearts, from their idol temples, whither they went up, v. 2. because they find little hope of help, or comfort there, or, rather, their eyes running down with tears, as Psal. 119.136. Jer. 9.1, 18. & 13.17. Lam. 1.16. & 3.48.

**V. 4.** *{And Heshbon shall cry*} Or, *Both Heshbon, and Elealah*, as Psal. 76.6. Jer. 17.26. Or, *For*: as Chap. 13.8. & 53.2. For he proceeds to show by enumeration of particular places, how general the lamentation should be. See Jer. 48.34.

*{Heshbon*} Of this, which was the royal city of Sihon, the Amorite king, as of the former, see Num. 21.23, 26. & 32.37.

*{shall cry*} Or, *crieth*: as ver. 1.

*{and Elealah*} Of this likewise, see Num. 32.3, 37. by *Heshbon*, and *Elealah*, is meant the inhabitants of either: as *Moab* for the *Moabites*, ver. 2. See v. 1.

*{their voice shall be heard*} Or, *is heard*: as before, *Crieth*. See ch. 10.30.

*{even unto Jahaz*} The utmost border of Moab's country, towards Sihon's land, Num. 21.23. called also *Jahazah*, and assigned to the Levites, out of the Reubenites' portion, Josh. 21.36.

*{therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out*} The cry shall be so doleful, and so great, that it shall make not the weak only, and such as are not acquainted with war; but even the soldiers, that are in arms, and the most courageous among them, to quail, and by crying with the rest, to discover their inward faintheartedness, and unwillingness to fight, and make resistance against the enemy. See Jer. 48.4, 14, 41.

*{armed soldiers*} The word signifies properly such as have their garments, and their harness, or weapons, as sword, and the like, such as they were wont then to wear, and to make use of, *girt up* to them, unto, or about their loins, Deut. 12.11, 41. & 13.18. Luke 12.35. as ready to go out into the field, or to enter fight, whensoever occasion should be, Num. 32.30, 32. Deut. 3.18. Josh. 4.13. The word, *soldiers*, is not in the text.

*{shall cry out*} Some of the Jewish writers expound it, *shall shout*, as men are wont to do for joy, and in triumph, Judg. 15.14. and as valiant men when they are joining battle, 1 Sam. 17.20. 2 Chr. 13.15, 16. as implying, that though the soldiers should show themselves, ready and forward to go out against the enemy, yet Moab, the king, and people, should have no heart thereunto. But the shouting here mentioned, as other of them well observe, is not of mirth, nor of alacrity, but of mourning, and dejection of spirit. See Jer. 48.32, 33. So is the word used, *to cry out*; for sense of pain, or fear of evil, Judg. 7.21. Mic. 4.9.

*{his life shall be grievous to him*} As if it were said, he shall be weary of his life, as Rebekkah, Gen. 27.46. and Job, Job 3.20, 21. & 6.8, 9. & 7.15, 16. Heb. *his soul shall be ill affected to him*, or, *for himself*. Which the Jewish writers, some of them expound: *Moab's soul shall be grieved for himself*, or, *each of the Moabites shall be in much grief* of mind, for the evil that is like to befall him: and some of them, as if an emphasis were in the last word; he shall have no list to look after any other: but *each soul sorrow for itself*. The fear, and affliction that shall surprise each party, being so great, that they should mind none but themselves. This latter seems somewhat too nice; yet see Jer. 47.3. & 49.5. Others, *it shall grieve within him*. There is in the text an elegancy in the sound of the words: between this, and that of *crying*, before used. The vicinity whereof has made some great Rabbins, and some of ours, treading in their steps, to expound it; *each one shall cry for himself*; referring it, some to the whole body of the people, some to the men of war, before mentioned. But the word in that form is not found so to signify. See Chap. 16.7.

**V. 5.** *{My heart shall cry out for Moab*} Or, *Doth cry out*; or, *did cry out*: (for the tenses are oft promiscuously used. See Chap. 14.25. ver. 1.) *for Moab*, or *unto Moab*, as ver. 4. *to him*, or, *for him*. This, most, both Jewish, and Christian interpreters, understand of the prophet's compassionate affection towards that people, albeit so great an enemy to God's people; their destruction and calamity being so grievous, that the very thought of it moved him to commiseration. Whence also one of the Rabbins observes a difference between the prophets of God, and the prophets of idols; between Esay, and Balaam; the one desired to be cursing God's people, Num. 23. whereas Esay was grieved to forethink what evil was to betide Moab. See chap. 16.9, 11. & 21.3. Jer. 47.6. But other, of both sorts understand them, not of the prophet; but of those, before mentioned, ver. 4. (and insert therefore, as to be supplied in the text, the word, *saying*, which is indeed sometime omitted; as Psal. 105.15. ch. 63.11.) Some of the men of arms, making profession of their forwardness to fight, and their crying to, and calling upon the people for that purpose, to reclaim them from flight, and encourage them to stand to it. Others, of the Moabites in general, professing their inward grief, even at heart, for the calamities, and ruin of their country. And this, to me, seems best to agree with the rest of the context, as well foregoing, as ensuing. See Jer. 48.31, 32, 36.

*{his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar*} *His fugitives*. Or as the Hebrew has it, *her fugitives*. (and so ver. 8.) as having reference, say the Jewish doctors, to the region. Of whom, some expound the words here used, as our version does. And as another from the same root, (which generally signifies to *flee*) does undoubtedly import, Ezek. 17.21. as also is this here used by many deemed to signify, Chap. 43.14. See also, Jon. 1.10. *shall flee*, is not in the original; but is supplied from the noun. Instead whereof, some supply from the former clause, or from what follows, *shall cry*. And others, *shall run crying unto Zoar*. The city that was saved, when Sodom, and her neighboring towns were destroyed. (Of which, and of Lot's fleeing thither, whereunto the prophet is here deemed to allude, see Gen. 19.20–22.) And thither those may well seem to flee, that stood in fear of, or had escaped the sword of the enemy, either hoping there to find shelter; as others at Heshbon, Jer. 48.45. or thereby intending a further escape: (See Jer. 48.6.) it being a bordering town of that state, Deut. 34.3. Whence also have divers taken occasion (the old Latin among the rest) to render the word here not *fugitives*, but *bars*, or *bolts*; as most commonly, indeed, it signifies, Exod. 26.26, 27. Psal. 107.16. So called, because they shoot, or run through the rings, or hollow places, made for the passage of them, Exod. 26.28. & 36.33. And some, thereby understand the *borders* of the land, which are to it, as *bars*: and read the text, *Unto the borders thereof, even unto Zoar*, to wit, *did I cry*. From the former branch supplied; as Gen. 1.16. But of this use of the word, (though great ones maintain it,) is no example produced. Others therefore and so some of the Jewish writers understand by it the *bars* of the city gates; which go commonly together, Deut. 2.5. 1 Sam. 23.7. 2 Chro. 8.5. Job 38.10. Psalm 107.16. Jer. 49.31. Ezek. 38.11. As *gate*, for *city*, Chap. 3.26. So *bar*, for *gate*, Proverbs 18.19. Or *stronghold*, Amos 1.5. As also some take it, Chap. 43.14. And *bars* said to cry here, says one Rabbin, as *gates* and *cities* to *howl*, Chap. 14.31. But another, rather referring it to the former branch, renders it, *My heart shall cry for Moab*; and for *her bars*, that is, *all her strength*, says he, or strongholds, because the bars are the strength of a gate, as the gates of a city. And the gate cannot hold out, when the bars are broken, no more than a city, when the gates are broke open, Psal. 107.16. & 147.13.) *even unto Zoar*; a principal one of them. In this variety of versions, and expositions, (and others also there are, besides these) I suppose with least straining of the text, the words may be thus rendered, *Her fugitives shall cry unto Zoar*. For of the cry passing to and fro, up and down, through the whole country, does this passage still speak. And so, Jer. 48.34. *From the cry of Heshbon, even unto Elealah, even unto Jahaz have they uttered their voice; from Zoar, even unto Horonaim*. Of which, see v. 5. They shall cry thither; that is, carry on the cry along thither: or shall *run crying* thither. Of which kind of defective speech, see examples, Gen. 45.14. *Benjamin wept upon his neck*; that is, fell weeping upon his neck: or, *fell upon his neck, and wept*; as the former part of the verse, more fully has it, 1 Sam. 7.2. *Israel lamented after the Lord*: that is, lamenting sought after him, 1 Cor. 5.2. *Ye have not mourned, that the man that hath done this deed might be taken away from you*: that is, you have not, sorrowing, or being grieved, taken a course for the removing of him from among you: as after there, ver. 13. See also Chap. 14.12. & 38.14, 17, 21. I shall only add, and leave it to the consideration of others, whether this branch, may not, with the next foregoing, be thus knit together, and rendered, *My heart crieth out for Moab*, (that is, I myself; as Psalm 25.17. & 27.8. and 28.7. cry out, or I cry out heartily for him) *and for his fugitives*, (that flee: or so as my voice may be heard) *unto Zoar*. See Chap. 43.14.

*{an heifer of three years old*} The words thus rendered, make it ambiguous, unto whom this branch is to be referred. Some refer it to the city Zoar: which, they say, is called here, *an heifer of three years old*, in regard of her strength and beauty, and the richness of her soil, Gen. 13.10. Because at those years, an heifer is in her prime: and therefore God bids Abraham take *an heifer*, and *a female goat*, and *a ram*, each of that age, for the sealing of covenants between them. Gen. 15.9. Yet some of the Jewish authors would have it, *a calf of the third birth*: as if such were usually the strongest. And would have Moab, or Zoar, likened to such a *calf*, for her wantonness: as Jer. 31.18. Hos. 10.11. See Jer. 48.11. But Jer. 48.34. where the same words are found, they are rendered, *as an heifer of three* *years old*. And it is there referred, not to the city, but to the criers, or the cry. I will cry out, as such an heifer, missing her calf, or her company, 1 Sam. 6.9, 12. Or, the cry of those that fly, shall be such, and so loud, that it should be heard unto Zoar; or it shall pass in that manner over the whole country, till it come thither. See v. 4. Of the defect of the note of similitude, see in the like case, Chap. 21.8.

*{for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up*} Heb. *he shall go it up*: or, *it shall go up* (to wit, the cry; as it is, Jer. 48.5.) by the *ascent*, &c. In which words, some suppose a reason to be rendered, why the men of war should cry so loud for the staying of the people: to wit, because all places should be so full of howling, and yelling for fear, and grief, that otherwise they could not be heard. Others, why those that fled, should not stay till they come to Zoar; because they found these places, on the way, so full of weeping, and wailing, that they well thereby perceived there was no safe tarrying there. But I suppose rather, that the prophet's intent is to show, that the cry was gone over the whole country, and was arrived at Zoar, by relating the places by which it had passed. See Jer. 48.4, 5.

*{Luhith*} Of this city or town, we find no mention in Scripture, save here, and in Jeremy. The Rabbins tell us, it stood high; which I suppose they gather from the words of the text. Some of ours tell us, that it was situate on a hill, and on that side of it that looked toward Judah, as Horonaim, on the other. But whence they have that, I know not.

*{for in the way of Horonaim*} Or, *to Horonaim*. So Jer. 48.34. *From Zoar unto Horonaim*. That is, all the way that lies between them. Hence it is thought, that Sanballat was called the *Horonite*, Neh. 2.10, 16. The name is in the dual, as you would say, *the two Horons*. The reason whereof, is by the Rabbins rendered; because there were two of them, the upper, and the lower. And of Beth-horon indeed we so find, Josh. 10.10, 11. & 16.3, 5. & 18.13, 14. which, by those places, seem to have been situate upon the confines of the Ephraimites, and the Benjamites. And might peradventure be the same with Horonaim, here mentioned: (as *Nimrah*, and *Beth-nimrah*, Number 32.3, 36.) if the situation of them would admit it.

*{they shall raise up a cry of destruction*} That is, men *shall raise* such a *cry*: or, such a *cry shall be raised*; as Chap. 2.19. & 14.30. So some of the Jewish writers, by a transposition of letters, deducing it from a root that signifies to raise, Chap. 14.9. Howbeit, others of them say, it is a Syriac word, and signifies *to cry*. And it has some affinity with the term of *shouting*, used v. 4. Whereunto also some refer it. And others again to a word, that signifies *to break asunder* with force or violence, Psal. 2.9. and render it, *They shall break*, or *rend themselves* with *crying*. A defect of the particle *with*, as Ps. 17.13, 14. with ver. 7.

*{a cry of destruction*} Heb. *of breach*, or *breaking*. That is, either a cry importing destruction; *Breach*, put for destruction, as Chap. 1.28. & 14.25. Or as some, *a broken cry*: such as vehemency of passion, and distraction, in a tumultuous multitude, does oft produce. But I incline rather to the former. See Jer. 4.20. The drift is, to show, that all places, and passages, high and low, from the one end of the land to the other, should be filled with lamentations, and outcries. See further, v. 8.

**V. 6.** *{For*} Or *Because*. One reason of their cry, the utter spoil of their pastures, at present, not, as some, their future desolation.

*{For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate*} Heb. *shall be desolations*; or, *shall be brought to extreme desolation*; as Jer. 48.34. See chap. 1.17. That is, as most, the waters and brooks near to that place, that watered the rich pastures, in the plains of Moab, shall be dried up. As of Egypt the like is said, Chap. 19.5, 7. But that was there done by diversion of the main stream of the river: whereof here, there is no likelihood; and falls out oft, in times of drought, 1 King. 18.5. Jer. 14.3. But that is not the thing here foretold. Others, therefore, by *waters*, do here understand that fat, and rich pastures and grounds themselves that lay near to those waters, as Eccl. 11.1. *waters*, for soil, or land, well watered, Chapter 32.20. For as for that which some of the Rabbins have of the brooks there, that they should be said to be *desolated*; because they were mixed with the blood of the slain, or choked up with their corpses. It seems somewhat too far-fetched. That which others have of the places adjoining, said to be *desolate*; because left by the inhabitants, either fled, or slain, is more likely; but suits not so well with the words following, which speak, not of the towns, but the grounds. See Jer. 48.34.

*{Nimrim*} There is mention of a town, called *Nimrah*, Numb. 32.3. joined there with divers other of those here mentioned. Called also *Beth-nimrah*, Numb. 32.36. (for names are oft times cut short, as *Sittim*, for *Abel-sittim*, Num. 25.1. & 33.49. *Hermon*, Psal. 133.3. for *Baal-hermon*, Judg. 3.3. *Ashan*, Josh. 19.7. for *Corashan*, 1 Sam. 30.30. *Sheba*, for *Beersheba*, Josh. 19.2. *Salem*, for *Jerusalem*, Psal. 76.2.) where it is reckoned up among those cities, that the Gadites possessed concerning which see on v. 2. It is here put in the plural number, for the grounds near to, or about that city. Or, it may be, for such fat pastures, as those about Nimrah were, as if he had said, the fat pastures of the *Nimrahs*, or *Nimrim*; towns so seated, as that was, in rich and fertile soils. See *Sittim*, Chap. 13.10.

*{for the hay is withered away*} Or, *the grass is withered*; as the word is usually rendered, Job 40.15. Psal. 104.14. & 147.8. Chap. 37.27. & 40.6, 8. otherwise *grass withered*, in an ordinary course, makes *hay*, and that is nothing amiss.

*{the grass faileth, there is no green thing*} Or, *the herbage* (that properly that is newly sprung up, and sprouted out of the ground, the tender sprout, Gen. 1.11, 12. Chap. 37.27. and 66.14. Jer. 14.5.) *is gone*, or *consumed*, (as Chap. 16.4. & 24.13.) *the green herbage is not*. So Gen. 1.30. and 9.3. the meaning is, the pastures, as utterly spoiled, either eaten up with the enemies' horse, or trampled on, and stamped down with their feet, and so beaten into the soil and mire, made of that which grew on them, that there is nothing green to be seen. See ch. 1.7. Ezek. 34.18.

**V. 7.** *{Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away to the brook of the willows*} Or, *Because* (as containing another cause of their outcry) *the abundance* which (the relative wanting should be supplied; as Gen. 42.28. Exod. 13.8.) Or, *the residue* of what (as Deut. 3.13.) *they have gotten*, (Heb. *made*, as Gen. 31.1. Deut. 8.18.) *and their wealth*, (so called, because the owner is as *master* of it, Jer. 20.1.) or, *their treasure* (so termed, as by the Greeks also, because wont to be laid up, Gen. 41.36.) *shall be carried away*; or, *is carried away*; (as ver. 5.) &c. This some understand of the Moabites themselves, who, either because the waters of Nimrim were dried up, and no pasture there to be had for their cattle, should drive them away, to seek water and pasture for them; about some *willow brook*, elsewhere. Or, as others, should for fear of the enemy, carry away the best of their substance, and of their treasure, so much as they well could, or so much as was left of it, to hide it in some low place by the *brookside*, yea, or in the *brooks*; such of it, as might without damage, or detriment, be there bestowed, in hope afterward to recover it again. But others rather understand it of the enemy, that should seize upon their wealth, and carry it all away, which is here brought in, as one cause of their lamentations, and outcries: as before the spoil of their soil; so now the loss of their wealth. And is spoken of, as a thing in doing, or done. This to be the true sense of the place, appears by that of Jeremy, parallel hereunto, Jer. 48.36. *Because the riches that he hath gotten, are perished*. See chap. 16.8. Howbeit, one of the Rabbins, in whose steps the old Latin treads, renders the words to this purpose, *According to that which Moab hath done, shall their visitation* (as Psal. 89.32.) or, *retribution, also be*. And so runs out into a large discourse of the manifold kindnesses, that Abraham showed Lot, and the unkind dealing of his issue, the Moabites, and Ammonites, with Abraham's posterity, for which they were deservedly thus to be destroyed. See Jer. 48.26, 27. & 49.1. But the genuine sense was given before.

*{to the brook of the willows*} So is the word used, Levit. 23.40. chap. 44.4. that is, say some of the Jewish commenters, and of ours after them, to Babylon; and so, those that expound the former part of the verse, of a retribution, expound this latter, *they shall carry them* (to wit, the Moabites) *unto Babylon*; because they find mention of *willows* growing by the waterside there, Psal. 137.1, 2. as if willows grew nowhere else besides brooks, but at Babylon only: besides, that, it appears not, that this prophecy intends any carrying at all to Babylon. Others understand it, of some *brook*, in the land of Moab, where the Moabites should hide their wealth, or whither the enemy should carry it, there to share it. But the words may as well be read, *unto the vale of the Arabians*: of whom, Chap. 13.20. either by the Arabians themselves, serving under the Assyrians; or, by the Assyrians sending them thither beforehand (for some part of Arabia bordered upon the Moabites' country) thence to convey them afterward into Assyria. See chap. 16.8.

**V. 8.** *{For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab*} Or, *Because*: as ver. 7. Heb. *border*; but taken collectively: as Judg. 11.22. This appears by the particular recital of the places, these especially here added to them, ver. 4, 5. *Heshbon*, being situate on the northeast side of that country; *Elealeh*, on the northwest; *Jahaz*, on the southwest; *Horonaim*, as some say, farthest east; and *Zoar*, the utmost west.

*{the howling thereof unto Eglaim*} Heb. *her howling*: to wit, Moab's: as *her fugitives* ver. 5. or, *the howling of it*: that is, of the cry: *and howling cry*: and so in the next clause: See Jer. 48.20.

*{unto Eglaim*} This most interpreters, Jew, and Christian, take for the proper name of a place: and the Rabbins affirm it to be a boundary town of Moab: but on which side, they say not. The word is nowhere else found. Yet some late writers of note take it, for a common term: and will have it to signify such places, where there is *a confluence* of divers streams: because the word *Egel*, Job 38.28. (where alone it is extant) signifies *a drop*, and they suppose it, to signify, those *watery places*, that were near upon the confluence of the *brooks*, or *streams of* the river *Arnon*, Numb. 21.14. which is there said, v. 13. to be *the border of Moab*, dividing them and the Amorites, who lay easterly from them, ver. 11. and it is not unlikely, that the place had its name from the springiness of the grounds thereabouts. To this nature of the Moabitish soil, the Psalmist seems to have an eye, Psal. 60.8. where he calls *Moab*, not his *washpot*; but his *washing pot*: his pot, or basin, to wash his feet in

*{and the howling thereof unto Beer-elim*} The word *Beer*, which signifies *a well*, some take here, for a common, or general term; and so render the words *the well of Elim*, as if *Elim*, not *Beer-elim*, were the name of the place; and of that name indeed, we have a place, in the Israelites' journeying from Egypt, Exod. 15.27. & 16.1. Num. 33.9, 10. but that cannot be the place here mentioned. It seems rather, that *Beer* here is part of the name of the place, for which also it is put alone, Num. 21.16. and may seem to have been called *Beer-elim*, that is, *The well of the mighty ones*: because it is said, *The princes* (who are so termed, Exod. 15.15. Ps. 29.1.) *digged it*, Num. 21.18. This *Beer-elim* seems to have been not far from some part of *Arnon*, Num. 21.13, 16. between which river, on the one side, and Jordan on the other lay the greatest part of the Moabites' country. See Num. 21.13. compared with Num. 33.48. & 35.1. though some parts, it seems, they were at this time possessed of, also beyond Jordan, as *Zoar*, ver. 5. Of which, see Deut. 34.3.

**V. 9.** *{For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood*} Or, *Because they are full*, or, *are filled with blood*: (as before, ver. 6, 8.) to wit, the blood of men slain by the enemy. See ver. 6. So Chap. 34.3, 6, 7. Jer. 46.10. Ezek. 32.6. This seems to be here specified, as one cause of this general outcry, that ran to and fro, from place to place; because the waters that came down from the place here mentioned, being dyed blood, showed how it went with them there.

*{Dimon*} The Jewish doctors tell us, that this Dimon is a river in the land of Moab: and that stream, say some, that appeared like blood to the Moabites, in the expedition of the three kings, against Moab, and was after indeed so dyed with their blood. 2 King. 3.22, 24. whence they imagine, that it was afterward so called. But it may well be questioned, whether any such stream continued there, after that extraordinary flood, by the prophet's prayer, at that time, in that their extreme necessity procured. Some again of ours say, that it is not a river, but a city, that belonged sometime to the Gadites. But we find elsewhere in Scripture none of that name. Others therefore lastly, suppose it, to be no other than that Dibon mentioned before, ver. 2. but by the prophet here so termed, with change of a letter, not Dibon, but Dimon: (as Merodach, for Berodach, Ch. 31.1.) in regard of the abundance of blood, that should be shed in it: and the streams about it, or near unto it, should flow with, a new name, is upon a new occasion given it: as Gen. 17.5, 15. & 25.30. & 32.28. Judg. 6.32. Ruth 1.10.

*{for*} Or, *moreover*: as ch. 16.8.

*{I will bring more upon Dimon*} This is spoken, as in the person of God. *I will bring*, says he, *more*. Heb. *additions*, or, *things added*: that is (says one of the Rabbins well) evils added, a defect of the subject as Prov. 18.23. *the rich answereth*, or gives out, *rough*, or *harsh things*, that is, *rough*, or *harsh words*. The meaning is, I will inflict more, and more evils upon them. See ch. 1.5. Though others, both of them, and ours, refer it to what was before said of blood, that the river should abound with blood, that should be *added* to the waters thereof, in great abundance running in, on either side of it; and that the word is plural, in regard of the several streams, that should run divers ways, not tainted with blood, only, but swelling with it: or, in reference to the story above mentioned, that he would make those rivers to run with blood, more abundantly, than at that time; and yet again with much more, than hitherto they had done. But I suppose rather, that by *additions* of evils, is here meant, more than had been before mentioned; to wit, the spoiling of their pastures, and the plundering of their goods, ver. 6, 7. even the slaughter of their inhabitants, partly, by the sword of the enemy; and partly also, by wild beasts that shall be sent in upon them: and it may be, that Moab itself, in the next clause mentioned, is here termed *Dimon*, that is, *bloody*, in allusion to the name of *Dibon*, one of her chief cities: as if it were said, all *Moab* shall be, as one *Dibon*, or *Dimon*, rather. It shall in all her streams run with blood; as Jerusalem is called *Ariel*, because it should be as one *Ariel*, or *altar*; in regard of the general slaughter, that should be in all parts of it. Ch. 29.1, 2. See of Edom, Chap. 34.5–7.

*{lions upon him, that escapeth of Moab*} Heb. *upon the escaping* or, *escape* (as Chap. 10.20.) *of Moab a lion*: that which some of the Jewish writers understand of Nebuchadnezzar, compared to *a lion*, Jer. 4.7. who should destroy whatsoever had escaped Sennacherib. But the word, *lion*, seems rather, as some of them also observe, to be taken collectively, for *lions*: as chap. 30.6. Jer. 5.6. Nah. 2.11, 12. put here for ravenous beasts in general, such as are wont to prey upon men, ch. 35.9. 2 King. 17.25. The meaning is, their land being much of it wasted, and desolate, God would cause wild beasts to abound in it, that should destroy many of those that had escaped the sword of the enemy, Exod. 23.29. Levit. 26.22. So that they should be no way able to escape God's hand; but he would meet with them, either in one kind or another, and by variety of judgments, execute his indignation upon them, Chap. 24.17, 18. Jer. 46.43, 44. Amos 5.9. & 9.1.

*{and upon the remnant of the land*} To wit, of Moab: the same (says one of the Rabbins well) in effect, though in other terms, with the former. For why another of them should say, *the remnant of Israel in their land*; I know not.

### CHAPTER 16

**V. 1.** *{Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land*} This chapter ought to be joined unto the former; as in some versions it is, because they make up but one prophecy, and that no long one, of one and the same subject, concerning Moab; who in the former part of it, is admonished; what course she should, and might have taken, for the aversion and prevention of the judgments here denounced against her, to wit, by paying their tribute duly to the king of Judah, and performing kind offices unto God's people, in the times, especially, of their distress, ver. 3, 4. both which things, because they had not only failed in, but had carried themselves haughtily and harshly, toward those, unto whom they ought to have performed such offices, ver. 6. they are further again menaced with the judgments before mentioned, ver. 7–13. and a certain time set for the execution of the same, ver. 14.

*{Send the lamb to the ruler of the land*} Or, *Send a lamb the ruler of the earth*: as the old Latin, and those that follow it, expounding it of Christ, that came from Ruth the Moabitess, Matth. 1.5. or, *Send the lamb of the ruler of the land*, or, *the earth*: which seems to suit best with the original. The great variety of expositions, that both Jews, and Christians, give of the words, were too long to relate, and lost labor to refute, they being many of them so absurd. I will pick out of them therefore one, or two only, that seem most probable; and pitch upon that, I deem most proper. Some therefore of prime note expound the words, as if the prophet should advise, or admonish the Moabites, to send *lambs* and the like, for sacrifice to God, the ruler of the whole world, 1 Chr. 29.12. as heathen princes sometime did, Ezr. 6.8–10. & 7.15–23. to make their peace, if they may, with him. Which some of them conceive to be spoken seriously, as exhorting them, to come in to God, submit to him, acknowledge him, by sacrificing to him, to be the only true God who is able to protect, and save them: as Chap. 11.12. which their idols cannot do, ver. 12. Others, as in way of derision, as if, do it, he might, but it should be to small purpose, to seek now to him, whom he had so despised, and despited before; and who had now passed an irrecoverable doom of destruction upon him. So it should be like that, Mal. 1.9. But the genuine sense seems rather to be that, which the sounder sort of the Rabbins have; and divers of ours also admit: that the Moabites are called upon, to pay that tribute to Ezekiah, which was due from them, to the kings of Judah. David had conquered Moab, slain a great part of them, made the rest of them tributary, 2 Sam. 8.2. this tribute, because they abounded in sheep, and goats, was paid in such cattle: but after the rent made in the state, upon Solomon's decease, the kings of Israel got this yearly pension into their hands, and enjoyed it quietly, without refusal, unto Ahab's decease; after whose death, they denied it to Ahaziah, and to Joram his sons, 2 King. 1.1. & 3.4, 5. The prophet therefore here minds them, of their duty herein, and wills them to send *the ruler's lamb*, that is, the present, or tribute due to him, as the lord of the soil, to whom of right it belonged, being of David's posterity, consisting in *lambs*, with *rams*, and *goats*. That which some add, that they are admonished now so to do, because there was no king of Israel now to receive it, Samaria being taken by Salmaneser, and that kingdom dissolved, 2 King. 18.9, 10. is not so certain; but that more unlikely, that the prophet's words should be spoken in way of derision, and insultation over them, after their destruction, and the desolation of their land: as if he had said, you refused before to pay your wonted tribute, consisting of so many thousand sheep, *send now*, if you can, but *a lamb* only, as implying, that they had scarce a *lamb* then left them, of such numerous flocks, as they were late possessed of. But *lamb*, is here put collectively, for *lambs*, as *lion*, for *lions*, ch. 15.9. and *lambs* here, for such cattle, as their tribute consisted of: as *lions* there, for such beasts, as are wont to kill and devour men. I am not ignorant that one of the Jewish great masters would have the word, *car*, here to signify *a swift beast* of the *camel* kind; pointing us to a place, 2 King. 11.4, 19. where the words are, *the carim and the runners*, which we render, *the captains and the guard*: as if the meaning were, that they should send in posthaste. See more hereof, on chap. 66.20. wherein, howsoever I suppose he be far wide, as well for the one place as the other, yet he gives a hint of that, which to me seems to minister an occasion of some doubt, whether the word *car* and *carim*, might not better be rendered both here and elsewhere, *ram* and *rams*, than *lamb* and *lambs*. My reason is, because by *carim*, *chieftains* and great ones, soldiers, and men of might at least, are commonly resembled by such; so styled, Chap. 34.6. Jer. 51.40. Ezek. 39.10. besides that, the word *carim*, is itself used for *captains* and *leaders*, such as are *rams* in the flock; as in that place of the Kings, and for those engines of battery, which both Greeks, and Latins call *rams*, Ezek. 4.2. & 21.22. yea so the old Latin renders the word *rams*, 1 Sam. 15.9. and some late interpreters of prime note, *leaders of the flock*. All that can be objected against this, is, that *elim* is used commonly for *rams*, and that *elim* and *carim*, are sometime found mentioned together, as Ezek. 39.18. & 2 King. 3.4. But hereunto may be answered, that in like manner *sheirim* and *athudim* are both used for *he-goats*, and yet there seems some distinction between them, and the latter, to be the *leaders*. See chap. 14.9. & Jer. 50.8. and the *carim* to be among the sheep, as the *athudim* among the goats. Besides that in the history which this relates unto, it is said *carim*, so many simply, (which some render *fat wethers*) *and elim with wool* so many. But this I shall submit to the judgment of the learned.

*{from Sela in the wilderness*} The Hebrew word signifies *a rock* or, *a fortress*, Num. 20.8, 10. Chap. 31.9. It seems here to be the proper name of a place, (as is *Petra*, sometime, both with Greeks and Latins, and so some here render it,) situate in the confines of Moab, and Edom, mentioned, as then in the possession of the Edomites, in Amaziah's time, and by him taken, and the name changed unto *Joktheel*, (of which name we find a city, anciently so called, in Judah's lot, Josh. 15.38.) annexed to the crown of Judah; but in aftertimes, it seems, gained unto Moab; and by them, at the time of this prophecy, possessed. Some say it was the head city of Moab; and is said here to stand on that part of the land, that overlooked *the wilderness of Moab*, Num. 21.11. Deut. 2.8. Others say, that it was the head city of Edom: and suppose that here is intimated, the full extent of the whole country of Moab: *from Sela* (the south end, to Edom-ward) *unto the wilderness*, (for so they render the words of the text) to wit, of Jordan: the north end to Judea-ward: as if he had said: Send all of you, out of all parts of the country, from the one end of your land to the other. I incline to the former, though I doubt whether *Sela* were the head city of either. See *Ar*, ch. 15.1.

*{to the mount of the daughter of Zion*} To Jerusalem: where God's seat was in his temple, and the king's in his palace, See ch. 1.8. & 2.2. & 10.32. & 14.13.

**V. 2.** *{For it shall be, that as a wandering bird, cast out of the nest; so the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon*} In these words the prophet foretells them, what will befall them, if they shall not follow the advice before given them, ver. 1. but persist in their rebellion, and refusal to come in: and the things menaced are two especially, confusion, and deportation. The words may be rendered; *Else it shall be, that as a wandering bird, as a nest forsaken; the daughters of Moab, shall be at the passages of Arnon*. Or, as some thus, *Or else Moab shall be as a wandering bird, as a nest dismissed; and the daughters of Moab shall be at the passages of Arnon*.

*{For*} Heb. *And*. As chap. 13.8. or, *Or*; as Gen. 2.6. Judg. 11.31. that is, *else*, *otherwise*: as some well render it here.

*{it shall be, that*} As chap. 7.21. & 11.11. or *Moab shall be*: as chap. 13.14. *Babylon shall be*.

*{as a wandering bird*} Prov. 27.8. that being driven from her nest, has no place to repair to. See of Babylon, ch. 13.14. of Ammon, Jer. 49.5.

*{cast out of the nest*} Or as *a nest* (that is, *a brood*, or *young ones* in a nest: as Deut. 32.11. Luk. 13.34.) *forsaken*, (as chap. 27.10. to wit, by their dam: having none to protect them) or *driven out*: or, *cast out*: as Exod. 12.33. 1 King. 9.7. See chap. 10.14. And there is in the Hebrew, an elegant allusion to the word of *sending*, ver. 1. as if he had said, Send away your lamb: or else yourselves shall be like *birds sent out* of their *nest*, expelled, and driven from the places of your present abode, Job 29.18.

*{So the daughters of Moab*} As, *the daughters of Zion*, chap. 3.16, 16, 17. and *the daughters of Jerusalem*, Luk. 23.28. that is, the Moabitish women: or, as some more generally, the promiscuous multitude of that people. The Jewish doctors understand it of the villages, or lesser towns, that are as *daughters*, to the mother cities: and are in Scripture commonly so styled, Num. 21.26, 33. & 32.42. But this suits not so well with the tenure of the text: unless we will say, that the people of Moab shall be *as wandering birds*: and her towns *as a nest forsaken*. But then, why not the great ones, as well, as the less? Of which, chap. 15.1, 2.

*{at the fords of Arnon*} Or, *passages* (as Josh. 2.7.) *of Arnon*, which bounded their country on the one side, Num. 21.13. there shall they be, either flying from the enemy, out of their land, towards the wilderness, Num. 21.13. or by the enemy carried captive, beyond the bounds of their country, See v. 8. and ch. 15.7.

**V. 3.** *{Take counsel, &c.*} The second branch of wholesome advice given the Moabites, for preventing of the judgments denounced against them: the sedulous performance of kind offices to God's people, in the time of their distresses, wherein they had been much failing, and faulty before, Deut. 23.3, 4. implying, that had they been careful so to have done, they should not have been now, in the like straits themselves.

*{Take counsel, execute judgment*} Or, *call a council*, (Heb. *make a council to come*: cause a council to meet, bring them together: as Ps. 2.2.) *and make a decree*, resolve upon a course to be accordingly taken, and put in execution: as chap. 28.7. So Psal. 106.30. Or, as some, deal equally, and uprightly, show the likeness of Abraham's posterity, as he did to Lot your ancestor.

*{make thy shadow as the night, in the midst of noonday*} Or, *at noonday*: as chap. 6.12. or, *noontide*, Jer. 20.16. *at high noon*, as we use to say. It is a proverbial kind of speech, as one of the Jewish writers well observes: whereby God, or men, are said *to make midnight, at*, or, *of, noonday*: as on the other side, God is said *to make noonday, of midnight*, Psal. 37.6. with 112.4. & 139.11, 12. Of some other uses hereof, see chap. 59.10. Amos 8.9. Here it is applied to protection, shelter, refreshment, concealment. The violent, and eager persecution of the enemy, is compared to the heat of the sun, at noonday, that is very grievous to a traveler, or wayfaring man, where no shade, or shelter is to be had, Psal. 121.6. Jon. 4.8. Rev. 7.16. the Jewish people fleeing from it, to such travelers, so distressed: the relief that Moab should have afforded them, to a shade: which is used in Scripture commonly, for protection, shelter, refreshment, concealment, Judg. 9.15. Job 32.22. Psal. 17.8. & 91.1. chap. 30.2, 3. & 32.2. and the night, being no other than the shadow of the earth interposed between us and the sun: and midnight consequently, the depth of that darkness, caused by the interposition of so vast a body, as the earth is: hence it comes to pass, that the closest concealment, and the most copious refreshment is here resembled by the making of high noon, as midnight. So that it is, as if the prophet had said, after serious consultation, resolve upon some course, whereby you may afford what shelter you are able, both for safety, and secrecy, to the distressed Israelites; be both a secure refuge to them, and a comfortable refreshing, See Obad. 14.

*{hide the outcasts, bewray not him that wandereth*} Or, *the wanderer* but collectively; taken as appears by the former word, being plural. The same in plainer terms that was before spoken. Harbor, and hide those that are driven from their places of abode, and constrained to wander: lest you yourselves undergo the like calamity, v. 2. Luk. 6.38.

**V. 4.** *{Let mine outcasts*} *The outcasts of Israel*, Psal. 147.2. Chap. 11.12. & 56.8. For it is spoken in the person, not of the prophet, but of God requiring this office, as of duty, in behalf of his people. The outcasts of my people, whom he owns yet as his; though he had caused them to be driven out of their land, for sins, and excesses, Ezek. 11.16. For I suppose not, (as some do) that to be the reason, why he here terms them his outcasts, as being cast out by him, but as whom, though cast out so, yet he accounted, and acknowledged still, as his. See chap. 52.5, 6.

*{dwell with thee*} Or, *sojourn with thee*. As Ruth 1.1. 2 King. 8.1, 2. Harbor them for a while.

*{Moab be thou a covert to them, from the face of the spoiler*} A metaphor, from such places of *covert*, as beasts use to retire and repair to, when they are hunted, and pursued, So Psalm 27.5. & 32.7. & 91.1. chap. 4.6. & 32.2. But who *the spoiler* here spoken of should be, or, when this office was to have been performed by them, is much questioned. See the next clause; and v. 14.

*{for the extortioner*} Heb. *the milker*, or *sucker*, or *wringer out*, Prov. 30.33. It is used of the wringing out of *milk*, by milking, or, sucking. Chap. 60.16. & 66.11. of *blood*, when it is not let out barely, but pressed, and crushed out, Levit. 1.15. & 5.9. of *water*, when it is not suffered to drop, or run out of a cloth, or fleece; but is *wrung out*; by some force used to it, Judg. 6.38. Of *drink* when not only the liquor, or thinner part of it, or what comes away of itself, is drunk off; but the lees, or thicker part of it, or whatsoever remains behind is *sucked* out, and so fetched out, that not a drop, as near as may be, is of aught left, which we usually call *a wringing of the pot*, or *cup*, Psalm 73.10. & 75.8. chap. 51.17. Ezek. 23.34. and it fitly expresses the nature and practice of an oppressing tyrant, that sucks and wrings from the people, over whom he tyrannizes; not the milk only of their substance, but the blood of their bodies; and leaves nothing unto them, whereby to subsist. See chap. 3.14, 15.

*{is at an end*} Or, *is brought to nought*: as ch. 29.20. or, *shall be no more*, chap. 33.1.

*{the spoiler*} One of the Hebrew doctors makes this word, not in common sense only, but in proper signification also, the same with the former; because the word is used sometime for *a pap*, or, *a teat*, Job 24.9. Ch. 60.16. but there is no place produced where it signifies *a sucker*, or *wringer*, as the former; but it is used commonly for *a plunderer*, *waster*, or, *spoiler*, Amos 5.9. and for *plunder*, *waste*, or, *spoil*, ch. 13.5. & 22.4. & 59.7.

*{ceaseth*} Or, *is consumed*, *is spent*, *is clean gone*, as Job 7.9. Psalm 73.26. Chapter 15.6. and 24.13. or, *shall be clean gone*, as before.

*{the oppressors*} Heb. *treader down*, or, *trampler upon*, for the word is singular, as the former, but taken collectively; and the verb therefore plural: or distributively, as if he had said, each one of them, chap. 26.19. a fit expression, to denote a cruel tyrant, as one that treads men under feet without mercy, Dan. 8.7, 10. Lam. 3.34. or that spoils and makes havoc of that which he cannot carry away or make use of; like beasts, that kill more than they are able to devour, Dan. 7.7. Mic. 5.8. See chap. 15.6. Howbeit a Jewish commenter, because the word also signifies *a creeper*, or *a worm*, Gen. 1.26, 30. Psal. 69.34. would have hereby meant *beasts*, or noxious and harmful creatures, which are sent oft in judgment upon a land; See chap. 15.9. but whether he mean properly, or metaphorically so taken, he tells us not. Such are tyrants and oppressors oft compared to in Scripture, Prov. 28.15. Ezek. 22.27. Zeph. 3.3. but the former sense seems the more natural.

*{are consumed out of the land*} As Psal. 104.35. or *they shall be utterly consumed*, there shall be an utter riddance of them *out of the land*, to wit, out of Judah, the land that God's people possessed. For it is commonly conceived, that the scope of the prophet here, is, to let the Moabites know, that neither the calamities and distresses of God's people, in regard whereof, the offices before mentioned are in their behalf required of them, shall last long, nor the performance of them, consequently, be overburdensome unto them: for that Sennacherib with his forces (who by the terms here mentioned is of the most deemed to be described) should not make any long stay with them, but should be suddenly sent away, and not one of his vast army left any more to molest them, or to restrain them from returning into their own country again, chapter 37.36, 37. But see further hereof, on verse 14.

**V. 5.** *{And in mercy shall the throne be established*} This is added, to assure the Moabites, that though the Jewish state might seem much impaired and weakened, by means of those calamities before intimated, yet it should be restored to its former strength, and luster again, either by the coming in of Ezekiah, after his father's decease, chap. 14.19. 2 Kings 18.7. or, by the settling of the estate again, after Sennacherib's overthrow, chap. 33.17. & 37.31. & 38.6. and Moab therefore might do well, to afford them this kindness, that he might expect the like favor again, at their hands.

*{the throne*} That is, *the kingdom*, as Psalm 45.6. with Psal. 145.13. to wit, of Judah, or Israel, 2 Sam. 3.10. called the *throne of David*, Chap. 9.7. Jer. 17.25. *God's throne*, 1 Chron. 29.23. as both settled by him, Psalm 2.6. and a type of his, Dan. 7.24, 27. Mic. 4.7. Luk. 1.33.

*{shall be established*} Or, *settled*, and restored again to its former strength and luster. See chapter 2.2. 2 Sam. 7.13. 2 Chr. 32.22, 23.

*{in mercy*} Or, *benignity*, or, *bounty*, Prov. 19.22. & 20.6. which some refer to God; by *mercy*, as it is rendered here, understanding God's free favor, and goodness; as Psal. 89.33. Chap. 54.8. Others to Ezekiah, understanding by it, his kind, and benign carriage, (opposed here to the cruel courses of oppressors, and tyrants) in relieving, and righting the poor oppressed, Psal. 72.3, 6, 7, 12, 14. Prov. 16.22. & 20.28. & 29.14. Dan. 4.27.

*{and he shall sit upon it*} Or *one shall sit upon it*: as chap. 8.21. & 14.30. a ruler shall not be wanting to it, Psal. 132.11. Jer. 33.25, 26. Ezekiah a type of Christ, for a time, ch. 32.1. Christ himself, forever, Luk. 1.33.

*{in truth*} That is, *firmly*, *surely*, as having reference to the establishment of the throne mentioned. So Prov. 11.18. *a reward of truth*, for *a sure reward*: and *a retribution in truth*, for *a sure*, and *certain retribution*. Chap. 61.8. or, *constantly*: as respecting the due, and daily administration of justice, a principal means of procuring that establishment, Jer. 22.1–4. So Prov. 29.14. *A king, that in truth*, that is, *constantly judgeth the poor; his throne shall be established for ever*.

*{in the tabernacle of David*} In the house, or palace of David; a type of the church, Amos 9.11. compared to *a tent*, or *tabernacle*, as a place, that people retire to, for shelter, against storm of rain, or heat of sun, Psalm 31.20. Chap. 4.5, 6. and such ought all courts of judicature to be, chap. 32.2. though oftentimes, through man's corruption, they prove nothing less unto those that repair to them for relief, Eccl. 3.16.

*{judging*} Or, as some render it, *who shall judge*: and so after, *who shall seek*, and *hasten*, *judging*, that is, hearing causes, and deciding them; the special office of rulers, in regard of their own people, from thence styled *judges*, Deut. 16.18. Judg. 4.4, 5. Act. 13.20. and so also, some here render it *a judge*. Howbeit, *to sit judging*, seems here to be mentioned as a note of peaceable times. The ordinary course of judiciary proceedings, being in times of war, and public disturbance, usually interrupted, and obstructed. So of David, 1 Chr. 18.14.

*{and seeking judgment*} Or, *procuring*: as Esth. 10.3. *procuring his people's good*: or, as some of the Hebrew doctors, not doing justice only to such poor, or other, that appear before him, to crave it, but making inquiry also after such wrongs, as are committed, but concealed and smothered, because the oppressed dare not come to complain, for fear of the power and greatness of those that wrong them; that unto such also he may do justice. See Neh. 13.10, 11. So God is said *to make inquisition for murder*, to avenge it, whether it be complained of to him, or no, Psalm 9.12. See chapter 1.17.

*{and hastening justice*} Dispatching and dispeeding causes, without needless delays, and hastening the execution of it. So *a ready scribe*, Ezr. 7.6. and *a quick*, or *a speedy writer*, Psal. 45.1. or, as some, *sedulous*, or *diligent*, in the administration of justice: as the word is rendered, Prov. 22.29. but that seems implied in the former branch. See of David, Psal. 75.2. & 101.8. A late learned annotator would have it rendered, both here, and in those other places, *skillful*, because the modern Syrians so use the word. But I see, as yet, no necessity of receding from the received version, which suits well with the former member.

*{judgment and justice*} So of David, 2 Sam. 8.15. and of Solomon, Ps. 72.1, 2. See ch. 1.27.

**V. 6.** *{We have heard of the pride of Moab (he is very proud) even of his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath*} Some suppose these words spoken by the prophet, in the person of other people, as professing not to wonder at the destruction of Moab; his extreme pride, and haughtiness calling for it, and justly deserving no less. Others, as in the person of God, as implying, his taking notice of their insolent, and outrageous carriages against his people: and so understanding it, the words would be rendered; *We have heard*, or, *do hear* (*I know*, Jer. 48.30.) *Moab's pride—and his haughtiness, and his pride; and his wrath*, or, *both his pride, and his wrath*: as chap. 14.22. that is his rough, and wrathful carriage toward my people, proceeding from his pride: as intimating the contrary practice of Moab, to that, which he was advised unto, ver. 1, 3, 4. together with the ground of it, the pride of his heart; in regard whereof, he scorned to stoop so low, as to do either of the offices before mentioned, unto those, whom he so much disdained. Yea we find express mention of him, as an assistant to the Chaldees, in their expedition against Judah and Jerusalem, under Jehoiakim, 2 King. 24.2. See Jer. 48.27, 29, 30.

*{but his lies shall not be so*} Heb. *not so his lies*, as Job 11.3. (see chap. 44.25. Jer. 50.36.) or, *his devices* (from a word that signifies *to devise*, 1 King. 12.33. Neh. 6.8.) *not so*. An usual defective form, Gen. 48.18. Exod. 10.11. Num. 12.7. Prov. 15.7. Luk. 22.26. Eph. 4.20. The meaning is, for all his proud, and swelling thoughts, his vain counsels, false confidences, covert carriages, and cunning devices, shall not take such effect, as in the pride of his heart, he imagines. So Jer. 48.30. *not so his lies*, or, *vain devices, they shall not so* (that is according to what he conceives) *do* aught. The Jewish doctors' various interpretations of this clause, I let pass; because they seem too far-fetched, and forced. Only that forementioned late writer of note, renders it, *his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath, are not rightly his bars*, they are matters of no might, and in vain for him therefore to confide in them. The particle is used for *rightly*, Numb. 27.7. 2 King. 7.9. the noun for *bars*, Exod. 25.14. & 27.6. the strength of gates and cities, Psalm 147.13.

**V. 7.** *{Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab*} Or, *to Moab*; as Chap. 6.3. The Moabites shall howl one for another, or one to another, as implying a vicissitude of howling on every side. For so the next branch has it.

*{everyone shall howl*} Heb. *all of him* (to wit, of Moab) *shall howl*; a general howling there shall be. See chap. 13.2, 5, 8. Jer. 40.20. *Moab for Moab*, or, *to Moab*: as *Egypt against Egypt*, chap. 19.2. and *the Lord from the Lord*, Gen. 19.24. and *the Lord with the Lord*, 2 Tim. 1.18. See Jer. 48.31.

*{for the foundations of Kir-hareseth shall ye mourn*} Or, as some, *of the foundations of it, shall ye meditate*, or *talk*. A change of the person as ch. 1.29.

*{the foundations*} As Jer. 50.15. Ezra 4.12. intimating, that that goodly, and glorious city, was not to be sacked only, but utterly razed, unto the very foundations of it. As Ps. 137.7. that which alone, of all the ancient cities of Moab, had escaped in the expedition of the three kings against Moab, 2 King. 3.25. Howbeit, that learned late writer would have it rendered, *for the bottles of Kir-hareseth shall ye mourn*, because the word is so used, Hos. 3.1. and those other terms for *foundations*, he conceives to rise from another root: and the words following speak of *wines*, vers. 8.

*{Kir-hareseth*} Called also *Kir*, chap. 13.1. and *Kir-heres*, hereafter ver. 11. and signifies, in all likelihood, *the city of the sun*, (as by the Greeks, *On*, in Egypt, Gen. 41.50. is called *Heliopolis*, and *Beth-shemesh* among the Jews, 2 King. 14.11, 13. *the house*, or *the temple of the sun*, so named, by ancient idolatrous inhabitants) being so called because the *sun* was in a more special manner there worshiped. Some stately temple being therein erected unto it; which in Scripture is sometime by a foreign term (as some suppose) called, *Heres*, or, *Cheres*; or, *Hersah*, or, *Charisah*, Judg. 8.13. & 14.18. Job 9.7. Howbeit, some there are, that would have it so termed, from a word that signifies *an earthen pot*, or, *a potsherd*, Levit. 15.12. Job 2.8. Psal. 22.15. chap. 30.14. & 48.9. Jer. 19.1. & 32.14. in regard of a number of potters there resident, and of the curious earthenware, there made: or, because the walls of it were built of brick, hardened in the sun, as were the walls of Babel, Gen. 11.3. and of those cities, that the Hebrews built for Pharaoh in Egypt, Exod. 1.11, 14. because stone, in those low and moist places, was not so plentiful. But the former seems more probable. See chap. 19.18. and Jer. 15.2.

*{shall ye mourn*} Or, *mutter* in a mournful manner. See chap. 8.19. So chap. 38.14. & 59.11. Howbeit, some render it, *ye shall meditate*, entertain thoughts of that strong city, as a place for you, to retire unto, as a city of refuge; hoping that that strong piece had yet escaped, as formerly it did, 2 King. 3.25. and others *ye shall speak* of it, or *talk*, and say of it, as follows: and the word indeed, does very commonly import *meditation*, and *speech*, or *communication* from thence proceeding, Josh. 1.8. Psalm 1.2. & 35.28. & 37.30. chap. 33.18. & 59.13. But the reading that our translators, with other interpreters of good note, here agree in, seems most consonant to the prophet's purpose, and the word is, by him, more than once, elsewhere, so used. Yea, and so some of those, who first otherwise here expound it, render it, Jer. 48.31. a parallel place in effect.

*{surely they are stricken*} Or, as some, of those that maintain the latter exposition of the former, word, *but they are contrite*, or *destroyed*, as the words of the prophet, implying a frustration of their hopes, and expectation of any relief there; the very foundation of that city being utterly ruined. But we need not alter our version in that behalf. The particle is used for a note of asseveration, or, confirmation; *surely*, 2 Sam. 21.31. 1 Kings 11.21. Yet instead of *stricken*, I should rather render it, either *lamed*, (as the word is used of a lame person, 2 Sam. 4.4. & 9.3.) and unable therefore to sustain their superstructures; or, *broken*, or, *bruised*; or (if our English word of a wall of stonework, or brickwork, would bear it) *contrite*; as of man's spirit, or mind, it is rendered, chap. 66.2. instead whereof is used, ch. 57.15. *a spirit beaten*, or, *broken*, or, *ground to dust*, or *powder*. Some make them the words of the Moabites, speaking so of them. Others, of the prophet, importing the cause of their mourning so for that city. So some make, that understand the place of bottles; they are broken.

**V. 8.** *{For the, &c.*} Or, *Moreover*: or, *Also*: as chap. 15.9. & 32.13. For the prophet goes on in relating the grounds and causes of their mourning, to wit, not the razing of the cities, only; but the spoil, and waste of the whole land, and country about them: as 2 King. 3.19. ch. 1.7.

*{the fields*} Or, as some, *the vines*: because they suppose it so to be taken, and is by divers so rendered, Deut. 32.32. but thereof there is no necessity, either here, or there. By collation of places, it is justly deemed to signify *fields*, not lying waste, but managed; and either tilled for grain, or set with fruitful and useful plants. See 1 King. 23.4. Jer. 31.40. Hab. 3.17. in which last place, *fields* and *vines*, are distinct.

*{of Heshbon*} Of this city, see chap. 15.4. it seems from hence to have been seated in a fat, and fertile soil. See Cant. 7.4.

*{languish*} A metaphor taken from persons so overmastered, and quailed, through infirmity, or fear, that they are ready to *faint away*, with qualms, and feebleness of spirit, Josh. 4.3. Neh. 4.2. 1 Sam. 2.5. Psal. 6.2. chap. 19.8. and it is applied to plants, chap. 24.7. Joel 1.10. to lands, chap. 24.4. & 33.9. Nah. 1.4. when their goodly beauty, wealth, fruits, crop, and verdure, is all wasted, and gone; to towns, and cities, when decayed, and destroyed, Jer. 14.2. Lam. 2.8. the word here used is singular; though the word foregoing it, and conjoined with it, plural; to denote a general waste of their fields; as if he had said, *the fields*, each of them *languisheth*; the very same manner of construction is, Hab. 3.17.

*{and*} A defect of the copulative: as ch. 14.5. & 15.1. Hab. 3.11. or, it may be rendered; *as for the vine*, &c. as 1 Chr. 28.2.

*{the vine*} For *vines*: as Chap. 7.23. & 24.7. to wit, they do likewise languish. Howbeit, some by *vine*, or *vineyard*, understand here, the city itself; so termed in allusion to the vineyards round about it.

*{of Sibmah*} A city sometime taken from the Amorites, and repossessed by the Reubenites, Num. 32.38. unto whom also it was allotted, for part of their possession, 13.10. See the note on c. 15.2. it seems hence to have been a place of note, for special good wine, which the vineyards about it yielded.

*{the lords of the heathen*} Or, *of the nations*. The great commanders of the enemies' forces, whether Assyrians, or Chaldeans, and other their associates.

*{have broken down*} Or, *beaten down*: as Ps. 74.6.

*{principal plants thereof*} *her choicest plants*. Of the term here used, see on Chap. 5.2. & 19.9. they have utterly wasted it; for the meaning is not, that they had picked out the choice plants, and left the residue; but that her plants and vines were generally such; though there want not, that expound the words metaphorically, for the persons of note, and name, abiding in those parts. The whole sentence may well thus be rendered; *Those choice plants of the vine of Sibmah, have the lords of the nations broken down*. For the pronoun is commonly in such constructions, superfluous, save that the use of that language, as a kind of elegancy, admits it. So Gen. 2.17. & 18.13. & 45.9.

*{they are come even unto Jazer*} Or, *which reached*, (Heb. *touched*: as Jer. 48.32. & 51.9. Mic. 1.9.) *even unto Jazer*: a defect of the relative; as Gen. 39.4. Exod. 13.8. ch. 42.1. This some understand of the men led away into captivity, and of the wealth of the country carried away out of the land by the enemy, ch. 15.7. Others rather, of the large extent of the vines, and vineyards growing in those parts, reaching for many miles along, even unto *Jazer*, a town situate in the confines of Moab, deemed to be that belonging to the tribe of Dan, whereof mention is made, Josh. 21.39.

*{they wandered through the wilderness*} Or, *that*, (as before) or, *and* (as ch. 14.5, 6.) *wandered* (that is, winded to and fro; as in wandering to and fro, men are wont to do, until they reached) *to the wilderness*, to wit, of Moab, Deut. 2.8. ver. 1. A defect of the particle from the former branch to be supplied.

*{her branches were stretched out*} Or, *sent out abroad*. So is the verb used, Num. 11.32. Judg. 15.9. 1 Sam. 30.16. 2 Sam. 5.18, 22. Some render it, *plucked up*, or *plucked off*, and *dissipated*, broken, lopped, and scattered here and there: alleging, Chap. 33.23. to that purpose; whereof see there. But from the signification of *spreading*, or *stretching out*, comes the word, used by Jeremy, in this argument, Jer. 48.32. and answering that other word, used by the prophet here, and nowhere else in Scripture found, for *branches*, so termed, from *shooting out* here, as from *spreading out*, there. See Ezek. 17.6, 7.

*{they are gone over the sea*} That is, carried away beyond the sea. So most interpreters; supposing the meaning to be, that all the Moabites' wealth (which consisted most, say some of them, in their vines, and their wines, whereof they had great plenty) was carried away out of their country, together with a great part of their people, into a land, far remote from theirs. See chap. 15.7. But the words may well, and (as I suppose, with some other) might better be rendered; *they passed over to the sea*, (as chap. 8.8. & 10.28. Jer. 2.10.) that is, to *the dead sea*, the *lake of Sodom*; whereon Moab bordered. See chap. 15.5. or, *the sea of Jazer*; as it is, Jer. 48.32. which some make divers from this. See further hereof, on Jeremy. For they may well be deemed to shoot wide, who, by the *sea*, would have here understood, either the Assyrian river; or the Mediterranean Sea. Meanwhile, I incline to the latter interpretation of this passage; to wit, that not a far deportation of men's persons, or of their goods, and chattels; but a large propagation, and extension of branches, seems here to be delineated. See the very like to this, Ps. 80.9–12. and the very same; but contracted with this, Jer. 48.32. both relating the former flourishing condition of the places there mentioned, to move unto commiseration, and to make the lamentation, for their present desolation, the more grievous.

**V. 9.** *{Therefore I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer, the vine of Sibmah*} Of this see Chap. 15.5. and ver. 11. Among those that thus read and render the words, there is some doubt moved, what *the weeping of Jazer* should be. And some of them would hence gather, that Jazer was sacked, and ruined, before either Sibmah, or the rest, hereafter mentioned. And so the meaning should be, that he should lament the destruction of these latter, in the same manner as that other had been lamented before. But the words are, by others, diversely rendered. Some read them, *I will bewail the weeping of Jazer*: the weeping (supplied out of the former branch) *of the vine of Sibmah*. That is, I will bewail the miseries of them both; or, I will bewail them, as their inhabitants did, when either of them were destroyed. And some again, *I will bewail the weeping*, (that is, the calamity) *of Jazer, and the vine of Sibmah*. But these take no notice of the particle, which in these forms has his peculiar sense, and ought not to be disregarded. The words therefore, to avoid all ambiguity, would be thus rendered; *I will with weeping bewail* (that is, very grievously bewail; as chap. 15.5.) *Jazer and the vine of Sibmah*. And this reading, the points in the text confirm, which stay the voice at, *weeping*: (for the article answering, our *the*, is not here.) Of the defect of the copulative, see chap. 15.1, 2. and both of it, the places mentioned, and the occasion of mourning for them, see ver. 8. See also further hereof, on Jer. 48.32.

*{I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh*} I will pour down streams of tears upon you; as the Psalmist, *I water my couch with my tears*, Ps. 6.6. See also Ps. 119.136. Jer. 9.1. And there may be some allusion here unto the famous fishpools at Heshbon, mentioned, Cant. 7.4. as if he should say, she should not want his tears, to water her, though she had water otherwise in abundance. Both of it and of Elealeh, which it seems stood not far from it. See on ch. 15.4.

*{for the shouting for thy summer fruits, and for thy harvest is fallen*} Or, *over thy summer fruits, and over thy harvest*. Such singing and shouting, as those were wont to use, that did reap their corn in harvest, or did cut, and tread their grapes at vintage, either to pass the time with, while they were in work, or to encourage one another, unto work, ver. 10. Jer. 25.30. Or the shoutings, and acclamations, that in mirth and sport they used to make, at the bringing in, and housing of their corn, and fruits, their harvest and vintage, chap. 9.3. shall fail and cease; none such shall be, because no vintage, no harvest, no reaping, no cutting, no bringing in, or housing of aught; the enemy having spoiled, and made havoc of all, chap. 1.6. ver. 10. Howbeit, some understand it of the enemies' shout, and that way most of the Jewish writers go, rendering the words, *Because upon thy summer fruits, and upon thine harvest is a shout*, or *an alarm fallen*: that is, because the enemy with a shout, such as is commonly used for encouragement, in joining of fight in the field; or, in way of jollity and triumph, at the surprisal of some place, has suddenly fallen in upon your fields and vineyards, to make spoil and havoc of whatsoever is found in them. So is the word used, Jer. 51.14. See Jer. 48.32. where instead of *the shout*, it is said, *The spoiler is fallen upon thy summer fruits, and thy harvest*; which confirms the latter sense. And Amos 2.2.

*{summer fruits*} Heb. *summer*, Gen. 8.22. So 2 Sam. 16.1. as *harvest*, for *crop*: and so Chap. 17.11.

**V. 10.** *{And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field*} Heb. *And joy and gladness is gathered up out of the Carmel*. That joy and mirth, that in harvest time they had wont to have upon the return of a plentiful crop, after their foregoing labors, and pains taken in tilling their grounds, Ps. 4.7. & 125.5, 6. ch. 9.3. & 24.8. See Jer. 48.33.

*{is taken away*} Heb. *is gathered up*, or, *gathered in*, Chap. 11.12. & 10.14. & 17.5. & 62.9. But the word signifies also, *taken away*, Jer. 8.13. & 9.22. & 16.5. And it seems here used, with some glance, at the gathering of their harvest, and the mirth then expected; as if he had said, Your harvest, and your harvest mirth, is all gathered in, beforehand; for you it is all gone, ere you can come to gather it yourselves. See ch. 57.1.

*{plentiful field*} Heb. *Carmel*. See ch. 10.18.

*{and in the vineyards, there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting}* Or, *in the vineyard, shall be neither singing, nor shouting*. No merry note, nor joyful noise, (for such the words, here used import, ch. 12.6. Ezr. 3.11.) the matter, and occasion thereof, being gone.

*{the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses*} Heb. *treader*; (but collectively put for *treaders*; as Chap. 6.2.) *and the presses*; to wit, of the Moabites. They trod out, as at this day, their grapes, not in such presses, as we use now for cider and verjuice, with weights and screws; but in open vessels, or vats, with their feet, Judg. 9.27.
