Neh. 13.15. and the *treaders* (Job 24.11.) used to chant merrily, as they trod, when they tasted the sweet liquor, Jer. 25.30. and 48.33.

*{I have made their vintage shouting to cease*} Heb. *the shout*. I have stilled their merry shout, partly, by taking away the ground and cause of it; and partly, by sending in upon them a sad shout, in the room of it. See Jer. 48.33. Howbeit, some interpreters of note, understand this, as spoken in the person of the Moabites, forbidding any such *shout*, to be used, which they could not endure to hear. But this seems not so consonant to the parallel place in Jeremy, before cited, where it is conceived, as spoken by God. See Jer. 48.33, 35.

**V. 11.** *{Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab*} Out of tender pity and compassion to Moab, whose miseries are so great and grievous, that they may well move an utter enemy to commiserate his condition; I will make doleful lamentation, such as is wont to be made with mournful kinds of music over the dead laid out, and at burials, Jer. 9.17–20. Matth. 9.23. Or, my bowels, upon the very apprehension of it, as rolling together, tumble, and make a noise within me, as the strings of an harp sound, when they are struck with the finger of him that plays on it. So ch. 63.15. Lam. 1.20. Hos. 11.8. See ch. 15.5. ver. 9.

*{and my inward parts*} Heb. *the midst of me*. That is, *my heart*, Ps. 22.14. & 62.4. My heart is troubled for him. His misery, and calamity goes to the very heart, with me; and makes my heart beat within me; Ps. 38.11. Jer. 4.19. Lam. 1.20.

*{for Kir-haresh*} See ch. 15.1. ver. 7. All this would some have spoken in the person, not of the prophet himself, but of the Moabites, whose confidence was most, of any place, in *Kirheres*, which they saw now, with all the country about it, wasted and ruined. But the collation of this passage, with Jer. 48.36. seems to infer the contrary.

**V. 12.** *{And it shall come to pass when it is seen, that Moab is weary on the high place, that he shall come to his sanctuary to pray*} Or, *It shall come to pass*, (Heb. *it shall be*; as Chap. 14.3.) or, *it shall come to pass, that* (as chap. 10.20.) *though* (as Chap. 1.15.) *Moab present himself*, (Heb. *be seen*; as Chap. 1.12.) *though he tire himself on his high place, and come to his sanctuary to pray*. The courses are here described, that Moab should, or might in this his distress take, to get relief and succor, against the enemy invading him, by repairing to his high places, and idol temples, and tiring himself out in his superstitious services, and all to no purpose.

*{Moab*} Either the prince thereof, or the people, Chapter 15.2.

*{is weary*} Or, *tire himself*; as Chap. 47.13. Either with running to and fro, from place to place; or by multitudes of sacrifices offered one after another, as he did when he desired to have God's people cursed, Num. 22.39, 40, 41. & 23.2, 14, 27, 30.

*{on the high place*} Put collectively for *high places*. Or, some place peculiarly so termed; as Ezek. 20.29. See ch. 15.2.

*{his sanctuary*} Abusively so termed. The temple of his chief idol Chemosh, 1 King. 11.7. Jer. 48.46. which was to that idolatrous nation, as the tabernacle and temple were to God's people, Exod. 25.8. 2 Chr. 20.8. Ps. 78.69.

*{but he shall not prevail*} Heb. *and*; as Chap. 12.18. Or, *that*; (as Chap. 13.2.) or, *yet*; as Chap. 17.6. *He shall not prevail*. Heb. *He shall not be able*. But so the word is used, Num. 22.6, 11. Hos. 12.4. His god shall not be able to do him any good. Though we need not, as some, insert that into the text. For the pronoun here has reference to *Moab*, before expressly named, not to his idol, not mentioned. See Chap. 46.7. Jer. 48.13. As for that, which some would have here intended; that he should *not be able* to reach thither, the enemy either intercepting him, or having already surprised the place where his idol temple stood, seems not so well to accord with the rest of the context, whether of the two ways, before propounded, we read it.

**V. 13.** *{This is the word that the Lord hath spoken concerning Moab, since that time*} The conclusion of this sad sermon, or prophecy against Moab. Not unlike that, wherewith the burden of Babel is concluded and consigned, Chap. 14.26. intimating this doom, concerning the utter destruction of Moab, to be a doom irrecoverable, passed, formerly, with God, and revealed to the prophet: for the stronger confirmation whereof, there is somewhat further now added, ver. 14.

*{This*} That which I have delivered concerning the land, and state of Moab, hitherto related. See the like close, Jer. 48.47.

*{the word*} The *doom*, or *sentence*; as 2 King. 9.36. Jeremy renders it, *judgment*.

*{concerning Moab*} Or, *against Moab*, Heb. *unto*; as Jer. 48.1. & 49.1.

*{since that time*} Heb. *from then*. Or, *since then*; as Psal. 93.2. Prov. 8.23. chap. 44.8. & 48.3, 5. Now by this form of speech here, some conceive no certain time to be understood; and therefore render it, *before time*: *heretofore*: *of old*: or, *from eternity*. And so in some of the places pointed to, it seems to be taken. Others suppose that some certain time is thereby designed. Some the time present, and render it, *from this time*; as also the first words of the next verse, *even now*; as an exposition of this clause. But most, some time past: (as indeed, the constant and general use of the phrase, requires it) either the time when Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, Num. 22.5, 6. Or, the time when God enacted that law against the Moabites, inhibiting the receipt of them into communion with his people, Deut. 23.3, 4. Or when being subdued by David, they became tributary to the crown of Israel, 2 Sam. 8.2. or since their revolt from it, 2 King. 3.4, 5. or, when their destruction was foretold by Amos, in the reign of Uzziah, Amos 1.1. & 2.1–3. or lastly, from the time that this judgment, passed upon Moab, was first revealed to the prophet; that which follows, ver. 14. being afterward added thereunto. The like whereunto, see Jer. 36.32. And of all these, the last seems to me the most likely to be intended; though the words would be rendered, as they sound, indefinitely, *heretofore*, or, *sometime since*, without restriction, or limitation.

**V. 14.** *{But now the Lord hath spoken, saying*} The Lord has now added somewhat further, to what he had formerly denounced against Moab; to wit, concerning a foregoing judgment to be shortly inflicted upon him, before, and besides that utter destruction, before mentioned; together with the time prefixed, and limited, for the execution of the same.

*{within three years*} About these three years, there is much dissension among interpreters. Some would have the words read, not *within three years*; but *in*, or, *for three years*. Expounding them, not, as setting a time, at which this misery of Moab should begin, or from whence it should commence; but importing only, whensoever it began, how long it should continue. That it should not last long, as Babel's, before, Chap. 13.19–22. it should not exceed a *three years* term. But this interpretation, has but few followers: and other places, parallel to this, as Chap. 7.8. & 21.16. (though a little difference there be in the particles used there, and here) carry it, rather, the other way, to wit, as designing a certain time, when this calamity should befall Moab. But among those also, that go this way, there is no small difference about the time therein designed. For some would have *the three years*, to commence from the destruction of Jerusalem, by Nebuchadnezzar, 2 King. 25.4–10. Their reasons are these: First, Esay and Jeremy, prophesy of one and the same destruction of Moab; for Jeremy uses many words and sentences, the very same with Esay. Secondly, Jeremy says that Moab had not been stirred to any purpose nor captived till then, Jer. 48.11. Thirdly, Josephus relates, in his *Antiquities*, lib. 10. cap. 11. That *three year* after the destruction of Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar invaded the Moabites. But to this it may be answered: First, that though Esay, and Jeremy, use many the same terms, and that of the devastation of one and the same land; yet it follows not necessarily thence, that they speak of the same time; yea, or the same particular destruction: in the book of the Revelations are many forms and expressions borrowed from the writings of the ancient prophets, yet applied unto the stories of other times, than those whereof those former prophets spoke. Secondly, it appears that Moab had been dispossessed of much of his land; not only before the times that Jeremy points at; but long before the times that Esay lived in: See Num. 21.26–30. Jeremy's words imply only, that he had been long at rest, before the overthrow then denounced; nor had endured, and undergone such a general deportation, as either the ten tribes, or the other two of God's people had done. Thirdly, Josephus says not, that *three year*, but that *five year*, after the fall of Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar invaded Coelosyria, and after that subdued, set upon the Moabites, and Ammonites, and made a conquest also of them. And lastly, (though it were granted, as I suppose it well may be) that the foregoing prophecy of Moab's utter devastation, was by Nebuchadnezzar to be accomplished; yet could it not be necessarily thence inferred, that the *three years*, here mentioned, might not commence from a nearer term, than the times of Nebuchadnezzar. There is no necessity therefore of drawing the period of these *three years*, so low: nor is there aught to countenance such a vast divulsion of them, from the time of the delivery of this prophecy. Whereunto other, with better ground of reason, reduce them; though they also are at much disagreement among themselves. For some would have them to commence from the first year of Ezekiah; supposing this prophecy to be of the same date, with the next before it, denounced against the Philistines, Chap. 14.28. and that Salmaneser in the fourth year of Ezekiah, when he came to besiege Samaria, 2 King. 18.9. took the Moabites' land in his way. But this seems not so well to sort with the advice given to Moab, by the prophet, for the prevention of this judgment; to succor, and harbor God's people driven out of their country, ver. 3, 4. there being no occasion given, of showing any such kind office to God's people, during the three, or four first years of Ezekiah's reign. Others therefore, drawing down these years a little lower, suppose this prophecy delivered in the fourth year of Ezekiah, what time Salmaneser sat down before Samaria, which having taken, after three years' siege, 2 King. 18.9, 10. he then fell, as they suppose, upon the Moabites. And this might carry with it a little more probability, than the former; because many, out of the ten tribes, might seek relief and shelter among the Moabites, in that Assyrian invasion. But it is deemed rather, that they were of the Jewish people more peculiarly so termed: in the behalf of whom, those offices are required by the prophet. Others therefore, go yet lower. Some fixing the date of this prophecy, much about the eleventh year of Ezekiah's reign, in whose fourteenth, Sennacherib came up against Judah, 2 King. 18.13. and withal executed on Moab, what was here denounced against it. So, the three years should come about, just together, with Sennacherib's invasion of Judah. But this opinion laboring of the same difficulty with the former; some to salve it, make them to commence from Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem, *three year* after, which, they imagine that Sennacherib invaded Moab; deservedly spoiled and plundered, through God's just judgment by him, for their harsh and unkind carriage toward his people, that had sought shelter among them, when their own country had been not long before overrun by him. And this indeed might well suit with that, which was from that passage of this prophecy, objected against the former. But there is another difficulty arising here, instead of that hereby removed. For Sennacherib, by that blow given him while he was minding, and attempting the siege, rather, than besieging, as yet, of Jerusalem, was so weakened and disheartened, that there is little probability, that ever he attempted aught that way again; especially being so soon after it, cut off by the hands of his own sons, ch. 37.37, 38. Amidst these dissenting opinions, concerning this place, I shall crave leave to deliver my conjecture, concurring much with the last; but supposing the judgment, here denounced against Moab, which these *three years* relate unto, to have been executed, neither by Nebuchadnezzar, (albeit the utter devastation of Moab, before denounced, were by him to be effected) nor by Salmaneser, nor by Sennacherib; but by his son and successor, Esar-haddon: who after his father's decease, having recovered some strength, it is not unlikely, but that he might again make towards those parts, and invade some of the neighboring states, and Moab, in particular; expecting some opportunity to be dealing with Judah, in revenge of his father's quarrel. Which albeit, warned by his father's defeat, he durst not attempt, during the reign of Ezekiah; yet after his decease, in Manasses his successor's reign, he did; when also, the better to clear his way thereunto, he swept away the remainders of Israel and Samaria; as was before shown, on Chap. 7.8. from Ezr. 4.2. I conceive therefore this prophecy to have been delivered about the fourteenth, or fifteenth year of Ezekiah; and that, in particular, which is in this last verse denounced, to have taken effect, about the eighteenth, or nineteenth year of his reign, being put in execution, by the Assyrian king Esar-haddon. To express my mind herein more fully; I suppose that the utter destruction of Moab, here before denounced, and by Jeremy, long after seconded, to have been executed by Nebuchadnezzar. But as the Lord uses sometime to give assurance of the the complement of some prophecies, of longer date, by some other prediction of a nearer term; (whereof see ch. 7.8, 16. & 8.4. & 14.25. Jer. 28.16, 17.) in like manner he seems to me, here to have done. For, having in the foregoing prophecy, threatened the utter ruin of the Moabitish state, which was many years after to be effected; he does here, to give the stronger assurance of the complement of the same, foretell that within *three years* after the promulgation of this prophecy, the state of Moab, by the Assyrian king, Esar-haddon, should exceedingly be impoverished, and impaired. That which being then effected, though at present, it may be, little expected, might help, to confirm the truth of the former denunciation, though not so speedily to take effect.

*{as the years of an hireling*} That is, *three years* precisely. Because hired servants are wont to keep a precise account of the time and term of years, for which they are hired; the expiration whereof, also, they are wont earnestly to expect, Job 7.1, 2. & 14.5. So ch. 21.16. For, as for that which the Jewish writers, and some others, would from this place compared with Deut. 15.18. collect, that the Jews, either might not, or used not to hire any for above *three year*; neither does that place of Moses, necessarily, prove any such matter; and that the phrase, here used, implies nothing less, may hereby appear, in that it is there also used, where mention is made only of *one year*, Chapter 21.16. See further there.

*{and the glory of Moab shall be contemned*} Or, it shall come to pass, that (as chap. 14.3, 4.) *the glory of Moab shall become mean, of light esteem*, or *of no repute*; as 1 Sam. 18.23. opposed to *honorable* Chap. 3.5. and there is in the words an elegant notion, though such, as cannot so well be expressed in our language; for the word *glory*, in Hebrew, has an intimation of *weight* in it: alluded to, by the apostle, when he says, *a weight of glory*, 2 Cor. 4.18. and the latter word of *contempt*; has affinity with that, which signifies, *lightness*, 1 Sam. 18.26. chap. 49.6. And they are both used promiscuously, Num. 21.6. Job 40.4. Nah. 1.14. So that it is, as if he had said, the great *weight*, that Moab now bears, shall then become *light*. He that weighs down so much now, shall then bear no weight, but fly up in the balance. For the metaphor is taken from moneys, or wares, brought to the beam to be weighed; as in payment, and sale, they used to be. See Jer. 32.9. Hos. 12.7. So Psal. 62.9. Dan. 5.27. The like elegancy is found, 1 Sam. 2.30. And not unlike it, is that which Luke has, where he says of the apostles, that they went from the consistory, where they had been ill entreated, rejoicing that they had been so much *honored*, or *graced*; as to be *dishonored*, or, *disgraced* for Christ, Act. 5.41. for so the words there run.

*{with all that great multitude*} Or, *with all that multitude*, (whereof he now so much glories: and wherein he so much prides himself, ver. 6. the glory of a state consisting in the multitude of people, Prov. 14.28.) *that is great*, or, *that is* now *so great*. For so the article redoubled ought to be, and is sometime, rendered: as chap. 15.16. which not observed, lessens the emphasis of it. See 2 Chr. 20.12, 15. See Jer. 32.18. A late writer renders it, *with all his much abundance*, or, *great wealth*, or, *his glory* consisting *in the great abundance of his wealth*. See chap. 5.13, 14.

*{and the remnant*} Or, *so that the remnant* (as ch. 10.19.) that shall be left of that multitude before so great. See ch. 10.22.

*{shall be very small*} Heb. *little small*. The notion redoubled, though in two different terms, to intimate, the great paucity that should be left of them. So chap. 10.25. See chap. 24.6.

*{and feeble*} Heb. *not many*: as the margin has it: or, as others, *not mighty*. See Chap. 10.13. few in regard of what they had been; the copulative is wanting: as chap. 14.5. & 15.1. The meaning is, that Moab should be brought very low; and his main multitude much diminished.

### CHAPTER 17

**V. 1.** *{The burden of Damascus*} Another heavy, and sad sermon or prophecy, called therefore *a burden* (of which term, see Chap. 13.1.) is in the former part of this chapter (for the three last verses are of a diverse subject) related, concerning Damascus the head city of the Syrians, Ch. 7.8. who had been from time to time sore enemies to, and grievous vexers of God's people, on whose country they bordered eastward, 2 King. 13.17. See Judg. 3.8. 2 Sam. 8.3, 5. 1 King. 11.24, 25. & 15.20. & 20.1. 2 King. 6.24, 25. & 8.12, 13. & 12.17, 18. & 13.22. & 15.37. & 16.5. & 24.2. Chap. 7.1, 5, 6. & 9.12. The like burdensome prophecies against Damascus, see ch. 49.23. Amos 1.2. Zach. 9.1.

*{Damascus*} Heb. *Dammesek*, Gen. 14.15. and sometime also, *Darmesek*, 1 Chr. 18.5. (as *Nebuchadretser*, for *Nebuchadnetser*, Jer. 21.2.) and so the Syrian calls it *Darmesuk*, Act. 9.2. Some of the Jewish doctors would have it so called because Abel was there slain, and the ground there *drank* in his *blood*, Gen. 4.11. Others, because Adam was there made out of the earth, the mold thereabout, being of a ruddy kind of clay, apt to be molded into any shape, such as his body was framed of, Gen. 2.7. Others would have it so named, as *a sack*, or *bag of blood*, from the abundance of rich wine, that the country thereabout yielded, called *the blood of the grape*, Gen. 49.11. Deut. 32.14. Whence the heathen also feigned, that their drunken god lay hid there, sometime, in a bottle. But these are mere fictions and fables. It is most likely, that the city had its name from the first founder of it: yet not Eleazar Abraham's servant, as some have supposed; who is said to have been *Damascus*, Gen. 15.2. as descended from parents, inhabitants of that city; and in all likelihood born, not in Abraham's house, but there: beside, that the city had been built; and bore that name before that time, though how long, uncertain, as appears by the story of Abraham's pursuit of those kings, that came against Sodom, Gen. 14.15. Being the chief city of Syria, it is put here for the whole country, ver. 3. as Samaria, for the land of the ten tribes, 1 King. 13.32.

*{Behold*} This note of attention, and consideration, is prefixed, partly to intimate the improbability of that which he was to deliver concerning the ruin of Damascus, in the conceit of those, that apprehended the Syrian principality, as a state, not like suddenly, or easily to be conquered, and that city, as an impregnable piece; and partly to give assurance of the certain accomplishment thereof, whatsoever conceits men might have, either of the impossibility, or improbability of it. See ch. 3.1. & 7.14.

*{Damascus is taken away*} This was effected, partly by Tiglath-Pileser, who took it, and sacked it, 2 King. 16.9. but more fully afterward, as some suppose, by Salmaneser, after he had taken Samaria; as others by Nebuchadnezzar, after the destruction of Jerusalem, Jer. 49.23.

*{from being a city*} Heb. *from a city*: as 1 Sam. 15.22. *from a king*; for, from being a king: and Jer. 48.2. *from a nation*, that is, from being a nation. It is so ruined, that it shall be no longer a city.

*{and it shall be a ruinous heap*} Or, *but* (as chap. 16.12.) *it is become* (for the prophet speaks in the prophetical strain, as of a thing already done. So chap. 15.1.) Heb. *an heap of ruin*. See the like, Psal. 79.1. Chap. 25.2. & 37.26. Jer. 26.17. Mic. 1.6. & 3.12. There is in the original, an elegancy in the terms of *city*, and *heap*, the latter wanting but one letter of the former; and the prophet using a word here, not elsewhere found in that form, to bring it up home to the former word, with the particle prefixed to it.

**V. 2.** *{The cities of Aroer are forsaken*} The cities situate in that whole tract, beyond Jordan, along by the brink, or near to the banks of Arnon, Deut. 2.36. & 3.12. the ancient possession of the Amorites, Josh. 12.2. but held afterward by the Reubenites, and Gadites, Num. 32.34. Josh. 13.8, 9. and recovered from them again, by neighboring people, the Moabites one while, the Ammonites another, Judg. 11.26, 33. and the Syrians another while, 2 King. 10.33. & 14.22. and 16.6. Jer. 48.19. Now hence some of the Rabbins would gather three *Aroers*, one belonging to the Moabites, Josh. 13.16. Jer. 48.6, 20. another belonging to the Ammonites, Josh. 13.25. a third in Syria, here mentioned: but some others, to take that conceit away, say rather and better, that *Aroer* coasting along upon the river Arnon, lay on the confines of Moab and Ammon; and was held sometime by the one, and sometime by the other; and at this time by the Syrians; and after by the Assyrians; as in the next note. For as for that Jewish doctor, that would by *Aroer*, have *Damascus* itself here meant; so called, because it was to be as *Arar*, Jer. 17.5. or as *Aroer*, Jer. 48.6. *in the wilderness*; of which term, see on those places; it is by the generality of them justly rejected.

*{forsaken*} The inhabitants of them (whether Syrians, or Israelites who were in confederacy with them) being expelled, and carried away captive by Tiglath-Pileser, the king of Assyria, 1 Chr. 5.8, 26. See chap. 16.12.

*{and shall be for flocks*} The Hebrew word comprehends as well *herds* of greater cattle, as *flocks* of less; as appears, Gen. 32.15–17. cattle shall graze freely, where towns, and cities before stood. ch. 32.14. Zeph. 2.14.

*{which shall lie down*} Heb. *and they shall lie down*: as ch. 4.6.

*{and none shall make them afraid*} Heb. *none shall be frighting*. They shall rest quietly there, the country being so depopulated, that there shall be none to disturb them, or chase them away: a defect of the pronoun, in such speeches frequent, Levit. 26.6. Deut. 28.26. Job 11.19. Jer. 7.33. & 30.10. & 46.27. Ezek. 34.28. & 39.26. Mic. 4.4. Nah. 2.12. Zeph. 3.13.

**V. 3.** *{The fortress also, shall cease from Ephraim*} That is, from the ten tribes. See Chap. 7.2. Their fortresses (for the word is collective; as Amos 5.9.) shall not be able to hold out against the enemy; but they shall be surprised, slighted, and dismantled by him. Heb. *they shall have their sabbath*, or time of *cessation*, and *rest*: as Levit. 26.43. Now the ten tribes are here mentioned, and threatened together with the Syrians, Ephraim and Damascus together; not so much, as some interpreters would have it, either to give the Syrians to understand, that if God spared not his own people, he would much less spare them: as Jer. 25.29. or because that Samaria was first to be destroyed by Salmaneser; and thereby the Syrians might know what should in the next place betide them; but because they were linked together in a joint confederacy against Judah; and the ruin of them both, therefore, by the king of Assyria, is, as in some former prophecy, so here again jointly foretold. See ch. 7.1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 16. & 8.4. as also 2 King. 15.29. & 16.5, 9. The time therefore of this prophecy seems mistaken by those, who suppose it to have been delivered after the death of Ahaz, about the second, or third year of the reign of Ezekiah: as if that date of the prophecy against the Philistines, ch. 14.28. did relate, not to that alone, but to the other also ensuing sermons: or, that those, that follow it, in the book here, upon record, must of necessity follow it, in course of time also. See ch. 1.1, 2.

*{and the kingdom from Damascus*} Damascus shall no longer be a royal city; nor Syria a kingdom; but a province. So Ezek. 30.18. and 33.28.

*{and the remnant of Syria*} Heb. *Aram*. So Chap. 7.1. either, *and from the remnant of Syria*; as intimating, that such of them, as remained, should have no royal power left among them, their king being slain, and none to succeed in his stead, 2 King. 6.9. or, the sentence being continued, and this branch joined (as it may well) to that which follows.

*{the remnant of Syria, they shall be as the glory of the children of Israel*} Or, *shall be* without *they*; which in the text is not expressed. The meaning is, that the Syrians, and Israelites, the joint enemies of God's people, should both of them, be alike brought low, and stripped of their former state and dignity, ch. 7.16. & 8.4.

*{saith the Lord of hosts*} As Chap. 3.15. & 5.9. the prophet's usual close, to assure the effect of the word delivered, ch. 14.24.

**V. 4.** *{And in that day it shall come to pass, that*} Or, *For* (as ch. 16.2.) *in that day*, &c. as chap. 7.11. For the prophet seems in these words, to render a reason of what he had said, ver. 3. that the state of Syria should be as the glory of Israel, to wit, because they should both be exceedingly impaired; and that much about the same time.

*{the glory of Jacob shall be made thin*} Or, *exhaust*. See ch. 10.2. the word is used of rivers, when their waters are spent, either drawn off, or drained from them, Job 28.4. chap. 19.6. or, of the bodies of man, or beast, when their moisture, flesh, or fat, is so wasted, that they are grown thin withal, and are nothing but skin, and bone, Gen. 41.19. 2 Sam. 13.4. their might, and multitude, wherein they gloried, should be much diminished, and abated. So Judg. 6.6.

*{Jacob*} As *Israel*, ver. 3.

*{and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean*} The like metaphor, see ch. 10.16, 18.

**V. 5.** *{And it shall be, as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm*} Or, *And he* (that is, Jacob, ver. 4. or, Israel, ver. 3. the ten tribes) *shall be*. It shall be so with him. See the like manner of syntax, ch. 29.7, 8. Mat. 25.14. They shall be cut down, and carried away captive, the main body of them, some few only left, as the corn is cut down, and carried away out of the field, where it grew, by the harvest workmen, that leave only some few gleanings behind them, Levit. 19.9. Deut. 24.19. they being no more able to stand before the enemy, than the corn before the reapers, Rev. 14.15, 16.

*{the harvestman*} Heb. *harvest*, for, *man of harvest*; as *prey* for, a man of *prey*, Prov. 23.28. and, *peace*, for, a man of *peace*, Ps. 120.7.

*{gathereth*} See ch. 16.10. Deut. 16.12.

*{corn*} The word properly signifies *standing corn*, Deut. 23.25, 26. Judg. 15.5. but there is in it, an ellipsis, of the substantive; *standing*, for, *standing corn*: as *parched*, for, *parched pulse*, 2 Sam. 17.28. *full*; for, *a full cup*, Psal. 73.10. *sure*, for, *a sure covenant*, Neh. 9.38. *strong*; for, *a strong hand*, Chap. 40.10. *fruitful*; for, *a fruitful vine*, Gen. 49.22. or, olive tree, ver. 6. See ch. 5.2.

*{reapeth the ears with his arm*} A defect of the instrumental particle: as Psal. 17.13, 14. or, *his arm reapeth the ears*. Gen. 41.7, 8, 23, 24. Ruth 2.2.

*{and it shall be as he that gathereth ears*} Or, *picketh up ears*. The former word is used of harvest workmen, that reap, and gather by armfuls, or lapfuls, Psal. 129.7. this of gleaners, that pick up ear, after ear, Levit. 19.9, 10. Deut. 23.22. Ruth 2.2, 3, 15–18. See chap. 27.12. Hereby is implied, that there should not only be a sweeping away of a great part of them together; but a second gleaning of them also, as is said of the Benjamites, Judg. 20.45. See the like, chap. 6.13. That which was effected first by Tiglath-Pileser, 2 King. 15.29. then by Salmaneser, 2 King. 17.6. these as two harvestmen: and lastly, by Esar-haddon; as one that gleaned after them, Ezr. 4.2.

*{in the valley of Rephaim*} A fertile valley, having good store of corn ground, lying on the west side of Jerusalem, Josh. 15.8. & 18.16. where it is rendered, *the valley of the giants*; and the word indeed seems so to signify, 2 Sam. 23.16, 18, 22. Deut. 3.11, 20. But the valley may well be deemed to have had that appellation, from the name of an ancient people called the *Rephaites*, that inhabited thereabout, Gen. 14.5, & 15.20. The prophet mentions it, here; because a place commonly known to the people whom he spoke to.

**V. 6.** *{Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it*} Heb. *And*, as ch. 8.9. or, *Yet, a remnant of clusters shall be left in it*, because the verb is singular, and the noun plural: and the noun is included oft in the verb: as Gen. 50.26. with ver. 2. The meaning is, that though God should cause them, by whole multitudes, at several times, to be carried away captive by the enemy, and of those that they had left, some again, to undergo the like calamity; yet he would not make an utter riddance of them, Jer. 30.11. he would deal with them, as he had enjoined his people to do, in gathering their grapes at vintage, Levit. 19.10. Deut. 23.20. some few clusters should be left, Chap. 65.8. a remnant should still be reserved for a church, chap. 1.9. & 6.13. & 7.3. & 10.21, 22. for even those also that glean, leave some behind them, Judg. 20.45, 47. Jer. 49.9. Obad. 5. See chap. 25.13.

*{as the shaking of an olive tree*} Heb. *according to the shaking of an olive tree*; or, *as* in *the shaking* of it. The word signifies properly, not so much *a shaking* of the tree, as *a shaking off*, or, *striking down* of the fruit, by beating of the tree, Deut. 23.20. the law here alluded to. See ch. 24.13.

*{two, or three berries*} A defect of the disjunctive; as 2 King. 9.32. chap. 38.14. a very small number, Matth. 18.20. to wit, are left.

*{in the top*} Heb. *in the head*: as ch. 2.2.

*{of the uppermost bough*} So called in the Hebrew here, and ver. 9. (for it is nowhere else read) because it is *lift up* above the rest, Ps. 94.4. ch. 61.6. where, by reason of the height, they cannot easily be reached.

*{four, or five*} As before, a small number, 2 King. 7.13.

*{in the outmost fruitful branches thereof*} Heb. *in the branches* (ch. 27.10. properly, *side branches*; or, *spreading branches*, Ezek. 31.6, 8. See Chap. 2.21.) *of her fruitful tree*: such an one, as has great store; and whence the more, therefore, might well be spared, and left; a defect of the substantive: as Gen. 49.22. See ver. 5.

*{saith the Lord God of Israel*} *Jehovah*; who both can, and will fulfill what he says, chap. 1.20. & 14.24, 27. and *the God of Israel* still, (but not of the Syrians) notwithstanding these heavy judgments inflicted, as well on the one, as on the other. See Deut. 30.7, 10. Levit. 26.44.

**V. 7.** *{At that day shall a man look to his Maker*} The residue of God's people, refined, and reformed, by these forementioned calamities, shall then, abandoning their idols, repair unto God, seek to him, trust in him, and depend upon him. So ch. 10.20, 21. God's end in the chastising of his, being, not to drive them away from him; but to reclaim them from their wanderings, and to bring them home to him, chap. 19.22. & 27.9. This was in part fulfilled in the reign of Ezekiah, 2 Chron. 30.11. and of Josiah, 2 Chron. 34.33.

*{that day*} As ch. 4.1, 2.

*{look to*} That is, *trust to*, *depend upon*; as Ps. 25.20. & 34.5. & 121.1, 2. & 123.1, 2. & 141.8. ch. 8.17. & 45.22. Because what men trust to, that they are wont frequently, and wistly to look after, and to have their eyes much fixed upon. See the contrary, wherewith God's people are upbraided, ch. 22.11. & 31.1.

*{his Maker*} Whom therefore he owes all duty unto, and ought wholly to depend upon, Deut. 32.6. Ps. 100.3. and 149.2. Eccles. 12.1.

*{and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel*} The same notion, in other terms. See ch. 1.4.

**V. 8.** *{And he shall not look to the altars*} Erected for idol service, chap. 27.9. Jer. 11.13. & 17.2. Hos. 8.11. Nor to the idols, for the worship of whom they were erected, chap. 30.22. and were placed therefore near to them, but above them, 2 Chr. 34.4.

*{the work of his hands*} Whether altars, or idols, 2 King. 21.5. Psal. 115.4. chap. 2.20.

*{neither respect that which his fingers have made*} See ch. 2.8.

*{either, the groves, or the images*} Heb. *and the groves, and the images*; or, *both the groves, and the images*; as Psal. 76.7. But the copulative is here put for the disjunctive; as Exod. 21.17. Neh. 5.8. These two words, rendered *groves*, and *images*, we find divers times joined together, 2 Chron. 34.4, 7. chap. 27.9. Of the former whereof is less doubt, or difference among the learned. Yet the word seems to be sometime used, not only for *a grove*, or a company of trees of lower growth, and less stature, growing thick, and close together, as on a cluster; of which kind, they were forbidden to plant any near to God's house, or his altars. Deut. 16.21. But for a model, or curious piece of workmanship of gold, or other precious metal, resembling such a cluster of trees. For some such, in likelihood, was that *grove* which Josiah found in the temple; but brought forth of it, 2 King. 23.6. And dealt with it, as Moses did with the golden calf, Exod. 32.20. and Ezekiah with the brazen serpent, 2 King. 18.4. not unlike to the *golden vine*, and *platane*, that the Lydian lord is reported to have represented Darius with, Herodot. lib. 7. Either of both may be termed, *the work of man's hand*; because, planted by man's industry, the one; and framed by man's workmanship, the other; whence the phrase of *making groves*, here alluded to, 1 King. 16.33. 2 King. 17.16. & 21.3. Howbeit, as before, the word *altars*, seemed to be put for the idols, worshiped at those altars; so here the *groves*, for the idols worshiped at, or in those groves. But, concerning the latter word, there is no small question: the word is not found, but in the plural, *Hammanim*, or *Chammanim*: and is derived from a noun, that signifies primarily, *heat*, Psal. 19.6. And in the second place, *the sun*, (unto whom it is also there, by the Psalmist, applied) so called, in regard of his heat, Job 30.28. Cant. 6.10. ch. 24.22. & 30.26. The Chaldee paraphrast renders it, *temples*: and so also does the Greek, Ezek. 6.4, 6. And some of the Rabbins, on Levit. 26.30. say that it signifies, *houses*, or *temples*, dedicated to the sun. But this seems not so probable, by the collation of other places; whence it may appear that they were rather some kind of *images*, than *temples*. For of Josias it is said, that he *brake down the altars of the Baalim* and cut down the *Hammanim, that were aloft above*, or *beside them*, 2 Chr. 34.4. Others therefore, of the Jewish doctors, do with more probability, conceive them to have been images. And *wooden images*, say some of them; as also the Greek renders the word, Lev. 26.30. because there is mention made of *cutting* them down, 2 Chro. 34.4, 7. Ezek. 6.6. but that is but a wooden ground. For the word, that is there used, is applied, as well to metal materials, as to wooden, or treen fabrics; as to *bars of iron*, Psal. 107.16. chap. 45.2. But the images, so termed, are by the Jewish writers, generally supposed to have been *images of the sun*; or such, at least, as were erected in honor of him, and whereby to worship him; as the heathen most of them did, Deut. 4.19. & 17.3. 2 King. 23.5, 11. Jer. 8.2. & 7.18. & 44.17, 18. Ezek. 8.16. And Joseph Ben-Gorion, in his *Jewish story*, tells us, that this *Hamman* was an image, and made like a man of a middle age, with horns on his head, like an ox, and a chin, or beard, like a dog. But other of the Jewish writers say, it was a picture made round, to represent the orb of the sun, like our signs of the sun. And Benjamin the Jew, in his *travels*, tells us of a town he met with, inhabited by *Cushites*, near whereunto were abundance of altars, and images, resembling the round orb of the sun, whom that people worshiped; which, by magical arts, at the sunrising, when people, men and women, came to burn incense to them, shined very bright, and made a great noise. And I remember to have read in Hero, a Greek writer, his *wind works*; how, by artificial device, an image may be so framed, that the sun shining on it, may cause it to yield some kind of sound. But I suppose this to be but a fiction of that Jewish author: whereof he has not a few. Howbeit, from this Hebrew *Hamman*, it is not unlikely that the Phoenicians had their idol, from whom the Greeks and Latins had their *Jupiter-Hammon*; or *Ammon*; of whom they tell many fabulous tales. But Macrobius relates, *Saturnals*, lib. 1. cap. 21. that the Lybians worshiped him, not at the *sunrising*; (as those Jews, Ezek. 8.16. and those other people the Jew speaks of) but at the *sunsetting*; and represented him with the horns, not of an *ox*, as the son of Gorion, but) of *a ram* on his head, thereby representing the rays, or beams of the sun: as both, in Hebrew and Greek the words of *horn*, and of *glittering light*, are of near affinity, the one with the other. See Exod. 34.29, 30, 35. (whence the gross error of painting Moses with *horns*) and Hab. 3.4. It seems therefore most probable, that these *Hammanim* were images, of what matter, or figure soever, made, thereby to adore the *sun*. Nor can I therefore readily assent to that, which some later writers have conceived this term to import. The idolaters, say they, had divers places for the worship of idols, according to the divers seasons of the year, and conditions of the weather; their *groves*, and shady places, which they used in heat of summer: and their *sun images*, set in sunshine places; which they made use of in colder weather; so called, say some, because they stood in the sun, and were *sunburnt*. And these two sorts, say they, are joined together, as including all sorts of idols, and idolatrous services, being reduced to these two heads. But for this distinction, I find little ground, either in Scripture, or elsewhere. Groves were commonly used, by the superstitious heathen, for idolatrous employment, in regard of a kind of awful dread, that such shady, and solitary places are wont to surprise people withal, especially prepossessed with a superstitious conceit of some deity dwelling there. Nor were they wont to make use of them, more at one time than another; the closeness of the trees, in them, affording, as well shelter, in the wintertime, as shade in the summer. And *Statuae subdiales*, as they render the word, signifying *images set in the open air*; having no covert, but what heaven affords, seems not so well seated for winter service, or for use, suitable to cold and blustering weather. I adhere therefore to the former; and suppose *groves*, and these *sun images*, to be joined together; because these idols were oft placed, as well in their *groves*, and *high places* abroad, as in their *temples*, and *houses* within doors. See 2 Chr. 34.4.

**V. 9.** *{In that day*} At that time, (as ver. 4.) when God shall execute the judgment before denounced. For to that the prophet now returns again, illustrating it further, by the procuring causes of it, ver. 10. and the sad effect of it, ver. 11.

*{Shall his strong cities be as a forsaken bough*} Heb. *his cities of strength*, (as Prov. 10.15. & 18.11.) shall be as the leaving a *side bough*, or *branch*; such as makes a shade, Ezek. 31.3. answering not unfitly to that other word used, ver. 6.) Or, *of a wood* or, *thicket*. For the word, here used, also sometime so signifies, 1 Sam. 23.15, 16, 18. 2 Chr. 27.4. As a bough or a branch that is *left* behind, to wit, by those that did lop, or shred a tree: or; as tree left for a stander, when the whole wood about it is felled. For the word *forsaken*, does not well suit here. In regard of birds or fowl, that nest, or roost in a tree; or, in regard of beasts that had shade and shelter, formerly, from it; may a tree, or bough, be said to be forsaken, Ezek. 31.4, 12. Dan. 4.12, 14. but not properly by the husbandman, who when he lops a tree, leaves some bough or branch, either neglecting it, or because he cannot well come to it; or because he has no need of it; or has further uses there for it. And although the cities, here mentioned, might in the former respect, be compared to *a forsaken bough*, because left by their inhabitants, being driven away from them, as birds chased from a tree, which was before their wonted harbor, chap. 16.2. Yet that seems not to be the thing that the prophet here aims at; but that their strong cities should stand solitary, left alone and desolate; (such of them, at least, as were not utterly razed, as Damascus was, ver. 1. and some of Israel, it may well be, were) the whole country, and smaller towns and villages, round about, being utterly wasted and ruined. See chap. 1.7, 8.

*{and an uppermost branch*} As ver. 6. A standing bough, that is left on the top of a tree, when the rest are all lopped away, naked and bare. Though some expound both this, and the former, of boughs and branches of fruit trees, left naked and bare; and many times also broken and mangled, despoiled wholly of their beauty, when the fruit is all beaten down. But the former seems to agree better, both with the prophet's scope, here, and the like elsewhere. See ch. 30.15.

*{which they left for the children of Israel*} That is, which the enemy left; God in his providence, so disposing things, out of his gracious affection to his people, of whom he had reserved a remnant to himself, ver. 6. that yet some places should be spared for them, when the residue should be destroyed. The verb is impersonal, and may well be rendered, *which shall be left* (See chap. 2.19.) *for the children of Israel*; as *for the anointing*, Chap. 10.27. Howbeit, some interpreters turn it another way, reading the words, *which shall be left*, or, *forsaken by the children of Israel*; as ch. 7.16. And others, yet, a third way, supposing this latter clause to have some reference to the ancient inhabitants of the land of Canaan, in Joshua's time, and their leaving the land, upon the Israelites' entrance thereupon; and this way the Jewish doctors generally go; and divers also of our interpreters, some reading the words, *as they left* them. The note of similitude supplied before the relative; as Exod. 34.18. Jer. 44.8. Some, *which they left*, (to wit, the Amorites, and Canaanites) *before the children of Israel*, that is, for fear of them, as Exod. 2.15. Chap. 21.15. That which some understand of their leaving their *tillage*, and their *fruits*, (because one of the words, beforegoing, has affinity with another word that signifies *plowing*, and the other belongs to a tree) and betaking themselves to their strong forts, and fenced cities for fear, Exod. 23.27, 28. Josh. 2.9, 11. & 5.1. Others, of the leaving of their forts themselves, and their fenced cities, being by the Israelites dispossessed of them. And thus most of the Rabbins. Some, also, making the two words, in the foregoing sentence, rendered, *bough* and *branch*, the proper names of two cities, in the land of Canaan, called *Horesh*, and *Amir*, whereof yet we find no record in Scripture. But these latter interpretations, though not wanting great authors, seem somewhat too coact.

*{and there shall be desolation*} As chap. 6.11. Or, *it shall be desolations*, that is, *most desolate*; (see chap. 1.7.) to wit, Samaria, the royal city, says one Rabbin; the land of Israel, says another. I suppose it has reference to the first words of the verse, *His strong cities*, &c. each of them *shall be desolate*, See chap. 20.2. and 26.19.

**V. 10.** *{Because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation*} The procuring cause of this their calamity, their forgetting, neglecting, disregarding, and rejecting him, that might, and would have saved them, had they been mindful of him, and faithful to him, Deut. 8.14. Psalm 106.13, 21. Jer. 2.32. & 3.21. & 13.25. & 23.27. Ezek. 22.12. & 23.35. Hos. 8.14. & 13.6. The person is changed; as chap. 14.3. and the words are in the feminine, directed to the land, or state of Israel, as to a woman, or a wife, that had forgot her duty and loyalty to her husband, Prov. 2.17.

*{the God of thy salvation*} Or, *thy saving God*. God your Savior. So Psal. 18.46. & 25.5. & 27.9. & 62.1, 2, 7. as, *the God of my mercy*; or, *my God of mercy*: that is, my merciful God, Psalm 59.10, 17. And *the God of my righteousness*; or, *my God of righteousness*: that is, my most righteous God, Psalm 4.1.

*{and hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength*} Or, *thy rock of strength*. Your strongest rock; as *the cities of thy strength*, or, *the cities of strength*: your strong cities, ver. 10. So Psalm 62.7. He that would have protected you more surely, than all those your strongholds, which you did mind and trust to, when you minded not him; for the one of them is here opposed to the other, see Deut. 32.4, 30, 31. Psalm 31.2, 3, 4.

*{therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants*} Heb. *plants of pleasant*; to wit, flowers, or fruits, as Gen. 30.14. Cant. 7.13. with chap. 2.12. A defect of the substantive, as there, in the Canticles; and here before, ver. 5.

*{and shalt set it with strange slips*} Heb. *and with a slip of a stranger*, or *foreigner, shalt thou sow it*. A defect of the instrumental particle: as ver. 5. a *slip*, for, *slips*, collectively; as Ezek. 8.17. and *plant*, for *plants*, ver. 11. It is used, more especially, for *a branch*, or, *slip* of a vine, Num. 13.23. Ezek. 15.2. *a slip of a foreigner*, for *foreign slips*; brought out of foreign parts, and in that regard, of more esteem. *Shalt thou sow*, or *set*: for the Hebrew uses the same word for both, Levit. 19.19. Deut. 22.9. *it*, to wit, your vineyard, or your garden; the pronoun, for the noun; as 2 King. 25.4. Chap. 30.8. He compares the state of Israel to a curious lady, that delights in beautiful flowers, affects choice fruit, desires foreign plants, is careful to procure them, to plant her places of pleasure with them, and sedulous in nursing and tending of them there; as the next words imply, ver. 11. See *a strange vine*, in another sense, Jer. 2.21.

**V. 11.** *{In the day shalt thou make thy plant to grow; and in the morning, shalt thou make thy seed to flourish*} All the pains you shall take and all the cost you shall be at, in making provision for the maintaining of your state, and the continuance of it, in a plentiful, beautiful, and flourishing condition, shall come to nought; it shall be spoiled, and destroyed all, by the enemy. There seems an eye had to that threatening in the law, Deut. 28.29, 30, 33.

*{In the day*} In the daytime: Day by day, as Psalm 42.8.

*{make thy plant to grow*} The single word signifies, *to grow much*, or *apace*, Job 8.7, 11. & 12.23. & 36.26. Psalm 73.12. & 92.12. But here it is in a redoubled form, as importing a double desire, endeavor and diligence, constantly employed, by all means that might be, to strengthen and advance their estate. See Chapter 9.10.

*{in the morning*} A phrase implying commonly much sedulity, and industry in pursuit of a business, Psalm 5.3. & 127.2. Eccl. 11.6. ch. 5.11. & 27.3. and it may here be referred, as well to the hastening of the growth, and putting forth of things, set, or sown, as to the early and constant care used about them: in allusion to Aron's rod, that being a dry stick overnight, was found budded, and blossomed next morning, Num. 17.8. or, to the practice of those, that use artificial means, and helps, for the forwarding of plants and fruits, See Ezek. 17.24.

*{make thy seed*} As before; *thy plant*. That which you have set, or sown. See ver. 10.

*{to flourish*} Or, *bud*, or, *blossom*: as Num. 17.8. Chap. 27.6. & 35.1, 2.

*{but the harvest shall be a heap in the day of grief, and desperate sorrow*} This clause is by divers, diversely both rendered and expounded. Those that read the words, as they are here rendered; do thus expound them: that in the day, or at the time of their calamity, and irrecoverable grief, which they shall sustain by the enemy, all that they had gotten together, should be suddenly consumed, as a small heap of corn is, when a great multitude, or, a whole army that have been long pinched with famine, shall light on it; or all that you have taken so much pains for, shall be laid together on a heap, for the enemy, to divide, and share among themselves. See Chap. 15.7. or, shall all be spoiled and destroyed, as such choice and precious matters are wont to be, when they are regardlessly jumbled together, and so cast upon an heap. See chap. 33.4. & Jer. 43.12. And this I suppose the genuine sense of the words. Which one of the Jewish commenters observes to have been a proverbial speech among them, concerning labor in vain. *Your crop is come to an heap*, or, *your whole crop is all on a heap*. But some others, and so of the Jewish teachers, render the words far otherwise, to wit, *The crop*, or, *the branches shall be removed in the day of inheritance, and* there shall be *deadly grief*; or, *The heap of the crop, in the day of inheritance*, shall be *deadly grief*: or, *The crop in the day of inheritance*, shall be *a heap and deadly grief*: that is, as some, your children, whom you have with so much care, and cost, brought up, as others, your wealth, which with so much pains and travail, you have raised, and brought to a height, shall be taken all from you, and carried away, when you should come to enjoy it, and reap the fruit of it, which shall be as deadly pangs, and pains unto you; it shall go so near to the heart with you, Deut. 28.34. Or, all the fruit, or crop, that for all your forepassed care, and cost, shall accrue unto you, shall be nothing else, but an heap of heart's grief, and sorrow, Eccl. 2.11, 17, 18.

*{but*} A defect of the adversative: as Psal. 119.69, 70, 78.

*{the harvest*} Or, *crop*: as chap. 16.9. Joel 3.13. yet, according to others *the branch*. For so is also the word used, Job 29.19. and *branch* for *branches*, or *boughs*: as Job 14.9.

*{an heap*} So the word commonly signifies, Exod. 15.8. Josh. 3.13, 16. Psal. 33.7. & 78.13. nor is it ever found otherwise used: and some put in here the restrictive particle, *but*; reading it, *but an heap* only: as Job 8.9. Jer. 46.17. Yet divers of the Rabbins, whom some of ours also, here, follow, would refer it to a root, that imports *removal*, ch. 10.31. & 16.2. & 22.3. & 33.3.

*{in the day of grief*} Heb. *of grievous*: a defect, as the Jews that go this way, note, of the substantive, *plague*, or *stroke*, expressed, Jer. 14.17. & 30.12. or, *wound*, or *breach*: as Jer. 10.19. Nah. 3.19. the like defects, see chap. 5.2, 4. ver. 5, 10. Jer. 17.16. Ezek. 13.14. Howbeit, the same word, but descending from another root, does ordinarily signify *an inheritance*, or *possession*, Num. 18.23, 24. Chap. 54.17. & 58.15. and so some would here take it: and the time of harvest, termed *the day of inheritance*, or *possession*; because the fruits of the earth, and of men's labors are wont then to be inned, and enjoyed, Deut. 16.13, 14. Joel 1.5. but little difference there is, in the vowel points, between the word, in the one use, and in the other.

*{and desperate sorrow*} Or, *deadly pain*. So Jer. 30.17. from the same root is *man* termed *Enosh*, *miserable*, or *mortal*. See chap. 2.9. Some suppose the copulative here to be, but a mere expletive: as 2 Sam. 13.5. and so they knit the first words of the clause, with these last: *The heap of the crop* shall be *deadly pain*, or *grief*. In which sense if we take it, it may better be rendered, *The crop* shall be *a heap, and deadly pain*, or *grief*; that is, *an heap of deadly pain*, or, *grief*: as *a cloud and smoke*, for, *a cloud of smoke*, chap. 4.5. Others make it, a distinct branch, *and* there shall be *deadly pain*: as the last clause of ver. 9.

**V. 12.** *{Woe to the multitude of many people*} Some would knit the ensuing passage, to the foregoing part of this chapter; as if in these words were contained a reason of the *desperate grief* mentioned, ver. 11. to wit, the multitude of strange people breaking in upon God's people; which the prophet should here lament. But by the most, and best, they are deemed to belong to a new sermon, or prophecy; in regard whereof, some interpreters, rent off the three verses following from this chapter, and glue them on to the next, as if this parcel, and that chapter, made up one entire prophecy, or sermon. The reason they give of it, is, because these three verses contain a denunciation of judgment, against those people of several countries that assisted Sennacherib, and served under him, in his expedition against Judah, and Jerusalem; and the eighteenth chapter is against the Ethiopians, whose destruction God would have beforehand denounced, that God's people might not expect any aid from them, or any means to be used by them, to divert the Assyrian, from his intended invasion of it. But this seems but a weak ground, to make them one sermon: being of so divers subjects. Howbeit these words seem to begin a new, but short argument; and clearly to intend the downfall of those forces, that Sennacherib led against God's people. See chap. 30.28. & 36. & 37. Although there want not, that understand them, of such nations, as joined with the Syrians, and accompanied them in Ahaz his time, in the oppugnation of Jerusalem, Chap. 7.1. But the tenor of the text, and all the circumstances of it well weighed, carry it rather the former way.

*{woe*} Of this particle, see ch. 3.11. & 10.5. & 18.1. Some would have it rendered, *Alas*: as Joel 1.15.

*{the multitude of many people*} Or, as some, *to the tumult*, or, *noise, of many peoples*; (for the word is plural, as intimating, a variety of people, out of several countries, that served under the Assyrian. So Chap. 10.13, 14.) that is, say they, *to the many tumultuous people*, and it is true indeed, that the word rendered *multitude*, is sometime used for *tumult*, or *noise*, as chap. 31.4. Jer. 47.3. Amos 5.13. as also, that it is derived from a word, that has a notion of *noise*, or *tumult*, used in the very next clause, because multitudes meeting are commonly tumultuous: but neither does it always necessarily imply or import noise, and tumult: as Gen. 17.5. nor is there any need here to depart from the ordinary reading, and most general acception of the word, designing here the vast *multitude*, or number of them, joined in one body: as the other addition of *many people*, the multiplicity of nations, whereof that body consisted. Howbeit, because the ensuing parallel member may seem to plead for the former translation: to accord both members, it may well be rendered more fully, the *streperous*, or *tumultuous multitude*: as implying both their multitude, and the manner of their demeanor, See the next clause, and the next member: and Ezek. 30.10.

*{that make a noise like the noise of the seas*} Heb. *according to the seas making a noise*, See chap. 5.30. Jer. 6.23.

*{and to the rushing of nations*} Or, *rustling*, or, *tumultuous noise*, ch. 5.14. & 13.4. & 25.5. or *outrage* (ch. 37.28.) *of nations*: that is, *to the rustling*, or *tumultuous*, or *outrageous people*. See Jer. 47.3. Or, (which I take to be the most natural syntax: for, the *woe* is denounced to the persons, or people) *to the rustling*, or *raging*, and raging company, the abstract, for the concrete, *rustling rage*, for rustling, and *raging* company, as *pride*: for *a proud man*. Jer. 50.31. *folly*, for *a foolish man*. Prov. 24.9. See chap. 13.4.

*{that make a rushing, like the rushing of many waters*} Or, *that make a rustling*: or, *that rage according to the rustling*, or *rage of many waters*, Psal. 93.4. chap. 8.7. & 28.2. Jer. 51.55. Rev. 1.15. & 14.2. & 19.1, 6. See chap. 16.14. a defect of the relative is in either branch; as chap. 42.5.

**V. 13.** *{The nations shall rush, like the rushing of many waters*} *Rush*, that is, break in with rage: or *rustle*: break in with much noise. They shall break in with such a hideous noise, as the sea, or, some great river is wont to do, when it has broken through, or got over its sea walls, or banks, as if they would with a rage, and violence irresistible, bear down, and carry away all before them, chap. 8.7, 8. & 59.19. Jer. 51.42. See in what a blustering, and boisterous manner, the Assyrian broke in, Chap. 36.1–20.

*{but God shall rebuke them*} Heb. *and*, (as chap. 16.12.) *he shall rebuke him*, or, *one shall rebuke him*, that is, *he* (to wit, Sennacherib, with all his forces) *shall be rebuked*: by whom, but by God? Chapter 59.19. whose rebuke is not verbal: but real, and efficacious: able, not to still only, the noise and rage of the sea, Psalm 93.3, 4. and that with a word; Matth. 8.26, 27. Mar. 4.39, 41. but to dry it up, so that men may walk through it dryshod, Psal. 66.6. & 106.9. chap. 11.15. & 50.2. and much more to bring down, and abate the rage, and to still, and calm the tumultuous outrage of any persons, or people whatsoever, Psalm 91.5. & 65.7. & 68.30. & 76.6. ch. 25.5. See this effected, ch. 37.36.

*{and they shall flee far off*} Heb. *and he shall flee far off*: to wit, Sennacherib, who upon the discomfiture of his forces, by the ministry of an angel fled to Ninive, faster by much, than he came out from thence, ch. 31.9. & 37.37.

*{and shall be chased, as the chaff of the mountains before the wind*} As *chaff*, that the least puff of wind will anywhere easily drive before it, Psalm 1.4. & 35.5. and not *chaff in the floor*; Dan. 2.35. Hos. 13.3. but as *chaff of the mountains*: or, *chaff on a mountain*: as chap. 18.3. on some high place, where the wind has most power, and nothing either to restrain the force, and violence of it, or to stop, and stay that that is driven by it, Chap. 41.15, 16. Jer. 4.11, 12.

*{and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind*} The Hebrew word is commonly used for *a wheel*, as chap. 5.28. & 28.28. but in this place some suppose it, to signify, *thistledown*; others more generally, *a round wisp*, to wit, of stubble; or some other suchlike light stuff, Psalm 73.13. Job 21.18. Chapter 41.16. Jer. 15.24.

**V. 14.** *{And behold*} Take notice of, and consider seriously: a most strange, and sudden change, See chap. 3.1. & 7.14.

*{at evening tide trouble, and before morning he is not*} There is in the Hebrew, a transposition of one copulative; as Gen. 22.4. and the defect of another: as chap. 16.14. which makes the sentence the quicker. And it is indeed a brief, and concise, but quick, and lively description of a great and sudden alteration, within the space of a night, both in the condition of Ezekiah, & those besieged with him; and of Sennacherib, and his forces, that lay without in siege against them.

*{at evening tide trouble*} Or, *terror*, as it is commonly, and constantly rendered elsewhere, Job 18.11, 14. & 24.17. & 27.20. & 30.15. Psal. 73.19. Ezek. 26.21. & 27.36. & 38.19. All within Jerusalem overnight affrighted, and damped, with Rabshakeh's blusterings, and menaces, together with the consideration of the state of the whole country, about them, and a puissant army of so many thousands set down before them; so that well they may be deemed, to have been even at their wits' end, ch. 22.2, 5, 7. & 33.7, 8. & 36.1, 22. & 37.3.

*{before morning he is not*} Ere morning appear, he, and his, are all gone, there is not an enemy to be seen, chap. 37.36, 37. Thus weeping at even, and joy in the morning, Psal. 30.5. And he seems to compare the Assyrian to a tempest of wind, that rises, and blusters towards the evening, but is laid again, before the next day. Though some understand the whole of the Assyrian forces, that they were frighted in the night, by that sad, and sudden work, that the angel made among them; and fled away in the morning. So *evening* should be taken for *night*: as Gen. 1.5, 8. But the former seems more familiar.

*{this is the portion of them, that spoil us, and the lot of them, that rob us*} A sweet and comfortable close to God's people; but sad and dismal to all their opposites. Such success are they all like, yea sure in fine to have, that maliciously oppose, and impugn, God's people. See the like, but in way of a vote, Judg. 5.31. Psalm 83.9–18. There is in the words, a metaphor taken from portions, either of allowance of meat, or drink, Jer. 52.34. Dan. 1.5, 8. or of land, rather, and inheritance, divided among coheirs by lot; as Psalm 11.6. & 16.5, 5. Jer. 31.25. Act. 8.21. See the very like, in plainer terms, Job 20.19. Of the other two terms here used, rendered, *rob*, and *spoil*. See c. 10.2, 6, 13.

### CHAPTER 18

**V. 1.** *{Woe to the land*} A new sermon, or prophecy, here begins, as most generally agree, but against whom it is denounced, or whom it specially concerns, is much questioned by many. Some understand it, as menacing the ruin of Egypt: which others reject; because the very next is peculiarly, and directly addressed against that state. Others suppose, that it threatens the Ethiopians, whom they deem to be described in the first, and second verses. Others would have it meant of the Romans, by whom Jerusalem was destroyed. The Jewish doctors, of Gog, and Magog, to be destroyed in the days of their Messiah, Ezek. 38.4. And lastly, some Spanish writers, of the inhabitants of the new world in America, whom they vaunt of, as their converts. I suppose the prophecy to contain a denunciation of destruction against the Ethiopians, to be inflicted by the Assyrians, chap. 20.4. (with a promise of future restitution, ver. 7. in the times of Christ's kingdom:) but directed to the Egyptians, as their neighbors, Ezek. 29.10. and confederates, Ezek. 30.5. advising them by their ambassadors to advertise the Ethiopians, of their ruin approaching, Ezek. 30.9.

*{Woe to the land*} As spoken by way of denunciation, like that, chap. 17.12. But they who so take it, observe not, that the denunciation of evils here mentioned, is darted, not against the land, or people in this verse, described; but against the people deciphered in the next verse, whom, they are there willed to send a message to, to acquaint them therewith: as appears by verse 7. For those, and no other, are threatened with destruction, in the one place, unto whom restitution is promised in the other. I suppose rather therefore, that the word is here used in way of compellation: as ch. 55.1. Zach. 2.6. and so both the Jewish doctors, and some of ours also, here take it; rendering the words, not, *woe to the land*, but, *Ho the land*, &c. to wit, of Egypt. See the like diversity of exposition, ch. 10.5. & 29.1.

*{the land shadowing with wings*} This many interpreters apply to Ethiopia; or some part of it; reading the words, *the land of shadow of wings*; and understand thereby, some, *a land shadowed*, with a circle of mountains environing it. Others, with locusts, and flies, that abound in it, chap. 7.18. Joel 2.19. or, with flight of fowl, that at time of year, out of the colder regions, fly in great flocks thither. Others, a land *shadowing*, either the sea, which it lay upon, with the sails of their ships, which to them, are as *wings*, or the countries they trade unto with wares, and commodities, cap. 45.14. or, the lands, they invade, like *locusts*, Judg. 6.5. 2 Chr. 14.9. & 16.8. with the multitude of their troops, as *wings*; for so are *troops* sometime termed, Dan. 11.12. beside that, some would have it termed *a land of wings*, because it was divided, say they, into two parts, by the Red Sea, or Arabian Gulf, that severed them, the one from the other; the eastern containing some part of Arabia, and the western, that bordered upon Egypt. But others, rather, (whom I concur with, for the reason above rendered) understand the land of Egypt to be here deciphered. Which some of them suppose to be called, *the land of shadow of wings*, because it used to put other people, and God's people especially, Ezek. 31.6. & 29.16. in great hopes of ample protection from it, chap. 20.5, 6. & 30.2. & 31.1. & 36.6. now *shadow*, Num. 14.9. Judg. 9.15. Psalm 91.1. Eccl. 7.12. and *wings*, Deut. 32.11. Psalm 91.4. and *shadow of wings*, Psalm 17.8. & 36.7. & 57.1. are emblems of protection, and the word *shadow*, is here, say they, in a double form, to denote the amplitude of protection, that Egypt was wont to promise. But because the word here used is nowhere found, so to signify: but is used commonly and constantly, for *a cymbal*, or suchlike musical instrument, that makes a tinkling, or jingling sound, being shaken, or stricken with the hand, 2 Sam. 6.5. Psalm 150.1. Others therefore, and so the old Latin, render it, *the land of a cymbal*. Which title, or term, some suppose, to be given unto Egypt, as implying, it to be but a *jingling wing*; that promised much protection, but answered not expectation, chap. 20.6. & 30.5. & 36.6. Ezek. 29.6, 7. was like *a tinkling cymbal*, 1 Cor. 13.1. according to that, Jer. 46.17. *the King of Egypt is but a noise*; makes a great noise; but does nothing. Others suppose the land of Egypt, to be termed *a land of cymbals*, or, *jingles*; (the word taken collectively, as others the like, chap. 5.12.) in regard of that great abundance of jingling instruments, by the Greeks and Latins, termed *sistra*, used perpetually, in the superstitious rites of their goddess *Isis*; and so rife among them, or peculiar to them, that by other people it was termed, *Egyptian music*; and the same of so near affinity for sound, and handling, to the *Cymbal*; that the old Greek glossaries interpret the one sometime by the other: the one also is supposed by some to be mentioned with the other, where it is in our English, very unfitly, and no less diversely rendered, *fiddles*, by the ancienter translators; and *cornets*, by the latter, 2 Sam. 6.5. for the word is nowhere else found; but signifies such a kind of instrument as by motion and agitation, yielded a musical sound, as both *cymbals*, and these *jingles* did; for so we shall make bold to term them, until we have a fitter name for them. The difference between them was, that the one was of a spherical, the other of an oval form, made hoop-wise, with little bells hanging on the brims, or edges of it, which some suppose here, to be meant by *wings*, and this kind of instrument to be termed here *a cymbal of wings*, or, *a winged cymbal*, to distinguish it from the other kind, commonly so called. In regard hereof, therefore, might Egypt well be termed *the land of cymbals*, or, *jingles*; such kind of music being nowhere so rife as there, though for the other term of *wings*, some of those that thus understand the word *cymbal*, conceive that to look another way: and the word, *land*, as having reference to both, they render the text *a land of cymbals, a land of wings*: as if it were said *that jingling land of wings*, deeming it so to be called, because by the river Nilus, running through the whole body of it at length, chap. 19.5. it was divided, and parted into two moieties, lying on either side the river, *as two wings*: for so is the word used, chap. 11.12. & 24.16. However certain it is, that not Ethiopia, but Egypt, is here described.

*{which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia*} That is, as some, beyond those rivers, that out of Arabia empty themselves, either into the red, or the midland sea, or, as others, *besides*, or, on the side of: or, *on this side of*; as the word is oft used, Num. 21.13. & 22.1. & 32.19, 32. Josh. 22.7. 1 Sam. 14.1, 4. Job 1.19. See chap. 9.1. & Zeph. 3.10. However, we read it, the words here rather seems to design some other land, bordering near upon the Ethiopian coast, as Egypt does, Ezek. 29.10. than Ethiopia itself, beginning at the last cataract, or downfall of Nilus.

*{the rivers of Ethiopia*} That is, either those rivers that run into Nilus, whereof Astaboras, and Astapus, are said to be two principal ones, Strabo, *Geograph.* lib. 17. or Nilus itself, called the *Ethiopic river*, because from, and through that country, it comes down into Egypt, and in the plural, styled *rivers* here, as also, Ezek. 29.3, 4. either in regard of the rivers, that by the way it receives; or, of the watercourses drawn out of it, partly above, to abate its violent current: partly, beneath, for the benefit of the bordering places, Chap. 19.6. or, in regard of the several streams, and channels, that it runs in, both above, in Ethiopia, where by branching itself, it makes sundry great islands, whereof Meroe a chief one: Strabo, lib. 1. & 16. Pliny l. 5. c. 9. as also below, in Egypt, where by seven famous channels, it empties itself into the midland sea, chap. 11.15. Or, as some; the rivers of that part of Arabia, which the Chusites inhabited, lying between Judea and Egypt, running, as the brook of *Rhinocorura*, into the lake of Sirbon, and *Besor*, into the Mediterranean sea, and *Ceris*, with some others, into the red sea. See Herodot. l. 2. & Strabo, l. 17.

*{of Ethiopia*} Heb. *Cush*, as Chap. 11.11; a country so called, because inhabited by the posterity of *Cush*, the son of *Cham*, or *Ham*, Gen. 10.6. 1 Chr. 1.8, 10. Who at first seem to have sat down in, and peopled some part of Arabia, Gen. 2.13. Num. 12.1. 2 Chr. 14.9, 14. and in process of time, not only to have extended their habitation unto the shore of the red sea, but to have pierced also, into the islands that are scattered here and there, about the mouth of the same: and from thence (which was no difficult matter for them to do) to have wafted over in the African continent: wherein, on the south of Egypt, they at length settled themselves: And hence that division of them, into the *Eastern*, and *Western*, the *Asian*, and *African Ethiopians*, or *Cushites*, of which may be seen Herodotus, liber 7. and Strabo, liber 1. and may help to reconcile the differences that are among writers, concerning the place of their abode.

**V. 2.** *{That sendeth Ambassadors by the Sea*} This *sending of Ambassadors by Sea*, some understand of the Ethiopians: on the one side of the red sea, sending over to them that inhabited on the other side, for the levying of forces to go forth with them, to war against the Assyrians, or some other common enemy. Others, of sending out heralds of arms, to defy the Assyrian, and bid them battle. To which purpose, they suppose to make, that rumor of Tarhakah, the Ethiopians coming against Sennacherib, Chap. 37.9. Others, of the Egyptians sending, as some, to the Jews, to put them in hope of supplies, and assistance against the Assyrians: or, as other rather, to the Ethiopians, to inform them of the Assyrian preparations against them, and the evils, that from them they were like to sustain.

*{Ambassadors*} As Josh. 9.4. Ch. 57.9. Jer. 49.14. or, *Messengers*; for the word is general, Prov. 13.17. & 25.13. Howbeit, because the word is found used for *images*, chap. 45.16. Some would have it here so to signify, understanding this passage, not of sending *messengers*; but of sending Osiris his head; as Lucian tells the tale: or an epistle, as some of the Greek Fathers (to bring it nearer home to their version) concerning the reviving of Adonis, put up in an earthen pot, and so cast into the sea, to arrive beyond sea, at Byblos, which by the Devil's help, within a few days, it used to do. But neither is this relation of any certainty, nor is there any mention of *images* in it: nor appear therein the *paper-boats* spoken of in the text: and what is called *Tsirim* here, is in the next branch termed *maleachim*, which is, questionless, *messengers*, and small reason therefore to depart from the version received.

*{by the sea*} The red sea; that runs along by the coast of Egypt, and Ethiopia, on the one side: and of Arabia, on the other side: called therefore, *the gulf of Arabia*, as that other beyond it, *the Persian gulf*. See Jer. 49.14.

*{even*} Heb. *and.* But some suppose the copulative to be here redundant; as ch. 17.11.

*{in vessels of bulrushes*} Heb. *of rush.* For the word is general, of all kind of *rush*, Job 8.11. so called, of a word that signifies *to drink*, Gen. 24.27. because *rushes* require moisture, and thrive not, but in miry and watery places, Job 8.11. chap. 35.7. But it is here taken collectively; for *rushes*; as Exod. 2.3. And some suppose it to be used here, in way of derision, as scoffing at the aid that the Egyptians should undertake to afford the Jewish people, against the enemy, whoever he were, as if it were said, You will send them supplies *in vessels of rush*, or, *in paper-boats*, as we use to say, (for their *paper* was a kind of *rush*) the matter of your shipping, and the supplies you send in them, will be the one like the other. But he seems rather to speak here of their ordinary manner of sending messages, and passing to and fro, in those parts, in boats, or vessels made of *paper*, (not such as we now use, but such as was anciently used; for writing, and was most plentiful in Egypt) and of other the like kind of *rush*, and *reed*, whereof they had great store, Ch. 19.6, 7. And of such kind of vessels they had much use, both in Ethiopia and in Egypt; partly, for expedition, and partly, for safety, in shallow waters especially, in regard of shelves and rocks, and in steep downfalls, and stiff streams of rivers, which other vessels, of matter less pliant, would not so well brook. These, both the Ethiopians, and Egyptians, much used, in the downfalls of Nilus, as Strab. lib. 17. The rather, because they could easily draw them ashore, carry them on their shoulders over land, and put them beneath into the water again, Plin. lib. 5. ch. 9. The Egyptians very much, also, in that river, as Plin. l. 7. c. 56. but especially in their yearly deluge, when their whole country, the cities only and higher ground excepted, lay all under water, and was, generally, on float: as Lucane, lib. 4. Of these *paper-barks*, Theophrast. lib. 4. c. 9. Strabo, l. 17. and Plin. l. 6. c. 22. & l. 13. c. 11. Though Herodote, l. 2. speaks of another kind of shipping, that they had for burden: and of some *earthen boats* of potters work, that they used sometime in the river, Strab. l. 17. and Juvenal, sat. 15.

*{upon the waters*} Heb. *upon the face*, or, *surface of the waters*; as Gen. 1.2. & 7.18. Here the phrase is the rather used, because these kind of boats or, barks, did rather float, and glide on the top of the water, than dive anything into it, not drawing much water, as those of plank and timber usually do.

*{saying*} This word is not in the original. Yet either the same as Ps. 105.14, 15. Act. 7.32. or somewhat the like, as Ps. 27.8. is necessarily to be supplied. Those that suppose the words following to be spoken in the person, either of the Ethiopians, or Egyptians themselves, as delivering instructions to those that they sent, supply, *saying*. Those that take them, as spoken in the person of God, or the prophet from God, supply, *say*, as enjoining, or advising the Egyptians; what message God would have them send to their friends and allies, as ch. 22.15.

*{Go ye swift messengers*} Heb. *light*; as ch. 19.1. Either alluding to the lightness of their passage-boats, above mentioned. Or, because lightness is a means of swiftness, as heaviness of slowness, in motion. In whose person they are spoken, was before specified.

*{to a Nation*} The Assyrians, say some, the Israelites, say others: but neither sort find any mention what their message should be: and so dispatch messengers without a message. I suppose it rather, the nation, here described, to be the Ethiopians, whom the Egyptians should send to.

*{scattered*} Or, as some, *outspread.* Heb. *protracted*, drawn out at length. Used of time; as Prov. 13.12. Ch. 13.22. Ezek. 12.18. Or of place, as Judg. 4.6. ch. 5.18. That which the Jewish doctors understand of the Israelites driven out of their country, and dispersed by the enemy. Some of ours, of the Assyrian, drawn far away from his country, and in war now against Judea, ch. 5.27. But others, rather, of the Ethiopians, called, *a scattered*, or *dispersed people*; in regard of the large territory, or land overspread with them, reaching part of it from the Persian gulf to the red sea, and part of it again from the red sea, to the main ocean. Though some expound it in a future notion, as spoken by way of prediction, *to be dissipated, and dispersed.* The like whereunto, see Psalm 137.7. ch. 27.13. Nor want there, that expound it *people of long stature*, from chapter 45.14. But I find not the word anywhere so used.

*{and peeled*} Or, as some, *to be peeled*; as before: that is, stripped of all. A metaphor taken from the pulling off hair; either from head, or beard, Ez. 9.30. Neh. 13.25. ch. 50.6. which some apply to the present estate of the Jews; some to the future, of the Ethiopians, by the Assyrian to be despoiled. Some to the Assyrian, as exhausted, and left bare of their soldiery. But it may well, in his native and proper sense, be understood of the Ethiopians, being *a peeled*, and beardless people. For the word imports a want of hair, Levit. 13.40, 41. Little whereof is found on Ethiopian bodies, by reason of the heat of their country. For the word *polished*, by which some render it, because it is of iron and brass, and instruments made of either, so used, 1 King. 7.45. Ezek. 21.9, 10, 11, 28. is not so fit here.

*{to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto*} Heb. *from him*: or, *from that, and further.* The phrase is used, either of time, as Levit. 22.26. Num. 15.23. Or, of place as 1 Sam. 10.4. & 20.22. Some take it, here, in the latter sense; and of these, some understand it of the Assyrians, that were terrible to other nations, as well on this side, as beyond them. Others, of those Ethiopians that dwelt farthest in the inland parts, more remote from the sea, and from society with other people. And therefore, as the more black and grim, so more horrid and savage. But the message seems to concern the Ethiopians in general, not any special part of them.
