Others therefore, following the Latin, read it, *Beyond whom there is no other.* Either in regard of situation say some, or in regard of fierceness, say others: but I see not how the text will bear either. Those that take the phrase in the former sense, understanding it of continuance of time, as our English, and many others do, apply it, some to the Jewish people, who were terrible to other nations, from the time that God first made a nation of them, and long after, in regard of those strange works, that God, at several times wrought for them, Deut. 4.34. Josh. 2.9, 10. & 5.1. 2 Chr. 20.29. or in regard of their dreadful judgments, that at sundry times he executed upon them for their sins, such as might well strike a terror into all that saw, or heard of them, Deut. 28.28, 37. Jer. 18.16. & 19.8. & 24.9. & 25.9, 18. as some would have it. Or, as some of the Jewish writers, in regard of both. But other again, understand it of the Assyrians, who had anciently been a terrible people, and subduers of other nations; the Assyrian monarchy, or tyranny rather, being of the greatest antiquity of any, at least, since the flood, Gen. 10.8–11. and endured, in likelihood, as long as any. But those that so apply it, may do well to consider, that the first founder, and raiser of that kingdom, was an Ethiopian, or a Cushite, Nimrod the great hunter, the prime son of Cush. Nor was it called the Assyrian monarchy, at first, as founded, or possessed by Ashur, the son of Sem, Gen. 10.22. or any of his issue; but might so be called, because Nimrod the Cushite, having in his conquests, (after the interruption of Babel, in which intended structure, he seems to have had a chief hand) pierced into that country, which Assur and his issue, at first, quietly possessed, did therein build the city of Niniveh, and made it the head-city of his dominions, and so is that of Moses to be understood, Gen. 10.10, 11. This application, therefore, of these words to the Assyrians, leads us home, as by the hand, to the right owners of it: and directly points, as with the finger, to the persons intended in them: To wit, the Ethiopians, or Cushites, a terrible nation from the first: and no other also, in succeeding ages: The greatest number of men, being brought into the field by their king, that is read of in Scripture, or, I suppose, in any other story. See 2 Chr. 14.9. & 16.8. There is an ellipsis, in the phrase, *from that*: that is, *from that day*, or time. As it is more fully expressed, Numb. 15.23. 1 Sam. 18.9. Ezek. 39.22. as having relation to their first original, since they began to be a people.

*{a nation meted out*} Heb. *a nation of line line.* And the word signifies sometime *a line* of letters, figures, or words in a book; as Chap. 28.10, 13. Whence some of the Jewish commenters, applying this to their own people, whom they imagine to be here intimated, would have it to contain a reason of their then low condition, because they had no more knowledge of God and his law, (Chap. 27.11.) than little children; (Chap. 28.9.) that must be taught, *line after line*, and letter after letter, Chap. 28.10. But neither is the phrase here and there alike, nor does it suit so well here, either with the foregoing, or the ensuing branches. But the word most usually, imports, *a measuring-line*, as in that very place also, Ch. 28.17. and elsewhere, Job 38.5. Jer. 31.39. Ezek. 47.3. And this was used, sometime, to build by, Zach. 1.16. Or, to rule, square, and cut out by, ch. 44.13. in which sense some take it here. A nation that takes upon it to give laws, and rules to others; applying it to the Assyrians, as usurping a power of command over other people. Sometime it is used to destroy by, to mete out, who, or what, how much, or how many, shall be destroyed: or having pulled down lofty and stately buildings, to lay the places, where before they stood, level with the other ground, 2 Sam. 8.2. 2 King. 21.13. Psal. 60.8. Ch. 34.11. Lam. 2.8. and so here some take it, but understanding it, some actively, *a nation, that meteth out* other people to destroy them: Others, passively, *a nation meted out*, or, *shortly to be meted out to conculcation*, or destruction. To which purpose also, one of the Jewish writers, affirming it to be a proverbial speech with them, and joining this, and the next branch together, expounds it, *by little and little to be destroyed*, and another of them, as implying the cause of their destruction, as in way of retribution, *measure by measure*: the evil of punishment being meted out unto them, according to the measure of the evil of their sin, which they indeed apply to their own people, but may with better ground, and more agreeably to the scope of the text, be understood concerning the Ethiopians, as designed by God to destruction: letting pass these latter niceties. I am not ignorant, that some of ours understand it of these, render the words, *dispersed here and there*, as having reference to the manner of the Ethiopian habitations, having no cities, but villages, scattered here and there, Hab. 3.14. which I should not reject, if the words of the text would yield it.

*{and trodden down*} Heb. *and of conculcation*, or, *treading down*: as Chap. 22.5. rendered also *destruction*, 2 Chro. 22.7. Now the nation here mentioned, is termed, *a nation of treading down*; either actively, as some, understanding it of the Assyrians, because they trod down, that is, vanquished and subdued other people, Chap. 10.6. & Psal. 44.5. & 60.12. or, as others, rather, passively, a nation trodden down by others, as the Jews expounding it of themselves, Chap. 5.5. & 51.23. or, a nation to be trodden down very shortly, understanding it of the Ethiopians, to be subdued, and captived by the Assyrians, Chap. 20.4. Or, lastly, as some other; an *abject* people, kept under in extreme slavery, both at home, and abroad: but the former, concerning their condition shortly to ensue, seems best to suit with the prophet's intent here.

*{whose lands the rivers have spoiled*} The form of the verb here used, being singular, and nowhere else found, has in part, occasioned variety of expositions. Some supposing it to be the same with a word used, Chap. 17.14. & 42.22, 24. that signifies *to spoil*, and *plunder*. Others, with another word used, Chap. 37.22. & 49.7. & 53.3. that signifies *to slight*, *to despise*: again to some, they seem to be part of the description of the nation before mentioned, whereas others deem them, to be the sum of a message sent to them. Those that take it the former way, applying it to the land of Israel, read the words, as we render them; and expound them of such direption, and spoil, as the Assyrians, and other their enemies, had made among them, chap. 8.4. & 36.1. But those of them, that understand it of Ethiopia, read the words in the present tense, *whose land the rivers spoil*, or *tear asunder*; and expound it of the great rivers, Niger, and Nilus, that cut through their land, and by their frequent inundations, wash away the fat of their soil. Howbeit, this may seem not so probable, because with the Egyptians, those deluges have a contrary effect, making their country, by the more watering of it, the more fat and fertile: the abate and restraint whereof, is therefore menaced, as a judgment, and a curse, ch. 19.5–10. Ezek. 30.12. As for those that take this passage, as the content of the message, sent by the messengers, before mentioned, they, some of them understand them, as to be delivered from the Ethiopians to the Assyrians, and read, according to the latter signification of the word, above noted, to tell them, (as in way of contempt and defiance) *that the rivers* (to wit, of Ethiopia; of which v. 1. that is, the people of that country) *despise* (contemn, and set light by) *his land*: howsoever dreadful and terrible he may appear unto other people. Not unlike to that, ch. 37.22. But other of them, conceiving it as a message, sent by God's direction, from Egypt to Ethiopia, read and render it, according to the former signification of the word, to tell them, *that the rivers*, or, *floods will spoil their land*: that is, that the forces of the king of Assyria, Ch. 20.4. breaking in upon them, like the strong streams of some great river, ch. 8.7, 8. will overflow their land, not as Niger and Nilus, or Astaboras, and Astaphus use to do, to water and enrich it; but to plunder and spoil it; to sweep all away before them, as great land-floods are wont to do. Ch. 28.2, 17. This, the rather, I concur with, because I find the like in Ezekiel of messengers, by God's appointment, to be sent unto the Ethiopians, informing them of great pains that should come upon them to make them afraid, Ezek. 30.9. The relative for the conjunction, *that*, as Deut. 4.40. Neh. 2.6, 7. For I cannot assent to that learned writer, who supposing the message to be sent, not from any one nation to another, but by God himself to one and the same people, described, v. 1, 2. would have the subject matter of it to be related, ver. 3.

**V. 3.** *{All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth*} After this warning, or advertisement, willed to be given unto Ethiopia, by Egypt, concerning those calamities that were to befall them; the prophet turns his speech unto the wide world; as in the name of God, calling upon the inhabitants thereof, to consider, and observe, the manner of his proceedings, and the passages of his providence, when he shall begin to muster those forces which he purposes to employ, for the effecting of the judgments denounced against that people, and to expect the issue of it. See the like, Psalm 46.8. Chap. 33.13. so thereby withal giving assurance, that the execution of the same should be so remarkable, and so conspicuous, that notice should be taken of it, throughout the whole world; that the whole world should ring of it. See the like, Jer. 49. 21. & 50. 46.

*{See ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains*} When God calls those together, whom he means to make use of, as by an ensign to that purpose set up on the top of some high hill, ch. 5. 26. & 13. 2. For the Hebrew commenters are wide, when they expound it of God's gathering his people together out of the places of their captivity: as ch. 11. 12. Or, *as when an ensign is lift up upon a mountain, ye shall see it*. The judgment executed upon them, shall be so conspicuous, that you shall as easily see it, as a banner erected on the tops of a mountain, for any special use, and purpose, is of all seen, far, and near.

*{when he lifteth up an ensign*} That is, when God shall lift it up, as most expound it, or *when I shall lift up*, as some render it. The Hebrew is, *as in lifting up*; or, *according to the lifting up of an ensign*; (for the infinitive in the Hebrew, is also as a gerund) that is, as when one lifts up an ensign, or, when an ensign is lift up. So 1 Sam. 15. 22. *as in obeying the voice of the Lord*; that is, as when one obeys the voice of the Lord: or, as when the voice of the Lord is obeyed. See also, ver. 5. ch. 64. 2. Jer. 5. 26.

*{on the mountains*} Or, *upon a mountain*: a defect of the preposition; as Deut. 33. 19. ch. 17. 13. and *mountains*, for, *mountain*: as Gen. 8. 4.

*{see ye*} Heb. *ye shall see it*. A want of the pronoun; as Psal. 37. 34. & 91. 8. ch. 9. 9. Hosh. 8. 4.

*{and when he bloweth a trumpet*} When God blows his trumpet to summon his soldiers, and servitors, to make their appearance, as Jer. 4. 5. & 6. 1. or, to set them on upon their service, as Zach. 9. 14. For the Jewish writers are too far out of the way, in expounding it, of the *trumpet* mentioned, chap. 27. 13. The Hebrew is, *as in sounding a trumpet*; that is, as when one blows a trumpet; or, as when a trumpet is blown; as before.

*{hear ye*} Heb. *ye shall hear*, to wit, *it*; as before: that which is now foretold you, ch. 12. 5.

**V. 4.** *{For so the Lord said unto me*} Or, *Thus hath the Lord said unto me*. God has, in these words, acquainted me with his counsel, and purpose herein; to wit, in letting out the rein unto the Assyrian, for some space of time, and permitting him to subdue, and make havoc of many people, ch. 10. 5–10.

*{I will take my rest*} Heb. *I will rest, or be quiet*, ch. 7. 4. & 14. 7. & 57. 20. I will sit still, not offering to interrupt the Assyrian, but suffering him to proceed in his designs, and attempts, for a time: See Psal. 83. 1.

*{and I will consider in my dwelling place*} Though I seem to sit still, as an idle spectator of what is done in the world; yet from the place of mine heavenly habitation, I behold and take notice of the courses and carriages of men on the earth, Psal. 2. 4. & 11. 4, 5. & 33. 13, 14. Or, *but*; or, *yet, I will look to, or, upon my dwelling*. I will have an eye to my church, the place of my special residence on earth, to Jerusalem, and mount Sion, where my temple is, to protect, to rescue, to relieve, to refresh it, Psal. 132. 13–17. Chap. 37. 29–31.

*{consider*} Heb. *behold, look to, or look after*, it implies a providence, and care, employed for the good of the thing looked to, or looked after, Psal. 102. 19. chap. 57. 15. & 66. 2. Or, *look upon*, so the rather, in regard of what follows, I will lift up the light of my countenance upon it, Psal. 4. 6. I will cause my face to shine on it, Numb. 6. 25.

*{my dwelling place*} Heb. *set, or, settled dwelling*; and this, with God, is heaven above, 1 King. 8. 39, 43, 49. his sanctuary, a type of his church, on earth, Exod. 15. 2, 17. 1 King. 8. 13. Dan. 8. 11.

*{like a clear heat upon herbs*} Heb. as some of the Jewish doctors, *upon the herb*; as they take the word, Chap. 26. 19. 2 King. 4. 29. as other of them, and so the most; *upon rain*, or *after rain*, as they suppose it to be used, Job 36. 31. & 37. 11. See chap. 24. 15. The meaning is, that the Lord would look out, and shine forth upon his church, though he suffered them, also, to be for a while under a cloud; as the clear sunshine (for from the word here used, has the sun its name, Chap. 24. 22. & 30. 26. See on chap. 17. 8.) upon tender herbs, and plants, after a shower of rain; which is wont to make them suddenly to sprout out, and shoot up. See 2 Sam. 23. 4. Psal. 72. 6. Hos. 14. 5. and of the complement, ch. 37. 31.

*{and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest*} A *cloud of dew*, or, a dewy cloud, not of rain, or rainy: such as may relieve the harvestman in the heat of the day, and yet not hurt the corn, chap. 25. 5. See chap. 4. 5. For rain in harvest is hurtful, Prov. 26. 1. See Jer. 5. 24. Nor can I here accord with them, though men of great note, that turn the text a clean contrary way, understanding the words; the former of such a torrid heat, as scorches, and kills herbs, the latter, of such a dew, or rain, as coming in harvest time, out of season, when heat rather is needful for the ripening and hardening of the grain, does corrupt, and spoil the crop. Prov. 25. 13. & 26. 1. Which they expound, some, to be a threatening of famine; other of them, a prediction of such evils, as from the Assyrian king, should befall God's people: and other again, of that destruction, that from God should befall the Assyrians. And to this purpose, a late writer of note thus reads the whole passage, *Should I rest, and look on in my place?* (To wit, while the adversary makes untimely havoc of my people, before my judgments are come to maturity, vers. 5.) that would be *as parching heat to herbs, as clouds* sending down *dew*, or, *rain, in harvest*; all then would be spoiled. But the words seem to me clear for the former sense.

**V. 5.** *{For afore the harvest, &c.*} He returns, here, to show the effects of God's sitting still, and looking on, while the Assyrian proceeded in his achievements; to wit, the untimely ruin and destruction of the Ethiopian estate, while it was yet in such a flourishing condition, as might seem to give great hopes of further growth, and afford fair promises of long continuance, and this set forth, by the resemblance of a vine, or other plant, that is pruned in an unseasonable time; or, a tree, that is lopped, and cut down, ere her fruit come to maturity, when she is full of leaves, and blossoms, in the prime of her pride, Job 15. 32, 33. & 18. 16. Psalm 37. 2, 35, 36. & 49. 14. & 52. 5. & 55. 23. & 73. 18–20. & 92. 7, 12, 13. & 94. 23.

*{For*} Or, *But yet*; as Psal. 118. 17. Chap. 9. 1. Though I have an eye to mine own; yet this people, whom I will have to be destroyed, I will leave to the enemy.

*{afore*} *Before harvest* comes; as 1 Sam. 9. 15. *before Saul* came: & Job 3. 24. *before my meat*; that is, before I eat. Heb. *at the face of harvest*, that is, as some take it, when the harvest is coming, is near at hand, as Prov. 18. 12. *at the face of destruction*, that is, when it is approaching: according to which acception, it might be rendered, *toward harvest time*, but the former sense the plainer, and more common.

*{the harvest*} The word includes, as well the time of plucking fruit, and gathering grapes, as of cutting, and inning corn: as well vintage, as harvest, strictly so termed. See ch. 17. 10, 11.

*{when the bud is perfect*} Or, *as when* (see ver. 3.) *the bud is gone*, (as Deut. 3. 14. for the word signifies either) as when the bud that first appears, is become a perfect, but a green, and unripe grape, which, says the Jewish doctor, is with them, in the month Sivan, which in part, answers our May.

*{and the sour grape is ripening in the flower*} Or, *and the unripe, or, green grape is producing* (so the word is used, Num. 17. 8.) *its flower*, or, *the flower*, See Gen. 40. 10. Cant. 6. 11. & 7. 12.

*{he shall both*} Heb. *and he shall*, as chap. 14. 22. Or, the copulative is redundant, as Zach. 2. 6. Howbeit, I suppose it may well stand in his native notion, and use, as a copulative, the words being thus rendered; *But yet afore harvest time, as when the bud is past, and the green grape is about producing its flower, and one cut off* (that is, *if one cut off*) *the sprigs*, and so forth.

*{cut off the sprigs with pruning-hooks*} Or, *the sprigs* (the small tender twigs: the word is nowhere else used) *shall be cut off with pruning-hooks*, so called from that use of them, chap. 2. 4. That which is not wont to be done with vines, or other plants, by those that prune them, for the bettering of them, and to make them the more fruitful, Joh. 15. 2. at such time, when their fruit is green upon them, and making on to maturity; for that were to destroy both fruit and plant: and the *cutting* therefore here intimated, being thus described, appears thereby to be intended, for the destruction of them, against whom it was denounced, not for their correction, or cure. The verb is impersonally, and indefinitely here used, of which manner of speech, see on ch. 2. 19. so that we need not supply either, *the Lord*, with some; or the *King of Assyria*, with others. Though it is true, that God, and by him, would do it, chap. 20. 4; much less, as some others do, to put in the *vine-dresser*, who is not wont to dress his vines, on this manner.

*{and take away, and cut down the branches*} Heb. *and the branches* (to wit, the great spreading boughs, resembling the better, or greater sort of persons with them, Jer. 48. 32.) *he will take away, and cut down*; or, *remove by cutting down*: this latter word, is nowhere else read in Scripture. But the Jewish commenters upon the place, tells us, that with their Talmudists it is used for *to cut off*, or, *to take away*, as when they say, *to cut off*, or, *to take away* one's *head*, and a word drawn from it, for *an evil spirit*, that takes men's wits away from them: according whereunto, the words may be here rendered; *the spreading branches he will remove, and take away*; that is, *they shall be removed, and carried away*: the verb is, as the former, indefinite. So Gen. 41. 13. Luk. 12. 20.

*{sprigs, and branches*} Both the small, and the great ones, ch. 9. 14. & 10. 33.

**V. 6.** *{They shall be left together, unto the fowls of the mountains; and to the beasts of the earth*} To wit, the sprigs, and branches, so cut off, and cast away, like matter of no use or worth; as the cuttings, or shreddings of a vine, or other plant, oft-times are, by those that regard them not, ch. 17. 9. & 27. 10. Ezek. 15. 2–4. especially, when the fruit that is on them, is immature, and unfit for man's food, and are let lie therefore, on heaps, not looked after, for birds to sit, and beasts to browse on, and both to make meat of; the birds of the fruit, and the beasts, of the branches, Ezek. 31. 13.

*{left together*} One with another; without respect had to their former, either meanness, or greatness, as if they made all but one heap, Chap. 17. 11.

*{fowls*} Heb. *fowl*, as Ezek. 39. 4. properly, fowl of prey, Gen. 15. 11. 1 Sam. 14. 33. & 25. 14. chap. 46. 11. Jer. 12. 9.

*{of the mountains*} On which fowl of prey, especially, do usually breed, and abide.

*{beasts*} Heb. *beast*, as Jer. 15. 3. and as *fowl* before.

*{of the earth*} Opposed to the fowl of the *heaven*, or, of the *air*, Deut. 28. 26. Jer. 15. 3. or, *of the land*, of the country they lived in; as Exod. 23. 29.

*{and the fowls shall summer upon them, and all the beasts of the field shall winter upon them*} That is, both the one and the other, shall abide by them, find harbor with them, and feed upon them, all the year long. For we are not so to conceive it, as if the meaning were, that the fowl, and the beasts should divide the year between them; that the fowl should summer, but not winter with them; the beasts should winter, but not summer with them, but that both winter, and summer, either of them, should make their abode with them, finding matter sufficient, such as they desire, and delight in, to detain them there, from summer to winter, and from winter to summer, from the one end of the year, to the other. Of such like distributions, in this prophet very frequent, see on cap. 5. 1. 4. and we need not therefore stand upon that nicety of some of the Jewish commenters, of fowl abounding more in summer time, and beasts in winter. The words import a great, and continued waste: Which some understand of the wealth of the land, and the people therein abiding; being exposed as a prey, to those by whom they were subdued, or to the spoil of thieves and robbers, either of their own, or from abroad. Others, of the carcasses of men slain in great multitudes, and so left to be devoured by birds and beasts, Psalm 79. 2. Thus they, who expound it of the Ethiopians. For I pass by those of the Jewish writers, and some also of ours, who understand it, either of the host of Gog, and Magog, Ezek. 39. 4. or of Sennacherib's army, chap. 37. 37. neither of which I conceive to be so probable. Both the verses I suppose, may be thus rendered, and knit together; But yet, with those other people, it shall be, (see the like ellipsis, Matth. 25. 14.) *as when afore harvest-time, the bud being gone, and the green grape about producing the flower, and the sprigs be cut off with pruning-hooks, and the spreading branches be removed, and taken away, they are left together*; (to wit, those sprigs, and branches, so cut off) or, (as some other likewise render it) *So shall they* (to wit, those people, like to those sprigs, and branches) *be left together*, &c.

**V. 7.** *{In that time*} That is, after this judgment executed upon the Ethiopians, in the days of the Messiah; as chap. 11. 11. & 19. 18, 19. A prophecy of the conversion of the Ethiopians unto Christ, by the ministry of the gospel: the firstfruits whereof, we have in that noble courtier instructed by Philip, Act. 8. 27, 39.

*{shall the present be brought to the Lord of hosts*} The Ethiopians shall yield up themselves to God, (whom they shall then know, and acknowledge, to be the Lord of hosts, Psal. 24. 8, 10. Ezek. 30. 8.) and to his Christ; and shall show, and manifest their submission by spiritual sacrifices, and oblations offered unto him, Psal. 68. 31. Zeph. 1. 10. Mal. 1. 11. Act. 8. 27, 37. as subjects declare their homage, and allegiance to their sovereign, by presents; 2 Sam. 8. 6. 2 King. 17. 4. 2 Chr. 17. 11. Psal. 68. 29. & 72. 10. & 76. 11. chap. 16. 1. That which yet some expound of the prey taken from Sennacherib's army, ch. 33. 23. consecrated to God's service: as Num. 31. 28–47, 50–54. see Jer. 51. 44.

*{of a people scattered, and peeled*} Or, *from a people scattered, and peeled*, the word, *from*, here wanting: as ch. 2. 2. is supplied from the next clause: as ch. 13. 13. & 30. 17.

*{from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto, a nation meted out, and trodden under feet*} See of all this, v. 2.

*{whose land the rivers have spoiled*} That being now effected, whereof before they were advertised, v. 2.

*{to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts*} To the place, where God's worship shall then be settled; as sometime it was at Jerusalem, Deut. 12. 5, 11, 14. Act. 8. 27. Joh. 4. 21, 23.

*{the mount Zion*} A type of the church, ch. 2. 2, 3.

### CHAPTER 19

**V. 1.** *{The burden of Egypt*} An heavy prophecy concerning Egypt. See ch. 13. 1. As the prophecy in the foregoing chapter, was against Ethiopia; so this is against Egypt: and the next after it, against both jointly, in regard of their vicinity, and mutual confederacy. See likewise against Egypt, Jer. 43. 10. & 44. 30. & 46. 2, 13. Ezek. 29. & 30. & 31. 2, 18. & 32.

*{Egypt*} Heb. *Mitsraim*. So termed, from one of Cham's sons of that name, Gen. 10. 6. whose posterity seated themselves in that country: the name, Egypt, we have from the Greeks, whose grammarians and historians say, some of them, that it had that name from an ancient king that there reigned: Others, from the river Nilus, that runs through it, as being at first the name, not of the country, but of the river; and that from the color of the water thereof, black like a *vulture*. See Sihor, ch. 23. 3. Jer. 2. 18.

*{Behold*} An usual beginning with the prophets, this especially; requiring attention to God's messages, brought by them, and stirring up men's minds to a serious and sedulous consideration of the matter therein contained. So ch. 7. 14. & 24. & 32. 1. The chapter consists of two parts; the former, concerning the calamities and ruin of the Egyptian state: the latter, concerning their restitution, and return unto God, v. 18. &c.

*{the Lord rideth*} A description of God coming in judgment against Egypt, together with the sad and dismal effects thereof.

*{the Lord rideth*} Heb. *riding*; as speaking of a thing present: as ch. 3. 1. and a thing that he saw, Chap. 2. 1. as if he beheld the Lord riding in pomp and state toward Egypt, as judges use to do unto the places, where they are to hold their session, or assize, Judg. 5. 10. & 12. 14. 1 Sam. 7. 16. or, in a warlike manner, leading his troops, and riding before them, as princes do, when they go out into the field, 2 Sam. 18. 9. Psalm 18. 10. & 45. 4. Hab. 3. 8. Rev. 6. 2. & 19. 11, 14.

*{upon a swift cloud*} Heb. *light*, as chap. 18. 11. Jer. 2. 23. because lightness causes swiftness. God is said *to ride*, as *upon the heavens*, Psal. 68. 4, 33. so, *to make the clouds his chariots*, Psal. 114. 3. and here, *to come riding into Egypt upon a cloud*, as to intimate an impossibility of keeping him out, from entrance upon any land he comes to invade; who comes riding not on the ground below, but aloft in the air, Psal. 18. 11, 12. Matth. 24. 30. Rev. 1. 7. so more specially here, to note his sudden and unexpected coming, against Egypt, because clouds must needs be very rare in those parts, where ordinarily, it never rains, Deut. 11. 10, 11. See Ezek. 30. 3. and, not on a cloud only, but on *a light, or swift cloud*; as elsewhere, *upon the wings of the wind*, Psal. 18. 10. & 104. 3. thereby to signify, the speedy execution, and accomplishment of the judgment against Egypt, here denounced. So chapter 13. 22. Ezek. 12. 27, 28.

*{and shall come into Egypt*} Or, as the word may well be rendered, *and coming into*, or *entering upon Egypt*, yea, or, *coming against Egypt*; as Gen. 33. 1. *behold Esau coming*; for the preposition is wanting: as 2 King. 8. 7. & 10. 17. 1 Chr. 19. 13. and the prophet speaks it, as if he saw God, in some visible, but stately, and majestical manner, either marching on against Egypt, or falling in upon it, not unlike one of the *Levant spouts*, as they commonly call them, wherein a vast cloud full of water, suddenly falls, and bears down all that it lights upon: peradventure alluded to, Ezek. 30. 18. where mention is of *a cloud, that should cover Egypt*. See the like expressions of things; as in present view, chap. 7. 14. & 10. 18–32. & 13. 4, 5.

*{and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence*} There were two things that the Egyptians trusted much unto; the multitude of their idols, and the might of their men; but the prophet here tells them, that neither of these should stand them in any stead. For that the one of them; to wit, their idols, should be shaken and shattered; and the other, to wit, their mighty men, should faint and fail.

*{idols*} Of the word, see on ch. 2. 8.

*{shall be moved at his presence*} Or, *shall tremble, or quake*; as chap. 7. 2. or, *stagger, or reel*, as chap. 24. 20. & 29. 9. (for so the same word is in those places rendered, and would rather so be here, to express the emphasis of it) *before*, or, *from his face*, as the Hebrew has it; that is, *because of him*, as it is rendered, Psal. 38. 3. or, *for fear of him*, as chap. 21. 15. The Egyptian idols shall be no more able to stand before the face of God, than the Philistine Dagon before the ark of God, 1 Sam. 5. 3, 4. See Exod. 12. 12. Jer. 43. 12, 13. & 46. 15. Ezek. 30. 13.

*{and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it*} That is, the courage of the Egyptians shall be utterly quailed, Jer. 46. 5, 12, 15, 21.

*{heart*} For *courage*. Whence also that English term, 2 Sam. 17. 10.

*{Egypt*} For *Egyptians*: as v. 2.

*{melt*} As chap. 13. 7.

*{in the midst of it*} *Within them*: as Psal. 22. 14. v. 3.

**V. 2.** *{And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians*} The prophet now speaks, in the person of God: who in these words, threatens to set the Egyptians at odds, and disagreement, to destroy one another, by intestine jars, and wars, among themselves; as he did the like, sometime, with other nations, that came to invade his people, Judg. 7. 22. 1 Sam. 14. 16, 20. 2 Chr. 20. 23. Chap. 49. 26. This some suppose to have been done under Psammetichus; who living about these times, and being a petty king, among others, of a particular province in Egypt, upon some indignities offered him, by the princes of the other provinces, to revenge himself upon them, called in some foreign forces, and by help of them, overpowering the rest, at length made himself lord of all Egypt, Herodot. lib. 2. Diodor. lib. 1. Others imagine it, to have thus fallen out upon the Assyrians invading the country, some being willing to receive him, and another party opposing them: as some also deem the like to have been, on the like occasion, in the state of Judah, chap. 8. 6. But the former seems more probable.

*{set*} Heb. *mingle*, sometime in confederacy: as ch. 9. 11. sometime in war, and jar, and so here. See on chap. 9. 11.

*{the Egyptians against the Egyptians*} Heb. *Egypt against Egypt*, as, *Moab for Moab*, chap. 16. 7.

*{and they shall fight every one against his brother; and every one against his neighbour*} They shall *war* (so the Hebrew) one with another, and seek one to destroy another, without any regard had, either to vicinity, or alliance, chap. 9. 19, 20. Jer. 31. 34.

*{city against city*} As *city of city*, 2 Chr. 15. 6. and *house against* *house*, Luk. 11. 17. but there *house against house*, is an house against itself: here *city against city*, is one city against another.

*{and kingdom against kingdom*} One province against another. For Egypt before she was raised by Psammetichus, consisted of twelve provinces, Herodot. l. 2. *Kingdom against kingdom*, one against another, as Matth. 24. 7.

**V. 3.** *{And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof*} Not their courage, and valor only; ver. 1. but their wisdom, and policy also, shall falter, and fail, ver. 11, 13. God will infatuate them, and turn their wisdom into folly, 2 Sam. 15. 31. Job 5. 13, 14. & 12. 17, 20, 24, 25. chap. 44. 25. Rom. 1. 21, 22. 1 Cor. 1. 26, 25, 27. & 3. 19.

*{fail*} Heb. *be emptied*, as chap. 24. 3. Jer. 19. 7. it is as if he had said; their wits shall be drained: alluding to their folly, in draining, and diverting the course of their river, and thereby causing the waters thereof to fail them, v. 5, 6.

*{in the midst thereof*} *Within them*: as ver. 1.

*{and I will destroy the counsel thereof*} Heb. *swallow up*: as chap. 3. 12. & 10. 7. that is, either bereave, and deprive them of that faculty, by which they might be enabled to give any prudent and wholesome counsel, for the safety and welfare of the state; called *the spirit of counsel*, Ch. 11. 2. ver. 11, 13. or, overthrow, defeat, and frustrate their counsels, that they shall never take effect, Psal. 33. 10, 11. Pro. 21. 30. ch. 8. 10.

*{and they shall seek to the idols*} When they are thus, either puzzled in their counsels, or defeated in the issue of them, being at their wits' end, they shall betake themselves to their idols; as Moab to his, chap. 15. 2. & 16. 12. but with like success, both, and to their magicians, as Pharao did, Exod. 8. 18. & 9. 11. but neither of them shall be able to afford any aid or advice to them: no more than in the like case unto Babylon, ch. 47. 12.

*{idols*} Unable to help them, being not able to subsist themselves, v. 1.

*{and to the charmers*} The word here used is nowhere else found; and is by divers therefore diversely rendered. The Jewish doctors here give us little light, only one of them tells us, that his father told him, that it was an Arabic term, signifying some kind of magicians, it seems to come from a root that has a notion of doing things *quietly, softly, gently*, Gen. 33. 14. 2 Sam. 18. 5. 1 King. 21. 27. ch. 38. 15. Whence some conjecture, that it should import some such kind of witches, as did disturb, and endamage men, when they were at rest in their sleep. Others, such as used *fair, smooth, and gentle* words, as some are said, by praising, and blessing things to bewitch them. It may rather be, that they had this name given them, from that *soft, and low*, or, *slow and drawling* speech, that they used, either in their spells, or in their answers to those that consulted them. See chap. 8. 19. For I cannot concur with them, that hold it to be the name of some idol.

*{and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards*} Of these two, see on ch. 8. 19.

**V. 4.** *{And the Egyptians will I give over into the hand of a cruel lord; and a fierce king shall rule over them*} These words the most, both of the Jewish, and ours, generally expound, of those foreign kings, by whom Egypt should be subdued. Some, and some Rabbins unanimously, of the king of Assyria, c. 20. 4. Others, of the king of Babylon, Jer. 43. 10. & 44. 30. & 46. 13. Ezek. 29. 19. & 30. 10, 24. Others, rather, of their own kings, by their cruelty, and folly, rigorous courses, and unadvised projects, oppressing their subjects, weakening their kingdoms, and by intestine jars working the ruin one of another. That which the sequel of the context seems most fitly to agree with.

*{the Egyptians*} Heb. *Egypt*: as before, ver. 1, 2.

*{give over*} Heb. *shut up*, or, *close*, Gen. 8. 2. Psal. 63. 11. The Jewish writers expound it, by another of near affinity to it, and of the same with it, 1 Sam. 24. 18. & 26. 8. Psal. 31. 8. Nor seems wholly improbable, the conjecture of those, that suppose the prophet made use of this word, rather than the other, though more usual, in allusion to the *sluices*, or, *stews* rather, mentioned, ver. 10. wherein the Egyptians used to keep their fish: as intimating, that the rulers here spoken of, should keep them shut up, and restrained, as they kept their fish in their stews.

*{into the hand*} *In the power*: as Psal. 78. 61.

*{of a cruel lord*} Heb. *Lords*, in the plural, *hard*, Deut. 26. 6. in the singular. Which yet the Jewish writers, as our version has it, understand but of one; as if it were said; *Some one hard, and harsh lord, or other*, or, *an hard lord* simply, alleging divers places, where the word is in a plural form; though speaking but of some one, as Gen. 24. 29. & 42. 30. Exod. 21. 4, 6. 1 King. 22. 17. 2 Chr. 18. 16. which they expound of Sennacherib, as others, also, of ours, do, of Nebuchadnezzar, Jer. 46. 6. and some of Psammetichus before mentioned, whom also each of them respectively understand to be the *fierce king*, spoken of, in the next clause; the same thing, but in divers words, being intended in both. But on the other side, there want not, that take the word in a plural, as well notion, as form; and read the text; *Lords hard*, or, *harsh*, each of them; a manner of speaking in Scripture very usual. Of which, see on ch. 2. 20. So Psal. 78. 15. & 119. 137. Chap. 16. 8. and they understand it, to be spoken of those twelve princes, or lords, who as petty kings, ruled Egypt, divided amongst them, into so many provinces, after the death of Sethon, who had been king of the whole country before. See Herodot. lib. 2.

*{a fierce king*} The Hebrew epithet is sometime taken in the better part; for *powerful*, and *strong*, Gen. 49. 3. Num. 13. 28. & 22. 24. cap. 25. 3. sometime, in the worse part, for *fierce*, and *cruel*, Gen. 49. 7. Deut. 28. 50. and thus here. This fierce king, is by some supposed, to be Psammetichus, the father of Nechoh, by whom the good King Josias was slain, 2 King. 23. 29.

*{saith the Lord, the Lord of hosts*} See chap. 10. 16.

**V. 5.** *{And the waters shall fail from the sea*} There were two principal means of upholding the Egyptian estate, in wealth, and plenty; their traffic by sea, and the overflowing of Nilus, that, instead of rain, which they utterly wanted, watered their ground for them; and by such slimy stuff, as it brought down along with it, made the soil, which it overspread, exceeding fertile, and fruitful. In regard whereof, the inundation of it was anciently celebrated; and is yet to this day, with a great deal of solemnity; and a yearly account was taken, and kept, how high the river was risen; the expectation of a plentiful, or penurious crop, much depending thereupon. See Pliny, l. 5. c. 11. & l. 35. c. 7. But with the failing of both these, their principal props, and means of support, are the Egyptians here threatened. The former, some suppose to have been effected, partly, by the hostile incursions of the enemy; partly by their own jars, and divisions among themselves; and partly, by pirates of other people, lying upon their coast, and disturbing their trade. Of which, falling out, much about these times, see Herodot. l. 2. The latter, by the folly of their own princes, and rulers, of which, further hereafter. I am not ignorant, that some late interpreters, refer all that is here said, to the latter only; reading the text, some, *For they shall destroy the waters from running into the sea*. Others, *For they shall diminish the waters from the sea*, or, *of the sea*; (that is, of the river Nilus; all great waters being by the Hebrews termed *seas*. See chap. 9. 1.) *So that the river shall be dried up*. Which they understand of the fond, and unadvised practice of those twelve rulers, who for the making of a vast lake called the lake of *Moeris*, and the building of two stately *Pyramides*, in the midst of it; and *Labyrinth* near unto it, for bigness, and workmanship almost beyond belief; (and all this, only, out of an ambitious humor, to leave a memorial of themselves and their greatness, to posterity) both put their people to excessive labor and pain; and so weakened their river, by water drawn from it, that it could not so freely, and plentifully water the country, as formerly it had wont to do, and for this they cite Herodot. l. 2. And it may well be, that somewhat of this kind may be intimated in the latter part of the verse: of which, more anon. But for the former part of it, I adhere unto that, as most probable, that was formerly propounded.

*{the waters shall fail from the sea*} Or, *shall be dried up*; as some of the Jewish doctors expound it, from chap. 41. 17. and so the old Latin renders it. They shall be deprived of their sea trade, it shall be no more beneficial to them, than as if the sea had no access to them. See somewhat the like of Tyrus, chap. 23. 1, 4. See also, ch. 11. 15.

*{and the river shall be wasted, and dried up*} The *river*, to wit, *Nilus*, called *the river of Egypt*, Amos 8. 8. & 9. 5. because it runs down along clean through their country; and both fattens their soil, stores them with fish, Num. 11. 5. and enriches them by traffic. See on chap. 18. 1. Heb. *shall be dried up*, (as ver. 6. ch. 37. 25. & 50. 2. & 51. 10. for applied to water, it always so signifies) *and become dry*: become as *dry land*; from this word so termed, Gen. 1. 9, 10. So Job 14. 11. Some of the Jewish commenters expound all this, of the waste of men, that the Assyrian king should make in Egypt, by reason whereof, there should be no more trading there, than as if sea, and river, were both dried up: See Ezek. 30. 11, 12. And some Christian writers understand it, of a great dearth, that God would, through drought, bring upon them, by restraining the river, from his accustomed course of overflowing; at least, in such measure, as was needful for a competent supply. To which purpose, they allege some passages out of a panegyrical oration of Pliny the younger, not altogether unlike to those of the prophet in this place. But the prophet seems rather, as others, before mentioned, to speak here of errors, committed by their kings, and rulers, to the prejudice, both of themselves, and their people, in draining the river, at several passages, and in several places, for the effecting of their own vain, and ambitious designs. And of this kind, as by the prophet here intended, is by some interpreters of note, supposed to be the digging of that vast lake of Moeris, by those twelve rulers, or tyrants, before spoken of. But first they fail much, both in the time, and in the author of that stupendous work. For it was done a long time before their date, by a king, whose name it bears, who, as Herodot. himself relates, lived some hundreds of years before them, though by occasion of the Labyrinth, by those twelve, built near to it, he takes occasion to make a further, and larger relation of it, as a work far surpassing the erecting of that Labyrinth, which might otherwise seem a matchless masterpiece. Beside that, the making of that lake, in that place, in that manner, is deemed to have been a work of much use, and of great benefit to the country; both for the restraining of the river, when it surrounded beyond measure, and for the helping of it, by an outlet, when it was likely to fall short. See Diodor. lib. 1. But (to pass by other works of less note, in the same kind, done by others) of this nature, was that ditch, or watercourse, digged, after the reign of those twelve, by Psammetichus, as some, Strabo, lib. 17. or by Necho his son, and successor, as others, Herodot. l. 2. attempting thereby, to make a free passage by water, from Nilus, into the Red Sea; in the pursuit of which attempt, Herodot. reports, that he lost an hundred and twenty thousand of his people; and at length left the work unaccomplished. And to the impairing of the river, and the impeaching of the state, by such vain and fond courses as these, the prophet's words may well be deemed, to have reference, in this place. See ver. 6.

**V. 6.** *{And they shall turn the rivers far away*} This seems to confirm the latter exposition of the words beforegoing. For who are *they* that should do this? *The sons of men*, says one of the Jewish interpreters: and those in likelihood here intended, that drew away the streams of the river, into places far remote, from the main channel, it ran in. Howbeit, the verb being taken indefinitely, the text may be read, *the rivers*, or, *streams, shall be turned far away*: or, *shall go back*: to wit, by the falling of the water: as some here render it. See ch. 2. 20.

*{rivers*} For, *river*; or the *streams* of it: as chap. 11. 15. or, as some, the *watercourses* drawn from Nilus, for the watering of their grounds: but the former seems more probable.

*{and*} The copulative is not in the original: but were it to be supplied, it might rather be rendered by the finitive, *so that*; as chap. 11. 3. & 13. 2. If it be supplied, as a copulative, it should rather have been inserted before the last branch of this verse; or at the beginning of the next.

*{the brooks of defence*} That is, say some, *the rivers*, or, *streams of Egypt*, in general: Egypt say they, being elsewhere so termed. And true it is, that the word here used, is in sound, and letters, somewhat like to that name, that Egypt bears in Hebrew. But neither are they the same, nor of the like form, nor in likelihood arising from the same root: for as for those other places: (which yet in effect are but as one) where the very same words are found, that are here used, to wit, 2 King. 19. 24. & ch. 37. 25. Though some of the Jewish writers would by *Matsor* there, understand Egypt; yet others, of their own, therein control them: and there is little reason, in either place, so to expound it. The word signifies, either *obsession*, as Deut. 28. 52. or *munition*: as Deut. 20. 20. And some therefore by the *brooks*, or *rivers* here mentioned, understand such watercourses, as environed strong cities, or holds, in regard whereof, they could not be so easily surprised; termed therefore *rivers of obsession, or siege*, say some; because places encompassed by them, could not be stormed nor taken, but by long siege; or, *of munition, and defence*, as others; because they were no small strength unto those places; yea, were the main strength of Egypt, Ezek. 29. 3. & 30. 2. Howbeit, others understand them of *watercourses*, kept in with banks, and dams; and they render the words, some of them, *rivers of obsession*, or, *siege*; because environed and beset with those banks, as cities besieged are with the enemy's camp. Others *rivers of munition*, because fenced, and mounded, by such works raised about them, to preserve and keep them from diminution, and decay, v. 10. See Chap. 22. 11. Of whether of the two we take them, they could not but be wasted, when the main river, that fed them should fail.

*{shall be emptied*} Or, *wasted, or drained*: or, *exhausted*. See chap. 12. 2. & 17. 4. Some render it, *they shall waste, or, exhaust the rivers*; to wit, the persons before spoken of. But the word is never used actively. See Job 28. 4. Psalm 79. 8. & 116. 6. & 142. 6. and it is nowhere else found.

*{and dried up*} As ver. 5. and so constantly, Gen. 8. 13. Job 14. 11. Psal. 106. 9. Ch. 44. 27. Jer. 2. 12. Hos. 13. 15. and it is amiss therefore rendered by some, *they shall dry up*, as before: the verb being never active, in the form here used.

*{the reeds and flags shall wither*} Or, *decay*. See chap. 33. 9. These water-plants, or shrubs, must needs fade, and decay, when the waters, that nourished them, failed. So of the like, Job 8. 11. and these were of much use with them; for of these, were their boats and barks usually made. See chap. 18. 1. In regard whereof, some interpreters suppose, that a decay of shipping is here denounced: of these also, were mats for their bedding, weels for their fishing, and baskets of all sorts, commonly made with them.

*{the reeds*} Heb. *reed*, or *cane*: for so is the Hebrew, and ours, from it, ch. 36. 6. & 42. 3.

*{and flags*} Heb. *flag*, or, *reit*; such as grew about the brink of the river Nilus, Exod. 2. 3. and other the like watercourses. Whereof also, the Red Sea has its name in Hebrew. See chap. 18. 1.

*{shall wither*} So chap. 33. 9. *Lebanon is withered*. The word is nowhere else found: though some render it, both here, and there, *cut down*. But the former seems the more probable.

**V. 7.** *{The paper reeds by the brooks, by the mouth of the brooks*} To wit *shall wither away*. For that is here intended: and may be supplied, either from the verse beforegoing: or from what follows in this.

*{paper reeds*} The word is nowhere else found in Scripture: and is in that regard the more ambiguous. The most expound it, *grass*, instancing for proof thereof, in a word near unto it, Judg. 20. 33. or *green things*, as having reference to a word used, Psal. 37. 35. and this way the Jewish critics generally run; with whom ours also have formerly unanimously concurred. Howbeit, the places they point us to, seem rather to look another way. And some later interpreters, whom our version follows, understand by it, *the paper reeds*, or *canes*, or *rushes*; (for a kind of *bulrush* also some make it) so called, because they afforded sheets of paper to write on; before such paper, as we now have, or parchment, were for that purpose, in use. Now this kind of shrub being peculiar to Egypt, proved a rich commodity to that state, all civil people desiring to have traffic with them for it. Nor is it likely, therefore, that the prophet would omit the failing of such a water-plant, for which the land was so famous, and that was so advantageous unto it. The Hebrew word they suppose to be deduced from a word, that signifies *an hide*, or, *skin*, Gen. 3. 21. Exod. 34. 30. because the sheets of paper were made of the rind, or coat of it. I should rather derive it from a word, that signifies *to strip*, or *make bare*, ch. 3. 17. & 32. 11. because it was stripped to make writing-sheets for books, and tables, and other the like uses as hemp, and flax, is, to make linen in these times; though after a far diverse manner. See Pliny, lib. 13. ch. 11, 12.

*{by the brooks*} Heb. *brook*, or, *river*; either the river Nilus itself, as some here understand it, so termed, Gen. 41. 1, 2. Exod. 4. 9. & 7. 15, 18. or, the *watercourses*, derived from it: (the word being taken collectively) of which before, ver. 6. or both.

*{by the mouth of the brooks*} Heb. *brook*, or, *river*, as before; that is, say some, *by, or, about, the fountain of the river Nilus*; at which the water issues out, as at a mouth; where, if moisture fail, it cannot be expected in the places more remote, that must have all their water thence: and so infer hence, a stupendous waste, and consumption of that river, reaching up to the very first head of it. But this seems nothing probable; nor does the prophet seem to speak, here, of the river itself alone, but, as our version renders it, of the streams, and watercourses also, derived from it. Besides that the *mouth* of the river might seem rather to import those streams, or channels, whereby it disgorges itself into the sea, (whereof, see chap. 11. 15.) being in other languages so termed: and being applied to the *watercourses*, thence derived, those passages, whereby the water of the river made its entrance into them, or whereby they emptied themselves again into the river. But by *mouth*, I suppose simply to be understood the *brinks*, or *banks* of either, called as here, the *mouth*, so elsewhere, the *lips*, Gen. 41. 3. Exod. 2. 3. Ezek. 47. 6, 7. and the two brinks, as lips, on either side, seem to make up a mouth, are at least, to the river, or watercourse, as lips to the mouth, of man, or beast.

*{and every thing sown by the brooks shall wither*} Heb. *every thing sown beside the river, or brook, shall be dried up*: Places near to rivers and brooks, are wont to be most fertile, and fruitful, and near them, men desire usually to sow, and plant, Chap. 32. 20. alluded to, Eccl. 11. 1. but the things there sown, and planted, must needs fail, when the water fails, that made the places adjacent so fertile. This comprehends such grains, herbs, roots, and other useful plants, as hemp, flax, and the like, as they used to set, or sow there. See Exod. 9. 31, 32. Num. 11. 5. ver. 9. as the former, those that grew there of themselves, v. 6.

*{be driven away, and be no more*} Heb. *and not be*: as Psal. 37. 36. & 39. 13. shall so fade away, that they shall be, as if there never had been any such thing there. Though there be, that understand it of the spoil that the enemy shall make of them: but the course of the context seems to carry it the other way.

**V. 8.** *{The fishers also shall mourn*} As chap. 3. 26. Because the fish shall fail: as they must of necessity, when the element fails, out of which they cannot live; and which formerly did abundantly furnish them with fish, Num. 11. 5.

*{and they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament*} The same thing in other terms.

*{cast angle*} Heb. *hook*, as Job 41. 1. Hab. 1. 15. there being two kinds, or courses, of catching fish, most commonly used; *by hook*, or, *by net*, the one is pointed at in this branch; the other in the next.

*{the brooks*} Heb. *brook*, or, *river*, as before, ver. 7.

*{and they that spread nets upon the water shall languish*} All sorts of fishermen shall be disheartened, and much grieved, because their trading shall decay.

*{nets*} Heb. *net*: as Hab. 1. 15, 16. and as *hook* before.

*{upon the water*} Heb. *upon the face, or, surface of the water*: as Gen. 1. 2. Eccl. 11. 1.

**V. 9.** *{Moreover*} Heb. *And*: as chap. 7. 10. & 8. 1.

*{they that work in fine flax, and they that weave net-works shall be confounded*} Because the materials shall fail, that should set them on work.

*{in fine flax*} The epithet given to the flax here mentioned, is elsewhere used of vines, and their branches: and is deemed to import the choicest of them, chap. 5. 2. & 16. 8. and in like manner, being here applied to flax, it seems to imply the finest, and choicest sort of it, as in Arabic, the choicest sort of silk, is by some of the Jewish critics, reported so to be termed: though some of them render it, with the Chaldee, *combed, or dressed flax*; because the Talmudists commonly use the word in that sense. But that which one of them adds, that of it they made nets to fish with, is as ridiculous, as to imagine, that men should use to fish with silken nets, or to angle, as he said sometime, with golden hooks. That *fine linen and linen yarn*, was a principal commodity in Egypt, appears, 1 King. 10. 28. Prov. 7. 16. Ezek. 27. 7. Of the several sorts whereof, and the gain that Egypt anciently made thereof, see Pliny, l. 19. ch. 1.

*{net-works*} The word here used, is by some supposed to come from another, that signifies *an hole*, Chap. 11. 8. Ezek. 8. 7. and some of them, therefore, understand by it, *nets*, to fish with; so called because full of holes to let the water pass at, while they held fast the fish: thus the rather; because, say they, it follows, vers. 10. *the nets are broken*: but of that, when we come to it. Others of them, with more probability, conceive it, to import cloth, or garments, wrought or woven of purpose, with many holes in them, such as our network cauls, and loom-works ordinarily are. See chap. 3. 18. But others deducing it from a word, that signifies *white*, Esth. 1. 6. & 8. 15. render it, *white-works*; that being one special commendation of linen, lawn, and the like, to be pure white: and such, therefore, were men of chief note wont to be clad with, Esth. 8. 16. Dan. 7. 9. whereof also, the name taken from this, is very frequently given them in Hebrew, 1 King. 21. 8, 11. Neh. 2. 16. & 4. 14. Eccl. 10. 17. ch. 34. 12. Jer. 26. 19. & 39. 6. and this to me seems the most probable.

**V. 10.** *{And they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices, and ponds for fish*} These words are very diversely rendered, and expounded, in regard of some terms in them very ambiguous; we will first therefore discuss the words, and then draw up the expositions, that seem to be most probable.

*{in the purposes*} The word signifies *foundations*, Psal. 11. 3. Hence some expound it, *projects*, or, *purposes*. Which are wont to be the foundation and ground of action, and practice. Others, the *walls, and mounds*, or, *dams*, and *sluices*, raised and built, to keep in the water, in the *stews*, or *ponds*, hereafter mentioned. The one of these two, seems to be most likely here intended. For little show or color of reason is brought for their opinion, by those, that render it *nets*; and yet not a few are they, that go this way: and they derive it from a wrong root, that translate it, *irrigations*, or well-watered places: as if it came from a word, that imports *drinking*, which the analogy will not bear.

*{thereof*} Or, *of it*, to wit, of Egypt, their kings, and rulers, of whom before, v. 5, 6. and hereafter, v. 11, 13.

*{all that make*} Or, *of all that make*.

*{sluices*} Or, *dams*. So some render it; as from a verb, that signifies *to shut*, or *stop up*, Gen. 8. 2. Psal. 107. 42. Others, *for hire*, or, *gain*, as the word is very commonly used, Jon. 1. 3. Mal. 3. 5. the preposition *for*, supplied: as Mal. 2. 5.

*{and ponds*} Or, *stews*, to keep fish in; either for sale, or, to make use of otherwise, when they please.

*{for fish*} Heb. *of soul, ponds of soul*, or, *of souls*, that is, living things: the word taken collectively, for *ponds of fish*, according to that, Gen. 1. 20. *let the water bring forth gliding creature of soul*; or, *ponds of desire, delight, or pleasure*, as Gen. 23. 8. *if it be your pleasure*: and Deut. 23. 24. *thou mayest eat according to thy desire*, or, *pleasure*, ponds serving for delight and pleasure. The whole then, may thus be rendered; *And through her foolish projects, they shall all be broken that make sluices, or dams, for ponds of fish*. Or, *her, or their banks, or dams shall be broken, with all those that make for hire, or, gain, ponds*; or, *that make gain of ponds*, or, *stews, of fish, or, for pleasure*. Whether way we render it, the meaning is, that all the pains and cost that men had been at, about the making of ponds, and stews, to keep fish in, and about dams and sluices, to secure them, should come to nothing, the water being drained away from them; neither yield them any gain, nor stand them in any stead: and in a word as before he intimated, that there should be no catching of fish, ver. 8. so here, that there should be no keeping of fish with them. Howbeit, some expound it, as if the meaning were, that the people were worn out, by working about those lakes, and watercourses, above mentioned, and all to no purpose: the like whereunto, see Jer. 51. 58. But the other sense before given, sorts better with the main current of the context.

**V. 11.** *{Surely the princes of Zoan are fools: the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharao is become brutish*} The prophet, in these words, directs us unto one main cause of the calamities of the people and state of Egypt, before related; to wit, not so much any foreign hostility, or invasion from abroad, as their own folly; the witless carriage of their nobles, and counselors at home, who by their fond flatteries, soothed up their kings, and put them upon such inconsiderate designs, as tended to the impoverishing of the land, and the ruinating of the state.

*{Zoan*} Heb. *Tsoan*, a very ancient city in Egypt, Num. 13. 22. one of their kings' seats, that gave the name unto the whole province about it, Psal. 78. 12. it was from the Syriac form, by the Greeks, called also *Tanis*, by the loss of a letter; as of *Tsor*, or *Tsur*, *τύρος* and *Tyrus*: and from it, the Tanaitic division; and the Tanaitic stream, one of the principal ones, by which Nilus makes its way into the sea. See Herodot. l. 2. Strabo. l. 17. Pliny, l. 5. ch. 9, 10.

*{the counsel of the wise counsellors*} Heb. *of the wise of the counselors of Pharao the counsel*. That is, the counsel of those that are the wisest among them; as *the wise of women*, Prov. 14. 1. that is, the wiser sort of them; such as are wiser than many, or the most, or, as wise as any, Prov. 31. 10. Eccl. 7. 28. and, *the wicked of the earth*, Ezek. 6. 21. for the wickedest upon the earth. *The fierce of the nations*, Ezek. 28. 7. for the fiercest among them. They impair the force of the sentence, that render it with a needless interposition, *the wise*, or *wise men and counselors*; there being no copulative in the text.

*{is become brutish*} Not foolish only; but sottish: such as might better seem brute beasts than men endued with common sense, Jer. 10. 14, 21. & 51. 17.

*{How say ye unto Pharao*} The prophet turns his speech unto the king of Egypt's counselors and nobles, taxing them, by way of expostulation, for their groundless opinion, overweening conceit, and vain vaunting and boasting to their king, of their wisdom, coming upon them, as by descent, and the antiquity of their houses; thereby to commend both their selves, and their advices, to him; and to procure the greater regard to what they suggested. Or, as some, for their gross and palpable flatteries, wherewith they wrought into their king, the like vain conceit of his own extraordinary wisdom, as derived to him from his ancestors; and of the antiquity of his stock, drawn down by a continued line of many descents, through a multitude of ages, and a vast number of years, from some of their imaginary deities.

*{say ye*} Or, *can ye say*, as Jer. 2. 23. with what face can you say it? So Jer. 8. 8.

*{say*} Or, as some, *dictate*. Put such words, as these, into your king's mouth; as 2 Sam. 14. 3.

*{unto Pharao*} Or, as some, *of Pharao*: as ch. 39. 33.

*{Pharao*} A common name of the kings of Egypt, in the more ancient times, it being, as it may seem, a term of sovereignty amongst them, Gen. 12. 15. & 40. 2. & 41. 50, 44. Exod. 1. 8, 11. For it may justly be doubted, whether they shoot not wide, that give the word, either an Hebrew, or a Chaldee original. Yet, by some other peculiar surnames, they were wont to be distinguished; as *Pharao Necoh*, 2 Kings 23. 29. and *Pharao Hophra*, Jer. 44. 30. in latter times about the time of the Macedonian empire, they came to be called, *Ptolomys*, not in regard of any *warlike* disposition, from a Greek poetical term, so signifying, as some have imagined; but from a name of great antiquity, in those Eastern and Southern parts, *Talmai*; which, among others, one of the sons of Anak bore, Num. 13. 22. Josh. 15. 14. So the Talmudists call *Ptolomy*, that caused the law of Moses to be translated into Greek, and from thence the apostle *Bartholomew*, had his name, *Bar-talmai*, or *Bar-tulmai*, as the Syriac pronounces it, Matt. 10. 3. that is, *the son of Talmai*, or, *Ptolomy*; after the Greek phrase; as *Bar-Jona the son of Jona*, Mat. 16. 17. and *Bar-Jesus, the son of Jesus*, Act. 13. 6. and *Bar-Timeus the son of Timeus*, Mar. 10. 46. Both names, it may be, came at first, from some great one of special note, in those places, of that name; as the name of *Abimelech*, to the kings of Palestine, Gen. 20. 2. & 26. 1. Psal. 34. 1. and of *Benhadad* to the kings of Syria, Jer. 49. 27. Amos 1. 4. Of *Candace*, to the queens of Ethiopia, Act. 8. 27. (See Plin. lib. 6. c. 29.) and of *Cæsar* to the Roman emperors, Mat. 22. 17. Luk. 2. 1. John 12. 12. Act. 11. 28. & 17. 7. & 25. 10. Phil. 4. 22. Being, through use, a note and title of sovereignty, but having otherwise no notion of any such thing in itself, as the name, *Abimelech* has.

*{Pharao*} The Pharao, here mentioned, some suppose to have been *Sethon*, a foolish king, say they as Herodotus shows; who yet says little of him, save that he neglected his military men. See further of him, on ch. 37. 37. Others with more probability, take him to be Psammetichus, spoken of ver. 4. and under whom, and those twelve, between Sethon and him, the calamities here threatened, as those former affirm, were to befall them. I suppose, it need not be restrained to any one particular king, but may well extend itself unto those kings in general, that ruled Egypt in those times, and those more specially, by whose fond and unadvised courses these mischiefs were procured; of which number, Sethon appears not to have been any.

*{I am the son of the wise*} Heb. *a son of the wise*; as *a son of the gods*, Dan. 3. 25. & *a son of man*, Rev. 1. 13. for so those places should be rendered. Or, *a son of wise ones*. That is, wise men; (a defect of the subject, as ver. 12. Gen. 41. 8. expressed, Deut. 1. 13, 15.) and having their wisdom by inheritance. The words are either of the king's counselors, concerning themselves, or his own, suggested to him, in parasitical manner, by them, concerning himself. Yet it is somewhat over-harsh to render it, as some would, *a son of wise ones, thou art*, or *he is*. The Egyptians, anciently, for wisdom and learning, arrogated much to themselves, Act. 7. 22. And out of other remote parts, many that were greedy of knowledge, and variety of learning, did for their better satisfaction, therefore travel into Egypt, to have conference with the wise men there. See Diodor. lib. 1. Plat. *in Timeo*, Clemens, *Strom.* lib. 1. and Eusebius *præpar.* lib. 10.

*{the son of ancient kings*} Heb. *a son of kings of antiquity*; as Deut. 33. 15. Chap. 23. 7. The Egyptians vaunted much of the antiquity of their nation, their kings and priests, especially, who reported themselves, about these times, to have records of their descent from the gods, that in human shape, sometime, conversed there, by 341 generations, under no fewer kings containing 10341 years, beginning at their first king of that divine issue, unto Sethon's decease; and that within that period of time, the sun had four times changed his course, from East to West twice: and twice back again, from West to East, Herodot. lib. 2. But these fabulous relations were but mere fictions, devised by their priests, to puff up their princes, and to gain credit to themselves.

**V. 12.** *{Where are they? where are thy wise men?*} A tart and sarcastical interrogation; like that, 1 Cor. 1. 20. What is become of your wise counselors; why do none of them appear, to acquaint you with these evils that will betide you? For so it follows,

*{and let them tell thee now*} The copulative, some deem here, redundant; as Gen. 36. 24. Exod. 1. 1. Levit. 7. 16. Others suppose a defect of some word, to be supplied: *Let them now appear*, or *arise* (as the usual phrase in Scripture is, Jer. 2. 27, 28.) *and tell thee*. See the like, Zach. 2. 6. But the words may well be rendered, *That they may now tell thee*; as ch. 11. 3. & 13. 2. See the like speech to Babylon, ch. 47. 12, 13.

*{and let them know what the Lord of hosts hath purposed against Egypt*} Or, *that they may know*, or, simply with reference to the former branch, *that they may tell thee, and know themselves*; or, *or know*, as Gen. 2. 6. Judg. 11. 31: (in both which places, in the margin of our Bibles, there wants an *or*) That they may either tell you, or take notice themselves, as having that taught them, which they were before ignorant of, and which all the great wisdom they boast of, is not able to acquaint them with, ch. 41. 22, 26, 28. & 47. 11. Or lastly, By *telling* you, *make known*. See Jer. 9. 13.

*{the Lord of hosts*} Ch. 14. 27.

*{hath purposed*} Heb. *consulted*, or *counseled*; as Jer. 3..20.30.49. Here, the rather to answer the term *counselors*, ver. 11. and because they pretended to be of counsel with their gods, and to be acquainted with such matters as were concluded in the court of heaven; as false prophets also usually did, 1 King. 22. 6, 24. Ch. 36. 10. & 40. 14. & 47. 13. Jer. 23. 18, 22.

*{upon Egypt*} Either *against*, as ch. 5. 30. Or, *concerning Egypt*, as ch. 1. 1.

**V. 13.** *{The princes of Zoan are become fools*} Or, *dote*, as it is rendered, Jer. 50. 36. where the same is said of the princes, or wizards of Babel. See the like of other the heathens, professed wise ones, Rom. 1. 22. The word is, by some, deemed to import, *a willful*, or obstinate disposition in, or course of *folly*, or, *a presumptuous folly*, because the same word, in another flexion, signifies, sometime, *to will*, Hos. 5. 11. sometime, *to presume*, Gen. 18. 27, 31. Of *Zoan*, see on ver. 11.

*{the princes of Noph*} A famous city in Egypt; built, as some say, by their first king Menas, Herodot. lib. 2. Though others ascribe it to a latter; Diodor. lib. 1. It might be founded by the one, beautified and enlarged, made, in some sort, anew, by the other: but agreed on to be one of the goodliest, and famousest cities in Egypt, wherein their kings, therefore, many of them, held their ordinary residence. It is mentioned by this name also, Jer. 2. 16. & 44. 1. & 46. 14, 15. And is, by some, deemed to have its appellation from an Hebrew word signifying, *a tract, coast, or, region*: (as a word of near affinity with it imports, Josh. 12. 23. 1 King. 4. 11.) rendered *situation*, Psal. 48. 2. And for its situation, some highly commend it. But to force Egyptian terms to Hebrew notations, is not proper. It is elsewhere, in Scripture, called, *Moph*, Hos. 9. 6. whereof the Greeks, and Latins, have framed their *Memphis*. Howbeit, Strabo, lib. 17. informs us, that there were two several cities in Egypt, the one called *Memphis*, and the other, *Momemphis*, (peradventure, *Momphis*:) that their sacred ox Apis, was kept, in the former; their holy cow, in the other. Whether *Noph*, might not be the one, and *Moph* the other, I leave it to the consideration and conjecture of others. For as concerning the mountain, *Mophi*, whence some would have Memphis to be called, *Moph*, with his mate *Crophi*, between which Nilus his head-spring should rise, and run in one channel, to Ethiopia, in another, toward Egypt; they are both alike figments, having no existence out of the brain of the temple treasurer, that to Herodot. related it; nor does he profess to esteem any otherwise of them. *Noph*, or *Memphis*, formerly so termed, is, by some, deemed to be that most populous city, which we commonly call, *Grand Cairo*, as *the great city*, say some; though others, render other reasons of that name. The Arabian writers are reported to call it, *Misr-hadith*, that is, *New Egypt*. Zoan, and Noph, are by some, supposed to be specially here mentioned; because the one, to wit, Noph, was situate near to the utmost border of Egypt, upward, toward the land of Ethiopia; the other, to wit, Zoan, in the nether part of the country, toward the fall of the river into the Midland Sea, which, for the latter, is true enough: (See on ver. 11.) but for the former, seems not so. For though Memphis be situate about some twenty miles above the head Delta, where the river Nilus divides itself into two main channels, (See on ch. 51. 9.) which afterward branches into seven several streams, ch. 11. 15. yet is it some hundred of miles distant from Siene and Phile, the confines of Egypt and Ethiopia. See Strabo, lib. 17. and Plin. lib. 9. ch. 7. But these two, seem rather here to be mentioned, because they were principal and royal cities, and might therefore fitly comprehend all the rest. See the like, Jer. 2. 16.

*{are deceived*} The pride of their hearts has deceived them: as God, of Edom, Obad. 3.

*{they have also seduced Egypt, even they that are the stay of the tribes thereof*} Or, *the stays, or, princes of the tribes thereof have seduced Egypt*. That is, their princes, and wise counselors; either by their ill-grounded advices, and flattering suggestions; or by their vain and false predictions, and promises of prosperous successes, have deluded the whole land, and led them into courses destructive to the state, which they ought to have supported. See ch. 3. 12. & 9. 16.

*{the stay*} Heb. *corner*. So the word properly signifies, 2 Chr. 28. 24. Job 1. 19. Jer. 31. 40. Then a *stone*, laid in the corner of a building, where two walls meet, and are therewith united, Eph. 2. 14, 20, 21. called therefore *the head of the corner*, Psal. 118. 22. and *the corner-stone*, Job 36. 6. Jer. 51. 27. & *a corner*, simply, Zach. 10. 4. See chap. 28. 16. And because such stones, so placed, are a principal stay, strength, and support to a structure; hence it comes to pass, that the same term is used, as for *towers*, or, *bulwarks*, 2 King. 26. 15. Zeph. 1. 16. & 3. 6. So for princes and rulers, or persons of prime place; for to them also it is given, Judg. 20. 2. 1 Sam. 14. 38. There, in the plural number; here, in the singular; but joined to a verb plural, to comprehend them all, and take in each of them, See on ch. 2. 20. Some would have the word, here used, to signify, not so much *a corner*, as *an end*, and render the text, *unto the end, or utmost part thereof*: as implying, no province, or region throughout the land, to be free from this seducement. And it is true, that the corner of a building, is the utmost part of it. But beside a needless addition to the text, I find not where the word is used in that notion, for as for Judg. 20. 2. & 1 Sam. 14. 38. *The extremities, or utmost ends of the people*, seem to sound somewhat harsh in either place.

*{of the tribes thereof*} The prophet speaks here of Egypt, according, not to their language; but his own country dialect; with whom the several *tribes* had this term. The word signifies *a rod*, Chap. 10. 5, 15. & 14. 29. But this commonly used, where it is rendered *a tribe*, for such a number of people united into a body, as descended from any of Jacob's twelve sons; whose posterity therefore was divided into twelve tribes. And this appellation therefore given them, as some think; because they were as *rods*, shooting forth, and branching out from one stem, or stock, the prime patriarch Jacob, or in reference to those *rods*, on which their names were written, Num. 17. 2. But the term seems more ancient than so, Gen. 49. 16, 28. I rather suppose, that this denomination was given to the tribes, in regard of the judiciary power and government belonging to each tribe respectively, and residing in the head, or heads of it. For the word signifying, not so much *a walking*, as *a ruling rod*, a scepter, as we say, Psal. 2. 9. & 110. 2. implies power, and authority, Psal. 45. 6. Ezek. 19. 11, 14. And this these words of Jacob seem to import where he says, *Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel*, Gen. 49. 16. As our prophet therefore calls Cyrus, *God's anointed*, Chap. 45. 1. in way of allusion to the rite of anointing kings among God's people, 1 Sam. 10. 1. & 16. 15. though no such ceremony was in use among the Persians: so in reference to the Jewish tribes, he gives this title, to those several *Nomi*, as the Greeks call them; or *precincts*, and *prefectures*, as the Latin terms them, into which the land of Egypt was divided; the rather also, for that they were just as many in number, about those times at least, as the Jewish were. See Herodot. lib. 2. and Pliny, lib. 5. chap. 9. though some other reckon many more. See Strabo, lib. 17.

*{thereof*} This addition overthrows the interpretation of those, who understand the last words of this verse, *the stay of tribes*, or *the corner-stone of states*, as spoken of Egypt, who professed herself to be a stay and shore to other states. Of which, see on ch. 18. 1. for it shows evidently, that the speech is of those, that either were, or ought to have been, in their several places, and within their several precincts, respectively, the supporters of the state, Psalm 75. 3.

**V. 14.** *{The Lord hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof*} The prophet here declares a principal ground of this distraction, in the Egyptian estate, the unadvised counsels, and courses, that their princes took, and the calamities, that by means thereof, the whole country sustained; to wit, a secret hand of God; his just judgment following them for their pride and insolency; and infatuating them in their projects, and purposes. See v. 10. So Rom. 2. 21, 22, 24, 26.

*{mingled*} Or, *poured out*; given them to drink. Of the use of the word, see on chap. 5. 22. God's judgments in Scripture, are oft-times resembled by a cup, containing such liquor, as being strong and heady, so distempers men, that it makes them either so brain-sick and giddy, that they turn round or stagger with it, as not able to stand steadily; or so outrageous, that they fare like madmen, and mischief both themselves, and others. See Psal. 60. 3. & 75. 8. ch. 51. 17, 21, 22. Jer. 25. 15, 16, 27, 28. Lam. 4. 21. Ezek. 23. 32–34.

*{a perverse spirit*} *A spirit of error, or seducement*, as the Chaldee, and the Greek render it, or, *of giddiness*, as the Latin, either of which, suits well with what here ensues: The Hebrew word, nowhere else found, comes from a verb, that signifies *to pervert, turn away, or make crooked*, chap. 24. 1. Lam. 3. 6. it is plural, and of a duplicate form: as if he had said, *a spirit of extreme perversities*. Instead of that spirit of wisdom which they so much boast of, God has made them drunk with a spirit of stupidity, and erroneousness, which being possessed with, they run headlong into perverse and crooked courses, whereby they carry all things awry, unto the great disturbance of the state, chap. 29. 10, 14. Rom. 11. 8. See Ezek. 21. 32. where a word of near affinity to this, is thrice repeated. This is supposed to have been fulfilled, a great part of it, in the time of those twelve, that shared the kingdom among them, after Sethon's decease: who falling at variance among themselves, did exceedingly distract, and disturb the whole land, until Psammetichus, at length, overpowered and mastered them all, and so made himself absolute lord of all. See v. 4.

*{in the midst thereof*} Or, *into it*, to wit, Egypt, her princes especially, or, *among them*, as ver. 3. ch. 5. 8.

*{and they have caused Egypt to err, in every work thereof*} The effect of this spirit of error, and giddiness, wherewith the princes were possessed, redounding to the prejudice of the main body of the whole state, and disturbing all employments. When the head is distempered with drink, the whole body staggers; and no member is able to carry itself steadily, in any work, or office belonging unto it, Chapter 24. 19, 20. and 29. 9. Psalm 107. 26, 27. Jer. 23. 9.

*{as a drunken man staggereth in his vomit*} Heb. *wandereth*: that is, wallows, or rolls to and fro, and cannot get out of it, Job 12. 24, 25. Jer. 48. 26. like a wandering man, that has lost his way in a wood, or a wilderness, where he can find no issue out, Gen. 21. 14. Psal. 107. 4. See ch. 28. 7, 8.

**V. 15.** *{Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head, or tail, branch, or rush, may do*} All estates and conditions, shall be so distracted and disturbed, that they shall have no mind, nor opportunity, to mind or attend aught. So 2 Chr. 15. 5, 6. Zach. 8. 10. *head, and tail, rush, and branch*: a proverbial speech, for high, and low; strong, and weak. See ch. 9. 14.

**V. 16.** *{In that day*} In those times, wherein this judgment shall befall them: as ch. 17. 9.

*{shall Egypt be like unto women*} The Egyptians, their men, yea their military men, shall turn milksops, shall become as fainthearted as women, ver. 1. Jer. 51. 30.

*{and it shall be afraid, and fear, because of the shaking of the hand of the Lord, which he shaketh over it*} Heb. *from the face of*, &c. as Psal. 38. 3. Joel 2. 6, 10.
