By reason of the judgment before mentioned, by the Lord inflicted on them, vers. 14. illustrated here by an allusion to Moses stretching out of his hand, at God's command, over the Red Sea, to bring the sea back on the Egyptians, to drown, and destroy them, Exod. 14. 24, 25, 26–28. It shall not be like Sennacherib's shaking his hand at Jerusalem, ch. 10. 32. that proved ineffectual, but as God shaking his hand over the Egyptian troops, in time past, that took effect, to the ruin, and overthrow of them; (see ch. 10. 24. & 11. 15.) and as his shaking of it over the Assyrian forces, chap. 30. 32.

**V. 17.** *{And the land of Judah shall be a terror unto Egypt*} Not that the Jews should put Egypt into any such fear, or fright, in regard of aught by them done, or attempted against it, but that the judgment of God executed and inflicted on the Jews; whom the Egyptians had undertaken to protect, chap. 20. 5, 6. & 36. 6. shall, beside their intestine broils and combustions, further exceedingly dismay them: they shall tremble for fear, when they see the land of Judah, that relied on them, chap. 30. 2. & 31. 1. overrun, and distressed by the Assyrian forces, chap. 36. 1. as expecting the like to betide them too; partly in regard of their confederacy; which, between those two states, was over-frequent, and constant, chap. 30. 4, 5. 2 King. 17. 4. & 18. 21. Jer. 2. 18. & 37. 5. Ezek. 17. 15. and partly also, of their vicinity, Josh. 13. 3. & 15. 4. 1 Sam. 27. 7, 8. the Philistines' land only lying between them and it: and the rather so, here, for that the land of Judah lay in the Assyrian's way to Egypt, 2 King. 23. 29. which being subdued, therefore, by the Assyrian, would make his passage unto Egypt the more free. So Ethiopia is said to be affrighted and afflicted at the fall of Egypt, in regard of their nearness to them, and conjunction with them, Ezek. 30. 9, 10. and other neighboring nations, at the fall of Tyre, chap. 23. 5. Ezek. 26. 15–18. Beside that the Egyptians might justly expect the like, or worse, from the hand of God, when they should behold, and consider how he had dealt with his own people, ch. 7. 17, 19. & 8. 7, 8. See Jer. 25. 29. Howbeit, some draw down this prophecy lower, to the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem, by the Chaldeans, Jer. 37. 10. & 39. 2, 8. and the conquest of Egypt also by them, Jer. 43. 10–13. & 44. 30. & 46. Ezek. 29. 19, 20.

*{a terror*} The word here used, but nowhere else found, (a condition common to it, with many others, in this prophecy, as if the prophet had of purpose coined them, to make his style the more emphatical) as a term very pregnant: and signifies such a trembling, quivering, and quavering, as is wont to befall men, when being surprised and overmastered with fear, they cannot stand still; but do, as it were, *dance* with their feet, and their heart seems likewise to *dance* within them; the very same, that the term of *trepidation*, in Latin, does in its original import. For as that, so this comes of a word, that signifies first *to dance*, as at feasts is usual, 1 Sam. 30. 16. and then to intimate such a dancing, through fear, Psal. 107. 26. where it is applied to just such a disposition, in persons distressed and distracted, as is here intimated; and resembled by the same similitude, that is here also, ver. 14.

*{every one that maketh mention thereof, shall be afraid in himself*} Or, rather, *every one* (to wit, of the Egyptians) *that calleth her to mind, with himself*, (that does seriously call to mind, and consider with himself, what is befallen the land of Judah) *shall be afraid*, or, *shall fear*, the very thought of it, shall strike a terror into him: and to this reading, the points in the text lead. So 2 Chr. 17. 10. & 20. 29. Act. 5. 11.

*{because of*} As ver. 16. or, *for fear of*. Heb. *from the face of*: as ch. 21. 15.

*{the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he hath determined*} Heb. *is consulting*; or, *decreeing*. See ch. 14. 24, 26.

*{against it*} Heb. *against*, or, *concerning him*: either the Jewish people, which the Egyptians themselves, shall then see executed; or, the Egyptians, expecting thereupon, their own ruin to come next. See v. 12. Some suppose an allusion in this clause, to the acknowledgment of God's hand against them, Exod. 14. 25.

**V. 18.** *{In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan*} A gracious prediction of the conversion of Egypt unto the service of the true God, in the latter times, after the judgments here denounced, fulfilled, and executed on them. See the like comfortable closes, Chapter 6. 13. and 17. 7. and 18. 7. and 23. 17, 18. and in particular, concerning Egypt, Jer. 46. 26.

*{In that day*} Not while these calamities lie thus heavy on them; but in aftertimes, when these evils are over. So are the same words used, chap. 4. 2. & 18. 7. This some suppose to have been fulfilled, not long after the time of this prophecy, in the days of Ezekiah, when upon Sennacherib's invasion of the land of Judah, many Jews fled into Egypt, and having liberty there for exercise of their own religion, were the means of converting many Egyptians to God, (not unlike to that, Act. 8. 4. & 11. 19, 21.) being the rather wrought upon, and prevailed with, upon that miraculous, and most remarkable defeat, given by God to Sennacherib's forces, and the deliverance of Jerusalem. For thereupon it is said, *that many strangers brought gifts unto the Lord, to Jerusalem, and presents to Ezekiah*, 2 Chr. 32. 23. So Esth. 8. 17. Psal. 138. 4, 5. chap. 59. 19. Or, as others, (and so the Jewish writers) that many Egyptians, that serving under Sennacherib, having escaped in that mighty slaughter; and being kindly used by Ezekiah, (as those Syrians by Joram, 2 King. 6. 23.) at their return into their own country, abandoned their wonted idolatries, and addicted themselves wholly to the service of the true God; as did Naaman, 2 King. 5. 17. But because there is little footing found of aught in this kind, in the records of antiquity, either sacred, or profane, (for as for that, which one of the Rabbines produces, from c. 45. 14. seems little to this purpose;) it is rather to be referred unto the times of the Messiah, under whose kingdom, the gospel was planted in those places, and as well in Ethiopia, Chap. 18. 7. and in Assyria, as in Egypt, verse 23–25.

*{five cities*} A certain number, for an uncertain; as all generally agree: *five* for *many*, say some: but in Scripture, *five* is more commonly used for a small number; especially, when *five* are either culled out, or opposed unto far many more: as Levit. 26. 8. Chap. 30. 17. 1 Cor. 14. 19. in which last place if *five* be reckoned, as a very small number, in regard of a *thousand*, and of *ten thousand* much more; sure *five cities of Egypt* must needs, consequently, be deemed a very small scantling, in regard of that whole country, which by some authors is reported to have had above *ten thousand*, by some *twenty thousand cities*. See Herodot. l. 2. & Mela, l. 1. c. 10. To this, therefore, some say, that as there were among the Philistines, *five* principal, or head cities, though many other inferior, and less ones besides, 1 Sam. 6. 4. so there were *five* mother-cities in Egypt, *Memphis, Tanis, Alexandria, Bubastis*, and *Heliopolis*. Which they would gather out of Ezekiel, 30. but there are more than six mentioned in that chapter, ver. 13, 14, 16, 17, 18. Others, that the meaning is, that *five* cities, only, or simply, are not meant, but five of six, as if five cities for one should come in unto God, or one city of six only, should stand out, and perish in, and for their sin: but how the text will bear this, I see not. Albeit, therefore we need not admit that excessive number of cities, which from their priests' report, these authors relate to have been sometime in Egypt, no more, than we are bound to believe those thousands of years, that they affirmed their state, in a succession of kings and priests, to have stood; nor again on the other side, have we any good ground, to reduce their prime cities to so precise, and narrow a number, as bare five: Yet it is not improbable, that their principal cities, and royal seats, were not very many, suppose some twelve, as they might well be, about this time, when into twelve principalities was all Egypt divided. The meaning of the prophet then may well be, that a considerable number, (such as is five of twelve) of the chiefest cities in Egypt, should embrace the faith and service of the true God: and that the prophet's intent is to design a number of such, appears by his express nomination of *Heliopolis*, in particular, to be one of them.

*{speak the language of Canaan*} What is here meant by *speaking the language of Canaan*, is questioned. That there is an allusion to the Hebrew tongue, as we term it; the language wherein God was then served by his people, is generally agreed on: but there is some controversy among the learned, why that tongue should be called *the language of Canaan*. The common, and almost generally received opinion, both of Jews and Christians, has been, that it is so termed, because it was the native language of God's people, who then were possessed of, and lived in, the land of Canaan, and in that language, then, and there, served God; which language being that which our first parents spoke, and was in general use before the division of tongues, Gen. 11. 1. remained still in the line of Sem, among those of Eber's posterity, (whom a special mark is set upon, as the prime man in Sem's issue, there recorded, Gen. 10. 21. with memorable note also, subjoined, concerning Peleg his son, that *in his days, the earth, or, world, was divided*, Gen. 10. 25. and from whose name Abram, is called *an Hebrew*, Gen. 14. 13.) and was termed Hebrew, because continued constantly in his family: Howbeit, in these latter days, some men of great note have not stuck to affirm, that the Hebrew tongue is termed here *the language of Canaan*, because it was the native language of the posterity of Cham, descending from him by Canaan, who first inhabiting and peopling those parts, both retaining that language in the division of tongues, and transmitted it to their posterity: and that Abram was wholly unacquainted with it, as being not his native language, until leaving his kindred, and father's house, where he was born, he came to live in the land of Canaan. But this opinion, though maintained by great authors, seems to me very improbable, that the ancient tongue, spoken commonly, yea, generally, before the building of Babel, which procured the ensuing division, should be lost in that family, that in all likelihood had no hand in that business, and should continue in the line of those that were most deeply engaged therein; and in all probability, drew others thereunto, Gen. 10. 10. The arguments brought to confirm this new conceit, seem very weak, and inconsequent, and would require longer discourse to discuss, than the present work will well afford. Suffice it may, for our present purpose, that the Hebrew tongue, in ordinary use with God's people then residing in Canaan, is the language, if not intended, yet alluded to in this place: called also the *Jews' language*, Neh. 13. 24. chap. 36. 11, 13. A new question arises, what is here meant by speaking this language; And there want not, that understand it, of studying, learning, and making use of the Hebrew tongue. Which some writers, therefore, testify to have been very common in some Egyptian towns, bordering upon Palestine, and to have continued, though not without some alteration, even unto their times; and the meaning is, says one of ours, as if it were said of some persons or places, in Hungary, or Transylvania, that the people are so affected and taken with the Mahometan religion, that they wholly addict themselves to the study of the Arabic tongue; because Mahomet's law is written in it, and so here of the Egyptians, that out of love and affection to the Jewish religion, and the worship of the true God, they should desire to learn, and make use of that language, wherein the law of God was written, and wherein he was served by that people. But the prophet's intendment seems rather to be, though alluding indeed to that language, that the Egyptians converted by the ministry of the gospel, should, whatsoever language they spoke in, make the same profession, and confession of their faith, with other of God's people, that were before them in Christ, Rom. 10. 9, 12, 18. & 14. 6, 9–11. 2 Cor. 4. 11. their speech and communication, should now be no longer profane, as it had been; but circumcised, and pure, chap. 6. 5. the very same that is prophesied, and promised, Zeph. 3. 9. that after God's judgments there before denounced, and then executed, he would *turn people's lip*, (that is, *language*, as it is also here;) and give them *a pure lip*, that is, *a pure language, that they may call all upon the name of the Lord, and serve him with one shoulder*: that is, with joint consent they should all concur in praising of God, as if they all spoke with *one mouth*, Rom. 15. 6. or, had all but *one lip*, spoke all the same language; as before that unhappy division of tongues, the whole world did, Gen. 11. 1. *lip*, for *language*: as Job 12. 23. ch. 28. 11. Jer. 33. 19.

*{and swear to the Lord of hosts*} Not, *swear by him*, Jer. 4. 2. & 5. 2. and not by false gods, Exod. 23. 13. Josh. 23. 8. Jer. 12. 16. though that be mentioned, as one prime piece of God's royal prerogative, to be sworn by, and a principal part of man's duty to him, to swear only by him, Deut. 6. 13. & 10. 20. Psal. 63. 11. chap. 65. 16. but *swear to him*: as Psal. 132. 2. that is, bind themselves by solemn oath to depend upon him, and be loyal subjects unto him, 2 Chr. 15. 14, 15. Ezra 10. 5. Neh. 10. 29. Psal. 119. 106. (as people, and princes also, are wont to do, their liege lords, and sovereigns, 2 Chr. 36. 13. Ezek. 17. 13–18.) abandoning their former idolatries, and superstitions, 2 King. 5. 17. Act. 19. 19. See Ch. 45. 23. Zeph. 1. 5.

*{one shall be called the city of destruction*} There is a double reading here, in the Hebrew. Some read *Heres*, with *He*, which signifies *destruction*, or *overthrow*: and though that word itself is nowhere else read, yet a word, not much unlike it, is in that sense found, ch. 49. 19. Amos 9. 11. descending from a verb that signifies commonly to *pull down*, or *destroy*. This reading our translators follow; though the former version, in received use, before the Geneva, render it, by way of inversion, *the city of destruction shall be called one of them*. But by those that maintain this reading, the words are diversely expounded. Some, that a sixth city, remaining unreformed, when five of her neighborhood were converted, should be allotted to destruction, for not following their good example. Others, that each one (as chap. 6. 2.) of the five, before mentioned, *shall be a city, saved from destruction*, Heb. *a city of destruction*, as *wine of lees*, for, *wine*, drawn off the lees, cap. 25. 6. Other read the word *Hheres*, or, *Cheres*, with *Het*, or, *Cheth*, as the Greeks commonly render it; which the old Latin, and some others, among which our ancientest English follow: and the word signifies, sometime, *an earthen pot*, Levit. 6. 28. Jer. 19. 1. or, *a potsherd*, Job 2. 8. chap. 45. 9. and so some render it here, *ostracian, the earthen city*, as *earthen vessels*, 2 Cor. 4. 7. but the word there used: sometime *the sun*, Job 9. 7. Jer. 19. 2. and thus the old Latin, and not a few others, here understand it; rendering the text, *Heliopolis*, or, *the city of the sun, shall be*, or, *shall be accounted one*. Heb. word for word, *the city of the sun shall be said to one*: that is, the city of the sun shall be called one of that number, shall be reckoned up among them: as Psal. 87. 5, 6. So ch. 62. 4. *forsaken shall not be said unto thee*, that is, you shall not be so called, or accounted. There were divers cities in divers countries, consecrated to the sun, and that bore therefore his name, being deemed one of the heathens' principal gods, 2 King. 23. 5, 11. Ezek. 8. 16. See chap. 17. 8. Of this sort was *Bethshemesh*, among the Canaanites, Judg. 15. 10. & 19. 38. *Kir-heres*, and *Kir-Haresheth*, among the Moabites, chap. 16. 7, 11. and among the Egyptians, *Heliopolis*, as the Greeks term it, being for signification, the same with those other, (of which see many more in Steven of Byzantium) and by the Latins, *Solis oppidum*, Pliny, l. 5. c. 9. and l. 6. c. 29. in Scripture it is sometime called by the Egyptian appellation, *On*, Gen. 41. 45. and sometime, by an Hebrew, of the same signification in effect with this here, *Bethshemesh*, Jer. 43. 13. and *Aven*, Ezek. 30. 17. though this latter, it may be, by an Hebrew term of ill presage, coming near the Egyptians, the like whereunto, Hosh. 4. 15. and 10. 5, 8. as if he had said *On, that may well be termed Aven*, as Amos 5. 5. *Bethel shall become Aven*, that is, *vexation*, or *vanity*, or, *a thing of nought*, this city so called anciently, but in latter times, *Damiata*, was a city much addicted to idolatry, and is reckoned by Herodot. for one of the six, unto which the Egyptians used, at some set times, out of all quarters, to repair, as the Jews to Jerusalem, because there was their famous *temple of the sun*, and there was kept *Mnevis*, one of their sacred bulls, which they worshiped for a god, as *Apis*, the other of them, at Memphis; so that the prophet's intendment, is, to intimate, that even some of those Egyptian cities, that had, with idolatry, been most polluted, should receive the sincere service, and worship of God. Howbeit, Josephus is much mistaken, who imagines, that this prophecy was fulfilled under the Ptolomies, when *Onias* the Jewish priest, being driven out of his country, built a stately temple, with an altar, not unlike that at Jerusalem, within the principality of *Heliopolis*, in Egypt, to draw other of his countrymen into those parts. See Joseph. *antiquities*, l. 13. c. 6. and *of the Jewish war*, l. 7. c. 30. The Chaldee takes in both readings here, thus rendering the words, *The city of Bethshemesh, which is to be destroyed shall be said to be one of them*: the like does the Greek, ch. 16. 1.

**V. 19.** *{In that day*} In those times: as ver. 21.

*{shall there be an altar to the Lord, in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof, to the Lord*} The meaning is, that the true worship of God, prescribed by him in his word, shall be as amply settled among the Egyptians, as it was then among the Jews, See Joh. 4. 21–24. described here, as usually elsewhere, by the rites and ceremonies and manner of service, that by God's appointment, was among God's people, then in use. So c. 18. 7. & 60. 7. & 66. 20, 21. Mal. 1. 11.

*{an altar*} Not for sacrifice, say some; (for that might not be out of Jerusalem, Deut. 12. 13, 14. and yet upon extraordinary occasions, was by God's, not permission only, but approbation, and secret instigation, if not manifest injunction, at sometime, built elsewhere, 1 King. 18. 30, 32.) but for memorial, and resemblance only, ver. 20. not unlike that of the Reubenites, and Gadites, Josh. 22. 10, 11, 23–26. But why not an altar for sacrifice, then, when the Jerusalem altars should be all, not demolished only, but out of date? Jer. 3. 16. Heb. 9. 9, 10. for why not a spiritual altar, for spiritual sacrifices? v. 20. c. 56. 7. & 60. 7. Ro. 12. 1. & 15. 16. Phil. 2. 17. Heb. 13. 10, 15, 16.

*{in the midst of the land of Egypt*} As Jerusalem stood in the heart of the land of Canaan, for the more easy resort unto it, out of all parts, Psalm 122. 4, 5. or in the land of Egypt, among the Egyptians: as Chap. 5. 12. ver. 20, 24. But here rather, in the former and stricter sense, in regard of the next branch.

*{and a pillar*} Evident tokens and signs of God's true religion, settled with them. An allusion to such altars, and pillars, as the ancient patriarchs, in times fore-past, erected for the solemn service and worship of God, in all places where they came, but in those more especially, where God appeared unto them. Gen. 12. 7. 28. 18, 22. & 31. 13. & 35. 7, 14. Exod. 17. 15. & 24. 4. where mention is of twelve pillars in one place: and *pillar*, may be for *pillars*, in this place as it is also there.

*{at the border thereof*} Alluding to that, Josh. 22. 10, 25. where it is said, that *at the borders of the land of Canaan, by Jordan, that altar was built*: The meaning is, that monuments, and evidences of piety and devotion, should be frequent among the Egyptians, not in the heart of the land only, but in the skirts of the country; so that, no sooner should a man set his foot on Egyptian ground, but he should perceive how piously, the people were affected, and to what Lord the land now belonged. See Zach. 14. 9, 20, 21.

*{to the Lord*} Not to idols, and false gods, as formerly; unto which imaginary deities pillars were in Egypt very rife.

**V. 20.** *{And it shall be*} To wit, that altar, and pillar; or, those altars, and pillars, ver. 19.

*{for a sign, and for a witness to the Lord of hosts in Egypt*} To signify, and testify, that the Lord the only true God, the sole Sovereign of heaven and earth, Gen. 2.1. Psal. 146.6. is there acknowledged and served. An allusion to that altar built by the Reubenites, Josh. 22.24,27. and to that stone, or pillar, erected by Joshua, Josh. 24.26,27. of both which, the same in effect is said. Yet there are, that refer this, not to the verse before going; but to the words there ensuing: to wit, that God's hearing them, and sending deliverance unto them, when they called upon him, in their distresses, should be an evidence and argument of God's favor towards them, and reconcilement to them; not unlike that, Psal. 41.11. & 147.43. But the former more naturally flows from the text. That which follows, seems rather to be here intimated, as a motive and inducement to them, to serve him, and adhere unto him, of whose powerful and ready help, they had had so pregnant proof. So Exod. 15.2.

*{for they shall cry unto the Lord for the oppressors*} Or, *when:* (as chap. 1.3.) or, *because when,* (as Jer. 4.30. & 12.15.) *they shall cry;* that is, say some, when the Jews shall cry to God, being by Sennacherib besieged, and distressed, chap. 37.4,15. 2 Chr. 32.20. But few herein concur. The tenor of the context shows, that it is spoken of the Egyptians, who being, by reason of those that oppressed them, grievously afflicted, and distressed, when they found no relief from their idols, or their wizards, ver. 1,3. as was with others, in the like case, ch. 16.12. they shall then, leaving them, seek unto the true God, with better success. So Judg. 10.16. ch. 10.20,21. & 17.7,8. Psal. 107.6,13,19.

*{for their oppressors*} Or, *because of.* Heb. *from the face of:* as ver. 16,17. as the Egyptians sometime made the people of God among them, to cry unto him, by reason of those that then oppressed them, Exod. 3.9. so should they themselves be enforced to the like, in regard of those that should oppress them. For the same word is used in both places, and the prophet may seem here to glance at that story.

*{and he shall send them a Saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them*} Or, *he shall then send them* (as ch. 8.3,14.) *a Saviour, and a great one;* that is, *a great Saviour:* as *a cloud and smoke,* for *a smoky cloud,* chap. 4.5. a great one to be their Savior; or, *even a great one:* as Jer. 17.17. such an one, as in regard of his power, and greatness, shall be able to effect what he undertakes to do for them, ch. 63.1. What great ones were, by God, at several times raised up in succeeding ages, from time to time, as there were for his own people, Judg. 2.16. & 3.15,31. 2 King. 14.27. Obad. 21. Mic. 5.5. to give them some ease and relief, from their oppressors, which might be, as a presage and some shadow of their future spiritual deliverance, and in whom this prophecy might, in part, be fulfilled, is not so clear by the records of antiquity, sacred or profane; especially, while the Assyrian, and Chaldean monarchies stood; of which times we have few monuments of worth and credit, remaining. Howbeit, to pass by what some have conjectured of the conversion of many of them, upon the defeat given to Sennacherib; it may well be deemed, that some notice of the God of Israel came in among them by the Jews' commerce with them; and in the latter times, under the Ptolomies, especially, after the law of Moses was translated into a language; which the Grecian Empire had, in those parts, made more familiar: and divers temporal deliverances, might, from God, be vouchsafed them, in regard of his faithful ones among them; as in Ethiopia; we know also that some proselytes there were, Act. 2.5,10. & 8.27. But certain it is, that the Lord Jesus, that *great Saviour,* Tit. 2.13. is here principally intended, by whom they were delivered from the spiritual servitude and bondage unto sin and Satan; under which they had long lain, as other Gentiles also were, through the ministry of the gospel, Act. 26.17,18. 1 Cor. 6.9,11. & 12.2,3. Eph. 2.2,3. Col. 1.13. 1 Thess. 1.9. Meanwhile, they seem to stray from the text, that expound this of the Angel, who, by the slaughter made in the Assyrian camp delivered those of Jerusalem out of their present distress, chapter 37.37.

**V. 21.** *{And the Lord shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the Lord*} He seems to say the same thing in a divers form, or frame of speech. Yet two distinct things may be implied, their notice of God, and their acknowledgment of him. First, that their service of God, it should not be an ignorant devotion, a blind obedience, like that of those at Athens, Act. 17.23. but God should manifest, and make himself known unto them, Psal. 9.16. & 76.1. Ezek. 29.8,25,26. The knowledge of him, being the ground of all true devotion, and sincere service of him, Jer. 31.34. Hos. 6.3,4. Rom. 16.25,26. 2 Cor. 4.4,6. Gal. 4.8. Eph. 1.17. & 3.19. And then, that God being made made known unto them, (because man may know a thing, and yet refuse to be acknown of it, or to make profession of what he knows, Joh. 12.42.) they shall make acknowledgment of him, whom now they knew; but were ignorant of before, Gal. 4.8. 1 Thess. 4.5. by their performance of service to him, such as he himself requires, Deut. 26.17,18. Joh. 17.3. Rom. 10.9,10. *To know;* for, *to own,* or, *acknowledge,* Psal. 30.7. & 142.4. ch. 59.12. Jer. 3.13. Mat. 7.23. & 25.12.

*{in that day*} As ver. 18,19.

*{and shall do sacrifice, and oblation*} The word, here used, in the Syriac dialect, signifies, indeed, *to make,* or *to do,* as Dan. 3.1. & 4.35. but in Hebrew, most generally, *to worship,* or, *serve,* Deut. 4.19. & 6.13. & 10.12. See ver. 23. It would rather therefore be rendered; *And shall serve,* or *worship him with sacrifice and oblation.* Of the difference whereof, see on chap. 1.11,13. Put both here, as the one there, and the other, Psal. 51.16. and elsewhere collectively, for *sacrifices,* and *oblations:* metaphorically, for such spiritual services, as were thereby, sometime, typified, and are correspondent thereunto. See ver. 19. Zeph. 3.10. Mal. 1.11. And this is that, whereby they should acknowledge God for their Sovereign, and their Savior, and testify their duty and engagement unto him, 2 King. 5.15,17. A defect of the pronoun, *him,* as Hos. 6.5. Job 3.34. Of the particle *with,* as ch. 37.5,10.

*{yea, they shall vow a vow unto the Lord, and perform it*} Heb. *and they shall,* etc. Look what vows they made unto God in the time of their troubles they shall perform and make good, upon deliverance, by God, vouchsafed them, Psal. 66.13,14. & 116.8,16,19. Another evidence, and acknowledgment of their dependence on God, and loyalty to him. Of the former, by making vows now to him, as to their false gods they did before. Vows being a special part of religious worship, in those times, especially, Gen. 32.20. & 35.1,3. Levit. 27.9–25. Numb. 6.2–21. The latter, by their due payment, and performance of what they had vowed, Deut. 23.21,22. Psal. 65.1. & 76.11. Eccl. 5.4,5. Mat. 5.33.

*{perform it*} A defect of the affix, or pronoun; as v. 22. ch. 9.9. Hos. 8.4.

**V. 22.** *{And the Lord shall smite Egypt, he shall smite, and heal it*} Heb. *smiting and healing.* It may therefore be thus rendered, *Thus* (after this manner, as Jer. 7.34. Prov. 17.3.) *the Lord shall smite Egypt, smiting and healing it.* The particle is supplied; as ver. 21. God shall so afflict them by the evils above mentioned, as that he shall yet, by those afflictions, work a gracious work upon them, give a good issue of them, and deliver them, not out of those alone, but out of others also worse than them, Deut. 32.39. Psal. 60.2. ch. 6.10. Hos. 6.1.

*{and they shall return even to the Lord*} Or, *for* (as ch. 13.8. & 16.2.) *they shall return to the Lord.* Have recourse to him for mercy and deliverance in their distresses, ver. 20.

*{and he shall be entreated of them*} As he was of Manasses, 2 Chr. 33.20.

*{and shall heal them*} By vouchsafing, as well spiritual health, as temporal deliverance, unto them, chap. 57.18,19. Jer. 3.22. See Jer. 46.26. Ezek. 29.13,14.

**V. 23.** *{In that day*} As ver. 19,21.

*{shall there be an high way out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrians shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptians into Assyria*} Whereas there had been much dissension, and bloody wars, between the Assyrians and the Egyptians, 2 King. 17.24. & 18.19,21. & 23.29. & 24.7. Jer. 44.30. & 46.2. Ezek. 29.19. & 30.10. They should now, being both converted unto God in Christ, abandon all such hostility, one against another, and maintain free commerce, and friendly intercourse, either with other. See chap. 11.13. Some such thing, some deem to have been in Psammetichus his reign; but it was more fully accomplished in the kingdom of Christ, Act. 2.9,10. Rom. 10.18.

*{an high way*} Or, *causeway,* as ch. 11.16.

*{and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians*} They shall both *serve,* that is, *worship,* as ver. 21. one, and the same God, with one and the same worship, in one and the same manner, such as he requires, ch. 2.2,3. & 46.7. Zach. 8.23. Joh. 4.24. The old Greek and Latins, read the words, *The Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians.* That is, say some, not as the Israelites did the Egyptians, Exod. 1.14. & 14.12. but as Christians do one another, with the voluntary service of love, Gal. 5.13. But the former is the better. For why should Egypt serve Ashur thus, rather than Ashur Egypt? The intercourse before was mutual, the service now joint; as Zeph. 3.9.

**V. 24.** *{In that day*} As ver. 23.

*{shall Israel be the third with Egypt, and with Assyria*} That is, say some, the Jews, in the latter part of Ezekiah's reign, shall be in peace and amity with both of them, on either side, 2 King. 20.19. But, nor does any such thing appear, yea, or is likely, nor does that place imply it. The meaning is, that whereas the Jews were formerly disjoined from other nations, who lived then without the pale of God's church, and without that knowledge and worship of God, which as a special privilege the Jews, in those times, enjoyed, Deut. 4.7,8,33,34. & 7.2,3,6. Psal. 76.1,2. & 147.19,20. & 148.14. Act. 10.28. & 11.3. Rom. 3.1,2. & 9.4,5. Eph. 2.12. Now the pale being plucked up, and the partition wall pulled down, the hatred abolished, and both in one body reconciled, there should be no more any distinction of Jew, or Gentile, whether Egyptian, Assyrian, or other, but they should all be in a spiritual confederacy, and communion, one with another, Zach. 8.23. Act. 10.28. & 11.18. & 15.9. 1 Cor. 12.13. Gal. 3.28. Eph. 2.13–19. Col. 3.11.

*{the third*} Heb. *a third.* Which because it seems to be in a feminine form; some would have understood *sister;* and put the word into the text, *a third sister.* As Cant. 8.8. Jer. 3.8,10. Ezek. 16.45,46,48,51,52. & 23.2,4,31–35. But this seems not necessary; because of states, nations, and countries, the Scripture uses to speak promiscuously, sometime in the one form, and sometime in the other. See chap. 15.1,4,5. But what if we render it, *God's third:* as *God's tenth,* ch. 6.13. See the note there; as also, Jer. 2.3. where a word of the self same form and notion, is found,

*{with Egypt, and with Assyria*} These two people are supposed to be more specially mentioned; to show a conjunction of the posterity of Cham, (from whom the Egyptians were descended, Gen. 10.6.) with the race of Japhet, and both of them with the posterity of Sem, according to Noah's prediction, Gen. 9.27. But here is no mention, at all, of any of Japhet's issue: for Ashur was of Sem's race, Gen. 10.21. as well, as Arphaxad, from whom Israel descended, by Eber, and Abraham, Gen. 11.13,16,26. It seems rather to intimate, that even the most accursed people that were in the world, should, in God's good time of grace under the gospel, partake in the blessing by Christ, Gen. 12.2,3. and 22.18.

*{even a blessing*} This may seem to have a special respect to Israel: and is then to be understood actively, as a means of conveying, and imparting a blessing unto the other two; as the word is used, Gen. 12.2. Psal. 21.6. & 72.17. and that partly, in regard of the Messiah, to descend from them, Rom. 9.5. in whom they were to be blessed, Gen. 22.18. And partly, in regard of God's church established among them, and in former times, confined to them; in respect whereof, they are said to partake of the blessing, by their abode in Sem's tents, Gen. 9.27. and adhering unto them, Chap. 56.2,3,6. Zach. 2.11. Or if it be extended unto all three, it must be taken passively; for one that has a blessing bestowed upon him, or partaker of, and in, a blessing; as ch. 65.8. Zach. 8.13.

*{in the midst of the Land*} Or, *earth:* as Gen. 12.3. For this blessing extends itself unto the whole world, chap. 49.6. *in the midst of it:* either *on earth,* in the world; as Psal. 74.12. See ver. 19. Or if there be some emphasis, more than ordinary, in the phrase, I should say, it were, not as some, because these lands lie all three in the middle of the world, which God would have to be as leaven, to spread into the whole lump of it, on every side, Matthew 13.33. for two of them, Israel and Egypt, coast on the sea: but because the land of Judah lay in the midst, between Assyria and Egypt; See ver. 17. For, as for that frivolous and ridiculous conceit of the Jews, wherein the Chinois are said to concur with them, that their country and Jerusalem, more especially, should be the navel of the world, (abusing, to that purpose, some passages of Scripture, Ps. 74.12. & Ezek. 5.5. & 38.12.) it is scarce worthy taking notice of.

**V. 25.** *{whom the Lord of Hosts shall bless, saying*} Or, *For the Lord shall bless him.* That is, each one of them; as chap. 2.20. The relative for the conjunction causal; as 1 Sam. 15.15. Or, *whom,* each one, *the Lord shall bless.* That is, both of pronounce, and make blessed, chap. 61.9.

*{Blessed be Egypt my people*} The title that Israel engrossed before, Deut. 7.6. Ps. 78.71. but should now be common to the Egyptians, with them, Deut. 32.21. Hos. 2.23. Rom. 9.26.

*{and Assyria the work of my hands*} As Israel is so called; not as created only, at first, in Adam, but as made, and molded into a state, Deut. 32.6. chap. 43.7. & 44.2. Psal. 138.8. So are the Assyrians here termed, as being new molded, and new created by him, in his Christ, 2 Cor. 5.17. Gal. 6.15. Eph. 2.10. & 4.24.

*{and Israel mine inheritance*} My portion, my peculiar people, Exod. 19.5. Deut. 4.20. Ps. 74.2. & 135.4. See Jer. 12.7. A privilege, yet now not to be appropriated to them alone; but to be extended unto people in all parts abroad, Ps. 2.8. & 82.8. Eph. 3.6. All three terms used, for variety and elegancy, come home, in effect, and fine to the same.

### CHAPTER 20

**V. 1.** *{In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod*} In the eighteenth Chapter, was a prophecy of evils to befall Ethiopia: in the nineteenth, of the like to betide Egypt. Now in this Chapter, is a prediction of calamities, that both of them, were, from the Assyrians, jointly, to endure, with a more special intimation of the time, at which this prophecy was delivered, prefixed in this verse.

*{Tartan*} A commander of some forces, under the king of Assyria, one of the three, that Sennacherib sent unto Ezekiah, to summon him to a surrender of Jerusalem, 2 King. 18.17.

*{Ashdod*} Or, as the Greeks and Latins term it, *Azotus,* Act. 8.40. A chief city of Palestine, or the Philistines' country: famous for their idol Dagon, who had his temple there, 1 Sam. 5.1,2. & 6.17. Yet it seems to have belonged, sometime, to the Israelites, and to have been part of the portion, and possession of the posterity of Judah: as also, some other, of the Philistine cities, Josh. 13.3. & 15.47. See c. 15.2,4.

*{(when Sargon the King of Assyria sent him)*} Who this Sargon should be, is much questioned. The most suppose him to be Sennacherib; and to have had two names: as many others, in like manner, mentioned in Scripture. See on chap. 1.1. *Uzziah.* Though, beyond all probability, they multiply the matter, who tell us, from Jerom, that Sennacherib had no less than *seven names:* yea, some of the Jewish writers, say, *eight:* and mold the Assyrian monarchs, many of them into one. But there want not those, who deem this Sargon to have been, not Sennacherib: but one of his predecessors. And some of them, thus reckon the succession of the Assyrian rulers. *Phul,* 2 King. 15.19. 1 Chr. 5.26. *Tiglath-Phileser,* 2 King. 15.29. 1 Chr. 5.26. *Jareb,* Hos. 5.13. & 10.16. *Sargon,* Esay 20.1. *Salmaneser,* 2 King. 17.3. & 18.9. *Sennacherib,* 2 King. 18.13. Other, omitting *Jareb,* thus order them: *Phul, Tiglath-Pilneser, Sargon, Salmaneser, Sennacherib.* See on Chap. 14.29. But, as it may justly be doubted, whether *Jareb,* who, in the former descent is reckoned after *Phul* and *Phileser,* were not ancienter than either of them; so I suppose, it will better suit with the course of the sacred story, (for foreign helps, in a manner here, wholly fail us) to place this Sargon, between, *Salmaneser,* and *Sennacherib:* as the successor of the one, and predecessor to the other. The name seems to be the same with *Serug,* or *Sarug,* the name of Abraham's grandfather, Gen. 11.22. *Sarug, Sargon;* as *Tirakah,* ch. 37.9. *Tarchos, Jesua* Zach. 3.1. *Jason,* Act. 17.5. and the like.

*{and fought against Ashdod, and took it*} This some suppose to have been done in the twelfth year of Ezekiah, under Sennacherib, when he bent himself against the strong cities of Judah; among which, they suppose Ashdod to have been one, as being lately from the Philistines recovered, by Ezekiah, 2 King. 18.8. Others and so some of the Jewish doctors, draw it down to the fourteenth of Ezekiah; at which time, say they, Sennacherib hearing of Tirhakah, the king of Ethiopia, coming against him, ch. 36.1. & 37.9. sent Tartan to take Ashdod, and went himself to meet Tirhakah, whom having discomfited, and subdued Egypt and Ethiopia, within the space of three years, he returned, with those he had captived of them, to the siege of Jerusalem. But this no way suits well with the Scripture story. Which to help, therefore, some say, that the Ethiopians, led by Tirhakah, made an inroad into Assyria, about that time, in Sennacherib's absence; after whose decease, Esar-haddon, who succeeded him, made war upon the Ethiopians, and took many of them captive, together with such Egyptians as were assistant to them. That which carries much more probability with it, than the former. But others carry up, far higher, the date of this prophecy, unto the fourth year of Ezekiah, and the sixth of Hosea, at which time they suppose, that this Sargon, Salmaneser's predecessor, invaded Palestine, and sent Tartan to besiege Ashdod: but died before it could be surprised. And true it is, that the words may not amiss, for the syntax of them, be so read, casting out the parenthesis, *In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod, when Sargon sent him to fight against Ashdod, and take it.* For we have the very like frame of words, Josh. 24.9. where it is said, that *Balack the king of Moab arose, and warred against Israel, and sent and called Balaam to curse them.* Yet Jephthah asks the king of Ammon, whether *Balak did ever fight against Israel,* Jud. 11.25. And it is apparent, he never did; nor dared do it; because he could not induce Balaam to curse them; which otherwise he would have done, conceiving some hope to prevail, if he could have drawn him so to do, Numb. 22.5,6. But the meaning of the place is, *he arose and warred;* that is, *he arose to war:* assayed, or attempted to do it, but never did. So Mal. 1.9. *Do ye now beseech God: and he will be gracious unto us.* For so, word for word, the text runs in the original. The prophet therein intending nothing less, than that God, at their request, would deal graciously with his people, in remitting his wrath towards them, incensed by their sins, whereof they themselves had been principal promoters and abetters; as he afterward affirms; and were very unfit, therefore, to sue for others, and very unlikely to prevail in their behalf. But the prophet's meaning is, as our Bibles aright render it, *Beseech God that he will be,* or, *to be gracious unto us:* and so *he arose, and warred;* that is, *arose, that he might war,* or *to war:* and the like might be here. Howbeit, unless aught could be produced, whereby it might appear, that Ashdod was not taken by Tartan: we need not decline that sense of the words, that is most ordinary and common. And since, that in places where we have so little light of certainty, we must of necessity go by conjectures, as those before mentioned interpreters all do; I shall make bold to add my conjectural thoughts also to theirs. I suppose, therefore, this prophecy was delivered about the eighth, or ninth year of Ezekiah, when Salmaneser, who, in his sixth year had taken Samaria, and carried Israel away captives, 2 King. 18.10,11. being now deceased; Sargon his successor, desirous to prosecute his father's designs, and to enlarge his dominions, began to set upon the Philistines, that bordered upon them, to the West, (see ch. 9.12.) and began with Ashdod: to the relief whereof, the Egyptians, their next neighbors, together with the Ethiopians, their confederates, coming in no small companies, were by the Assyrians defeated and carried captive, in such scornful and despiteful manner: as is here after described, ver. 4. the rather, to be revenged upon the Egyptians, because they had so lately before, been assistant to the Israelites against the Assyrians, in the reign of Salmaneser; and an occasion of their revolt, 2 King. 17.4. And the siege of Ashdod might well continue three years, as well, as that of Samaria, 1 King. 17.5. being one of the strongest cities in Palestine; nor is it unlikely, that Sargon the rather attempted this city, if it were one of those that Ezekiah had subdued and regained, that he might pick a quarrel with him, and so be dealing with him, as his predecessors had done with the other ten tribes before; that which might also, the rather move Ezekiah, to seek to shake off the Assyrian yoke, 1 King. 18.7. thereby discovering their ambitious and tyrannical intentions. But Sargon, it seems, being taken away; before that his purposed design could be effected, Sennacherib, his successor, went on with the same; 2 King. 18.13. and this my conjecture I leave to the consideration of others, ready to yield unto any, that can bring surer grounds, or afford better light. The Egyptians, after their wonted manner of ascribing to their kings conquests, achieved by others, seem to attribute this taking of Ashdod to Psammetichus, who, about these times, reigned in Egypt, reporting of him, that invading Syria, he sat down, not three, but thirty years, wanting one, before the strong city of Azotus, which endured the longest siege that had been known, and at length took it. See Herodot. lib. 2.

**V. 2.** *{At the same time spake the Lord by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying*} Heb. *by the hand,* (that is, the ministry; as Hag. 1.1. Mal. 1.1.) *of Isaiah the son of Amos;* See chap. 1.1. That is, by me, and to me; the noun, for the pronoun; as chap. 2.1. Gen. 19.24. God's will and commands, were sometime made known to the persons, that were to put them in execution by others; as 2 King. 9.1,2. Sometime immediately to themselves; as Jer. 19.1,10. And so to Esay here; who is enjoined, not only to do somewhat that might shadow out that which he was to deliver; but to tell his people, withal, what was thereby designed, ver. 3,4.

*{Go loose the sackcloth from off thy loins*} An act enjoined the prophet, that was symbolical and significative; not unlike that, Ezek. 12.3–7. foreshowing, in what sort, the Egyptians and Ethiopians should be carried captive, by the Assyrians, ver. 4.

*{Go*} The word in these kind of injunctions does not always imply some motion from place to place; especially, when the thing enjoined may without any such change be accomplished; but a speedy, and sedulous address to the doing of the thing enjoined, Gen. 19.32. & 31.44. Num. 24.14. Jer. 19.1. Hos. 3.1.

*{loose*} The word signifies, first, *to open,* chap. 50.5. then to *loose;* either captives out of prison; which is done, by opening the prison doors, chap. 14.17. & 51.14. & 61.1. or garments from the body, by opening, and untying the girdle, or whatsoever they were fastened to the body with before, Job 12.18. and lastly, more generally, *to put off* any garment, whether girt close to the body, or hanging loose about it, 1 King. 20.11. Ps. 30.11. and so here.

*{the sackcloth*} Heb. *sack:* as chap. 3.24. Now sackcloth was used in times of heaviness, for a mourning weed, chap. 22.12. & 37.2. Joel 1.13. Whence *to loose,* or *to put off sackcloth,* for to leave mourning, or to give cause so to do, Psal. 30.11. but here it is not so used; but for such an upper garment, made of coarse, and hairy stuff, as the prophets ordinarily were wont to wear, 2 King. 1.8. Zach. 13.4. Matth. 3.4.

*{from off thy loins*} Whereunto, or about, such garments, loose otherwise, were sometime girt, 1 King. 20.46. 2 King. 9.1.

*{and put off thy shoe from thy foot*} Or, *loose,* Deut. 24.9. because the latchet, or shoestring is loosed, for the pulling of it off, Mar. 1.7. Luk. 3.16. *shoe,* and *foot:* as Josh. 5.15. for *shoes,* and *feet:* as it is, Exod. 3.5. Heb. *from off,* or *upon:* as Deut. 25.9.

*{and he did so, walking naked, and barefoot*} Albeit, it be expressly said, that he did so; yet there want not a few, among whom, also, some of the Jewish writers, who suppose, that this was not done indeed by the prophet, but in a vision only seemed to be done by him. See the like conceit, cap. 8.3. One cause, why they so imagine, is because they conceive, that the prophet should be enjoined to walk stark naked: whereas indeed, there was no such matter intended. For first God enjoined him only to put off his prophetical robe or mantle; such, as fell from Elias, when he was carried up to heaven in a whirlwind, 2 King. 2.13. then, it had been in vain, to add *barefoot,* if he had before meant all naked. Secondly: it was to signify, how the Egyptian and Ethiopian captives should be handled; he was therefore to go stripped, as a prisoner, or captive; now captives are not wont to be led stark naked; but ill clothed, in single, and sorry suits, or in ragged apparel. And lastly, the word *naked,* is in Scripture commonly so used; to wit, when a man goes in his coat, or inner raiment only, without upper garments, gown, cloak or mantle, such, as at other times he ordinarily uses. So it is said of Saul, that in a prophetical rapture, *he stripped off his clothes,* that is, his upper garments, or garment, (as *yokes,* for *yoke,* Jer. 27.2. & 28.10.) and *lay down naked before Samuel,* 1 Sam. 19.24. So chap. 32.11. the women are commanded *to strip themselves bare,* (that is to put off their bravery, or their better apparel, Exod. 33.4,5.) and *to gird on sackcloth.* So Peter is said to cast on his *short fisher's coat,* (for such an one, the learned observe the word there used, to signify, as frequent among them, of that employment, in those parts) *for* (says the text) *he was naked;* yet not stark naked, though without it, Joh. 21.7. nor in any other sense, does Micah say, that *he would go stripped, and naked;* or, our prophet here, that *he went naked, and barefoot.* See also Act. 19.16.

*{barefoot*} Or, *unshod.* The habit, when affected, of mourners, 2 Sam. 15.30. when enforced, of captives, Jer. 2.25.

**V. 3.** *{And the Lord said*} Unto the prophet, and by him, to those whom he preached and published this unto: either when, at first, he enjoined him to walk up and down in that manner, which could not but seem strange unto those that beheld it, or afterward, when he had for some space of time so done, and was demanded of his people, what, by so doing, he meant, or intended: as Eze. 12.9,10. & 24.19.

*{like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked, and barefoot, three years, for a sign, and wonder upon Egypt, and upon Ethiopia*} In the words ensuing, God declares what he intended to signify unto them, by this his command given to the prophet, and his acting according to the same. A relation of what was done by the prophet, together with the end of it, and whom it concerned, is in this verse: the application of it, to that which was to befall those two people, to wit, the Egyptians, and the Ethiopians, is in the next.

*{my servant*} Not in general only as are all men, yea, all creatures; in regard of creation, Ps. 119.91. or, in somewhat more special manner, in regard of a voluntary addiction, and obstriction; as are all, that are in special covenant with him, Neh. 1.11. Psal. 79.2. & 116.16. but in a more special rank yet, in regard of his place, and office, as a prophet, as Num. 11.7,8. Jer. 7.25. So, *Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ,* Rom. 1.1. Phil. 1.1. that is, an apostle, 2 Cor. 1.1. Eph. 1.1. *A servant of God, and an Apostle of Christ,* Tit. 1.1. the one explicates the other.

*{naked, and barefoot*} See on ver. 2.

*{three years*} Concerning these words, there is much discrepance of opinion among interpreters. Some annex them to the foregoing sentence, and apply them to the prophet's carriage. And of these, some suppose, that all this was done in a vision; as, say they, those things of Ezekiel, his lying so long on either side; and making, and baking his bread in such and such sort, Ezek. 4.4,6,10,15. and doing of a thing three years together, might, by a vision, be represented in a moment. Other of them, affirm it to have been really done, and exhibited. How else could it be a sign and wonderment unto any? Yet are these also divided; for some of them suppose, that he went constantly thus; as well within doors, as without, for three years together: other; that he went so during that time, only then when he went out about the discharge of his prophetical employment. Thus they, that affix these words to the former, understanding them of the prophet's continuance in that habit. But there want not, that prefix them to the clause ensuing, *for three years a sign, and wonder,* or, *a three years sign, and wonder, upon,* or, *concerning the Egyptians and Ethiopians:* conceiving them to be meant, not of the prophet's act, but of that which was thereby designed: and this reading is strengthened by the pauses, in the Hebrew, the middle distinction concluding at the word next before going. Howbeit, these, again, are not all of one mind, concerning the thing thereby designed. For some suppose that thereby is implied, when this calamity should befall those two nations, which is the more probable (to wit, *three years* after the publication of this prophecy: as the like, chap. 7.8. & 21.16. Others, how long it should continue; to wit, not above *three years,* as the like, chap. 23.15. & 31.10. the like difference of opinion, concerning the same term of years, which some also draw to this, See on chap. 16.14. Howsoever, the question is with these again moved, how long the prophet was to walk thus naked? the rather, for that the text thus read, seems not to determine it: and they deem it unfitting, that the typical act should be of equal extent, for term of time, with the thing itself, thereby typified; no example in Scripture exhibiting any such parallel. Some of them therefore conceive, that one day might suffice for him, to walk abroad in that manner; here being no time limited in the injunction that God gave him. As Jeremy's wearing a yoke on his neck, but for a day, might suffice to denote a captivity of seventy years continuance, Jerem. 25.12. and 27.2. and 28.10. Others would have it done by him, three days, correspondent to the three years designed, either unto the commencing; or, for the consummating of that, which by the prophet was denounced. This is most agreeable to the usual manner of Scripture, *a day for a year,* so *forty days,* for *forty years;* Num. 14.33,34. Ezek. 4.6. and 390 days, for as many years, Ezek. 4.4,5.

*{three years*} Some would have it read, *a third years sign,* etc. because the cardinal number is put sometime for the ordinal, as they term it, as *one;* for *first:* Gen. 1.5. Matt. 28.1. but I find not, where any cardinal so used is joined with a substantive plural: and that *enallage,* therefore, can have no place here.

*{a sign, and wonder*} These two words oft joined together, Deut. 6.22. & 7.19. & 13.1,2. & 26.8. & 28.46. Neh. 9.10. Psal. 135.9. Jer. 32.20. Chap. 8.17. are as *genus,* and *species;* the former of larger extent than the latter. For the former may be, where nothing future is foreshown: as Num. 2.2. Ezek. 20.12. whereas the latter is ever, for the foretelling, and ascertaining of something to come, 1 King. 13.2,3. the former may be some common and ordinary thing; whereas the latter is ever of something, if not miraculous, as Exod. 7.9. 2 Chr. 32.24. yet strange, and unusual, at least, Ezek. 4.2,3. & 12.3,6,11. & 24.16,17,24. and so here. See chap. 8.18.

*{upon Egypt, and upon Ethiopia*} Or, *concerning Egypt, and Ethiopia:* as chap. 1.1. concerning what was to befall the Egyptians, and Ethiopians. See on ver. 1,4. yet concerning the Jews also, unto whom it was exhibited, to dissuade, and deter them, from relying upon these two people; which they were overprone unto. See verse 5,6.

**V. 4.** *{So shall the King of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captive, young, and old, naked and barefoot*} An exposition of this strange, and unwonted demeanor of the prophet, and application of it, to the sad, and sorry condition of the Egyptians, and Ethiopians; which, within a short space of time, they were from the Assyrians to sustain.

*{the King of Assyria*} Whether Sargon, or Sennacherib, or Esar-haddon, his successor, uncertain. See on ver. 1.

*{lead away*} As men are wont to lead, or drive beasts, and cattle: for of such it is most commonly used, Gen. 31.18. Exod. 3.1. 1 Sam. 30.20. 1 King. 4.24. ch. 11.6. and where allusion is thereunto, Ps. 93.52. & 81.1. And it is therefore, not unfitly applied to poor captives, that are led, or driven, like beasts, Gen. 31.26. Deut. 28.37. ch. 61.11. Lam. 3.2.

*{the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives*} Or, *captive.* Heb. *the captivity of Egypt, and the captivity,* or *deportation of Cush: captivity,* for *captives:* as Neh. 1.2,3. Jer. 24.5. For we must not imagine, that the one were *prisoners,* and not *captives;* the other *captives,* but not *prisoners:* (see on chap. 5.13.) for both the words in the original, import one and the same thing: variety of terms, is for the greater elegancy only used. This the king of Assyria should do, either having discomfited their joint forces, or subdued their countries, bordering the one upon the other. See ver. 1.

*{young, and old*} Showing no mercy to any, in regard of tenderness, through years, or weakness through age. See 2 Chr. 36.17.

*{naked, and barefoot*} Stripped of their apparel, and left, in a manner, stark naked, in base rags, scarce able to cover their nakedness: that which is wont to be the lot of captives, in fight taken, and pillaged by the enemy, Deut. 28.45. ch. 3.17,24. Job 24.7,10. Jer. 2.25. Amos 2.16. See ver. 2.

*{even with their buttocks uncovered*} Heb. *fundament;* a word not unusual with us: for it is of near affinity with that, which signifies *foundations,* Psal. 11.3. that part, which man's body sits upon, and rests on in sitting. The meaning is, having not raiment, so much, as to hide their shame. See on ch. 3.17. So in despite were David's messengers used by the Ammonites, 2 Sam. 10.5. And herein, sure, the thing signified outstripped the sign; for the prophet, doubtless, walked not so naked, as to have his shame seen, Rev. 16.15.

*{to the shame of Egypt*} Who assisted them, and in likelihood, undertook to protect them. See on ch. 18.1.

*{shame*} Heb. *nakedness,* 1 Sam. 20.30. Exod. 32.25. because nakedness, since man's fall, is shameful, Gen. 2.25. and 3.7.

**V. 5.** *{And they shall be afraid, and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory*} The event of this overthrow given by the Assyrian, unto the joint forces of the Ethiopians, and Egyptians; to wit, that it should strike a terror into those, that had sought to them for aid against the Assyrian, and make them ashamed, that they relied so much upon them for relief. See ver. 6.

*{they*} That is, say some, the Jews; who trusted too much to them, chap. 30.2. & 31.1. & 36.6. Ezek. 29.6,7,16. See chap. 19.17. Others, the Philistines, and Ashdodites, that expected relief from them. It may well be both, and such others, as they undertook to protect. See on Chap. 8.1. *wings;* for the word is used indefinitely; as others oft are, Chap. 2.19. Mal. 1.4.

*{afraid*} Because they shall have no hope of ability to hold out against an adversary so potent, and prevalent, whom the joint forces of two such kingdoms were not able to withstand, 2 King. 10.4. and it is matter of dread, to see supporters, and confederates to fail, chap. 19.17.

*{ashamed*} To find their expectations frustrate, and those defeated, of whose help, they had been overconfident, and had much gloried therein before, chap. 30.5. Jer. 2.36.

*{their expectation*} The people from whom they expected succor, and safeguard. Heb. *their looking unto,* or, *looking after:* and so ver. 6. for the word is no where else found, but the root it comes of, is used oft in that sense, Psal. 34.5. & 142.4. and so other words of the same notion: *expectation,* for, persons, from whom aught is expected, Psal. 71.5. Jer. 14.8. & 17.13.

*{their glory*} *Glory,* for them, of whom and their help, they gloried; So Psal. 3.3. with 44.8. Chap. 10.3. & 17.4. yet *expectation* is not here so appropriated to the one, and *glory,* to the other, as if they did not, as well expect help from, as glory in, either. But it is an elegant form of speech, very usual with this prophet, intending the same thing of either; Of which, see before, ver. 4. & chap. 5.13.

**V. 6.** *{And the inhabitant of this Isle shall say in that day*} *Inhabitant,* for *inhabitants:* as chap. 5.3. *in that day,* for, at that time, as ch. 9.18. But the question is, what the *isle,* or *island,* here spoken of, should be. The word is deemed, most properly, to signify an island, that is, some land on every side environed with water, as *lake,* some great water encompassed with land; whence arises that question, among the ancient geographers, whether the earth were an *island,* or the sea a *lake,* that is, whether the sea encompassed the land, or the land the sea, and hence in Scripture, *the Isles of the Sea,* Esth. 10.1. chap. 11.11. and, *the Isles in the Sea,* Ezek. 26.18. but it is used also, as is generally agreed on, for such countries, and regions, as lay upon the seacoasts: so it seems to be taken, Jer. 25.22. Ezek. 27.3,15. Hence some gather, that the Philistines' country should be here meant, because it lay upon the midland sea, See Jer. 47.7. but so did the land of Israel too, Josh. 13.4,12,47. and that reason some of the Rabbins render, why it should here be so termed: nor is it a sufficient argument to prove, that the Jewish land should not be here intended, because that their country had no where in particular, this name given it, when as the word is granted to be of so large an extent, as to take in all regions bordering on the sea, as theirs did. Yea it is used yet more largely; for lands, or countries in general; and for *inlands,* as well as *islands.* See chap. 41.1,5. & 42.4,10. & 49.1. & 51.5. & 60.9. Jer. 47.4. And *this land* may seem rather to carry it to those, unto whom, than to the Philistines, of whom, he spoke.

*{Behold, such is our expectation, whither we flee for help, to be delivered from the King of Assyria; and how shall we escape?*} See on ver. 5. Thus it fares with those, on whom we relied, or expected help from. Nor do these words evince, that this is not spoken in the person of the Jewish people; because Ezekiah trusted not on Egypt, but on God alone; and Jerusalem therefore was delivered: but Ashdod, which trusted to the Egyptian aid, was not. For it is not unlikely, that Ezekiah, though a good king, and one that *trusted in God,* 2 King. 18.5. as well as Asa, who did so also, 2 Chr. 14.11. & 16.7,8. might be somewhat faulty this way, as well as another way, that savored of some diffidence, upon the very same occasion, 2 King. 18.6,14–16. See ch. 3.2,4.

*{from the King of Assyria*} Who shortly after, surprised a great part of Judea, Chap. 36.1. Heb. *from the face of:* as Chap. 21.15.

*{and how shall we escape?*} Or, *how should we escape?* What hope can we have to be secured by help from them, who are not able to save themselves? Psalm 60.11. & 146.3,4. their shame appeared in the former branch; in this latter, their fear. See ver. 5.

### CHAPTER 21

**V. 1.** *{The burden of the desert of the Sea*} Here begins a new prophecy, another sermon. Of the word, *Burden,* see on Chap. 13.1. That this prophecy concerns Chaldea, and Babylon, appears evidently, as well by the name of it expressly mentioned, ver. 9. as also by the nations precisely named, by whom it was to be destroyed. But here are two questions moved concerning this prophecy. The former is, why the prophet should have another sermon against Babylon, when as he had so large an one against it, before. To which it is answered; for two causes especially: First, because the people of God were too prone to trust to, and seek amity with, as the kings of Assyria, though they smarted for it, 2 Chr. 28.16,20,21. so the kings of Babylon, who afterward stood up in their stead, 2 King. 20.12,13. chap. 39.1,2. And again, because they were to sustain very heavy things, at their hands, 2 King. 20.17,18. chap. 39.6,7. The prophet therefore, or God rather, by the prophet, does the rather oft mind them of the ruin of Babylon; partly, to withdraw them from relying on a state that was itself, to be ruined; and partly, to comfort them, in regard of those evils, that from that city and kingdom they were to endure. For the same cause, may seem so many predictions to have proceeded from this our prophet, of the Assyrians' downfall, chap. 10.5–20,24–34. & 30.27–33. and of the Egyptians, as from the same prophet, chap. 19. & 20. & 30.3. & 31.3. so also from Jeremy, Jer. 43.8–13. & 44.29,30. & 46. The latter question is, why Babylon, or Chaldea, should be termed *the desert of the Sea.* To this, a late writer of some note, answers, that though the prophecy concerns Babylon, yet by these terms is designed, neither Chaldea, nor Babylon; but Idumea, or the country of the Edomites, who inhabited the desert of Sur, or Etham, Exod. 13.20. & 15.22. Numb. 33.8. But had he shown how this sad prophecy had concerned these Edomites, or where any mention had been therein made of them, there might have been some color of ground for the turning of it that way: now having produced nothing from the matter of it, to back, or second this his conceit, we see little reason to afford entertainment unto it, and taking that for granted, that others, as well Jews, as ours, generally agree in, to wit, that it is Babylon, or Chaldea, at least, that is in these terms described; we shall proceed to consider why it should be so termed: and because the word *desert,* is first in the text, we shall begin with it. Chaldea therefore is here termed a *desert,* as most interpreters imagine, for two causes; the one historical, or geographical, not because it was a wild, or waste country: For it was a very rich, and well watered soil, but because there lay a large desert, or wide wilderness, between Chaldea; wherein Babylon stood, and the countries of Media, and Persia; by the people whereof, it was afterward invaded. The other prophetical: not because it was at present so: because it was in time to come to be laid waste, and desolate, chap. 13.19–22. and as it had made the whole *world a wilderness,* ch. 14.17. in like manner, by way of just retaliation, to be made a *wilderness* itself. So Psal. 137.8. Jer. 51.29,36,37,43. I shall make bold to add mine own conjecture, and leave it to the learned. The Hebrew word signifies as well a *plain,* as a *wilderness,* chap. 63.13. Jer. 13.24. Lam. 4.19. & 5.9. and the notation of it, from a word, that is in the Chaldee, more common, signifying to *lead* cattle out to the places where they are to feed, carries it more specially, unto such plains, as had pasture grounds in them, or consisted of such. So the word seems to be taken, 1 Sam. 17.28. & 24.1,3. & 25.1,15. Psal. 65.12,13. Jer. 9.9. Joel 1.19,20. & 2.22. Luk. 15.4. compared with Matt. 18.12. I suppose therefore, that Chaldea has this term given unto it, not as a *desert,* but as a *plain:* and such indeed that country was, wherein the building of Babylon was first set on foot, as Moses testifies, Gen. 11.2. in regard whereof, also, it is commonly deemed, that the Chaldeans proved so skillful in astronomy, the situation of their country, which lay all in a plain, without any notable interruption of hills, or mountains of height, affording a great help to the more exact observation of the motion, as well of the fixed stars, as of the planets, and the times of the rising, and setting of either. And thus much for the former term of *desert,* or, *plain:* and the reason why Chaldea might be so termed. The latter word, is that of *the sea.* Now this term is given to Chaldea, or Babylon, as some think, metaphorically, *a sea,* that is, *as the sea,* in regard of that great abundance of wealth, that Babylon was stored with; (as we use to say, *a sea of good*) all the kingdoms, and countries under that vast monarchy, Jer. 27.5,6. sending in their treasures to Babylon, as all rivers empty themselves into the sea, Jer. 51.44. some also, in regard of her unsatiableness; though receiving all, yet having never enough; as the sea is never the fuller, for all those waters, that out of all parts are swallowed up in it, Eccl. 1.7. See Jer. 51.13. and Herodot. l. 1. Some also prophetically, in regard of those manifold, and immense evils, that were to befall her, as we use to say, *a sea,* or, *an ocean of evils; the Sea is broke in upon Babylon,* Jer. 51.42. or, because the seat of the city was to become as a sea, to be turned into *water-pools,* chap. 14.23. Thus they; but, as to me seems, with no great probability; for neither the land of Chaldea, nor the city, are here termed *the sea;* but *the desert,* or, *plain of the sea,* as *the Isles of the Sea,* Esth. 10.1. for lands situate in, or beside, the sea. See on chap. 20.6. Others therefore rather deem Chaldea, or the seat of the city, so termed, in regard of the situation of it. And here, in regard that *the sea,* in Scripture language, is very commonly used, for *the West,* Gen. 13.14. & 28.14. Exod. 10.19. chap. 49.12. Ezek. 48.17. the reason whereof is, because the midland sea lay to the West of Judea, and was the western border, or boundary of it, Josh. 15.12. Deut. 34.2. Some of the Rabbins therefore would have it so called, because it *lay west* or northwest, from the land of the Medes, and Persians, by whom it was to be destroyed. See chap. 41.25. But this seems rather, to others, a little too far fetched: who rather suppose this term to allude to the situation of Babylon, and the plain whereon it was built, standing the one, and lying the other, situate either of them, near unto, or upon the banks of, *the great river Euphrates,* as it is styled, Gen. 15.18. Deut. 1.7. and the vast lakes made out of it. For any great confluences, or receptacles of water, are in the Hebrew tongue termed *Seas,* Gen. 1.10. hence *the Sea of Galilee,* chap. 11.1. Matth. 4.18. & 15.29. which yet was but a *lake,* Luk. 5.1. and the great laver belonging to Solomon's Temple, is called, *a sea,* 1 King. 7.23,24. Jer. 52.17. The country of Chaldea, therefore, that part of it especially, that lay near to Babylon, is not unfitly termed, *the plain of the sea,* in regard of those meres, and pools, the country lying all on a flat, that that great river Euphrates, that ran round about Babylon, as also, through the midst of it, made on every side of it, which yet in part to remedy, two queens especially, were at infinite cost; the one of them, to wit, Semiramis, by raising mounds, and banks of strange height, and strength, on either side the river, to keep it, so much as might be, within compass, the other, to wit, Nitocris, who came long after her, (besides what in this kind, she also did, even to wonderment) partly, by diverting the course of the river from his direct passage, and through new channels of great depth, by man's industry sunk, winding it to and fro, and enforcing it to fetch many compasses, before it came down to Babylon, to break the violent force of the stream, running downright before, and partly, by digging a lake near unto it, three hundred and twenty furlongs broad. Of which things, see Herodot. l. 1. Strabo, l. 16. Plin. l. 6. c. 26,27. Hence is Babylon said *to sit upon many waters,* Jer. 51.13. Whereunto may be added, what Abydenus an ancient writer, cited by Eusebius, in his *Evangelical preparative,* l. 9. c. 41. reports, to wit, that it was by tradition commonly received, that the whole country about Babylon was *all water,* a very *sea,* until Belus (supposed to be Nimrod, Gen. 10.9–11.) having drained it, divided it, and built Babylon upon it: as also what God himself says by the prophet, speaking to Babylon, *I will dry up thy Sea,* Jer. 51.36. And thus much for the title, or inscription of this prophecy.

*{As whirlwinds in the South pass through; so it comes from the desert, from a terrible land*} Or, *As whirlwinds in the South; he passeth.* A prediction of the Medes and Persians, their violent irruptions, in a furious and tempestuous manner breaking into Chaldea.

*{whirlwinds*} Or, as some, *Some one grievous whirlwind,* or, *tempest,* the plural, by way of eminency, used for the singular; as Prov. 1.20. & 9.1. Mic. 5.2. Yet in a plural sense, it may well stand here; as another word of the same notion, which, with it, is used, Zach. 9.14. though in that form, this word be no where else found, *wind,* in such similitudes, is a note of swiftness, Psal. 18.10. & 104.3. A *whirlwind,* such as whisking about, involves all on every side, and bears all down before it, a note of vehemency, and violence, forcibly breaking through, and beating down all opposition, Psalm 83.15. Prov. 1.27. Chap. 5.28. and 29.6. Jer. 4.13. Nah. 1.3.

*{in the South*} Of *whirlwinds of the South,* is mention made also, Zach. 9.14. Howbeit, the word here used, is ambiguous. For albeit, that it be frequently used for the South, or Southern parts, Exod. 26.18. & 27.9. Num. 34.3. Josh. 15.1,2. Judg. 21.19. yet it seems properly, and primarily to signify *highlands,* or *dry lands,* opposed sometime to the *vale,* or, lower grounds, Josh. 10.40. Jud. 1.9. Jer. 17.26. sometime to the *springy,* and well watered lands, Josh. 10.40. & 15.19. Judg. 1.15. and the Southern parts are so termed, because commonly such, as being nearer to the scorching heat of the sun, either may here be meant: partly, because the Southern winds are oft in those parts tempestuous, Job 37.9. as also, for that in such uplands, the wind is wont to have the greater power, Jer. 4.11.

*{pass through*} Heb. *to pass through;* that is, are apt, or are wont *to pass along,* without stop, or stay; there being nothing usually in such places to hinder, or to restrain them, Jer. 9.24.

*{So*} A defect of the redditive particle; as Prov. 25.12. and 26.11. but here it needs not, the text being rendered as before.

*{it cometh*} To wit, the calamity of Chaldea, or a tempest upon it. Or, *he cometh,* that is, Cyrus with his forces breaking in fiercely and furiously upon it, Jer. 50.42,44. and 51.28,30.

*{from the wilderness*} Either, because winds oft blow suddenly and fiercely, from waste places, Job 1.19. Jer. 4.10,11. or in regard of a wilderness, that lay betwixt Persia, or Media, and Chaldea, which Cyrus and his forces, must of necessity pass through. Xenophon, l. 3. or, of the country itself, both of Media, and Persia, the northerly part of either, wherein their soldiery was most bred, being much of it waste, and mountainous, Herodot. l. 1. and Strabo, l. 11. and 15.

*{from a terrible land*} To wit, out of Media, the people whereof, the Babylonians much feared; and their queen Nitocris, therefore, above mentioned, a woman of prudence, and providence, above her sex, by all means, endeavored to keep them from having any commerce with her people, by the Assyrians, that lay between them and the Medes, Herodot. l. 1. Of their fierceness, see ch. 13.17,18.

**V. 2.** *{A grievous vision is declared unto me*} Grievous matters concerning Babylon, are, in way of vision, revealed unto me: and this prophecy, therefore is not without good cause, entitled, *a burden,* ver. 1.

*{grievous*} Heb. *hard, harsh,* or, *cruel,* ch. 19.4.

*{vision*} See ch. 1.1.

*{the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously; and the spoiler spoileth*} Heb. *The treacherous dealer, a treacherous dealer;* or, *dealing treacherously; and the spoiler, a spoiler,* or *spoiling.* These words some join with the words going before; reading them on this manner, *A grievous vision is declared unto me;* for the *perfidious person dealing perfidiously, and for the spoiler, that spoileth:* as spoken of the Chaldeans, and pointing to their sins, for which they were to be destroyed; to wit, their treachery, and their inhumanity, chap. 47.6. Hab. 2.5. Or, *a treacherous one, dealing treacherously; and a spoiler spoiling.* Understanding it of the Medes and Persians, their dealing with the Chaldeans, thus, in either kind, as the subject matter of this prophecy. Others fasten it unto that which follows, as spoken in way of compellation; *O thou treacherous dealer, and notable spoiler; thou Elam,* I mean, *go up; thou Media besiege:* as inviting them to go instantly about the business assigned them. But most read them; and so they run best, apart by themselves. Yet some on this wise, much to the same effect with the first of the former: *This perfidious person dealeth perfidiously, and the spoiler spoileth.* That is, the Babylonian that persists in his impiety, (so understanding the former branch, Dan. 3.5,6. & 5.3,4,22,23.) and in his oppression, ch. 14.16,17. Dan. 4.27. Others thus, *The perfidious person,* that is, the Babylonian, *dealeth perfidiously; and the spoiler,* or, *plunderer;* that is, the Mede or Persian, *plundereth,* or *spoileth.* God, for her perfidiousness, punishes Babylon by the Persian sword. Or, which sense seems most natural, *The treacherous dealer, hath found a treacherous dealer; and the spoiler, one that spoileth.* The perfidious plunderer, the Babylonian, is now paid in his own coin; has now met with his match; is, through God's just judgment, now dealt with himself, as he had dealt before with others. See chap. 33.1. Jer. 50.15. That which some expound of Cyrus, and Darius, whom they suppose to have been, if not, in some sort, under the Babylonian monarch, yet in confederacy, at least, with him; yea, as some say, though without all color of probability, guests with him at table, in that fatal supper, whereat he was slain. But others, deeming it to be too great a blemish to so generous a person, as Cyrus seems to have been, and to cast a wrongful aspersion upon him; (besides, that the last branch of it, has no footing in story, sacred or other; but is refuted, rather, by either) they expound it rather of such, as fled over from the king of Babylon, to Cyrus, of whom Gadatas and Gobrias, were two principal ones, who being of the first that entered the city, and well skilled in the passages, made, directly, with their followers, to the king's palace, whom they there suddenly surprised, and slew. See Xenophon, lib. 7.

*{Go up, O Elam; besiege, O Media*} The Persians, and Medes, joint subjects to Cyrus, are called upon, and incited to go up, instantly, against Babylon, and to sit down before it. See chap. 13.2–4. 17.

*{Go up*} A military term, used commonly of those, that go out upon any expedition unto any place whatsoever. See on chap. 7.1. and the like, ver. 5. The rather, here used, in a way of elegancy, alluding to the name of Elam, which our English cannot express. The like is, Mic. 1.1,14,15. Zeph. 2.4.

*{O Elam*} Or, *O Elamite.* The Elamites put for the Persians, because they held that part of Persia, which bordered upon the Medes. See on ch. 11.11.

*{besiege*} Beleaguer Babylon. The prophet, as God's campmaster. Not that the one should march thither, and the other sit down there, when they were come thither: but that both, jointly, should do either. Of this manner of speech, very rife in this prophet; See on ch. 5.13. & 20.4,5.

*{O Media*} Or, *O Mede,* as Dan. 5.31. For the name of the country, and of the inhabitant thereof, is, in the Hebrew, all one: and the old Latin here so renders it. Howbeit, in regard that the verbs, here, are both feminine; the words may have reference to the lands, in the first place, Elymais and Media; but put here for the inhabitants of either. Of the Medes, see on chap. 13.17.

*{all the sighing thereof have I made to cease*} This is spoken in the person of God; I am determined, by this your service, against Babylon, to put a final end to the affliction of my servants, which they have, a long time, sustained by their captivity in Babylon. See ch. 14.1,2. He speaks of a thing, as present, not in doing only, but even done, though not to be effected, till, 170 years after, and names the people, expressly, by whom it should then be accomplished.

*{the sighing thereof*} Or, *of her.* To wit, of Babylon: Not wherewith she sighed herself, but wherewith she made others, God's people, especially, to sigh. The sighing of people, by her cruelty procured. So, *the cry of Sodom;* for, the cry of poor persons, oppressed by Sodom, Gen. 18.20. And, *my terror,* not wherewith I am terrified, but wherewith I might terrify you, Job 33.7. And, *your fear, and your dread;* for, the fear and dread of you, Deut. 11.25. Not wherewith you fear, or dread others, but wherewith others stand in fear of you.
