For they seem to strain it overmuch, who expound it, *of her,* that is, of my people; as if the pronoun had reference to them, of whom no mention is made before. Or, that understand the *sighing,* here mentioned, of the solemn mournings wont to be made at the solemn exequies of great persons. Which the king of Babylon should want, ch. 14.18,19.

**V. 3.** *{Therefore are my loins filled with pains*} These words are, by some, conceived, as the prophet's words, concerning himself; exceedingly terrified with the dreadful apparition, in a vision represented unto him, of the surprising and sacking of Babylon. So Hab. 3.15. Some, again, make them the speech of God's people, relating the ground of their sighing, the great misery they endured in the Babylonian captivity, Psal. 66.11,12. Lam. 1.2,3,12. But others, rather, suppose them to be spoken in the person of the Babylonians, intimating in what an heavy and heartless condition they should be, upon the sudden, and unexpected surprisal of their city; See ch. 15.5. & 16.7,9–11. Ezek. 21.6,7.

*{my loins are filled with pains*} Diseases, and pains in the loins are generally, very grievous, and such as disable, either to stir, or to stand upright, Deut. 33.11. Psal. 38.6,7,8. & 69.23. ch. 45.1. Ezek. 21.6. & 29.7. Dan. 5.6. In this place, those parts especially, mentioned, because pains there, are more eminent in childbearing and birth, here especially aimed at. So Nah. 2.10.

*{pangs have taken hold of me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth*} See the like description of persons in distraction, and distress, Psalm 46.6. Chapter 13.8. and 26.17. Jerem. 48.42.

*{I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it*} Heb. *I am writhed,* or, *wrung:* (and so, Psal. 38.6.) *with hearing; I am affrighted,* (as Job 21.6.) *with seeing.* It should be rendered in the present tense, that it may suit with the former. The pronoun is wanting; as Chapter 9.9. Hos. 8.4.

**V. 4.** *{My heart panteth*} Heb. *wandereth;* as ch. 29.24. & 53.6. Or, *staggereth,* as chap. 28.7. Or *fluttereth to and fro,* as another word like, for notion, to this, and in the like case used, Psalm 38.10. It is not able, for fear, to keep in its proper place and posture.

*{fearfulness affrighted me*} Or, *horror* (as Jer. 49.16.) *affrighteth,* or, *terrifieth me,* as Job 9.34. & 33.7.

*{the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me*} The nighttime, usually desired for rest, yet affords me no rest, for terror and fear, Deut. 28.67. Job 7.4,13,14. Or, our festival night is turned suddenly, into terrors; our mirth and jollity being interrupted by the unexpected irruption of the adversary. For in a festival night, in the midst of their merriment, was the city of Babylon, by Cyrus, surprised, Jer. 41.39. Dan. 5.1,30. See Xenophon, lib. 7.

*{the night of my pleasure*} Heb. *the evening* (*evening,* for, *night;* as *morning,* for, day, Gen. 1.5,8.) *of my desires;* as 1 King. 9.1,19. *Desire,* for *delight;* as ch. 2.16. & 32.12. though another word be there used. Here so, the rather, because the word, here used, properly signifies a vehemency of desire, and amorous affection, Gen. 34.8. Deut. 21.11. Ch. 38.17. The revelling night, that we had so much longed for, making full account in it, to satiate ourselves with all variety of delights, proved a dreadful, and dismal night to us.

*{hath he turned*} That is, the enemy, say some; God, say others: and both true. But the word is indefinite; *He hath turned it:* that is, *It is turned:* as Gen. 15.6. *He imputed it:* that is, *It was imputed,* Rom. 4.3. and *they shall call them;* that is, *they shall be called,* Mal. 1.4.

*{turned*} Heb. *put;* as Ps. 107.33.

*{into fear*} Or, *trembling:* for so the word, properly, signifies, Gen. 27.33. 1 Sam. 14.15. Dan. 10.7. And great variety of terms does the prophet here use, to set forth the dreadfulness of that fatal night.

**V. 5.** *{Prepare the Table; watch in the watchtower; eat, drink; arise ye Princes, and anoint the shield*} In whose person these words are spoken, is questioned. Some make them God's words to the prophet, as enjoining him to do that, which he was to foretell should be done: For what the prophets denounce, they are said oft to do, Jer. 1.10. & 18.7,9. Others, would have them spoken in the person of the prophet, as either in way of derision, bidding the Babylonians go on with their feasting; but withal, implying, that in the midst of their revelling, they should be interrupted with the clamors of those, that should call upon them to betake them to their arms. Or, as others, admonishing them and their king, instead of giving order to have their tables spread and furnished, to set a strict watch for fear of the enemies' approach: instead of eating and drinking, to stand upon their guard, ready armed, to receive, and repel any enemies' assault. Others, lastly, divide them, making the former part of the verse, king Baltasar's words, giving command, as for the royal banquet to be made ready, so for a watch withal to be set; and inviting his guests to make merry, and feast without fear, notwithstanding the siege: and the latter of it, the words of the prophet, as calling upon the Medes and Persians, not to overslip the opportunity offered them; but to set upon them, and surprise them, in the midst of their drunken feast. And this last, to me, seems to come nearest to the mind and purpose of the prophet. Howbeit, I suppose, the words should be rendered somewhat otherwise, than generally they are: For the verbs, in the former part of the verse, are not imperative; as those in the latter part, but of an infinitive form. Thus, therefore, the whole passage may run, *In furnishing the table, setting the watch, eating, and drinking;* (that is, while the Babylonians are thus busied; and thus employed) *arise ye Princes, and anoint the shield:* Set you suddenly upon them. The like row of infinitives ranked, and ranged together. See ch. 59.13.

*{Prepare the Table*} Furnishing it with provisions: as Ps. 23.5. & 78.19. ch. 65.11.

*{watch in the watchtower*} Heb. *watching the watch.* Though some of the Rabbins expound it, *a light;* such as was set up in some high place, in manner of a beacon, to give notice, thereby of the approach of any adverse force: the noun is no where else found. Some understand this branch, not of setting a watch, or of having an eye to the light; but of Baltasar's eying the hand that wrote his destiny on the wall, in the midst of his feast, Dan. 5.5. as calling on him, to view and consider well of it. But that seems not to suit well with the rest of the context.

*{eat, drink*} Wonted words of invitation, at feasts, Cant. 5.1. But it is in the infinitive form, as in the former branches, the like which argues a defect of the same verb, in another form, to be supplied: as if it were said, *eating, eat, and drinking, drink:* that is, eat, and drink, freely. So *remembering remember:* that is, be sure to remember, Exodus 20.8. Deuteronomy 5.12. Josh. 1.13. and *seeing, I saw;* for, I wistly saw, Eccl. 9.11. See Chap. 22.13.

*{arise*} A form of speech, not implying, necessarily, any alteration of any present posture, but inciting unto the speedy, and sedulous addressing of a man's self, unto some present design, Gen. 13.17. and 19.14,15. See the like, of *going up,* ver. 2.

*{Princes*} Darius Cyrus, and those that command under you: for such also are so termed, ch. 10.8.

*{anoint the shield*} Or, *furbish the shields; shield,* for, *shields:* as chap. 22.6. Jer. 46.3. prepare for fight: address yourselves to an assault. The Hebrew doctors, some of them, under the term, here used, suppose *helmet:* and *harness* also, to be comprehended, as well as *target,* or *shield:* because they all conduce to the protection of man's body, which the word, in its notation, imports, ch. 31.5. & 37.35. And for the word of *anointing,* though they grant it to intend *scouring,* and *polishing,* whereunto the use of oil is well known to conduce; yet they add, that they made use of oil also, for another end, to make their arms the more slick and slippery, that the enemies' shafts and javelins, might not, so easily, fasten on them. To which purpose, they wrest that, 2 Sam. 1.21. *The shield of Saul is cast away, as if it had not been anointed with oil:* as they expound that place. Howbeit, others of them, turn this, both *anointing,* and *shield,* another way; expounding the words, *anoint a shield,* that is, set up another king in the room of Baltasar, Dan. 5.30,31. For, as God is called *the shield,* that is, the protector of his people, Gen. 15.1. Psalm 3.3. & 84.11. So kings and princes, say they, are likewise so termed, Psalm 47.9. Hos. 4.18. (for so they understand this word in those places.) As also from another word of the like notion, to wit, *shelet:* (whence our *shield* seems to have descended. Jer. 51.11. Ezek. 27.11.) They are called, *Shalits;* or after the Arabic manner, *Sultans:* Gen. 42.6. Eccl. 10.5. because they either do, or ought to protect their subjects, Lam. 4.20. But the simple, and plain sense, is here, for either branch, the best. The whole verse runs along, clean through, in six members, without any copulative, to make the sentence the quicker, and to intimate the speedy dispatch of the business. See the like, Exod. 15.9. Judg. 5.27.

**V. 6.** *{For thus hath the Lord said unto me*} Or, *Thus the Lord enjoined me.* For so the word is sometime used, 2 Sam. 16.10. Esth. 7.9. Dan. 3.20. I deliver these things thus confidently, because I have good warrant from God, for what I say. So ch. 8.11. ver. 16. Or, because God, by a second vision, has further confirmed, and given me stronger assurance of what he had revealed to me before. So ch. 8.1,5.

*{Go set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth*} Because the word, in the foregoing branch, is not *Jehovah,* but *Adonai,* which signifies, *Lord,* or *Master,* and is communicable to men, Exod. 21.4,8. Mal. 1.6. Some understand these words, and all that follows, with relation to that of *a watch set,* ver. 5. Of the watchmaster, by the king's appointment, commanding a sentinel to ascend on some high tower, and relate, what from thence he should espy; who accordingly, being there set, should thence give notice of Cyrus and Darius, their approach, with their forces toward Babylon. But neither does this seem to suit well with the course of the context: nor was that watch, before spoken of, set before their approach; but after they had sat long before the city, the same night that it was taken. Others therefore, and so most understand them; as God's words to the prophet; commanding him, as some suppose, to set some other prophet on work, to attend on this sacred and mysterious business, as a watchman on a watchtower, expecting, what, by vision God should reveal to him; as Jer. 6.27. Hab. 2.1. And this watchman, some of the Jewish doctors, would have to be one of the prophet's scholars, and some of them, by a trick of theirs, (of which more, on ver. 8.) to be *Habakkuk,* the *lion* there mentioned; because of his standing on a watchtower related, Hab. 2.1. But some of ours from the Greek, (which by a vicious reading, ver. 8. for *Aryeh,* that is, *a lion,* has *urias*) would have this watchman to be the high priest *Urias,* mentioned before, chap. 8.2. But the conjecture, with the ground of it, may both go together. Others understand it of the prophet himself, as if God had willed him to stand, as on a watchtower, to see what he could descry. And God's prophets are generally so termed, because, by the spirit of prophecy, they are wont to see afar off, and foresee things to come, and that, sometime, for many generations after, which others, neither by the help of nature, or art, are able to descry and discover, Ezek. 3.17. & 33.2,7. Rev. 1.1,10. as men, standing aloft, can see far and near many things, which others that are below on the ground, cannot see. But I conceive all this to be done in a vision; as that, 1 King. 22.19,20,21. and chap. 6.1–13. For to what end is it, to induce a multiplicity of visions, where one only is related. Sufficient it was, for the prophet, to relate; as chap. 6.1. what in vision, himself had seen.

*{Go*} See on ch. 20.2.

*{set a watchman*} This, as in a vision enjoined; so in a vision was done. For a watchman could not be set at Jerusalem, that could see what was at Babylon.

*{let him declare what he seeth*} Or, *that may tell what he seeth.* A defect of the relative: as Gen. 39.4. Exod. 13.8. ch. 42.5. & 47.15.

**V. 7.** *{And he saw*} The watchman, set in this vision, saw in a vision as ch. 6.1. Dan. 7.2. & 8.2.

*{a chariot with a couple of horsemen, a chariot of asses, and a chariot of camels*} He saw troops of horsemen, with beasts, as well for burden, as service, approaching to Babylon.

*{a chariot with a couple of horsemen*} That is, say some, a chariot with two riding in it, to wit: Darius, and Cyrus: or, as others, Cyrus alone with two drivers: the chariot being drawn by an ass, and a camel: an emblem of Cyrus, as a mongrel mix of two nations, a Persian by his father, and a Mede by his mother: and termed therefore a *mule:* as well, in a frantic prophecy of Nebuchadnezzar's, as also, in an old oracle of Apollo, given to the Babylonians, that their city should stand, till a mule were king of Media: and some such things, though not altogether thus, are related by Eusebius, in his *Evangelical preparative,* l. 9. c. 41. out of Megasthenes, and Abydenus: and by Herodot. l. 1. & l. 3. Others deeming it, an unfit matter to crowd two such great commanders into one chariot, suppose *a chariot* to be put for, *chariots:* two at least, with *two riders* respectively, the one in the one chariot, and the other in the other: or two, to wit: the rider, and the driver, in either: Cyrus riding in the one: drawn with *asses,* or *mules;* which were of most use in Persia and Elymais: Darius in the other drawn with *camels,* which the Medes, and the Bactrians their neighbors, most abounded in. Others are of the mind, that these *chariots of camels,* and *mules,* should allude to a stratagem, that Cyrus should put in practice against the Chaldeans, who because they were strongest in horse, Cyrus placed in the front of his army, against their horse troops, his camels, whose sight and scent the horse could not brook, and with them also, his mules; which, in those Eastern parts, are famous for swiftness; as appears by the story of Absolom, 2 Sam. 18. & 13.29. But howsoever of camels somewhat is related, to this purpose, with Herodot. l. 1. as contrived by Cyrus in his expedition against Crœsus; yet neither does he, or any other author, that I can light on, mention aught in this kind attempted by him, either with mules, or camels, in his invasion of Chaldea. But to pass by these and divers other, either overcurious, or frivolous descants upon this Scripture, the plain song or genuine sense of it, thus arises. The verb *racab,* the root whence this word *recab* here used, springs, signifies, in general, *to ride,* whether on horse, ass, mule, camel, or any other beast, used to bear a rider; and whether in chariot, coach, or litter, indifferent. See Judg. 10.4. 1 Sam. 25.20. & 30.17. Esth. 6.8. & 8.10. 1 King. 1.38. chap. 66.20. See also ch. 19.1. and hence *a rider,* sometime for *an horseman,* Job 39.18. 2 King. 9.17. sometime, for *a coachman,* 1 King. 22.24. Hag. 2.22. The word *recab,* therefore, thence derived, and here used, comprehends in general, all *riding* forces, whether on horseback; and on other beasts, or in chariots, coaches, and the like; for it is a collective word, as *equitatus* in Latin, with us, *horse,* and *foot:* in English, and in foreign terms, *cavalry,* and *infantry:* nor is it found above once, in a plural form, and that in a poem, Cant. 1.9. See Exod. 14.7. 2 Sam. 1.6. & 8.4. Now these *riding forces,* are here first divided into two ranks: whereof the former is for fight, or field service, said to consist of two troops of *horse,* or *horsemen:* and may represent the distinct companies of Cyrus, and Darius: marching as under two commanders: the latter, chiefly for burden: and that again subdivided into two sorts, the one consisting of *asses,* the other of *camels;* both used much for that purpose in those parts, Gen. 37.25. 1 King. 5.17. ch. 30.6. and a multitude of such beasts were necessarily required to carry along all manner of provisions, for so great an army as they led, both in regard they were to pass through many waste places, and to continue a siege of uncertain length, against a city of great strength; and having purposely gathered into it most of that store, which the country round about it afforded; partly, to furnish it for a long siege; and partly also, to starve those that came to besiege them. The words therefore may be rendered, *and he saw a company of asses, and a company of camels.*

*{a chariot*} The word is sometime used for *a chariot* or *coach,* Exod. 14.6. 1 King. 22.35. sometime for *horses,* that draw in a *chariot,* or *coach;* 2 Sam. 8.4. sometime for *wares,* that lade a *wain,* or a *wagon,* 1 King. 10.29. sometime, for *an army,* or *company of riders,* in *chariots,* such as in those days, were much used in war, where from horsemen they are distinguished, Exod. 14.9. 1 King. 10.26. 2 Chr. 12.20. and sometime, lastly, for all *cavalry,* or *troops riding,* whether on horse or in chariot; opposed to those, that serve on foot. Exod. 14.7. 1 King. 4.21. 2 King. 5.21.

*{a couple of horsemen*} The word signifies *a yoke of oxen,* 1 King. 19.19. or, *a couple of oxen,* 1 Sam. 11.7. or of *asses,* 2 Sam. 16.1. or, *a couple of men:* that go, or ride together, 2 King. 9.25. here used, for a couple of troops, or companies of *horsemen: horsemen,* for, *troops,* consisting of such: for so the singular also is sometime used, Jer. 4.29. Ezek. 26.10.

*{a chariot*} Or, *company:* as before, and after.

*{of asses*} Heb. *ass:* as ch. 32.20. See ch. 1.3.

*{of camels*} Heb. *camel:* as Zach. 14.15.

*{and he hearkened diligently with much heed*} Heb. *and he considered with consideration, even with much:* or, *great consideration:* a defect of the participle *with:* as ch. 17.5,10. This some understand of Cyrus, viewing of Babylon, when he was set down before it, considering which way it might best be assaulted, and most speedily surprised. Others, of the prophet Esay himself, making profession of his own sedulity, and diligence, in attending the business that God had set him about, and promising therein to persist. Others lastly, of the watchman set to watch in the vision; and upon the representation of such companies to his view, observing diligently their motion, which way they bent, and what they intended to do; that which seems to be the proper intendment of the prophet, in this place.

**V. 8.** *{And he cried a lion*} Some of those, that thus read these words, suppose that the watchman, whether set up by the Babylonians, to keep sentinel, while they revelled it; or by the prophet, appointed to attend what he could descry: at first beheld, but confusedly, a great company coming on, as in two troops; after upon nearer approach, and better view, perceived them to consist of mules the one; and of camels the other: and lastly, upon a third, and more accurate view, saw *a lion* leading them, and by an outcry signified as much. And this *lion,* some would have to be either Cyrus, or Darius, that took Babylon. Dan. 5.30. called *a lion* for his fierceness, Jer. 50.44. Others, to be Christ, *the Lion of the Tribe of Juda,* Gen. 49.9. Rev. 5.5. the destroyer of the spiritual Babylon, and deliverer of his people: of whom Cyrus was a type, ch. 45.1. Nor want there, that dream of a *lion,* that should be coming on the stage to affright, and disturb the sentinel; who though by a loud shriek, he gave notice of it; yet would not desert his station; unlike to the hireling, that flees when he spies the wolf coming, Joh. 10.12. or that somebody, to terrify him, should tell him of *a lion;* as Dalilah Sampson, of the Philistines, Judg. 16.9,12. which yet he should not regard; unlike therein to Solomon's sluggard, Prov. 22.13. But the Jewish doctors have two other readings, the one more light: the other more weighty. For some of them by *Geometry,* as they term it, or *Arithmetic* rather, reading the words, *and the lion cried:* (wherein some of ours also concur with them, supposing the watchman, for his vigilancy, to be termed a *lion*) expound it, of *Habbakuk:* And *Habbakuk cried.* And if you ask, how they find *Habbakuk* in the text. The answer is, just as they find *Jacob and Esau,* in *Ishto,* or *his wife,* Gen. 25.21. for because there is a transposition of the words from their ordinary sequel, running thus in the original, *Rebeccah conceived, his wife.* They would have in this last word, which is in Hebrew, *Ishto,* to be intimated what it was, that she conceived: and if we demand what that was, they tell us, it was *fire,* and *stubble,* and why so? Because forsooth, the letters of these two words, *esh ve-kash:* that is, *fire and stubble,* do make up just the same number, with the letters of *Ishto,* his wife, to wit, 707. And if we ask further, what this *fire and stubble* should be; they tell us, it is *Jacob and Esau,* for it is said, Obadiah 18. *the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Esau, stubble:* and thus you have *Jacob and Esau,* in *Ishto,* and clear Scripture for it too. In like manner here, because the letters of the word *Aryeh,* here signifying *a lion,* amount just to the same sum, that the letters of Habbakuk's name do: to wit, 216. therefore he must needs be the *lion* here mentioned, and the watchman, consequently, as was before said. Nor should I mention this idle dotage, but to show how these addlebrained doctors, whose mysterious expositions many begin to dote on, and are so much taken with in these days, do ridiculously and irreverently wring and writhe the words of God's sacred oracles, as if they were descanting upon, or making sport with some light poem, or satirical pamphlet, for the exercising of their wanton wits. Meanwhile, this is no better than that of the Greeks, of which also before, who for *Aryeh* here, read *uriyah,* all the difference is, that the one is a gross mistake, the other a studied, but frivolous device. But instead of this fond and far fetched conceit. Others of them give a more solid reading and sense; which the most, or best at least, of ours, also embrace; thus rendering the words, *And he cried, as a lion,* that is, aloud, like a lion. The note of similitude being supplied which is oft times wanting; as Psal. 11.1. Nah. 3.12,13. So Lam. 3.10. Hos. 11.10. by his hideous noise, implying, and expressing much fear and terror to those, whom it concerned, from great danger then approaching. So Amos 1.2.

*{My Lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower in the daytime; and I am set in my watch whole nights*} Or, *on the watchtower, Lord, I stand continually by day:* for the word *Lord,* as it is here written, seems to have no pronoun affixed to it; but is in a form commonly deemed peculiar to the Deity. The words are the watchman's words, whether, as some, of him at Babylon, set to keep sentinel; or, as others, rather, of the watchman set in the vision by the prophet, to observe; either, as the most, professing his constant vigilancy, and assiduous attendance in his station; to give the firmer assurance of what he had seen: or, as some, complaining that he had so long watched, in contemplation of Babylon's downfall, and had not the full accomplishment of it revealed, as yet, to him. So Habbakuk seems to complain, that he had long watched, and waited for some comfortable vision, but as yet could see nothing but of affliction and grievance, Hab. 1.2,3. & 2.1. Howbeit, the former seems in this place the fitter, well suiting both with the last clause of the verse before going; and with what follows, ver. 10.

*{whole nights*} Or, *every night;* as ch. 1.5.

**V. 9.** *{And behold, here cometh a chariot of men, with a couple of horsemen*} Some understand these words, as no more than a repetition of what the watchman had seen, and related, before, ver. 7. But others suppose, somewhat more to be in them, that should more certainly import, and portend the ruin of Babylon. Some therefore expound them, as the former also, of God's people, making out of Babylon, and marching away by troops, with bag and baggage, on such beasts, as were before mentioned, Jer. 50.8. & 51.45. Others rather, (and so some of the Jewish doctors also) of the forces before spoken of, piercing into, and entering upon Babylon, part of them, on the one side of it, and part on the other, Jer. 51.31.

*{And behold, here cometh*} Or, *behold, even now are gone in.* He speaks, as of a thing suddenly done: as if he had said, while I am yet speaking this, some of the retinue before mentioned, are gone in, to wit; into the place, toward which they were bound; the issue whereof, I so sedulously, and solicitously had all this while expected, ver. 7,8. the pronoun here found, is oft used, to denote a thing at present done, and fully effected, Gen. 31.38,41. Num. 14.22. & 22.32.

*{cometh*} Or, *goeth in,* or, *is gone in:* So the word is oft used, for *to go unto,* or, *go into,* Gen. 7.1,13. & 16.21. & 19.23. & 24.31. & 30.3.

*{a chariot of men*} Heb. *of man:* as Num. 26.10. ch. 5.4. *chariots of men,* (for both words are collective) such as men ride in; to distinguish them from such as were used for carriage. Here by an hypallage, *chariots of men;* for those men that were before seen riding in the chariots: as *silver of shekels,* for, *shekels of silver,* Levit. 5.15. & Levit. 7.21. *uncleanness of man,* for, *a man of uncleanness;* that is, a man unclean. See ver. 7. and Chap. 22.6.

*{a couple of horsemen*} See on ver. 7. the troops under the command of those two great princes, Darius and Cyrus; either having left their horses, to scale the walls, and so surprising the city; or, after surprisal of it, entering in on horseback, by the gates, set open for them.

*{and he answered, and said*} By the person here said to answer, some understand the watchman, further adding; what he was now assured of, that the downfall of Babylon, was that, which was in this vision represented. Others, God's people, who coming out from thence, relate, and publish it to others, Jer. 51.50. Some, the prophet Esay himself, assuring himself now, of what before he expected, upon the report made by the watchman, whom, in the vision, he had set to observe what he could see. And lastly, (which to me seems most probable) God himself, expounding more fully to the prophet, what this apparition, all, tended to.

*{answered*} The word in Scripture is used, not for the returning of aught to some foregoing question, only; but for adding aught, to somewhat before spoken, Job 34.1. Mat. 17.17. & 19.27. & 22.1. Luk. 5.22.

*{Babylon is fallen, is fallen*} To wit, by the hands of those, who were seen coming against her, and entering into her, Jer. 51.48. and it is repeated, as for assurance; so in way, also, of rejoicing, Rev. 18.20. So Rev. 14.8. & 18.2.

*{and all the graven images of her gods, he hath broken unto the ground*} All her idols are fallen; and come down with her; being either become a prey to the enemy, in regard of the rich matter whereof they were made, and the ornaments that they were dressed with; or beaten down, and broken; or burnt, in a bravery, by the conqueror; as seeming to triumph; not over the people, and princes, only, but their gods, also, ch. 10.11. & 37.19. See ch. 46.1. Jer. 50.2. & 51.44,47,52.

*{the graven images of her gods*} Heb. *the gravenings,* or, *graven works of her gods;* that is, *her gravened gods:* as ch. 30.22. *the gravenings,* or, *graven works of thy silver;* for, *thy graven works,* or idols, made of *silver.* So also, Deut. 12.3. See Chapter 2.10. *graven* ones, put for all sorts of them, Jer. 8.19. Mic. 1.7.

*{her gods*} Her idols; whom Baltasar, a little before, had so much extolled; when in contempt of the only true God, he drank with his concubines, in the cups taken out of his Temple, Dan. 5.2,4.

*{he hath broken*} God, say some; Cyrus, say others. But the verb (as the Jewish Doctor well observes, paralleling it with that, Num. 26.59.) is indefinite; and it might well therefore be rendered; *and all her graven gods are broken.* See chap. 2.18,19. and 18.5. ver. 4.

*{broken unto the ground*} Or, *broken, and thrown down, unto the ground:* as Ps. 89.39. ch. 14.12. & 22.18.

**V. 10.** *{O my threshing, and the corn of my floor*} These words some interpreters make the words of God, speaking unto Babylon, and foretelling what now should befall her; as if he had said; You Babylon, by whom I have formerly threshed; that is, grievously afflicted, and trodden down, other people, (as chap. 25.10. & 41.15.) are now yourself to be threshed, or to be made a place, wherein your princes, and people, shall be threshed by the Medes and Persian, as corn in a threshing floor, Jer. 51.33. Mic. 4.13. But others rather suppose them to be the prophet's words, speaking unto God's people, and comforting them against those grievous afflictions, which they had from the Syrians, Assyrians, or others, formerly sustained, and were from the Chaldeans, and Babylonians, further to suffer; assuring them, that what he had foreseen, and foreshowed them of the ruin of Babylon and the Chaldeans, was no dream, or relation of his own devising, but what by revelation he had received from God. And indeed the latter part of the verse, which cannot, without apparent force, be pulled away from this, of necessity enforces to carry it, this way.

*{O my threshing*} How this might be spoken by God; either concerning Babylon, by whom he had threshed, and whom he meant now to thresh, by others: Or, of his own people, whom he had threshed already, and intended further to thresh; though not utterly to destroy them, ch. 28.28. as he did some others by them, ch. 26.14,19. & 41.15,16. Jer. 50.11. it is not hard to conceive. But how the prophet should speak in this manner, of his people, as to call them, *his threshing,* there seems some difficulty in it. This to clear, and assoil, some would have it understood, not effectively, but denunciatively: as Jeremy is said *to build, and pull down, to plant, and pluck up;* not by way of execution of aught in that kind, but by way of denunciation, alone, Jer. 1.10. & 18.7,9. so, say they, does Esay call this people, *his threshing:* not because he himself had threshed them, but because he had from God denounced those heavy judgments, wherewith they were to be threshed, for their sins. But I suppose we need not have recourse unto any such far fetched interpretation. It is agreed on: and the very next word evinces it, that by *threshing,* (a word in this place only found) is here meant, not the act of *threshing,* as by another word of the same stock, the time, Levit. 26.5. but the object of it, as the corn, straw, and grain; so such persons, or people, as either have been, or are to be threshed in such manner, as is in the words here intended. So *captivity,* for, *captives,* chap. 20.4. *escaping,* for persons *escaped,* Neh. 1.2. chap. 15.14. now this being granted, I see not what should hinder, but that the prophet may well call them, *his threshed* ones, though not threshed by him; as well, as he might also have termed them, *his afflicted* ones, albeit he had no hand in the afflicting of them; and that without reference to any threshing, or affliction by him, ministerially, denounced against them.

*{and the corn of my floor*} The same thing says the Rabbin well, in divers terms. Heb. *my son of the floor; the son of the floor;* for, the corn that is threshed in the floor: as, *the sons of the quick coal,* for, the spark that fly from it, Job 5.7. *the son of the bow,* for, a shaft shot by it, Job 41.28. and, *the sons of the quiver,* for arrows, that are laid up in it, and drawn out of it, Lam. 3.13. *my son of the floor,* as, *my mountain of holiness,* chap. 56.7. and *his idols of silver,* ch. 2.20. and, *my God of mercy,* Psal. 59.10,17. in all which places, and many more, the words run in the very same strain, with these here, and it is *son,* not *daughter,* as of Babylon he is wont to speak, ch. 47.1. and so the Psalmist, Psal. 137.8. and in the feminine form, ch. 13.19. and in the verse next before going. Whereby also it may well be deemed, that he speaks here, not of her, but of his own people, whom, he might, not unfitly, call; not, *the son of his floor;* (for none such, as is here intended, he had) but, *his son of the floor;* that is, his poor countrymen, and much commiserated brethren, that had been oft under the flail, or, (as their manner of threshing was) under the cartwheels, and the beasts' hoofs, in the floor, and were so to be again. See ch. 28.27,28. As for Jerom's conceit of an allusion, in these terms, to *Araunah's threshing floor,* on which the Temple was built, 2 Chr. 3.1. I suppose it to have no place here.

*{that which I have heard from the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you*} I tell you nothing, but what God has told me. It is like that of the apostle, 1 Cor. 11.23. The prophet's fidelity, in the delivery of God's message, without addition, or detraction of aught, Jer. 23.26,28. & 26.2. And the certainty of the matter, delivered in it, to be, in its due time, accomplished: as that which comes from him, who is both *the Lord of Hosts,* and able, therefore, to effect it, chap. 14.24,26,27. and *the God of Israel* also; and though he suffer his people, therefore, to be under the threshing instruments in the floor for a while, yet he will not permit them to lie always there: but will send deliverance at length, ch. 27.7–9. & 28.27,28.

**V. 11.** *{The burden of Dumah*} The title of another prophecy, distinct from the former: The subject matter whereof, is intimated in the word, *burden,* to be some sad and heavy tidings. See ch. 13.1. The object, or land or people, whom it concerns, are described by the word *Dumah:* concerning which, interpreters are at some variance. For some fetch it from *Dumah,* one of Ismael's race, Gen. 25.14. 1 Chr. 1.30. His posterity, as his brother *Kedar's,* ver. 13,16. had seated themselves in some part of Arabia, which, in regard thereof, bore the name of that their ancestor, and is here called, *Dumah.* And we read, indeed, in Ptolomy, lib. 6. of a seatown in Arabia, called *Duma:* as also of an inland town, called *Domana:* and in Pliny lib. 6. c. 39. out of Juba, the Mauritanian, of a city situate in that part of Ethiopia, which he assigns to Arabia, as possessed by Arabians, called *Dumana.* And further also, in Stephen the Byzantine, out of Glaucus his *Arabian antiquities,* of *Dumathea,* a city of Arabia, which may well be all one with either of the former, (the manner, both of Greeks and Latins, being to mold foreign terms, as they please) and the same with this *Dumah,* that of Steven comes nearest home to the Hebrew: *Dumath,* for *Dumah,* as *Elisabeth,* for *Elisheba,* Exod. 6.23. and *Goliath,* for *Goliah,* both in the Greek and Latin, 1 Sam. 17.4. Of this people, therefore, called not *Idumeans,* but *Dumeans,* do some writers of note, both among the Jewish and ours, expound this prophecy. Yet others again, by *Dumah,* understand here *Idumea,* or *Edom. Dumah,* say they, by an *Apheresis,* or detraction of the first letter, for *Idumea,* or *Edomea:* as *Ram,* or *Aram,* 1 Chr. 2.9. Job 32.2. *Pasdammim,* 1 Ch. 11.13. for *Epasdammim,* 1 Sam. 17.1. But I find not in Hebrew Scripture, where the land of *Edom* is termed, either *Edomah, Adomah,* or *Idumeah,* for *Edomeah,* and *Idumeah,* Mar. 3.8. as *Judea,* Mat. 2.1,5. are words of a foreign frame. As for what is objected, that the next prophecy, is concerning the Arabians, and therefore not this? is no good consequence; for this concerns the *Dumean* Arabians, and that, the *Kedarens.* The main reason of any weight, that may induce to this supposal, is the mention of *Seir* in the next words, of which more there. Howbeit, Jerom tells us, that not the whole province of Idumea; but some region, or part of it, which lay Southward, and was not above twenty miles distant from a city of Palestine called, in his time, *Eleutheropolis,* was thus termed. Nor is it improbable, that some of Ismael's posterity, might seat themselves in some portion of that country, which the Edomites, their kinsmen, in those times, inhabited. Of whether of the two, the word is here used; there may seem to be in the use of it, here, some secret allusion, to what the word, ordinarily, imports, to wit, either *excision;* as Ezek. 27.32. or, *silence;* but such as is caused by dissolution and destruction, Psal. 94.17. & 115.17. See on ch. 15.1. as implying the ruin of that state, which this sad prophecy concerned.

*{He calleth to me out of Seir*} The prophecy is as well short, as sharp, wrapped up in two verses; and neither of them of any length; but very obscure: and that the rather, because little light is afforded us, for the clearing of it, from the stories extant of those times.

*{He calleth to me out of Seir*} Or, as the Hebrew runs, *One is calling to me from Seir.* Or, *A cry,* or, *A call* is made, or comes to me *from Seir.* I am cried unto, or called upon from thence. For the speech is indefinite; as ver. 9. This those that understand this prophecy of the *Dumeans,* interpret, either of a voice that should come from God to the prophet, concerning the destruction, that from the Edomites should befall them; as of Edom, the like, Jer. 49.14. Or of a noise, and clamor of warlike preparations, heard from mount Seir; the Edomites intending to invade and surprise *Dumah.* But those that by *Dumah,* understand Edom, or Idumea, expound it of the Edomites speaking unto the prophet, either in serious wise, or in derision.

*{from Seir*} *Seir* was (as *Shenir,* Cant. 4.8.) the name of a mountain, possessed by Esau, and his posterity, Gen. 36.8. Deut. 2.4,5. Josh. 24.4. So called, not as some have thought, from Esau, who was born rough and hairy, which the notation of the word imports, Gen. 25.25. or from the roughness, and *horridness* of that rocky mountain, though alluded unto, Jer. 49.17. but from the ancient lord, and possessor of it, *Seir, the Horite,* Gen. 36.20. in whose race it continued, Gen. 14.4. until the Edomites, or posterity of Esau, thence expelled them, Deut. 2.12. Esau, in likelihood, at first, having got some footing there, by the marriage of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, by Zibeon, descended from Seir, Gen. 36.2,20,24,25. which his issue well liking, and loath either to quit the place again, or to be cooped in some corner or scantling of it, at the will and pleasure of others, dispossessed the right owners, and made themselves absolute lords of it.

*{watchman, what of the night? watchman, what of the night?*} Some suppose these words to be the Dumeans, who, in regard of the great dangers and fears they were in, having set a watchman to keep sentinel, night and day, as ver. 8. were ever and anon calling on him, to tell them whether he descried aught, or no, whereby they might be endangered. Or, as others the Idumeans calling to the Dumean watchman, (as sentinels are wont to be set in bordering places) inquiring of him, as being in the like fears with them, and likely, in regard of neighborhood, to run the same hazard with them, whether aught were represented to him, that concerned either of them. Implying, as they imagine, that there were hostile forces abroad that had made foul havoc in the countries about them; and it might be expected, would do the like with them also. And this fits not amiss, with the matter of the prophecy next ensuing, concerning the Kedarens, their neighbors and near allies, ver. 13,16. which might well be of the same date with this, as well for delivery, as for accomplishment also. Some again would have them to be the words of some Edomite, that came as a spy, to view the confines, and see what watch and ward was there kept; but making, as if he were one of the country, and had some occasion, either of journey, or of some other business abroad: or of some Dumeans, that thus called upon the sentinels, to see whether they were awake, or no; or demanding of them, how far the night was spent, as hoping to be in some more quiet composure, being freed from the fear of a nightly invasion, as more dreadful, and not unusual, where the enemy is near at hand, and lying in wait for opportunities, and ready to lay hold on any advantage, for assault, Cant. 3.7,8. ch. 15.1. Or of such as were in arms, and stood all night attending the approach of the enemy, inquiring how near it is to break of day, that they might be, either relieved, or discharged of that their wearisome employment, Psal. 130.6. And these are, divers of them, the expositions of the Jewish doctors; but admitted and approved, the most, by some of ours also, among whom, yet, there are not a few, who understand them, as spoken, either by the Dumeans, or Idumeans, to the prophet Esay himself; and that either in scoffing manner, by way of derision, as if they had said, You prophet, that profess yourself to be a warder, and to watch for the good of your people, what tidings have you for us? What say you to the calamities, that other of your fellow prophets, have so oft said should befall us? You threaten us with nights of affliction, and heaviness; but we enjoy fair daylight of prosperity, peace and liberty, since that, in Joram's time, we shook off your yoke, and set us up a king of our own, 2 King. 8.20. Or seriously, and solicitously, as being in great difficulties and danger, in regard of a prevailing conqueror, that bore down all before him, and had seized upon many provinces, adjoining near to them, and desirous, from the prophet to understand what he saw, or foresaw concerning them or what advice he could give them: for even to God's prophets, as to God himself, Judg. 10.10,13,14. Jer. 2.27. Hos. 5.13,15. sometime, in such cases, they that otherwise did not relish, nor regard him or them, were content to repair, 2 King. 3.12,13. & 5.3,5. & 8.7,8. & 13.14. Thus have I delivered, though not all, (for there are many more) yet the principal, and most probable expositions of these words; leaving them to the judgment of others, to pick out, and pitch upon, which, in a Scripture of so great difficulty, they shall deem to be most likely; only professing myself to incline to the judgment of those, who suppose them to imply, a distracted and hazardous condition of those, by whom they were delivered, unto whomsoever they were directed.

*{watchman*} The word is not the same, that was used before, ver. 6. that signifies, properly, *a viewer,* or *a spier:* But the word, here used, is one, that, properly, signifies *a warder,* an *observer,* or *a keeper,* 1 Sam. 1.12. & 17.20,22. That which, therefore, has given occasion, here, of divers misinterpretations, especially, among the Jewish expositors. Some understanding here, by the *warder,* or *keeper,* God, *the keeper of Israel.* Psal. 121.4. Some the ruler of the country, the keeper of his subjects, as the shepherd of his sheep, 1 Sam. 17.20. Others, some soldiers; because the soldiery are the keepers of the country; whence Achish to David, *I will make thee keeper of my head,* 1 Sam. 28.2. But we need not run out to these far fetched interpretations, inducing strange senses; which because they have little show of probability, we have formerly omitted. The word does here, either imply the prophet himself, one of Israel's *watchers* and *warders,* *an observer* of them, as well as Jeremy, Jer. 6.27. or, *a watcher* for them, as well, as Ezekiel, Ezek. 3.17. & 33.2,7. Yea, and *a keeper* of them, as well as their soldiery; *the chariots and horsemen of Israel,* as well, as either Elias, or Eliseus, 2 King. 2.12. & 13.14. Or some *watchman,* as the former represented in a vision; so questioned and so answering, as is here expressed. For the word here found is of such *watchmen,* also used, as the former, Neh. 3.29. Psal. 130.6. and our prophet delights much in variety of terms.

*{what of the night?*} How much of it is past, or yet remains; How far is the night spent? Or, *what in the night;* or *by night,* as we use to say, have you seen, or observed? *Of the night,* for *in the night;* as *of a book,* for, *in a book,* Job 19.26. and, *of the city,* for, *in the city,* Psal. 72.16. or, *concerning the night,* to wit, of affliction, (as Job 5.14. & 17.12. & 35.10. Ps. 30.5. & 112.4.) that at present lies heavy on us.

*{watchman, what of the night?*} The same, as most interpreters redoubled, after the manner of those, that move such questions, unto those, especially, that stand far above them, as doubting whether, at first, they hear, or no; or as those are wont to speak, that are full of fear and solicitude, asking oft the same thing, chap. 33.18. only the contract is put for the entire word, though standing entire, without leaning on any other. Which, as in some other the like, *Chel,* for *Chayil,* chap. 36.2. Obad. 20. So in this word, *Lel,* for *Lajil,* is not unusual. See ch. 15.1. & 16.3. & 30.29. Yet, because the word *millel,* signifies, sometime *to speak,* Job 8.2. Psal. 106.2. whence the term *millah,* that signifies *a word,* Psal. 139.4. Some interpreters, of good note, render the words here: *The watchman, what saith he?* (for so lie the words in the text) or, *what saith the watchman,* as, *who would have said to Abraham?* Gen. 21.7. where the same word is found. But the syntax runs more smoothly, the former way.

**V. 12.** *{The watchman said*} The watchman's answer to the question, before moved to him, follows: Which whether it be delivered, as returned by the prophet himself, to those that did solicit him for advice; so (as repeating their words) calling himself by the term, that they before gave him; or, as by the watchman, in the vision represented unto him, unto those that inquired of him, either concerning the time of the night, or of aught he saw in the night, is to be taken as a divine oracle, intimating what was to befall that people, whom he spoke to.

*{the morning cometh, and also the night*} The watchman's answer consists of two parts; containing an assertion, the one; an advice, the other: very obscure either; and much canvassed by interpreters, as well Jewish, as others. This former part laid down in these words, must import some sad and heavy tidings to those whom it concerned. The prophecy else should not answer its inscription: *a burden,* or *burdensome* vision, or prophecy. The title should not be suitable to the contents of it. Some, therefore, expound the words, as if he should say, The morning indeed, approaches; but such a morning, as shall afford you no light or comfort at all, as little comfort shall you have of it, as if it were dark night, or midnight still with you, ch. 8.22. & 51.30. & 59.10. Job 5.14. & 24.17. Amos 4.13. & 5.8. Others, though morning be come as you suppose, with you, having, as Isaak, your great grandfather sometime foretold, shaken off that yoke, wherewith Jacob's issue kept you under, Gen. 27.40. Yet this fair morning will not last long with you, a night of calamity, and misery, will, by the Assyrians, ere long seize upon you, worse than that you were in, under the Israelitish yoke. Others, I have nothing to impart unto you, save that, as sure as the night succeeds the day, so certainly will affliction and destruction shortly surprise you: either coming and commencing, or to be accomplished and concluded, within a set compass of time, like an entire day, consisting of morning, and night: *morning,* for, *day,* as *evening,* for *night,* ver. 4. and it well suits with that of the Kedarens, their kinsmen. Ver. 16. *morning,* and *night,* for an entire day: and *a day,* for a *year,* as Ezek. 4.6. See on Chap. 20.3.

*{if ye will inquire, inquire ye; return, come*} As many several senses of these words, are given, as of the former. I will present you with one, or two only. Some knit this clause to the former branch, as noting the inevitableness of the evil therein menaced; the night, I foretell you of, will come, *though* (so the particle is found used, Job 14.7,8. & 16.6. & 17.13. & 27.16.) you inquire, and inquire never so oft, never so earnestly, and go to and fro, and come again and again; or, retaining the former reading, you may inquire further, if you please, and return and come again, as oft as you will; but other answer cannot be returned you. Others, if you will needs be inquiring, inquire seriously, not in mockery; or, inquire of that that concerns you, and may be for your good: to wit, how you may make your peace with God, before this night seize upon you, Jer. 13.16. and the only way whereby that may be effected, is by returning to him with sincere repentance of your sins, and adjoining yourselves to his people, ch. 55.6,7. Jer. 18.7,8,11. Dan. 4.27. Jon. 3.4,10.

*{inquire*} The word is, by some of the Rabbins, here noted, to be a Syriac, by other, a Kedarene, or an Arabic word: and it is indeed in the Chaldee paraphrast of the Old Testament, and the Syriac version of the New, very frequent. It seems to import an earnest, eager, and ardent inquisition; when a man's mind is restless, and his heart boils so within him, that he cannot be quiet, but is continually inquiring after somewhat, that his mind is wholly taken up with: for the word in his first (as may seem) and original sense, signifies *to boil,* chap. 64.2. whence, as bubbles arising upon the surface of boiling water; so blisters from inward heat, breaking forth, and swelling upon the outward parts of the body, have their name in Hebrew, Exod. 9.9,10. and that it implies a very narrow, exquisite, and exact inquiry; see Obad. 5,6. It is therefore, as if he had said, *since that* (so is the particle also rendered, Job 14.5.) you are so inquisitive, or so eager upon inquiry, inquire, and ask what you please, but so inquire, as that your inquisition be not vain and fruitless. Which that it may not be.

*{return, come*} That is, say some, no more than *come again.* And indeed the word of *returning,* oft times, imports no more than a reiteration of that which it is joined with. So *Isaak returned and digged;* that is, he dug again, Gen. 26.18. *return, lie down,* for lie down again, 1 Sam. 3.5,6. *he returned and lodged there,* for, he lodged there again, Judg. 19.7. being not yet gone out of the house. But in such forms of speech, the words are wont to be knit together; which here they are not, and imply, therefore, two distinct acts; *A return* (not, as some, to those that sent them, but) to God, who alone was able to relieve them: And *a coming over;* (not as some, of the Idumeans, to the Dumeans, either to fight for them, as confederates, craving their aid, or with them, as enemies to be destroyed; but (whether of Dumeans, or Idumeans) unto God's people, among whom the prophet abode, and with whom, alone, protection was to be had, ch. 4.5,6. & 10.24. & 56.6–8.

**V. 13.** *{The burden upon Arabia*} Another prophecy, concerning either Arabia, in general, whereof Dumah before mentioned, ver. 11. might be a part: or concerning that part of it, more specially, which the Kedarens possessed, ver. 16.

*{The burden*} See on ch. 13.1.

*{upon Arabia*} As Neh. 2.12. To be laid upon Arabia; as a burden is laid upon a beast, ch. 30.6. Or, *against Arabia;* as *against Egypt,* Exod. 14.25. (And *Arabia,* for the Arabians, (as *Egypt* there, for the Egyptians) and *against thy neighbor,* Exod. 20.16. and *against Moses,* Numb. 12.1. for the particle is the same. And the Latin goes wide, that renders it here, as he should after have done it, *in Arabia;* as if *the burden* were not *the burden of Arabia,* but of some other, that should flee thither for succor.

*{Arabia*} Whence this region had its name, at first, is uncertain. The fabulous Greeks in Eustathius, tell us of one *Arabus,* of the race of Apollo; and Solinus would make us believe, that the word signifies *an holy country;* but in what language, he tells us not. The name in Hebrew has affinity with a word, that is used for the *West;* supposed therefore, by some, to be so called; because that it lay toward the Western part of Asia, trending along over against Ethiopia, and Egypt: as also with another word that signifies *a plain,* or, *a desert,* Chap. 51.3. Jer. 50.12. which suits well with some part of it; and hither some of the Rabbins draw that, Jer. 3.2. *as the Arabian in the wilderness.* But I take it rather to have had this appellation, from the name that signifies *a mixed multitude,* Exod. 12.38. Jer. 50.37. because the region was, much of it, peopled by such, some of Cham's posterity, Gen. 10.7. and some of Abraham's issue by Keturah, Gen. 25.2,3. and by Hagar, from Ismael, Gen. 25.13,14. being therein intermingled, the one with the other; whence the ambiguity, and variety of readings, and versions, 1 King. 10.15. 2 Chron. 9.14. Psal. 68.4. Hab. 1.8. Zeph. 3.3. See Jer. 25.24. For as, for those that imagine, they should be so called of the word *Arab,* that signifies *lying in wait;* though it carry a fair show with it, as if the words were the same, and it suit well with the condition of that people, living much by robbery to this very day, and to that purpose waiting for passengers, to surprise them, Jer. 3.2. yet the roots of either, in the original, are divers; and the initial letters differ as in *Amoz,* and *Amos,* chap. 1.1. which not observed, bred a gross mistake in the Greek version, Josh. 8.14. The whole region lying, a great part of it, between the Persian gulf, on the Eastern side; and the Red sea, thence called the Arabian gulf on the West; is commonly divided into three parts, *Arabia the fertile, the rocky,* and *the waste.* But Strabo, l. 16. seems to make a dichotomy of it, as nature itself, in a manner, has done, dividing it into two parts, *the fertile,* and *the barren;* which latter may well include those two, which others divide; being for infecundity much at one; in the wilderness whereof, the Israelites so long wandered to and fro, after their cutting the Red sea, before they arrived on the coast of Canaan, and of this part of Arabia do most understand this prophecy; (though peradventure, yet, of a larger extent) because bordering upon Palestine, it is probable, that the Assyrian king overran this also, when he invaded that country, ch. 20.1. Of *Arabia,* see also on ch. 13.21.

*{In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim*} This prophecy foretelling the calamities that should befall the Arabians, from the Assyrian invading them, relates how they should be driven, leaving their abode in the champaign, to seek shelter in the woods; calls upon some of them, to relieve their neighbors in their flight, ver. 14,15. and prefixes a time, wherein this disaster, betiding them, should much impoverish their estate, ver. 16,17.

*{the forest*} Or, *wood;* as 1 Sam. 14.25. *wood,* for *woods:* or, *forest* consisting of *woods:* as chap. 7.2. the woody part of the country, whither, as well men, as beasts, use to betake themselves for covert and retreat, in times of danger and distress, when invaded, or pursued in the plain; or expect so to be, where they lie more open to assault, Gen. 3.8. 1 Sam. 22.5. Josh. 17.18. *though it be a wood,* or, *forest,* apt to shelter, and more difficult therefore to surprise: for so the particle should there, as after in the same verse, be rendered. The meaning seems to be here, that not only for fear of the enemies, but being stripped, by them, of their tents, which they usually lodged, and dwelt in, ch. 14.20. they should now be compelled to take up their lodging in the woods. See Jer. 49.28,29.

*{in Arabia*} The woods, that are in that country; or, *of Arabia: in Arabia,* for, *of Arabia:* as, *the mountains in Gilboa,* 2 Sam. 1.21. for *of Gilboa:* and, *in thy people,* Exod. 22.28. for, *of thy people:* as it is rendered, Act. 23.5. and it may, as well, be rendered, *ye in Arabia,* or, *of Arabia shall lodge;* as well inhabitants *of Arabia,* as *woods of Arabia:* referring the words *in,* or, *of Arabia,* not to the *woods,* wherein they should lodge, but to the people, that should lodge in them. The Latin, deceived by the nearness of the word, translates it, *at evening:* and the word that signifies *evening,* is supposed indeed, sometime, to be put for *Arabia,* 1 King. 10.15. but this of *Arabia* never for *evening:* and the word is the same here with that before. As for the Popish interpreter, he did but play here, (as many of them oft do;) who because the word *Arab,* is not far in sound from *Oreb,* that signifies *a crow,* or, *a raven,* (for the word seems to include either, Levit. 11.15. so called it may be, for *his blackness,* Cant. 5.11. resembling the Arabians' smoky tents, Cant. 1.5.) would have it here intimated that the Arabians' destiny was, like Pharao's chief baker's, to be hanged; and made meat for such fowls, Gen. 40.19. Prov. 30.17. Thus do wanton wits, as well among professed Christians, as apostate Jews, in profane manner dally, and make sport with God's sacred oracles.

*{shall ye lodge*} This some, and so the Rabbins also, divers of them, understand of the Jews, who, in the Assyrian invasion, fled into those parts for relief. Whom the Arabians (here upbraided, therefore, for their inhumanity towards them, as was Moab before, ch. 16.3,4.) refusing to entertain; should constrain them to lodge abroad in the wide, and wild woods. Others understand it, of caravans, or troops of people, that used to travel that way with merchandise, Gen. 37.25,28. Job 6.19. and to take up their lodgings among them; but now finding the country full of soldiery, in regard of whom they could not pass with security, and safety, as formerly they had done; (See Lam. 5.9.) or rather, all rifled and wasted by the enemy, should be compelled to lodge in the woods. But I suppose it rather to be intended of the Kedarens, or Arabians, inhabiting in the lower parts of the country, towards Palestine; who being expelled from the places of their wonted abode, in the plain, should be enforced to flee up into the higher parts of the country, to seek shelter there in the *woods.*

*{O ye travelling companies of Dedanim*} The word here used, signifies first, and properly, *paths, ways,* or *passages,* Gen. 49.17. Job 6.18. Chap. 2.3. and so some interpreters here understand it; rendering the words, *in the ways,* or *passages of Dedanim;* by the ways, that lead thither. The particle is wanting: as Hos. 6.9. *in the way,* or *upon the way;* or, *by the highway side to Sechem,* that is, say they, *in the woods,* that are about the way toward Dedan. Howbeit, as the word *Oreach,* arising from the same root, (but once read, Job 34.8. having a notion of journeying, and there used of such, as travel, in society, or company together) does signify *a traveller;* whence *a lodge for travellers,* Jer. 9.1. and, *like a traveller, that turns in to a lodge for a night,* Jer. 14.8. so the word *Orchah* here used is, by a metonymy deemed to be put for *a company,* or *troop of travellers,* that journey together, Gen. 37.25,28. Job 6.19. in which latter place also, *walks,* or *marches,* for so the word properly signifies, Ps. 68.24. seems to be put for *companies marching,* or *journeying,* as another the like also, 2 Sam. 12.4. where *a walk,* or, *a way,* for a man to walk, or journey in, is put for a *man of the way,* or, *by the way,* that is, *a wayfaring man,* and made the same, with *oreach, a traveller,* there also used. The text therefore may well be so read here as our English renders it; though I see no necessity of departing from the proper, and most frequent signification of the word.

*{Dedanim*} Or, *Dedanites:* a people descended from *Dedan,* one of Abraham's issue by Keturah, Gen. 25.3. and they are reckoned up with the *Temanites,* and other people of *Arabia,* Jer. 25.23,24. though among the *Edomites* also together with the *Temanites;* as near neighbors to them, and mixed also, it may be, with them, Jer. 49.7,8. Ezek. 25.23. So the *Dumeans,* and *Idumeans,* before, ver. 11. See of them and their merchandise, Ezek. 27.5,10. & 38.15. by which places, it may be deemed, that they dwelt near upon the fertile part of Arabia. Howbeit; from the former place of Ezekiel, some observe two several people; of countries far distant one from another, both bearing that name; the one descended from Cush, by Raamah, Gen. 10.7. seated Eastward from the gulf of Persia on the Indian seacoast, where a region is called *Dedan* unto this day, that traded at Tyre in *ivory,* and *ebony,* the wares of those parts, v. 15. The other, as before, descended from Abraham by Keturah, whose seat was, as has been said, and their trade in *clothes* only, v. 20.

**V. 14.** *{The inhabitants of the land of Temah, brought water to him that was thirsty; they prevented with their bread, him that fled*} The Jewish doctors conceiving these *thirsty* ones to be of their own countrymen, understand the words to be spoken with an intimation of duty, relating what they should have done: *The inhabitants of Tema should have brought water to* the *thirsty* Jews, their kinsmen, *and should have prevented with their bread, those of* them *that fled* away from the Assyrians: or, as some of them would have it, *as they prevented* them with their bread; that is, as they expound it, whereas being athirst they wanted drink, and they should in the first place have supplied them with that; they did not, but first tendered salt meats, that increased their thirst; and when they had so done, then offered them empty bottles, which putting to their mouths, in hope to meet with drink in them, they drew nothing but wind from them; and so died. These are Jewish fictions and fables. As far from the truth of story, do those run another way, that would have it understood, of their helping to relieve the Assyrians, their confederates, pursued by the Medes. The words may well be rendered, from the Hebrew: *Bring forth water,* wherewith *to meet the thirsty; with your bread prevent those that flee.* Which is spoken by the prophet, to intimate unto the Temaites, what distress their countrymen of other parts of Arabia should be in, being constrained to leave suddenly their wonted places of abode, and to flee either to them, or along by them, being destitute of all necessary provisions, in those waste regions especially, to seek for some shelter, and relief elsewhere.

*{the land of Tema*} As *Dumah,* v. 11. so *Tema;* was one of Ismael's race, Gen. 25.15. from whom the land, that the people descended of him did inhabit, was so called; Job 6.19. Jer. 25.23. They misread here *Teman* for *Tema,* with the Greek, who after the old Latin render it *The land of the South.*

*{brought*} Or, *bring.* Heb. *come:* as Jer. 12.9. and so taking it, in the first form it should be rendered, and *come O water,* as some very unfitly; but, *come with water:* a defect of the particle: as ver. 7,10. as some, *come, and bring water:* as Gen. 27.9. *take me* (that is, take, and bring me) *two kids;* Or, it may be here, in the second, or active form; and then it is, *make to come:* which is all one with *bring.* I rather choose the former, *come with water,* partly, because the verb in Jer. 12.9. (and in this form it is no where else found) so sounds, *come to eat;* and partly, because the Hebrew has it more fully than our English expresses it, *come with water to meet the thirsty:* as 1 Sam. 25.34.

*{water*} A commodity, in those parts, very scanty, Exod. 17.1. Num. 20.2. Job 9.18,19.

*{thirsty*} Heb. *thirsty one:* as afterward, *the fleer:* but both taken collectively: as chap. 32.6. & 16.3. In this condition their neighbors then were, partly, in likelihood, being stripped of all necessaries; partly not daring for fear, to stay to eat, and drink, or, to take any provision along with them; and partly also wandering in those hot, and dry places; such as their country for the most part was. So 2 Sam. 17.28,29. Ps. 107.4. Heb. 11.37,38.

*{they prevented*} Or, *prevent ye.* Which whether way taken, does not imply, as the fond Rabbin would have it, a tendering of meat, or bread to them, before meat; but a speedy, and spontaneous act of beneficence, not staying till they were cried unto, or called upon for it; but freely of their own accord, without delay doing it, and with their voluntary tender, anticipating their suit for it. So Deut. 23.4. & Neh. 13.2. *because they prevented not the children of Israel, with bread, and with water* by the way: not amiss rendered in either place *met,* being the same, that is implied in the former branch, by *coming to meet,* importing a going voluntarily to meet them, before they were come at them, or arrived with them: as Gen. 46.29. Prov. 7.15.

*{with their bread*} Or, *with your bread:* one person for another: the third for the second: as Job 18.3. *O thou that tearest his soul in his anger;* (for, *thy soul,* or *thy self with thine anger:*) *shall the earth be forsaken for thee?* and Job 17.10. *return ye all them,* for *all of you.*

*{him that fled*} Or, *that fleeth.* Heb. *the fleer,* or *wanderer:* as Prov. 27.8. Jer. 49.5. See ver. 15.

**V. 15.** *{For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war*} It is no groundless fear, that makes them flee thus, like that, 2 King. 7.8. but the dread and terror of a potent enemy, not making towards them, but fallen in upon them, with an over-powerful army.

*{they*} Which shows the word before going, ver. 14. to be collective.

*{fled*} Or, *flee:* as Ps. 31.11.

*{from the swords*} Heb. *from before the swords.* That is, for fear of the sword, ready to seize on them; as 1 Chro. 11.13. ch. 31.8. Joel 2.6. and so in all the branches following. *The sword* is put frequently for hostile invasion, Levit. 26.6,25. chapter 1.20. and 51.19.

*{the sword drawn*} So the Chaldee. Heb. *left,* or *let go,* as the verb sometime signifies, Deut. 32.15. Gen. 31.38. or rather *stretched out;* at them: and ready to fall upon them, as the verb is used, Num. 11.31. 1 Sam. 4.2. chap. 16.8. or, *diffused,* and spread abroad, over the country: (so one of the Rabbins) as the participle is used, 1 Sam. 30.16. and the verb also, Judg. 15.9. 1 Sam. 4.2. 2 Sam. 5.18,22. the word is no where else found applied to *a sword:* and some therefore suppose *netushah,* to be put here, for *letushah,* that signifies *sharp,* or, *sharpened,* Ps. 7.12. & 52.2. but that is a needless boldness.

*{the bent bow*} Heb. *the trodden bow.* See ch. 5.28. *sword,* and *bow,* as elsewhere, so here; for all manner of warlike weapons; being two of the most principal, and in those times most commonly used; the one to smite, with at hand; the other, to reach afar off; joined frequently together, Gen. 48.22. Ps. 37.14. & 44.6. & 76.3. ch. 13.15,18. & 41.2. Hos. 2.20.

*{the grievousness of war*} That is, *a grievous war.* Heb. *heaviness:* as ch. 30.27. *heavy,* for *grievous,* as Gen. 18.20. & 36.8.

**V. 16.** *{For thus hath the Lord said unto me*} See ver. 6. & chap. 37.4.

*{within a year, after the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail*} In these words, is a short space of time set, a bare year, within compass whereof this sad prophecy should take effect; and the heavy doom, in the verses foregoing, closely, and darkly described, now more expressly, and in plainer terms denounced, should be executed upon the Arabians.

*{within a year*} Heb. *in yet a year;* that is, while the year, that now is, is yet in being: before a year be come about; or be complete. A shorter time, than that assigned to the Moabites, chap. 16.14. or, that to the Ethiopians, and Egyptians, jointly together, chap. 20.3. the Assyrian, whether Sargon, chap. 20.1. or Sennacherib, ch. 36.1. falling in, it seems, sooner upon those parts of Arabia, than upon those people; if those several prophecies, at least, were delivered about the same time with this. For I cannot assent to them that conceive this prophecy, to intend the calamities on this people, inflicted by the Chaldeans, above an hundred years after Esay's days; foretold by Jeremy, Jer. 49.28. and that the time here mentioned does not tell when this heavy doom should be executed; but how long the execution of it should last.

*{after*} Or, *according to the years of an hireling;* Who so soon as his years are run out, expects instantly his wages, Gen. 29.21,22. See on ch. 16.14.

*{and all the glory*} Or, *shall all the glory.* For as our English runs, the *all* is superfluous: *within a year, and all the glory shall fail.* Or, if we retain the copulative, which in the original is not unuseful, it may be rendered: *As yet a year, and all the glory shall fail.* So ch. 10.25. Jer. 51.33.

*{all the glory*} Their wealth, might, and multitude: or whatsoever it is that they glory in, or procures them any note, or name: as ch. 16.14. Their wealth seems to have consisted most in their cattle, not the greater sort, but the lesser, to wit: sheep, and goats; that will thrive in places, though somewhat bare; and affording but short commons, where they may have scope enough: and some camels, beasts, that will endure hard feeding, and hold out long without water: See ch. 60.7. Ezek. 27.21. Jer. 49.29.

*{of Kedar*} The name of one of Ismael's sons, Gen. 25.13. whose posterity seated themselves, in the less fertile part of Arabia, as well the waste, as the rocky: that which this our prophet intimates, ch. 42.11. there they lived most in tents, therefore called *Scenites:* which they were wont to remove from place to place to procure change of pasture for their cattle. Hence, *the tents of Kedar,* Ps. 120.5. Cant. 1.5. and their *curtains,* whereof their tents consisted, Jer. 49.29. Hab. 3.7.

*{fail*} Or, *be consumed:* as it is rendered, Ps. 37.20. ch. 1.28.

**V. 17.** *{And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar shall be diminished*} There shall be a very small company left among them, of any might; or fit for military service.

*{the residue*} The small remainder, like a remnant, of a large piece of cloth or the like: See ch. 10.22.

*{of the number*} The word is used sometime as a note of fewness, such as may easily be numbered, Deut. 33.6. ch. 10.19. sometime, of multitude, a number not easily told, Numb. 23.10. Ps. 147.4. and so here: as also *numbers,* in the plural, Ps. 71.15.

*{of archers*} Heb. *of the bow,* that is, *of men of the bow;* or, *bowmen:* as, *harvest:* for, an *harvest man.* Chap. 17.5. See Chap. 22.3. yet the word may be taken here in his proper sense, without that trope, if we carry on the sentence, without interruption, thus; *the number of the bow* (that is, *of the bows;* as ver. 15. for the word, howsoever taken, is collective) *of the mighty men,* etc. as the very like is, 1 Sam. 2.4. that is, the residue of the multitude of the bows, that is, the arms, and the might, consequently of their martial men shall be diminished. So Jer. 49.35. *I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might.* The bow was these Kedarens' chief arms, therein imitating their ancestor Ismael that was trained up in that trade; and living in the wilderness, (it is not unlikely) lived much by it, at first, Gen. 21.20.

*{of the sons of Kedar*} The Kedarens, his posterity. See ver. 16. as, *the sons of Lot,* Ps. 83.8.

*{shall be diminished*} Not utterly destroyed. So of Moab, chap. 16.14.

*{for the Lord God of Israel hath spoken it*} See Chapter 1.20. & ver. 16.

*{God of Israel*} The only true God, Jer. 10.10.

### CHAPTER 22

**V. 1.** *{The burden of the valley of Vision*} A sad prophecy against Judah and Jerusalem: as appears by ver. 8,11. Of *burden,* see ch. 13.1.

*{the valley*} It is here questioned why Jerusalem should be called *a valley,* when as it seemed to stand upon an hill, whereof that, Psal. 87.1. *Her foundation is on the holy mountains,* or, *hills.* To which some answer; that though the city stood, the chief part of it, on a knoll, or rising ground, and might therefore be termed an hill, the Temple built on mount Moriah, whereon Abraham was to have sacrificed Isaac, and Sion the city of David being an hill of some height, Gen. 22.2. 2 Chr. 3.1. 2 Sam. 5.7. Psal. 48.2. & 68.1,16. chap. 2.2. & 14.13. yet, in regard that the place in which it was seated, was environed with mountains, far higher than it, or any part of it, it is in regard of them said to stand in a vale, and is here termed *a valley.* See Ps. 121.1. & 125.2. chap. 52.7. Jer. 3.23. Others, would have it so termed, both Jewish, and ours, in regard of the dejected estate, and low condition, that it should be brought unto, by the troubles here foretold, in regard whereof, it might well be called, not a lofty, or stately mount, now, as sometime; but a depressed, low valley. See Jer. 17.3,12. & 22.23. the former seems the genuine sense.

*{of Vision*} It is called *the Valley of Vision,* as most think, in regard of the abundance of visions, or divine revelations, from time to time, there imparted to God's prophets: for Jerusalem (as one well says) was as *a Seminary of Seers:* and there was the place from whence God was wont to give oracles; whence that sacred room, or closet in the Temple, was so styled, 1 King. 6.5,19,20. & 8.6,8. Some, a little more nicely, proceed somewhat farther; because thereinto from heaven, as from an hill, into a vale, did those divine revelations, in great plenty descend. Nor are there wanting, who suppose it might be so termed, not as the subject only, but as the object of such visions; because so many visions either went before, or were delivered concerning it, Exod. 15.17. Deut. 3.25. & 12.11. 2 Sam. 7.10,23. Psal. 87.2,3. & 132.13,14. According to this first exposition, which seems most genuine; *Vision* is put for *Visions:* as chap. 1.1. Howbeit, some think, there is in this title, an allusion to the name of *Jerusalem,* upon the apparition made to Abraham, in that place named thereupon by him, *Jehovah-jireh,* Gen. 22.14. for *Jerusalem,* say they, may well signify, *Salem* (so it was anciently termed, Gen. 14.18. Ps. 76.2.) *where God appeared;* which words both joined together, make up *Jerusalem,* Josh. 10.1. 1 Chr. 11.4.

*{what aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?*} The former part of this Chapter contains a prophecy, concerning the distress and distraction, that should befall the Jewish state; and more specially, the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem; with whom the prophet here parleys, demanding of them (for to them he directs his speech) what the reason might be of so sudden a change with them; that whereas, but a while before they were set wholly upon revelling and jollity, ver. 13. they should now be generally possessed with such fears, and so full of distractions and disturbance. Now some suppose this to be a prophecy of the surprisal and sacking of the city, under Zedekiah, by Nebuchadnezzar, Jer. 39. & 52. Others, of the distress of it, under Ezekiah, by Sennacherib, chap. 36. & 37. and this latter is most likely; because the whole tenor of the Chapter does most fitly agree thereunto.

*{what aileth thee?*} Heb. *what to thee:* that is: what is the matter? what has betided, or is befallen you? So Judg. 13.23. Psalm 114.5.

*{gone up to the housetops*} To burn incense to the host of heaven, say some of the Jewish doctors; which indeed, sometime, they used to do. See Jer. 19.13. But this is not here intended. To lament, and bewail themselves, say others: as chap. 15.3. that, more likely than the former: Or to look abroad, to see what the enemy does, as those are wont to do, that are begirt with hostile forces: or, to look about, to see whether they can descry any aids coming to their relief, Psal. 121.1. Jer. 3.23. or, to safeguard themselves there: for unto the higher places, as more defensible, people in such cases are wont to retire, Judg. 9.51. or, to call thence, for aid or advice, to neighbors, or others near to them; or, to crave relief and help, at God's hand, Act. 10.9. For some one, or more, or the most of these ends and purposes, it may be, that this running up to the tops of their flat-roofed houses at this time, was; importing, howsoever, much fear, and distraction, throughout the whole city.

**V. 2.** *{Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city*} Or, *That thou art full of stirs, thou tumultuous city, thou joyous city?* What is the matter, that your note and tune, is so altered? that you are now so full of outcries, and clamors, that were so full of mirth and jollity before. See ver. 13.

*{full of stirs*} Or, *clamors,* or *noises.* The word is used, sometime for joyful acclamations, Zach. 4.7. sometime, for doleful exclamations: and so it is by some deemed here to signify. It may well be taken either way; either, that they had been before full of the one, or, that they were now full of the other.

*{a tumultuous city*} Or, *thou tumultuous,* or, *streperous, city:* For some refer this branch to the former, supposing it to denote, in part, her present condition, because the word sometime implies a mournful noise, Psal. 55.2. chap. 11. Other, carry it on to the branch next ensuing, as describing, her former condition and estate; the word is used of such noise, as revelers amidst their mirth make, Prov. 20.1. Zach. 9.15. the word seems here to imply, a hideous confused noise, whether of the one, or of the other. See ch. 17.12. and, 51.15.

*{a joyous city*} Or, *thou reveling city.* See Chap. 5.11,14. So chap. 32.13.

*{thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle*} Those that conceive the siege, and sacking of Jerusalem, by the Chaldeans, to be here intended, understand this passage, the former part of it, of those that died with plague and famine, in the time of the siege, Jer. 14.18. & 38.2. the latter, of those that were slain at Riblah, after the surprisal of the city, Jer. 39.6. Others, that apply it to the Assyrian invasion, suppose the meaning to be, that they were so dismayed and disheartened, that they had no spirit or life in them, than as if they were slain men, ere the sword touched them; stark dead with fear, ere they came to any fight, Josh. 2.11. & 5.1. 1 Sam. 28.20. Dan. 10.17.

*{thy slain*} Or, *that thy slain ones;* (for *men* is not in the text) as carrying the text on in a continued tenor, from the first verse, unto the end of the third. *Thy slain;* either slain indeed; or, as slain with fear, Ps. 88.4,5. ch. 59.7. Lam. 2.12.

*{with the sword*} Heb. *the slain ones of the sword;* as Num. 19.16. Lam. 4.9. For the former word is put substantively, and governs the latter: and the like is in the next clause.

*{dead in battle*} Heb. *the dead ones of war,* or, *battle:* as 2 Sam. 18.8. *dead of battle,* for, *dead in battle;* as *woods in Arabia,* for, *woods of Arabia,* ch. 21.13.

**V. 3.** *{All thy rulers are fled together*} This perturbation and affrightment, has seized upon, not the common sort of people alone, but your captains also, your commanders, your military men; chap. 33.7,8.
