*{All thy rulers are fled*} Or, *That all thy captains do flee;* as continuing still the question, at first propounded, ver. 1. *Rulers;* as chap. 1.10. & 3.6,7. Or, *Captains, Leaders;* as Josh. 10.24. Judg. 11.6,11. Prov. 6.7.

*{are fled*} Or, *flee;* as Chap. 21.15. Or, *wander;* as Job 15.23. Prov. 27.8. Either they wander, and run to and fro, as men in a maze, or at their wits' end, chap. 8.21,22. seeking one while to the Assyrian, to make their peace with him, chap. 33.7,8. another while to the Egyptian, to crave aid against him, chap. 30.2,4. (so Jer. 2.18,36.) or, that they flee to Jerusalem, out of all parts, not daring to stand it out against the Assyrian, bearing all down before him; ch. 39.1. (so Jer. 8.14. & 10.17.) or, (as those that refer it to the Babylonian invasion) they flee out of the city, to shift for themselves, Jer. 6.1. & 39.4.

*{they are bound by the archers*} Or, *that they are bound:* (carrying the sentence still on) Heb. *of,* or, *from the bow.* Which those that apply the prophecy to the times of Zedekiah, expound, *from,* that is, *of,* or; *by:* as Psal. 78.64. *the bow,* that is, *the bowmen,* the archers: as chap. 21.17. and understand it of those that were taken, and bound by the Chaldeans, after the surprisal of the city, Jer. 39.5,6,7. But those that suppose it to concern Ezekiahs days, expound it, some, *from the bow,* that is, *for fear of the bowmen,* referring it to the former verb, *they flee from the bow;* and so the words indeed lie in the text. Other of them, referring it to the latter verb, read it, *from the bow they are bound:* which they expound, by an Hebraism, not unusual, *they are bound from the bow:* that is, bound from making use of it: as, *from speaking,* that one cannot speak, 1 Sam. 25.17. *from seeing,* Psal. 69.23. *that they cannot see,* Rom. 11.10. *from a King,* from being a King, 1 Sam. 15.22. *from ministering as a Priest,* Hos. 9.12. *that thou shalt no more do it.* Thus understood, the sense is, that their hands are so restrained, and tied up with extremity of fear, that they are not able to manage, and make use of their bows.

*{all that are found in thee, are bound together*} Or, *that* (as before) *all that are found in thee,* that is, are in you, as Est. 1.5. Chap. 39.2. *are bound together;* either in fetters, Jer. 52.11. or with fear, Ps. 76.5. Though some expound it, of a conspiracy of the princes of Judah among themselves, not to fight, but to flee, and make their peace with the enemy, ch. 8.12.

*{which have fled from far*} Or, *that they flee from far;* that is, that they flee hither to Jerusalem, from the farthest part of the country; or, that they flee away, so fast, from an enemy afar off, before he come near to them; or, simply, *that they flee far away;* (for so is the word used, ch. 23.7.) that they withdraw themselves, and get as fast, and as far as they can, out of the way: as Ps. 55.7,8. and so it is not unlikely that divers of them did.

**V. 4.** *{Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly: Labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people*} The prophet's speech of himself, setting himself upon a solemn and settled course of mourning, in regard of the calamities that he foresaw would shortly befall his people: So ch. 15.9. & 24.16. The wonted manner of God's ministers to mourn, as for the sins, so for the sufferings also of God's people; Jer. 4.19. & 9.1. & 13.17. Luk. 19.41.

*{look away from me*} So Cant. 6.5. but in another sense, *turn thine eyes away from me:* here, as if he should say, speaking to his friends about him, endeavoring to take him off from his grief; look another way, betake yourselves to some other employment, and let me alone, leave me to my mourning, whereunto I have with a firm resolution abandoned myself. Whence, also, some here render the word, *cease from me:* as also, Job 7.19. & 14.9. Psal. 39.13. which places are parallel to this.

*{I will weep bitterly*} Or, *that I may weep bitterly:* a defect of the final particle: as chap. 5.11. & 10.2. Heb. *I will;* or, *that I may, embitter myself in,* or, *with, weeping:* a *bitter weeping;* for, a sore, and grievous lamentation, Jer. 6.29. & 31.15. Ezek. 21.6. & 27.30,31. Zach. 12.10. Matth. 26.75. So Exod. 1.14. *they made their lives bitter to them:* and, *God hath dealt very bitterly with me,* Ruth 1.20.

*{labour not to comfort me*} Heb. *urge not,* or, *press not to comfort me:* so the word is used, Gen. 19.35. Exod. 4.13. Jer. 17.16. press not comfort upon me. So Jacob, Gen. 37.35. *he refused to be comforted:* and Asaph, Psal. 77.2. *my soul refused to be comforted:* and Rachel, Jer. 31.15. Thus passion prevails sometime overmuch, even with the Saints.

*{because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people*} Because of the spoil made by the enemies' forces, among my countrymen, as dear to me, as to tender parents, any daughter, ch. 1.8. Jer. 9.1. Rom. 9.3.

**V. 5.** *{For it is a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity, by the Lord God of hosts, in the valley of vision, breaking down the walls, and of crying to the mountains*} These words relate to, and further dilate, what he had touched upon, and given some hint of, in the close of the former verse. That therefore his so great professed grief might not seem groundless, he does in this verse very pathetically, and rhetorically, lay forth the grievous distresses and distractions, that his people should be in, when these dismal evils should befall them.

*{a day*} That is, *a time:* as Jer. 36.7. Joel 2.2.

*{of trouble*} So it is rendered, Ezek. 7.7. Prov. 15.16. Or, *tumult:* as Amos 3.9. Zach. 14.13. or, *vexation:* as 2 Chron. 15.5. Ezek. 22.5. or, *discomfiture:* as 1 Sam. 14.20. or, *destruction:* as Deut. 7.23. 1 Sam. 5.9. the verb it comes from, used in that place of Moses, signifies *to break,* or, *destroy:* and so ch. 28.28. See ch. 37.3.

*{of treading down*} As ch. 18.2. See ch. 10.6. where Sennacherib has a commission signed from God, thus to deal with his people: and ch. 14.25. where with *breaking* (that is discomfiture) and *treading down* as a further degree of harsh, and disgraceful usage, Sennacherib himself is threatened. See also, ch. 63.6.

*{of perplexity*} As Est. 3.15. Mic. 7.4. it is a metaphor from man, or beast, entangled in a thicket. So Pharaoh, of the Egyptians; *they are entangled in the wilderness,* Exod. 14.3. there is in the original, an elegant parechesis, or similitude of sound, between this word and the former; which our English cannot express.

*{by the Lord God of hosts*} Who has given commission for it, ch. 10.6. and whose instruments and officers they are, who are hereafter mentioned, ver. 6. chap. 10.5,15. that which makes the evil to be unavoidable, and unconquerable. See chap. 13.6. So Zach. 14.13.

*{by the Lord*} Heb. *to the Lord:* to him, for *by him:* or *from him:* as Ruth 3.10. 1 Sam. 23.21. Ps. 2.8. & 115.15. Jer. 15.8.

*{breaking down the walls*} Heb. *wall:* but taken collectively: as 1 Chr. 14.1. where *wall-wrights,* is put for *masons.* Hence a city, or walled town, may seem to be termed *Kir.* See chap. 16.7,11. and thence also, the word here used, not to *build up,* but to *pull down a wall;* (as, *to branch,* for, *to lop;* or *cut down branches,* ch. 10.28. See also, ch. 66.2.) and consequently, to *destroy,* Numb. 24.17. It is that which God before threatened; to wit, that he would *break down the wall* of his vineyard, & suffer it to be trodden down, ch. 5.5.

*{in the valley of vision*} See on ver. 1.

*{and of crying to the mountains*} Not, *a noise from the mountains,* Ezek. 7.7. either a hollow sound only, such as mountains usually yield; or, a noise of mirth and jollity, such as in vintage time the vintagemen are wont there to make: but *a crying to the mountains,* such loud shrieks, and outcries, as shall reach the neighbor mountains, and cause them to ring again, with them, chap. 15.4,5,8. Jer. 48.34. Or, a crying of persons making toward the mountains, for shelter and safety; and crying out unto their friends, and others, after the usual manner of people, in such cases, as they go along; *to the mountains, to the mountains:* one usual place of retreat and refuge, for man and beast, being here put for all other of like kind, Gen. 19.17,19. Judg. 6.2. 1 Sam. 13.6. Psal. 11.1. and 104.18. Jer. 13.16. & 16.16. Matth. 24.16. Though there want not, that expound it of the noise of houses, and buildings ruinated, and either beaten, or burnt down; or, of the clamor and shouts of the enemy, falling in, upon, and sacking the city, Ps. 137.7. See ch. 16.9. But the former seems more probable.

**V. 6.** *{And Elam bare the quiver, with chariots of men, and horsemen; and Kir uncovered the shield*} In these words, the prophet further shows what people, among others, were to be employed in this expedition against Judah.

*{Elam*} The *Elamites,* or *Persians:* at that time subject unto the Assyrian monarch; and serving under him in this expedition. Of them, see on chap. 11.11.

*{bare the quiver*} Served as bowmen: That people being of special note for archery, in those days; as appears by Jer. 49.35. like as the Parthians, their neighbors, have been also, in all ages: and of the Elamites Strabo, lib. 16. testifies as much.

*{with chariots of men*} Heb. *with the chariot of a man:* as chap. 21.9. Save that the word is *Ish* there; *Adam* here. Of which words, see on chap. 2.9. *chariot of man;* for, a company of chariots, (as ver. 7.) with military men; commanders for the most part, in them, Judg. 4.15. 1 King. 22.31,34. 2 Chr. 35.24. so termed, to distinguish them from such as were employed for carriage of provisions, or other necessaries: and so also, ch. 21.7,9.

*{and horsemen*} A defect of the copulative: as chap. 21.7. See more there.

*{Kir*} Not that of Moab; whereof before, chap. 15.1. but another city of that name situate in Media, and under the dominion then of the Assyrian, 2 King. 16.9. Amos 1.5. The Medes and Persians are here joined together, being neighboring nations; as Chap. 21.2. For those that would have this *Kir,* to be Cyrene, (whereof, yet, some of note seem very confident) consider not well, how far Lybia, wherein Cyrene is situate, and these regions lie asunder.

*{uncovered the shield*} Heb. *made naked:* or, *bare:* as ch. 3.17. & 32.11. that is, they uncased it, they took off the case, wherewith, out of times of use, and service, arms are wont to be covered, to preserve them from dust and rust; and fitted them for service, chap. 21.5. or, because the course of the context seems to import, not a preparation for war, but matter of present action, (see ver. 7.) the words may be rendered, *Kir discovered the shield;* that is, appeared in the field, with their shields in sight, to the terror of the other party, before those places which they came to assault. Thus it sorts well with the former branch; *Elam bare the quiver, and Kir bare up the shield.* For as men may be said to *conceal their arms,* when they come with sword, or dagger, under coat, or cassock, or with their pistols in their pockets, or, when they carry shield or buckler, hanging behind them, at their backs: so they may well be said to *reveal* or *discover* them, when they bear them in open view, or advance, and lift them up to make use of them in battle: and so do some of the Hebrew commenters expound the word here. And of some such *uncovering,* and *discovering* of arms in fight, see Hab. 3.9. as also of making the *arm bare;* by stripping of it up to the elbow, for the fitting of it to fight, or smite with. See chap. 52.10. Howsoever, they are wide, who taking the word *Kir,* here, not for the name of a city, or the men of that country, wherein it stood; but for a *wall,* render the words, either after the old Latin, *the shield made bare the wall;* that is, the shield-men pillaged the walls of their houses, of all their rich hangings and ornaments: or, after some of the rabbins, *they made the wall bare of the shields:* taking them from the walls, where they were hung up before: and those other of this latter rank, no less, that following the Chaldee; and because the verb here used, in their Talmudic language, does frequently signify, *to adhere,* and *be annexed unto;* though they produce no clear text of Scripture for it, render the words, *the shield stuck to the wall:* or, *they fastened their shields to the wall;* to wit, that under the covert thereof, they might with more safety either assault the defendants, or undermine the walls.

*{the shield*} If it be demanded, why *Elam* has the *quiver* assigned him; and *Kir* the *shield:* it may be supposed, because the Elamites were the better, generally, at bow and arrows, and these of Kir, at sword and target. But we are not so to understand it, as if the Elamites were archers only; and those of Kir, none but swordmen: though it is not unlikely, that the use of the one sort of weapons might be more rife in the one country, than in the other: but that yet there was use of the *quiver* also with them of *Kir,* and of the *sword* with them of *Elam.* It is an elegancy of phrase, whereby our prophet is wont in way of distribution, to assign several attributes, to several subjects: although both common, to them both. See on ch. 5.13. & 18.6. & 20.4. & 21.14. so likewise, ver. 7.

**V. 7.** *{And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots; and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate*} The state and condition, is here described, of the land of Judah, invaded by the people before mentioned, ver. 6. and what should be done by the chariots and horsemen there spoken of, to wit, that their rich vales should be spoiled by them, and their cities besieged, and assaulted.

*{it shall come to pass, that*} Heb. *it shall be that:* as ch. 16.12.

*{thy choicest valleys*} Heb. *the choice of thy valleys:* as *the choice of our sepulchers,* Gen. 23.6. *the choice of his fir trees,* ch. 37.24. and *the choice of thy cedars,* Jer. 22.7. their valleys which were of special note and regard, as well for pleasure, as profit, ch. 28.1,4.

*{chariots*} Heb. *chariot,* or, company of chariots: as ver. 6.

*{horsemen*} Of which before, ver. 6.

*{shall set themselves in array*} Heb. *shall setting, set:* or, *disposing, dispose* themselves, to wit, in warlike manner, to assault and surprise: as Psal. 3.6.

*{at the gate*} Heb. *to the gate-ward:* as, *to the wilderness-ward;* ch. 16.1. So also, ch. 28.6. either toward the city; (*Gate,* for, *city:* See ch. 3.26.) or, toward the gate of the city, (both collectively taken) to force entrance thereby, into the city, Judg. 9.44,52. Yet, the meaning is not, that the chariots stayed in the valleys, and the horsemen only approached the cities; but chariots and horsemen both, spoiled the one; and assaulted the other. See on ver. 6. And although true it be, as one of the Jewish doctors well observes, that the chariots were more useful in the vale than on the hills: yet it is apparent, that they made use of them, in, and on either, Josh. 17.18.

**V. 8.** *{And he discovered the covering of Judah*} In this verse, and those that follow, is related the courses that were taken by those of Jerusalem, especially, in those calamitous times; the mere worldly sedulity of some, ver. 8–11. and the deep security, and brutish sensuality of other some, ver. 12,13. joined with a neglect of God, the one; with a contempt of him, the other.

*{he discovered the covering of Judah*} Who did it, is not expressed. God did it, say some: the enemy say others: the verb seems to be put indefinitely: and it may well be rendered, *the covering of Judah was discovered,* See vers. 19. By *covering,* some understand the city of Jerusalem itself: to which the people had repaired for shelter, ver. 3. but was broken up by the Chaldeans, Jer. 39.2. Others, the Temple, or Sanctuary, (and the vain confidence they put therein, Jer. 4.4.) being surprised, and rifled together with the city, Jer. 52.13,17–20. Lam. 1.10. Others, God's protection, formerly spread over them, Chapter 4.5,6. but now withdrawn from them, Exod. 32.25. Num. 14.9. 2 Chron. 28.19. Mich. 1.11. Others, their strongholds, and fenced cities, which were unto them as the covert is, in the forest, unto the beasts, that there abide, Ps. 29.9. but were now laid open, being seized upon, and dismantled also, it may be, some of them, by the enemy, chap. 36.1. and this I take to be the genuine sense of the place: it being, (as the sequel concerning Shebna, shows, vers. 15.) intended for the times of the Assyrian invasion: wherein, though a main part of the country was overrun by their forces, yet neither was the city of Jerusalem surprised by them: nor God's protection withdrawn from it, Chap. 37.33,35. Howbeit, there want not, that by the *covering,* here, understand their armories, and storehouses, wherein their arms and ammunition were bestowed, and laid up out of sight: which were unlocked, and set open, and the armor, and weapons, brought forth, to be in a readiness, for warlike use: which might sort well with that which follows, save that the course of the context, duly weighed seems to imply a passage unto the relation hereof, as a divers act from this, and occasioned by it. I should rather prefer, before this, what a Jewish doctor suggests: to wit, that by *covert,* should be meant their power, in general, wherein soever it consisted: discovered now, to be but feeble, and unable to stand before so potent an enemy, as was broken in upon them. See chap. 37.3.

*{and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest*} When you perceived that the enemy was broken into your country, and had taken many of your walled cities: You supposed it was high time, for you of Jerusalem, to look about you, and bestir you: by making the best preparation that might be, for the defense of your city, 1 Chr. 32.1,2.

*{thou didst look*} You, (as vers. 9.) the inhabitants of Jerusalem, 2 Chr. 32.3. did look after those outward means of provision and defense; as your sole, or principal, at least, means of safeguard. See ch. 17.7,8. and ver. 11.

*{in that day*} At that time, as ch. 17.9. when the country was full of foreign forces, ver. 7.

*{of the house of the forest*} That this was the name of an armory situate within Jerusalem, is generally agreed on. But whether it were that which Solomon called, *the house of the forest of Lebanon,* 1 King. 7.2. is questioned. For some of note there are, who deem, that house which Solomon built, was so called, because it stood in mount Lebanon; built by him for a summer-house, or house of pleasure, to retire unto when he hunted, or desired to take the air; and that this spoken of here, bears the name of that, because it resembled it, and succeeded it in some sort, and for some use, as for an armory, among others. That situate on Lebanon, being long since lost, and at this time held, if in being, by strangers. But I see no reason, why this may not be the very same with that which Solomon built, not in Lebanon, but in Jerusalem: for, to omit, that by the relation of the structure of it, the porch, wherein his throne stood, seems to have been adjoining to it; and his dwelling-house, not far from either, 1 King. 7.2,6,7,8. Certain it is, that the shields and targets of beaten gold, made for show, not for service, for his guard and attendance to bear about him, in state, were in this house of the forest of Lebanon; or, some part of it, laid up, where they might be at hand to make use of, upon occasion. See 1 King. 10.16,17. and there is no reason to imagine, that his guard should run, or ride for them, to mount Lebanon, so oft as the king should please to go abroad in state. Besides, that in his son's days, after the defection of the ten tribes, the king of Egypt found them, and seized on them, not at mount Lebanon, but in Jerusalem; 2 Chron. 12.9,10. Nor is it improbable, but that this may be the same that is called *the tower of David,* said to be *built for an armory;* and to be stored with *thousands of shields and targets,* for warriors, Cant. 4.4. So called, either because built in that place by David, at first, or because belonging to the house of David. And if it shall be further demanded, why the house should be so called, *the house of the forest of Lebanon,* if it were not there situate? I answer, it is not certain why; but it might well be, in regard of some resemblance it had of mount Lebanon, in wild walks about it; or, the loftiness of it, or some other circumstance, now unknown: and this is the more probable, because the city of Jerusalem itself, or the royal palace, at least, in it, is sometimes termed, for like reasons, by the name of Lebanon, Jer. 22.23. Zac. 11.1.

**V. 9.** *{Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many*} You viewed and repaired the decayed places, in the upper city; especially, the fort Zion, which had been neglected in time of peace, and not regarded, when no invasion feared, or expected. See 2 Chron. 32.5.

*{Ye have seen also*} Heb. *And,* but may well be rendered *also,* as Chap. 12.4. *Ye have seen,* or, *did view,* that it may run in the same tenor with the former branch, ver. 8. *thou didst look;* but that *looking,* and this *seeing,* seem somewhat to differ; that looking to their arms, as confiding in them; this seeing, or viewing the breaches, or decays in their fortifications, to repair and make them up: *to see,* for, *to view,* or *consider,* as Exod. 32.9. Job 34.21. Rom. 11.22. Some read this whole verse, as in a continued tenor, thus. *And considering, that the breaches of the city of David were many, ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool;* as if the former branch implied no special act of provision, but related only the ground, or cause of the act, mentioned in the latter. But I take it rather, to be a zeugmatical term, importing a twofold act, *ye viewed the breaches,* to repair them; as *Moses viewed his brethren's burdens:* to relieve them, Exod. 2.11. the plain syntax of the text, carries it this way, and the story itself strengthens it, 2 Chr. 3.25. Of the former speech, see Chap. 14.12. But they divert this branch of the prophet's words, far away from the main stream of the text, as well as the truth of the story, that render them, on this manner, *ye shall see the breaches of the city of David,* to wit, which the enemy shall make in your sight.

*{the city of David*} The fort of Zion, which David dwelt in, after he had taken it from the Jebusites, 2 Sam. 5.7,9.

*{that they were many*} Or, *for,* (as Psal. 12.1.) or, *because,* (as Ps. 14.6.) *they were many,* and the more need therefore of diligent view, and due repair.

*{and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool*} For the better, both strengthening the city, and supplying it with water, if it came to a siege: as also to withdraw, and derive it from the enemy to themselves. See 2 Chr. 32.4,5. Some of the Jewish commenters, add, to make brick & mortar therewith, for the repair of the walls.

*{the lower pool*} Two pools of note there were near to Jerusalem, Nehem. 3.15,16. the *upper pool,* 2 King. 18.17. Chap. 7.2. & 36.2. and *the lower,* of which, 2 Chr. 32.30. See on Chap. 7.3. & ver. 11.

**V. 10.** *{And ye have numbered, the houses of Jerusalem; and the houses have ye broken down, to fortify the wall*} Another course taken by them, to make the city the more defensible.

*{Ye have numbered the houses*} Or, *ye numbered,* as *ye gathered,* verse 9. or, *ye surveyed,* for so the word also signifies, 1 Sam. 14.17. Job 14.16. Psal. 119.26. (so it should there be rendered) Chap. 33.18. It is questioned, to what end this numbering of the houses should be. Some say, to take a muster of the men, fit for service, in every family; and to assign each one his employment. Others, to see what provision of victuals they were furnished with; and to know what quantity, both of water, and of bread, would be requisite against a siege. Others, to see which might well be spared, to afford timber and stone, for the repair of the wall. Others, to consider, what houses standing might hurt, or hinder; or be advantageous to the enemy; and which of them stood fit to be employed, and fortified for defense. And again, which might be set apart, for the receipt of those, whose houses were to be demolished, either without, or, within the city. And these, or some of these, might well be the occasion of this survey.

*{the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall*} Or, *Ye brake down* (as *ye made a ditch,* ver. 11.) *the houses,* (such of them as you thought good, or saw fitting) *to fortify the wall;* either by making use of the stone, and timber of them, to that purpose; or, because, joining upon the walls, as Rahabs did, Josh. 2.15. they could not well come to search, or make up the defects that were in the wall, without removal of them. Though there want not, that understand it, of such houses, as stood without the wall, in the suburbs, which are wont to be, on such occasions, demolished, that the enemy may not find harbor and shelter in them, with more safety, and security, to undermine, or assault. See Jer. 33.4.

**V. 11.** *{Ye made a ditch, also, between the two walls, for the water of the old pool*} For the better, and further, both security, and supply of the city: and that the enemy for want of water, might be the less able to maintain any long siege, 2 Chro. 32.3,4.

*{a ditch*} Heb. *a receptacle,* for confluence of waters, Gen. 1.9,10.

*{between the two walls*} Of which, See 2 Chro. 32.5. Jer. 39.4.

*{the old pool*} This seems to have been the upper pool, Chap. 7.2. & 36.2. from whence water was afterwards drawn to the lower, 2 Chro. 32.30. which was made long after, Neh. 3.16.

*{but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof; neither had respect to him, that fashioned it long ago*} Hitherto were the outward provisions they made, for the repelling of hostile assaults, and the safeguarding of themselves, and their city against them: which all so exactly, and precisely, in all circumstances, agreeing with the historical relation, concerning the courses taken by King Ezekiah, his princes, and the people assisting them, upon the expectation of Senacheribs coming with his forces, to besiege Jerusalem do clearly evince this prophecy to belong unto, and to concern his times. Nor were these preparations and provisions, of themselves, evil, or unwarrantable: Yea, it would have been a sin in them, and a tempting of God, to have neglected them. But here comes in their failing, in that, as Asa, in his sickness, sought unto physicians, and sought not unto God, 2 Chron. 16.12. so that they looked after these outward means, with a neglect of God; as if these means were sufficient to secure them and their city, without him, which yet by experience, afterward, they found, and acknowledged to be otherwise, Chap. 37.3. See Prov. 18.10,11. Howbeit, some of the Jewish interpreters, conceiving this prophecy to have reference; not unto the Assyrian, but to the Chaldean invasion, propound an objection, in the person of those that should then live; as if they might say to the prophet; Why do you tax us for the taking of such courses as these, for the safeguard of ourselves, and of our city? did not Ezekiah do the like? And this they suppose the prophet does, in way of anticipation, meet with in these words; as if he had said, It is true indeed, that Ezekiah did the same, that you do; as by the story of his times appears, 2 Chron. 32.3–5. But it it is added withal, that *he trusted in God,* 2 King. 18.5. which you, in Jehojakims, and Zedekiahs days, do not. But it is evident enough, as has been said, what times the prophecy belongs unto: and though Ezekiah trusted in God, yet might he have many hollow-hearted princes and officers, whereof Shebna was one, of whom, hereafter, in this chapter; nor might the people's hearts, for the main multitude of them, be so upright with God: beside, that Ezekiahs own faith somewhat faltered, when in such submiss manner, he sent to Sennacherib, and pillaged God's house, to pacify him, 2 King. 18.14–16.

*{looked unto*} Sought to, and relied upon, Psalm 34.5. Chap. 17.7,8.

*{the maker thereof*} As Chap. 45.18. or, *the doer thereof;* as Mal. 3.17. & 4.3. Heb. *makers,* or, *doers.* Which, because the word is in a plural form, the Jewish writers, some of them, understand it of David and Ezekiah; the one that took the fort of Zion, and built about it, 2 Sam. 5.8,9. the other, that made those conveyances for water, 2 King. 23.20. 2 Chron. 32.30. these they looked not after, to tread in their steps. But the plural form hinders not, but that the words may be, and indeed must be, understood of God. For the same word (whether to intimate a plurality of persons in the deity, or in way of excellency and eminency, I stand not now to dispute) is in the same form frequently used of God, Job 35.1. Psal. 149.2. Chap. 54.5. and though this be in a plural form, yet that in the next branch, spoken questionless, of the same party, is in a singular. The only doubt is, what the pronoun, rendered, *thereof,* or, *of it,* has reference unto. Some refer it to God, who in his secret counsel had disposed of these occurrents, and accordingly by the enemy, whoever he were, inflicted on them this judgment, Chap. 10.5,6. 2 King. 24.2. Others, to the pools, and waterworks, before mentioned; which God, by the careful provision of those kings, had furnished them with; the rather ascribed unto him, because fed much with rainwater, which is in Scripture, made his peculiar gift, Lev. 26.4. & 28.12. Chap. 30.23. Jer. 5.24. & 14.22. Joel 2.23. Zach. 10.1. Mat. 5.45. Others, lastly, which seems most probable, the city of Jerusalem, a type of his church, which he had settled, and made the seat of that kingdom, and the special place of his more solemn service and worship, Psal. 76.2. & 87.2. & 122.3–5. & 132.13,14. See Chap. 37.26.

*{that fashioned it*} Heb. *the potter of it:* or, *the framer of it:* he that fashioned, or framed it, as the potter does clay, or the like stuff, to make an earthen vessel of it, Chap. 64.8. Jer. 18.6. and God is said, here, either thus, to have framed, and fashioned, that is, devised, and produced the evil, that was befallen, or was to befall them; as the like phrase is used, Jer. 18.11. or, as to have *made,* so to have *framed* the city; to be the *maker,* and *framer,* or *fashioner* of the city; as elsewhere, the *maker,* & *fashioner,* or *framer* of that state, chap. 44.3.

*{long ago*} Heb. *from afar.* The word is used sometime of place; ver. 3. chap. 5.26. sometime, of time, chap. 25.1. Jer. 31.3. *long since,* as having reference to the first constituting, and settling of that city. See chap. 37.26. The Jewish doctors, some of them refer it to God's purpose, at the time of Creation, when he had Jerusalem, and his Temple there, in his head. Yea, their Talmudists run higher, and tell us here of *seven things that God framed before he created the world, the garden of Eden, the Law, the just ones, Israel, the Throne of glory, Jerusalem,* and *Messiah, the Son of David.* And this the prophet, if you please to afford credit to their fancies, had respect unto, in this place.

**V. 12.** *{And in that day did the Lord God of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth*} In the foregoing passages, was described the sedulity of one party, in making of preparations to withstand the enemy, when they perceived that he was bent to come and besiege them, and could not, by such rich presents, as their king had sent him, be diverted from that his purpose, 2 King. 18.15–17. 2 Chr. 32.2–5. together with their neglect of God, whom in the first place, they should have sought unto; as if with these provisions, they might do well enough without him. Now follows the security, and sensuality of another party among them, or it may be, also, the same; abandoning themselves unto all manner of mirth and jollity, riot, reveling and excess, as deeming themselves now sufficiently secured, by the courses they had taken, against any enemy whatsoever; and that in an open, and professed contempt of God, his messages and menaces, who by his prophets foretelling what evils hung over their heads, called upon them for humiliation, and repentance of their sins, and reformation of their lives, for the prevention, and aversion of the same. See ch. 5.11,12.

*{in that day*} At that time, either when this, or some other the like prophecy, was delivered, giving warning of such calamities, as would shortly, and suddenly befall them. For to some such prophetical sermon, or sermons, do their words in the next verse, relate: or, when they had dispatched those their forementioned designs, for the safeguard of the city, esteeming themselves now to be sufficiently secured against all occurrents that could be. So ver. 8. For I cannot concur with those, that make such a distraction between the branches of this prophecy; as if this calling upon them for humiliation, were not in regard of the evils then eminent; but in regard of those that had befallen them, in King Ahaz his time, 2 Chr. 28.5–8,17–20. Albeit, it may not amiss be said, that God did call upon them for humiliation and repentance, by those heavy things, that, about these times, befell their brethren of Israel, by Salmaneser, 2 King. 18.9–12. which they ought to have taken notice of, and to have taken to heart, Jer. 3.8–10. Amos 6.6. But in this place, the approach of their own calamities menaced, seems to be the *call* mentioned.

*{the Lord God of hosts*} As ch. 10.24.

*{call*} God is said to *call,* two ways: sometime, by way of operation, and execution; and so it is said, *he called for a famine,* Psal. 105.16. that is, he caused it; sometime, by injunction, and direction; and so here, when by his ministers, and messengers, giving warning of evils impendent, he requires means to be used, for the preventing of them, chap. 55.6,7. Zeph. 2.1,2. though there may be an allusion in the word here used, to the solemn proclaiming of a fast, which was usual with them, in times of danger, or distress, 2 Chron. 20.3. Joel 1.14. & 2.15. as implying, that there was just cause for them, so to do. But see an express *calling,* in those very times, by this prophet himself, hereunto, ch. 32.11.

*{to weeping, and mourning*} So Jer. 6.26. and 9.17–20. Joel 2.12,13.

*{to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth*} Signs of much grief and sorrow, ch. 3.24. & 15.2,3.

*{to baldness*} Either, by shaving the head, as Job 1.20. or, by tearing of the hair: as Ezr. 9.3. But it may be demanded, how God is said here to call for *baldness;* when as, elsewhere, he seems to forbid it, Levit. 19.27,28. & 21.5. Deut. 14.1. To this there are two answers given: 1. That it is forbidden to be done, upon private deceases, or departure of friends; not upon occasions of public lamentation, for calamities of like condition, Mic. 1.16. 2. That it is condemned, when it is done out of a desperate disposition, or out of impotency, and impatiency of spirit; not when it proceeds from a zealous and pious indignation against sin, as in Ezra, Ezr. 9.3. or from a spirit, surcharged with abundance of sincere contrition, and sanctified sorrow for sin, and God's wrath thereby incensed; as it ought to have been here.

*{sackcloth*} Heb. *sack:* as Chapter 20.2. See on Chapter 15.3.

**V. 13.** *{And behold*} Or, *But behold.* The copulative for the adversative, as Chap. 5.12. & 11.14. The direct contrary practice in this people, to that which God, by his judgments denounced against them, and ready to seize on them, did then call for: ushered in, not undeservedly, with a note of admiration; as from one astonished at their stupendous security, and horrible contempt of God, and his dreadful menaces; *Behold.* So ch. 5.7.

*{joy, and gladness*} Instead of *weeping, and mourning,* that God called for, ver. 12. abundance of mirth, or, nothing but mirth: two words of the same notion, implying an excess, or eminency of it. So ch. 35.10. & 51.3,11. Jer. 7.34. & 16.9.

*{slaying oxen, and killing sheep*} To feast, and make merry with, Amos 6.4.

*{sheep*} The word imports both sorts of lesser cattle, as well goats, as sheep, ch. 7.21.

*{eating flesh*} Which was not so ordinary with them, in those parts, among the meaner sort especially, save at invitations, and feasts, Gen. 18.7. Deut. 12.15,20. 1 Sam. 28.24. 2 Sam. 6.9. Luk. 15.23,27,29,30.

*{and drinking wine*} Reserved for feasts, and special occasions, Neh. 5.18. Est. 1.7. & 5.6. Eccles. 10.19. Amos 6.5. otherwise water was their ordinary drink, Gen. 21.14. & 24.17. Exod. 17.1–3. Deut. 2.6,28. Joh. 4.7–15.

*{eating, and drinking*} Feasting, and making merry together: as Job 1.4,18. but here, as Matth. 24.38. *they were eating and drinking;* the words imply a constant and continued practice, as if they did nothing else; minded nothing else; but addicted and abandoned themselves wholly to such riot and excess, without regard of aught beside. See ch. 5.11,12. Amos 6.4–6. and the phrase is here emphatical; the verbs running all in an infinitive form: as ch. 21.5. & 59.13. which yet some would have all to be conceived, in an imperative, or invitative notion; as those the like, chap. 21.5. And, indeed, so divers read and render this last branch; saying, *Let us eat and drink:* and so the ancient Greek has it, and the apostle from them, 1 Cor. 15.32. which if we admit, there must be a supply of the verb redoubled in the Hebrew: *Eating, let us eat; and drinking, let us drink;* that is, let us eat and drink freely: as where the word repeated, is expressed; *Eating, thou mayst eat,* that is, *thou mayst freely eat,* Gen. 2.16. See chap. 21.5. & 56.12. the word, *saying,* is oft wanting: as Psal. 105.14,15. Act. 7.32. and so ver. 14,15.

*{for to morrow we shall die*} Or, *we must die:* as it is rendered, 2 Sam. 14.14. Some understand them, as words of men in a desperate passion, making an account, that there is no way but one with them; that within a day, or two, they shall undoubtedly be swept, or snatched away, an enemy coming on them, whom they cannot escape; and that their best and wisest course therefore is, to enjoy themselves, and make use of that which they have, while they may, and have opportunity so to do. But I suppose it rather to be here, the speech of profane mockers, and scoffers, that believed nothing less, than what the prophet threatened them with, whose words they esteemed to be no other than wind, Jer. 5.12,13. 2 Pet. 3.3,4. (see ch. 5.18,19.) and speak therefore thus in mockery; The prophets say we must all die, and be destroyed ere long; let us take us pleasure therefore, while we have time for it: and it is the common language of loose and debauched persons; our life is short, and it will soon be gone, (not that they have any serious thought of their end, or aught that ensues it, which either they believe not, or have no list to think on) and let us be merry therefore while we may. So 1 Cor. 15.32. See Wisdom, 2.1–9. and see also, ch. 28.15.

**V. 14.** *{And it was revealed in mine ears by the Lord of hosts*} So some; as if the prophet should in these words meet with an objection, that some might make, against what he had charged them with; How do you know that we thus think, or say? why? God himself, says the prophet, has acquainted me with it, has revealed it unto me. So Jer. 11.18,19. or, *it was,* that is, this heavy doom that is now to be passed upon you, for this your vile impiety, and horrible profaneness, was revealed to me from God, it was uttered by him, in my hearing. The particle, *by,* is not indeed in the text; but it is oft in like manner supplied: as Psal. 44.2. Others, supposing that supply here needless, read the words as spoken in the person of God, and thus render them, *it is revealed in the ears of me the Lord of hosts;* that is, this your height of impiety and contempt of God, and his Word, is ascended up into heaven, and entered into his ears, and does cry to him for vengeance, as Gen. 4.10. & 18.20,21. & 19.13. 2 Chr. 28.9. Ezra 9.6. Jon. 1.2. But that which seems the genuine sense, and reading of the words, is this, *the Lord of hosts, did in my hearing reveal himself,* saying, as the words of the prophet, relating what God had revealed to him, concerning those lewd wretches, that thought thus to jest out God's judgments: *in mine ears:* for, in my hearing: as chap. 5.18. where see the like form of speech: *saying,* supplied: as ver. 13.

*{it was revealed*} Or, *he revealed himself:* for the passives are oft used in a reciprocal sense: so, *God was revealed,* that is, revealed, himself, *to Samuel,* 1 Sam. 3.21. and, *the King of Israel was revealed,* or *uncovered:* that is, revealed, uncovered, laid himself open, *as one of those vain fellows, is revealed,* or, *laid open,* that is, discovers, and lays himself open, *to his shame,* 2 Sam. 6.20.

*{the Lord of hosts*} See ch. 1.9.

*{Surely, this iniquity shall not be purged from you, till ye die*} A dreadful and direful doom, passed by God himself, upon these profane scoffers, and bound with an oath to make it irrevocable, that this high and hideous contempt, and contumely, offered by them to his Majesty, shall by no means be expiated; but that they shall without hope of mercy, be destroyed for it. See the like, 1 Sam. 3.14. Deut. 29.18–21. Matth. 12.32. Heb. 6.4–6. & 10.26–29.

*{Surely this iniquity shall not be*} Heb. *if this iniquity be,* etc. a concise form of an oath, frequent in Scripture. Of which see on chap. 5.18.

*{purged from you*} Heb. *propitiated to you,* or, *expiated for you:* and there is, as the rabbins suppose, an allusion in the word to the solemn day of *propitiations,* or *expiations,* Lev. 23.27,28. and the legal rites used, for expiation of delinquents, Lev. 4.20,26,35. & 16.30–33. intimating, say they, that no repentance, no prayer, no sacrifice, should serve or be available to expiate this sin, Num. 15.28–31. 1 Sam. 3.14. Heb. 6.6. & 10.28. 1 John 5.16.

*{till ye die*} Eternally, says the Chaldee: captivity shall not serve your turn; but you shall die by the sword of the enemy, says a Jewish doctor: but the former might befall them, as well as the later, Ch. 5.13,14. Amos 6.6,7. and the latter might be no less bitter than the former, Jer. 22.10. Lam. 4.9. the meaning is, that God's vengeance should pursue them, to their dying day, Psal. 140.11.

*{saith the Lord, the Lord of hosts*} I have said it, yea, have sworn it; (as Amos 6.8.) who am *the Lord, the Lord of hosts.* See Chap. 1.24.

**V. 15.** *{Thus saith the Lord God of hosts*} Or, *said,* to wit, at the same time, Chap. 8.11. ver. 14. For this prophecy concerning Shebna in particular, the displacing of him, and the substituting of Eliakim in his stead; seems to have been both delivered by God to the prophet, and by the prophet published at the same time with the former, concerning the state of those times in general.

*{Go, get thee unto this Treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say*} What this Shebna's carriage was, whereby he procured to himself the heavy doom here passed upon him of devestment and designment, to deportation and destruction, is nowhere expressed; only, the Jewish writers tell us, that he was one that complied, and had correspondency with the king of Assyria, and drew others into the same conspiracy with him, who should have betrayed the city into Sennacheribs hands; drawing hither those passages, which of him and his complices they expound, Chap. 8.6,12. But these relations are of little esteem, where there is nothing for them but their word. Certain it is, that he was a rotten-hearted man, and one that had much abused his power, and place, being, in likelihood, of mean parentage; and it may be, a stranger by descent. See ver. 16.

*{Go*} See Chap. 20.2.

*{get thee unto*} It may be questioned, Whether God's meaning were, that the prophet should repair unto Shebna's house, and there directly, by word of mouth, deliver him this message, as Nathan did to David, 2 Sam. 12.1. or, only so publish it, that Shebna might hear, or hear of it; as the apostle says, *say to Archippus,* that is, Let this be spoken to Archippus, let him take this as spoken in special to him, Col. 4.17. However, God's pleasure was, that this sad message should by some means be made known to him, and to others also, thereby to be warned of better and more upright carriage, in their places of trust and command.

*{this treasurer*} So most, both Jewish, and others, expound it, supposing that he had the oversight and custody of the king's moneys, provisions, and treasuries; because it comes of a word, that signifies, *to be profitable,* or, *useful,* Job 15.3. & 22.2. & 34.9. & 35.3. and from whence a term, that is used for *stores,* or, *provisions,* Exod. 1.11. 1 King. 9.19. 2 Chron. 8.4. & 16.4. & 17.12. & 32.28. There want not those that suppose some secret intimation of Shebna's corrupt carriage, wrapped up in the title here given him; as if it were said, the *money-man,* the man that meddles so much with money; or, that dangerous fellow; because the root it springs from, is deemed to import *danger,* Eccl. 10.9. and so the rabbins commonly use it, as in that common byword, *A knife in a child's hand is hazardous:* Which yet runs not so elegantly with us, as with them. But these I suppose but light and slight conjectures. I should rather incline to that which some of the rabbins suggest; that it was a name, not of the office he bare; (for his office comes after; and it is not usual to have a man in Scripture, described by two offices;) but of the place where he was born, which they affirm to be a town in Egypt, so termed, as some suppose, from one *Soches,* sometime king there, Plin. l. 36. c. 8. of whom the city was called *Sochen,* and from it Shebna born there, a *Sochenite:* and this some of ours seem not unwilling to admit. Howbeit, because I find little footing in Scripture, or story of credit for it; as also, for that names of Gentilism are of another stamp in Hebrew; and it should according to analogy, have been, not *Sochen,* but *Socheni:* as *Keni,* Judg. 4.17. and *Canaani,* Gen. 12.6. Therefore I waive it; and if in a point so dubious leave may be obtained, I shall make bold to add my conjecture: the word is nowhere found in a masculine form, save here only; but in a feminine form, it is found, 1 King. 1.2,4. where it signifies an *adjutress,* or, a *cherisher,* (for they can hardly be cleared from absurdity, that would make Abishag, Davids *She-treasurer,* and so there translate the word) in like manner may Shebna be here termed *this,* or *that co-adjutor:* but in way of irony; as importing what he professed to be to his sovereign, and what in regard of his place, he ought to have been; but implying withal: that in deed and truth, he was nothing less than what he professed, or pretended to be. See the like Psal. 55.13. Chap. 48.1,2. Rom. 2.19,20. So I should rather take it, than as some other, who (I suppose from the same ground) render it, *this adjutor;* and expound it, this favorer, and master of those profane varlets, before spoken of, ver. 13. or, as others, this *fomenter,* and *cherisher* of secret conspiracies, and compliances underhand with the enemy.

*{which is over the house*} Or, *high-steward.* By *house,* some of the rabbins, here, understand God's *house,* the Temple; called sometime, simply, the *house,* 1 King. 5.17,18. and hence gather, that Shebna was the High Priest; or, because no such name is found in the catalogue of High priests, some of them would have him to be one of those that had the charge of the temple-treasure; of which, 2 King. 18.15. 2 Chron. 32.28. Ezra 8.33. but other of them, and so the best approved writers, by *the house* here mentioned, understand *the house of David,* or, *the King's house;* to be over which, was one of the highest places in the kingdom. See Gen. 41.40. 1 King. 4.6. 2 King. 40.5. & 15.5. and this appears to be here meant by the office of Eliakim, his successor, described, ver. 21,22.

*{and say*} These words are not in the original; but are to be supplied: as the like oft, elsewhere, 1 Chr. 28.19. vers. 13. Chap. 18.2.

**V. 16.** *{What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here? that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulcher here, as he that heweth him out a sepulcher on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?*} The prophet is enjoined here to begin his message from God to Shebna, with a quick and tart expostulation, demanding of him what he means, being a stranger born, and a man come up of nothing, to hew him out such a stately monument for his corpse to be interred in, as if he were a man of great birth, and ancient descent, and made full account to enjoy his present dignities, so long as he lived, and to lay his bones there, when he died whereas God had determined to dispose far otherwise of him, to throw him down from his dignities, and to send him packing into a strange country, where he should die, far enough off from the place where he made account to be laid up, ver. 17–19.

*{what hast thou here?*} Or, as some render it, *what hast thou to do here?* as Psal. 50.16. Chap. 3.15. implying, say they, that he was unworthy of that high degree of honor, which, at present, he enjoyed, and should therefore be devested of it, and not retain it, till he died, as he hoped, and out of that hope, built him this monument: or, as others, rather, who retain the more received reading, implying, that, being an alien by birth, though in Ahaz his time, he had crept up under him, and so continued his greatness under Ezekiah, and was grown now so powerful, that the good king, though discovering his corrupt carriages, yet could not, or durst not wholly cast him off; yet he had no inheritance among God's people, nor lawful possession of land, but what might be redeemed, or, at the year of Jubilee, was to be released, Levit. 25.23–28.

*{and*} Or, *or,* rather: as Chap. 8.19. & 10.14.

*{whom hast thou here?*} Whom to help, or uphold you, says one of the Jewish commenters; but, as other of them rather, what brethren, or kindred? being a stranger born; which is also the more probable, because of the three courtiers sent by Ezekiah, to parley with Rabshakeh, the other two have their pedigree, or parentage mentioned; but of his there is no word, of his place in court only, ch. 36.3.

*{that thou hast hewn thee out a sepulcher here*} As if this were the place where your ancestors had lain before you, (for men of note had places of purpose set apart for the interment of them, and theirs, Gen. 23.4,6. & 9–20. & 46.29–31. & 50.13,25. Josh. 24.30,32,33. 2 Sam. 19.37. and were not buried in the common places of burial, Jer. 7.32. & 26.23.) and you made no doubt but here to die, and be entombed in the monument that here you have made you. Yet there are of the Jewish doctors, that by *sepulcher* here understand, not a burial-place, but a *palace;* but that conceit has no place here; and others of their own, therefore, therein justly control them. See further on the last clause.

*{here*} In the city of Jerusalem, the chief place of the kingdom; though I suppose those Jewish doctors overreach, who report that Shebna had made his sepulcher among those of the house of David, the kings of Judah, 1 King. 22.50. 2 King. 8.24. 2 Chron. 21.20. which honor yet we find, that Jehojada the High Priest obtained, 2 Chr. 24.16.

*{as he that heweth him a sepulcher on high*} Great men are wont, and that oft in their lifetime, to build them lofty and stately sepulchers, correspondent to their greatness. And such Shebna it seems would imitate; little deeming, or once dreaming, what is hereafter denounced of his dishonorable fall, and end; the note of similitude is not in the text, but is supposed to be so suppressed, that it ought to be supplied, by those, that thus read the words; and so it is indeed frequently elsewhere, see on Chap. 21.8. But the words may be read better, here, another way, without any such supply. *O he that heweth himself a sepulcher on high;* that is, *O thou that hewest thyself a sepulcher on high,* a change of the person, just like that of Bildad, Job 18.4. *O he, that teareth himself in his anger;* for, *thou that tearest thyself,* see on Chap. 21.14. *their bread.*

*{on high*} Aloft in some conspicuous and eminent place; as ch. 57.7.

*{and*} The copulative is not in the text, nor need be inserted.

*{that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock*} This some suppose to be spoken also by way of similitude, as well as the former. You hew you out a tomb, as one that were building him some strong and stately palace, to continue to all posterity, being founded on a rock, Ps. 49.11. Mat. 7.24,25. Others read the words by change of the person, as before, *thou that gravest thee out a dwelling place in a rock:* which some would expound of the sepulcher before mentioned. And of the Egyptians indeed it is reported, that they called, and accounted, their dwelling houses, their *inns;* their sepulchers, their *houses;* and their great men therefore built them more like palaces than places of burial: nor was it a thing unusual among the Jews, to hew them sepulchers out in rocks, Mat. 27.60. But we need not suppose the one put for the other, as well his mansion-house, as his monument, might be built on a rock, and the same rock: for their sepulchers were, usually, either within the walls of, or near adjacent unto their houses. See chap. 14.18. His affected magnificence, and ambitious humor of perpetuating the memorial of himself, as well by the one as the other, is commonly deemed here to be taxed: but his folly, I suppose, is principally aimed at, in making so full reckoning of that, wherein God was resolved directly to cross him, and to frustrate his designs. So Luk. 12.19,20.

*{in a rock*} *On high,* before for stateliness, as Jer. 22.23. *in a rock,* for firmness, as Mat. 16.18.

**V. 17.** *{Behold the Lord will carry thee away with a mighty captivity; and will surely cover thee*} Shebna's presumptuous folly, in being so confident of a firm, both seat and sepulcher was before tartly taxed. Now follows the doom of deprivation, and deportation, passed upon him by God, and discovering the vanity of these his insolent presumptions.

*{Behold*} A note requiring more than ordinary consideration, is prefixed, as to the relation of a strange and unexpected alteration. So Ps. 37.36. & 52.7. chap. 17.14.

*{the Lord*} You intend one thing, but God purposes another: so Luk. 12.19,20. You make account to live always in Jerusalem, and there to die: but God intends shortly and suddenly to remove you from thence, and to send you far away, to end your days elsewhere, ver. 18.

*{will carry thee away, with a mighty captivity*} Heb. *is casting,* or, *throwing thee out,* as Ch. 3.1. *with the casting,* or, *throwing out of a man;* or, *is casting thee out with casting, O man;* or, *O thou mighty man;* for so the word properly signifies. See on Chap. 2.9. & Jer. 31.22. which they expound, either God will cast you out in such a violent manner, as a man of might and strength is wont to throw aught away from him; or, he will cause you to be carried away captive, with such a captivity as men use to be captived with, who are carried away farther commonly than women, and are wont to have less favor and mercy shown them, than that weaker sex oft has; or, because the former noun of *casting,* or, *throwing,* is absolute, and should not therefore be conjoined with the word *man,* from which the point of distinction also withholds it: the genuine sense seems to be this. The Lord is preparing suddenly and speedily to throw you out of your offices, house, and place of abode, in a violent manner, (that the repetition, or reduplication of the same notion, in the noun annexed to the verb, commonly imports, as Psal. 53.5. & 76.5. Chap. 24.22. & Zech. 1.14.) *O thou mighty man,* (as Job 38.3. & 48.7.) you that are so high and powerful in your own conceit and apprehension: so Ps. 52.1. where the word deduced from this, and of near affinity to it, is used: or, *O man,* simply, and so the Italian renders it; *Behold O man:* as men use to speak to those whom they set light by, as not deigning to give them their name. And somewhat like hereunto is that of the apostle; *Thinkest thou, O man?* and, *who art thou, O man?* Rom. 2.3. & 9.20. But that sounds not so well, without such a trajection as the text has not; which seems to have put it off, as a more emphatical compellation, to the close of the sentence. The vulgar Latin renders it, *God will carry thee away as a cock is carried.* Whereupon a learned interpreter says, he wonders whence this *cock* flew into the text. But the answer is ready: It was by Jeromes overmuch credulity, in giving credit to his Hebrew-master, who told him, that *Gaber* here signified not a *man,* but a *cock.* And indeed so the Talmudists are said frequently to use it. And so some of the Jewish commenters in this place expound it; as if God threatened to drive him away like a cock, that is driven from place to place by the puttock: or to carry him away, as a cock, or capon, is by the countryman carried to the market, with his wings and legs tied together: a fit emblem of a captive, says a Popish writer, to set some fair gloss on this their absurd translation, which yet must not be refused, since the Pope has set his stamp upon it; though it be confessed, that the author of it was herein gulled by the Jew. But contrary to all this that has been spoken, concerning the sense of the place, some late interpreters, of no small note, understand it, as relating, not what God would do with Shebna, but what he had done for him: For they read and render the words thus, *God that covereth thee with a covering, as much as may be for a man;* or, (because the article is absent) *God covereth thee with a covering* (and because the word is in an absolute form) *even with the covering of a man:* that is, God, who now arrays you with most gorgeous apparel; for rich and goodly apparel is an ensign of honor, Gen. 41.42. Est. 8.9–11. Dan. 5.29. Mat. 11.8. and Shebna was in likelihood the second man in the state, as Joseph next Pharaoh, Gen. 41.40. The ground they give for this interpretation, is, because the word here used does, as they suppose, though in another form, signify *to cover,* Neh. 3.15. Where it is said, *the gate of the fountain he built, and covered it.* Whence also the dew has its name in Hebrew, because it covers the ground, Judg. 6.40. and though the word in the Hebrew be not so usual, yet it is found in the Syriac of Daniel, where it is said, *the beasts had covert,* or, *shade, under it,* Dan. 4.11. and both in the Chaldee paraphrase of the Old Testament, and the Syriac version of the New, the same word is used for *to cover,* and *to shadow,* Ex. 40.21. 1 King. 6.9. Ps. 80.10. Mat. 17.5. Luk. 1.35. But it is well observed, that the words used, in the most of, if not all these places, may well come from another root, that signifies a *shadow:* nor is any place produced, wherein it is found applied to *apparel.* The single word therefore, being so commonly used, for *casting,* or *throwing,* 1 Sam. 18.11. & Ps. 29.33. Job 41.9. Ezek. 32.4. Jon. 1.4,5,12,16. I see not why it should not in the doubled form retain the same sense; or, why it should not be so taken in this place, when as it suits so well with the main scope of the place; and the single word is there found used, where the same judgment is denounced, wherewith Shebna is here threatened, ver. 18. Jer. 16.13. & 22.26,28.

*{and will surely cover thee*} Heb. *and is in covering, covering thee.* The repetition, has ordinarily, an implication, either of certainty, or of eminency, vehemency, and the like; so before, and again, ver. 18. This also, those latter interpreters expound as the former, of God's conferring honor and dignities upon Shebna; rendering the words, *and doth clothing, clothe thee:* that is, does fairly, or gorgeously clothe you. And they have the more colorable ground for this their exposition here, because this word indeed is sometime found used of *putting on apparel,* 1 Sam. 28.14. Psal. 104.2. & 109.19. Chap. 59.17. & 61.3,10. But there seems no reason of weight appearing, that should necessarily force us out of the way of denunciation, which the prophet all along here, is commonly deemed to insist in. Some therefore read it, *he will wrap thee up.* So one of the Jewish writers also; because the word is supposed, sometime, so to signify, see Jer. 43.12. and a man may be said, to be wrapped up in his garments, as wares are wrapped up, in those things wherewith they are covered. See on Chap. 3.12. but it is taken, as they imagine, from those that intending to cast a garment, or some other loose thing away from them, are wont to wrap it up, hard, and round, that they may fling it the further. But that notion seems rather to be implied, in the branch following, ver. 18. Others therefore expound it, *he will chase thee far away,* into captivity, like a bird. So another of the Jewish commenters supposing the word to have a notion of flight in it, as indeed sometime it has, 1 Sam. 15.21. & 25.14. *the people flew upon the prey;* and *our master flew upon them,* for so the words there are; but then it has reference to another root, as another of them, controlling this exposition, well observes. Others again render it, *he will surely,* or, *to the purpose, cover thee,* with shame and confusion, instead of that honor you now enjoy, and make full account still to retain; and so much indeed the word imports, where those terms are expressed: as Psal. 89.45. & 109.29. but so it is not here. The received reading therefore, without any addition, does well: the only doubt is, what *covering* is here intended, or alluded unto. And here some would have it to be, the covering enjoined the leper, Lev. 13.45. hence gathering that Shebna should be smitten with leprosy, as Moses his sister, Numb. 12.10. Gehazi, 2 King. 5.27. and Urijah were, 2 King. 26.19. And such a tradition some of the rabbins tell us here that the Jews have. But of this there is no great probability. Others therefore refer it rather to such a *covering,* as persons fallen into disgrace, surcharged with shame, or sorrow, carried into captivity; or condemned unto death, were wont to have their faces covered with, as unworthy to see the light. See 2 Sam. 15.30. Est. 7.8. Job 9.24. Ezek. 12.6,12.

**V. 18.** *{He will surely turn, and toss thee, like a ball into a large country*} Heb. *he will wrapping, wrap thee up, with a wrapping.* There is a reduplication of the verb, as in the latter branch of the verse next before going; and to that an addition of a noun of the same notion, as in the former branch of the same verse; a defect of the particle *with* here, as there; and Chap. 21.7. The words may well be rendered, *He will surely,* or, *straitly wrap thee up, and toss thee like a ball.* The same word oft-times comprehends a twofold notion, as *take,* for, *take, and bring,* Gen. 27.9. *receive,* for *receive and give,* Psal. 68.18. with Eph. 4.8. so here, *wrap up, like a ball,* for, *wrap up,* and toss, or throw like a *ball, into a spacious land.* Heb. *a land large of hands,* or, *spaces,* as Psal. 104.25. Chap. 33.21. He will be sure to send you far away from the place of your present abode. An allusion to something made up round like a ball, or to a ball itself, that being tossed, or thrown, with more than ordinary stress, from a strong hand, into a spacious plain, where there is nothing to stay it, runs on an end forward, without interruption, or intermission, until either the force fail that it was thrown with, through the great length of the way, or it arrive at the land's end.

*{turn, and toss*} The word, though repeated in a twofold form, is but one; and it is nowhere else found, but here, and Lev. 16.4. where it is used of the linen *miter,* or, *turban,* wherewith the High Priest was to be attired; so termed, either because it was wound up, with many wreaths, as the Turkish and Persian turbans are at this day. Or, because the head of him that wore it, was therewith enwrapped. See chap. 3.23. and 62.3. Now because the word has so near affinity with such a kind of head-tire, as was used most by kings, priests, and persons of prime note, and place, some conceive a bitter taunt, to be closely couched in it; as if by it, the prophet had said, God will *attire thee,* or, *crown thee* (as the old Latin also renders it) with a witness; with another manner of attire, than that you now wear; he will wrap you up, in a bundle or fardel of miseries; and environ you with troubles, instead of a head-band of state. As on the contrary, God is said to *encompass* the godly with favor, loving-kindness, and mercies, as with a crown; or, the like head-band of state, Ps. 5.12. & 103.4. for so the word also there used, imports. Again, some of the Jewish writers, upon the same ground suppose it to be implied, that all his treasure, and honor, shall be packed up together with him, and so he, and they, both thrown out, or sent away together. But that seems not to sort so well with the subject matter intended; it is more likely, that he was first stripped of all, and then carried or sent bare enough into a foreign country.

*{as a ball*} A defect of the note of similitude: as ch. 13.8. & 21.8. the word is nowhere in Scripture found in this sense; though frequent with the Talmudists. Yet there are, that suppose no such defect; for that the word *dur* alone, signifies a *ball,* or, a *bowl;* and that in the Arabic it is frequently so used. See ch. 29.3.

*{into a large country*} What country this was, that Shebna was either carried captive, or exiled, and confined unto, or upon discovery of his evil carriages, and deposition from his dignities, should flee, and retire himself, for shelter, is not certain. The Jewish writers, some of them say, it was Cassiphia, Ezr. 8.17. some, Nineveh, in Assyria; some, Babylon; and this last, some of ours suppose not to be improbable: Yet, not imagining, as they, that he could be carried captive, in the Chaldean invasion, first, or last, under Nebuchad-nezzar; (for he must needs be dead long before) but that together with Manasses, surviving Ezekiah, he might be thither carried by the Assyrians under Esar-haddon, 2 Chr. 33.11.

*{there shalt thou die*} Not at Jerusalem, where you have hewn out your sepulcher, ver. 16. as you made account to do, when you so did. The Talmudists tell us, that this Shebna, with some others, made a defection to Sennacherib; by whom, after the slaughter made by the angel, in his camp, they were carried away, in much displeasure into his own country, where, after some despiteful usage, he put many of them to death: and this may be as true as what other of them say, that with Jehojakim, or Jehojachin, (and why not, as well Zedekiah?) he was by Nebuchadnezzar carried to Babel: or, what others, not that he died indeed abroad, but that being sequestered for his leprosy, he was *as a dead man;* as of Miriam, or Mary, (for the names are the same, Luk. 1.16.) it is said in the like case, Num. 12.12. yet after being recovered, he returned to the city, though not to his former office, and dignity again, now conferred upon another.

*{and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy Lord's house*} Some of the rabbins on this place, out of their Talmudic stories, tell us another story of Shebna, somewhat differing from the former; that when Shebna came alone to the Assyrians camp, and they asked him, where the rest of his conspirators were, he told them, that they were revolted again, and so had deserted him: whereupon they laid hold on him in a rage, and having bored through his feet, they dragged him, fastened to horse-tails, over brambles and briers: and that this is that, which the prophet foretells him here, of the stately chariots, that there he expected to have. But this may well go among the rest of their fondly-forged figments. Other of them more serious, expound the words thus, Your stately chariots, that are now your glory, shall be turned into shame, and ignominy, because you are the shame of your Lord's house; and so in him, say they, was fulfilled, what our masters say, *He that seeks the shame of his Master's house, his honor shall be turned into shame:* or, as other of them, whom many of ours also concur with, keeping closer to the text; *and there shall thy glorious chariots,* all your state and pomp, that you now glory in, die, that is, cease, and come to an end, O you that are *the shame of thy Lord's house.*

*{the chariots of thy glory*} Or rather, *thy chariots of glory;* that is, *thy glorious chariots:* your chariots of state, which as a great man, you ride in, up and down, through the city. So *thy Throne of glory,* for *thy glorious throne,* Jer. 14.21. and, *his eyes of glory,* for, *his glorious eyes,* ch. 3.8. *his chariots,* both his power and pomp: for *chariots* denote either, Gen. 41.43. 2 King. 9.25. & 10.15. Josh. 17.18. Judg. 4.3. 2 King. 2.12. & 13.14.

*{shall be*} Or, rather, *shall die:* supplied out of the former branch: as Job 16.21. & 22.24. & 23.6.

*{shall be the shame of thy Lord's house*} According to this reading, the meaning should be, that the honor conferred by the king upon Shebna, being such an one, as he was, should in fine, prove a dishonor to his Lord, and to his house over which he had placed him. But the old Latin reads it, inserting a copulative, instead of the verb substantive, *and the shame of thy Lord's house.* Which some following expound the whole sentence thus, *There shalt thou die; and there* also *thy chariots* with you; *and the shame of thy Lord's house,* to wit, shall also then cease, you being thrown out of it, whose honor was a disgrace to it, and a better man being set up in your stead, by whom it may recover its wonted honor again. But the proper sense of the place, seems to be that above, *O thou the shame of thy Lord's house:* you that by your corrupt courses, are a foul blemish to your master's honor, and a disgrace to his house, Ps. 12.8. & 101.4–7. Prov. 28.12,28. & 29.2. Eccl. 10.5,6.

**V. 19.** *{And I will drive thee from thy station*} The prophet speaks here, as in the person of God: in regard whereof, some render it, *For I will,* says he, as (looking back to vers. 15.) drive you from your station: and the copulative, is, indeed, put sometime for the causative: as Gen. 12.1. & Exod. 14.19. for the places are parallel, and should be rendered alike.

*{drive thee from thy station*} Depose you from your dignity; thrust you out of your office, wherein you think, that you stand so fast: you suppose yourself so surely seated, that you cannot be stirred. But *they cannot stand,* whom *God drives,* Jer. 46.14,15. there is in the word *station,* a notion of firm settling, and consisting, whence a *pillar* has its name: notwithstanding which, as he conceived it, God tells him, that he would not move him only, but remove him, as the like is threatened Queen *Huzzab,* that though her name imported the same, yet she should be removed, she should be carried away captive, Nah. 2.7.

*{and from thy state he shall pull thee down*} The same thing repeated in other terms: *from thy state,* that is, your *office:* as 1 Chr. 23.28. 2 Chr. 35.15. or, *standing:* as the word properly signifies. Whence a *pillar,* also has another name. Now because the person is in this latter branch, changed from the first to the third; the prophet speaking before, as in the person of God, now as himself, speaking of God; some read the words, saying, *from thy station shall he pull thee down:* and expound it, *he,* that is, the king, who before advanced you, shall by my appointment put you down: and this they suppose, was in part done, when of High Steward, he was made scribe, or secretary, which was a far inferior place, chap. 36.3. And it is true, that the word *saith,* or, *saying,* is oft necessarily supplied: as ver. 13,15. Job 8.18. & 9.20. But there is no such need here: and they wrong the text, by omitting the copulative, which is of use here. Others therefore say, *he,* that is, *God:* he will do it, whether your Lord the king do it, or no: Levit. 20.4,5. So Psal. 52.5. and, says one of the rabbins it is *he will,* for, *I will, pull thee down:* one person for another, as is the manner of Scripture in many places, 1 Sam. 6.4. 1 King. 22.28. Job 17.10. and this God did, says another, by smiting him with leprosy, as he did Uzziah, and so enforcing him to leave his place, 2 Chron. 26.19–21. But of that before: nor need we stand here, to inquire, who should do it, though whosoever were the instruments, it is sure that God did it; and no less sure, that it should be done; that which only seems here to be intimated: for the verb may well be taken indefinitely; *he will pull thee down;* that is, *thou shalt be pulled down. I will drive thee from thy station, and thou shalt be pulled down from thy standing.* I will do it; and it is therefore sure to be done, Ps. 115.3. & 135.6. Dan. 4.35,37. Of this indefinite use, see on ch. 2.19. & 17.13. ver. 8.

**V. 20.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah*} Hitherto was the deposition and deportation of Shebna. Now follows the substitution of Eliakim in his stead: after the devesting of the one, the investing of the other.

*{it shall come to pass*} Heb. *it shall be:* as chap. 2.2. & 3.24. & 7.21.

*{in that day*} At that time, ch. 2.20. & 4.1,2.

*{that I will call*} Heb. *and I will call:* as chap. 16.12. he shall not intrude himself into your place; but shall be called by God to it. So chap. 42.6. & 48.15. Rom. 1.1. Heb. 5.4. that which God does sometime immediately, as by word of mouth, or inward motion of spirit, Exod. 31.2,6,25. ch. 6.8,9. Jer. 1.5,7. Matth. 4.18,21. & 9.9. Gal. 1.1. sometime mediately, and so ordinarily, by the ministry of man, Exod. 16.18. & 11.14,15. Act. 6.3,6. & 13.3,3. and thus, in likelihood, was Eliakim called to this office, advanced thereunto by Ezekiah. Nor amiss, therefore does one of the rabbins here paraphrase it; I will put it into the heart of Ezekiah, to put him into your place. Who yet, I suppose, was mistaken; supposing great princes, to be termed *called ones,* when it is rather *renowned ones,* Ezek. 23.23. more likely so, Num. 1.16. & 16.2. & 26.9. but the word there does a little vary, and is doubtful too; and by most, rendered the other way.

*{my servant*} Not in general; or, at large, as are all men; yea, all things, Psal. 119.91. but in a more special manner, as one designed to do him and his people special service, in that place, which Shebna formerly had held. So Num. 12.7. Psal. 78.70. Phil. 1.1. Tit. 1.1.

*{Eliakim*} See 2 King. 18.18,26,37. chap. 36.3. & 37.2. the name well suits with the person. For Eliakim imports one *raised,* or *settled, by God:* as *Jehojakim,* also, does the same. See Jer. 22.18.

*{the son of Hilkiah*} This is added, to distinguish him from others, that might be in those times of the same name. For the name Eliakim was among that people, not unusual, as may appear, 2 King. 23.34. 2 Chron. 36.4. Nehem. 12.41. Matth. 1.13. Luk. 3.30. and it may well be also, because his father *Hilkiah,* was a man of some note.

*{Hilkiah*} Heb. *Hilkijahu;* as *Hannibal:* or, *Chilkijahu;* as *Charran,* Act. 7.2. Of the form, see on Chap. 1.1. there are divers other found in Scripture of the same name, 1 Chr. 26.11. Neh. 8.4. among the rest, the High Priest, in Josiahs reign, 1 Chr. 6.13. 2 Chr. 34.9. Ezr. 7.1. and Jeremy the prophet's father, Jer. 1.1. The word signifies, *God's portion.*

**V. 21.** *{And I will clothe him with thy robe*} God by the prophet directs his speech still to Shebna, into whose office Eliakim was to succeed (as the promise, or prediction of the saving seed is directed, not to the woman, but to the Devil, whom it was to destroy, Gen. 3.15. Heb. 2.14.) to vex him the more; ambitious persons hating such as are to succeed them; especially when to be deposed from their high and great places; and not enduring to hear the name of a successor. See 2 Sam. 19.13. & 20.9,10.

*{thy robe*} Or, *coat:* as Gen. 37.3,31,32. such a rich and goodly robe, or coat, as you now wear, correspondent to your place. So Gen. 41.42. Est. 6.8. & 8.15. Dan. 5.29. See on ver. 17.

*{and strengthen him with thy girdle*} I will give him that power and authority, that you now have: or, I will not only put him in your place, but I will confirm him also, and strengthen him in it, ver. 23. The *girdle,* and emblem of power. See chap. 11.5. & 23.10. & 45.1,5. Prov. 31.17. Though an allusion, as some not improbably conjecture, to such rich, as robes before; so girdling here; as great men used to wear; Exod. 28.39,40. Rev. 1.13. Howbeit, I suppose they go too far, who, because special mention is made of Aarons *robe,* or, *coat* rather, (for so the word properly signifies, both here, and there) and *girdle,* or *belt,* Exod. 28.4,39. would hence infer, that Shebna now was, and Eliakim was to be, High Priest; substituted in his place by Ezekiah, as Zadok, in the place of Abiathar by Solomon, 1 King. 2.27,35. But of this, see on ver. 15.

*{girdle*} Or, *belt.* Which may well be deemed to come from thence, by no unusual change of a letter; it is so called in Hebrew; because the *belly* is girt in with it.

*{and I will commit thy government into his hand*} Heb. *I will give:* as Job 9.24. This we find effected afterward in the story. For as Shebna is said to have been *over the house* here, ver. 15. so is Eliakim said to be afterward in that office, 2 King. 18.18. chap. 36.3. & 37.2. God, say the Jewish writers, revealed his treacheries and covert carriage, to Esay; by Esay to Ezekiah, who thereupon put him beside his place; and placed Eliakim therein.

*{in his hand*} Or, *hands;* for the word is collective: as Prov. 31.20. a metaphor from a coachman, or chariot-man, in whose hands the reins are, that guide and rule the horses that draw in the chariot, or coach, Jam. 3.3. or, from a pilot, that sitting at the stern, with the helm in his hand, thereby steers the ship which way he pleases, Jam. 3.2. So Ps. 78.72.

*{and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah*} Heb. *for a father;* that is, *a father,* simply: as Gen. 17.4. or, *instead of a father;* as a father, Judg. 17.10. & 18.19. 2 Sam. 7.14. As in regard of his command, and the eminency of his place; as all rulers are styled *Fathers,* Exod. 20.12. Num. 36.1. 2 King. 5.13. so more especially, in regard of his fatherly care of them, and tender affection towards them: a fit title for a good governor. See 2 Sam. 23.17. & 24.17. 2 Chr. 30.18,22. Neh. 2.10. & 5.8,13–19. The Persians used to say, of three of their kings, that *Darius* was a *trader, Cambises,* a *master, Cyrus,* a *father:* Herodote, lib. 3. But they strain the style here too far, who would hence infer, that he must needs be High Priest. For who else should be *father,* say they, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, but either the High Priest, or the king? For they might have considered, what the rabbin on this place suggests; to wit, Josephs speech of himself, that *God had made him a father to Pharaoh, and Lord of all his house, and a Ruler throughout all the land of Egypt,* Gen. 45.8. See Ps. 105.20,21.
