The words yet show, as those of Joseph, that the power of the place was not confined to the family, or household servants only: but was extended also unto other the king's subjects. See 2 King. 15.5. Of *Jerusalem* and *Judah,* see on ch. 1.1.

*{inhabitants*} Heb. *inhabitant:* as ch. 5.3.

*{the house of Judah*} As, *the house of Jacob,* ch. 2.5. and, *the house of Israel,* or *the house of Judah,* Jer. 5.11. & 11.10,17. not to the king's house only, but to the whole body of the people, that were as one joint family: so all the faithful make one family, Gal. 6.10. Eph. 2.19. & 3.14,15.

**V. 22.** *{And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder*} Hence it appears, that Eliakim now, as Shebna before, was to be controller, or High Steward of the king's house, as one of the Jewish commenters on this place, well observes: and not High Priest, as some other of them groundlessly affirm, whom yet some of ours follow: and much less one that bore both offices: which yet the Chaldee paraphrast asserts. It is as if he had said, I will commit unto him, the whole charge and government of the king's house: so as there shall not be done anything there, in one kind, or other, without him: nor shall any control him in what he does, Gen. 41.41,44. Ps. 105.21,22.

*{the key*} An emblem of power and authority, because none can come into a place, or go out, without the will and leave of him, that has the command of the key: and when a man therefore comes to take possession of a house, the key is wont to be given him. When rendition of a city, town, or castle, is made, the keys are commonly delivered. See Matth. 16.19. Rev. 1.18. & 3.7. & 9.1. & 20.1,2. *key,* collectively, for *keys,* Matth. 16.19. as after, *shoulder,* for *shoulders.* Some suppose, that the party who bore this office, either carried a key himself; or, had one of gold carried by some other before him, as maces before some in high place at court, are with us. Others, that he had the figure of a key woven into, or fastened unto, or embroidered upon his upper garment, as an ensign of his office. But these are but surmises, and groundless conjectures.

*{of the house of David*} See on chap. 7.2.

*{will I lay*} Or, *put.* Heb. *give:* as ver. 21. Jer. 23.40. Ezek. 37.7,14,17.

*{upon his shoulders*} See on ch. 9.6.

*{so he shall open, and none shall shut, and he shall shut, and none shall open*} The effect of this his authority in the execution of his place. Heb. *and he shall,* etc. which may well be rendered *that he may open,* or, *so that he shall open, and none shall shut,* etc. as chap. 10.19. & 11.3. & 19.12. A form of speech borrowed from the office of those, who having the keys of city, or castle, committed unto them, the gates thereof cannot be opened, or shut, without their direction, and special order from them. The meaning is, that he shall have power to dispose of matters, for the government of the royal palace, and execution of jurisdiction, appertaining to his place, without let, and restraint, or power in any other to reverse what he does. So Rev. 3.7. Job 12.14. and the like in some kind, Mat. 16.19. & 18.18. The rabbins gloss falls short, who expounds it, that he shall be of counsel to Ezekiah, who should do nothing without, or, but by his advice. For the place that Eliakim was to possess, was an office distinct from the place of a counselor. See 2 Chro. 26.21.

**V. 23.** *{And I will fasten him as a nail, in a sure place*} To the power of executing what belonged unto his place, (lest the due, and impartial execution of his duty therein, might prove prejudicial unto him) God further here promises such an establishment of him in it, that he should be sure to sit fast; and be able, not only to discharge his place, so as should be both for the king's honor, and the public welfare; but to support also those inferior offices, whether strangers, or of kin to him, that should have dependence upon him; contrary to that, which of Shebna is threatened, ver. 25.

*{as a nail*} The note of similitude is supposed to be wanting, as Job 11.12. Psal. 11.1. ch. 21.8. Yet I suppose the text may well be rendered without it; *I will fasten him a nail,* or, *a pin, in a firm place:* as, *to give us a nail,* or, *a pin in his holy place,* Ezr. 9.8. Because the verb *fasten,* here used, is sometime applied to the *pitching* of tents, Gen. 31.25. Some interpreters therefore would have this word rendered, not a *nail,* but a *stake:* supposing such a *stake,* or *post,* here intended, as being pight in the midst of a tent; besides that many necessaries may be hanged on it, supports the whole pavilion. True it is, that the word is also oft found used about tents; but it then signifies not such a *post* or *stake,* as supports it; but such an iron *nail,* or wooden *pin,* or short *stake,* (if you please so to term it) as the cords of a tent are wont to be fastened unto, chap. 33.20. & 54.2. as appears by the story of Jael, Judg. 4.21,22. & 5.26. But here the allusion is rather to such a nail, or, pin, as is fastened somewhere about the house in the wall, to hang such utensils upon, as are of ordinary use in the house; that they may not be cast about, and so wronged; but may there be safe out of harm's way, as we say, and at hand, when occasion is to make use of them, Ezek. 15.3.

*{in a sure place*} That he may not be, either shaken, or wrenched out of it, Eccl. 12.11. as you shall be, ver. 25. Heb. *in a faithful place,* Num. 12.7. 1 Sam. 2.35. such a place, as will not fail, but hold fast; as a faithful man, one that fails not the trust reposed in him; but is true and firm to them that confide in him, Deut. 7.9. Prov. 14.5. & 25.13. Prov. 31.11. One of the Hebrew commenters supposes a trajection in the words, which he would have therefore to be thus read, or rendered, *I will fasten him a sure nail in the place.* But, besides that the genders agree not, (for the one is masculine, the other feminine; and the Hebrew points carry the construction the other way: (the repetition of the same form of speech, ver. 25. does evidently refute it. See Zach. 10.4.

*{and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house*} As you were a shame to your Lord's house; so shall he be a grace, and an honor, not to his Lord's house alone: but to his father's house too.

*{for a glorious throne*} That is, *as a glorious throne:* or simply; *a glorious throne:* as, *for a father,* ver. 22. *for a glorious crown,* and, *for a goodly diadem,* ch. 28.5. Heb. *a throne of glory:* as 1 Sam. 2.8. Jer. 17.12. Some would have it read, *to the throne a glory:* understanding it of the king's throne, and consequently, of the king: that he should be an honor to him, by whom he had been to that height of honor advanced. But the points in the original, and frame of the context, will not easily admit it.

*{to his father's house*} His prudent and upright carriage shall make his whole stock and kindred, the whole family he came of, honorable, as was Josephs the like to his, Gen. 47.5,6,11. Some extend the word *family* here, to the whole tribe of Judah, called *the house of Judah,* ver. 21. but the term here used, seems narrower here, than that there: and the words following, run rather the former way.

**V. 24.** *{And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring, and the issue*} All his kindred and allies, with their issue, as well small as great, shall partake of his honor, in one employment, or other. So I rather take it, than, as some other, who expound it of the general care, that Eliakim should have in the execution of his office, of doing right to, and relieving, as well the mean, as the mighty, Exod. 23.2. Deut. 16.18,17. 2 Chr. 19.6,7. Ps. 72.2,4,13,14. & 82.3,4.

*{they shall hang upon him*} *they shall hang;* that is, there shall be hanged, as things are wont to be hanged on a pin, or nail; (for the verb is here taken indefinitely: See ver. 19.) *upon him;* or, *upon it:* in allusion to the *nail,* or *pin,* before mentioned, ver. 23. they shall have, all of them, dependence upon him.

*{all the glory of his father's house*} Either the whole family, which by his means should become honorable. See Chap. 4.5. or, those among them, that are of some note, otherwise, for wealth, wisdom, or the like; as ch. 10.16,18. opposed to the *little ones,* afterward mentioned.

*{the offspring, and the issue*} The former of these words, signifies properly, *plants,* that grow up out of the ground, chap. 34.1. & 42.5. or, *branches,* that sprout, or spring out from a root, stock, or stem, ch. 44.3,4. and in the next place, *children,* or *issue,* Job 5.25. & 21.8. & 27.14. & 31.8. chap. 61.9. & 65.23. so called, because they issue, and proceed from the bowels of their parents, of those, that breed and bear them, chap. 48.19. The latter in this sense, nowhere else found; but used for *excrements,* Ezek. 4.15. is deemed to come from a root of the same notion with the former; from whence also are words derived, that signify the same thing, ch. 4.4. Ezek. 4.12. so termed also, because they come out of man's body, Deut. 23.14. but this latter root seems to imply a more abundant issue, flowing out, as *streams* of water, from a fountain; because it has near affinity with another term, that signifies such *abundance,* Deut. 33.19. Job 22.11. chap. 60.6. And because the former word is of a masculine form, the latter of a feminine, some of the Jewish writers understand thereby, *sons and daughters,* and because it was before said, that he should be as a *father to the house of Judah,* ver. 21. some of them would have the people to be reputed, here, as his children; the men, his sons; and the women, his daughters: but of that formerly. Other of them, with the Chaldee paraphrast, understand *sons, and sons' sons,* or *nephews,* as that name properly signifies. But these are by other of them, not improbably, deemed niceties; supposing both words to signify (as our prophet's manner is, to use oft variety of terms) but one and the same thing. For, as for that which a learned late writer surmises, that these two should be the names of the keys, that Eliakim should have the command of; the former, of the *foregate,* by which they went in and out, of the word, that signifies *to go out:* the other, of the *back-gate,* by which they went to the backside; because of that use of the word, Ezek. 4.15. it is a conceit, so far fetched, and so improbable, that it is strange how it should enter once into any judicious man's brains.

*{all vessels of small quantity*} The prophet proceeds in the forementioned metaphor, of *nails,* or *pins,* on which, *vessels,* instruments, and utensils, eared ones especially, as flagons, pots, cups, and the like, are wont to be hanged: and it may be deemed, that the copulative should here be supplied, which is oft omitted, as chap. 21.5. ver. 6. *and all vessels,* (or, *utensils:* for the word is of a very large extent) *of a small* size, as some, *of little,* or, *less,* use, as others: for the word is here put substantively: as Gen. 44.20. 2 Chr. 34.30. and I suppose also comparatively: as Gen. 27.15,42. And so this branch will not unfitly answer the former: he shall support, and bear up, with honor and credit, not those alone of his stock, that are persons of note, and parts, fit for more honorable employments, together with those, that are of their issue, and partake therefore with them, in their honors: but even those also of them, that are of meaner parts, and less esteem, who yet, in regard of their alliance to him, should have respect given them, and have such employments assigned them, as they were found to be fit for. God the more to spite Shebna, declares how not Eliakim himself alone, but his whole kindred should be graced with him. Some expound the words of the great care that Eliakim should have in his place of securing, even the meaner sort of people: and not their persons only, but their goods and chattels also, even to the meanest of them. But the former I take to be the genuine sense of the place.

*{from the vessels of cups, even to the vessels of flagons*} This amplification continued in the former similitude, seems to argue both the great power and the fixed firmness, that Eliakim should be possessed of in his place. Even in the meanest men's houses: but in great men's much more, there are many pins and hooks of several sorts, to hang utensils, pots, and cups, of several sizes, and weight, on; and they are to be chary of hanging over many on the same hook, or pin, for fear of loosening, or breaking it. But this pin should be so strong, and so well fastened withal, that it should be able, without fear of danger, either to itself, or the things hanged on it, to bear all the vessels, or utensils in the house, though never so many, of several size, weight, and use. Some following the Chaldee paraphrast would have the meaning to be, that all those that had any sacred employment in the Sanctuary: as well the priests, that sacrificed, as the Levites that sang and played on instruments, should have their dependence upon Eliakim, supposing him to be High Priest. Others, that all the offices in the king's court, as well the higher as the lower also, should be at his disposal. And others again, that there should be nothing in the king's house, or palace, that should not be under his power. But the tenor of the context seems to run another way, and to admit none of these.

*{from the vessels of cups*} *vessels of cups;* that is, *cups,* simply, says one: as, *an instrument of viol,* (the very term here used) for, *a viol,* simply, Ps. 71.22. or, *vessels of cups,* for several *kinds,* or *sorts of cups;* or *bowls:* So the Jewish commenter; because there were, says he, divers sorts of them, different as well for matter, as for size. The word is not above twice found elsewhere in Scripture, Cant. 7.2. where the spouse's navel, is likened to *a round bowl,* or *goblet,* replenished with liquor. Whence it is with good probability deemed, that the word comes from the same root with that, which is used, for a *target,* or *shield.* Of which, see on ver. 6. in regard that the one did, in form, or roundness at least, resemble the other: and Exod. 24.6. where it is said, that Moses received into *basins,* the blood of the beasts, or bullocks, slain, for sacrifice, at mount Sinai. Whereby it appears, that it was a vessel, bowl, or basin of some large size, and of some good competent capacity: those used at table, were, in likelihood, of gold, as the rabbin here guesses, in great men's houses, or of silver, at least, and are mentioned here, as the principal. For those used at the altar of burnt offerings, might be of brass, Exod. 27.19. & 38.3. and so might the like for other uses, in private houses: but the former sort seems to be aimed at in this place.

*{even unto*} Heb. *and unto:* as ch. 1.6.

*{the vessels of flagons*} Or, *sorts:* as before; and for the cause there mentioned. The word rendered flagon, first, and properly, signifies a *bottle:* such, as they used commonly, to carry or keep wine in, 1 Sam. 1.24. & 10.3. & 25.18. 2 Sa. 16.1. Jer. 13.12. they were usually of earthen stuff, ch. 30.14. Jer. 19.1,10. & 48.12. and therefore of no great value, Lam. 4.2. put therefore here, for persons of the lowest rank, and least esteem: as the *bowls* before; for men of some prime note, and repute. The one answering to the honorable ones, spoken of before, the other to the small ones. Howbeit, because the same word is used also, for an instrument of music, a *viol,* so called, because it is bellied, somewhat like a *bottle,* of which, see on ch. 5.12. Hence, some would have it rendered, *the instruments of viols;* understanding it of musical instruments: and the rabbins most of them run this way, those especially, that dream of Eliakims High-Priest-ship; as also the Chaldee paraphrast, and the old Latin. But this agrees with the former, as harp, and harrow.

**V. 25.** *{In that day, saith the Lord of hosts*} In this last passage, wherewith the latter part of this prophecy concerning Shebna is concluded; the prophet returns to relate, as from God, the ruin now not of him alone, but of all those, that had dependence upon him.

*{in that day*} At that time: as ver. 20.

*{the Lord of hosts*} See ch. 1.9.

*{shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place, be removed*} Or, *shall the pin* (as ver. 23.) *that is fastened in a sure place,* (for there is no article here, more than there) *remove:* as Zach. 14.4. ch. 54.10. or *depart:* as Num. 14.44. Josh. 1.8. Judg. 6.13. ch. 59.21. The prophet resumes again the former similitude from a pin, or nail, driven into a wall, to hang some weighty thing on. To such an one surely fastened, that it might be able to hold whatsoever was hung on it; he compared Eliakim before, that was to be Shebna's successor; but Shebna, now, to such a pin, or nail; as though it might seem to be surely riveted into the post, or wall, yet should fail, and fall out of its place, when it came to the stress: and not be able to bear, or hold up that, that was hanged on it. For they are very far wide, that understand this of Eliakim, that he also should be removed, and taken away, as was Josias, 2 King. 23.26,29. for the sins of the people: as also those, that refer this to the Babylonian deportation, and expound it of the Priesthood, that seemed then to have failed, Hos. 3.4.

*{in a sure place*} As he accounted himself to be, when he hewed him out his sepulcher, ver. 23. as making no question but to live, and die there: and to hold his place, and state, to his end: as Job 29.18.

*{and be cut down, and fall*} See ch. 10.33. & 14.12.

*{and the burden that was upon it, shall be cut off*} As he compared Shebna to a pin, or, a nail: so his favorites, and his dependents, such as rested, and relied on him, in regard of his power, and place, (whether those of his family, or those of his faction) to some weight of bottles, or other utensils, that hanging upon such a pin, or nail, must needs, when that fails, and falls, fail together with it: and being brittle ware, break to pieces. So ch. 31.3.

*{For the Lord hath spoken it*} The prophet's usual close. See chap. 21.17.

### CHAPTER 23

**Ver. 1.** *{The burden of Tyre*} Of *Burden,* see c. 13.1. *Tyre,* the place, which this prophecy concerns, was a famous port, and mart-town, in Phenicia, the lower part of Syria; from which that whole country is supposed to have been so termed, (see on ch. 7.1.) lying upon the midland sea, and situate like Venice, within the sea, Ezek. 26.5. & 27.3,4. It is in Hebrew called *Tsor,* which sometime signifies *a rock,* Ezek. 3.9. because it was built upon a rock, Ezek. 26.4,14. and in that regard very strong, Josh. 19.29. in Syriac *Tsur,* whence *Suria,* and *Syria:* but by the Greeks, turning that first double letter into a single *T. Τύρος,* whence the Latin, *Tyrus,* and our *Tyre;* and by the Latins again, changing it into a single *S,* sometime *Sarra.* See the like prophecies against this town, and state, Jer. 25.22. & 47.4. Ezek. 26–28. Amo. 2.9. Zach. 9.2,4. denounced against it, among other their excesses, for their insolent and injurious carriages towards God's people, their neighbors, the Jews, Ezek. 26.2. & 28.24. Joel 3.4.

*{Howl, ye ships of Tarshish*} The prophet begins his sermon against Tyre, with a summons of such as had trade with her, and were maintained by her, to mourn for her, or over her, in regard of her ruin.

*{Howl*} Make a grievous lamentation, ch. 13.6. ver. 14.

*{ye ships of Tarshish*} Either the *ships* themselves; as by a rhetorical compellation, the senseless creatures are sometime called to mourn, ch. 14.31. and said so to do, Lam. 1.4. implying what they would do, were they sensible of such occurrents, whereby so much detriment accrues unto them. See Chap. 24.7. or the *ships,* put for those that are employed about them, and trade in them, who losing, and missing their former trade, with her, and a gain that thereby they got, should make grievous moan for Tyres fall, as being either wholly undone, or much endamaged thereby, Ezek. 27.29–32. Rev. 18.11–19.

*{of Tarshish*} That trade there, Ezek. 27.22,25. either of *Tartessus* in Spain; or of *Cilicia;* whose chief port town *Tarsus* was, (the Cilicians being anciently masters of those midland seas; as Strabo, l. 14. and Solinus, cap. 41.) or, of the main *ocean,* or great sea, from the one of those countries, in process of time, generally so termed; (as *Pontus,* with the Latins, from the like) or, from the color of the stone called *Tharshis,* Exod. 28.20. Ezek. 1.16. & 10.9. as some: but the stone, in more likelihood, had its name from the sea. See on ch. 2.16.

*{for it is laid waste*} When, or by whom, this calamity befell Tyre is much questioned among interpreters. The most draw it down to Nebuchadnezzars days, by whom they suppose it to have been effected, Jer. 47.4. Ezek. 26.7. Joseph *against Apion,* lib. 1. though other of them say, that it then indeed began; but was not fully completed until Alexanders time, by whom, after a long siege, having been taken with much difficulty, it was utterly sacked and ruined. See hereof, Diodor. lib. 17. Arrian, lib. 2. Plutarch, *in Alexanders life,* & Curtius, lib. 4. Yet some late writers suppose that what Esay here foretold, was effected and fulfilled by the Assyrian kings of those times, in which the prophet himself lived; to wit, by Salmaneser, and Sennacherib. To which purpose, they allege an ancient record out of the writings of one Menander, an Ephesian, cited by Joseph the Jew, in his *antiquities,* l. 9. c. 14. wherein it is related, that under Eluleus (or, as some out of Ruffinus read it, Eliseus) king of Tyre, the king of Assyria having subdued most of Phenicia, and having taken Sidon, and old Tyre, set upon Tyre itself too; which alone stood out against him, and so beset them, that they could come by no fresh water, for the space of five year, but what, by digging within the city, they got out of wells. Now this, says Joseph, was done, by Salmaneser, whose attempts against it, it is not improbable, that both Sargon, and Sennacherib, might after, pursue.

*{it*} That is, Tyre; whom this prophecy concerns.

*{laid waste*} Heb. *wasted,* or, *spoiled,* Psal. 17.9. chap. 33.1. Obad. 5. *wasted,* or *spoiled,* for, *to be wasted,* or *spoiled,* say some: as Psal. 137.8. *destroyed,* for, *to be destroyed:* but this nicety here needs not. It is the manner of the prophets, and their common language, to speak of things to come, as already done. So *Babylon is fallen,* ch. 21.9. Rev. 18.2.

*{so that there is no house*} Heb. *from house,* or, *from an house;* that is so, say some, that there is not one house left standing in her, Ezek. 26.4,14. Others no place of receipt, or harbor, Job 39.6. Psal. 104.17. or, *from* being *an house,* that is, *from* being *a city: house,* for, *city;* as *Beth-shemesh,* for *Kirheres: the house of the sun,* for, *the city of the sun,* See chap. 16.7. her wonted trading and state, thereby upheld, being gone. Of the phrase, see on ch. 7.8. & 17.1. Thus the most, which in the latter sense may import no more, than what might by those Assyrian kings well be accomplished. Some late writers, in exposition of this clause, go another way, expounding the words, *from house; from her domestics,* those that are of her own house, *is she spoiled:* according to that, Mic. 7.6. Matth. 10.36. and so, say they, it came to pass; when the state of Tyre, being much weakened by long wars between them and the Persians, their slaves joined in a conspiracy, surprised the city, slew their masters, possessed themselves of their wives, and goods, and set up such a king as themselves pleased, Justine, lib. 18. But neither does it appear, at what time this should be done; nor is it likely to be that, that the prophet here pointed at; and the text sounds rather the other way. See the next words.

*{no entering in*} Or, *nor entering in,* or *nor going,* to wit, in, or out. For the copulative wanting, as Psal. 110.3. would be supplied: as Hos. 9.11. Heb. *from going:* as 1 Sam. 25.26,33. or *from entering:* as ch. 24.10. a place parallel to this, *every house is shut up, from entering,* or, *going;* that is, so as none does, or can go in, or out. The meaning is, either Tyre is not frequented with repair of merchants, and traders, that pass to and fro, her wonted traffic being cut off, or decayed: or, it is so beset, and begirt by the enemy, that there can be no repair to it, or passage for it, or, from it, with safety. For it seems too forced a construction that some here give, to carry on their forementioned exposition, *from coming:* that is, *from men of coming:* as *wine,* for, a man of wine, a wine-bibber, Prov. 20.1. *wisdom,* for, a man of wisdom; a wise man, Mic. 6.9. men of *coming,* strangers: as, *the come Governor,* Dan. 9.26. the Governor stranger: so the meaning should be, Tyre is to be wasted by her own household servants, her slaves, and by strangers, the Chaldeans, Ezek. 28.7. But neither is any such phrase found in Scripture; *men of coming,* for, *strangers:* nor is the word of *coming,* or, *going,* here a noun, but a verb: and besides, that it seems somewhat improbable, that by these two terms, the prophet should describe two divers manners of devastation, by two several sorts of persons, at two several times, far distant the one from the other; the tenor of the text, according to the common phrase of Scripture, whereof the Jewish commenters, upon the place, afford examples enow, from 1 Sam. 15.23. 1 King. 15.13. Ezek. 16.41. to which many more also might be added; and the current of the context runs fairly, and familiarly, the former way.

*{from the land of Chittim*} As *Tarshish,* so *Chittim,* was the name, at first, of one of Javans sons, Gen. 10.4. from whom those lands, or countries, were afterward called, which by him, or his posterity, were possessed. Now because it is said, that among Japhets, or Javans issue, *the Isles of the Nations were divided,* Gen. 10.5. Hence it is supposed, that under the name of *Chittim,* are comprised some of the maritime coasts, bordering upon the Eastern parts of the midland sea, as well on the European, as on the Asian side, and of the isles that are therein. This they surmise, the rather, in regard of the ancient names of divers places, in those parts, as *Cittium,* a town in Cyprus, whence Zeno the philosopher was, Strabo, lib. 14. Joseph, *antiquities,* l. 1. c. 12. & Pliny, l. 5. c. 31. *Cyteum* in Candy, Pliny, l. 4. c. 12. the *Ceteans,* a people situate between the Cilicians, and the Pelasgians, Strabo, l. 13. so called, as some think, from the river *Cetus;* which they lie upon, Pliny, l. 5. cap. 20. or, from *Cetus,* whether a town, or province in Cilicia, of which Ptolomy, l. 5. nor want they, that draw in hither, some parts at least, of Achaia, and Macedonia; called anciently *Macetia,* as Hesychius informs us; and the inhabitants thereof *Macetians,* as Steven the Byzantine, out of Heraclides, as also part of Italy; because Suidas, out of some old author, reports, that Telephus the son of Hercules, brought some *Cetians* out of Asia, and placed them in Italy. Yet some there are, that would confine *Chittim* to the lands about Italy, in the utter, or Western parts of the midland sea; as *Tarshish,* to those about Greece, in the inner, or Eastern parts of it: which to me seems not so probable. See Num. 24.24. Dan. 11.30. 1 Maccab. 1.1. & 8.5. Nor is it unlikely, but that those of Chittims posterity, were dispersed into divers of those forementioned places, out of which merchants had traffic with Tyre. But this branch of the verse, concerning Chittim, is by divers diversely expounded. For some refer it to the words beforegoing: and of these, some to the first word, *is wasted,* or *spoiled from the land of Chittim;* that is, say some of them, *from Cilicia,* by which way Alexander broke into the Eastern parts; whereof, yet, I find no particular mention, in the stories of those times. Others, from Macedonia, whereof Alexander was king, and from whence, at first, he set forth: and so the author of the Maccabees constantly takes it; whatsoever a learned writer in his annotations, affirms, in the one place, by his own version, crossing himself in the other: and these both understand the place of that devastation, that by Alexander, and his forces, befell Tyre. But other join this passage to the words next beforegoing, thus rendering them, *so that there is no entering,* or, *coming, in from Chittim,* that is, so that the merchants, who had wont from those parts to repair to Tyre, can now find no entrance thither. Thus they, that annex it to the former words. But most refer it to the branch following, reading the text.

*{from the land of Chittim, it is revealed to them*} Which yet is diversely expounded. Some, from the merchants of Chittim, that are nearer at hand, is the overthrow of Tyre reported to those of Tarshish, that are further off. Others by the merchants of Chittim, trading to Babylon, the Babylonians have been informed of the wealth of Tyre, and incited to invade it: or, the Tyrians have by them been informed of the Babylonians evil purposes against them. Others, *from the land of Chittim it appears to them:* as Chap. 40.1. & 56.1. or, *it shall fall suddenly upon them,* to wit, the Tyrians, *to them,* for, *on them:* as Psalm 9.4. Exod. 15.15. or, as others, *on it:* or *on her,* to wit, *Tyre:* as Job 10.23. but the pronoun is in both places masculine. Others, lastly, *from the land of Chittim is the foundation discovered,* or, *laid bare, with them.* The word, *foundation,* supplied, as it is found complete, Ezek. 13.14. Mic. 1.6. for, as for those, that following the old Greek, render it, *it is,* or, *she is led captive,* or *gone into captivity:* or, more generally, *it is removed,* or *she is gone:* as the word is used, chap. 38.12. they take no notice of the last particle, *unto him,* or *unto them;* (for it may signify either: as chap. 53.8.) which yet is not here superfluous. Amidst this great variety, I incline to those, that join those words, *from the land of Chittim,* with the next before them, and understand the passage of all harbor in Tyre, or entrance, into it, denied unto such as had wont to have recourse thither: to which is added, *it is revealed to them,* to wit, to those that formerly traded with her; the report is come to them, how it fares with her, that she is sacked and spoiled, and there is, therefore, nothing for them to do there: and the whole passage may, as I conceive, be not amiss, thus rendered, taking the initial particle in a double notion: as Jer. 4.30. & 12.5. (of which, see on Chapter 18.3.) *for that she* (Tyre) *is spoiled, so that there is no house, nor coming in* for those *from Chittim, is made known to them:* as chap. 22.14. Dan. 10.1. So the words run smoothly without rub; and many needless difficulties are taken off, wherein most of the other readings received, do necessarily entangle us. I shall add only, what one of the Jewish commenters has on this place; because I find it seconded by a man of great note; to wit, that by the *Chittim,* or *Chittijim,* as they are termed, vers. 12. are meant the *Chuthei,* a people inhabiting some part of *Susiana,* to the East of Babylon, called also by the Greeks, *Cissia.* So the meaning should be, from Chaldea, and the parts adjacent shall this evil befall them. But this I shall leave to the judgments of others.

**V. 2.** *{Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle*} It is somewhat doubtful whom the prophet here either speaks of, or speaks unto. Most interpreters understand by the isle here mentioned, Tyre itself, so called, because it stood within the sea, environed round about with it, Ezek. 27.3,4. & 28.2. until by Alexander it was adjoined to the continent: as Pliny, lib. 5. c. 19. The inhabitants of Tyre, therefore, say some, are here advised to be *quiet,* and not trouble themselves, about courses to be taken for the defense of their city; since, that all would be to no purpose. See the like, Jer. 8.14. Psal. 4.4. But this seems not to suit well with the main current of the context, running all along in the prophetical strain, in speaking of things to come, as past and done; and of Tyre, as already, either spoiled, or destroyed: and others therefore on better ground, suppose, that the Tyrians are here called upon, (as were her merchants before) to mourn for her, and to be *silent;* that is, to leave their boasting of the state and wealth of their city, and their rioting and reveling that formerly they had used, ver. 7–9. (see the like, chap. 22.2,13.) and to sit down in silence after the manner of mourners, Job 2.8,13. chap. 47.5. Jer. 8.14. Lam. 3.28. and this I suppose to be the genuine meaning of the words. Yet some other, among whom one of the Jewish commenters, on the place, suppose the word, *isle,* to be taken here collectively; *isle,* for *islands:* as *ox,* and *horse,* and *ass;* for *oxen,* and *horses,* and *asses,* Gen. 32.5. 2 King. 1.10. chap. 1.3. and the place to be understood of those, who dwelling in sea-towns, or islands, had trading with Tyre; either said here, to sit down, and give over their trade; the city, with which their chief traffic was, being destroyed. For they read the words, not imperatively; but enunciatively; not as advising them what they should do: but as relating what they do; *they are still:* or, as others, called upon, and advised to *forbear* going to Tyre, or looking any more after her, as the word is used, Ezek. 24.17. or, willed to sit down, and mourn with her, and for her, as those, ver. 1.

*{thou whom the merchants of Zidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished*} Heb. *merchant that passeth:* as Gen. 23.16. Prov. 31.14. The Sidoneans being merchants, and trading also by sea, helped to fill the mart at Tyre with their wares, being not far from her; and finding a good market for themselves with her; though in Ezekiel, they are mentioned rather as her mariners, than as her merchants, Ezek. 26.8. but they might well be both. Some read the words, *the merchants of Zidon, that pass the sea, and fill thee,* O Tyre, are still, also, or silent: supplying the verb from the former branch. For Tyre falling, Zidon being so near it, and in some sort, a joint state with it, could not but fall with it. See on ver. 4. but this syntax seems over-forced.

*{that pass over the sea*} Or, as we use to speak, *that cross the sea.*

*{replenished*} Have haunted, and enriched; so Tyre speaks in her pride, upon the fall of Jerusalem, *I shall be replenished,* Ezek. 26.2. I shall grow great, and rich.

**V. 3.** *{And by great waters, the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river is her revenue*} Tyre further described, as before by her trade with Zidon, ver. 2. so here, by her traffic with Egypt. See Ezek. 27.7.

*{by great waters*} By the midland sea; by which the wares of Egypt were conveyed unto Tyre, Psal. 104.25. & 107.23. See chap. 18.1. and some therefore supply here, the word, *came,* or *was brought,* thus reading the text, *by great waters, came the seed of Shihor,* it was brought unto her: and the reading seems not amiss. See the like defects, Jer. 51.25. *Behold, I* come *against thee,* Psal. 120.7. *I* am, or, stand, or, plead, *for peace.* See ver. 5. Howbeit, the Jewish writers suppose here a trajection in the text; and by *great waters,* understand the waters of Nilus, reading the words, *the seed of Nilus beside those great waters:* as chap. 32.20. but the plainer reading seems the better.

*{the seed of Sihor*} The grain of Egypt; and whatsoever else the land of Egypt, being watered by the river Nilus, did afford, as fine flax, paper, and the like. Of which, see on ch. 19.7,9.

*{Shihor*} Or, *Shichor:* as *Achaz,* and *Achab.* See on chap. 1.1. This *Sihor,* some great ones would have to be, not Nilus; but a petty river, or brook, that ran between Palestine and Egypt, termed sometimes *the brook,* or, *the river of the wilderness,* or *plain,* Amos 6.14. the same they suppose, that by foreign writers is called *Rhinocolura;* and the Greek sometime so renders it; though that in those writers is the name not of a river, but of a town, situate indeed in the confines of Egypt and Syria, in a waste place, not far from the sea, so called, from the condition of those that were first placed in it. For an Ethiopian king having, as they report, sometime subdued Egypt, and finding the kingdom much pestered with thieves and robbers, to rid the land of them, being loath yet to kill them, especially, being so many, only cut off their noses, and placed them in that town, which there of purpose he built for them. So Strabo, lib. 16. Diodor. l. 1. c. 60. and Steven the Byzantine; Pliny also mentions it, l. 5. c. 13. and Ptolomy, l. 4. nor appears it, that this town stood upon any river of note. For Diodore writes of it, that it had no good water near it; nor was that very good, that they had from wells sunk within the city. *Sihor* therefore, (as this very place alone might suffice, were there no other argument to prove it) is no other than *Nilus,* as the old Latin also here renders it. For how absurd a thing were it to imagine, that either some sorry rivulet, of which scarce any record, because it lay on the skirts of the country, should give the name to the whole kingdom; as *Twede* to *England:* or, that the grain of Egypt should be termed the *seed* of some such petty brook, running along through waste places, where scarce any tillage at all could be had? Beside, that the ancient name, that the river Nilus was known by, intimates as much. For Dionyse the geographer testifies, as also Pliny, l. 9. c. 5. that by the Ethiopians it was anciently called *Siris,* that is, as those inform us, who are skilled in that language, according to their manner of forming words, *Shihri,* or *Shichri;* which comes very near to the Hebrew *Shihor,* or *Shichor.* Whence also so many names in the Egyptian tongue, of *Osiris, Busiris, Petosiris,* and the like: for an absurd thing it is, as Eustachius, on the geographer, observes, to give Greek notations of Ethiopian, or Egyptian appellations. The Hebrew name *Shichor,* has a notion of *blackness* in it, as appears by the common use of the fountain, whence it springs, and other the issues of it, Job 30.30. Levit. 13.31,37. Can. 1.5. & 5.11. Lam. 4.8. Zach. 6.2,6. and the color of its water seems to have given the river that name. Whence also, the Greeks are deemed anciently to have given it the name of Egypt, (as Eustathius observes that Homer does in his Odysseys, l. 14.) and to the land from it, (which the ancient writers called *the gift of Nilus,* as produced, all the lower part of it, by the inundation of the river, and the slime it brought down with it, and left there behind it, Herodot. l. 2.) and Strabo, l. 1.) not from Egyptus, a mere figment of a man, such another as Nileus; that should give Nilus his name, Diodore, lib. 1. c. 63: but from the color of the water, resembling, not so much the *Eagle,* thence so called by the Latins, as the *Vulture,* termed *Egypius* in Greek. To which purpose, also, Eustachius further informs us, that it was likewise upon the same ground, anciently by the Greeks, called *Melas,* which signifies *black;* and thence, by the Latins, in old time, *Melo;* as Festus, and Servius, on Virgil observe: so that both the present text, terming the Egyptian wares, either growing upon the banks of Nilus, or procured, and [produced], by the water thereof, bateling the Egyptian soil, *the seed,* and *harvest of Sihor;* as also the name, by the Ethiopians, given to the river; the very same, in a manner, with it; and the notation of the name concurring with those, whereby the Greeks anciently styled it: do all joined together, strongly evince *Sihor* to be no other than *Nilus.* All that can be objected against it, is this, that *the Egyptian Shihor,* or *the river of Egypt,* is mentioned, as one of the limits of the land of promise, Num. 34.5. Josh. 13.3. & 15.4,47. 1 Chro. 13.5. within compass whereof the land of Egypt came not, nor did the Israelites ever possess so far, as Nilus: To which may well be answered, first, that in like manner, is the river Euphrates recorded, as a limit of the same land, Gen. 15.18. Deut. 1.7. & 11.24. Josh. 1.4. and yet read we not, that God's people ever possessed, or inhabited, at least so far. Though of Solomon it is said, that *he reigned over all the kings, from the river,* (to wit, *Euphrates:* as Ps. 72.8.) *even unto the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt,* 2 Ch. 9.26. they attained not to the full extent of the boundaries by God assigned them: partly, through their own negligence and cowardice, Judg. 1.21,27–33. Psal. 106.34,35. and partly, through the just judgment of God, who for their transgressions and apostasies, after much of it surprised, refused to put them, into further possession of it, Judg. 2.20–23. Hereunto may be added, that when Nilus is mentioned, as a boundary of the promised land, it is not so to be understood, as if the limits thereof reached as far as the main body of that river, or any branch of it, ran: (for then it should take in the whole lower region of Egypt: which the river Nilus, as Pliny relates, l. 5. c. 9. branching itself into several channels, does on either side, by her embraces determine) but any such branch of that river, or stream, thence derived, as lay nearest unto the land of Canaan, and bounded Egypt on that side. Now the nearest main channel is that of Pelusium, as that of Canopus, the furthest; out of which a lesser stream issuing, makes the sea, or lake of Sirbonis, of a great length, and vast depth, dividing Egypt from the Edomites, that lay on the upper part of it, and the Philistines, that confined upon the lower: as Herodote, l. 3. Strabo, l. 14. Diodore, l. 1. c. 30. Pliny, l. 5. c. 13. from whence, as Leo the African, l. 8. c. 1. testifies, by a narrow passage, the water thereof through waste places, finds out a way to the sea: that which Brocard also c. 6. attests, having been an eyewitness of it: save that following the common error, he would have this little gut, or gutter, to be that, which is in Scripture termed *Sior,* and *the river of Egypt.* So in Scripture, Nilus should never be named; and obscure rill, or distill of water, derived from it, instead of it, should; which whether it be probable, let other deem. For howsoever *the river* without further addition, be in way of eminency, used sometime of Euphrates, ch. 7.20. Jer. 2.19. as it is also of Nilus, ch. 19.5. and in this verse; yet the name of Euphrates, is withal, frequently mentioned, Gen. 2.14. 2 King. 23.29. & 24.7. Jer. 13.4. & 46.2. & 51.63. nor does it seem to stand with reason to imagine, that Nilus, so famous, and so oft spoken of in Scripture; yet should not, so much as once, be therein named.

*{the harvest*} The word *harvest,* is here taken in a large sense; for whatsoever, either springing out of the ground, or from such plants as grow on it, is for man's use wont to be taken, at certain times, from either. See on Chap. 17.11. for they seem to cut out the text over-curiously, and needlessly to restrain the terms of it, who by *seed,* would have understood the *flax* alone; and by *harvest,* the *grain.*

*{of the river*} To wit, *Shihor,* or *Nilus,* before-mentioned. For the one branch speaks the same, in effect, with the former: save that the one has a glance, at the *seed-time,* and the other, at the *harvest: the river,* for Nilus: as Ezek. 29.3,9. called more fully, *the river of Egypt,* Amos 8.8. & 9.5.

*{is her revenue*} Or, *was her revenue:* Whatsoever Egypt, by help of her river could afford, it was brought, as commonly, and as plentifully, to her, as if it had been, both sown, or planted, and reaped, or plucked on purpose for her use. The word is general, for all kind of increase, of grain, fruits, or the like, Levit. 23.39. and 25.22. Num. 18.30. Deut. 14.22. and 22.9.

*{and she is a mart of Nations*} Or, *she was a trader with Nations.* The word translated *mart,* signifies properly, not a *mart,* or *market;* that is, a place of *trade;* but *trade,* or *traffic,* or *merchandise* itself, ver. 18. Prov. 3.14. & 31.18. chap. 45.14. and some of the Hebrew commenters, therefore, suppose a defect of a word to be supplied, a mistress, or owner, *of trade:* as, *defect cannot be numbered,* defect, for things *of defect;* or *defective,* Eccl. 1.15. and *spoil,* for, men or masters *of spoil,* spoilers, Judg. 5.30. and *fraud,* for men, or masters, of fraud, *fraudulent* persons, Ps. 109.2. and, *prey,* for, men or masters, *of prey:* such as use to prey upon others, Prov. 23.28. so *trade,* for a mistress, or owner of *trade:* and *mistress,* or, *owner of trade,* for, a *trader:* as, *a mistress,* or, *owner, of a familiar spirit,* for a *witch,* or, *great witch,* Nah. 3.4. And thus is Tyre termed; a *trader of,* or, *for,* or, *to,* or *with, nations:* (for it may be any of these ways rendered) because she had trading not with one or two, but abundance of several nations, far and near, being, in regard of her situation, a most convenient place for them; and was therefore the greatest mart of the known world, in those ages, for all manner of merchandise. Whereof, see at large Ezek. 25.

**V. 4.** *{Be thou ashamed, O Zidon*} The denunciations in this prophecy, are directed, and darted, as well at, and against *Zidon,* as Tyre: as the like is done also, Jer. 47.4. because it was a near neighbor to Tyre, and though it were not under the same government with it; (for it appears, that they had several kings, Jer. 27.2.) yet were they so linked together in commerce and confederacy, that they seemed as one state; in regard whereof, we find them so often joined in Scripture, Josh. 19.28,29. 2 Sam. 24.6,7. 1 Chron. 22.4. Ezra 3.7. Jer. 25.22. Joel 3.4. Zach. 6.1. Mat. 11.11. & 15.23. Mar. 3.8. & 7.24,31. Luk. 6.17. & 10.13. Act. 12.20. and the fall of the one, therefore, the more principal especially, must needs prove the overthrow of the other. Howbeit, Ezekiel has a sermon specially directed apart unto, and against Zidon, ch. 28.20–24. severed from those several ones, denounced against Tyre, Chap. 26. & 27. & 28.1–10. and vers. 10–19.

*{Be ashamed*} Or, *confounded.* As Ps. 25.2,3. & 119.6.

*{O Zidon*} Heb. *Tsidon.* for which the Greeks and Latins have *Sidon;* as for *Tsion, Sion,* Rom. 9.33. & 11.26. Mat. 11.21. This city for antiquity, was in likelihood ancienter than Tyre; for we find records of it, far ancienter than any of Tyre, Gen. 10.19. & 49.13. And it is observed by Strabo, lib. 16. that Homer makes mention of Sidon, but not of Tyre: which being at first but a small rocky island, was not much regarded, until sea-trade was grown rife; and it was then observed to be a place fit to settle a mart in, for the midland sea: and as some foreign histories report, until the Sidonians, being driven out of their country by the king of Ascalon, by shipping, betook themselves unto that island, as a place of defense, and thereon built, and peopled it, that lay formerly waste: Justine, lib. 18. And in Joshua's time, though Tyre had the name of *the strong city,* Josh. 19.29. yet had *Zidon* the name of *the great city,* Josh. 11.8. & 19.28. As, though far inferior to it for strength, yet for amplitude, far exceeding Tyre; in regard whereof Strabo tells us, that it was questioned in his time, whether of the two should be reckoned the chief city of Phenicia; mean while they are wide, that from that epithet given to Sidon, would produce us two *Sidons,* a greater, and a less; as there were two *Tyres,* the old and the new: and no less wide are they, who suppose that the city Sidon was so called from the store of fish that it abounded with, through the neighborhood of the sea: affirming withal, that *Sidon* in the Phenician tongue, signifies a *fish;* Justine, lib. 18. But neither does Sidon in that language, being of near affinity with the Hebrew, and derived from it, signify any such thing: nor had the city thence its name, but from *Sidon,* one of Canaans sons, Gen. 10.15. 1 Chron. 1.13. who either himself, or his issue settled in those parts, founded that city, and called it after his name.

*{for the sea hath spoken, even, the strength of the sea, saying*} Sidon is brought to shame and confusion, because Tyre, of whom she before so much boasted, and upon whose trading she much depended, ver. 2. is utterly wasted and ruined, ver. 1.

*{the sea*} The sea-coast say some, thereabout in general: or, those that trade by sea, As ch. 60.5. But the most, both Jewish, and ours, suppose Tyre to be here so termed, because she was situate, as an island within the sea, or, *in the heart of the sea,* as it is, Ezek. 37.4. & 28.2. Or, *the sea,* at least bordering on it, as lamenting the devastation of Tyre, her chief port, Ezek. 26.4,5,12.

*{the strength of the sea*} Or, *sea-fort,* as ch. 25.4. & 30.3. So is Tyre termed, in regard of her situation, being both founded upon a rock, Mat. 7.25. and environed with the sea, See on ver. 1. And it was famous therefore for strength; as well as Sidon for greatness, Josh. 19.28,29. and did rule therefore, and command the sea in those parts. But of the strength of Tyre, see Curtius, l. 4. c. 1.

*{I travail not, nor bring forth children; neither do I nourish up young men, nor bring up virgins*} Thus is the midland sea, as some, or that part of it near about Tyre, as other some, or, Tyre itself rather, as the most and the best, brought in, speaking by a rhetorical frame, and fineness of speech; as in the person of a woman bemoaning herself, and bewailing her present condition; that has had many children, but now either is wholly bereft of them, nor is like ever to breed any more: or, has as little comfort of them, and help from them, as if she never had borne any. Some read the words of the text in the present tense, as our version has them, implying, that howsoever she was plentiful in people, whom she bred up in so great abundance, that with her colonies she peopled many other places: (of which see Strabo, l. 16. Mela, l. 3. c. 6. Pliny l. 5. c. 19.) yet now she was so wasted and worn out, that she was not able to bear, or bring up, or send forth any more; like Naomi, Ruth 1.11,12. And this seems the plainest; and most natural sense of the place. Howbeit, others read them in the time past; and some, as spoken by way of interrogation, *Have I not travailed, and brought forth children, and brought up young men, and reared up virgins?* As complaining, that albeit she had so done, yet that none of them now had come in to her succor; like that of Jerusalem, *of all the sons that she had brought forth, and brought up, there is never a one to take her by the hand,* ch. 51.18. And this, say they, is that, which Sidon is willed to be ashamed of; that she had not offered herself, to the relief of her mother city: but Tyre was indeed rather a daughter of Sidon, than Sidon daughter to Tyre. Others conceive the words spoken, in an optative form and sense: as wishing, that she had rather been always barren, and had never bred or brought forth any: than to breed and bring up children: either for herself, to see the destruction of them, or for them to see her dreadful and shameful ruin. See Hos. 9.11,14. where Tyre and Ephraim are compared together: but this sense, how the letter will well bear, I see not: And others lastly, (to omit all others,) as lamenting her calamitous condition; being as one that had never borne, or brought up any children, her people and inhabitants being slain and destroyed, either in the siege, or in the surprisal of the city: of whom what havoc was by Alexander made in his rage, after he had taken the city; partly, for the long stay they had put him to in the siege; and partly, for their barbarous breach, of the law of nations, in murdering his ambassadors, and throwing their bodies in contempt into the sea: (the violation whereof, so much incensed David against the Ammonites, 2 Sam. 10.4. & 12.31.) See Curtius, l. 4. c. 4. See also concerning Nebuchadnezzors dealing with Tyre, (who might likewise be the more enraged against it, because he had spent thirteen years in the siege of it, as Joseph the Jew, out of the Phenician records *against Appion,* l. 1.) Ezek. 26.6,8,11,15. & 27.34. and see of Babylon, ch. 47.7,8.

*{I travail not, nor bring forth children*} Cities are in Scripture resembled to teeming women, ch. 47.8,9. & 49.19,21. & 51.18. & 54.1,3. & 66.4,5. & 66.7,8.

*{neither do I nourish up young men*} Heb. *greaten:* that is, *bring up,* till they are grown great (as ch. 1.2. & 49.21. & 51.18.) *choice young men.* See ch. 9.17. & 40.30.

*{nor brought up virgins*} Either reared them up to woman's state, till grown up to a height, and made fit for marriage, as of young men the like, in another word before, having in it, a notion of *greatness,* Psal. 144.12. as this of *height,* Ezek. 31.5. and so the same thing though in divers notions should be said of either: or, advanced them, as the word is most commonly used, 1 Sam. 2.7. Job 41.14. Psal. 37.34. Prov. 4.8. To wit, by giving or placing them out in marriage; that which with our English phrase well accords. Both the words, this and the former, are together found, Ezek. 31.4. and before here, chap. 1.2. See there. A large issue cannot be achieved, unless children be as well brought up, to maturity, and ripeness of growth, as before that, bred and born; nor, those of the female sex especially, in an honest and desirable way, but by advancement of them in marriage: that which it may be is alluded unto, the rather, by the prophet in these words, because, persons broken in their estates, have not now, those means and abilities to prefer their daughters, that formerly they might have had: So it is, as if Tyre had said, I am not able now to breed children, to bring up sons, or to prefer daughters, as I had formerly wont to do. The particle, as well negative as copulative, is in this branch wanting, to be supplied from the former, as Ps. 9.18. ch. 5.28.

**V. 5.** *{As at the report concerning Egypt, so shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre*} A second effect of the overthrow of Tyre, in regard of others, neighboring persons and people: to wit, that as her allies and associates were before smitten with extreme sorrow and shame, in regard of the loss and damage they sustained in their wealth and state, by her fall, Ezek. 27.34. ver. 1,4. So both they also, and others beside them, should be surprised with sore fear and pain, as not without cause, misdoubting that their turn might be next, at least, they could not sit sure, or be safe, when a place deemed so impregnable, as that, was pulled down. See Ch. 19.7. Some restrain this effect of Tyres fall, to Egypt only: thus reading the text, *when the report* (to wit, of the fall of Tyre) *came to Egypt,* they, that is the Egyptians, *were sorely pained,* or, *much affrighted at the report of Tyre* (at the hearing of her downfall:) or *according to the report of Tyre,* that is, according to the fear and amazement that the Tyrians were surprised with, when they heard of Nebuchadnezzars coming against them. The Egyptians, say they, were much amazed and troubled upon the tidings brought them, how it had fared with Tyre; partly, in regard they had much merchandise there; which must of necessity miscarry; and partly, because that block being removed, that lay in the Assyrian, or Chaldean king's way, he should now have freer passage, and readier access unto Egypt: and the particle translated, *as,* does sometime also signify *when,* or, *as soon as,* as it is rendered, Josh. 2.7. and for the defect of the verb, see on ver. 3. And this reading, besides some of the Jewish commenters, the ancient Greek, and old Latin have, whom many of ours also follow: But the effect here mentioned, seems to be, more general, as it is also by Ezekiel at large related, Ezek. 26.15,18. & 27.35. To wit, that as the fall of Egypt, or, the overthrow given the Egyptians, did terrify and affright many neighbor nations; yea, so many as came to the hearing of it; so should the fall of Tyre affright and astonish those, unto whom the report of it should come. Now against this version and exposition, the only objection is, that by Nebuchadnezzar Tyre was destroyed, before Egypt: as appears, Ezek. 29.18–20. To which (besides what might be returned, that it is not so clear, at what time, or by whom, the judgment here denounced, was upon Tyre inflicted;) answer is two ways returned; First, by some granting it to be spoken of the destruction of Egypt, by Nebuchadnezzar; that as other people should be affrighted at the fall of Egypt, when it should come: so should others also be, at the fall of this strong city. Secondly, by others it is answered, that what is spoken here concerning Egypt, has reference, not to that conquest of Egypt by the Chaldeans, but to an overrunning of it; say some, about Esays time, by the Assyrians, of which see on ver. 1. Or, as others, raising far higher, to the fearful judgments inflicted from God, on Egypt by the ministry of Moses, that ended in the destruction of Pharao, and all his forces, in the red sea; the report whereof is said to have struck *fear,* and *dread, pain, trembling,* and *amazement,* in the *Edomites, Moabites, Philistines, Canaanites,* and other people round about, Exod. 15.14–16. Josh. 2.9,11. And this latter way, go the greater part of the Jewish commenters, who yet some of them, fondly and needlessly busy their brains, in paralleling the ten plagues of Egypt, with those things that befell Tyre, See ver. 11.

*{As at the report concerning Egypt*} The particle *at,* is wanting, to be supplied, as Ps. 18.44. *the report.* Heb. *hearing,* as ch. 53.11. *concerning Egypt;* as the particle is used, chap. 8.12. *There was much affrightment;* or, *men were much affrighted,* is to be supplied in this branch, from the next: as in the like speech, the one branch is oft made up by the other. See Job 24.19. Prov. 9.7. & 13.1,2,11. Chap. 13.13. & 18.7.

*{so shall they be sorely pained*} The note of similitude is wanting, as oft, in the latter part of similitudes. See Prov. 25.22. & 26.11.

*{sorely pained*} The word properly signifies women's travail, wherein trembling and pain concur, Ps. 48.6. chap. 13.8. The verb is indefinitely here used; *they shall be in pain,* that is, *there shall be much pain;* or, *men shall be much pained.* See on Chapter 2.19.

*{at the report of Tyre*} Or, *according to;* as the particle ordinarily signifies, Ch. 1.7. & 8.20. & 10.26. but here rather, as our English renders it.

**V. 6.** *{Pass ye over to Tarshish, howl, ye inhabitants of the isle*} Whom these words are spoken to, interpreters are not agreed on. Some conceive them spoken all to those, that had trade and traffic with Tyre; expounding them, you that carry the tidings of Tyres fall, get you over beyond the sea; and you in the islands, and elsewhere, that had dealings with her, lament for her, upon the hearing of it. Or, you Egyptians, and others, that had wont to haunt Tyre, turn now over to *Tartessus,* or *Tarsus,* and mourn for your losses sustained at Tyre, by your wares there surprised, and your trade there at an end, Ezek. 27.27. Other suppose them to be spoken to the Tyrians themselves; either in whole, or in part, by this kind of speech insinuating what should befall them; as before the like, ver. 1,2. To wit, either that they should betake themselves to the sea, and by help of their shipping seek places of harbor, and shelter, elsewhere abroad; to which purpose some relate, that in the time of their siege (but by whom say not) they sent away many of their people to Carthage: or, as others, and so the Chaldee paraphrast, that they should be carried away captive by the enemy into transmarine parts, which sorts well with what follows after, ver. 7. nor need we divert, from them, to any other, the latter branch of the verse; as if the inhabitants of some other islands, which they either passed to, or passed by, in that manner, should howl for them, as the *ships of Tarshish* are said to *do,* ver. 1. when as this their transmigration, would undoubtedly minister matter enough, of howling and lamenting as well, if not much more, unto themselves, as unto others: and that they were before here called, *the inhabitants of the isle:* to wit, on which Tyre stood; whereof, and why it was so called, See on ver. 2,10.

**V. 7.** *{Is this your joyous city? whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn*} The prophet's words insulting over Tyre, and in bitter manner upbraiding the Tyrians, for their vain conceit, and presumptuous vaunting of, and confidence in their city, as well the pomp and pleasure, as the antiquities of it; as if having continued so long, in so prosperous and flourishing a condition, she were now past all hazard, or fear of any change; whereas now they might see her, in a very mean and sorry condition, compelled to travel on foot, far, at the pleasure of those, in whose hands she was fallen.

*{your joyous city*} Heb. *a joyous,* or *reveling one, unto you,* or *with you;* for *city* is not in the text, no more than in the next verse, nor ver. 11. yet may well be supplied, for so is Jerusalem styled *a joyous city,* Ch. 22.2. which one of the Jewish commenters parallels here with that, Psal. 48.2. *the joy of the whole earth;* as if the meaning were; the city, that you may all the country over glory of, and rejoice in. But I suppose, well weighing the prophet's words, and his wonted manner of speech, it will appear, that he speaks rather of the city, as of a stately and lascivious lady, that lives in all manner of bravery and jollity; *Is this your jolly,* or *reveling Lady,* as you accounted her, that lived in so great plenty and excess? See of Babel, ch. 47.1,5,8. and of Tyre, and her jollity, Ezek. 26.13. as also of Sidon, ver. 12.

*{whose antiquity is of ancient days*} Heb. *from days before,* or *days of antiquity,* as ch. 3.26. For the antiquity of Tyre, Joseph the Jew tells us in his *antiquities,* l. 8. c. 3. that it was built two hundred and forty years before Solomons Temple, that should be about Gideons time. Justine goes higher, lib. 18. and says, it was built by Agenor, the Phenician Cadmus his father; and that should be about Joshua's time; and so far, we are sure of its antiquity: for we find it standing, *a strong city* in his days, Josh. 19.29. and how long before it had stood, we know not. For, as for the fables of Annius, his counterfeit Berosus, who l. 5. tells us, that *Tyras* (the son of Japhet, Gen. 10.2.) built Tyre, and so brings the founding of it very near up to the Flood: We give as much credit to them, as to the tale, that the Tyrian priests told Herodote, as himself reports, lib. 2. that their town had then stood no less than two thousand and three hundred years, and so carry it up above the Flood. But of great antiquity it was, doubtless; for we have infallible record of about seven hundred and forty years past, when it was found built, and a place of special note, before the time of this prophecy: but a fond thing it was therefore, thence to conceive, that it must needs stand, and continue in that flaunting and flourishing condition, that she had formerly enjoyed. See ver. 13. So Babel, *I shall sit as a Lady for ever,* Chapter 47.7,8.

*{Her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn*} An elegant description of one of the weaker sex, having lived plentifully, daintily and deliciously: but now led captive into a far country, to live there in a sorry and servile condition. She shall not now, as heretofore (like some gallant nice lady, that out of state and delicacy either scorns, or will not adventure to set the sole of her foot once to the ground, Deut. 28.56.) be carried in her coach, or litter: or, in state, and pomp, ride out as a princess: but she shall be compelled to travel on foot, as a lackey, or some other obscure and mean person, Eccl. 10.7. and that not some short journey, but into some remote country, far distant from the place of her former abode; into Assyria or Chaldea, or some of their provinces: not there to rest, or have any place of settled abode: but to *sojourn* there as a stranger, in slavery hurried to and fro, at the will and pleasure of those that have power over her. See of Babel, ch. 47.2.

**V. 8.** *{Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city?*} This demand is made in way of admiration, as by some wondering, who either could endure to plot, or put in execution, such a design, against so noble and gallant a city as Tyre was; or was able to effect it, against a place of that impregnable strength, in which she had so long continued, ver. 7.

*{taken this counsel*} Heb. *consulted this,* that is, *contrived it,* as ch. 7.5. or, *devised it,* ch. 32.7. or, *purposed it,* as ch. 19.12. or, *resolved it,* as 2 Chron. 25.16. chap. 14.27. or, (which I conceive to be fittest here) *taken this course,* as Hab. 2.10. *thou hast taken a course to bring shame to thine house;* for all these being the wonted effects, and consequents of counsel, are oft contained respectively under that term; or, are taken in, together with it, so the word, *to consult,* is frequently used, for, by, or upon consultation, that is, counsel given, and taken, *to contrive, devise, purpose, resolve, take a course.* (Of which manner of speech see on chap. 14.12. and 22.18.) nor is the term of consulting in this notion unusual, as well in other learned languages, as in the Hebrew; for so both in Greek and Latin one is said to have *consulted well* or *ill for himself,* when the meaning is, that he has taken some course, either behooveful, or prejudicial to himself: which being not observed, has caused a misunderstanding of a proverbial verse, used both in Greek and Latin, whereby, as it is commonly taken, should be said, that *evil counsel is worst to the counselor,* or him that gives it; whereas the right meaning of it is, that *evil courses,* or *contrivements, are worst to the contrivers,* to him, or those, that contrive them, and take them, as Ps. 5.10. & 7.15,16. & 9.15,16. in the first of which places, the word *counsel* is also found thus used.

*{The crowning city*} Heb. *the crowning,* or *crowned one:* for the word *city,* as before, ver. 7. is not in the text: But so is Tyre termed, either as a stately princess (being a royal city, Jer. 25.22. & 27.3.) wearing a goodly rich crown, Ezek. 27.3. & 28.12–14. or, as one that crowns her followers, and favorites, her merchants, and inhabitants, with wealth and state, Ezek. 27.33.

*{Whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth*} With whom kings, princes, and great potentates trade; or, that makes those that trade under her, and with her, as rich, and as great as princes, Ezek. 37.21,33. See the Assyrian vaunts, ch. 10.8. and of Babylon, Rev. 17.2. & 18.3. Cineas one of King Pyrrhus his counsel, said of the Roman senate, it was *a council of kings.* Plutarch in *the life of Pyrrhus,* and Pyrrhus himself of Rome, that it was a *city of kings:* Jerome on this place.

**V. 9.** *{The Lord of hosts hath purposed it*} An answer to the former demand, ver. 8. declaring not only who it is that has contrived, resolved upon, and put in execution this design; (for the prophet speaks constantly of the overthrow of Tyre, as of a thing already done) but the end, and aim also that he had in so doing; to pull down the pride and insolency both of Tyre, and of those great states and persons, that were grown to a great height of haughtiness, the sin, that God most abhors, and can worst brook, Ps. 138.6. Prov. 3.34. & 6.16,17. ch. 2.12–17. Jam. 4.6. 1 Pet. 5.5.

*{Lord of hosts*} See ch. 1.9.

*{hath purposed it*} Heb. *consulted it.* See ver. 8. and his counsel shall stand, Ps. 33.11. ch. 14.24,26,27.

*{to stain the pride of all glory*} *to stain,* or *pollute,* by pulling down, or throwing down, as some polluted and filthy thing; to throw it down, as such, or by throwing down, to make it such, when it shall come to be trodden upon, and trampled under foot: so Psal. 89.30,44. chap. 14.12,19. and of Tyre, Ezek. 27.16,17. and 28.7. in both which places, the same word is used.

*{the pride of all glory*} The word translated *pride,* signifies first *excellency,* chap. 4.2. then *pride,* or *insolency,* ch. 13.11. because the one rises usually from the other: the latter, *beauty, loveliness,* such as pleases the eye, or the eye is wont to be taken with, as Gen. 3.6. Ezek. 24.16,21. 1 Joh. 2.16. of the word, see on ch. 4.2. All such goodly state, as people are wont to pride themselves in: And Tyre is principally taxed for her pride, Ezek. 27.3. & 28.2,5,12,13.

*{and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth*} Heb. *to make light,* properly, 1 King. 12.4. Jon. 1.5. then *to set light by, to contemn,* Ezek. 22.7. or, *to cause to be set light by;* to make contemptible, *to bring into contempt,* 1 Sam. 2.30. See Job 12.21. Ps. 107.40. Mal. 2.9.

*{all the honourable of the earth*} Or, *of the land,* as ver. 10. and chap. 5.8. and 9.19. either those of Tyre, and within her territory, as some; or more largely, and generally, of a great part of the known world; as others; which the subject matter of the next chapter seems to confirm: And indeed by the Assyrian was much done to that purpose, much about this time, chap. 10.9,10,14. & 36.18–20. as after, the like by the Chaldeans, Jer. 27.3,8. there is in the Hebrew an elegant antithesis, between *light,* and *weighty;* as if he had said, God is resolved to make *light,* or to bring into light account, all that bear *weight* in the world: for that the word properly imports. See ch. 3.5.

**V. 10.** *{Pass through thy land, as a river, O daughter of Tharshish*} These words some take, as spoken to the Tyrians, or inhabitants of Tyre advising them with all possible speed, to quit their country, and to betake themselves to some other place for safety, or implying, as some would have it, that they should pass away before the enemy into captivity. Others rather conceive them, to be spoken to the multitude of merchants, or traders by sea, whether of *Tarsus, Tartessus,* or other places, that had dealings at Tyre, to withdraw themselves from thence, and betake themselves to their own homes. See before on ver. 6.

*{Pass through thy land*} Or, *from thy land.* So those that understand it of the Tyrians, either fugitives, or captives: against which is objected, that the particle *from,* which is not here in the text, is never omitted, where mention is of motion, from place to place; to which may be returned; First, that in somewhat the like passages, as this, it is sometime suppressed, as chap. 18.7. and 52.2. And again, that the particle *from* is not of necessity here; *through,* which our English version has, will suffice, and is sometime omitted, as Chap. 47.2. Jer. 2.10. and lastly, that it may be simply rendered without either, *Pass,* or *Pass over thy land, like a river.* Make no stay in it: for the word of *Pass,* in this notion, of a motion from place to place, does frequently admit an accusative case attending it, Gen. 32.31. Num. 35.10. Deut. 2.4. the note whereof, is very commonly omitted. But others supposing the text not to speak of the Tyrians at all, but of those that traded with them, render it, *Pass away,* or *depart,* or *return to your own land,* go back to your own country, as Num. 22.26. Josh. 6.7. 1 Sam. 27.2. 2 Sam. 16.9. the particle *to,* or *unto* being oft-times concealed as Exod. 4.19. and 10.29. 1 Sam. 20.6. Jer. 20.6. See ver. 3.

*{as a river*} By this some understand, a swift, hasty, and speedy flight, alluding to the current of rivers, or land-floods, that falling by steep passages from higher grounds, run with a swift and strong stream, chap. 59.19. Amos 5.24. or, *as a river* that does not stop, or stay, but runs on without intermission until it arrive at the sea, Eccl. 1.7. Others conceive it, to intimate the flight of multitudes (understanding it of those that traded at Tyre) as in flocks, or shoals, in their passage overspreading the seas; because the term of *a river,* is used in Scripture; as also in other authors, to note abundance, and plenty, chap. 8.7. and 48.18. and the word here used, is not a word that is general, common to all rivers; but peculiar to Nilus, the river of Egypt, (which one of the Jewish doctors supposes to be here intended) used of the main body of it, in the singular form, Gen. 41.1,2, etc. Exod. 1.22. and 2.3. and 4.9. and 7.15, etc. and 8.5,7. and 17.5. chap. 19.7,8. ver. 3. Jer. 46.7,8. Ezek. 29.3,9. Amos 8.8. and 9.5. Zach. 10.11. of the many streams of it, in the plural, Exod. 7.19. and 8.8. Psal. 78.44. Chap. 7.18. and 19.6. Ezek. 29.3, etc. and 30.12. Now Nilus, though it rise high, and with abundance of water overspread the land, Jer. 46.8. Amos 8.8. and 9.5. yet it runs not swiftly, but gently and smoothly, as Pliny, l. 5. c. 8. Howbeit, all this hinders not, but that the phrase here may have a notion of speed, and haste, as well as of shoals and multitudes: Since that it is found used in the one notion, as well as in the other: nor is the word here used so peculiar to Nilus, but that it is used also, of other *rivers* and *streams,* as well in the singular form, Dan. 12.5,7. as in the plural, Job 28.10. 2 King. 19.24. chap. 33.21. and 36.25. nor does Nilus wholly run so, either slowly or quietly; but as is generally well known, with much violence, and exceeding swiftness in some places, at its falls especially, as Pliny in the same place relates; who says only, that as it comes down lower, where it finds more freedom, as wearied with its long passage, by so many turnings and windings, at length it runs more calmly, and quietly than before it did. As for those, that render the words, *pass through thy country, as men pass over a river;* or, as a *shallow brook* that men pass over on foot: they carry little show of probability with them, and I forbear therefore to insist on them.

*{O daughter of Tarshish*} By this circumlocution, some understand *Tyre,* or the inhabitants of it, (for the place is put commonly for those that therein abide. See chap. 1.27.) called *the daughter of Tarshish;* that is, of *the main sea,* or the *ocean,* because situate in the sea, maintained by the sea, and the famousest sea-town, and mart, for sea-traffic, in all those parts. See on ver. 1,2,6,7. Others, *Tarsus,* or *Tartessus* (the *daughter:* whether *Tarsus,* or *Tartessus,* or *of Tarsus,* or *Tartessus,* for *Tarsus,* or *Tartessus* itself, as the like, ver. 12.) as if the Tyrians were advised to flee thither, leaving their own land, the particle *to* or *unto,* being, though suppressed, yet to be supplied, as before. But against this, is objected, that where this form or metaphor of *daughter* is used; there, not so much the place itself, as the people, or persons, there residing or inhabiting is implied; which yet, it may be, need to be no bar to this exposition of the place; since that as well to the people of a place, as to the place itself, men may betake themselves for refuge. But others conceive it to signify the shipping that used to Tyre, *the daughter of Tarshish,* that is, *the ships of Tarshish,* as ver. 1. ships in heathen authors also being called *virgins,* or *damsels* of the sea; or the merchants that had trading at Tyre, so styled, either as some, from the principal place, that they belonged unto: whether *Tarsus,* or *Tartessus:* put here, to comprehend under its name, all places, whence any repaired to Tyre for traffic: or as other some, from *the main sea,* the midland especially, on which, their places of abode lay, and by which they traded to and fro.

*{there is no more strength*} The reason, why either the Tyrians should quit their country, or foreign people should leave them; to wit, because there was no place of shelter, or means of protection, and safety there, either for the one, or the other. See Ezek. 26.4. ver. 11,12. and somewhat the like, chap. 47.1.

*{strength*} Heb. *girdle.* as Psal. 109.19. where only, and in this place, it is in this form found; and in another, Job 12.21. by it, is understood, either the wall and rampire of Tyre, wherewith the city was begirt, ver. 4. but now gone, ver. 11. or her former might and power, whether by fortifications within her, or the sea about her, or her shipping, or her soldiery, or any other means whatsoever, now utterly impaired, ver. 4. the *girdle* being a usual emblem of might and strength, Job 38.3. chap. 11.5. and 22.21. in particular, some from the Chaldee paraphrast, would have the *girdle* here mentioned, to be their *soldiery,* because the military *belt,* or *girdle,* was a badge of that profession, 2 Sam. 20.8. Psal. 45.3. Others, the sea, wherewith it was begirt, until the enemy besieging it, by strange devices, and stupendous works, joined the isle it stood on to the continent, thereby to render it assailable from the shore: whereof see Curtius, l. 4. c. 3,4. and Pliny, l. 5. c. 19. but these two latter, though somewhat far fetched, yet without any such straining of the word, do of themselves, fall within compass of the former; for, as for their interpretation, it seems to me over-poor, and slender, (though some of good note mislike it not) who taking the word *girdle,* in its native notion, because they find *girdles* among other petty commodities, that merchants sometime trade in, Prov. 31.24. would have the meaning to be, that Tyre had been so rifled, and her wares so plundered, and swept clean away, that there was not so much as a *girdle* left in her.

**V. 11.** *{He stretched out his hand over the sea, he shook the kingdoms*} Or, *He hath stretched out his hand over the sea, and shaken the kingdoms.* The prophet returns again, after the former digression, or interjection, conceived as in way of advice, ver. 10. to show who it was, that had both contrived, and brought about that design against Tyre, ver. 8,9. or to fasten the words of this verse to that that went next before, unto the very close of ver. 10. he renders a reason, why Tyre was not able to retain her wonted strength, or to afford shelter, and safeguard any more, either to others, or her own, because the Lord has lifted up his hand against her, and the other states and kingdoms thereabouts; and has set out, and sent against her military forces, to make an end of her.

*{He*} That is, the Lord, to be supplied from ver. 9. or from the next branch. See the like, Hos. 13.9,10.

*{stretched out his hand over the sea*} Or *against the sea,* as Ezek. 16.27. that is, against Tyre, say some, situate within the sea, as ver. 4. or against the islands and provinces bordering upon the sea; to strike at her or them, or both, and to destroy either; as Jer. 15.6. and 51.27. Ezek. 6.14. & 14.9. & 16.27. & 35.7. & 35.3. And who can stay, or turn back his hand? ch. 14.27. Dan. 4.35. Howbeit, there seems to be an allusion to God's hand, that was sometime stretched, or held out over the red sea, when as Pharao, and his forces, were therein drowned and destroyed, Exod. 14.26,27. & 15.6,12. alluded to also, ch. 10.26. & 11.15. though I concur not with those of the Jewish commenters, or others, who suppose that story to be here intended, as produced to show, that God was as well able to destroy Tyre, and her allies, now, as he was to destroy Pharao and other great ones, then.
