See ver. 13.

*{He shook the kingdoms*} Or *made them quake;* as Deut. 28.65. 1 Sam. 14.15. Hab. 3.7,16. or as some render it, *he raised up,* or *moved the kingdoms:* as chap. 14.9. which they expound of God's stirring up Nebuchadnezzar, and the kings, or princes, of the provinces under him, to come against Tyre, Ezek. 26.7,12. But the word here used, is nowhere found to signify such a *moving,* or gathering together, as this exposition implies; but such a *shaking,* as is joined with *trembling,* and *terror,* Deut. 2.25. chap. 32.11. Jer. 33.9. Joel 2.10. Jer. 50.36. or such a *moving,* as is joined with *removing,* Job 9.6. 2 Sam. 7.10. 1 Chr. 17.9. not unlike that *shaking,* spoken of Hag. 2.21,22. Heb. 12.26,27. The kingdoms therefore here spoken of, are either the kingdoms of Tyre and Sidon, and those other on the sea coasts, that God had shaken and shattered, whether by the Assyrian, or the Chaldean, ver. 1,12. for Tyre and Sydon were two kingdoms, Jer. 37.3. beside that they may both seem to have had inferior kingdoms, or provinces, also under them, Jer. 25.22. and the prophet speaks of these things, as past, and done. See on ver. 3,4,5. or they are rather, as some other, those kingdoms and provinces that were made to *tremble,* and *shake,* being stricken with fear and terror, at the fall of Tyre. So Ezek. 26.15,18. than which, no other commentary needs on this place. And, howsoever I take it to be no relation, as some would have it, of what God did for his, either in Canaan, Josh. 12.7–24. or in their way to Canaan, after they had passed the red sea, Josh. 12.1–6. in shaking the kingdoms on either side Jordan: yet I suppose there is an allusion unto the stories of those times; and withal, as to the dreadful earthquakes, and shakings of the mountains, that seem to have accompanied some of those things then done; (See Psal. 77.16–18. & 114.4. Hab. 3.6,10.) so to the fear and terror, that upon the same, surprised the kingdoms and countries about them, Exod. 15.14,16. Josh. 2.9,11. See v. 5.

*{the Lord hath given a commandment against the merchant city, to destroy the strong holds thereof*} Or, *the Lord gave:* because the charge, in course of carriage, precedes the execution of the thing given in charge; it is the Lord of hosts, ver. 9. that set his soldiery, whether Assyrians, or Chaldeans, on work to do it; and therefore it could not but be done, ch. 14.27. and 55.11.

*{given a commandment*} Heb. *commanded,* or *charged:* a military term, as we also use it; whence the term of *a commander;* and it imports, by a kind of zeugmatical form, a *sending* of forces *with a charge.* So Amos 6.11. & 9.3,4,9. Some of which places are not so clearly rendered through want of this observation. The consultation, as at a council of war, and resolution upon it, was before, ver. 9. now there is a commission given out, for the putting of it in execution, and a mission of forces, with a strict charge to effect it: so ch. 10.6. & 13.3.

*{against*} Heb. *unto:* as Jer. 51.3. or *concerning;* as Jer. 22.11. but used also for *against:* as Est. 7.7.

*{the merchant city*} The word *city,* is not in the text, ver. 7,8. The term used here, rendered *merchant,* is *Canaan,* (whereof see chap. 19.18.) which some therefore retain, rendering the words, *against Canaan;* yet by *Canaan,* understanding *Tyre,* as so termed, because it stood within the compass of the country that was commonly called, and known by that name, Psal. 150.11. & 135.11. and fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, Josh. 19.29. see Mat. 15.21,22. or more generally, the relics of the Canaanites, abiding in Tyre, and Sidon, and the coasts thereabout. But it is by others rather deemed here to signify, as we render it, *a merchant;* for because the Phenicians, or Canaanites (compare Mat. 15.22. with Mar. 7.26.) were their land lying fit for navigation, much addicted to merchandise: hence it came to pass, that the word *Canaan* was used for *a merchant;* so it is taken, Hos. 12.7. Job 41.6. v. 8. and Tyre is so termed here, because a principal place for mart, and market for merchandise and merchants: see on ver. 2,3,8.

*{the strong holds thereof*} The strength of this place, how great and extraordinary it was, may appear by the long and sore pains, that it put Alexander and his whole army to, ere he could be master of it: whereof see Curtius, l. 4. c. 2,3,24. And this the prophet to express, seems to have coined a new word, nowhere else found, but here; and drawn it out in length longer than any, from the same root; as if one should say, with us, *her strengthednesses,* or *her fortificationnesses.*

**V. 12.** *{And he hath said, Thou shalt no more rejoice, O thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon*} Or, *He hath also said,* as ch. 8.8. & 23.9. because the prophet turns his speech from Tyre to Sidon, foretelling her overthrow, together with Tyres: see Ezek. 28.21. Jer. 47.4. Joel 3.4.

*{He*} The Lord, ver. 11.

*{hath said*} Has passed this doom or sentence upon you, as chap. 15.14.

*{thou shalt no more rejoice*} Heb. *thou shalt no longer add* (as ch. 1.13. & 7.10.) *to exult,* or *to revel;* to wit; as formerly you were wont to do, and as Tyre your daughter did, ver. 7. yet *no more,* or *no longer,* rather (because that solves the ambiguity) does not intend a perpetuity, but an intermission, or intercision, for the present, or for some space of time, at most, as some of the Jewish writers well observe, pointing us to the like forms, 2 King. 6.23. Prov. 31.7. for it is not unlikely, that as Sidon fell together with Tyre, so with Tyre she also rose, and recovered again: see ver. 17.

*{O thou oppressed*} Or, *O thou grievously oppressed:* for the word is in that form, that aggravates the simple notion of the theme, in which form the same is nowhere found, but here only; and our prophet is in his terms very pregnant and precise. This some suppose spoken, in regard of the damage that the Sidonian merchants should sustain by loss of their wares remaining at Tyre, when it was taken by the enemy: but it seems to imply much more than so; no less, than the like surprisal, and sacking also of their own city: as Ezek. 28.22,23. Some suppose that there is in the word an allusion to a virgin, or damsel, forced and ravished, Deut. 22.25. 2 Sam. 13.14. and this suits not amiss with the term here given to that state, or city; nor is it unusual, that such things are over-frequently acted in the surprisal of such places, Lam. 5.11. but I find not the word anywhere so used, or applied.

*{Virgin daughter of Zidon*} Or *Damsel, daughter Sidon.* By *virgin, daughter of Zidon,* most of our interpreters here understand Tyre, so called, say they, because founded at first by those of Sidon; as Justine, l. 18. see on ver. 4. Whom I should willingly assent unto; did I not observe the constant tenor of Scripture in forms of this kind, concerning states, and cities, without exception, running perpetually another way; which therefore induces, or enforces me rather, to go with those though fewer, Jewish writers, and ours, who conceive not Tyre, but Sidon itself here intended, called a *virgin,* or *damsel;* (for the word seems to be taken sometime not so strictly, as Joel 1.8.) either because she had hitherto continued untouched, unsubdued, unacquainted with any yoke of servitude, or any such grievous pressures as now she sustained; or because, for state and beauty, she was like to some young beautiful damsel of noble parentage, daintily brought up, and living at ease and in pleasure; *daughter of Sidon,* for *Sidon* itself; as *daughter of Sion,* for Sion itself: see on chap. 1.8. and *virgin,* or *damsel, daughter of Sidon;* as *virgin,* or *damsel, daughter of Sion,* chap. 37.22. and *virgin,* or *damsel, daughter of Babel,* ch. 47.1. and *virgin,* or *damsel, daughter of Egypt,* Jer. 46.11. where it may be observed, that the word *virgin,* or *damsel,* in such phrases, is constantly in a contract form, and has in a way of regiment therefore, a reference, as well as the word *daughter,* unto the noun following both of them: which I find no grammarians to have taken, or given notice of, by any rule for the like: and as *daughter* apart, so is *virgin,* or *damsel,* found apart, in this manner of speech; for so we read *the virgin,* or *damsel of Israel,* Jer. 18.13. and 31.4,21. Amos 5.2. in which frame of speech, *the virgin of Israel,* is not to be understood as *a virgin of Israel,* Deut. 22.29. that is, an Israelitish virgin, or a virgin that is some Israelites daughter, though the terms be just the same: but by *the virgin of Israel,* is to be understood, *Israel the virgin,* or *the virgin Israel;* as by *the city of London, the city London;* or, *London the city.* And it would further be observed, that these kind of forms, *the virgin,* or *damsel,* or *daughter of Sidon, Sion, Judah, Israel, Jerusalem, Moab, Edom, Egypt,* and the like are not found, but in the poetical and prophetical books of Scripture; or where something of either nature is inserted into the story.

*{arise, pass over to Chittim*} The like advice is here given to the Sidonians, that was before to the Tartessians, or Tarsenses, as some; to the Tyrians, as others, ver. 10.

*{arise*} This term does not always imply any particular present posture of body to be changed: as sitting, lying along, or the like: but it imports only, a speedy and sedulous addressing of oneself, without delay, and setting all other business aside, unto some special act, or work, employment, or journey, that he was not at, or on before, Gen. 13.17. and 19.15. and 27.19. Jon. 1.2. Mic. 4.13.

*{pass over to Chittim*} Leave Tyre, say some, for there is no more mart, or market, for you there, and seek out some other place for you to trade in: or, as others rather, leave your own place and seat, and seek you some place of shelter, and harbor elsewhere: the particle *to,* is wanting, as oft elsewhere: see on ver. 10. But some read the words, as spoken to Chittim: and the same advice given it, that was given Sidon before: *O Chittim, arise, and pass,* or *depart:* and the order of the words, as they lie in the original, seem to favor this interpretation: but the former I suppose to be genuine, and more agreeable to the tenor of the context: of *Chittim,* see on ver. 1.

*{there also shalt thou have no rest*} Having no assurance of safety anywhere, as Deut. 28.65,66. either the enemy's sword pursuing them, and following them whithersoever they flee, which some suppose shadowed before by the similitude of a river, that finds no place of rest anywhere, till it come to the sea, ver. 10. See the like, Lev. 26.33,36–38. Jer. 42.14–17. or the enemy every way, and on every side so prevailing, that no sure place of succor, or shelter, can anywhere be had: so Jer. 25.15–26. and 27.6–8. and 43.10,11. A learned author understands it, of the deportation of them unto Babylon, and other countries thereabout, Cissia, or Susiana among the rest; where yet they should not long be at rest, in regard of the Medes invading those parts: See on ver. 1.

**V. 13.** *{Behold the land of the Chaldeans: this people was not, till the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness*} The scope of the prophet in these words, by divers diversely expounded, seems to be, to meet with an objection; or to remove a doubt at least, that many might make, or have, against the verity, or concerning the certainty of that that is here denounced against Tyre and Sidon, as deeming it a thing, considering the present state and strength of them, if not utterly impossible, yet almost incredible, that they should be by any other people or power thus destroyed. This therefore the prophet shows, to be no such, either impossible, or incredible matter: either by pointing at those, by whom it should be done, a people of more antiquity and greater power than themselves, and that had been the first founders of them, and their state, as some; or as others, rather, by telling them of other states, to wit, the Chaldeans, or Assyrians, or both, which being far more ample and potent than theirs; yet had either the one by the other, or either of them, by some other, in like manner been destroyed: see the like, Ezek. 31.3–21. Amos 6.2. But that learned author, of whom, on vers. 12. supposes this to be subjoined, as rendering a reason, why in Chaldea they should not be long quiet, being that that land, also, God had devoted to destruction, chap. 13. & 14.

*{Behold the land of the Chaldeans*} This some understand of Tyre, as affirming it to have been sometime the Chaldeans: who, as they at first founded and peopled it, so now come to destroy it: Others, rather, of Chaldea, or, the Chaldeans by whom Babylon, and Nineveh, were then possessed, though not the first founders, or owners of them; and that, for all their greatness, were to be destroyed by the Medes and Persians, ch. 13. & 14. Jer. 50. & 51.

*{this people was not*} The Tyrians, say some, were neither so ample, nor so ancient a people, as the Chaldeans, or Assyrians, whom they suppose to be here the same; But the most go another way, or other ways rather: Some, the Chaldeans were not a people of any great note, or name, at first: See of their original, on chap. 13.19. Others, *there was not any like this people,* the note of similitude supplied; as ch. 22.18. there was no people comparable to them, as 2 King. 18.5. & 23.25. Others again, *this people now is not;* they are not now a free people, but a province, governed by an inferior king under the Assyrian, 2 Chr. 33.11. Dan. 2.37,38.

*{till the Assyrian founded it*} *it,* or *her,* that is, Tyre, say some; nor does that, say others, cross what is elsewhere related of its founding by others; of which, see on ver. 7,12. because those others were then under the Assyrian command: But others, *the land of the Chaldeans,* before mentioned; wherein the Assyrian, not Assur the son of Shem, Gen. 10.22. but Nimrod, the son of Cush, Gen. 10.8. built Babylon, and other cities, whose successors were called *Assyrians,* and their empire, *the Assyrian Monarchy;* after he had subdued that country held by Assur, and his before; and made Nineveh, there by him erected, the principal seat of his empire, Gen. 10.10–12. But some read the note, not *till,* but *since, since that the Assyrian founded it,* for *strange* people, that is, placed strange people in it, which they expound of the Samaritans, there seated by Salmaneser, 2 King. 17.16.

*{for them that dwell in the wilderness*} The word here used sometimes signifies *ships,* Num. 24.24. ch. 33.21. Ezek. 30.9. So some would have it here taken, that the Assyrian kings finding Tyre a fit place for shipping, did for that purpose at first build it. But it signifies also *deserts, waste,* and *dry* places, Psal. 63.1. & 74.14. and those that abide, or dwell in such places, whether persons, or other creatures, Psal. 72.9. chap. 13.21. Thus most here take it, that the Assyrian kings built cities in it; either for such people as were scattered abroad, here, and there, living in wild and waste places, after the Flood, Job 3.14. & 15.28. or; that dispersion caused by the division of tongues, Gen. 11.1–4. that they might convene, and be cemented, into a people, or a state: or, for such people of other nations, as having subdued, they there placed in the room of such colonies as they thence removed, and transplanted in other places, 2 King. 17.6,24. & 18.11.

*{they set up the towers thereof*} Properly, *watch-towers,* chap. 32.14. Jer. 6.27. they fitted them, not only for habitation, but for defense: Heb. *they set up his watch-towers,* that is, each company of people their own; as ch. 2.20. though some understand it of the princes of Babylon, endeavoring each one to strengthen his part what he could, in that city.

*{they raised up the palaces thereof*} To wit, of the land, or of the city: the former particle, or affix, was masculine, this feminine. See ch. 25.4. they built further, as for strength, so for state, chap. 13.19,22. Dan. 4.29,30. Howbeit, some read the words, *they have destroyed,* or, *demolished her palaces:* So the Chaldee paraphrast, whom some of the rabbins follow; and so the old Latin, whom some of ours, as if it came from the root that signifies *to raze,* Psal. 127.7. Jer. 51.58. Hab. 3.13. not from that *to raise,* chap. 14.9. Zach. 9.13. for they are near in sound, and letter, the one to the other; or, somewhat more rather, in Hebrew, than in English; but in this latter notion, I never find it applied to walls, or buildings; and I therefore embrace rather the latter sense, and read the words, *yet,* (as chap. 17.26.) *they razed her palaces;* or, *were her palaces razed,* as chap. 22.24.

*{and he brought it to ruin*} He that first founded it, to wit, Tyre, can, and shall ruin it, as some; or, as others, rather the Chaldean, or Assyrian state, Babylon, or Nineveh, or both, either already are, or shall be ruined: See chap. 13. & 14. Jer. 50. & 51. Nah. 1,2,3.

*{he brought it*} One brought it; or, *it was brought,* as chap. 22.8. Heb. *put it;* or, *made it, to a ruin,* or, *a ruin;* that is, a ruinous heap, as chap. 25.2. Jer. 12.11. See on chap. 1.7. So rather, than (as a learned man of late renders it) *cottages:* supposing the Punic word for *cottages,* deduced from the word of *ruin,* (for both the root, and the use of it show that it so signifies) here used: but neither does the notation of it, so well suit with the thing, thereby expressed; and the skillful in that language affirm, that it comes from a word, only by change of a letter, that with them signifies *an house.*

**V. 14.** *{Howl, ye ships of Tarshish*} As he began this denunciation of Tyres ruin, with an invitation of the ships of Tarshish, to howl in regard thereof; so he closes it here again with the like: concerning which, see on ver. 1.

*{for your strength is laid waste*} Or, *your fortress;* rather; and so ver. 4. to wit, Tyre, ver. 1.

**V. 15.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day*} At that time, wherein this prophecy shall be fulfilled: as ch. 10.20. & 22.20. In the passages following, there is first an extent with limitation of Tyres calamities, here foretold, how long they should continue, in this verse; and secondly, a gracious promise of her restitution, after that term of time expired, in the verses following.

*{that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years*} *forgotten,* that is, neglected, not regarded, not looked after, either by God or man: as Psal. 13.1. & 49.10. chap. 49.14. Jer. 2.32. Hos. 2.13. & 4.6. & 8.14. because things forgotten, are not regarded: hence, those caveats, so frequent, Exod. 20.8. Deut. 4.9,23. & 8.11,18. nor is it improbable, or impertinent, that one of the Jewish commenters here suggests, that the prophet should have some allusion to the condition of a harlot, *forgotten,* and forsaken by her lovers; since that it suits so well with what immediately follows, v. 16. so the word *forgotten* should have special reference to her merchants, whom her trade was with, before, ver. 17. see the like, Jer. 30.14. Howbeit it seems more general, and to include also God's disregarding of her, who is said to *visit* her again, v. 17.

*{seventy years*} Concerning this number, and the fixed terms of it, there is difference amongst interpreters: One surmises some corruption in the text; and that, as ch. 7.8. there is, as he conceives, *sixty,* for *six:* so here, *seventy,* for *seven:* and these *seven* years, he supposes to have been under Salmaneser, of whose invasion of Tyre, and interruption of their trade for five years together, see what was out of Menander alleged, on v. 1. But this seems to be somewhat overbold dealing with Scripture, both here, and before. Other interpreters therefore generally, reading the text, without any such alteration, deem these *seventy years* to concur with those of the Jewish captivity in Babylon, Jer. 29.10. Dan. 9.2. and that the rather, because not the kingdom of Judah only, but the other kingdoms also thereabouts, and those of Tyre and Sidon, among the rest, are said to be by God given, for the like time, into the hands of the Babylonian empire, to serve it, Jer. 27.3–8. and a commission to be made out from God to Nebuchadnezzar by name, for the taking, and sacking of Tyre, Ezek. 26.7–14. and Egypt assigned to him, as pay, for him and his forces, in way of recompense for their service, therein performed, Ezek. 29.18–20. Howbeit, that prediction of Tyres destruction in Ezekiel, seems to reach further than this, since that this goes with a limitation, and a promise of restitution at the expiration of those years; whereas there is denounced a final and perpetual devastation, without any restitution, Ezek. 26.14. as of Babylon, ch. 13.20.

*{according to the days of one king*} This one king, a late writer would have to be Salmaneser, during whose reign and life, Tyre was never able to recover the damage that by him she sustained, whereof above. But this sandy conceit I let pass, because it is founded on that which directly crosses and controls the text. The Jewish interpreters that hold to it, yet are of divers minds about the meaning of it; some of them understand it of David, who is said to have lived *seventy years,* being thirty years old when he came to the crown, and holding the kingdom forty more, 2 Sam. 5.4. which put together, make *seventy.* But one of them confesses ingenuously that he knows no reason, why Davids life should be there intimated, as the limit of such a time: which yet another, to meet with, says it might be; because there was a league of amity between their king and David, 1 King. 5.1. to mind the Tyrians of the breach of it, which had brought this calamity upon them: See on ver. 1. And some Christian writers, who take this way, say; because the name of David was exceeding precious among the Jews, and all his acts and occurrents, of special observation with them: But these reasons seem to be of very small moment: Others therefore suppose, that the ordinary limit of man's life is here aimed at, as it is circumscribed, Psal. 90.10. by Moses, and by heathen men, as Macrobius on Scipio's dream, l. 1. c. 6. but said, *of a king,* rather than of a man; that is, of such an one, as lives freely, and choicely, not tired out with pains-taking, not exposed to such occurrences and inconveniences as are wont to shorten man's life, in such manner, as others usually are: and the rather (adds the rabbin) he says, *of a king,* because Tyre, whom he speaks of, had lived as a queen, or a princess, ver. 8. But the most probable, and, as I take it, the genuine meaning of the words, is that, which another of them gives, *according to the days,* that is, the reigns, or continuance in reign, as chap. 1.1. *of one king,* that is, of one kingdom; as Dan. 7.17. & 8.21. to wit, in the days or reigns of Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his son's son, who successively held the Chaldean empire, during the time of those *seventy years,* Jer. 17.7. For those writers of ours wrong them, who would father such an absurd opinion upon them, as if by *the days of one king,* they should understand Nebuchadnezzar, supposing him to have reigned himself full *seventy years,* which indeed is most untrue; for he reigned but forty three years in all, both with his father, and by himself; as out of Berosus his *Chaldean,* or *Babylonian stories,* Joseph *against Apion;* which agrees well with the holy story, wherein we find upon record, that in the *eighth* year of his reign, he carried Jehojachin away captive, 2 Kin. 24.12. and withal, that he reigned not above *seven and thirty* year after that, 2 King. 25.27. which put together, make up much about the same sum, but come far short of seventy: Nor could those Jewish writers be ignorant of this: nor do they say, that Nebuchadnezzar is this *one king,* but expressly, that *he, his son, and his son's son, are accounted as one king.*

*{after the end of seventy years*} The time set for her desolation, and the discontinuance of her wonted state being expired, what time the Babylonian yoke shall be broken; she also among other people, that had formerly been in bondage under that empire, shall recover her liberty, and return to her former trading again.

*{shall Tyre sing as an harlot*} Heb. *it shall be to Tyre, according to the song of an harlot.* Or, as some, *there shall be with Tyre, as the song of an harlot.* Which some understand of a song sung to a harlot: such a song shall be sung to her, as men use to sing to a harlot, that has for some space of time been left, and not looked after, in regard of some disease, or other like disaster, which she has now overcome, and is recovered of again, inciting her to use means for the regaining of her lovers: and such a song they suppose to be that, which follows, ver. 16. But most take it, for a song used by a harlot, to draw those again to her, as they pass by, who had formerly abandoned her: and some therefore render it, *there shall be in Tyres* mouth, *as the song of an harlot,* which our English well expresses. The meaning is, that Tyre, upon the ruin of that empire, which had at the first rising of it to its height, subdued her, and till that time kept her down, having now recovered her liberty, shall by all means labor to set up her former market and trade, and to draw merchants and customers to her again. Howbeit, I suppose they are over-nice on the one side, that would have Tyre, that was termed a *virgin* before, while yet unsubdued, ver. 12. to be styled now a *harlot,* as forced and deflowered: for neither was it Tyre, but Sidon, that was so termed; nor is she considered as unsubdued, where she is so termed; nor is it violent enforcement, but voluntary prostitution which makes anyone a harlot. As also do those mince it too much on the other side, who by the word here used, would not have to be meant *an harlot,* but one that earns her living by some honest, but mean employment; as by being a hostess, or a huckster, or one that cries some sorry wares about, which they use to do sometime with a song, and some also, in some countries, with the tinkling of a pan, or the like, as tinkers do, thereof so termed with us: that which they think also alluded unto, ver. 16. So they suppose the word to be taken, where it is given unto Rahab, Josh. 2.1. & Heb. 11.31. (and it is not improbable, that the word there signifies a *hostess,* or *victualer,*) and of those two women that contended before Solomon for the child, 1 King. 3.16. of which yet, more doubt may justly be made. And it is true indeed, as appears by a poem ascribed commonly to Virgil, that hostesses in those times did usually by such singings and jinglings, invite customers to them; but those that so did, were commonly light housewives; such as are alluded to, Prov. 9.13–17. and the words following here, ver. 17. where it is said, *She shall return to her hire, and commit fornication with the kingdoms of the world,* do evidently show, that no other than a harlot is here meant: not as if merchandise were a dishonest or unwarrantable course, being of great and necessary use, and in the Word of God not approved only, but commended too, Ps. 107.23. Pro. 31.14,24. Eccl. 11.1,2. which last place seems to intend traffic, rather than alms-deeds: but the one is resembled by the other, because gain is intended as well in the one as in the other: and in regard of some similitude, or proportion, in some particular that the one has to the other, are good and commendable exercises, sometime compared unto courses evil and unjust. See Luk. 16.1–8,9. for I fear they go again a little too far, who would have the comparison here intended, to hold in regard of the fraud and iniquity; or, the tricks and devices, found and used commonly in either; whence *the mammon of iniquity,* Luk. 16.9. as also that of Solomon, Prov. 20.14. and that of Sirachs son, Ecclus. 27.2. For merchandising is here considered simply, as a gainful course; and the gain thence arising, not as evil-gotten gain, but as such gain as might warrantably come into God's treasury, where *the hire of a harlot* might not be admitted, Deut. 23.18. such as might well go for an offering unto God, who abhors an oblation made of ill-gotten goods, Ch. 61.8. Jer. 7.9,11. Mic. 6.6,7,11. See ver. 18.

**V. 16.** *{Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot, that hast been forgotten*} The prophet proceeds in his former similitude, comparing Tyre to a harlot, that having grown out of request, uses all means, as melodious music of voice and instruments, among the rest, to come into some request again; yet he may withal seem to allude to her wonted music mentioned, Ezek. 26.13. & 28.13.

*{harp*} See Chap. 5.12.

*{go about the city*} To seek customers, Prov. 7.11,12. see the like, in a honester and fairer way, Cant. 3.2. & 5.6.

*{harlot, that hast been forgotten*} See on ver. 15.

*{make sweet melody*} *good striking,* or, *hand-music,* so the word properly imports. See Chap. 38.20. the Hebrew phrase is, *do well to strike,* for, *strike well,* skillfully, cunningly, pleasantly. So 1 Sam. 16.17. one *doing well to strike;* for, one that can strike skillfully, play cunningly; and *do well to strike,* for strike skillfully, play cunningly, sweetly, pleasantly, Psal. 33.3.

*{sing many songs*} Heb. *multiply song;* as, *multiply soap,* for, use much soap, Jer. 2.22. *multiply sin,* for, commit many sins, 2 Chr. 33.23. and *multiply vision,* for, afford many visions, Hos. 12.11.

*{that thou mayest be remembered*} Thought upon, sought to, regarded, visited, as ver. 17. brought to remembrance with those, that had forgotten you, and grown into some request again. So Gen. 30.22. & 40.23. with 41.9. 1 Sam. 1.19. Ps. 22.27. See ver. 15.

**V. 17.** *{And it shall come to pass after the end of seventy years*} Or, *at the end.* Heb. *from the end:* as Gen. 8.6. Exod. 12.41. Deut. 5.1. when so many years are once expired. See on ver. 15.

*{that the Lord will visit Tyre*} God's visitations are of two sorts; either of mercy, as Ruth 1.6. Psal. 65.9. Luk. 1.68,78. & 7.16. & 19.44. or, of judgment, Exod. 20.5. & 34.7. Chap. 13.11. & 26.14. See Ch. 24.21,22. This of Tyre here, is in mercy; and it is said not that her merchants shall visit her, repair to her, and renew their former trade again with her; but that *the Lord shall visit her,* to show that this her recovery, and rising again, shall not be effected, or come to pass by mere casualty, or her own might, or skill and the means mentioned, or intimated to be used by her, but a gracious and powerful passage of God's providence, in mercy minding her, and making the means used by her, successful and effectual to that purpose. See Deut. 8.18. Ps. 127.1,2. Prov. 10.20.

*{and she shall turn to her hire*} Heb. *return,* and so it would be rendered, as Levit. 22.13. chap. 6.13. for it has reference apparently to Tyres former trading, ver. 2,3,6. she shall return to her wonted trading.

*{hire*} The word signifies not properly only, but generally, the hire of a *hore* (for so should it be written, according to the true and due notation of it, not *whore*) or, a harlot: either given to her, or given by her, for impure purposes: So Deut. 23.18. Ezek. 16.31,34,41. Hos. 9.1. Mic. 1.7. nor is the verb, from whence it comes, used any otherwise, Hos. 8.9,10. Howbeit, it is used in way of similitude, or resemblance, for gain arising from commerce and traffic, and consequently trade and traffic itself; as another word of very near affinity to it, of the same family, and of the self-same notion with this, is used Hos. 2.14. (being nowhere else found) in the like way of similitude for such commodities as the Israelites had, and received by their commerce and trade with other neighboring nations; the main matter taxed in them there, being not simply, that they had trade with them, and such commodities thereby from them, but that they ascribed them wholly unto those whom they dealt with, and not to God: nor to him from whom they received those commodities by them, Hos. 2.7,8. As in Nehemiah's time, they are blamed, not simply for trading with Tyre and Sidon, but for violation of God's day, in their trading with them, Neh. 10.31. & 13.16–21.

*{and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the world*} Or, *play the harlot,* as the word is rendered, Genes. 38.24. she shall have commerce with people of all kingdoms and provinces, as a common strumpet has with all comers, Ezek. 16.15,25. & 23.43,44. for the prophet persists still in his former comparison: Nor does this note here, an insatiable excess of wickedness, as some would have it, as Rev. 17.2. & 18.3. but an amplitude of commerce and trade, such as before she had. See on ver. 8.

*{world*} Heb. *earth:* as Ch. 37.16,20. but here rendered *world,* because *earth* follows: so Rev. 11.15.

*{upon the face of the earth*} The word seems more specially to imply the earth tilled, trodden, and traded on, by mankind, Psal. 104.24. Chap. 13.14. & 24.21. & 30.23,24. This clause some refer to Tyres trading, she shall trade with them, not in corners privily, but in open sight and view, publicly: or, with much pride and pomp, as ch. 57.7–9. Ezek. 16.15,16,24,25,31. But others rather with the Chaldee paraphrast, to the kingdoms next before, as noting the generality of them, from whence out of all the habitable parts and quarters of them, people had recourse to Tyre, as recourse is wont to be even from foreign parts, to some strumpets of special note. Ezek. 16.15. See Deut. 14.2.

**V. 18.** *{And her merchandise, and her hire shall be holiness to the Lord*} In this last passage, as in the close of other sad prophecies before, chap. 18.7. & 19.18–25. the prophet subjoins an intimation of the conversion of the Tyrians unto God, in the kingdom of his Christ, yet delivered in forms, alluding to the manner of God's solemn service, then in use: as Chap. 60.9,10,13,14. Mal. 1.11. And to the days of the Messiah, do some of the rabbins refer it, though some other of them, to the times of their return from captivity under the second Temple.

*{And*} Or, *Yet:* as Chap. 17.8.

*{her merchandise, and her hire*} Heb. *hires,* the word before used, but here plural; that is, the gettings, earnings, or gains of her merchandise: or, thereby accruing to her: of the phrase, see Chap. 4.5. and hence appears, what before was meant by *hire,* ver. 17.

*{holiness to the Lord*} It shall be a great part of it, devoted and consecrated to God's service; set apart for pious and sacred uses. There is an allusion in the words, to the motto engraven on the High Priest's golden frontlet, Exod. 39.30. so Levit. 27.30. Josh. 6.19. Jerem. 31.40. Zach. 14.20. For it is a very absurd conceit that a Popish writer has, that Tyres gain gotten by her trading, should be called *sacred,* as an accursed or abominable thing, like the goods of Jericho, Josh. 6.17,18. or like the hire of a harlot, Deut. 23.18. because the word signifying *sacred* in Latin, is sometimes used for detestable; and one in sound somewhat like the word of *holiness* here used, does signify an impure person, in that place of the Law before mentioned, and elsewhere, Gen. 38.21. 1 King. 15.12. & 22.46. and that therefore it was not to come into God's treasury; directly contrary to what immediately follows.

*{it shall not be treasured, nor laid up*} It shall not be reserved or laid up for any profane use, either public, or private. One of the Jewish writers thus distinguishes the words, It shall neither be carried into the king's treasury, nor reserved (as durable substance; so the word properly signifies, chap. 33.6.) for issue, for posterity, 2 Chron. 12.14. the former word is used commonly of public reserves, Neh. 10.39. Ch. 39.6. Mal. 3.10. the latter of private, Pro. 15.6. & 27.14.

*{for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the Lord*} *for,* or, *but,* as chap. 2.6. *her merchandise,* that is the gain thence arising, Prov. 3.14. *for them that dwell,* or, sit, or, *abide before the Lord's presence,* or, *in the Lord's presence,* for his ministers that attend upon him in his house, the place of his special presence and residence among his people, Deut. 10.8. 2 Sam. 7.18. Psal. 27.4. & 42.2. & 61.7,8. & 84.4. & 134.1.

*{to eat sufficiently*} Heb. *to eat unto satiety,* or *fullness,* as Levit. 25.19. & 26.5. Prov. 13.25. that God's ministers may have food sufficient, even to the full, 2 Chron. 31.10. Malac. 3.10. Some expound it, of the Tyrians making great feasts after the time of their recovery: by occasion whereof, they should lavish out their money upon corn, wine, and flesh, which the land of Israel abounded in, and so their earnings should fall into the hands of God's people; if it had been said, they should bring them to Jerusalem, and spend them there in sacred feasts; that God's ministers might feed, and feast with them with it, it had been somewhat to the purpose. See Deut. 14.23–29. & 16.11,14. But the exposition given, as before, is not only forced, and far fetched, but it is clean beside the intent and scope of the place.

*{and for durable clothing*} Heb. *covering,* as the like term imports, Gen. 8.13. Exod. 26.14. so is raiment called, in regard of the principal use of it to cover the body, and to shelter it against outward annoyances, Hos. 2.9. 1 Tim. 6.8. Rev. 3.18. & 16.15. The word rendered *durable,* as Prov. 8.18. does in his prime notion signify *old,* 1 Chron. 4.22. Psal. 6.7. but sometime *hard,* or *harsh,* and *stiff,* Psal. 31.18. & 75.5. whence some render it *thick;* such, say they, as the wool, in Palestine, made. The rabbins *precious,* or *of worth,* from that in the Proverbs, such as ancient things sometimes are, as in regard of their worth, kept and reserved. Others, as ours, *durable;* such as will last long, as the original word has a notion sometime of *continuance* only, not of decay, Job 21.7. See the like form, Chap. 65.22. The meaning is, that from the Tyrian trade, they being converted to God, means and maintenance should be freely and largely afforded unto God's ministers, as well for apparel, as for food.

### CHAPTER 24

**Vers. 1.** *{Behold the Lord maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof*} Here begins a new sermon, or prophecy, more general than those going before; and seems to comprehend not the land of Israel alone, or Judea alone; (unto which some would restrain it) but the countries also on every side near to either; and such of them, especially, as had exercised enmity with them, or been unuseful stays to them, as the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Philistines, the Syrians, the Ethiopians, the Egyptians, the Idumeans, the Arabians, the Tyrians, the Sidonians, against whom he had formerly, in more particular manner prophesied; and to have been executed, partly by the Assyrians, and partly by the Chaldeans, the two principal instruments and executioners of God's judgments on those people, Chap. 10.5,14. and 14.12,17. Jer. 50.23. and afterward also, by others, upon them. See the like Jerem. 25.15–38. & 27.2–8. Howbeit, as those straiten it too much, that confine it to the narrow limits of Judah and Israel, so they over-widen it much more, that would extend it to the general day of doom, which many passages in it do clearly control. The whole sermon reaches unto the end of the 27. Chapter.

*{Behold*} The prophet's usual preface to the relation of remarkable acts, either of judgment, or of mercy. See Chap. 7.14. & 17.1.

*{the Lord maketh the earth empty*} Heb. word for word, *Behold, Jehovah emptying the earth, and laying waste;* as himself, by the Spirit of prophecy, seeing God already in doing it, and inviting others by the eye of faith grounded on this prophecy, revealing as much to them, to behold the same with him. So Chap. 3.1. & 13.9.

*{maketh the earth empty and waste*} For, *the earth,* see on Chap. 13.5,11. *emptying* it of its inhabitants, either slain on it, or removed out of it: *laying it waste,* by destroying, and spoiling all of worth, or use in it, and on it; as if he were bringing it to its first condition, without all form and furniture, Gen. 1.2. See the like, Nah. 2.10. where both words are found; the latter here, and there, only; which though most of the Jewish interpreters here expound, as we do, yet some of them would from the Arabic give it other far fetched notions, which I forbear to recite. See ver. 3.

*{turneth it upside down*} Heb. *perverteth the face of it;* as Lam. 3.9. where, and here, only, the word is found in that form: he so transforms it, that it has not that face and fashion, that before it had. Which some apply more specially, to what follows, ver. 2. and expound of a preposterous disposition of states and conditions; that whereas in due course, the master should lead, and the servant follow, the mistress lead, and the maid attend; the ruler be respected, and the subject less regarded: all should now be turned a clean contrary way.

*{scattereth the inhabitants of it*} By flight from their enemies invading them, or deportation by the enemy, having surprised them. So Gen. 11.8. Deut. 28.25. 2 King. 17.6. & 18.15. Jer. 13.24. & 18.17. Ezek. 5.10.

**V. 2.** *{And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest: as with the servant, so with his master, as with the maid, so with her mistress*} Heb. word for word: *as the people, as the priest,* or, *prince;* as Hosh. 2.9. and so in the rest: whence some read, *there shall be like people, like priest,* and so forward; supposing the sense to be, that there should be a general confusion, no order, no distinction, or regard of persons, in church or state; as chap. 3.5. whereof some expound, that perverting the face of things, ver. 1. But others rather as ours render it, *it shall be, as with the people, so with the* *priest,* or, *prince;* and so on. The sense being, as they conceive, that all estates and conditions should fare alike, none, in regard of eminency of place, or state, spared, Chap. 2.9. & 5.9. 2 Chron. 36.17. Lam. 5.12.

*{the priest*} The priests being such, say some, as Jeroboam made, of the meanest of the people, 1 King. 12.31. or such, as by their miscarriages, and God's just judgment thereupon, were become vile and contemptible with the people, 1 Sam. 2.12,17,22,30. Mal. 2.3,8,9. Or, *the prince;* for so the word sometime signifies. See Gen. 41.45. Exod. 2.16. & 3.1. and on such does God oft-times, for the like causes, cast contempt, Job 12.21. Psal. 107.40. But this seems to look another way, to wit, that neither priest nor prince, or this latter rather, here, principally, I suppose, intended, should escape more than any of the common sort of people: see the same word used in the same place; but distinctly for both offices, 2 Sam. 8.17,18. & 20.25,28.

*{his master*} Heb. *Lord,* but so used, Gen. 39.20. Exod. 21.4,6. Deut. 23.15.

*{as with the buyer, so with the seller*} Or, *so with the buyer, as with the seller;* for the very same particle is in either member, and admits either notion here rather thus, than as before; because in the three former branches, the better condition, and more likely to do well, to wit, *the prince, the master, the mistress,* were in the latter place; whereas in these three latter branches, the better estate, to wit, *the buyer, the lender, the letter,* are in the former. He that by purchasing made account to mend his estate, shall be in no better plight, in regard thereof, than he that has made it away, and embezzled thereby his means. See Ezek. 7.12,13. and see somewhat the like, but in another notion, 1 Cor. 7.30.

*{as with the lender, so with the borrower*} Or, *so with the lender, as with the borrower;* neither having any surety of what he owns, or what he owes; nor any man more of what is in his own hands, than of what is in another's. Of the use of the words, see Ps. 37.1. & Pro. 22.7.

*{as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him*} Or, rather, *so with the letter on usury, as with him, to whom he letteth on usury;* for so it is, word for word in the text: as also, Deut. 24.11. *the man to whom thou lendest,* or *lettest;* for, the word is in either place the same, and the word both here and there used, is of a large extent, comprehending as well free *lending,* as *letting* upon consideration, as the Greek *δανείζειν,* which it answers unto, also sometime does. See Lu. 6.34,35. The Hebrew commenters therefore to distinguish this branch from the former, say some of them, that the former spoke of those that *let,* or *lent out money:* this latter of those that *lent,* or *let out* victual, or any such other thing, Deut. 23.19. others of them, that the former is meant of such as *lend* what they have freely: this latter, of such as *lend* upon pledge or pawn, as Deu. 24.11. where yet no consideration is mentioned, or necessarily implied; but the contrary rather: for it speaks of *a brother,* of whom they were forbidden to take interest, Deut. 23.19. so that the pawn seems to be there intended only as security for the principal. Howsoever, this latter distinction here seems more probable than the former. But though the parties here and there mentioned, are for good cause to be distinguished, yet the particle, or note of similitude, is the very same here, that was in all the former branches; and that learned scholiast was much mistaken (though not the first that here tripped) in supposing the term here to be altered; and the word *caasher* to be no more here, than (as in other places oft it is) the same with the Latin *sicut,* or *quemadmodum;* the English, *as,* or, *in like manner;* whereas indeed it is more than so, and it is to be taken asunder, as oft elsewhere; the *ca* itself alone, as in the former branches, importing as much as he would have signified by the whole; and the latter part, to wit, *asher,* being here a relative distinct from it, and looking forward, not to the particle next it, but to the pronoun demonstrative, by an elegant redundancy, in that language very usual, subjoined in the close of the sentence, the very like construction whereunto is precisely found in that parallel to this, Deut. 24.11. Howbeit herein I concur with that learned writer, for the reason before rendered (which yet by him is here crossed) that albeit in the three first branches, the former particle is to be rendered *sicut, as,* the latter, *sic, so;* and that therefore in the former part of the verse, the sentence runs aright, as our version has it, *as with the people, so with the prince;* and so forward: yet in the three latter branches, (and not in the two latter only, as he grounding upon his forementioned mistake would have it) the text ought rather to be rendered, *so with the buyer, as with the seller;* and so forward; as if he had said, as the prince, or priest, shall fare no better than the common sort of people; the master or mistress than the man or maid-servant; so it shall be no better with the richer sort, with well-monied men (such as use to purchase, are able to lend, and are wont to let money out to use) than with those of poor and meaner condition, such as are fain to sell, and are constrained oft to borrow, or to take money up at interest: either of which to be enforced unto, is made a note of penury, Deut. 15.6–8. & 28.12. Nehem. 5.3,4. Prov. 22.2,7. & 29.13. Thus a mistake has yet ministered a hint of that, which gives some light for the right conceiving of the text. Nor were the mistake so much to be regarded, but that it has bred another more material, as one error usually begets another. As therefore there was before observed some difference among the Jewish writers about the distinction of this branch from the former; so is there no less variance among them about the stating of the two terms used in this branch. For one of them misled by that former mistake, would have by the former term here used, to wit, *nosheh,* to be understood, *the taker up* of money at interest, or the *borrower;* and by the latter term, to wit, *nosheh bo,* the *letter out,* or, the *lender,* therein controlling another that had gone before him, and went a diverse way; and with him concur some great masters in that language; as also some late interpreters of prime note; and the Chaldee, and ancient Greek, seem to go the same way with him. But that ancienter critic by the former term *nosheh,* understands the *creditor,* or *letter out,* the *money-master,* as he terms him; and by the latter, *asher nosheh bo,* that is, *he to whom he letteth out,* or, *lendeth,* the *debtor,* the *taker up,* or the *borrower;* and in his steps tread most of the Latin, and all our English versions; as also the order of the terms in the former branch pleads for it; where the *lender* stands before the *borrower,* as the *letter* here before the *taker;* the *creditor* in either before the *debtor:* and the constant use of the word *nosheh,* never found used any otherwise than for one that *lends,* or *lets out,* does abundantly confirm it. See Exod. 22.25. Deut. 24.11. 2 King. 4.1. Ps. 109.11. nor does the word itself taken apart by itself, signify any other thing in the one member than it does in the other; but the self-same thing in both: Howbeit, the words taken entirely together, as they make up the latter member of the sentence, *he whom he letteth to him,* as Deut. 24.11. *the man whom thou lendest to him;* (for so in either place the words expressly are) they do evidently design the *debtor:* all the difference between these two parallel places is, that there is a defect of the antecedent (such as is found, Ruth 1.16,17. & 2.9. 1 King. 18.12.) in the one, which is expressed in the other. But so lastly, 1 Sam. 22.2. where it is said, as our version renders it, *every one that was in debt;* it is in the original, word for word, *every one whom a lender,* or *letter, was to him* (the redundancy before observed, there also found) that is, *every one that had a creditor,* or *every one that was indebted.* And thus much for the precise notion of the terms. Now from hence some observe, that those of the ten tribes (whom alone they suppose this prophecy to concern) had not regarded to observe the Law of God, by Moses enacted, against taking *usury* of their brethren, Exod. 22.25. Lev. 25.36,37. Deut. 23.19,20. as also many other of God's ordinances, v. 5. And it is true indeed, that not they alone, but the Jews also were oft-times very faulty that way, as appears, Neh. 5.2–7. Ezek. 22.12. as well as in not releasing their servants at the six years end, Jer. 34.8–11. But this prophecy, though it concern the Israelites among others, yet it respects other nations besides them, as was before said: nor is this here mentioned, more than any of the former, as a matter of iniquity, but as a note of some men's more plentiful estate than others, and an occasion of their commerce and dealing with others, usually of meaner and lower condition, with gain and advantage to themselves; notwithstanding which, yet they should be no more secured in these distracted times, than the poorest of those they dealt with. See Jer. 15.10.

**V. 3.** *{The land shall be utterly emptied, and utterly spoiled*} *The land.* Heb. *earth;* as ver. 4. of Israel, say some; of Judah, other some: but all that circuit of land, rather, devoted to destruction, against the same here denounced. See ver. 1,4. Heb. *shall emptying, be emptied; and spoiling, spoiled,* the word in either branch doubled, for the more emphasis, as the like, Gen. 2.17. & 37.33. Exod. 18.18. & 19.13. 2 King. 3.23. Cant. 8.7. and the latter word here confirms the exposition given of the second, in ver. 1. *emptied,* as ch. 19.3. *spoiled,* as ch. 10.6. & 17.14.

*{for the Lord hath spoken this word*} God has passed this doom upon it. See ch. 21.17. or, as some, *hath spoken this thing,* as Num. 30.1. & 36.6.

**V. 4.** *{The earth mourneth and fadeth away*} Or, *It fadeth away;* for so runs the Hebrew without the copulative; *the earth it mourns, it fades away;* there is a fineness of language in the original, which our English cannot so fitly express; as if it were said, *it wails, it fails;* or, *it quails.* The former may have reference to the *emptying* forementioned, by voidance of her inhabitants, as ch. 3.27. Lam. 1.4. the latter, to the spoil, before pointed at, of her fruit, and other furniture, as ch. 1.30. See ver. 1,3.

*{the world languisheth, and fadeth away*} By *the world* here, some still press to have understood the land of Israel, being as a little world within itself, sequestered and severed from other people, by those special rites and ordinances assigned them by God, which other nations had not, Deut. 4.7,8,34. & 7.6. & 26.17,18. Ps. 147.19,20. Rom. 3.1,2. and 9.4. but they produce no place, where it is so termed; and the term, as it is of a far larger extent; so it evinces this prophecy to reach far further, than they would have it. Of the word, see ch. 13.11. & 14.17.

*{languisheth*} See chap. 16.8. & 19.8. Ezek. 7.17.

*{and fadeth away*} The text runs here, also, elegantly on the letter, *it faints, and fails,* or *falls;* but there is a metaphor from the faintness of a feeble and crazy body, pining, and spent in a manner, with some long and lingering disease, in the one, 1 Sam. 2.5. Neh. 4.2. Ps. 6.2. See ch. 17.4. from plants that withering and fading, shed their flowers and their leaves, ch. 1.30. or, from the leaves and flowers themselves, that so wither and fall, in the other, Ps. 37.2. ch. 28.4. & 34.4. & 40.7.

*{the haughty people of the earth do languish*} Heb. *the height,* or, *haughtiness of the people of the earth,* not, does, but, *do languish.* Which some of the Jewish commenters taking in the former sense, for *height,* which it first, and properly signifies, ver. 21. ch. 2.13,14. & 14.10,13. & 22.16. expound it of great ones, in power and place, set higher than others: as, *the height of his cedars,* for, the *highest,* and *tallest* of them, chap. 37.24. so, *the height of the people,* for, the *highest,* and greatest among them: they that sit loftiest among them faint, as well as those that lie lowest; as even the tallest men, and the greatest bodies stoop, and grow faint and feeble with sickness, as well as the lowest, and the least. So chap. 1.5. & 2.9. & 5.14. But the most take it in the latter sense, for *haughtiness:* as Deut. 8.14. Psal. 131.1. Prov. 30.13. as *pride,* for a *proud person;* or, *proud* persons, Jer. 50.31. Psal. 36.11. and, *might,* for, *mighty* ones, chap. 3.25. so, *haughtiness,* for, *haughty* ones; and, *the haughty ones of the people of the earth,* for, the *haughtiest,* among the people upon earth: as, *the wicked of the nations,* for, the *worst,* and *wickedest* among them, Ezek. 7.24. The haughtiest, those that heretofore carried their heads highest in any place among them, do now droop, and hang the head. See chap. 2.12,17. It may well include both; the one usually causing, and accompanied with the other, ch. 5.13. Ezek. 31.10.

**V. 5.** *{The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof*} A reason of the former denunciation is here rendered, why God was resolved thus to proceed against the world, and the people thereof; to wit, in regard of their sins, and grievous transgressions, whereby both those other nations, and his own people, violating as well the Laws of Nature in general, as his special institutions and ordinances, had defiled and polluted the places of their respective abode, which should, therefore, cast them up, and spew them out, as some impure and loathsome matter, that made them sick, and qualmy, until they were rid and eased of them, Levit. 18.25–28. Lam. 3.13–15.

*{The earth also*} Or, as some, *The land also;* that is, say they, even the land of Israel and Judah; not of other nations at large only: that land, that should have kept itself free from such defilement as other people are polluted with, Lev. 11.43,44. & 18.16,18. Ezek. 14.11. and so indeed, is the copulative used, chap. 13.4. & 22.9. but the article is no other here, than was, ver. 1,4. Heb. *And the earth;* which may well be rendered, *For the earth:* as ch. 13.8. & 16.2.

*{is defiled*} Either with the gore-blood, and carcasses of men, slain, and sacrificed on it; in the execution of these judgments, Ezek. 7.21,24. & 9.7. & 39.14–20. or, rather, with the impieties, impurities, murders, rapes, violences, and other like wickednesses, committed by those that live therein, Levit. 18.25,27. Numb. 35.33. Psal. 106.38. chap. 1.10,15,21. & 4.4. & 54.3. Jer. 3.1,2. Ezek. 20.30,31.

*{under the inhabitants thereof*} As if they were so contaminated with sin, that their very footings defiled the ground that they trod on; not unlike those things, or persons legally impure, whereof Levit. 11.31–35. & 15.4,12,20–27.

*{because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinances, broken the everlasting covenant*} Because all God's laws, both general, and special; civil, and sacred, have been grievously and extremely violated by them; that which has made them so impure, Levit. 18.24. Ezek. 14.11. & 20.26,43. & 23.7,13. & 24.6,13. Zeph. 3.1. Mat. 15.18–20.

*{transgressed*} The word signifies properly to *pass over,* or *beyond,* Josh. 4.1. & 15.3. applied to sins and trespasses, because by commission of them, men pass the bounds and limits prescribed them by God; as Shimei the circuit, assigned him by Solomon, 1 King. 2.36,37.

*{the laws*} Either in general, written, or unwritten, concerning man's duty, both to God and man; which even the heathen also have engraven in their hearts, Rom. 2.14,15. or, as some, the moral, and civil laws delivered to God's people; distinguished from the *ordinances,* afterward mentioned: as 2 Chr. 33.8.

*{changed*} So the word, sometime, signifies, Gen. 31.7,41. & 35.2. but not in the form here used; where it signifies *to pass away,* or, *pass by,* Job 4.15. & 9.26. & 11.10. and so seems to intimate, properly, *neglects,* or *passings by:* sins of omission, as the former *passings over:* or, *beyond,* sins of commission: and it would therefore be rendered, *passed by the ordinances.*

*{the ordinances*} Heb. *ordinance:* but taken collectively: as Ezr. 7.10. rendered sometime *statute,* and *statutes,* Deut. 4.5,8. Josh. 24.25. supposed, here, to intend sacred rites, and observances, more specially by God prescribed to his people: as Neh. 9.13,14.

*{broken*} The word properly signifies, *to annul, frustrate,* or *make void,* Numb. 30.12,15.

*{the everlasting covenant*} Heb. *the covenant of eternity:* as chap. 55.3. that is, a covenant, never to be broken, or annulled, Jer. 50.5. This some understand of the covenant of circumcision, made with Abraham and his seed. So called, Gen. 17.7,10,14. Others, of the covenant made with the Israelites in mount Sinai, at the giving of the Law, Exod. 24.7,8. Jer. 11.2,4. and this seems more probable than the former. Others, of the Law of Nature, concerning all men in general, which was from the beginning, and shall last to all eternity, Psal. 119.89. Matth. 5.18. and they suppose, that these three several branches intend one and the same thing only, in divers terms, as is usual with this prophet. But I find not where the word *covenant,* is thereof used in Scripture; and incline therefore rather to the former.

**V. 6.** *{Therefore*} To wit, for the sins and transgressions before-mentioned, ver. 5. and so in the next branch.

*{hath the curse devoured the earth*} Or, *land:* as ver. 1,4,5. *the curse,* that is, the wrath of God, by these dismal effects, manifested and executed therein. It seems to allude, either to the curse denounced in the Law, taking hold of the willful breakers of it, Deut. 27.26. & 28.15–68. & 29.20. or, to the curse, together with the oath conceived by them, in their covenanting with God, as now for the violation thereof, justly inflicted, Neh. 10.29. See Jer. 23.10. Zach. 5.3,4.

*{and they that dwell therein are desolate*} Being stripped, and bereft of all those comforts and commodities, that from it they formerly enjoyed, Lam. 4.5. or, pined, wasted and consumed for want of necessary sustenance, Ezek. 4.17. Joel 1.18. or, *destroyed:* as Ezek. 6.4,6. according to another reading, *they sustain* the punishment of their *trespasses;* they suffer for their sins: as Prov. 30.10. Jer. 2.3. See the like ambiguity, Psal. 5.10. & 34.21,22. Hos. 5.15. & 10.2. & 13.16. See also, ver. 9.

*{therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burnt*} *burnt up;* consumed with fire and sword, by hostile invasions, Ezek. 5.2,4. & 24.10,11. or, with the fire of God's wrath, chap. 9.18. & 10.16. or, dried up, and exhaust; as the body of man, or beast, through want of moisture, Ps. 69.3. & 102.3. or, a brook, by means of drought, 1 King. 17.7. Jer. 50.38. & 51.32.

*{and few men left*} The words are all singular, but collective; as Ps. 8.4. ch. 2.9. & 5.15. See ch. 16.14.

**V. 7.** *{The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth*} The prophet proceeds, in particular, to instance in some special outward comforts, that the creature is wont to afford men; to wit, in *wine,* that is said to cheer man's heart, Ps. 104.15. but should now be taken away, both it, and the vines that yield it, being both spoiled.

*{the new wine*} So it properly signifies; whereof the month *Tishri,* the seventh month, answering to our September in part, is, by some deemed to have its name; because then their vintage was: but is put here for *wine* in general: as ch. 36.17. Jer. 31.12. Hos. 7.14.

*{mourneth*} The wine is said to mourn, being spilled and spoiled by the enemy: as *the land,* or, *ground,* is said to *mourn,* Joel 1.10. implying what it would do, were it sensible of what is done unto it. See ch. 23.1.

*{the vine languisheth*} Being trodden down, and despoiled by the enemy. See ch. 16.8. ver. 4. Joel 1.12.

*{all the merry-hearted do sigh*} The wine-drinkers, ver. 9. (so called, because wine makes the heart merry, Ps. 104.15. 2 Sam. 13.28. Esth. 1.10. Zach. 10.7.) *do sigh,* and *mourn:* because the means and matter of maintaining their mirth, are gone, ver. 8,12. Amos 5.19. instead of their wonted singing, ver. 9. now they sigh: *to sigh,* for, *to mourn:* as Ezek. 9.4. Lam. 1.21.

**V. 8.** *{The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth*} Their music and melody, that they used at their banquets, and merry meetings, is all at an end. See ch. 5.12. & 16.10. Jer. 7.34. & 16.7. & 25.10. Ezek. 26.13. Hos. 2.11. Amos 6.5,7.

*{tabrets*} Or *tabors.* See ch. 5.12. and of *harp,* there also.

*{the noise of them that rejoice*} Or, *the tumultuous clamor* (the confused noise, that they use to make, when they are drunk, Psal. 78.65. Zach. 9.15.) *of the revelers:* styled, *the sons of clamor,* Jer. 48.45. See ch. 22.2. & 23.7,12.

**V. 9.** *{They shall not drink wine with a song*} Heb. *the song:* such songs as they used to sing in their merry meetings, and at their feasts. They shall not revel it as they had wont to do; either with voices, or other music, ver. 8.

*{drink wine*} To drink *wine,* for, *to feast:* as Job 1.18. Chap. 22.13.

*{strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it*} Little pleasure shall they take in any strong drink, by reason of the calamities and distractions of the times. See ch. 5.11.

**V. 10.** *{The city of confusion is broken down*} Or, *The city of emptiness;* as it is rendered, Job 26.7. or, *of wasteness;* as Deut. 32.10. Job 12.24. or, *of desolation;* as ch. 34.11. Jer. 4.23. or, *of vanity;* such, as things void of soundness, or virtue, are, 1 Sam. 12.21. chap. 41.29. & 44.9. & 45.18,19. & 59.4. and because such things are as good as naught, and nothing worth, the word is used also for *nothing,* Job 26.7. chap. 40.17,23. So, *cities of wasteness,* that is, wasted, made or laid waste, chap. 61.4. Hence, some understand here, the city Bethel; which, both in regard of the idol, by Jeroboam there erected, 1 King. 12.29,32,33. as also of that desolation that was denounced against it, and made good upon it, 1 King. 13.2. Hos. 5.5. is by the prophets called *Bethaven,* that is, *the house,* or *city of vanity,* or *of desolation and emptiness,* Hos. 4.15. & 10.5,6. Others would have it to be Jerusalem, said to have been broken up by the Chaldees, 2 King. 25.4. Jer. 39.2. and as having been guilty of the like sins with Bethel, did undergo the like judgment, Jer. 7.17,20. & 21.13. & 32.28–35. And these seem justly to others over-narrow; but they may no less justly be deemed to range, as far over-wide, that would thereby have understood the whole world; because all that is in it, is *vanity of vanities*, and nothing but *vanity*, Eccl. 1.2. and to be brought unto its first emptiness again, Gen. 1.2. The most, and best, suppose it to be spoken, not of any one city; but by the word *city*, taken collectively, as ch. 25.2. & 27.10. the several cities of the kingdoms and countries respectively, which this prophecy concerned; so termed, as some of the Jewish commenters, because their inhabitants ran after idols, and other *vanities*, of whom this word is used, 1 Sam. 12.21. ch. 44.9. or, as others of them, rather because *ruined, emptied, [*and *isolated]*, by the enemies *breaking* into them, and *breaking* down [unclear], though the word *down* is not in the text. See ch. 3.26. & 34.11. and it is observed by one of them, that by a kind of anticipation, it is said, *the city of desolation is broken*; albeit, it were not such before it was *broken*, but being *broken*, and so *ruined*, came to be such, to which he supposes a parallel place to be, ch. 44.19. whereof see there. But such anticipations are found manifestly, Gen. 28.19, 22. Levit. 15.16. Judg. 4.21. ch. 37.9. & 28.1. & 32.6. & 40.19. Ezek. 3.3. Nah. 3.5. Howbeit, others would have it to be termed *the city of desolation*, because designed, or destinated to desolation, as *the city of destruction*, because thereunto designed, ch. 19.18. See ch. 23.12.

*{every house is shut up, that no man may enter in*} Or, *that there is no going in, or out*, Heb. *every house is shut up from entering*, as ch. 23.1. Which some understand of being shut up, to keep out the enemy having broke into the city, ch. 26.20. Joh. 20.19. Others, so shut, that none goes in, because there is no business there to be done, as ch. 23.1. or, stand shut up, and neither going in, or out, for fear of the enemy, as 1 King. 15.17. 2 Chr. 15.5. & 16.1. or, because the inhabitants are gone, either captived, or slain, ch. 27.10. I suppose it may well be rendered, *all houses are as shut up, so that there is no going out, or in*; there is no more going in or out, than as if the houses were all shut up. See c. 22.3. Jer. 13.19. See also, ver. 22.

*{every house*} That is, many, or the most of them, as Gen. 41.57. so one of the Jewish commenters. Howbeit, if rendered as before was intimated, there will no such restriction need.

**V. 11.** *{There is a crying for wine in the streets*} This passage, among others, shows that this prophecy is not to be understood of the universal destruction of the world at the last day, 2 Pet. 3.10, 11.

*{a crying for wine*} Or, *because of the wine*; not calling for it, but yelling and lamenting; not, as some, for the present want so much, Hosh. 7.14. as because of the spoil, and loss of it, Lam. 5.18. Ezek. 27.30. where it should also be so rendered. See ch. 16.7–10. for they seem to wander much out of the way, who would have it understood, either of passengers, or those few left in the city, crying up and down in the streets, *who hath any wine to sell*; as intimating, both the scarcity of that liquor, and men's greedy desire of it, notwithstanding the calamities of the times; that which yet some of the Jewish commenters suggest, and some of ours admit.

*{all joy is darkened*} Extinct, put out. See ch. 8.22. & 9.19. word for word, it is *eventide* with it, because at even darkness comes, Ps. 104.20, 23. their mirth shall set, as the sun does at even, and end in mourning, Amos 8.9, 10. Howbeit, because the verb is in that notion nowhere else found, there may be some suspicion, that by a transposition of letters, which in Scripture is sometime observed, (see Lev. 3.7. & 4.32. 1 Chr. 4.9, 11.) the word may signify here *to pass away*, which with that alteration, it most frequently does, and would suit very well with the next branch. See Job 30.15.

*{the mirth of the land is gone*} Together with the liquor that helped to maintain it, v. 8, 9. Heb. *is gone into captivity*, ch. 5.13. as alluding to the captivity of the people of the land carried away by the enemy: the like allusion is in the word of Eli's daughter-in-law, when the Ark of God was taken, 1 Sam. 4.21, 22. See also, Hos. 10.5.

**V. 12.** *{In the city is left desolation*} Or, as some render it, *He that is left in the city shall be desolate*. Heb. *desolation*, as ch. 1.7. or, *unto desolation*, as Jer. 4.7. or as others, *that is left in the city, shall be destroyed with desolation*, supplying the verb from the branch ensuing, as ch. 13.13. & 18.7. and the particle oft wanting, as ch. 21.7. & 22.17, 18. which way soever we read it, the sense is plain; there is nothing left in the city, city and country are both alike stripped and plundered of all, *city*, for cities, as v. 10.

*{and the gate is smitten with destruction*} The same, in effect, is in divers terms repeated.

*{the gate*} Either the gates of the city, broken open and destroyed by the adversary, Judg. 9.52. Neh. 1.3. Ezek. 21.22. or, *gate*, for city, as ch. 14.31.

*{is smitten*} Heb. *broken to pieces*, as Mic. 1.7.

*{with destruction*} So the rabbines, affirming this and the former word to be sisters, and so the most take it, yet some render it, *with a noise*, or *a crack*, such a noise as soldiers are wont to make in the assault of a fort or city, Ezek. 21.22. Amos 2.2. or such a crack, as gates or walls, being violently broken asunder, or broken down, are wont to give, alluded to, Jer. 49.21. Ezek. 26.15. The reason of the ambiguity is, because both the root whence this word comes (it being nowhere else found) and some others derived from the same, and in sound coming near it, have in them, not unusually, a notion of either: the reason whereof, may seem to be, because such assaults, whereby desolation is wrought, are commonly accompanied with fearful outcries on either side. See on ch. 16.9, 10. The particle, all grant, is to be supplied, as before.

**V. 13.** *{When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, there shall be, as the shaking of an olive-tree, and as the gleaning of grapes when the vintage is done*} Or, *For so* (as Gen. 15.5.) *it shall be in the land among the people, as in the beating of an olive-tree, as with clusters left, when the vintage is done*. Thus, or so, as was before said, it shall be, when these judgments shall be executed in those places, and with those people where they are put in execution, that a very small company shall be left, or escape; which may here come in, either in way of conformation of the former relation, and further amplification of the judgment therein related, by a lamentable effect, to wit, the paucity of those that should therein escape, or in way of mitigation and limitation of those sad denunciations of desolation and destruction, that yet God would not make an utter riddance of all, but reserve a remnant, that he might have a people to praise him, v. 14. The former I conceive to be principally intended, though with an intimation of the latter. See ch. 1.9. & 6.13. & 7.3. & 10.21, 22. Jer. 3.14. This some suppose to have reference to those that Tiglath-Pileser captived, 2 King. 15.29. Others, to the Jews, that either by the Chaldees were carried captive to Babylon, Jer. 39.9. or that voluntarily of themselves went down into Egypt, Jer. 43.5–7. both which I leave to the judgment of others.

*{in the midst of the land*} Or, *earth*, as Ps. 74.12. whereby some understand Jerusalem, situate (as the Jews say) in the very midst of the world, or the navel of the earth, Ezek. 39.12. near to which, say they the last judgment, or ecumenical assize, Act. 17.31. shall be held, Joel 3.2, 12. Zach. 14.4. But these are groundless conceits; *in the midst of the land*, is no more, than *in the land*, as ch. 6.12. & 7.22. as *in the midst of the people*, or *peoples* rather, (for so the text has it, as ch. 25.6, 7.) is no more, than *among the people*, or *peoples*, as Jer. 39.14. & 40.1, 5, 6. which yet argues the prophecy to concern more, than any one people.

*{as the shaking of an olive-tree*} Or, *as in the beating of an olive-tree*; it seems to have been a proverbial kind of speech: see ch. 17.6.

*{as the gleaning of grapes when the vintage is done*} Or, *as clusters left, when the vintage is done*, a defect of the epithet *clusters*, for *clusters left*, as *sheep*, for *lost sheep*, ch. 53.6. See ch. 5.2. and the clusters so left, are called *the clusters of the vintage*, Mic. 7.1. as, *a corpse* left by the soul, is called *a soul*, Num. 19.13. and wines drawn off the lees, are called *lees*; by the name of that they left, ch. 25.6. See ch. 17.6. Jer. 6.9. & 49.9. The *vintage*, the time of cutting grapes has thence its name in Hebrew, as the *harvest*, being the time of *mowing* grass, or reaping corn, is thence also so termed, and but one letter difference between the one and the other. See ch. 17.5, 11.

**V. 14.** *{They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the Lord, they shall cry aloud from the sea*} In this verse, and some ensuing, is described the condition and carriage of those few, the remains among each people, that should be preserved in, or delivered out of the common calamities and afflictions of those times; they should abundantly rejoice, and out of the joyful sense and apprehension of God's might and mercy therein showed them, break forth into praises of him. So ch. 12. & 25. & 26. This some restrain to those that were delivered in Sennacherib's invasion, ch. 37.31, 32. some to those that were freed from the Babylonian captivity, Ps. 126.1, 2. But it seems to be of a larger extent, and some extend it unto the times of the gospel, which yet seems not so clear.

*{They*} Or, *these*, for there is an emphasis in the word, the pronoun not only expressed, which seldom is, but with an additional adjection also to it; as Eccl. 3.18. ch. 35.2. the persons so left, as ver. 13.

*{lift up their voice*} The phrase is used to signify an expression, either of great grief, as 1 Sam. 11.4. Job 2.12. or, of much joy, and so here, as the like, ch. 40.9.

*{sing*} Or, *make joyful acclamations*, as ch. 12.6. & 54. Ps. 35.27.

*{for the majesty of the Lord*} Or *excellency*, as Amos 8.7. or, *magnificence*. See ch. 2.10. the supereminent greatness of his might, and mercy showed, both in the destruction of some, and in the deliverance of others. These words, according to the distinctions in the original appertain not to this branch, but to the next.

*{cry aloud*} Of this word, see on ch. 12.6. Some suppose, that it alludes there to the shoutings in vintage and harvest, ch. 16.9. Others, to the shouting of seamen, at their coming into harbor, because of the next words.

*{from the sea*} That is, say some, after their deliverance from their former afflictions; compared in Scripture oft to *a sea*, Ps. 42.7. & 69.1, 2, 15. & 88.7. & 93.3. and 130.1. Rev. 15.2, 3. when the *sea* shall be no more, Rev. 21.1. of this use of the particle, see on ch. 38.15. & 53.8. But other rather understand it of the place, from whence those voices of joy and praise should be heard, which some understand of those that are upon the sea, Ps. 65.5. & 107.23. as if the sense were, that God should be magnified both by sea and land, Ps. 96.11. & 98.9. Others, *from the sea*, that is, *from the west*, as ch. 49.12. from Palestine, which lay west from Judea, ch. 9.12. or the sea coast, the utmost bound of the land of Israel westward, Josh. 1.4. and 15.47. or, the isles of the midland sea, verse 15. or lastly, which is most likely, the transmarine lands, or sea coasts in general, where any of those shall be found that were partakers of this deliverance.

**V. 15.** *{Wherefore glorify ye God in the fires, even the name of the Lord God of Israel, in the isles of the sea*} The faithful delivered, and escaping the forementioned calamities, as they celebrate God's name, for both his judgments on the wicked, and his goodness to themselves; so they incite others also to do the like with them, and encourage one another thereunto: so Ps. 34.3. ch. 12.4, 5.

*{in the fires*} You that abide yet in the fire of tribulation, Ps. 66.10, 12. ch. 48.10. despair not, nor be discouraged; but by your patient sufferings glorify God, and depend upon him for deliverance, Ps. 94.19. Mat. 5.12. Act. 5.41. & 16.25. Rom. 5.3. 2 Cor. 4.8, 9. & 6.9, 10. Phil. 1.18, 20. & 2.17. Col. 1.24. Jam. 1.2. 1 Pet. 1.6–8. & 4.12–14. Or, *in the valleys*, so termed, as some, by way of antiphrasis, as a *grove* in Latin; because they enjoy less light that live in them, than those that dwell in higher places on the hills; or as others rather, for the plenty of herbs, and green things that there grow, ch. 18.4. & 26.19. So divers of the Jewish doctors understand that, Gen. 11.28, 31. *Ur of the Chaldeans*, that is, *the vale* wherein the *Chaldeans* dwelt, for their country lay low: see ch. 21.1. and they suppose the *valleys* here mentioned, because more cities are usually in valleys, for conveniency of watering and feeding, Ps. 64.12, 13. & 104.10, 14. than on hills, ch. 32.19, 20. and this seems most probable. Though there want not Jewish critics that would have the word signify *holes*, as two other words somewhat near it do, both found together, ch. 11.8. expounding it either of such *holes and caves*, wherein they lay hid, 1 Sam. 13.6. & 14.11. or of such *holes* and dungeons wherein they were held, ch. 44.22.

*{the name of the Lord*} The Lord himself, as Ps. 9.2. & 69.30. his power and majesty, Deut. 28.58. 1 King. 8.41, 42. see ch. 30.27.

*{the God of Israel*} By his judgments manifested to be the only true God, 1 King. 18.39. Ps. 9.16. & 83.18. ch. 45.6. Zach. 14.9. but therefore, says the rabbine, here so styled; because for his Israel he does all this, ch. 43.3, 4. & 45.4.

*{in the isles of the sea*} The isles, whereof great store in the midland sea, Ps. 97.1. or, the regions bordering upon the sea, see v. 14. ch. 21.6.

**V. 16.** *{From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs*} Or, *of the land*, as v. 3. The generality of the joy, and praises of God, from that scattered remnant, out of all places, far and near, where any of them are found: there is nothing but singing with them; all the land over they sing so loud, that they may be heard even from the land's end: see the like of lamentations and outcries, ch. 15.4, 5, 8. Jer. 49.21.

*{the uttermost part*} Heb. *wing*, as ch. 11.12.

*{songs*} Songs of deliverance, Ps. 32.7. such ditties properly, as are made to be sung unto some musical instrument, and those are in Greek also peculiarly termed *Psalms*, Col. 3.16. see ch. 12.2.

*{even glory to the righteous*} Some make this the subject matter of their singing, to wit, *Glory be*, or *be given, to the righteous*, that is, to God the righteous One, whose righteousness has been manifested and magnified in the execution of judgments above mentioned, Ps. 19.9.4. Apoc. 7.12. & 15.3, 4. & 19.1.
