Others understand it of the godly and righteous, by those deliverances made beautiful, delightful, amiable and honorable: see Ps. 149.4, 9. and they read the words, *a beauty*, or *beautiful ornament, to the righteous*: see ch. 28.5. and of the term itself, ch. 4.2. righteous, for righteous ones, as ch. 3.10.

*{But I said, my leanness, my leanness*} After the relation of this great glory that should fill the hearts of those that should escape so, as to survive the judgments before denounced; the prophet, in an abrupt manner, breaks off that his cheerful and gladsome discourse; and to show how full his heart was of grief and regret for the miseries that were the whilst to befall his people, he falls to lament their condition, as well in regard of their grievous sins as of the great variety of dreadful and unavoidable judgments, that for the same should be inflicted upon them; withal, making a very pathetical profession, and affectionate expression of his own present affliction, upon the very foresight thereof; so Jer. 9.1.

*{My leanness, my leanness*} The old Latin, following the Chaldee, renders it, *My secret to myself, my secret to myself*. And the Chaldee expounds it of a secret revealed to the prophet, concerning the retribution of the wicked in one kind, and of the righteous in another; but neither is the last letter in it a pronoun but the formal and usual termination of the word, as in others of the like stamp, nor is the word ever found without in Hebrew, as it is, when it signifies *a secret*, in Chaldee; nor has either the root itself, from whence the word rises, or any other of the same stock, any other notion, but of *leanness*, as our English therefore well renders it. See Num. 13.21. ch. 10.16. & 17.4. Ezek. 34.20. The meaning is, that, the grief of his mind was so great, for the perfidiousness of his people, and God's wrath thereby incensed, and sure shortly to seize on them, that even the flesh of his body was also wasted and consumed with it, as with some emaciating and pining disease. So Ps. 69.9. and 119.139. See also the like expression, upon other occasions, Ps. 22.15, 17. & 32.4. & 102.3–5. & 139.83. The repetition is only to manifest the vehemency of his affection: see the like, Jer. 4.19.

*{woe unto me*} Or, *wo is me*, or, *alas for me*; for it is spoken, not in way of denunciation, as ch. 29.1. but in way of lamentation, as Lam. 5.16.

*{the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously*} Heb. *dealing treacherously, have dealt treacherously*, as Jer. 5.11. that is, they have dealt exceeding treacherously; or, have dealt treacherously oft times, again and again. He cannot multiply words sufficiently, to express the extreme perfidious courses and carriages of his people towards God; whom by so many special and peculiar obligations, they stood so deeply endeared unto, and had so oft, and so solemnly engaged themselves: that which made their trespasses and transgressions far the more heinous than the sins and excesses of any other people, Ps. 81.11. Amos 3.2. See the like heaping up of various expressions to the same purpose, Dan. 9.5, 6. For it cannot be so fitly understood of other persons dealing perfidiously with God's people; albeit it be true, that divers of them so did, ch. 21.2. & 33.1, 8. Lam. 1.2. and so some apply it; as if the prophet mourned not so much for their treacherous dealing with God, as for others' treacherous dealing with them.

**V. 17.** *{Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth*} Heb. *Fear, and pit, and snare*. The heinousness and grievousness of their sinful courses was before, the dreadfulness of God's inevitable judgments upon them, for the same, now ensues. Thus when sin is come to a height, judgment follows it at the heels, Gen. 15.16. Ezek. 7.10, 11. Mat. 23.32, 36. 1 Thess. 2.16. In these words, a variety of perils, of sundry sorts, is implied, and they are knit together with a copulative reiterated, as pursuing the same persons; that if they chance to miss in the one, yet they may be sure to take in the other, v. 18. The words run very elegantly, in a near affinity of letter, and sound, in the original; as if we should say, *Scare, and sewer, and snare*, or the like; yea, the words come so near, in letters and sound, one to another, that sometime one of them is, in some copies, read for the other, as Lam. 3.47. See the same, Jer. 48.43.

*{O inhabitant of the earth*} *Inhabitant*, for *inhabitants*: as ch. 5.3. but there is some emphasis, here, in it; as if each one should be exposed to the same perils: of the earth, or land, as v. 16. which the Jewish commenters would, by all means, put off from their own nation, to the people abroad in the world.

**V. 18.** *{And it shall come to pass, that*} Heb. *And it shall be*: as ch. 17.4.

*{he who fleeth from the noise of the fear, shall fall into the pit, and he that cometh out of the midst of the pit, shall be taken in the snare*} The meaning is plain, he that escapes one danger, shall fall into another: as if he said, he that flees for fear of the enemy, either breaking in upon him, or pursuing him, shall fall into some well, or ditch; as those, Gen. 14.10. and if he get out of that, (though he may then think himself safe,) shall fall into the hands of some that lie in ambush for him, or the like, as Judg. 20.42, 43. See the like, 1 King. 20.30. Amos 5.19. & 9.2, 3. and an allusion to somewhat the like, Prov. 29.25. There seems to be, in the words, a metaphor, taken from the manner of hunters' dealing with deer, or other wild beasts, whom, when they have digged pits for, and covered with some loose, or light matter, and set toils, or gins and snares, not far from them, that if they escape, either passing by or getting up out of the one, they may be surprised with, and held fast in the other, do then, with noise and clamor raised, rouse up their prey, and so drive them, while they flee to save themselves, for fear of the noise, into these pits, or gins, that they have beforehand prepared for them, to intercept them in their flight. Hereunto are frequent allusions in Scripture, Ps. 9.15. & 10.8, 9. & 35.7, 8. & 57.6. & 64.5. & 91.3. & 124.6, 7. & 140.3, 11. Jer. 16.16. Lam. 3.52. & 4.18, 20. Howbeit, I cannot concur with those, who in the word *fear*, suppose an allusion to such feathers and papers, as hunters use, with us, to blanch the deer with, or that string or line, furnished with the like, which they are wont, anciently, to scare wild beasts with, to the same purpose that ours do; because in Latin, it is termed *formido*, that is, *the fright* or *the scare*, for it suits not well with the words of the text, wherein it is said, not, *from the sight*, as it should be, if that were intended, but, *from the noise* (which that makes none) of the fear: and indeed, *the noise*, or *voice of the fear*, is nothing but the *fear of the noise*: as, *the uncleanness of a man*, for, *a man of uncleanness*, Levit. 7.21. *the oath of obligation*, for *the obligation of an oath*, Num. 30.14. and *to flee from the sound*, or *the noise of the fear*, is no other, than *to flee for fear of the noise*: as *for fear of the sword*, ch. 21.15. or, *to flee from the dreadful noise*; as ch. 33.3. a *noise of fear*, for *a fearful noise*, or, a noise, or report of some fearful evil approaching, as Job 15.21.

*{out of the midst of the pit*} For, *out of the pit*, simply; as Prov. 5.15. Jer. 51.6. with Rev. 18.4. Ezek. 32.21. Amos 6.4. See Jer. 41.7.

*{for the windows from on high are opened, and the foundations of the earth do shake*} This is further added, more fully to illustrate the unavoidableness of God's judgments; the vengeance of God breaking forth, and surprising them, both from above, and from beneath, as well over their heads, as under their feet; and as no shelter for them, against the one, so no steady standing for them, in regard of the other.

*{the windows from on high are opened*} *From on high*, that is, from heaven. So ch. 32.15. Lam. 1.3. *the windows from heaven*, for, *the windows of heaven*: as, *a boar from the wood*, for, *a boar of the wood*, Ps. 80.13. Or, *the windows from above pour down, being opened*, or *are opened, and pour down, from above*. Of which concise and comprehensive form of speech see on ch. 14.12. & 38.17. The *windows of heaven* are said to be *set open*, to intimate, sometime, abundance of blessings, Deut. 28.12. Mal. 3.10. sometime, to express as large measure of unavoidable judgments; and so here, in way of allusion, either to the general deluge in Noah's days, Gen. 7.11. or, to that dreadful destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Gen. 19.24. See Ps. 11.6. Rom. 1.18.

*{the foundations of the earth do shake*} An hyperbolical phrase, very frequent in Scripture; whereby is represented that exceeding terror and astonishment, wherewith people are surprised and transported, upon the manifestation of God's might and wrath, in some extraordinary judgments; as if the earth, to the very center of it, shook under their feet. See Ps. 18.7. ch. 2.19, 21. and 13.13.

**V. 19.** *{The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly*} The prophet proceeds, still, in the rhetorical amplifications of the ruins and subversion of the kingdoms and states coming within compass of this prophecy, so subverted, and all things with them turned upside down, as if the earth itself, that bears them, were rent, and torn asunder and shattered, and not able, any longer, to consist, or to subsist. So v. 1, 18, 20.

*{is utterly broken down*} Heb. *in breaking asunder*, or *to pieces, is broken asunder*, or, *to pieces*. For that is, the more proper notion of the word, and better suits with the object here, the earth. So Ps. 2.9. Prov. 11.15. & 13.20. & 25.19.

*{is clean dissolved*} Heb. *in dissolving, is dissolved*, or, rather, *in renting*, or, *tearing, is rent*, or torn asunder. For though the word in one form signifies to *dissolve, break, frustrate* or *make void*, vows, covenants, and contracts, Num. 30.3, 12, 13, 15. v. 5. yet in the form here used, it signifies to rent, or tear asunder, some solid body, Job 16.12. Ps. 74.13. and there, of the word for *clefts*, or *ruptures* in the ground, ch. 2.20. yet there may be a glance at the former, here, in this latter, as noting a retaliation of transgression, and penalty; the earth is broken, and rent asunder with them; because they have broken and violated their covenant with God. v. 5.

*{is moved exceedingly*} Heb. *in moving, is moved*. The word is used for such *a moving*, by which a man staggers, so as his feet are scarce able to keep him standing upright, Deut. 32.35. Ps. 13.5. & 17.1. & 66.9. & 98.18. or, for such *a moving*, where somewhat is removed, out of its former fixed seat, ch. 54.10. Applied to the earth, or land, and the states and kingdoms thereof, Ps. 46.6. and 60.2.

**V. 20.** *{The earth shall reel to and fro, like a drunkard*} Or, *reeleth*: that it may run in the same tenor with the former. The future is frequently used of things spoken of, as past, or present, Ps. 1.2. & 18.6, 11, 13, 16, 20. Heb. *reeling reeleth*, the same term is used, ch. 19.1. & 29.9. and the same similitude, Ps. 107.27. ch. 19.1. Jer. 23.9. It is the same in effect, but clad under a new notion in other terms, that was before, v. 19.

*{and shall be removed like a cottage*} Or, *is removed*, as before. The word properly imports a flitting, or removing from place to place; the curse of Cain, Gen. 4.14, 16.

*{a cottage*} The word is used, ch. 1.8. for *a shed*, that a gardener, or keeper of a garden, sets it up in it, there to repose, or to shelter himself in a storm; or from thence to watch the fruits, or plants in it: and it is there rendered, *a lodge*: but it seems here to be taken for *a tent*; either *a soldier's tent*, as some, that is taken down and removed, when they are to march, or are quitting of their quarters; or, *a shepherd's tent*, which he removes from place to place, as he finds conveniency of feeding for his sheep, ch. 13.20. and 38.12.

*{and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it, and it shall fall, and not rise again*} Or, *that it shall fall, and not rise again*; as Judg. 7.13. the judgments of God, by the transgressions of its inhabitants procured, shall lie so heavy on it, that it shall sink down under the weight of them, and not be able to recover again its former estate. See v. 5, 6.

*{the transgression*} That is, punishment of it: as Gen. 4.7, 13. Prov. 29.22.

*{heavy*} In the punishment of it, Ps. 38.4. Ezek. 33.10. a metaphor taken from weighty burdens, so heavy, that a man cannot stand upright under them.

*{not rise again*} Heb. *not add to rise*. So Jer. 25.27. & 51.64. Amos 5.2.

**V. 21.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that &c.*} As ch. 10.27.

*{the Lord shall punish the host of the high ones, that are on high, and the kings of the earth, upon the earth*} None so great, or high, in power, or place, that shall escape in this judgment of God, v. 2. ch. 5.15.

*{punish*} Heb. *visit upon*: as ch. 28.14.

*{the host of the high ones, that are on high*} Or, *The host of that high one*, (that is, as some think the king of Assyria, ch. 10.12.) *that sitteth on high*, so far above other princes, ch. 36.4. or, as the king of Babylon, in his own haughty conceit, ch. 14.13, 14. or, *the host of each high one, with the high one himself*, not their hosts alone, but themselves also: as Ps. 68.12. ch. 34.2. So is the particle used, 1 Sam. 1.24. Jer. 11.19. Or, each *high one, in his height*, that is, the highest of men, in their highest estate. And so the latter part of the verse, should expound the former. But some would have it meant of the celestial bodies, the sun, and the moon, that are said to be darkened, v. 23. the darkening whereof is counted a dismal sign, ch. 13.10. Joel 2.21. to the heathen especially, Jer. 10.2. Some, of the angels, that stand for several kings, and seem concerned in their affairs; them in heaven opposed to, yet joined with, the kings on earth. So some of the Jewish commenters, from Dan. 10.13, 20, 21. Of Christian writers, not a few, of the devils, those *principalities, and powers*, that are said to be *in high*, (as our last edition renders it,) or rather, *in heavenly* places, that is, aloft, in the air, Eph. 2.2. (as, the *birds of heaven*, Ps. 8.8. Matth. 13.32. that is, *of the air*,) and are to be judged at the last day, 1 Cor. 6.3. Jud. 6. And some again, of their idols, set usually aloft, 2 Chron. 34.4. or their images of the celestial bodies, ch. 17.8. and 27.9. Amos 5.26. Act. 7.43. See ch. 19.1. and 46.1. Others, of *the heavenly host* here on earth, that is, the church militant, which should be visited, as well as the world, and the princes of it, Lam. 2.1. Dan. 8.10. Rev. 12.1, 3, 7. Among this great variety of interpretations, to which divers others might be added; I suppose that most probable, that by *the host of the high one*, (the word collectively taken; for *those, that sit aloft*, ch. 26.5.) are meant, those great monarchs and potentates, such as the heads were of the Assyrian, and Chaldean empire, styled not barely *kings* but *kings of kings*, Dan. 2.37. and whose *dominion* is said *to reach up unto heaven*, Dan. 4.20, 22. whose resplendent state and majesty, is also compared to the luster and brightness of those celestial bodies, ch. 13.19. with 14.7. v. 23. and whose dejection and downfall, therefore, is resembled by similitudes, taken from, and glancing at the dissolution and alteration that those heavenly substances shall, in likelihood, undergo at the last day. See ch. 34.4. Rev. 6.12–14. as on the other side, the restitution and restoration of God's church, and children, after some long captivity, or grievous calamities, is wont to be deciphered by resemblances drawn from, and alluding to, the general resurrection, and glorious condition that the whole body of the faithful, shall, at the last day, attain, ch. 26.19. Ezek. 37.1–14. Dan. 12.1, 2.

*{and the kings of the earth, upon the earth*} Or, *that are upon the earth*; that it may answer the former branch: those kings and princes, who though great, and high, in regard of those that are under their command; yet seem to have their thrones on the ground, in comparison of those their superiors, so far above them, that they seem to have *their thrones set among the stars, or above the clouds*, ch. 14.13, 14. See ch. 10.9.

**V. 22.** *{And they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered together in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison*} These great ones, of both sorts, or sizes, when God shall have executed judgment thus with them, shall, as common people captived, be kept down, and kept in so by his almighty power, that they shall no more be able to stir abroad, or to act aught, as they had wont to do, until he please to release them, and set them at liberty again, than as if they had been all that while kept fast shut up in some dungeon, or some strong and close prison. See Zach. 11.9, 12. Rev. 20.1–3. and of such like executions of judgment on such, 2 King. 23.33. & 25.7. 2 Chr. 33.11. & 36.6. Ps. 149.7, 8. ch. 38.33. Jer. 52.12. Ezek. 19.4, 9. Lam. 4.20.

*{be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered together*} Heb. *gathered together with the gathering of a prisoner*, as some render it; and so it should be like the phrase used, ch. 10.26. & 27.7. & 62.5. but because the former noun is not in a form of regiment, it would rather be rendered, as the rabbines conceive it, *they shall be gathered with a gathering*, (that is, exactly, or strictly gathered, so as none shall escape; as *throw with a throwing*, ch. 22.17. and as, *Gathering gather*, Mic. 2.12. besides that, the verb is in a form also implying no less, and so ch. 33.4. Zach. 14.14.) *as a prisoner*, (to wit, is gathered) or, *as prisoners* (the word taken collectively, as Ps. 79.11. & 102.20.) are gathered together, a defect of the note of similitude, as ch. 22.18. yet some render it without any such supply, *they shall be collected, being collected, bound*. Heb. say they, *a collection bound*: but this sounds very harsh; unless we read, *and bound*; but the word is not a particle, but a noun, and that singular; and so also, the text seems overforced. Nor does that, which some of the rabbines suggest, come off any more smoothly, to wit, that those great ones, Israel's enemies, when they are gathered together, shall be *as a man in bonds*, not able to stir hand or foot, until they have submitted themselves to God's people. See somewhat the like, ch. 22.3. For as for the Latin, *they shall be gathered with the gathering of one bundle*, it cannot be admitted, since that the word here used, does nowhere signify *a bundle*, but *a prisoner* always, or *one in bonds*, ch. 10.4. & 42.7. nor any interpretations therefore grounded thereupon.

*{gathered together*} That is, say some, *destroyed*, because the word sometime seems to have some such like notion, ch. 57.1. Jer. 8.13. Hos. 4.3. Zeph. 1.2. but the most take it, in the ordinary and most common sense, *they shall be gathered together* as malefactors are oft times out of several places, to be laid up fast in some jail or prison, until the day, either of assize, or of release.

*{in the pit*} Heb. *on the pit*; yet the particle is also so used, ch. 38.20. and in the next branch; and if it be so taken here, it may seem, that somewhat else should be supplied, and the text thus read, *they shall be gathered together—and cast into*, or *laid up in the pit*: of which manner of concise speech, see v. 18. Otherwise it may be rendered, *they shall be gathered together—for the pit*; as malefactors for the jail.

*{the pit*} That is, say some, *the grave*, which men's carcasses are wont to be cast into, ch. 14.16, 20. & 38.18. others better, the *dungeon* or *hole*, wherein prisoners are cast and kept, Jer. 37.16. & 38.6. Zach. 9.11.

*{and they shall be shut up in the prison*} Or, *in prison*: for there is no article in the text; nor does it suit so well here: or, *as in prison*, as in the former branch; *as a prisoner*, they shall be as surely and narrowly restrained and curbed, as if imprisoned and mured up in the strongest and strictest place of restraint. There is in the Hebrew a near affinity between the verb and the noun; the word rendered *prison*, signifying *a shutting up*, or, a place of *shutting up*, Ps. 142.7. ch. 42.7. and the verb is in the more weighty form, as Josh. 6.1. v. 10. Jer. 13.19. importing a strict and sure shutting up.

*{and after many days shall they be visited*} What manner of *visitation* it is that is here intended, is among interpreters much controverted: Some, and those not a few, both Jewish and Christian writers, understand it of *a visitation*, not for good, but for evil: so divers of the rabbines, of whom, some suppose it to allude to the manner of men's dealing with captives and slaves, whom they keep shut up all night, and in the morning let out to labor: Others, unto the wonted manner of proceeding with malefactors that are committed to prison, and there kept until they be brought forth unto execution, or to trial. Where in the main, to wit, that the *visitation* here mentioned is no matter of mercy, those Christian writers concur with them that interpret this whole prophecy of the general judgment at the last day; which yet because this passage seems to oppugn, some of them seems to make use of a rabbinical exposition, though not naming the author, rendering the words *from*, or, *for, many days*; and expounding it, of being questioned, and upon trial condemned to suffer for the sins that had been, *in many days*, committed by them, or, committed not many days after their commitment before mentioned; but *many days* before they were brought to their trial, 2 Cor. 5.10. But the most of ours, and the most judicious, expound it of *a visitation* in favor and mercy; such as is intimated in the like phrase, Gen. 21.1. & 50.24, 25. Exod. 4.31. Ruth 1.6. Zeph. 2.7. which the Jewish writers, that go this way, expound, some of their own nation, that though they were held in bonds and captivity, for some space of time, both princes and people; yet, at length, God would in mercy visit them, and set them at liberty again, ch. 27.12, 13. Jer. 29.10. & 32.37. & 52.31–33. Others more largely of other nations and states, that should, after these judgments executed upon them, being bettered by them, adjoin themselves to God's people, and find mercy and grace. Wherein we willingly concur with them, acknowledging the same to be fulfilled under the kingdom of Jesus Christ, the true Messiah, in those other nations; and desire to see accomplished, also, in them, ch. 2.3, 4. & 18.7. & 19.20–22. & 23.17, 18. & 60.3, 11, 12. But here a rub would be removed, cast in our way by a late interpreter of prime note, that may else impeach the free progress of this exposition; the rather, because our late translators have afforded it admission into the margin, though not into the text. This learned man, therefore, renders the word here, not, *they shall be visited*, but, *they shall be missed*, or, *found wanting*; that is, for many days, or, for a long time, they shall not be extant, as he expounds it. And it is true, indeed, that such a notion the word here used sometime has; it signifies, first, and properly, *to visit*, or *to survey*: and in the next place, upon survey, to take notice of the absence, or presence of those things, or persons, that come within compass of the survey, and to dispose of them, this way, or that way; for evil, or for good. Hence it comes to pass, that sometimes it signifies *to miss*, and *to be missing*, as Num. 31.49. 1 Sam. 20.18. & 25.7, 15. 2 King. 10.19. ch. 34.16. But that cannot be made good, which to strengthen this interpretation, here, is averred, that in that form which is here used, put absolutely, it never signifies otherwise: nor if it were so in all other places, where it is so put, would it necessarily follow, that it cannot otherwise be understood here. For first, it is apparent that it is used otherwise, where put absolutely, without any addition, in a place parallel to this, Ezek. 38.8. where it is said, *After many days thou shalt be visited*, that is, as this author himself renders it, *execution shall be done upon thee*; and that indeed is the genuine sense of the place, *thou shalt be visited*, to wit, *with evil*, as Solomon more fully, Prov. 9.23. where the same word is in the same form used, *he shall not be visited with evil*; and if it do so signify, when *good* or *evil* is added; why not where neither is expressed, since that in the active, it is so frequently used without either? Again, it seems but a harsh exposition, *After many days, they shall be missed*; that is, they shall not be extant for many days: and lastly, the like term used, but in the active, of Tyre, ch. 23.17. *after seventy years the Lord will visit Tyre*, helps much, both to confirm that which we have here in the text, and to enervate that which the margin suggests.

**V. 23.** *{Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously*} This chapter containing the first part of the present sermon or prophecy, the prophet closes after his wonted manner, with a passage concerning the spiritual, yet conspicuous glory, and magnificence of the gracious kingdom of God, in the times of the gospel, ruling in his church, by his Christ, the brightness and majesty whereof should be such, as no light of sun, or moon; no glory or magnificence of any worldly state, should be comparable thereunto.

*{Then*} When God shall have manifested his might and majesty, both in dejecting, and in restoring again kingdoms and states; in visiting them in wrath first, v. 21. and then in mercy again, v. 22. Heb. *And*, as ch. 8.3, 14.

*{the moon*} So called in regard of her *whiteness*, as here: so Cant. 6.10. ch. 30.26. an emblem of worldly state and glory, subject to change and variety, Rev. 12.1.

*{shall be confounded*} Or, *blush*; as alluding to the notation of her name; she shall blush for all her white or pale face; or, *be ashamed*; for that the word properly signifies, and so is it rendered Ps. 34.5. & 71.24. ch. 54.4. Jer. 50.12.

*{the sun*} So termed in regard of his *heat*, Ps. 19.6. both here, and Job 30.28. ch. 30.26. an usual type of the greatest and most resplendent glory, Jud. 5.31. Mat. 13.43. & 17.2. Act. 26.13. 1 Cor. 15.41. Rev. 1.16. & 12.1. for the sentence rises here, from the moon to the sun, as Cant. 6.10. ch. 30.26. from the less light to the greater, Gen. 1.16.

*{shall be ashamed*} Or, because this suited well with the former; *shall be abashed*, which both in letters and sound, comes very near to the Hebrew; whence in likelihood also, it has its original, both words are oft conjoined, as of a near or common notion, in some of the places above recited, and elsewhere. The less lights lose their light or luster, at least, upon the appearance of some far greater and more glorious one; which by its eminent splendor dims their former bright, but far inferior beauty: so the taper burns dim in daylight, and the moon and stars appear not when the sun shines forth, Joh. 3.30. & 5.35. 2 Cor. 3.10.

*{when the Lord of hosts shall reign*} Ps. 33.1. & 97.1. when *the kingdoms of the world*, shall be the kingdoms *of the Lord, and of his Christ*, Rev. 11.15.

*{in mount Sion, and in Jerusalem*} The types of his church, see ch. 2.2, 3.

*{and before his ancients gloriously*} Or, *in glory*, or, *with glory*, as most conceive it to run in the Hebrew, the defect of the particle being frequent, as ch. 22.17, 18. v. 22. or, as some other, *and there shall be glory, before*; or, *in the sight of his ancients*, or, *the ancients thereof*, that is, of the church of Israel, a type of the main body of the faithful, Rev. 4.4. & 5.8, 9. among whom, and in whom, God more specially manifests his glory in his ordinances, and the passages of his providence, in the regiment of his church, Ps. 29.9. See ch. 4.5. for they narrow this precious and pregnant prophecy overmuch, that restrain it to God's magnifying himself, his might and his mercy; in relieving Jerusalem, by the slaughter of those that besieged it, ch. 37.36. and the elders of Israel, their going up with their rich robes unto the temple in triumph, there solemnly to bless God for it, ch. 38.19, 20.

### CHAPTER 25

**V. 1.** *{O Lord thou art my God, I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name*} The prophet in the former part of this chapter, as one transported with the apprehension of the transcendent majesty, might, and mercy of God manifested, in the just execution of his vengeance on the insolent and obstinate wicked of all sorts, and the gracious protections and deliverances of his poor distressed, despised, and dejected people, and with the consideration of his admirable and unexpressible wisdom, most clearly revealing itself in the passages of his providence concerning either, does abruptly break off the file of his prophetical discourse, and falls into a solemn celebration and praising of God for these his wonderful works, as well of judgment as of mercy; and in the latter part, so returns again to his former discourse, that it is not easy to design or fix the precise lists or limits of either, they are so artificially interwoven the one with the other.

*{O Lord thou art my God*} Some suppose this sacred hymn to be conceived, as in the person of the elders, or ancients, mentioned, ch. 24.23. and so those words wanting to be supplied, *In that day it shall be said*, as v. 9. or, *In that day shall this song be sung*, as ch. 26.1. But I conceive it rather to be an expression of the prophet's own affection and disposition, much taken with the mercy and goodness of God in these counsels and courses of his showed to his people; such like holy breathings may be observed to break oft from God's children amidst other their discourses, Jer. 10.7. & 16.19. 1 Tim. 1.17. Rev. 1.5, 6.

*{thou art my God, I will exalt thee*} So Moses, Exod. 15.2. *thou art my God*, the pronoun for the verb substantive, as Ps. 44.4. *I will exalt thee*, so Ps. 30.1. & 141.1. God exalts his, Ps. 37.34. ch. 1.2. and they exalt him: he them, by making them high and great; they him, by acknowledging and celebrating his sovereignty and his greatness.

*{I will praise thy name*} That is, *thee*, as ch. 12.1. So Ps. 54.6. out of a full assurance of what will be done, he praises God for it, before it is done. So Ps. 13.5, 6.

*{for thou hast done wonderful things*} Heb. *a wonder*, as ch. 29.14. but here taken collectively, as Ps. 77.11. see ch. 9.6.

*{thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth*} Or, *counsels of old faithful and firm*: Or, *even thine ancient counsels*, or, *purposes*, done *in faithfulness and truth*. For some read the words, as an entire proposition apart by itself, *what you had determined*; or, (as those that conceive them spoken as already done in the person of God's surviving people) *what things you did foretell long since, are all faithfully and really fulfilled*. Others, as an additional by way of amplification, to the former, showing what those *wonders* done were, to wit, things consulted and resolved on long ago, most faithful and most firm *counsels*, or *contrivances* or *purposes*, (see ch. 23.8.) for things *consulted, contrived, and purposed*, as Ps. 81.12. Mic. 6.19. *Of old, long ago*, as ch. 22.11. *faithfulness and truth*, or *firmness*, for things, or *counsels, contrivances* (supplied by repetition, as Ps. 111.7.) *of faithfulness, and truth*, or *firmness*, that is, *most faithful, and firm*, or *true*, as Deut. 32.4. Ps. 119.30, 87, 142, 151. yet *firm* and *firmness* there, rather than *true* or *truth*, because the word in the singular nowhere else found, is in the plural used for *pillars*, 2 King. 18.16. or *counsels, contrivances, and purposes*, things consulted, or contrived and resolved on; in *faithfulness and firmness*, a defect of the particle *in*, as ch. 24.22, 23. & 41.2. *faithfulness and firmness*, says a rabbine, one and the same thing, in two terms of the same stock, and the same sense; as the like, Jer. 16.19. But I suppose yet, there is in either place some difference; *faithfulness* is one thing and *firmness* another; and though the one is with God, ground sufficient for the other; yet with men, oft it is otherwise; faithful enough a man may be in his purposes; and yet his designs may prove infirm: but in God's counsels, both concurring, give good and sure ground of praising him, for the doing of them, though not yet done, when so faithful and firm; and as sure therefore to be done, as if accomplished already, Matth. 5.18. Mar. 13.30, 31.

**V. 2.** *{For thou hast made of a city, an heap; of a defenced city, a ruin*} Or, *Thou dost make*. You manifest your might in overthrowing and ruining the cities and strongholds of your enemies and the enemies of your people. A learned late writer thus renders the words, *Thou hast from being a city*, (or that it may no more be a city) *brought a fenced city to an heap, to ruin a palace of strangers, from being a city*: or, that it may no more so be.

*{a city*} Collectively for cities, as v. 3. ch. 26.5. though some restrain it to Jerusalem, Ps. 79.1. a most unlikely thing, that the prophet should praise God for the destruction of Jerusalem, which the psalmist there so much laments. Others, to Babylon, ch. 13.19–21. Jer. 51.25, 26. with more probability. But it seems here to be more general.

*{an heap*} Heb. *to an heap*, and so after, *to ruin*; and it might therefore be rendered, *thou hast brought it* (oft wanting, as ch. 9.9. & 21.3.) *from a city to an heap; from a fenced town to ruin*, that is, to *a ruinous heap*, as ch. 23.13. where the same phrase is so rendered. So, *to be unto desolation*, is, *to become desolate*, Jer. 12.11. the latter repeats the same thing only with some emphasis, implying, that no strength of the creature can stand out against God, ch. 2.15. & 27.10.

*{a palace of strangers to be no city, it shall never be built*} Heb. *from a city*: of which phrase, see on ch. 23.1. & 24.10. the latter part may be rendered, *that it be not built forever*, Job 12.14. a defect of the particle, as ch. 5.11. & 10.2. *forever*, here may imply, not simply at any time, but for a long time, or *an age*, as Exod. 21.6. 2 King. 5.27. Ps. 37.18, 27. ch. 34.10. for as for that commentitious distinction of the word here used, that being written at full, as it is here, it should signify *eternity*, when otherwise, some *long time*, but finite; it may by manifold places of Scripture be controlled and confuted: it is full written in most of the Scriptures above mentioned; it is otherwise, Exod. 3.15. & 15.18. Deut. 32.40. and elsewhere; where yet of necessity, it must signify *eternity*, when otherwise, some *long time*, but finite; it may by manifold places of Scripture be controlled and confuted: it is full written in most of the Scriptures above mentioned; it is otherwise, Exod. 3.15. & 15.18. Deut. 32.40. and elsewhere; where yet of necessity, it must signify *eternity*. By *the palace of strangers*, some Jewish writers would have Babylon here meant in particular; and some of ours, Rome; (the former words they understand both more generally) so called, say they, because there the Chaldean court was to which strangers from all parts repaired, ch. 13.22. But the most take the word *palace* here, as *city* before, collectively: so ch. 32.14. The *palaces*, for royal cities, seats of great kings, as ch. 23.13. called the *palaces of strangers*, that is, possessed by strange people of other nations, than Israelites; as *strangers*, and Israelites do commonly counterdivide, 1 King. 8.41. Jer. 5.19. Lam. 5.2. Eph. 2.12. so v. 5. Or, as some, *strongholds* furnished and guarded with foreign forces, ch. 13.14. Jer. 51.9. Ezek. 27.10, 11. But I see not how the version of these latter, sorts well with the text.

**V. 3.** *{Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee*} The stoutest and strongest of them, that before would not acknowledge you, either escaping and surviving in the states and kingdoms subverted, or living in remote places, and hearing the report of their fall, shall be enforced to give glory to you; and they that were formerly a terror to others, shall then stand in awe of you. So Exod. 5.2. & 8.8. & 9.27, 28. & 15.14, 15. Ps. 18.44, 45. & 66.3. & 83.16. *city* for *cities*, as v. 2. and *cities* for *inhabitants*, as ch. 19.18.

**V. 4.** *{For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress*} Or, *because thou hast been a stronghold*, or *fortress to the poor, a stronghold*, or *fortress to the needy*, for so the word properly signifies, ch. 23.4. & 30.3. distinguished from *strength*, Jer. 16.19. That which shall gain so much glory to God, will be, not only the consideration of the destruction of those mighty ones, with their states and kingdoms, that opposed him and his people, v. 2. Dan. 2.44, 45. but the observation also of his powerful protection of his poor despised and dejected ones, formerly oppressed by them; and of his strange deliverances wrought for them in their deepest distresses, Ps. 9.9. & 18.27. A very conspicuous and remarkable example hereof, does the raising of the siege of Jerusalem, if it were, at least besieged by Sennacherib; the raising of his camp, howsoever, intended for the siege of it, afford, ch. 37.36. Yet to restrain it to that, I suppose it to be a needless narrowing of the text.

*{a refuge from the storm*} What he had said before of God's protecting, and delivering his poor people, is here illustrated by certain elegant resemblances, this taken from such places of covert and shelter, as in storm and tempest of wind or rain, men or beasts are wont for succor and safeguard to retire to, ch. 4.6. & 32.2.

*{a shadow from the heat*} See ch. 4.6. & 32.2. v. 5.

*{when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall*} Or, *for the blast of the violent ones, was like a storm against a wall*, as rendering a reason, why there was no small need of such shelter and safeguard; because the violent rage of the wicked, until by God repressed and suppressed, Ps. 76.10, 12. was like some furious gust of wind, or storm of rain or hail, that beating on a wall, and that but a weak one, either wholly shatters, or shrewdly shakes it, ch. 28.2. Ezek. 13.10, 11, 14. Mat. 7.25. *a storm of a wall*, for *a storm against a wall*; as, *a covert for a storm*, for *a covert from*, or *against a storm*, ch. 32.2.

**V. 5.** *{thou shalt bring down the noise of strangers, as the heat in a dry place*} Or, *But, as the heat, in a drought*; or, *dry place, so the tumultuous noise*, or, *tumult, of the strangers, didst thou abate*. The adversative, oft wanting, is to be supplied; as Ps. 119.103, 113. to clear the connection of this verse, with the close of the former. You did suppress their tumultuous noise and rage; as the extreme heat of the sun, in an open plain, or on some heath, putting passengers to much pain, is much abated, by the intervention of some thick cloud, or, the shade of some shroudy tree. See ch. 4.6. & 32.2.

*{the noise*} Or, *tumult*: as Ps. 74.23. See ch. 22.2.

*{of strangers*} Of whom, v. 2.

*{in a dry place*} Heb. *drought*: and so ch. 32.2. Ps. 68.6. for land, or place of *drought*: as more fully, Ps. 63.1. ch. 41.18. Ezek. 19.13.

*{even the heat with the shadow of a cloud, the branch of the terrible ones shall be brought low*} I join these two branches together, because they make up the latter part of the verse, divided by a middle stop from the former. The words may well be rendered, *as the heat* (is abated) *with a thick shadow; so the song*, or *chanting of the terrible ones was abased*: for this latter part runs exactly in the same tenor with the former: the former note of similitude is supplied from the former part; the latter as before, and oft in the like, Prov. 25.12. & 26.11.

*{with the shadow of a cloud*} Or, *of a thick cloud*. See ch. 14.14. & 19.1. or, as some render it not amiss, *with a thick shade*, whether of cloud, shroud, or the like: for the word is more general. See Exod. 19.9. Hab. 2.6.

*{branch*} Where the word is so used, I find not: nor, were it elsewhere so used, would it fit here: for *song* it is used, Cant. 2.12. it is put here for *triumph*, well sorting with the precedent *tumult*: their roaring and reveling, their shouting and triumphing shall be quelled and quailed, ch. 23.11. & 24.8, 9.

*{the terrible ones*} The same with *the strangers* before.

*{brought low*} Or *abased*, *dejected, humbled, cast down, laid low*, so is the word used, Ps. 116.10. *I was much dejected*, and, *before I was humbled*, or, *brought low*, Ps. 119.67. compare this with Ps. 7.4, 23. there their *tumult* is said to go *amain up*: here their triumph is said to come as fast down, and but one letter difference between the one and the other. They, though great ones, that would have it to signify, *to answer*, and thus render the words: *which* (to wit, heat) *answered* (or *was fit for*) *the branch of the violent*, seem to writhe and wring the text too hard. For I spare to spend further words, in relating how strangely the rabbines, some of them, and some of ours also, tear it asunder: Only I will adjoin what a learned late writer suggests. He would have the text thus rendered; *As the heat in a dry place, is the tumult of strangers, the heat wilt thou bring down with the shade of a thick cloud, the cutting off of the terrible ones shall testify it*. He confesses, the pauses, as they are in the text, go against him: but he denies it necessary to stick constantly to them: and yet when they afford a plain and fair sense, I should not lightly depart from them.

**V. 6.** *{And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees: of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined}* Or, *Moreover*; For the prophet having finished his former digression, wherein he had directed his speech unto God, in way of praising of his name for such passages of his providence, as he had formerly related: He does at this verse return again to his former prophetical discourse; and in these words, foretells what the Lord will do further: When having vanquished his enemies, and enlarged his kingdom, and begins to manifest himself in more glorious manner, than formerly, among his people, ch. 24.23. he will do as great princes and potentates are wont to do in such like cases, 2 Sam. 6.18, 19. 1 King. 8.65. Est. 1.2–9. Dan. 5.1. he will entertain his subjects of all sorts, out of nations reduced now unto his obedience, with a most royal and magnificent spiritual feast, described here by such worldly dainties, as are wont to be the materials of such solemn and sumptuous banquets; thereby figuring those celestial viands, wherewith God feeds his people by the ministry of his word and sacraments, and the comfortable presence of his Spirit in his church here, Ps. 22.26, 29. & 36.8. Prov. 9.2. Mat. 22.2–4. Luk. 14.16, 17. Rom. 14.17. and will yet further satisfy them, even to the full by the immediate communicating of himself unto them hereafter, Luk. 22.16, 30. Rev. 19.9.

*{in this mountain*} *Mount Zion*, God's court, ch. 24.23. unto which this looks back; a type of the church, ch. 2.2. Rev. 14.1. & 21.2.

*{the Lord of hosts*} See ch. 1.9.

*{unto all people*} Heb. *peoples*, as ch. 2.3. & 56.7. as well Gentiles as Jews, Rev. 7.9.

*{feast*} Not *a sacrifice*, as a learned late writer would have it, expounding it of God's vengeance executed on his enemies, who are thereby consumed, as meat at a feast, and whose destruction is as pleasing to God, as is any meat and drink at a feast to a man; though it be true, that the word *sacrifice* is sometime used of *a feast*, Gen. 31.54. and the slaughter of God's enemies is termed *a sacrifice*, ch. 34.6. for that is not the word here used; but one that has no such ambiguity, signifying no other thing than *a feast*, or *a drinking*, as the Greek word also does, Gen. 21.8. Est. 2.18.

*{fat things*} Fit for, and reserved commonly for feasts, Neh. 6.10. Luk. 15.23, 30.

*{wines on the lees*} The Hebrew text has no more than *lees*, as Ps. 75.8. Zeph. 1.12. whereby some would have to be meant strong wines, wines not racked, but remaining still upon their lees, Jer. 48.11. and it is true indeed, that as wines cannot be clear till they have some time to settle; so they cannot attain their full strength, until they have rested some space of time, upon their lees, which for some time, are said to preserve and feed them; whereof also it may be supposed, that they are so termed. Howbeit, I rather conceive, by wines of lees (for that is to be understood) are meant *pure wines*, wines drawn off from the lees (the prophet himself afterward seems so to expound it) as by *a city of destruction*, some conceive to be meant, *a city saved from destruction*, ch. 19.18. and as ch. 32.2. *a hiding place of the storm, and a covert of the tempest*; for a hiding place from the storm, and a covert from the tempest; or, as a corpse is termed *a soul*, from the soul that it formerly held, though now gone from it, Num. 5.2. & 9.10. and as *vintage clusters*, for clusters remaining when the vintage is past and gone, Mic. 7.1. Of wine at feasts, see ch. 5.12. & 22.13.

*{full of marrow*} Heb. *marrowed*, or *well marrowed*; for there seems an emphasis in the word, the word is nowhere else found; the word *marrow* whence it comes once only, Job 21.24. and another from it, signifying *fat ones*; because such commonly have most marrow, Ps. 66.15. ch. 5.17. whence also some expound the word here, *fatted*, or *crammed*; not fat of themselves, and their own feeding; but fed of purpose, to make more than ordinarily fat. So Mat. 22.6. Luk. 15.23. in *marrow*, not fatness only, but sweetness also exceeds; so they conceived, that rendered another word *marrow*, Ps. 63.5. but the word there used does not so signify.

*{wines on the lees well refined*} Heb. no more, than *lees refined*, or, *well*, or, *thoroughly refined*: for the word is in the form of weight: and in its original notion, it imports such *a refining*, as is used about metals, for the purifying of them, by melting out of them, whatsoever drossy matter is mixed with them, 1 Chron. 28.18. & 29.4. Ps. 12.6. Mal. 3.3. but here, being applied to wines, it must of necessity, signify a drawing of them clear, and clean off from their lees, that being the thing, wherein the purity of that liquor consists. The Jewish rabbines, divers of them, refer all this to the execution to be done on Gog and Magog, Ezek. 39.4. and by *fat things*, therefore would have understood, such cloying meats, as man's stomach abhors; by *lees refined*, not wine drawn from the lees, but lees drawn from the wine, Ps. 75.8. and apply hereunto, that passage, ch. 49.26. But the tenor of the context, which they little regard, does, of itself, readily, and clearly refel them.

**V. 7.** *{And he will destroy in this mountain, the face of the covering cast over all people, and the veil that is spread over all nations*} The prophet further proceeds, to relate the spiritual benefits that should accrue unto those of the Gentiles that shall be, by the ministry of the gospel, brought home unto God, and joined unto his church. The first whereof is, that they shall be freed from that ignorance and obstinacy, wherewith their minds and hearts were formerly possessed, and that kept God and them aloof, Eph. 4.17, 18. For they narrow the text unreasonably, that restrain it, to the removal of that great terror from Sennacherib's forces, that blinded men's minds, and made them at their wits' end.

*{destroy*} Heb. *swallow up*, or *swallow down*, as v. 8. ch. 19.3. & 49.29.

*{in this mountain*} Whereof before, v. 6.

*{the face of the covering*} Or, *wrapping* rather, as 1 Sam. 21.9. and there seems to be a transposition in the words, not unusual, *the face of wrapping*; for, *the wrapping of the face*; or, the *face of wrapping* or *wrapper*, as Gen. 3.24. *a flame of sword*, for *a sword of flame*, or *a flaming sword*, Lev. 5.15. *silver of shekels*, for *shekels of silver*, Num. 6.9. *his head of consecration*, for *the consecration of his head*, and this *face wrapper* may seem to allude either to the face cloth of death, wherewith dead men's faces are wrapped up, Joh. 11.44. or of condemnation, wherewith malefactors, after sentence passed upon them, had wont to have their head wrapped up by the hand of the executioner, or some other, as unworthy longer to see the light, Est. 7.8.

*{cast over*} Or, *wrapped over*: covering them so, as it does enwrap them withal: as in mourning, men wrap up head and face, 1 Sam. 19.4. and Elias wrapped up his head and face, with his mantle, 1 King. 19.13.

*{all people*} Heb. *peoples*: as v. 6. and so after, *nations*; all of them, being destitute of the light of grace, and sound knowledge of God, while they abode wrapped up in their natural blindness of mind, and hardness of heart, and spiritual deadness in sin, Eph. 2.1–3, 12. & 4.17–19.

*{and the veil, that is spread over all nations*} The same thing in divers terms.

*{veil*} Or, *covering*, as ch. 28.2. & 30.1. Of this *veil*, or *covering*, now resting upon the Jewish nation, as in times past, upon the Gentiles; yet promised, in time, also, to be taken from them: See the apostle, 2 Cor. 3.14–16. alluding there, to another *veil*: whereof, Exod. 34.33, 34. For the Jewish doctors run wide here, that understand all this, of much evil and misery, that should befall the nations, who had lived quietly and securely hitherto, as under a sure and safe covert, Zach. 1.11. which as *a veil*, cast over their faces, had kept them from the foresight of their future afflictions, ch. 47.7, 8.

**V. 8.** *{He will swallow up death in victory*} Or, *And he will*, or, *he will, also, destroy death forever*. That the copulative is to be supplied, both the connection of the context, and the use of the verb in Hebrew, show. The second benefit accruing to the convert nations, a freeing of them from the power of death, Hos. 13.14. Heb. 2.14, 15. and putting them into a condition of life, yea, into possession of eternal life inchoated here, Joh. 3.18, 36. & 8.51. & 10.15, 26. and to be entirely completed, and fully consummated, hereafter, 1 Cor. 15.26, 54. 2 Tim. 1.10. Rev. 20.24. & 22.4. For they straiten the text, and give it a very slender sense, that expound it only of freeing the Jews, at Jerusalem, from fear and danger of death, from Sennacherib's forces, by the dissolution of his camp, ch. 37.35. & 38.6.

*{swallow up*} Or, *destroy*: as v. 7.

*{in victory*} Or, *unto victory*; until an utter conquest be made of him. So the Greek, which the apostle retains, 1 Cor. 15.54. because the sense is sound and good; though it do not exactly render the letter: for the Hebrew is, as the old Latin well yields it, *forever*: and so, indeed, the word in this form of speech, constantly signifies, Job 4.20. Ps. 9.18. ch. 13.20. & 34.10. which they cut too too short, that expound, so long as Ezekiah lives, and so limit it, by the narrow last of his life, ch. 39.8.

*{and the Lord God will wipe away tears from all faces*} A third benefit accruing to the godly converted ones, (not, as some, to the besieged, by Sennacherib, at Jerusalem, only,) that they shall be freed from all occasions of such anxiety and anguish, as they were formerly surcharged with, and drew tears oft from them, which shall then be dried up, fulfilled, partly, in this life, by the inward comforts, and spiritual joys, from time to time imparted unto them from above, Mat. 5.11, 12. Joh. 16.21, 33. Act. 2.41. & 8.8. & 16.34. Rom. 5.2, 3. & 12.12. & 14.17. 2 Cor. 6.10. Phil. 3.1. & 4.4. 1 Thess. 9.16. 1 Pet. 1.6, 8. 1 Joh. 1.5. but perfectly in the next, when all grounds and occasions of grief and heaviness, shall be utterly abandoned, ch. 30.19. & 35.10.

*{God will wipe away*} As an affectionate father would, with handkerchief, or the like, wipe the tears from the face, and eyes of his child, when it lies weeping out of pain or grief. So Rev. 7.17. & 21.4.

*{tears*} Heb. *tear*: as Ps. 116.5. Jer. 9.1. Mal. 2.13.

*{faces*} For *eyes*, Rev. 21.4. as *eyes*, for *face*, ch. 1.15. so *face to face*, Gen. 32.30. and, *eye to eye*, ch. 32.8. are used for one and the same: or, *faces*, because with weeping and tears, the whole face, the cheeks especially, are oft blurred and besmeared, Lam. 1.2.

*{and the rebuke of his people, shall he take away from off all the earth*} Or, *and the reproach*: as it is rendered, Ps. 31.11. & 44.13. & 89.50. Jer. 31.19. and so in most places: nor was there any sufficient reason, of swerving from the usual and most common acception, and expression of it, here: *rebuke*, or *reproof*, (for they are, in a manner, one, Prov. 9.8.) is a friendly and neighborly office, Levit. 19.17. Ps. 141.5. Prov. 28.23. *reproach*, a spiteful and enemy like taunt, Ps. 42. 10. & 89.51. & 102.8. and therefore suits well here: for that is the fourth favor God vouchsafes to honor his reconciled people with, a removal, and riddance of those outward afflictions, whereby God's enemies and theirs, did ordinarily take occasion to reproach, and taunt both him, and them. See Ps. 74.22. ch. 37.3, 23. & 54.4. Ezek. 36.15, 20, 30. and of the phrase, see Gen. 50.23. 1 Sam. 17.26. ch. 4.1. Luk. 1.25.

*{all the earth*} Not Sennacherib, and the Assyrians alone, ch. 37.3, 23. but the enemies of his church in general, Ps. 79.4. & 89.40. Joel 2.19, 26, 27.

*{for the Lord hath spoken it*} As ch. 21.17. & 21.4. See Ezek. 36.36.

**V. 9.** *{And it shall be said in that day*} The thankful and joyful acknowledgment made by the people of God, partakers of these his favors and mercies in those times, is by the prophet here expressed, though somewhat more succinct; yet the same in effect, with that in his own person before conceived, v. 1, 5.

*{And it shall be said*} Heb. *And he*, or *one*, or *each one*, (to wit, of God's people, so delivered, v. 8.) *shall say*, which some therefore supply, and put into the text, reading it, *And God's people shall say*, which yet is not needful. Some others render it, *that he may say*; so knitting it unto the former words, concerning God's taking away *the reproach of his people*, and making a parenthesis of the clause lying between; but such forced connections make no smooth seaming. The word here is impersonal, or indefinite; and it is therefore well and fully enough rendered, as our version yields it, containing in it as much as the word in such form of speech imports: so Deut. 32.37. where being not observed, it has caused a foul mistake, making that to be God's speech, which the tenor of the text duly considered, will appear to be the bitter taunt of his malignant adversaries, and the enemies of his people. So also, ch. 45.24. & 57.14. & 65.8. Ps. 42.3.

*{in that day*} In those times, as ch. 26.1.

*{Lo, this is our God*} As ch. 12.2. v. 1. It is he, and he only, that has done all this, Ps. 118.23. See also, ch. 35.4. & 40.9. for what is spoken by way of encouragement there, as sure to be effected, is uttered in way of acknowledgment here, as being really accomplished.

*{we have waited for him, and he will save us*} As ch. 8.17. & 33.22. or, *we waited for him*, (Ps. 33.20. & 40.1. ch. 26.8. & 30.18.) *and he hath saved us*, v. 4. for he speaks in the person of the people delivered, upon their deliverance now achieved. See ch. 26.8, 9. & 33.22.

*{this is the Lord, we have waited for him, we will be glad, and rejoice in his salvation*} Or, *we are glad, and do rejoice*. For it is the same thing, for the greater emphasis again reiterated, with expression of their inward disposition thereupon. So Ps. 118.23, 24. Though some understand it, as spoken of a hopeful expectation of future, preservation and protection, v. 10.

*{be glad, and rejoice*} Two words of the same notion, to express the abundance of their joy, Ps. 14.7. ch. 65.18. & 66.10.

*{in his salvation*} In the deliverances afforded us by him. So Ps. 9.14. & 13.5. & 21.1.

**V. 10.** *{For in this mountain shall the hand of the Lord rest*} These words render a reason of the rejoicing and triumphing of God's people, and of the assurance of their safety; to wit, because the hand of God's power and providence, is continually, and constantly stretched out over them, both for their protection, and for the destruction, also of those that attempt aught against them, Zach. 2.5, 9. And this branch is, therefore deemed by some, to be as a passage from the relation of the gracious exhibition of mercy and magnificence, to the one, unto the declaration of the just execution of such grievous judgments as should be inflicted upon the other. Those other interpretations, either of those that expound it of God's smiting hand only, in afflicting and chastising of his own people, which, say they, shall then *rest*, that is, *cease*, Gen. 2.2, 3. Num. 10.36. or, in taking vengeance upon their enemies, which it shall *rest* in, that is, shall be long about: as Ps. 125.3. Zach. 9.1. or of those that understand it of the eternal *rest* of the saints, with God, in heaven, Heb. 4.4–11. they seem none of them to express the genuine sense of the place.

*{in this mountain*} Whereof before, v. 6, 7. for in heaven (as some will have it) such a powerful protection will not need, no more than strong guards, where no enemy either is near, or can approach.

*{the hand of the Lord*} His powerful protection, ch. 49.2.

*{rest*} Reside; make its constant abode: so Ps. 132.14. Prov. 14.33. ch. 11.2. See Deut. 33.12. ch. 4.5, 6.

*{and Moab shall be trodden down under him, even, as straw is trodden down for the dunghill*} That hand of his, that is spread over his people to protect them, shall be stretched out against their adversaries, to destroy them, ch. 11.13, 15. & 19.16. & 26.11.

*{Moab*} The Moabites here, as the Edomites elsewhere, ch. 34.6. & 63.1. and both together, ch. 11.14. are put for the enemies of God's people in general; because they were of the chief of those bad neighbors, Jer. 12.14. that disturbed God's inheritance, and were ever and anon, plotting and attempting against them, Num. 22. & 23. & 24. Deut. 23.3. Josh. 24.9. Judg. 3.13, 14. Mic. 6.5. and ready to join with any other that invaded them, Ps. 83.7. 2 Chr. 20.1. 2 King. 13.20. & 24.2.

*{trodden down*} Or, *crushed*: as Job 39.15. or, *threshed*. So the word properly signifies, Deut. 25.4. 1 Chr. 21.20. ch. 21.10. & 28.28. but so used, as here, Judg. 8.7. 2 King. 13.7. ch. 41.15. Amos 1.3. Mic. 4.13. Hab. 3.12. Howbeit, a learned writer would have that of *treading*, the first and native notion of the word; because the Syrians mostly so use it: that of *threshing*, the secondary; because with cattle, they used to tread it out in threshing, Deut. 25.4.

*{under him*} Under his feet, Ps. 110.1. ch. 26.6. Mal. 4.3. or, as some interpret it, *in his place*, to wit, Moab's, wheresoever he shall be found; or abiding. So is the word used, Exod. 16.29. ch. 46.7. and may do not amiss here.

*{as straw is trodden down*} Or, *threshed*: and by threshing, bruised and broken with the iron teeth of the cartwheel, that is drawn over it, ch. 28.28. and 41.15. or the hoofs of the cattle, that tread it out, Deut. 25.4. Hos. 10.11. Mic. 4.12, 13. See somewhat the like resemblances used, of subduing and destroying, Ps. 18.42. and 44.5. and 60.12. and 108.13. Zach. 10.5. but here, rather, *trodden down*: because the *dunghill* follows, on which it is not wont to be threshed, but trodden, Matthew 5.13. Luk. 14.35.

*{for the dunghill*} There being less regard had of such straw, as is destinate to the dunghill, than of that, that is intended to be reserved for the foddering, or littering of beasts, or other the like uses, Gen. 24.25. 1 King. 4.28. ch. 11.7. or, *in the dunghill*, that being cast out thither, is there trodden down, and trampled upon, with the feet both of men and beasts, Mat. 5.13. There is, in this place, some variety of copies; the writing is *bime*, with a *jod*; but the Masoretes would have it read *bome*, with a *vau*: and so it is precisely, *in*, or, *on, the dunghill*. Howbeit, a learned late writer, retaining that which the writing exhibits, renders it, *in the water of the dunghill*, as the Chaldee, *in the dirt*: for dung and water makes dirt; nor is chaff, or stubble, wont to be laid on some dry, but on some moist dunghill, the sooner to rot it, and make the better soil of it: So he. But some conceive it, to be the proper name of a place, before mentioned, ch. 10.31. which they deem to be a town of Moab, the same with that, Jer. 48.2. though assigned to Judah, Josh. 15.35. and so read it, *as straw in Madmenah*; supposing mention to be made thereof, because being situate in a corn country, there was both great store of straw, and in that regard, the less regard had thereof there. The root it comes of, signifies *dung*, 2 King. 9.37. Ps. 83.10. Jer. 8.2. and thence the Jewish critics suppose this word, being here only so used, to signify the place of dung, the *dunghill*. Howsoever, in the words here, there is a pleasant consonancy, between the word used for straw, here, (in that form, nowhere else found, as made choice of, by the prophet, for that purpose) and this *Madmenah*, which our English cannot express.

**V. 11.** *{And he shall spread forth his hands in the midst of them, as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim*} Some, as well Jewish, as Christian writers, understand these words of Moab; but diversely, either that he should strive and endeavor by all means, but in vain, to get from under those pressures, that from God's hand, lay heavy on him, Ps. 38.2. as one in danger of drowning does, to get safe to the shore, Act. 27.43, 44. or that being subdued and thrown down, he should lie sprawling on the ground resembling the manner of a swimmer; or that being so subdued, he should in like sort, as a suppliant, spread abroad his hands to God in prayer; as ch. 1.5. Others, of either sort, conceive it rather to be spoken of God; he shall as one that in swimming with all his might, stretched out his arms, in powerful manner, reach and smite his enemies, on either side, Zach. 5.3. or, he shall as easily destroy them, as the swimmer parts the waters with his hands, they being no more able to make resistance against him, than the water against the arm, or the stroke of the swimmer, Ps. 110.2. ch. 14.26, 27.

*{and he shall bring down their pride*} Which reigned so much before with them. See ch. 16.6. Jer. 48.29. as a man in swimming easily dips, or thrusts down aught, that he meets with in the water.

*{together with the spoils of their hands*} So some; or, as others, *with the lying in wait*, or *wiles of his hands*, (to wit, Moab's,) understanding it of the wealth of the Moabites, gotten by robbery, and lying in wait, to prey, and spoil, Prov. 1.11, 13. both the pride of Moab's heart, and the fetches of his hands, shall be pulled down. To somewhat the like purpose, do some other expound the word, but with reference to God, *with*, or, *by, the lyings in wait of his hands*, that is, *with his hands, that lie in wait*: and they suppose it to be a metaphor taken from wild beasts, that lie lurking in dens, and covert, watching for prey; which when it comes in their way, they suddenly start out, and surprise it with their paws, Ps. 10.8, 9. so the meaning should be, that he would be to Moab, as he is said to have been sometime to his people; *as a bear, or lion, lying in wait in his covert*, Lam. 3.10. But, because a word somewhat near to it, and of the same stock with it, signifies *windows*, Josh. 13.3. 2 King. 7.2. ch. 24.18. which were in those parts of *lattice*, 2 King. 1.2. Cant. 2.9. some thereby understand the *fingers*, that being spread abroad, are as lattice: and so it should be, *with the lattice*, or *fingers, of* *his hands*: and because the same word applied to waters, seems to import *sluices*, or *dams*, that keep in water; (so they render it Gen. 7.11. & 8.2.) some would have the word, here used, so also to signify; and translate it, *with the cataracts*, or *sluices, of his hands*: Which, to me, seems to sound very harsh, and not to suit well with the context; the use of such *sluices*, or *dams*, being to keep in, and to keep up water contrary to what is here intimated, of depressing and bringing down. The word, therefore, being nowhere else read, I concur with those Jewish critics, who inform us, that the word here signifies not the *arm*, as many of our interpreters mistake them; nor the *cubit*, as some other; but the *elbow*, or, more largely, the *nooks*, or *bendings* of the arm, whether at *elbow*, or *armhole*; for the word seems indifferent to either, coming from a root, that signifies *to lie in wait*: as in *nooks* and *corners*, both men or beasts use to do, Ps. 10.9, 10. and so it sorts well with the similitude of a *swimmer*; and may be rendered, *with the elbows*, or *armholes*: and consequently, more familiarly and plainly, *with the bowings*, or *bendings*, that is with the *motions*, or *strokes* (as both the Chaldee, and old Latin interpret it,) *of his arms*. The only difficulty is, how it should be fitly said, *with the elbows*, or *armholes, of his hands*: but that is easily solved: for in those places where the word is used, whereby they interpret this, and is generally acknowledged to signify one of these twain, the very same phrase is used, *the elbows*, or *armholes of the hands*, Ezek. 13.18. Jer. 38.12. In which places, the learned also observe, that *hands* are put for *arms*: and so the old Greek translators took the word, Ps. 128.2. when they rendered it by a word, that signifies the forepart of the arm, next the hand, or *wrist*; which word, also, usually signifying *fruit*, gave, by mistake, occasion of that absurd translation, in the old Latin; *Of the labor of thy fruit shalt thou eat*: out of which, the ancients pick mysteries. Thus have I endeavored to clear this dark and difficult passage; which, as many, on the one side, strain and stray in; so, as many on the other side, slight and let slip, as if nothing were dim, or doubtful in it. I shall add only, what I find since this note here inserted, in the posthumous annotations of a famous writer very deeply seen in the oriental languages. He would not have the word here questioned, to be applied to God. His reason is, because the particle here ushering it in, is (as he supposes) never taken in an instrumental notion. Yet so is it found used, Est. 9.25. *He commanded by letters*. The word, for the sense and use of it, here, he interprets it much in effect, as I do; but fetches it about another way, and applies it to Moab. For because he finds in Schindler's *Pentaglotte*, that with the rabbines, *arboth*, (the word here used) or *arubboth* rather, (for to *arubbah* Schindler subjoins it,) *of the feet*, does signify *the secrets*, or *secret parts* of the body, and that a word in Arabic, somewhat near it, is used for the same; he thence conceives the term to come from a root, that has a notion of *muchness* in it; (the first letter in it, as in *arbeh* for *a locust*, being not radical, but additional,) and to signify those parts of the feet, that have most flesh on them; to wit, *the thighs*: and consequently, by proportion the *arboth*, or *arubboth of the hands*, to be those parts thereof, that are most fleshy and brawny, to wit, those which the Latins call *lacertos*, *the arms*. So, because man's strength consists most in his arms, Ps. 18.34. the meaning to be, that God would put down Moab, together with all his might: and so he threatens, indeed, to *break Moab's arm*, Jer. 48.25. Now about these his criticisms, I will not contend with so great a scholar, being, in these studies, but a novice to him. Howbeit, well knowing the word *feet*, to be frequently used in some forms, for those parts, not with the rabbines only, but in the sacred Scriptures, as I have showed on ch. 6.2. & 7.20. I conceive that those Jewish masters, where they apply this *arubboth* to the word *feet* so used, understand nothing thereby, but *foramina*, the *holes*, or *issues* of, or in those parts taken from that acception of the word, whereby it is in Scripture used for such *holes* in the wall and house side, *windows*, and *loopholes*; or in the roof and house top, *louvers* and the like, whereby light issues, and is let in; smoke issues, and is let out, 2 King. 7.2, 19. Hosh. 13.3. See on ch. 24.17. & 60.8. and according to this notion, there is no fit application of it unto the hands. Besides, should it be referred to that other root, as he would have it, I should rather deem the term given to those parts in a notion of *multiplication* than of *muchness*; because they are instruments of propagation, whereof that root is most frequently used, Gen. 1.22, 28. & 9.1, 7, 8. Exod. 1.10, 12. What from some of the Jewish critics I have observed, concerning the genuine notion of the word in this place, was above showed; and how fitly it agrees to the course of the context, I leave, together with what has been here annexed, to the judgment of others.

**V. 12.** *{And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls, shall he bring down, lay low, and bring to the ground, even to the dust*} The prophet here turns his speech to Moab, (as the variation of the person, is in this prophecy, very frequent. See ch. 1.29. & 10.3, 4, 25, 26.) telling him, that notwithstanding his pride and haughtiness before touched, ch. 24.21. & 16.6. and the height and strength of his walls and fortifications, which he so much relied upon, he should find God too strong, both for him and them, who would pull them both down, lay them level with the ground, and reduce them to dust: and this he delivers in variety of terms, and expressions, close packed together, without any intervening particles, (which needed not, therefore, to be inserted) to make the sentence the quicker.

*{the fortress of the high fort of the walls*} That is, your fenced and lofty walls; for both words have reference unto *walls*. See ch. 26.5.

*{shall he bring down, lay low*} Or, *shall be brought down, laid low*, as v. 9.

*{bring to the ground*} Or, *brought to the ground*, as before, Heb. *make to touch the ground*: as Lam. 2.2.

*{to the dust*} Laid in the dust: as Ps. 7.5. & 44.25. So ch. 26.5. *he maketh them touch the dust*; or, dissolved, and turned into dust: not broken down only flat to the ground, but battered, also, so to pieces, that they are nothing but dust: as Job 10.9. Ps. 22.15. & 18.42. ch. 27.9. & 41.15. 2 King. 23.7, 15. *dust*, for, *rubbish*: as Neh. 4.2, 10. Thus if we take it, (which would add much emphasis) somewhat is to be supplied: but the former, because of the parallel place, there cited, seems sufficient.

### CHAPTER 26

**V. 1.** *{In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah*} As before, the prophet did, by the way, briefly relate, what affections and meditations God's people should have, when they should so plentifully partake of the mercies of God above mentioned, ch. 25.9. so here through this whole chapter, he delivers them a large song, of purpose penned by him, for them, suitable to their affections, before related, then to be made use of, what time these benefits should betide them. See the like, ch. 12. The psalm, or song, is wholly spent, in the relation and acknowledgment: 1. Of their former extreme misery, in their forepassed difficulties and distresses. 2. Of God's gracious mercy and free goodness, in the supporting of them under them, and delivering them out of them. 3. Of the obstinacy of the wicked under God's hand, together with his just judgment inflicted on them for it, to their endless destruction.

*{in that day*} As ch. 25.9. & 27.1.

*{in the land of Judah*} In the church: as Jer. 31.23.

*{we have a strong city*} To wit, Jerusalem, while God protects it, ch. 37.35. and the church of God, thereby typified, Ps. 125.1, 2. Matth. 16.18. Heb. *a city of strength*; as, *a fort of strength*, for, *a strong fort*, Prov. 18.10.

*{salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks*} Heb. *salvation he setteth*; that is, *salvation is set*: as ch. 25.9. the main ground of the city's strength, not her walls, or moats between the walls, or her outward means of defense, ch. 22.9–11. but God's protection, his salvation, sufficient instead of all these, and without which, none of these were able to secure them, Ps. 121.1, 2. & 125.1, 2. ch. 60.18. Zach. 2.5.

*{walls and bulwarks*} Heb. *bulwark*: or, whatsoever it is, that the word here used, signifies. So Lam. 2.8. where *wall*, and it, are likewise joined together, and is rendered *rampart*. Some would have the word to signify *a ditch*, or *trench*, ch. 22.11. as our English renders it, 2 Sam. 20.15. Some, the *counterscarp*, or the outer, and lower wall, that stands before the inner, and higher. For their cities were many of them double walled, ch. 22.11. and so those take it, 2 Sam. 20.15. that understand the words there of the city: Some, the *parapet*, or bank of earth, or some other like fortification raised within the wall to strengthen it. Others, lastly, the coping of the wall. Whereof, see Vitruvius, l. 2. c. 8. and Curtius, l. 9. c. 4. for the shooting of the rain, making the fence firmer, and entrance over it, the more difficult. The Jewish rabbines seem doubtful of it, and differ much about it; and though it be here, and elsewhere, in the two latter places above mentioned, distinguished from the wall; yet it seems to be used for the wall in general: and is so rendered, 1 King. 21.23. though some Jewish doctors would have the text there altered, and a letter added to make it agree with, 2 King. 9.36. Howsoever, this, and *wall* here, are used to comprehend all means of fortification, which God's safeguard is alone sufficient to countervail, where wanting; and to add strength sufficient for safety, where weak: and these seem here, as to be opposed to those strong and stately walls of Moab, that were to be battered and broken down, ch. 25.12. wanting that principal strength, which this city is from God said to have; and withal, to have some eye to the naked, and undefended estate of that city, that continued still dismantled for some space of time, even after the people's return from the captivity, to assure them of God's protection, and to strengthen their faith in him, as all sufficient to secure them, notwithstanding the want, or weakness of such outward means of defense, Neh. 1.2. & 2.13. & 4.2, 3. See Zach. 2.4, 5. a good comment upon this place.

**V. 2.** *{Open ye the gates, that the righteous nation which keepeth the truth may enter in*} He wills either the gates of Jerusalem, a type of the church, to be set open for the receipt of those returning from dispersion or captivity that had continued faithful with their God, or by repentance returned to him; thereby intimating, both the multitudes of those that should be reserved in those calamitous times, to replenish and recruit that city and state; as also, the confluence of others together with them unto God's church, when the limits thereof should be enlarged, ch. 60.11. Zach. 2.11. & 8.4, 5, 22. Or, as some, of the temple that the people preserved, and returned, might enter thither, to praise God for his mercy toward them, in the deliverances vouchsafed them, Ps. 24.7, 9. & 118.19, 20. But the former seems the better, and is the more received; for they draw it out too far, that understand it of setting heaven gates open at the last day for all the faithful, Mat. 25.10, 34.

*{the righteous nation*} As ch. 60.21. & 61.11. a reformed and upright people; such righteousness is here intimated, as is spoken of, Mat. 5.20. Luk. 1.6. what some add of imputed righteousness, seems not here aimed at.

*{that keepeth truth*} Heb. *truths*, or *faithfulnesses*, as Prov. 13.17. & 14.5. & 20.6. that have continued constantly faithfully with God. Ps. 31.23. Hos. 11.12. Rev. 2.10, 26. & 3.8, 10. & 14.12. Some expound it of faith, as well to man, as to God; in the former whereof, the Pharisees failed, Mat. 23.23. as also, hypocrites usually do. See ch. 1.14, 15, 16. But this I suppose is too nice.

**V. 3.** *{Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee, because he trusteth in thee*} Or, *The stayed mind wilt thou keep in continued peace*. Or, *To the stayed mind wilt thou preserve constant peace*. So, the most, referring the first words unto the godly man's constancy, in adhering unto, and depending upon God, and assuring all, that so do, of a continued course of peace, and prosperity from God; Or, as others, who suppose (but without ground) that there would be a tautology in the latter part of the verse, if the former were so understood, and require therefore to have the former applied unto God; *By a firm thought*, or *purpose, wilt thou preserve constant peace unto them*, (that is, to the faithful before mentioned, v. 2.) *because they trust in thee*, Ps. 37.40. Rom. 11.29. 2 Tim. 1.9.

*{whose mind is stayed*} Heb. *a stayed thought*, or *imagination*, or *mind*, or *purpose*, the word signifies properly a *frame*, or *fashion*, or *thing framed and fashioned*, by the potter's art and skill, ch. 29.16. Hence it is translated, and applied sometimes to man's body, and the frame and model of it, Job 17.7. Ps. 103.14. sometime to the soul, and to the mind more specially, that is as a mint or forge in it; and so it signifies any thing whatsoever is *framed*, conceived, or contrived in it, be it thought, imagination, deliberation, determination, or the like, Gen. 6.5. and 8.21. Deut. 31.21. 1 Chron. 28.9. and 29.18.

*{stayed on thee*} As ch. 48.2. they *stay themselves upon God*, but that is in another form. Or simply *stayed*, applied to God's precepts and purposes, Ps. 111.8. to the godly man's heart and mind, Ps. 112.8. here, *a stayed mind*; for, *a man of a stayed mind*, a firm or constant minded man: as *firmness*, for hands of *firmness*, hands firm and steady, Exod. 17.12. and *firmness*, or *faithfulness*, for *precepts of firmness* or *faithfulness*, firm and faithful precepts, Ps. 119.86. so *folly*, for *a man of folly*, a fool, Prov. 24.9. and *wisdom*, for a man of *wisdom*; a wise man, Mic. 6.9. and *peace*, for a man of *peace*, a peaceable man, Ps. 120.7. and *prayer*, for a man of *prayer*; a devout man, Ps. 109.4.

*{perfect peace*} Or, *constant continued peace*; or all manner of true and sound peace, Joh. 14.27. & 16.33. Rom. 5.1. & 14.17. Phil. 4.7. Heb. *peace, peace*, as ch. 57.19. *peace*, for *prosperity*, as ch. 48.18. Ps. 119.165.

*{because he trusteth in thee*} So Ps. 37.40. 1 Chr. 5.20. 2 Chr. 13.18. & 16.8. See also, Ps. 9.10. & 22.4, 5. & 32.10. & 33.21, 22. & 34.22. & 125.1. The word here, is, *he*, or *it; is trusted in thee*, that is, by trust or confidence, fixed or fastened upon you, as Ps. 112.7. (and the form is nowhere else read, but here, and there) *his heart is fixed, it is trusted* (or by trust and confidence fastened or settled) *upon God*.
