**V. 4.** *{Trust in the Lord for ever*} Upon assurance of God's readiness, to confer all sure and sound peace and prosperity upon those that sincerely rely on, and keep firm and faithful to him; and of his constancy, in continuing the same incessantly to them, they incite and encourage one another perpetually in all estates, and at all times to rely and depend upon him. So 2 Chr. 20.20. Ps. 31.3, 5, 7. 32.6–10. & 55.22. & 62.8. Prov. 3.5. & 16.3.

*{for in the Lord Jehovah is everlasting strength*} Heb. *for*, or *because in Jah, Jehovah, is a rock of ages*, or, as the old Latin renders it, *for Jah Jehovah is a rock of*, or, *unto eternity*, that which a learned late writer approves, deeming the particle *bet*, here redundant, as Exod. 32.22. Job 18.8. Ps. 55.18. Hosh. 13.9. as also, Ps. 68.4. not *in Jah*, but *Jah is his name*, or, *whose name is Jah*, as ch. 47.4. & 48.2. An argument to induce and persuade to trust constantly and perpetually in the true God, because he continues forever a God of infinite power, able ever to save, ch. 63.1. Heb. 7.25.

*{Jah, Jehovah*} Two names of God; the former found also, Ps. 68.4. and constantly in *Hallelu-jah*, that begins and ends divers psalms, as Ps. 111.1. & 112.1. & 113.1. and 104.35. & 105.45. & 106.48. Rev. 19.1, 3, 6. the latter, as frequently throughout all the books of the Old Testament, so expressly in our versions, Exod. 6.3. Ps. 83.18. nor is the one, as some have deemed, an abbreviation only of the other; but they are two distinct names, arising from two distinct roots, though both of the same signification, and have a notion of *being* in them, and either name therefore belongs unto the only true God; both in regard of his own eternal and immutable *essence*, or *being*, which he has from no other, but in, and of himself only, and is no other than himself, Exod. 3.14. and in regard also of his works, the creatures which have their being all from him, Gen. 1.1. & 2.1. Ps. 146.6. Act. 17.25, 28. Rom. 11.36. Rev. 4.11. and of his word and counsels, and their accomplishments, which he never fails to give being to, in their due and appointed season, Exod. 6.3. & 12.41. Ps. 33.11. & 146.6. ch. 14.24, 27. & 55.11. Those of ours, that would have the one to signify here God the Father; and the other, God the Son; and render the text, *in the Lord, the Lord is strength everlasting*; that is, the Son in the Father; according to that, *I am in the Father, and the Father in me*, Joh. 14.10. *The Lord in the Lord*; as the *Lord from the Lord*, Gen. 19.24. and, *the Lord with the Lord*, 2 Tim. 1.18. seem to pick that out of the text, that the prophet therein never intended, and to alter the genuine syntax of it.

*{everlasting strength*} The word translated *strength*, signifies primarily *a rock*, Deut. 32.13. Job 18.4. It is given oft to God, in regard of his invincible and unmovable firmness and strength, sometime simply and absolutely *the rock he is a faithful God*, Deut. 32.4. and, *The rock that begat thee, the God that formed thee*, Deut. 32.18. and, *Their rock is not as our rock*, Deut. 32.31. that is their God, as our God: sometime, with some special reference to the creature, as he who alone is able to secure them, and support them: and such a one therefore, as they may alone confidently repair to, and rely upon. Hence those speeches, *Who is a rock*, (that is one to be trusted to, or relied upon) *save our God*; and, *There is no rock like our God*, 1 Sam. 2.2. and this phrase alludes, partly to such places, as men or beasts are wont to repair to for succor and safeguard, Judg. 15.8. & 20.47. Ps. 104.18. Prov. 30.26. and hence is God styled, as *a rock of salvation*, that is, *a saving rock*, Deut. 32.15. 2 Sam. 22.47. partly to such firm grounds and bottoms, as men are wont to make choice of to build upon, that their foundation may be firm, and their structure stand sure, ch. 22.16. Mat. 7.24, 25. and to this, more especially, the prophet seems here to have had an eye: as also, ch. 28.16. & 33.16. So Mat. 16.18. Rom. 3.33. Eph. 2.20. 1 Pet. 2.6.

*{everlasting*} Heb. *of ages*, such as continues firm, and the same throughout all ages, Ps. 102.27. & 146.10. So, *a kingdom of ages*, for an everlasting kingdom, Ps. 145.13. and *salvation of ages*, for everlasting salvation, ch. 45.17. and, *righteousness of ages*, for everlasting righteousness, Dan. 9.24.

**V. 5.** *{For he bringeth down those that dwell on high*} An argument to persuade men to trust in God, and to give them assurance of his ability to protect those that depend upon him, against the proudest and most prevalent of those that oppugn or oppose them, taken from a present and pregnant proof of his power, in pulling down such mighty potentates that sat aloft so high above others, and ruinating their strongest and best defended cities, and enabling such of his, as were in regard of their seeming wants and weaknesses in the eyes of flesh and blood accounted contemptible, and unable to effect aught to prevail against those, and even to trample upon them that had so mean an esteem of them, and had formerly oppressed them, God then suffering it for their sins.

*{he bringeth down*} Or, *hath brought down*; for it is spoken, as of a thing now done and past. See v. 1.

*{those that dwell on high*} Or, *that sit aloft*, either that dwell in high walled towns, and high built palaces; see Jer. 51.25, 53, 58. or, sit on high thrones, in state far above others, see ch. 14.13, 14. & 24.21. & 25.11. Dan. 4.37.

*{the lofty city he layeth it low*} Or, *hath laid it low*, a redundancy of the pronoun very frequent, as Gen. 5.29. Ps. 1.4.

*{he layeth it low even to the ground, he bringeth it even to the dust*} Or, *he hath laid it low even to the ground, he hath brought it even to the dust*. Heb. *made it to touch even the dust*. See ch. 25.12. & 32.19. The whole verse may be thus rendered, as some give it, *For he hath brought down those that dwell on high, and the lofty city he hath laid it low, he hath laid it low even to the ground, he hath brought it to the dust*; and this best agrees with the distinctions in the original.

**V. 6.** *{The foot shall tread it down, even the feet of the poor, and the steps of the needy*} Or, *So that the foot treadeth it down*, that it is trampled upon, and that by those that seem poorest, and of least ability, or were formerly such. See ch. 14.30. a defect of the particle, intimating the effect or event; of which, see on ch. 7.25. The copulatives are wanting, nor need be inserted, because the sense is plain enough without them, and their absence makes the sentence the quicker. The sum is, he sets up his poor formerly afflicted ones over the power of their proud oppressors, Josh. 10.41. 1 Sam. 2.8. Luk. 1.52. & 10.19. Rom. 16.20. Rev. 2.26. that which is set forth by a similitude taken from cattle that tread down the grass, which even the lesser can do with the rankest of it. See ch. 37.29. Ezek. 24.18. Mal. 4.2, 3.

*{foot*} For, *feet*, as Job 39.15. Ps. 9.15. & 36.11. Put collectively, as also *poor one*, and *needy one*, for poor and needy persons, as Ps. 9.18. & 10.9.

**V. 7.** *{The way of the just is uprightness: thou most upright dost weigh the path of the just*} From this verse the prophet directs his speech unto God, and so runs on through the greatest part of it that follows, relating therein the various passages of his providence, and acknowledging his goodness in going along with them, in them, and in due time giving a good issue of them. This verse some expound of the just and upright courses that the faithful take in all estates: yet so, that their ability so to do, is from God who strengthens them therein, and enables them thereunto, Ps. 37.23. Phil. 3.13. Col. 1.10, 11. Others rather, of God's gracious providence out of his free favor towards them: so disposing of all occurrents befalling them, that in all their courses, and the passages of this life, they find a way made for them, and such impediments removed as might prove prejudicial unto them, or hinder their free progress, set forth by a metaphor taken from ways that are leveled, for the more ease and conveniency of passengers, and the stones or other like matter removed that may offend them in their passage, see Ps. 5.8. & 18.32. & 27.11. & 143.10. ch. 40.3, 4. & 62.10. Some read the verse, not disjoined in two several axioms, as we have it; but in one continued sentence, *Thou dost level the way of the just with all evenness*, or, *with most even courses, the path of the just with an even poise or balance*. So there should be a defect both of the particle *with* in either member, which is common: see ch. 24.22, 23. and of the subject, or substantive also, in the latter: the like whereunto, see ch. 5.2. But I rather divide it, as our English does.

*{The way of the just is uprightness*} Or, *a most even*, or, *straight way*. Heb. *evenness*, or *straightness* for *a way of evenness*, or *straightness*: the word supplied in the predicate from the subject, as Ps. 111.7. *the works of his hands are works of truth and judgment*, and *thy law is a law of truth*, Ps. 119.142. and *thy precepts, precepts of righteousness*, Ps. 119.172. and *a way of evenness*, or *straightness*, for *a most even way*, as *a place of plainness*, or *evenness*, for *a plain* or *even place*; Ps. 26.12. without rubs or hillocks: so Jer. 31.9. *in an even way where they shall not stumble*, or *a most straight way*, without windings and turnings, Prov. 4.26, 27. as, *a land of straightness*, or *evenness*, for *a most straight*, or *most even land*, v. 10. See Prov. 21.10. where the same, in effect, is said, that is here, and may serve as a comment for this place.

*{of the just*} Such as were before described, v. 2, 3.

*{thou most upright dost weigh the path of the just*} This way the Jewish commenters most of them go; yet the words might peradventure better be rendered, *Thou dost with evenness balance the path of the righteous*: *with evenness*, that is, *evenly*: for the word is sometime also used substantively, as Ps. 111.8. and we need not take in *poise* or *balance*: or thus, *the even path of the righteous thou dost balance*, or *level* rather, for there is no use of a balance here; that is, you O Lord, do by your leveling of them make them thus even: of the phrase, or manner of speech, see on ch. 24.10. This I conceive to be the genuine, both sense, and syntax of the place. For the further clearing whereof, we are to take notice of the use of the word rendered *weigh*; which though it seem properly so to signify, in regard of a word that either comes from it, or it comes from, (for in Hebrew, verbs sometime come from nouns) signifying *a balance*, Prov. 16.11. ch. 40.12. where it is rendered *weight* in the one place, *scales* in the other, and it may be, would be better *beam* in either: Yet in that sense properly, it is never found used in Scripture, but another in the room of it, whereof the *shekel* has its name: but by a metaphor thence taken, it is used for *to consider a thing exactly*, and *to decide*, or *do it evenly*: to which purpose, see on Ps. 58.2. where it is very elegantly used; and being applied to *a way* or *path*, it has a twofold notion: for sometime it signifies *to consider exactly* what manner of way it is, whether good or bad, right or wrong, that is, as we use to say, to *weigh it well*, as in a balance, or to *ponder* it; as it is rendered, Prov. 4.26. & 5.6, 21. sometime to *level* it, or to make it exactly even: so it is taken, Ps. 78.50. where it is but slenderly translated, *he made a way*, whereas it should be, *He leveled a path for his wrath*: he cleared a passage for it, that it might without let or interruption (as Exod. 32.10.) proceed to do execution on the obstinate Egyptian: And so it is to be here understood, *Thou dost by leveling make the just man's path even*. As for weighing them out as in a balance, a just and due proportion of chastisements and deliverances, or carrying an even hand in chastising of them when they do amiss, and relieving them again upon their repentance; neither of them seem to be proper to this place, no more than of the *weighing of men's spirits*, or *pondering of their hearts*, Prov. 16.2. & 21.2. where another word is used, which yet some would also draw hither.

**V. 8.** *{Yea, in the way of thy judgments O Lord, we have waited for thee*} Or, *Even*. An effect of their faith, and confident assurance of such dealing of God with his people, which they formerly professed, v. 7. to wit, that in consideration hereof, even then, when God seemed to lead them along through rough and rugged ways, yet they still depended upon him, and their hearts and affections hung continually after him, and kept close with him, hopefully expecting an issue out of them, and patiently waiting until the time thereof should come.

*{in the way*} Properly, *the highway*, or *traveler's way*, ch. 35.8. God's way of chastisement, is an ordinary way with his, Ps. 73.14. & 89.31, 32. a defect of the particle; as Hos. 6.9.

*{of thy judgments*} That is, chastisements, 1 Cor. 11.32. so called, either because dispensed with moderation, Jer. 10.24. & 11.30. See ch. 27.7, 8. or, because in inflicting of them, God seems to carry himself, as a judge; and for the subject matter of them, they are the same oft with those things that in a judiciary way, he inflicts upon the wicked, Jer. 30.14, 15. Lam. 1.15. & 2.5. & 3.3.

*{we have waited for thee*} See ch. 25.9. & 33.2. & 64.4.

*{the desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the remembrance of thee*} These words may thus be knit to the former, *Even when in the way of thy judgments we waited for thee, the desire of our soul was* (for it would be conceived in the time past) *unto thy name, and unto the remembrance of thee*. Our affections were not estranged from you, but our hearts were still towards you, and our minds on you, Ps. 44.17, 18. Job 13.15. ch. 64.5.

**V. 9.** *{With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early*} Or, *with my soul I desired thee; and with my spirit I sought thee*: because they speak of their forepassed carriage, during the time of their troubles. Our thoughts of you, and our desires after you, have been continual, night and day, Ps. 42.1, 2. & 63.1, 6. Mal. 3.16.

*{With my soul*} An affectionate form of speech. So Gen. 34.8. Ps. 63.1. a defect of the particle; as ch. 24.22, 23. The rabbine here observes, that a man has both a *soul*, and a *spirit*, and makes them here two distinct faculties: and it is true, that sometime they are distinguished the one from the other, 1 Thess. 5.23. but here they seem only mentioned, by an elegant variety, to make the speech the more passionate.

*{in the night*} When others are taking their rest, Ps. 63.6. & 119.62, 148. Cant. 3.1. & 5.2. They that by *night*, here understand the night of affliction, I suppose, swerve from the intendment of the prophet in this place.

*{with my spirit within me*} Heb. *in the midst of me*: a phrase here emphatical: as ch. 25.11. and would therefore have been expressed, Ps. 143.3. Dan. 7.15.

*{will I seek thee early*} The word is taken from, not the lightsome, but the dim and dusky morning; scarce twilight, (for of *duskness* it has its name,) implies both an earnest and early seeking. It is used, Ps. 63.1. Prov. 8.17. where desire is sincere, there endeavor will be serious, and seeking early, and earnest, Ps. 119.47. & 130.5, 6.

*{for when thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness*} Such a disposition and affection, not they alone, but others also, ought to have, under God's hand; and when his judgments are abroad in the world, thereby to learn the fear of God, and amendment of their lives, Job 37.23, 24. Rev. 15.4.

*{when*} So is the word used, Josh. 2.5.

*{thy judgments*} The word is general, and comprehends as well the effects of God's avenging wrath, as of his fatherly displeasure. See on v. 8.

*{in the earth*} Or, *on the earth*: and so it would be rendered, Mat. 6.10. the preposition itself there requiring it: as, *on the throne*, Ps. 9.4. & ch. 3.26. *on the ground*.

*{the inhabitants of the world*} Not we only, your peculiar people, Ps. 9.16, 19, 20. & 83.16, 18.

*{will learn*} Or, *should learn*. Heb. *have learned*. But that tense is used also in signification of duty; as Jer. 2.7. & 23.2. or in a potential form: as ch. 37.26. and as the future is oft, Mal. 2.8.

**V. 10.** *{Let favour be shewed to the wicked; yet will he not learn righteousness*} Having intimated what should be done, when God's judgments are in the world; he subjoins, now, the contrary disposition and carriage of many, so perverse in their demeanor towards God, and so desperately bent to, and set upon, evil, that neither God's mercies, nor his judgments, have any gracious or kindly work upon them, they take the more liberty to live loosely from the one; and they stand out obstinately against the other, until at length, they bring destruction upon themselves, deservedly for either, v. 11. See a pregnant proof hereof in Pharaoh, Exod. 7.12, 14. The like texture of sentence, as it is here conceived, may be found, Job 13.15. *Lo, let him slay me, yet will I trust in him*. Howbeit, it may be rendered, with some others; *Yet when favor is showed the wicked, he will not learn righteousness*: or, *Though favor be showed him, he will not learn righteousness*. See Rom. 2.4, 5. The particle is oft omitted: as Deut. 8.12. ch. 17.6.

*{learn righteousness*} To do righteously, to walk uprightly: as ch. 1.17. Phil. 4.10, 12.

*{in the land of uprightness will he deal unjustly*} Or, *in the plainest*, or *evenest land*, or *ground, he will deal perversely*. He will persist in his wicked courses, though he live among a reformed people, or in a land, where godliness is professed, and means of instruction are. So interpreters, the most, both Jewish and Christian. Or, in a land, or place, where all is plain and clear, and nothing either to offend a man in his way, or to force him out of it, even there will he go awry, or turn aside to crooked bypaths, there will he betake himself to his wonted wicked courses, where there is nothing to press him from walking uprightly, or to put him upon such practice: and this I take to be the true meaning of the prophet's words in this place, insisting still on the similitude of *a way*, or *path*, before used, v. 7, 8. God's children walk evenly and uprightly with God, even in rough and rugged ways: the wicked will tread awry, and run out, though the way be never so straight and clear, Ps. 125.5.

*{in the land of uprightness*} Heb. *a land of straightnesses*, or *rightnesses* (as ch. 59.14. *right*, or *equity cannot enter*, and Amos 3.10. *they know not to do*, or *cannot do right*, and ch. 30.10. *prophesy not right things*) that is, in Jerusalem, or in Judah say the Jewish commenters; in the church where righteousness reigns, say ours, ch. 60.21. Rom. 5.21. 2 Pet. 3.12. Or, *a land*, or *ground of straightnesses* or *evennesses*, that is, *a most straight*, or *even*, or *plain land*, or *ground*, where all is fair, and clear, and straight, and even and plain; so that a man may walk right on with ease; that which David alludes unto, when he says, Ps. 5.8. *Lead me for thy righteousness, because of those that watch me*, to do me some mischief: *Make plain*, or *even before me, thy way*, that is, the way that you lead me. And Solomon, when of wisdom he says, Prov. 8.8, 9. *All the words of her mouth are just, there is nothing perverse or crooked in them; they are all plain to an understanding man, and straight to the finders of knowledge*, to knowing men: See v. 7. He will stray, and go out of God's way, even where it is straightest, plainest, evenest, clearest, easiest, both to find, and to follow, Jer. 2.25. & 6.16. & 14.10. & 18.14, 15.

*{deal unjustly*} Or, *unequally, and perversely* (the verb is found here only) as Ps. 71.4.

*{and will not behold the majesty of the Lord*} Or, as some, *and he shall not see the majesty of the Lord*, as if it were spoken by way of commination, that such wicked shall never attain to that beatifical vision which the saints enjoy in heaven, Mat. 5.8. Heb. 12.14. 1 Joh. 3.2. and some frame here a dialogue between God and the prophet, as debating with God about the toleration of the wicked here; and suffering them to thrive, and rise, as Jer. 12.1. and God at length stopping his mouth, with this close. But the sense seems to be that plainly, which our version affords: they refuse to take notice of any hand of God in his work, either of mercy, or judgment: though his majesty shine forth never so eminently in either, Ps. 28.5. ch. 5.12. The next following passage plainly confirms it, for we may observe an elegant reiteration, or epanalepsis, wherewith the prophet chains and links together the several branches of his discourse, with the close of the precedent sentence, making entrance into the subsequent, and that in a constant course, from v. 7. to v. 11. the like may be observed in the beginning of John's gospel, Joh. 1.1–12.

*{majesty*} See ch. 12.5.

**V. 11.** *{Lord, when thy hand is lifted up, they will not see*} Or, *Lord, thy hand is lifted up but they will not see it*, (*it* supplied, as ch. 21.3.) Or, *thine high hand*, or *hand lifted up they will not see*; as Deut. 32.17. *Our high hand, and not the Lord, hath done all this*. Though the workings of your mighty power in these admirable and remarkable occurrents, as well the destruction of your proud and potent foes, as the deliverances of your poor despised people, be so conspicuous, as might well wring an acknowledgment thereof from your adversaries themselves, Ps. 118.15, 16. Deut. 32.31. yet they willfully shut their eyes against it, and refuse to regard it. See v. 10. They that restrain this, as some do, either to the destruction of the twelve tribes, by the Assyrians, for their sins, 2 King. 18.11, 12. or, to the slaughter made in the Assyrian camp, ch. 37.37. do too much in my mind, straiten the text.

*{but they shall see, and be confounded for their envy at thy people*} Or, *Yet they shall see it, and be confounded*, Or, *they shall see*, (and be confounded at the sight of it) *thy zeal for thy people*. They shall at length, will they, nill they, to their pain and shame, be enforced to take notice of, and acknowledge, what now they will not, when God's vengeance shall seize upon them, to their utter confusion, Ps. 83.16, 17. Or, they shall with shame and confusion, or to their shame and confusion, be compelled to see and take notice of the zeal that God bears to his people, ch. 9.7. & 37.31. in the strange protections and deliverances vouchsafed to them, Ps. 86.17. & 112.10.

*{shall see*} Be enforced to take notice of, Ps. 48.5. or *shall see*, that is, shall feel it to their cost and smart, 1 Sam. 5.6–12. ch. 30.30. so, *to see death*, for *to suffer death*, Ps. 89.48. Joh. 8.51. *to see affliction*, for to suffer it, Lam. 3.1. See the next branches.

*{for their envy at the people*} Their envious and spiteful carriage towards God's people, ch. 11.13. that *bitter zeal*, of which, Jam. 3.14. Or, *the zeal of the people*, that is, your zeal or ardent affection which you bear to your people; and in behalf of them, against those that oppose, or oppugn them, Zach. 1.15. and 8.2. a metaphor taken from those, that having an ardent affection, set upon some person that is very precious in their eye, cannot endure to see any affront offered them, or the least injury done unto them, Num. 23.21. Ps. 105.15. ch. 43.3, 4. Zach. 2.5, 8.

*{zeal of the people*} Not whereby they are zealous for God, as Num. 25.11. 1 King. 19.10. 2 King. 2.16. Ps. 119.137. but wherewith with God is zealous for them, ch. 63.15. and whereof they are not the subject, but the object, as *the zeal of God's house*, Ps. 69.9. which David has for it, whereof David is the subject, God's house the object: so Joh. 2.17. See the next branch.

*{the people*} That is, *thy people*, the pronoun supplied from the latter branch, as ch. 58.13. from the former.

*{Yea, the fire of their enemies shall devour them*} That fierceness of wrath wherewith you are wont to proceed against your enemies, shall for their obstinacy destroy them, ch. 42.13. & 59.17, 18.

*{the fire of thine enemies*} That fierce wrath of yours compared frequently to fire, whereof they are the object, wherewith you are wont to proceed against your enemies, Deut. 32.22. Ps. 21.9. & 97.3. as before, the *zeal of thy people*, which you bear unto them: so, *my wrong*, Gen. 16.5. Lam. 3.59. not done by me, but done to me; and *thy curse*, Gen. 27.13. not, wherewith you curse, but, which you may incur, wherewith you may be cursed; and of the wicked man, Job 18.10. *his snare*, and *his trap*, not laid by him, but laid for him; as appears, v. 8, 9. and as there, *the snare of the wicked*, for the *snare set for the wicked*: so here, *the fire of thine enemies*, for the *fire prepared for thine enemies*. See ch. 30.33. Mat. 25.41, 46. Rev. 20.9, 10.

**V. 12.** *{Lord thou wilt ordain peace for us*} From God's just prosecution of his obstinate enemies with the fiery fierceness of his wrath; the prophet speaking still in the person of God's people, proceeds to his gracious administrations, for the benefit, comfort and welfare of his people. Some read the words in form of a prayer, *Lord dispose peace for us*: for the future seems sometime so to be used, as Job 6.23. Ps. 74.19, 20. But the most, as in way of profession of their faith, and hopeful expectation of peace, and prosperity from God, on whom alone they depend for it. See v. 3.

*{for thou also hast wrought all our works in us*} This, many, the school divines especially, expound of God's working by his Spirit in the hearts and souls of his people; of which Phil. 2.13. Heb. 13.21. But that seems not to be the genuine sense of this place. The meaning is rather, as most interpreters, that all those gracious protections and preservations of them, in the times of their troubles, and all those strange deliverances out of their troubles, which hitherto had been afforded them, they had been all wrought by God, and to him alone they do ascribe them. So Ps. 18.32, 36, 47–50. & 44.3, 7. and 55.28. and this experience of the former favor and goodness of God, formerly exhibited to them, they lay here, as a ground whereon they build, either their petition for, as Ps. 22.9, 10, 11. & 27.9. & 71.4, 6. and 85.1–4. or their assurance and expectation of future favor, as continuance of peace and prosperity, from his hand: so 1 Sam. 17.36, 37. 2 Cor. 1.10. 2 Tim. 4.17, 18.

*{our works*} Not wrought by us, but for us: as *my violence*, for the violence done, not by me, but *to me*, as it is well rendered, Jer. 51.35.

*{in us*} Heb. *unto us*, as in the former branch; as we say, *to our hand* or *for us*, as Ps. 47.4. ch. 6.8.

**V. 13.** *{O Lord, our God, other lords, beside thee, have had dominion over us: but by thee only will we make mention of thy name*} Or, *Though other lords beside thee have had dominion over us, yet through thee alone we now celebrate thy name*. This passage many expound of the carriage of God's people in time of their afflictions; that though they were harshly and cruelly handled by those whom God had given power over them for their sins; yet they had constantly, even then also depended upon him, and sustained themselves by the frequent remembrance, and serious meditation of his might, and his mercy; and so it should be in effect the same, with what we had before, v. 8. But the words seem rather to look another way, and to proceed in what was intimated in the latter part of the verse, next before going, to wit, that howsoever God had suffered wicked men to tyrannize over them for a time; yet through his gracious providence, being protected and preserved, they now survived to praise his name, Ps. 66.11, 12, 13. & 71.20.

*{other lords*} Foreign tyrants, 2 Chr. 12.8. Jer. 27.7, 9, 12. & 50.17. Lam. 5.8. a defect of the word *other*: as 2 Chr. 32.22.

*{besides thee*} Other than you, who are our sovereign Lord, and King, Ps. 44.4. & 74.12. ch. 33.22. or, than you had appointed to be rulers over your people, Deut. 17.15. See Jer. 30.21. Some refer it, not to the rulers, but the manner of ruling; they have ruled over us harshly, cruelly, otherwise than according to your word and will. But I nowhere find the word used for *otherwise*, to distinguish the manner of doing aught: but for *besides*, as secluding party from party, and thing from thing; it is frequently found, 1 Chr. 17.20. ch. 45.5, 21. & 64.3.

*{but*} A defect of the particle here: as v. 11.

*{by thee only*} Or, *through thee*: as Ps. 44.5. & 60.12. without whom, all human helps are unavailable, Ps. 33.16, 17. & 60.11. Prov. 21.31. Some read it, with a supply, as a defective speech, *but trusting in thee*: but such insertions are superfluous, where the context runs full enough, and smooth without them.

*{will we make mention of thy name*} Or, *we celebrate thy name*: We now survive to celebrate your name; to publish and praise you for your might and mercy. So is the word frequently used, 1 Chr. 16.4. ch. 63.7. See ch. 12.4.

**V. 14.** *{They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased; they shall not rise*} The people of God do here amplify God's gracious dealing with them in their deliverance, albeit, he had permitted some cruel tyrants, as rigid taskmasters, to use them harshly for a time, with his contrary carriage towards, and dealing with other people, and other persons, whom he had irrecoverably destroyed, Ps. 36.12. ch. 24.20. Jer. 25.27. & 51.64. See ch. 27.7.

*{They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise*} Or, *Their dead shall not live; their deceased shall not rise*. Or, *Being dead, they shall not live; being deceased, they shall not rise*. When they are once destroyed, they shall no more be able to recover themselves and their former estate again, than a man, when he is once dead, is able to recover, and to return to life again, 2 Sam. 12.22, 23. & 14.14. Job 14.7, 12, 14.

*{deceased*} Of the word here used, see on ch. 14.9.

*{rise*} *Shall the deceased arise*, Ps. 88.10.

*{therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish*} The reason is here rendered, of this their irrecoverable destruction, to wit, God's severe, but just proceeding in judgment against them, Ps. 9.6.

*{therefore*} To wit, that they might not recover, and return again, to oppress and wrong God's people, as formerly they had done. See ch. 14.21. Ezek. 28.24. Or, *because*, because you have, in your heavy visitation, taken such a course with them; that they are utterly destroyed. So is the particle found used, Gen. 38.26. Num. 10.3. & 14.43. Ps. 42.6. Jer. 48.36. and so the context runs smoother.

*{visited*} See ch. 24.21.

**V. 15.** *{Thou hast increased the nation, O Lord; thou hast increased the nation*} They return again to relate God's dealings with them, though in somewhat a harsh and rough manner, for some space of time, v. 15–18. yet in a far other manner of issue, than with those other before mentioned, v. 19. These words are by divers, very diversely expounded. The Hebrew is, word for word, *Thou hast*, or *hadst, added to the nation*. Some understand them of God's manifold benefits, conferred upon that people, the people of the Jews. *Thou hadst added to them*, blessing upon blessing; you have laded them with variety of benefits, Ps. 68.19. Others, of the enlargement of God's church, by adding multitudes thereunto, ch. 2.3. & 60.3–12. Zach. 8.20–23. Act. 2.41, 42. & 4.4. & 5.14. Others, of the restitution of them, opposed to that of other people, v. 14. *Thou hast added* (that is, restored) *life to this nation*. See v. 19. But others, again, understand them of variety, not of blessings, but judgments; either of vengeance, as some, executed upon the people before mentioned; God pursuing them with a continued course of calamities, until he had utterly consumed them, Jer. 30.11. or of chastisement; in way whereof, God had exercised his people with variety of evils, adding one affliction to another, Jer. 45.3. See the phrase, Ps. 69.27. And this last interpretation I take to be most likely.

*{thou art glorified*} You did glorify yourself, or gain glory, to yourself, by the good you did, or have done for your people, both in the destruction of their enemies, and in the deliverance of them, and restoring them, as to life again, Exod. 14.4, 17, 18. & 15.1, 6, 11. ch. 20.18. & 59.19. & 63.12. Ezek. 28.23. & 38.23. So some. Others, *Thou didst glorify thyself*, by your judgments executed upon your people for their sins and excesses: for thereby, also, does God vindicate the honor of his name, which by means thereof, is oft dishonored, Levit. 10.3. 2 Sam. 12.14. And others again, render the word to another sense, *thou wast aggrieved*; to wit, with their sins: and the word, indeed, does also so signify, to be pressed, vexed, and grieved, as with some weighty thing, that lies, or hangs heavy upon one, Exod. 18.18. 1 Sam. 5.11. Ps. 32.4. ch. 24.20. and in such manner, is God said to be vexed and grieved, yea, broken and tired out with the sins of his people. See the note on ch. 1.13. See also, ch. 44.20. & 63.10. Jer. 15.6. & 44.22. Ezek. 6.9. Amos 2.13.

*{thou hast removed it far unto all the ends of the earth*} This, the most, and best, understand to be spoken of removing the people of God out of their land, and dispersing them far and wide into foreign parts. So is the word here used, applied unto them, ch. 6.12. and in particular, to those of them, whom yet he intended mercy unto, Ezek. 11.16. See Deut. 28.64. & 30.4. yet some expound it of the dilatation of the church of God into all countries to the world's end, Ps. 72.8. ch. 54.1–3. Matth. 24.14, 31. Mar. 16.15. Rom. 10.18. Col. 1.23. Rev. 14.6. But the former seems more consonant to the tenor and current of the context. The pronoun is wanting, as v. 11. the preposition, as Deut. 33.17. Ps. 45.6. Those that expound the whole verse of the defeat given to Sennacherib's forces, with the effects thereof, and restrain it thereunto, may seem, at the first sight, to have the text run smoothly for them; *Thou hast added to the nation*; (many of other people joining themselves to God's people upon that overthrow given them; as upon Haman's downfall, Est. 8.17.) *thou hast glorified thyself*, (both in their destruction, and in your people's deliverance) *thou hast enlarged all the ends of the land*: the limits and borders of the Jewish territory; they taking occasion thereby, to bring in and under, some neighboring nations; or have liberty now to enlarge themselves; and whereas before they had been penned up in the city, to go abroad freely to the remotest parts of their country; ch. 33.17. But, beside that we find no mention in story, either of the accession of any foreigners thereupon, to God's people; or of their subduing any neighbor country; the word does nowhere signify *to enlarge*, but ever in the one form, *to go far away*, in the other two, *to remove far away*: as Jer. 27.10. Ezek. 43.9. (where if it were rendered *enlarge*, it would make a most absurd sense) and elsewhere, and the subject matter both of this song, and the whole sermon, seems to be of a far larger extent, than that particular passage of providence, or the consequents of it.

**V. 16.** *{Lord, in trouble they visited thee; they poured out a prayer, when thy chastening was upon them*} In this verse, and the two next, is described both the great straits that they were sometime in, during their afflictions before specified, v. 8, 15. and their religious, also, and earnest addresses unto God under them, for deliverance out of them.

*{in trouble*} Or, *in their straits*, or *distress*, as the word properly signifies. See ch. 38.2. & 25.4. a defect of the pronoun: as Ps. 81.7. ch. 13.22. more fully expressed, Hos. 5.15.

*{visited thee*} Or, *minded, remembered*; as the word is rendered, 1 Sam. 15.2. See v. 8. or, *looked after*: as 2 King. 9.34. Jer. 23.2. you, whom they had forgotten, Hos. 8.14. and did not look after, but neglected too much before, ch. 17.7. See 2 Chron. 20.12. Ps. 25.15. & 123.1, 2. The prophet seems, in the use of the word, to have had an eye to God's visitation of them, by his fatherly castigations, Ps. 89.32. it is, as if he had said; they then visited you thus with prayer, when you visited them with afflictions, Ps. 78.34, 35. Jer. 2.27. Hos. 5.15. & 6.1.

*{they poured out*} The phrase of *pouring out*, implies a large quantity of the thing so dealt out: so when God is said to *pour out his Spirit*, it argues a more than ordinary, or formerly usual measure of it, to be dispensed, ch. 32.15. Joel 2.28. Act. 2.18, 33. and when persons are said, *to pour out their spirit*, or their prayer, unto God, it implies a large and earnest drawing out of their spirits and affections, in prayer, with plenty, oft, of sobs and tears, 1 Sam. 1.15, 16. Ps. 42.4. & 142.2. it is a metaphor taken from water, that men making no great reckoning of, where it is not scant, are wont not to be sparing of, as of some other liquor more precious; but to pour it out freely and largely, where occasion requires it, Ps. 22.14. or, to the pouring out of water, for the quenching of a fire, when it has seized upon some building, at which times men are wont to make no spare of it, though it be somewhat geason; but to pour on as plentifully as they can, to prevent greater mischief: and may well seem to have an eye to that abundance of tears, that fear and grief are wont, not so much to wring out of, as to pour out by, the eyes in such cases, as are here spoken of, Judg. 2.4, 5. 1 Sam. 1.10. & 7.6. Ps. 6.6. & 42.3. & 80.5. & 102.9. ch. 15.5. & 16.9. & 22.4. Jer. 9.1. Lam. 1.2, 16.

*{a prayer*} Heb. *a spell*, or, *a charm*, that is, either *a passionate*, and *persuasive speech*; such, as orators and eloquent persons are wont to work upon people's affections with, ch. 3.3. or a humble, submiss, and *lowly speech*, such as proceeds from dejected persons, ch. 29.4. or, *a bemoaning, muttering* manner of speech; *a mussitation*, such as those spell mongers were wont to use, that men might not understand what they said; ch. 8.19. such a prayer as Anna's was, 1 Sam. 1.13. *she spake in her heart, and her lips moved; but her voice was not heard*: such as Ezekiah's was, ch. 38.14. when he *mourned like a dove*: as the like is said, also, of this people, Ezek. 7.16. such a prayer, as the apostle describes, Rom. 8.26. that has more spirit and fervor, than words and language.

*{when thy chastening was upon them*} Heb. *in thy castigation of them*. See v. 8.

**V. 17.** *{Like as a woman with child, that draweth near the time of her delivery, is in pain, and crieth out in her pangs; so have we been in thy sight, O Lord*} The extremity of the pain and grief they were in, either by God himself inflicted upon them, or while he stood by, and seemed to neglect them, is further illustrated by the sharp pangs and throes of a woman in travail. An expression very rife in Scripture. See ch. 13.8. & 21.3.

*{a woman with child*} Or, *one great with child*. See on ch. 7.14.

*{that draweth near the time of her delivery*} Heb. *approached to bring forth*, or, *to be delivered*; as 1 Sam. 4.19.

*{and crieth out*} As ch. 42.14. The usual form, whereby we are wont to express women's travail.

*{pangs*} The word signifies such pains, as pinch like *cords*. Whence, some ambiguity now, and then, because the word signifies either, 2 Sam. 22.6. Ps. 18.5. and 119.61. Act. 2.24. It is commonly used for *pangs of birth*, Job 39.3. Jer. 13.21. & 22.23. Of death, Ps. 18.4. & 116.3.

*{so have we been*} Or, *so were we*; to wit, in the time of our distress, v. 16. That it may run on in the same tenor with the former; though the person be altered in the form of speech, (as formerly) yet the persons themselves, with the circumstance of time, being still the same.

*{in thy sight*} Heb. *from thy face*. Which some expound simply, *from thee*: or, *by reason of thee*: as Gen. 6.13. By occasion of these chastisements, which from you we suffered, v. 16. Or, *from thy wrath*: *face*, for *wrath*; as Ps. 34.16. The consideration of God's wrath, discovering itself in those things that they suffered, being more grievous unto them, than the sufferings themselves, Job 6.4. & 13.26. Ps. 38.1–3. Others render it, as our version, *Before thee*, or, *in thy sight*; as Gen. 31.35. Which might aggravate their grief; when as God should not seem to stand aloof off, and not look after them, as sometime they complain, Ps. 10.1. which yet must needs be very grievous; but, (that which could not but much further enhance their grief and misery) that God should seem to stand by and look on, and see in what extremity they were, and yet afford them no succor, Ps. 10.14. & 35.22. Hab. 1.13. It is a grievous disheartening to a woman in sore travail, to have her friends out of the way, that should be helpful to her in that extremity; but a far greater heart breaking unto her, to behold them at hand about her, but to stand gazing on her, and as not regarding what extremity she endured, or caring what became of her, refusing to lay hand once on her to help her, to afford her any relief, or to further her delivery.

**V. 18.** *{We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind*} They proceed to describe, and amplify the distress they were in, pursuing the former similitude, by the state and condition of a woman in labor, that has pang upon pang, and throe upon throe; and is now upon pitch of delivery, when the throes are sorest and sharpest, but has no power to deliver herself of that she goes with. See ch. 37.3.

*{we have been with child*} Or, *were with child*, or *went great*; as v. 17. The old, both Greek and Latin, render it, *We have conceived*: which many wrest to a mystical sense, and expound of a spiritual conception of grace in the soul. But neither is the translation right, and the exposition much more unsound. See on ch. 7.14. Yet it may well be expounded, as some do; We had many thoughts and devices, in our heads, and conceived great hopes of bringing them about, and meanwhile were as in travail with them. See the like, Job 15.35. Ps. 7.14. ch. 59.4.

*{we have been in pain*} Or, *we were in pain*; as v. 17.

*{we have as it were brought forth wind*} Or, as some, *we did in a manner bring forth our spirit*: that is, we were ready to give up the ghost, we were as at point of death, past hope of life; as 2 Cor. 1.8, 9. & 4.11. Or, as others, *we were, as if we went with wind*: we were in continual pain, as one tormented with inward gripes of the wind colic, beating to and fro within the bowels, and putting to extremity of pain whereof they can attain no ease. Or, as others again; *but we brought forth, as it were, wind*; or, *we did no more, than as if we had brought forth wind*: that is, nothing but wind, or some windy matter. It was not with us, as with women ordinarily going with child: they are in pain indeed for some time; but when they have brought forth what they went with, there is an end of their pain; they are at ease then, and enjoy the comfort of their former travail, Joh. 16.21. But it was otherwise with us, we wanted not for pain; but we found no issue; our pains were easeless, and endless; and all our attempts, and endeavors to relieve, or deliver ourselves, proved weak and windy, unable to wind us out of our present distresses. Vain hopes and helps, are by a proverbial form of speech, termed *windy* ones, both in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, by a metaphor taken from seeds, or eggs, that will not take, or produce aught. See Hos. 8.7. & 12.1. Job 15.1.

*{we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth*} Or, *we could not effect any deliverance for the land*. He tells in plainer words, what he intended in the former, to wit, that by all their consultations, and casting about, by all their devices and designs, they were not able to compass, or accomplish aught for the succor, or safeguard of themselves and their country. So 2 Chr. 20.12. ch. 36.1. and 37.3.

*{have not wrought*} Heb. *will not do*. But the future is put oft potentially. For willing enough, questionless, they were to have done somewhat. *we could not do*, or *effect*, as Ps. 56.4, 11. *I will not fear what flesh*, and *what man will* (that is, can) *do unto me*: and, *I will not fear: what will* (that is, can) *man do to me?* Ps. 118.6. See the like, ch. 30.5. Job 9.3. & 14.4, 14. & 15.3. & 22.14. Jer. 2.11, 23. & 11.12. Mat. 12.23, 23. compared with Mark 3.24.

*{any deliverance*} Heb. *salvations*, Ps. 74.12. 2 Sam. 22.51. or, *deliverances*; as it is rendered, Ps. 18.50. it is thus used in the plural number most commonly, in way of extension, and augmentation, to intimate a concurrence of all manner of *salvation*, and *deliverance* fully and perfectly accomplished, Ps. 28.8. and 42.5, 11. and 44.4. But here in way of extenuation, and restriction, for *any salvation*, or *any deliverance*; as it is well rendered. So *all*, for *any*, Exod. 20.10. Job 1.11. Ps. 49.17. And *understanding*, for *any understanding*, ch. 27.11.

*{in the earth*} Or, *for the earth*, that is, *the land*: (neither in, nor on is in the text) *earth*, for, *land*; as v. 10. *land*, for their *land*; as ch. 13.22.

*{neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen*} Or, *neither did the inhabitants of the world fall*, as they did before David, when God assisted him, Ps. 18.38. We were not able to beat down, or to bear down our enemies; those are meant here by the *inhabitants of the world*; as v. 9. opposed to the *land*, to wit, of Judea, before mentioned. And these it was that they were not able to master; it was God alone that was able to effect that for them. See Ps. 18.17. & 44.5. Hence that confession before, *through thee alone we survive, to celebrate thy name*, v. 13. and that now follows in the next verse.

**V. 19.** *{Thy dead men shall rise*} Hitherto was described the calamitous condition of God's people, under God's chastising hand; together with their utter inability of doing aught that might free them from the same. Now in this last passage, wherewith the prophet shuts up this psalm, is subjoined a gracious promise, or profession of confident assurance, concerning the power of God, to be showed in reviving, and raising them from that their extreme, low, feeble, and forlorn condition, wherein they seemed to be no better than men dead and buried, and even dissolved into dust. Now this is, by most, conceived here to be delivered to God's people, by the prophet, as a promise from God, whereby they might be supported in that their helpless, and as it might seem, hopeless estate, assuring themselves of a comfortable issue of their present afflictions, and of certain deliverance out of that their distressed condition, though, in the eyes of flesh and blood, it might seem a thing utterly impossible. Ezek. 32.3, 11. Zach. 8.6. And they suppose it to be spoken in the person, either of God himself, or the prophet from God, and directed to his people. But some other conceive it to be the voice of God's people, in whose person, the words next before, were conceived; as relating what out of their faith and confidence in God, with Abraham, *above*, or *against hope, believing in hope*, Rom. 4.17, 18. they then suggested unto themselves, wherewith to stay their minds, and settle their distracted thoughts, amid those doubts and difficulties, before rehearsed. And they render the words, therefore with some supply, thus, *Yet said we, Thy dead shall revive*. And such supplies are oft very requisite, for the fitter connection, and clearer conception of passages in Scripture, not a few. See Neh. 13.25. Job 8.18. Ps. 27.8. & 38.16. & 105.15. ch. 22.13. Act. 7.32. The words are conceived thus, in way of opposition, to what was spoken of their enemies, v. 14.

*{Thy dead men*} Heb. only *thy dead*. And so it would rather be rendered, as including, both either sex, and each age. In Scripture, extremity of misery, and anxiety is spoken of as a kind of *death*; 2 Cor. 1.10. & 11.23. because it takes away all the joy, and comfort of this life; and makes it little better, if not worse, and more bitter than death; and death, than such a life, more desirable, Deut. 28.65–67. 1 King. 19.4. Job 3.20, 22. & 6.9. & 7.15. Jer. 8.3. Jon. 4.3. Rev. 9.6. And those that live in such a sad and disconsolate condition, are deemed, and spoken of, as *dead*, Ps. 31.12. & 88.5, 6. Yea, as buried, and consumed, and dissolved into dust, Ps. 22.15. and 71.20. and 137.3. Ezek. 37.2, 11, 12. Dan. 12.2. and in this sense is the word used in this place, as also in the two prophets, last quoted.

*{Thy dead*} If spoken in the person of God to his people; it is to be understood with relation to them; those of you that seem dead; as, *thy children*, to Rachel, Jer. 30.17. If in the person of God's people speaking to God, it must have relation to God; those that you intend mercy to, and own for yours, as *thy people*, Jer. 31.7. Howsoever this particle is added, to distinguish these *dead*, from those *dead*, before spoken of, v. 14. and the old Greek, and the Chaldee therefore did not well in omitting it.

*{shall rise*} Heb. *shall live*; as Ps. 69.32. & 119.175. As the sad and dismal condition of people, in grievous afflictions and distresses, is compared unto *death*; so the freeing of them from the same, and restoring them to a more comfortable and gladsome estate, is said to be a reviving of them, and a restoring of them unto life again; Ps. 71.20. & 80.18. & 85.6. & 138.7. Ezek. 37.5, 14. Dan. 12.2. Hos. 6.2. Rom. 11.15. So is it here to be understood, not of the general resurrection at the last day, though many so expound it; and yet in way of allusion, in likelihood to it, and shadowed out by a resemblance taken from it; in regard whereof also, the rather here the word would be translated *shall live*; as having reference to *the resurrection of life*, as it is termed, Joh. 5.29. that is, peculiar to the faithful; and opposed to that, v. 14. *Their dead shall not live*: that is, shall not be revived.

*{together with my dead body shall they arise*} So rendering it, there should be a defect of the preposition; as Ps. 54.4. so one of the rabbines, who yet adds another reading by supplying the note of similitude, oft wanting, Ps. 11.1. ch. 21.8. and in the next branch but one; *as my dead body they shall arise*: they shall as surely rise as I know that my body shall: so Job of himself, Job 19.25. But others read the words without any such supply. And here one of the Jewish doctors makes these words, God's answer to the prophet's prayer. The prophet, says he, had before prayed against the wicked, that *their dead might not live, nor their deceased rise again*, v. 14. but here he prays, in the behalf of the righteous, that they may be revived, and raised again; *Let thy dead live*: and God, in these words, returns him an answer, as granting his suit for them, *My dead corpse shall rise again*. But of any suit or prayer, rendered to God, here, or there, there is no great likelihood. Others therefore, to pass by those that apply it, to the last resurrection, and so expound it of all those that are members of Christ's spiritual body, 1 Cor. 15.22, 23. 1 Thess. 4.14, 16. Or, with the Jewish doctors, that understand it of a resurrection at the Messiah's coming; either corporally, as they; or spiritually, as others, Joh. 5.24. of which latter, yet it is not denied, but that this might be a type. Those that understand it (as the whole tenor of the prophecy requires it) of the restitution of the Jewish people, some would have it meant of the city Jerusalem, and render it, *My carcass shall rise again*; my city, that now seems to be but carcass, or a dead body, shall be raised out of her dust, and restored to her former state and luster again, Ps. 102.13, 14. ch. 52.1, 2. & 54.11, 12. and we read, indeed, in foreign authors, both Greek and Latin, of *carcasses of cities*; and somewhat looking that way, of Babylon, ch. 13.19. but the verb plural, here, will not admit this reading. And because there is some seeming incongruity between the noun and the verb, the former being singular, and the latter plural, some would alter the text, and with the change of a vowel make the singular noun plural, reading it, *My corpses*, or *dead bodies shall rise*; but such alteration is not needful: the manner of speech in collective, or distributive notions, is very common, as has been showed on ch. 2.18, 20. and so some of those that expound it of the body of the Jewish people, (whether the speech be God's, or theirs) do well render it, *My corpse*, or *dead bodies, each of them shall arise*: the same thing, in other words repeated, as exactly answering in way of opposition, to what was said before of their enemies, v. 14. and with a more exquisite application unto each particular person, by God's gracious election designed unto this deliverance, that no one of them shall fail of having his share in the same. There shall not one of them be wanting, whom God has preserved, and reserved to partake in this national resurrection, alluded unto, Rev. 20.6. See ch. 27.12, 13. Dan. 12.1. Amos 9.9. The change of the person as in the Greek lyrics, so in this, and other sacred poems recorded in Scripture; and with this prophet, also out of his poems, is very rife.

*{awake, and sing ye that dwell in the dust*} Here again, some not unfitly, supply somewhat, as before; and that of the same nature, with that there supplied, rendering the text. *Thou wilt say, Awake*, &c. as, when you did say, *Seek my face*, Ps. 27.8.

*{awake*} From the depth of your affliction, which is as death unto you; and death, whereby it is resembled, as a deep sleep, Ps. 13.3. Act. 7.60. & 13.36. So of the natural death, 2 King. 4.31. *the child is not yet awaked*; and of the spiritual, *awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead*, Eph. 5.14. See also, Job 14.12. So ch. 51.17. & 52.1. & 60.1. the phrase implies, that it is as easy a thing for God, with a word of his mouth, to raise up from death, or from the greatest depth of affliction, as desperate an estate as the state of death, as for one man to awake another out of his sleep. The damsel slept; but to him, that was able to awake her with a word, Luk. 8.52, 55. Joh. 11.11, 14, 43, 44.

*{sing*} For joy, ch. 12.6. & 24.14. Jer. 31.7. Zeph. 3.14. Zach. 2.10.

*{Ye that dwell in the dust*} Heb. *dwellers*, or, *inhabitants of the dust*, as also, Dan. 12.2. not only as some would paraphrase it; you that are cast down to the ground, and sit in the dust, as Ps. 7.5. & 44.25. & 119.25. ch. 14.12. & 47.1. Job 16.15. but that are as men buried, that are as laid up, and lie sleeping *in the dust*, as Job 7.21. Dan. 12.2. For to such is the state of this people compared, Ezek. 37.11, 12.

*{for thy dew is as the dew of herbs*} This last word is ambiguous; in the singular it is found used for *light*, Est. 8.16. Ps. 139.12. and so would some, both Jews and Christians, take the plural here, and so render it, *as the dew of lights*, that is, of the morning; or, that is accompanied with the light and warmth of the sun; Ps. 110.3. and it is true, that *God is light*, 1 Joh. 1.5. yea *the Father of lights*, Jam. 1.17. and that the light of his countenance shining forth upon persons and people does not enlighten only, but enliven them, and is able to turn the heaviest and saddest condition into a cheerful and gladsome estate, Num. 6.25, 26. Job 29.3. Ps. 4.6, 7. & 36.9. & 43.3. & 63.3. & 89.15. & 60.1, 2. Joh. 1.4, 5. But this metaphor does not so well suit here. Others therefore, of either rank, take it in another sense, as the plural is used, the same with this here, 2 King. 4.39. and the masculine singular, with little variation, ch. 18.4. for *herbs*, as our English well renders it. Little difference else is between the most that go this way, save that some few make it the speech of God's prophet to his people, and expound it *thy dew*, that is, the favor that God shows unto you: the rest, conceive it as the speech of the people to God; as rendering a reason why they expect such a strange and sudden alteration of their present condition, upon God's being in mercy reconciled unto them; because, say they, *thy dew*, that is, the favor and grace that you show unto yours, (which, in effect and substance, also, comes home to the former) is like unto the dew that refreshes and revives the herbs, that were parched and withered with the heat of the sun in summer; or, that in springtime, causes them to revive, and to shoot up, and sprout out again, when as they seemed to be in the wintertime stark dead, and lay buried under ground, as in a grave. See Gen. 27.28, 39. Deut. 32.2. & 33.13. 2 Sam. 23.4. Ps. 133.3. Prov. 19.12. ch. 18.4. Hos. 14.5. of the defect of the particle of similitude, see the branch next but one, before going, and the expression of it in the like form of speech, ch. 65.22.

*{and the earth shall cast out the dead*} This version has very few fautors, or followers: Nor will the signification of the verb here used, well admit it: For it signifies in its first form *to fall*; in the next active here used, *to make to fall*, or, *to cast down*: the nearest use I can find of it, to that here given it, is where it is used of *striking out a tooth*, Exod. 21.27. or where of *casting a lot*, Est. 3.7. & 9.24. as if it were said, *the earth shall cast out her dead*, those that lie dead and buried in her, as the lots do in the lot pot, until they be drawn or cast out. But this seems somewhat far fetched, and harsh. It is true indeed, that some other render the word, *cast out*, as alluding to creatures that going with young, *cast* that they go with before their time, Exod. 23.26. in regard that the word signifying *an abortive*, is from the verb here found derived, Job 3.16. Ps. 58.8. Eccl. 6.3. But another word is used for such *casting of young*; not this: nor is the *abortive* so termed from the dam's *casting* of it, but from its *falling* from her that goes with it: and is turned another way, by those that so expound it, as shall afterward be showed. Nor does it seem to be a fit similitude, to resemble God's gracious deliverance; used rather to set out the dread, and terror of his voice casting into fits, and pangs of travail, Ps. 29.9. not the calmness of it, awakening and enlivening dead creatures. The most therefore waive this sense; and albeit they agree much at one in the signification of the verb; yet they vary much in the acception of the noun, and in the designation of the time, and the persons here intended. Some by the word *Rephaim* here used (of which, somewhat before, ch. 14.9. & 17.5.) understand the enemies of God's people; of whom the word was used before, v. 14. so called, because mighty and giant like men, such as the Rephaites are reported to have been, Deut. 2.11, 20. Or, because given to oppression and violence, as those great ones before the flood were, Gen. 6.4, 13. and some of these render the text, *and the land of the violent ones is fallen down*, which fits not well with the form of the verb. Others, *The land shall cast out the giants*, as an abortive birth, of the ground whereof before. Others, *But thou hast overthrown*, Or, *wilt overthrow the land of those violent ones*. Others, conceiving the former branch also, in the future; *for thy dew shall be as the dew of herbs; when thou shalt have thrown those giants*, or *great ones, to the ground*; the destruction of their potent adversaries and oppressors, ordinarily making way for the deliverance of God's oppressed people. See ch. 14.1. Heb. *and*, for *when*; or, *after that*, as Judg. 2.19. Hos. 1.11. Zach. 12.2. and a defect of the particle *to*, as Amos 9.9. and this last, to me, seems the likeliest to express the prophet's mind: Yet some take the word *rephaim* here, for *dead*, or *deceased*, as v. 14. and the word is so taken, Ps. 88.10. Prov. 2.17. & 9.18. and they thus render the text applied to God's people; *after that thou hast cast down the deceased into the ground*, that is, after you have brought them so low, and wasted them so by afflictions, that they seem as dead, and laid up in their graves in the ground, Ps. 71.20. a metaphor taken from corn that is cast into the ground, and there dies before it revive and fructify, Joh. 12.24. 1 Cor. 15.39. And here ends this pious song composed by the prophet, for the use of God's people.

**V. 20.** *{Come my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee, hide thyself, as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast*} The two last verses of this chapter, being no part of the psalm, or song therein comprehended, would rather have been joined with the chapter ensuing, as some interpreters therefore have also disposed of them. For in them, the prophet having made an end of his song, returns again, to proceed in his former discourse, and being to relate what dreadful judgments God was to execute abroad, far, and near, in the world, and even in those places, among the rest, where many of his own people abode; he begins his speech, directed unto them, with an wholesome advice, admonishing and exhorting them, to seek and provide shelter for themselves, against the great and general storm that was coming, retiring themselves as to some secret place of security and safeguard; and keeping close there, partly by sincere reformation, and renewing of their repentance, that all occasions of breach between God and them, might be removed, Zeph. 2.1–3. and by fervent prayer repairing to him, for his gracious preservation, and powerful protection, Mat. 6.6. and partly by serious meditation of their future deliverance, with a quiet and patient expectation of it, ch. 30.15. and that the rather, because it would be after a while over, Ps. 30.5. ch. 10.25. & 54.7, 8. Hab. 3.3. 2 Cor. 4.17. Heb. 10.37, 38. That which is here set forth by allusion to the usual practice of people, if they perceive a storm towards, when they are abroad, to get home speedily to their houses, Exod. 9.19, 20. and in times of peril, to retire into the secretest and surest rooms in the house, and to make all fast after them, Judg. 9.51. 1 King. 20.30. & 22.25. Ps. 18.45. Joh. 20.19. Or, it may well be, more specially to the Israelites, keeping their houses close in Egypt, while the destroying angel passed over, throughout the whole land, Exod. 12.22, 23. Some of the Jewish writers expound it, of their being shut up in Jerusalem by Sennacherib, ch. 36.2. See Jer. 8.14. But this is neither intended here; and in regard of comprehension, it is overstrait.

*{Come*} Or, *Go*, ch. 6.9. but *come*, rather here; as Num. 10.29. as if God himself went along with them, and led them by the hand, as a father his children, to conduct them to a place of safety, and there to shut them in, as he did Noah in the ark, Gen. 7.16.

*{thy chambers*} Or, *closets*, distinguished from chambers, 1 Chr. 28.11. the chambers of God's providence and protection, Ps. 31.22. & 143.9. Prov. 18.11.

*{about thee*} Or, *upon thee*; as 2 King. 4.4.

*{hide thyself*} Or, *lurk, lie hid*; the word is nowhere else found in this form.

*{as it were for a little moment*} Or, *for a little space*: as it is well rendered, Ezr. 9.8. or, *for a little while*, for the particle here seems rather a preposition, than an adverb of similitude, as Gen. 18.10. Ruth 1.4. Heb. *a little of a moment*, (as, *a little of water*, Gen. 18.4.) the least imaginable particle of time, 1 Cor. 15.52.

*{the indignation*} The storm of God's wrath, ch. 10.25. Dan. 11.36.

**V. 21.** *{For behold*} The reason why they should do, as the prophet advised; ushered in with a mark prefixed before it, implying it to be as sure, as if they saw it present, (see ch. 7.14.) because there is a grievous storm coming; God himself is setting out, to sit in a general session, and to execute judgment all the world over, Ps. 50.1–6.

*{the Lord cometh out of his place*} From heaven, Ps. 68.35. & 76.8. Rom. 1.18. So Mic. 1.3. A metaphor taken from a king that comes down out of his palace, to sit in judgment, hear, decide, and censure, 2 Sam. 19.8. Jer. 38.7. Gen. 18.20, 21.

*{to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity*} Heb. *to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth upon him*. See the like phrase, Exod. 20.5. & 34.7. *inhabitant*, for *inhabitants*, as ch. 5.3. & 24.17. *inhabitants of the earth*; those that dwell far and near: of whom, ch. 24.6, 17. v. 18.

*{the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain*} Some expound this of the severity of God's judgment, and the large execution that shall ensue; as if it were said, there shall so much blood be shed, that the earth shall not be able to receive, or drink it in: and so many slain, that there will want ground or room to bury them, Jer. 7.32, 33. But it is rather spoken, to show the strict inquisition that God will then make, for the oppressions and wrongs that have been done, and murders that have been committed, Ps. 9.12. that they shall be as surely brought to judgment, and avenged, as if the earth should spew up the blood she had taken in, and cast up again the bodies of the slain buried in her, to appear in judgment, and to give in evidence against the murderers, Gen. 4.10, 11. and it may well withal intimate, that no murder, though never so secretly committed, or closely carried, should then be concealed, but all brought to light; as if he had said, the blood that had been not shed on a rock, and there left to open view; but poured on the ground, and covered there so with dust, Lev. 17.13. that no sign of it could be seen, Ezek. 24.7. should all then come to light: see Job 16.18. and the murders not of those alone, whose bodies had been left lying upon the open surface of the earth, without burial, Ps. 79.2, 3. but of those also that had been privily slain, and secretly buried, should then be discovered.

*{her blood*} Heb. *bloods*. See ch. 1.15. *her blood*, which she had taken in, or was shed upon her; and so *her slain*, buried in her, or slain upon her.

*{no more*} Or, *no longer*, as Jer. 44.22.

### CHAPTER 27

**V. 1.** *{In that day, the Lord with his sore, and great, and strong sword, shall punish Leviathan the piercing serpent, even Leviathan, that crooked serpent, and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea*} As the murders and oppressions of God's people, shall then come to trial, so justice shall accordingly be done upon those, be they never so great, that have been the murderers and oppressors of them.

*{In that day*} At that time, when God shall hold that his great assize, ch. 26.21. as ch. 25.9.

*{sore*} Heb. *hard*, or *cruel*, ch. 19.4. our old English *heavy*. There is a great deal of emphasis in the words, as they are in the Hebrew: for thus they run there; *with his sword, that sore*, or *cruel one, and that great one, and that strong one*; able to do execution to the purpose. See the like, Ezek. 21.9, 10, 14.

*{sword*} An allusion to that sword, not which soldiers use in the field, 2 Sam. 11.25. ch. 1.20. & 3.25. but wherewith, for capital crimes, kings and magistrates are wont to execute malefactors, 1 King. 2.8, 32. Act. 12.2. Rom. 13.4. for God is here described as proceeding in a judiciary way; not as Ps. 45.3. And I suppose, therefore, that the *sword of the Spirit*, that is, the *spiritual sword, the word of God*, Eph. 6.16. Rev. 1.16. is not properly here intended, but that power of God, wherewith he takes vengeance, and does justice on the obstinate wicked. So ch. 34.15. & 66.16.

*{shall punish*} Or, *do execution upon*: that it may come nearer home to the Hebrew, *visit upon*, or, *do justice*, or, *execute vengeance upon*; to express the better a judiciary process; as Ps. 149.9. So ch. 26.21. and 24.21.

*{Leviathan*} The word seems properly, to import *a whale*, of the greatest sort and largest size, Job 41.1. Ps. 104.26. & 74.14. for in these places only, is the word certainly found, that, Job 3.8. is ambiguous. Of this *Leviathan*, the greatest of all living creatures, Job 41.33, 34. So called, as containing an addition of many creatures, put together, and made up into one: and of the *Behemoth*, or *elephant*; so called likewise, as a composition of many beasts, Job 40.15. being the greatest, that lives on land; and concerning their huge bigness, and making sport, by fighting together before their Messiah, when he comes, the Talmudists tell us prodigious tales out of Ps. 50.10. & 104.26. by them grossly abused; as also, of the killing of them both afterward, to make a great feast, for the just ones, from this place, and ch. 25.6.

*{the piercing serpent*} Or, *a piercing serpent*. The word *serpent*, is in the Hebrew, a general term, common to all living creatures in water, or on land that glide along in the one, and on the other, with a wriggling kind of motion, without use of feet, or fins. For such, only, seem properly to be so termed. Of the lesser sort whereof, are the *eel*, and the *snake*, of the greater sort, the *whale*, and the *dragon*; of which, more anon.

*{piercing*} The word here used, signifies, properly, *a bar*, or *bolt*. So called, of a word, that signifies *to flee*, (whence the ambiguity, ch. 15.5. & 43.14.) because it swiftly flees, or shoots the bolt into the staple, the bar, from the one end or corner of the thing barred, or borne by it, to the other, Exod. 26.28. & 36.33. Hence, diversity of versions here, some rendering the word *fugitive*: as ch. 15.5. so our former English, after the old Greek, some, *slippery*, or *gliding*: some, *long*, like a bar, or bolt: some *round*; as bars and bolts use to be: some, *strong*, like a bar of iron, or brass, Ps. 107.16. & 147.13. Prov. 18.19. ch. 45.2. to which purpose, our ancient English, *invincible*: some, *shooting*, from the one end of the sea, to the other; so the Jewish critics: some, *crossing*; because a bar, or bolt, runs across: ours, here, *piercing*; and so the Geneva version. Which whether it be meant of piercing the water, by such a quick motion, from place to place, or of piercing and insinuating itself into holes and bodies, where it finds any the least way for entrance, (which is noted, as a special property, in snakes and serpents) is uncertain: the word is found used, as the epithet of *a serpent*, here only, and Job 26.13. and from that which signifies a *bar* or *bolt*, it varies only in one vowel: the old Latin yields it not so fitly, *a bar*: some other, better: *barlike*, or *like a bar*; which, I suppose to be best: The Hebrew critics observing that variation, to intimate, the one to be a substantive, signifying *a bar*, or *bolt*, the other, an adjective, importing some resemblance of the same: as the *serpent*, or *whale*, does in divers of the particulars above recited.

*{even Leviathan, that crooked serpent*} Or, *and upon Leviathan, that crooking serpent*. Some, that retain the most common use of the copulative, suppose two *Leviathans* to be here intended, the one whereof, they conceive to be the king of Assyria; the other, the king of Egypt. Some others, as our version, rendering it *even*: as Deut. 4.32. suppose one and the same to be in both branches intended, which some would have to be Pharaoh the king of Egypt, compared to *a whale*, Ezek. 29.3. & 32.2, 6. in regard of the river Nilus, that runs through his country, is a chief strength of it, brings it in much wealth; and by overflowing it, makes it fertile: as was also another of them termed before him, Ps. 74.14. Others would have it to be Sennacherib, king of Assyria; so termed, because his country lay upon the great river Euphrates. See ch. 8.7. Others, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, situate upon the banks of the same. See Jer. 51.13. Others, taking the word collectively, conceive it to be intended, not of any one particular person alone, but of sundry great tyrants, that had been principal oppressors of God's people; of whom, ch. 26.13. compared to these huge devouring sea creatures, because they make havoc of men, Ps. 14.4. & 124.3. as those vast bodied ones are wont, even as by shoals to swallow down the lesser sort of fish; Hab. 1.14. Howbeit, some understand all here spoken, of Satan, the devil; of whom, Rev. 12.3, 9. But I suppose the devil no more intended by the *Leviathan*, here, than by *Lucifer*, ch. 14.12. that is, no otherwise, than as such tyrants were his instruments, Eph. 2.2. and as they might some way be types of him. See the notes on Rev. 12.3, 7.

*{crooked*} Or, *crooking*, or, *winding*; not crooked, in regard of the native shape of his body; but winding and crooking many ways in the motion of it; not going straight forward, but with wriggling to and fro, making his way. It is taken from byways, full of windings and turnings, one while to the right hand, and another while to the left, Judg. 5.6. Ps. 125.5.

*{and will slay*} He will not amerce them, with some pecuniary fine; as in some lighter trespasses is wont to be done, Exod. 21.22, 30, 32. strip them of their wealth, nor scourge them, as in some greater offenses is usual, Deut. 25.2, 3. lay some more grievous afflictions on them; but as in capital crimes, the proceeding is unto death, Exod. 21.12, 15–17. so here, he will *slay*, he will destroy them; he will make use of, not the rod, or the scourge, but the sword; and that not to wound, as in war it sometime only does, Joel 2.8. but, as in judicature, the use of it, is ever to slay, Mat. 26.52. Rev. 13.10. Or, he will not imprison them only, and restrain them for a time: as ch. 24.22. Rev. 20.2, 3. but utterly so destroy them, and rid the world of them, that they shall never return to oppress his people again, ch. 26.14.

*{the dragon*} The word *dragon*, though used sometime in foreign authors, poets especially, for any serpent in general, yet, more peculiarly seems to denote a long snaky kind of serpent, usually of great length; not such as they paint, commonly, with wings and legs. Of the strange length of them, see Aelian, lib. 2. ch. 21. and lib. 15. ch. 21. and lib. 16. ch. 34. and Pliny, lib. 8. ch. 11, 13, 14. and such a one does the word here import, when it is applied to land creatures: as ch. 13.22. so that the former word rendered *serpent*, seems the genus to this; and this, to comprehend only the bigger and larger kind of them: but here there is no place for such land creatures; for there is express mention in the text, of their abode *in the sea*: and as for the *sea dragon*, of which, Pliny, lib. 9. ch. 27. and Aelian, lib. 5. ch. 37. and lib. 14. ch. 12. it seems no great fish; not much unlike to our *wiver*; but the word, applied to sea creatures, signifies *a whale*; and those of a snaky shape, or serpentine figure of the like size with it. So Gen. 1.21. Ps. 44.19. and 74.13. ch. 51.9. Lam. 4.3. and would so be here rendered; not the *dragon*, (for we never so use the word) but the *whale*, or *the whirlpool, that is in the sea*: in which latter word, though there may be an allusion to the situation of Egypt, or Babylon, great waters usually in Hebrew bearing that name, whereof, see on ch. 19.15. & 21.1. Yet it is here enough, for that which the prophet here intends, that those devouring fishes, by which the prophet represents these great tyrants in them here intended, abide generally in the sea.

**V. 2.** *{In that day sing ye to her, a vineyard of red wine*} From the prediction of the destruction of God's people's greatest enemies, he proceeds to relate the flourishing and fructifying estate of God's people, now enjoying rest and peace. And this he enters upon, with an exhortation, whereby he excites and incites all that wish well to God's church, and rejoice in the prosperity of his people, by gladsome songs and acclamations, to express and show forth the same, ch. 52.9. & 66.10. Zach. 4.7. The words, as they are here read, seem to intimate the latter part of them, to be the sum of the short song, or acclamation itself, as, *Grace, grace to it*, Zach. 4.7. But some rather read the words, as one continued speech; *to the vineyard of new wine, sing ye to it*: a redundancy of speech in Hebrew very usual: as Gen. 2.17. ch. 8.13. Ps. 1.4. & 74.14. & 144.2. Others, which I suppose the best, as divided, but another way, into two branches, the one containing a prediction, *In that day there shall be a vineyard of red wine*, the other, an adhortation, *sing ye of it*, or *to it*.

*{In that day*} At that time, when the potent adversaries of God's people shall be destroyed, v. 1. and God's people, by their former afflictions, pruned and purged, ch. 1.25. v. 8, 9. ch. 48.10. Joh. 15.2.

*{a vineyard of red wine*} Or, as some, *hot*, or *strong wine*; because the word in Chaldee has a signification of *heat*: but it seems rather, to intimate the color, expressed plainly, Prov. 23.31. *red wine*, in those parts, being usually the strongest, and the best; called *the blood of the grape*, therefore, Gen. 49.12. Deut. 32.14. In regard whereof, also, the Jewish doctors advise their people, at the celebration of the Passover, to make use rather of *red wine*, than of *white*; because this is usually the weaker. So Ps. 75.8. The meaning is, the church, God's vine, Ps. 81.8. ch. 5.7. that had formerly degenerated from her native excellency, and brought forth vile and noisome grapes, Deut. 32.32, 33. ch. 5.2, 7. Jer. 2.21. should then recover her primitive generosity again, and bring forth such fruit, as should be of good esteem, useful and acceptable, both to God and man, Judg. 9.13.

*{sing ye to it*} Or, *of it*; as Num. 21.18. where the same term though in another form, with the same particle in like manner diversely rendered is found; spoken there of the *well* as here of the *vine*: and the one seems to allude to the other. Of the latter use of the particle see ch. 8.12. & 23.5. the word signifies, properly, *to sing by course, answering* one to another, Exod. 15.21. 1 Sam. 18.6, 7. Ezr. 3.11. Sing together, as in a choir. Concerning it.

**V. 3.** *{I the Lord do keep it, I will water it, every moment; lest any hurt it, I will keep it night and day*} Or, as some, *I the Lord will keep it*: as others, knitting the two first members into one sentence, *I the Lord, the keeper of it, will every moment water it; that it may not be hurt, I will night and day watch it*. That this vineyard of God thus restored, may have some good assurance, not of present prosperity only, but of future security, God himself is by the prophet brought in, undertaking the charge and custody of it. And whereas there are two evils especially, that may be prejudicial to a vineyard, and impeach the thriving of it, the one drought, and want of water to refresh it, ch. 1.30. the other, the violent breaking in, or, privy stealing in, of man or beast, that may annoy it, Ps. 80.12, 13. Cant. 2.15. God here engages himself to his church, to provide for it abundantly against either. For he that before had forbidden the clouds to rain upon it, ch. 5.6. would himself, now, be continually watering of it, by the gracious dews, ch. 26.19. and spiritual refreshments of his word and Spirit, and with a comfortable supply of whatsoever should be needful to keep it in a fruitful and flourishing condition, Gen. 2.9, 10. Deut. 11.10–12. ch. 58.11. Ezek. 47.1, 9, 12. Hos. 2.21, 22.
