Rev. 22.1, 2. and he that before had pulled down her wall, and plucked up her hedge, Ps. 80.12. ch. 5.5. would now himself be as a wall and fence unto her, Ps. 125.2. ch. 26.2. Zach. 2.5. he would keep such a constant watch night and day about her, that none should either by day openly force and break in, or in the nighttime, by some wile and sleight, privily steal in to wrong her, Ps. 121.3, 4.

*{do keep it*} Or, *that watch it*, or, *the keeper*: as the word is rendered, Jer. 4.17. or, *watchman of it*: as, 2 King. 17.9. the *keeper of Israel*, Ps. 121.4.

*{water it*} For it is his watering alone, that can make fertile, and fruitful, that can give thrift and growth, ch. 44.3, 4. 1 Cor. 3.6, 7. and without him, as no watching can secure, Ps. 127.1. so no watering can avail, ch. 17.11.

*{every moment*} Heb. *at moments*, or, *by moments*: as Job 7.18. Ezek. 26.16. & 32.10.

*{lest any hurt it*} Heb. *lest he visit on it*: *to visit upon*, for, *to punish, vex*, or *afflict*: as Jer. 19.21. & 30.20. *lest he hurt it*, for, *lest it be hurt*: the word is taken indefinitely, as Job 19.26. Ps. 7.2. and so the old Latin renders it; for they are wide, that think this form, and that, 2 King. 14.8. parallel, *let us look either other in the face*; the phrases are nothing alike.

*{I will keep it*} Or, *watch it*: as Job 7.20. Prov. 24.12. Mat. 26.36.

*{night and day*} Constantly, continually, without intermission. So 1 Sam. 25.16. ch. 21.8.

**V. 4.** *{Fury is not in me*} The prophet in these words, and the rest of his ensuing discourse, seems to meet with an objection, that might arise in men's minds, concerning these gracious promises of God, and his serious professions of his affection to, and care of his church, and to strengthen the hearts of the truly faithful against it. For it might be demanded, how these things could stand with those predictions and denunciations of such grievous calamities and distresses, that were to befall God's people themselves, whereof mention, also, had formerly, in this sermon, been made, ch. 26.8, 13, 15, 18. To which the prophet returns answer: First, that God neither, is of himself, prone to wrath, nor implacable. Secondly, that there are those among God's people, that by their obstinacy enforce God to severe courses, v. 4, 5. Thirdly, that God's sharp proceedings against such, are for the benefit of the rest, v. 6. Fourthly, that God's dealings with his people, in chastisement, do much differ from his proceedings with others, v. 7, 11. And lastly, that there shall, in due time, be an entire deliverance of them, v. 12, 13.

*{Fury is not in me*} *Wrath*, or, *heat*. See ch. 42.25. & 51.17. Either my wrath against my people, is no fury, no rage, no implacable wrath, like that of a husband towards a disloyal wife, Prov. 6.34. I am prone, and ready to do, what in such case a man will not do, Jer. 3.1. or my anger and displeasure, conceived against my people, is now over; since that by their forepassed sufferings, they are humbled for their sins that procured them, reclaimed from them, and reformed, ch. 12.1. & 40.1, 2. & 54.8, 9. Ezek. 16.42, 63. Zach. 1.15–17. and 6.8.

*{who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle? I would go through them, I would burn them together*} Or, as some, *who so shall set me briers and thorns in it, in battle will I march against them, and will burn them together*. But this agrees not so well with the pauses in the Hebrew. Others, *Yet if any with brier and thorn*, or *like brier and thorn, shall induce me to battle, I will warily enter into her*, or, *through her, and burn them, out of her together*. This some understand of the enemies of God's church, that it is folly for any, that are but as briers and thorns, fit to make fuel of, or matter to feed the fire, Ps. 58.9. Eccl. 7.6. to offer to oppose themselves against God, or against those whom he protects; and if any such therefore shall so do, or shall prove like pricking briers or thorns unto his people, Josh. 23.13. Ezek. 28.14. God will be as a fire to burn them up, and destroy them, Ps. 21.9. ch. 26.11. Zach. 2.5. & 12.6. Others, of his church and people, that albeit God be thus graciously affected towards it and them, yet if there shall those spring up in it, and be found among them, that like briers and thorns shall vex him, and provoke him to wrath, by their profane and sinful courses, 2 Sam. 23.6. Mic. 7.4. they shall find him to be a consuming fire, Deut. 4.24. ch. 33.12. he will in hostile manner set upon them, or enter, to that purpose, into his vineyard, and burn them up together, and by that means rid it of them, 2 Sam. 23.7. ch. 1.25. & 9.18. which yet he will so wisely and warily do, that his vineyard shall receive no damage thereby; he will withal have a due regard to those that continue faithful to him, Zach. 2.3. 2 Pet. 2.9. Many other versions and interpretations are given, too long to relate; these I suppose the most probable.

*{who would set against me*} Heb. *give me*, or, *set me*, some would have it read, by way of wish, as Job 19.1. Jer. 9.1. *who will set me?* that is, *I would some would set me*. I suppose it rather to be spoken, either in way of interrogation, Jer. 9.12. Hos. 14.9. or, by way of supposition; as Ps. 107.43. so Ps. 25.12.

*{the briers and thorns*} Heb. *brier, thorn*, as ch. 5.6. which some understand, as spoken of one kind only, as, *brier of thorn*, that is *thorny brier*: but both words being in an absolute and entire form, admit not well that construction: the most, therefore, rather take it, as intending two sorts; and either taken collectively, with defect of a copulative; as Hab. 3.11.

*{I would go through them*} The word here used, being nowhere else found; only two terms derived from it, the one, signifying *a step*, 1 Sam. 20.3. the other, *a hip*, 1 Chr. 19.4. so it would there, more properly, and more modestly be rendered; because it peculiarly points to that place, whence the motion in going seems to descend. Some here take it, to import a *warlike march*: Others, a *wary stepping*, as alluding to one, that entering into a garden, or orchard, to pluck up the weeds and thistles, and to grub up the briers and brambles, that pester the ground, is careful how, or where he treads, for hurting the useful plants, the more tender especially therein; and to this sense, I the rather incline, because the pronoun is here feminine. *I will go in her*, or *in it*, or *step into her*, or *into it*, to wit, the vineyard, v. 2, 3.

*{I would burn them together*} Heb. *I will burn her*, or, *it, together*; which because it cannot here be understood fitly of burning up the vineyard itself, as a ground altogether forlorn, Heb. 6.8. (notwithstanding what is said, Lam. 4.11.) must of necessity be meant, of burning those briers and thorns out of it; and may well, therefore be rendered, *I will burn them out of it*; for the preposition is, in such manner, oft implied either in the verb, or in the pronoun, or affix: so Ps. 53.5. *encamping me*, for *encamping against me; dwell thee*, for *dwell with thee*, Ps. 5.4. *come us*, for *come at us*, ch. 28.15. so Ps. 65.5. where the same particle is necessarily supplied, that is here wanting; though in a diverse use, than here.

**V. 5.** *{Or, let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me, and he shall make peace with me*} Some read the words, *Or, who will*, or *can grapple with my strength? let him make peace with me*, &c. as if he had said, who is able to stay my hand, by laying hold on my arm, or can hope to make his part good against me? Job 9.4, 12, 13. Dan. 4.35. 1 Cor. 10.22. and it is their wisest course, therefore, to make their peace with me, Job 11.13. & 22.21. The interrogative particle, supplied from the words before going, the future, for the potential: as ch. 26.18. Others, *Or, he shall take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; that he may, I say, make peace with me*: understanding it, as in allusion to one who perceiving some offended person ready to smite him, or give fire upon him, in a humble and submissive manner, lays hold on his arm, and by earnest suit, with prayers and tears, endeavors to stay him from smiting, or discharging on him, and by allaying of his wrath, to make his peace with him. See Exod. 32.6. Hos. 12.4. Jon. 3.8–10. as if he had said: So will I proceed against such as thus provoke me; unless by humbling of themselves, and seeking timely to me, they make their peace with me, and so prevent it, Zeph. 2.1, 2. Luk. 14.32. a defect of the finitive particle *that*; as ch. 5.11. & 10.2. Hos. 1.6. and the latter branch, for the greater emphasis, repeated: as ch. 26.3. Cant. 6.13.

**V. 6.** *{He shall cause them, that come to Jacob, to take root, Israel shall blossom and bud, and fill the face of the world with fruit*} The prophet returns again to the gracious promises of God, to be made good to his people; either of his restitution of them, or upon, and by means of his judgments executed upon the wicked, among them; their taking deeper root, thriving better, and growing so abundantly fruitful, that their fruit should fill the whole world.

*{He shall cause them, that come to Jacob, to take root*} Or as some others, *He shall cause those of Jacob, that come to take root*, Or, as some other again, *He shall cause them that come from Jacob, to take root*. Or, *Jacob shall take root in his posterity*. The first, understanding the text of Jacob's proselytes, ch. 2.3. & 56.3–8. The second, of those that return from captivity, v. 13. ch. 35.10. The third and fourth, of their posterity, ch. 44.3, 4. & 48.19. But the words, especially as they lie in the original, will not well bear any of these versions. The best interpreters concurring therein with the Jewish commenters, thus read them; *Hereafter*, or, *In times coming shall Jacob root*, or *take root*; or, to knit them, the more aptly to the former discourse; *That in time coming Jacob may take root*: as an effect of God's purging of his vineyard, his church, from such noxious plants as cumbered the ground, and hindered the growth and welfare of it. See ch. 4.2, 4. Of the usual defect of the particle, see on v. 5.

*{them that come*} Heb. *in the coming*; to wit, days, or times: as, *Behold the days coming*, Jer. 30.3. & 31.27, 31, 38. a defect of the particle; as in this very phrase, Eccl. 2.16.

*{he shall cause those that come to Jacob, to take root*} To wit, God, Ps. 80.9. *thou madest it to take root*; or, taking it indefinitely, *he*, or, *they shall be rooted*, as Jer. 12.2. so v. 3. *lest he hurt it*; or, *Jacob shall take root*, as Job 5.3. *I have seen the foolish taking root*; where the word is the same, and in the same form; see ch. 37.31.

*{Israel shall blossom and bud*} So ch. 35.1, 2. & 66.14. of the word, see ch. 5.24. & 17.11. *Israel*, and *Jacob*, are here the same; to wit, the posterity of *Jacob*, called also *Israel*, as ch. 14.1.

*{and fill the face of the world with fruit*} Heb. *and they shall fill*, to wit, the posterity of Jacob; either naturally descended from him, or by profession of faith adjoined to him, Ps. 24.6. Rom. 9.6. Gal. 6.16. *the face of the world*; the surface of the habitable part of it. See ch. 13.11. & 14.21. & 23.17. they shall be dispersed, and enlarge themselves through all parts of the world, fulfilled in the converts of the Gentiles, in all places by the ministry of the gospel, called here *fruit*, by a metaphor taken from the *fruit*, or *revenue of the field*, Deut. 32.13. Ezek. 36.30. See Joh. 15.16. Col. 1.6. See also, ch. 37.31. Job 14.7, 9.

**V. 7.** *{Hath he smitten him, as he smote those that smote him*} Another argument of God's mercy to his people; albeit he did, and had, sometime severely chastised them, yet does he not therein deal so roughly and rigorously with them, as he does usually with their enemies, when he comes to take vengeance upon them.

*{Hath he smitten him*} That is, God his own people, his Israel.

*{as he smote those that smote him*} Heb. *according to the stroke of him that smote him*, or, *struck him*, as ch. 10.26. *him that smote*, for, *those that smote*. The word taken collectively: Such as God had made use of, as instruments, rods, and cudgels for the chastising of his people, ch. 10.5, 20, 24.

*{or is he slain according to the slaughter of them, that were slain by him*} The same thing is, as oft, again, but in other terms, somewhat more emphatically, repeated.

*{or*} A defect of the disjunctive; as Job 6.6. which yet here may well be spared.

*{is he slain*} Or, *hath he* (that is, Israel, God's people) *been slain*. That it may run in the same tenor, with the former branch.

*{according to the slaughter of them*} As he slew, or, has slain them, or, as they have been slain, or slaughtered. Heb. *his slain*, or, *his slaughtered ones*; as, *her slain*, ch. 26.21. These *slain*, all agree to be of the enemies of God, and his people: but whose *slain* they are said to be, is questioned. Some say, the slain of the Leviathan, of the king of Babylon, before spoken of; not slain by him, but belonging to him. The Hebrew commenters, *the slain of him*, that is, of God that slew them; as is said, v. 1. Or, *of him*, that is, of Israel; not because slain by them, but because slain for them, for the wrongs that they did them. I suppose it may well be read, *as those* (that is, those other, before mentioned,) *slain by him*. And the interrogative implies a more vehement negative, as if he had said; God has in no wise, so either smote, or slain his people, as he has smote, and slain those other, his, and their enemies, ch. 26.14. v. 1. The version of many, who render this latter branch, *Hath he been slain, as they have been slain, that slew him*: the particle, being passive, will not admit. But those swerve further from the scope of the prophet, that turn over all this to the Leviathan, above mentioned, as if the prophet should say, *Hath he smitten him*, (to wit, the Leviathan) *as one smiting himself?* (as, says he, God does his people himself, feeling what on them he inflicts:) Or, *hath he slain him, as he slayeth his own slain?* That is, his people, his friends. Prov. 27.6. Hos. 6.2, 3. Zach. 13.3, 6. But this is all clean beside the cushion.

**V. 8.** *{In measure, when it shooteth forth, thou wilt debate with it: he stayeth his rough wind, in the day of the east wind*} The prophet having affirmed, that God in his chastising of his people, deals otherwise with them, than he is wont to do with others, whom he has not the like respect, or relation unto: he now proceeds more distinctly, to show, wherein the difference consists, between God's dealing with the one, and with the other. One point of difference, here laid down, is, that God deals in way of discretion, and in much moderation with his, Jer. 10.24. & 30.11. meting out their sufferings in a due proportion, like those that do things exactly, by weight and measure; physicians, especially, in prescribing pills, or potions to their patients, having a respect, as well to the ability of the patient, as to the nature and quality of the disease: not according to the greatness of his power, and his wrath answerable thereunto, Job 23.6. & 37.23. Ps. 78.38. & 90.11. or to the heinousness of their sin, Ezr. 9.13. Job 11.6. Ps. 103.10. Lam. 3.22. but according to the ability of the chastised, to bear that which is inflicted, Ps. 103.13, 14. 1 Cor. 10.13. Whereas in dealing with the other, he is nothing so cautious; but proceeds, as those that pour out, or lay on, without regard of stint or measure, ch. 65.6, 7. Jer. 10.25. See Joh. 3.34. He deals with the one, as a father, in correcting his children when they have done amiss, regarding their weakness, as well as their wantonness; and laying less on the more infirm, though all alike faulty, Ps. 103.13. Mal. 3.17. With his enemies, as a judge with delinquents, who proceeding according to the strict rule of law and justice, regards not the person of the offender, but his offense only, and according thereunto, dispenses justice equally unto all alike delinquent, though not alike able to sustain what their offense calls for, ch. 59.18. and 65.6, 7.

*{in measure*} The word here used, is derived from one, that signifies a certain measure, one of the lesser sort of those that they used, in measuring out of dry wares, meal, grain, or the like; and contained, as most suppose, the third part of an Epha, (and yet why should they then say, three seaes, Gen. 18.6. that, it seems, being the ordinary rate of one batch, Mat. 13.33. and not rather in one term, *an Epha*?) that is, according to the received estimation of the Jewish Epha, much about, but somewhat above, our peck. Of it, see 1 Sam. 25.18. 1 King. 18.32. 2 King. 7.1, 16, 18. and in the places before mentioned. The word is a duplicate, as many other of the like stamp in that language: which most of the Jewish masters would have to be a noun, as if it should be said, *By peck-peck*, that is, delivering out, not the whole *bushel*, or *strike* together; but by peck after peck, as a man does in meting out meal, or grain, out of a great heap, or tun, into vessels of a smaller size. Some make it a verb with a pronoun affixed to it, and render the text, *in measuring*, as it were, by the peck out *to it*; as afterward, in sending out of it. The former seems the better, and that the rather, because there wants that point in the belly of the last letter, which the pronoun wontedly has. The word, as many other in this prophet, has no mate.

*{when it shooteth forth*} The word, in the original, is very ambiguous. That which has bred much diversity, both of version, and interpretations amongst those that write upon the place. Some, *In due measure, using the sword wilt thou debate it*. Because a word used for a sword, so called of putting it up, or drawing it out, comes near to the term here used, 2 Chr. 23.10. Neh. 4.17. Joel 2.8. Others, *In measure, with her plantations dost thou contend*: Because of those things which the earth itself, as plants growing on it, *sends out*, the like word is also used, Neh. 3.15. ch. 16.8. Est. 17.6, 7. As if the meaning were, that God in chastising his people, did rather smite them, in the fruits of the field, than in their persons, Joel 1.4. Amos 4.6–9. but this is not sound. Others, *In her shooting forth*; that is, when she grows luxuriant, he prunes her, but warily, as the husbandman does his vines, or his fruit trees; so as not, either to hurt the heart, or kill the root of the plant, Joh. 15.2. Others, *in sending* (that is, inflicting judgments) *upon her*; as 2 Sam. 24.15. Ezek. 14.19, 21. The preposition included in the verb, or affix: as v. 4. And in the very next word, *debate it*, or *contend it*, for, *debate*, or, *contend with it*. The like whereunto see, Deut. 33.8. Job 10.2. ch. 49.25. Others, lastly, *In casting, dismissing*, or, *sending her out*; as the word, most properly, and usually signifies. Which I conceive to be the genuine sense of the place. The gender of the pronoun, altered here, from the masculine to the feminine; because in the foregoing verse, was relation had to the people, v. 6. in this to the land, or vineyard, v. 2. And some suppose an allusion here to a father, who displeased with his son, though he purpose not to disinherit, or cast him utterly off, yet either excludes him, for a time, from his presence, as David did Absalom, 2 Sam. 14.24. or sends him out into the country, and there holds him to hard meat, and keeps him in servile employments, until he have made his peace with him, Jer. 2.14. Others to a husband, who for ill carriage, or misdemeanor, dismisses his wife for a time, but with a purpose to receive and entertain her again: As God having the like affection and disposition towards his people, even then when he seemed to cast them off, as no longer his, and to have given them a peremptory bill of divorce, Ps. 44.9. ch. 50.1. Jer. 3.1–14. It is most probable, that the prophet had an eye unto God's sending, or casting them out into captivity, which though the heaviest affliction that ever he exercised his people with, was yet tempered with mercy towards them, towards the best, at least, of them, as were his reserve, Jer. 15.12. & 24.5. Lam. 3.22. Ezek. 11.16. They run wide still, both Jews and Christian commenters, that expound this passage, also, of God's dealings in exact rigor of justice, according to their demerits, or in way of retaliation, measure for measure, with the enemies of his people, Jer. 50.15. Rev. 16.5, 6. & 18.6, 7.

*{thou wilt debate with it*} Or, *dost*, or *didst thou* (for he seems to speak of what was past) *debate with it*; to wit, by your judgments; as Amos 7.4.

*{he stayeth his rough wind, in the day of the east wind*} Most interpreters apply this also, to God's proceedings with his people. The first word is ambiguous, and makes the sense the more uncertain. Some taking it in its most usual sense of *meditating*, render it, *when in his Spirit, he meditateth*, or, *mindeth, harsh*, or, *rough things toward them*. Others, eyeing another use of the word, whereby it signifies, sometime, *to make a noise*, ch. 8.20. & 31.4. & 38.11. & 59.11. *when he whistleth*, or, *though he blow with his stiff gale of wind*. Others, following a third notion of the word, whereby it is used, for *to remove*, or, *take away*, 2 Sam. 20.13. Prov. 25.4, 5. (and some of the Jewish commenters here so take it) *when he* (that is, the enemy, or God himself by the enemy) *took her away with that his stiff*, or, *boisterous wind*. Or, when with such a tempestuous storm, she was borne, or carried away into captivity, Jer. 4.11, 13. & 18.17. Ezek. 5.2, 12. (for the text, so read, would be best taken indefinitely, as the like, v. 3.) And they knit this latter clause thus to the former; which yet others sever, and make this latter an entire sentence, by itself. Some, whom our version follows, applying it to God's people, *he stayeth*, or *restraineth his rough wind*, that is, in fanning his people, he allays and slackens the stiffness and boisterousness of it; that it may not carry all away before it, Ps. 78.38. *he did not raise up all his wrath*: see ch. 48.9. Others understanding it, of the enemies of God's people, render the words with an adversative prefixed, as Ps. 119.23. Prov. 11.23. *but*; or, *whereas, with a rough wind he carrieth them away*: he sweeps them away, to their utter destruction, with a stiff blast of some tempestuous wind, that rends or tears up trees by the roots; such as passed by Elias, 1 King. 19.12. and that carries all before it, as that did the locusts in Egypt, Exod. 10.19. (alluded to, Joel 2.20.) which with a stiff blast of wind, he blew into the Red Sea, and there drowned them, as he did Pharao also after them, with the like, and all his forces, Exod. 15.10. See Job 27.20, 21. ch. 41.15, 16. Jer. 49.36. A defect of the pronoun *them*; as Prov. 8.13. and this last I incline to.

*{in the day of the east wind*} At such time as the east wind blows; noted for a blasting, boisterous, and blustering wind, in those parts, Gen. 41.6, 23. Ps. 48.7. Ezek. 17.10. & 19.12. & 27.26. Heb. *eastern*, for, *eastern wind*: as *standing*, for *standing corn*, ch. 17.5.

**V. 9.** *{By this, therefore, shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged, and this is all the fruit, to take away his sin*} Another difference between God's dealings in this kind with his people, and with those other. All that he does herein to his people, is not to destroy them, but to chastise them for what they have done formerly amiss, and for the future, to reform them; to wean, and withdraw them from their sins, that they may not perish by them, ch. 1.25. & 4.4. & 48.10. Prov. 21.30. Ezek. 18.31. & 33.11. Dan. 11.35. Mal. 3.3. 1 Cor. 11.32. Heb. 12.9, 10.

*{By this shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged*} Or, *Hereby is*, or, *hath the iniquity of Jacob* (that is, of God's people; as v. 6.) *been done away* (as ch. 28.18.) or *expiated*, as Num. 35.33. Prov. 16.6. ch. 6.7. & 22.24. the guilt of it is remitted, and God's paternal indignation and displeasure satisfied, and pacified, upon their sincere repentance, and serious humiliation, thereby procured, and produced in them, Job 5.17, 18. & 33.16–24. ch. 26.8, 9, 16–18. & 40.2. & 43.25. and 54.8, 9.

*{all the fruit*} *All the fruit thereof*, a defect of the pronoun, as Deut. 25.12. ch. 26.15. & 30.27. All the end that God aims at, in afflicting his people, to wit, their amendment, *fruit* being the end, for which men plant, set and sow, ch. 5.2. 2 Tim. 2.6. Heb. 6.7. Jam. 5.7. and the benefit that thence redounds to God's people; the *fruit*, that they thereby reap and receive; and in regard whereof, they are thereby in themselves also bettered, Ps. 94.12. & 119.67, 71. Heb. 12.10, 11.

*{to take away his sin*} Or, *taking away*: that he may *taking away, take away*: as ch. 5.5. that he, that is, God, may utterly take away, may thoroughly purge sin out of them, Job 33.17, 18. ch. 1.25. & 28.10. a twofold defect, both of the verb finite; as ch. 59.13. and of the finitive particle; as v. 5. or as others render it, *when he shall have taken away his sin*. When he, to wit, God's people, shall have abandoned the practice of those sins, that formerly they had fallen into; a want of the adverb of time; as ch. 17.6. & 26.10. or, taking it indefinitely, as v. 3. *when his sin shall be abandoned*; *sin*, say they, that is, the subject matter, means, and instruments of his *sin*, mentioned in the next branch: as, *Your sin*, for, the calf wherein you sinned, Deut. 9.21. but we need not depart from the proper sense of the word; the words relate to the former branch, what was termed *iniquity* there, is *sin* here: as Ps. 51.2. only there seems intended a removal of it, in regard of guilt and wrath, by free remission, on God's part; here an abandoning of it, by sincere repentance, and serious reformation on man's part, Ezek. 6.9. & 36.31.

*{when he maketh all the stones of the altar, as chalk stones, that are beaten in sunder*} When he shall have made the sincerity of his repentance (without which no reconcilement of God and man, ch. 59.2.) to appear, by abandoning his idols, together with the instruments and monuments of his former idolatries, ch. 30.22. Deut. 7.5. & 12.2, 3. 2 King. 18.4. & 23.4–20.

*{all the stones of the altar*} Or, *all his*, or, *their, altar stones*; for there is no particular altar designed; but the word without any particle prefixed, taken collectively: the *stones*, whereof their *altars* were made, whereon they sacrificed to their idols, ch. 65.3. a defect of the pronoun: as ch. 13.22. Jer. 5.49.

*{chalk stones*} Heb. *stones of chalk*, or *lime*; for so the word properly signifies: (though nowhere else found in the Hebrew text of the Old Testament; but another used for it, ch. 33.12.) as appears both by the word of *pargeting*, and a *pargeter*, among the Talmudists, thence deduced; and by the Syriac, in Daniel, where it is used in the Syriac form, for the *parget*, or *plaster* of the wall, Dan. 5.5. *as limestones broken in pieces*, that is, as chalk stones, broken in pieces to make lime, wherewith to parget. So ch. 24.10. and the participle is in such a form, not elsewhere read, as implies a breaking to pieces, as such stones, for such uses, are wont. So Deut. 9.21. 2 King. 23.12.

*{the groves and images shall not stand up*} These words are so joined to the former in our version, as if the meaning were, that when the altars should be demolished, then the groves and images should not stand up. Which yields a sense, that seems but flat: they would rather be rendered with supply of a copulative: as ch. 26.17. *and the groves and images*, or *sun images: stand not*: as Ps. 1.5. Nah. 1.6. but are likewise beaten and broken down, or *abide not*: as Gen. 45.1. or, *continue not*: as Job 15.29. but are also utterly abandoned, are demolished, and abolished. Of these *groves* and *sun images*, see on ch. 17.8.

**V. 10.** *{Yet the defenced city shall be desolate; and the habitation forsaken, and left like a wilderness*} This verse, and the next, are by divers diversely taken. Some, and so the Jewish commenters themselves, expound them, of God's dealing with Israel, his own people. Others, rather, of his proceedings against his and their enemies; because he speaks, in the close of it, of judgment, without any allay of mercy: as Jam. 2.13. which if it be applied, therefore, unto God's people, must be understood of, and restrained unto, those obstinate ones among them; of which before, v. 4. See Deut. 29.18–21.

*{Yet*} As ch. 9.4. or, *But*: as ch. 2.6. as either foretelling what should betide God's people, before they were thus reformed; or, as passing to the relation of God's dealing with others in a rougher manner, than with them: as v. 7.

*{the defenced city*} Jerusalem, say some: Samaria, say others: and others, again, Babylon; or as those of either judgment, that take the words more largely; the strongest cities, as well in Judah, as in Israel, Samaria, and Jerusalem, themselves not excepted; 2 King. 17.5. Jer. 34.1. or, the strongest cities of God's enemies, Babylon, and others of them, ch. 24.10. & 25.12. & 26.5, 6. the word being collectively understood, their *defenced cities*, and afterwards, their *habitations*: as Jer. 50.45.

*{desolate*} Heb. *solitary*; left alone: either all the towns and country about her being wasted and destroyed, ch. 1.8. or forsaken of those that formerly replenished her, and whose company and presence in times past she enjoyed, Lam. 1.1.

*{the habitation*} This some apply to the sanctuary or temple at Jerusalem; to which it seems applied, by way of prophecy, Exod. 15.2, 17. Jer. 31.23. Others conceive it spoken of the stately palaces, (the word being collectively used) of the city, or cities, before intended: used of Babylon, Jer. 50.45. or, more generally their *habitations*, as well without, as within their cities: for the word is very general, Job 5.3. Hos. 9.13. Yet some render it, *their sheepcotes*. Which albeit, the word oft elsewhere seems to import, 2 Sam. 7.8. ch. 65.10. yet I conceive not to have place here. We read, indeed, in Scripture, of *the habitations*, or *sheep walks*, if you please, rather than *sheepcotes, of the wilderness*, that is, *of the waste*, or the plain, where cattle use to graze, Ps. 65.12. Joel 2.22. but because the places here intended are opposed to the *wilderness*, or *wastes*, I suppose, rather, such *pleasant places* to be here intended, (see Hos. 9.13. where the same word is used) as either within their cities, or about their countries were choicely planted, and charily kept for their pleasure and delight. See ch. 32.13. so that the meaning is, that their strongest places should be ruined, and the pleasantest defaced.

*{forsaken*} Ch. 16.2.

*{left as a wilderness*} Ch. 6.11, 12. & 32.14. & 64.10. Ezek. 36.4. Jer. 9.12.

*{there shall the calf feed, and there shall he lie down, and consume the branches thereof*} Cattle shall feed, and lodge, and browse, where men now dwell, where houses now stand; threatened to Jerusalem, ch. 32.13, 14. Jer. 26.18. Mic. 3.12.

*{the calf*} Put here, for cattle of all sorts; as ch. 11.6.

*{feed, and lie down*} Quietly, without restraint, or disturbance; all lying open, and none to chase away, or affright, ch. 17.2.

*{consume the branches thereof*} Browse upon the shrubs, that shall be there growing, when the cities and dwellings ruined have lain long waste, ch. 32.14. or upon the pleasant plants, and choice slips, that their orchards and gardens had been planted and furnished with within the city, Neh. 3.15. Cant. 2.5. ch. 17.11. Some restrain it to the famous Babylonian gardens; whereof see Diodore, lib. 2. ch. 10. and they may well come in among the rest. Howbeit, some expound it, of the persons of men; as if all sorts, from the greater boughs, resembling men of note and place, to the lesser spigs or spray, that is, the meaner sort of people should be exposed to destruction; as ch. 10.33, 34. and others, that utter ruin is threatened to the state; compared to a tree, that is by beasts browsed upon, while it is green; and made fuel of, when it is sere. See ch. 18.5, 6. and of the word here used, ch. 2.21. & 17.6. But I suppose, that these notions do not suit so well with the prophet's present discourse, describing the devastation of the places, rather than the destructions of the persons there inhabiting, save as the deportation or destruction of the one, is a means to produce the desolation of the other.

**V. 11.** *{When the boughs thereof are withered, they shall be broken off, the women come, and set them on fire*} The prophet proceeds in the relation of that desolation and wasteness, that should befall the city, or, cities, here intended.

*{the boughs thereof*} Heb. *Harvest*: as Ps. 80.11. the name *harvest*, being common, as well to the plucking of trees, as to the cutting of corn. See ch. 17.11. and of some trees, no other *harvest* is, than their *boughs*, Neh. 8.15.

*{they shall be broken*} The verb is plural; the noun singular. Whence some render it, *each one of them shall be broken*, as ch. 26.19. none escape; but because the noun is masculine, and the verb feminine; and again, the noun of such a comprehensive notion, as admits not well, such a distribution, as to say, every one of a *harvest*, meaning, ear, bough, or fruit: Some, therefore, deeming the speech to be defective, and a word to be supplied, fitting the verb, and found, ch. 18.5. read the words thus; *the sprigs shall be broken*: and this the rather is to be admitted, because the prophet seems to speak, not of boughs, decayed on the tree, and then because grown sere, broken off, but of trees felled, or broken down, for the use of cattle, while yet green, the sprigs whereof, when they have barked them, growing sere, are easily snapped asunder: and as spray good for nothing else, are picked up for the fire.

*{the women come*} Or, *and women come*. For there is no article in the text, the copulative supplied, as v. 10. Some find mysterious matter in the word *women*, to wit, that the enemies of God's people should be so dejected, that they should be destroyed, even by a weak woman's hand; as was Sisera by Jael, Judg. 4.9, 21. and Abimelech by the of woman Thebez, Judg. 9.53, 54. and Pyrrus, by a woman seeing her son in danger to be slain by him; and some bring it home to the Babylonians, subdued by the Medes formerly, deemed but an effeminate people: and somewhat in the prophets may seem to sound this way, Jer. 50.45. But the plain literal sense seems most agreeable to the prophet's mind; and the ordinary practice in all places, may inform us, that where boughs lopped lie, till they be sere, unregarded, it is the usual manner of women and children, to gather up the spray, either to make fire of, or to kindle fire with, Jer. 7.18.

*{set them on fire*} Heb. *set it on fire*: and here the former version, by way of distribution, may not do amiss, *it*, that is, each one, or any one of the sprigs, either bigger, or less, as before.

*{set on fire*} Or, *on a light fire*, such a light fire, as such light stuff is wont to produce; having oftentimes more light, than heat; more blaze than warmth, Eccl. 7.6. the word properly signifies *to enlighten*, or *make light*, Ps. 18.28. but because there is little difference between the two words in Hebrew, of one and the same stock, that signifies *light*, the one, ch. 5.20. and *fire*, the other, ch. 44.16. yea the one is used, sometime, for the other: *fire* is put for *light*, ch. 50.11. as *light* for *fire*, Mar. 14.54. and that *light* and *fire* commonly go together; and no sooner is the fire kindled, but it presently gives light. Hence it is, that in Hebrew, the word that signifies first, and properly, *to lighten*, or *give light*, is used also for *to kindle*, or, *set on fire*, Mal. 1.10. The plain meaning of the place seems to be, that those places that had been before so curiously planted, and carefully fenced, that none might have access unto them, to touch aught there, should now lie open, for man and beast, ch. 5.1, 5. & 7.25. and that which now grew there, whether left of what had been formerly there planted, or had, since the land was overrun, sprung up of itself, should be so neglected, that it should be free for any, other beast, to browse on, while it was green, or people, to make fuel of, when it grew sere: an argument of extreme waste, and utter neglect.

*{for it is a people of no understanding*} Heb. *not a people of understandings*; that is, not of *any understandings*; understandings, for any understanding: as ch. 40.14. and as *salvations*, or *deliverances*, for *any salvation*, or deliverance, ch. 26.18. and, *righteousnesses*, for *any righteousness*, at all, Dan. 9.18. a people that has no understanding at all, ch. 1.3. that understand nothing, take no notice of, nor regard at all, either God himself, his dealings with them, and their duty to him; or aught that does truly and really concern their own good, Deut. 32.6, 28, 29. Ps. 28.5. & 82.5. ch. 5.12, 13. & 42.18, 20–25. & 44.19. Jer. 4.22. & 5.4, 5. & 8.7. & 10.8, 14. The reason is here rendered, of God's so severe proceeding against them, whether foreign nations, or those among his own people; as the like also in the other places pointed to. See Hos. 4.14.

*{therefore he that made them, will have no mercy on them, and he that formed them, will shew them no favour*} A heavy close, and a sad sentence; which therefore might seem to confirm the judgment of them who conceive this whole passage to be understood of foreign nations, and not of God's own people. But those terms of *making* and *forming*, are so frequently, in a peculiar manner, applied unto God's people, as importing, and intending, not so much the creating of them, as men in the loins of our first parents, or the procreating of them, by their several next parents, common to them with all manner of mankind, Gen. 1.27, 28. & 2.7. Job 10.8–10. Ps. 119.73. & 139.13–16. Jer. 1.5. but the making of them such a nation, as they were, and the framing of them into such a state, as well ecclesiastical as civil, as God had settled among them, and advanced them unto; these terms, I say, in a more special manner attributed in regard of God's peculiar dealings with them, to that people, makes me incline to think, that they are the people here meant, whom God would so severely proceed against. See Deut. 32.6, 15, 18. Ps. 149.2. ch. 22.11. & 43.1, 7. & 44.2. & 45.11.

*{will have no mercy on him*} Or, *will not have mercy on him*: a kind of extenuation, as some would have it. *I will not have mercy on them*, for, *I will punish them*: but it seems to me, rather, a very full and emphatical phrase, as if he had said, I will punish them unmercifully: my judgments inflicted on them, shall have no mixture of mercy. See ch. 9.17. Hos. 1.6. So in that of Solomon, Prov. 17.21. *He that begetteth a fool, begetteth himself grief*, or, *sorrow*: (so it would be read) *the father of a fool shall have no joy*, has no small emphasis in it, as some learned observe: the like may be said of the other branch; in sense with this the same. See on v. 10.

**V. 12.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that &c.*} In this verse, and the next, the prophet, after his wonted manner, concludes this long sermon, with a gracious promise of God's restitution of his people, after the main body of the obstinate wicked, by his judgments destroyed from among them, and the residue reformed, which is the day, or time pointed to in these words; as ch. 11.11. The particle *that*, is wanting; as ch. 7.21, 22. and so also, v. 13.

*{the Lord shall beat off from the channel of the river, unto the stream of Egypt*} This some expound of God's chastising his people, partly by the Assyrians, and partly, yea principally, by the Chaldeans, who should overrun their land, and beat them out of it, from the one end of it, to the other; and thus they rather conceive it to be understood, because the land of their inheritance is usually thus bounded. See on ch. 3.3. Others understand it, of a beating over all those parts, lying between Euphrates and Nilus, Assyria and Egypt, by the Medes in their expedition against Babylon. And others lastly, of a search that God would make for his people, and a beating of them out, or, a separation to be made of them, from other people, among whom they were dispersed in all parts, that they had an ordinary notice of.

*{the Lord shall beat off*} Or, *beat out*, a metaphor taken either from trees, whose fruit is in the gathering of it beat off, Deut. 24.20. ch. 17.6. & 24.13. or, from corn; the grain whereof, is beaten out of the ear from the chaff, Judg. 6.11. Ruth 2.17. with the staff, or the flail, ch. 28.27. for they had other kinds of threshing also: see ch. 28.27, 28. now because *threshing* is an ordinary emblem of affliction; of which, see ch. 21.10. & 25.10. and the beating of trees likewise, ch. 17.6. many suppose that afflictions should of necessity here be intimated, if not of God's people, yet of some to be beaten off, as fruit from the trees, from the places of their former abode; and of those nations at least, from whom they were to be reduced, as being thence brought forth, as grain out of the threshing floor: neither of which, yet, I suppose, is necessary. There may well in this term be intimated, no more than a severing of God's dispersed people from the nations, among whom they remained, and with whom they were intermingled; as by beating, the berries are severed from the tree; by threshing, the grain from the ear, the straw and the chaff, not to hurt, or destroy either, but that they may be gathered, carried in and laid up, the one in the storehouse; and in the granary, the other, Mat. 3.12. & 13.30. And the *beating*, here consequently, seems to imply no more affliction to God's people, than the *reaping* at the last day, Mat. 13.38,39. albeit, that *reaping* and *cutting* in Scripture be an ordinary resemblance of the execution of God's wrath upon the wicked, Job 24.24. Ps. 37.2. Joel 3.13. Rev. 14.15,19. Thus the Jewish commenters take it, and the word of *gathering* that follows, seems to confirm it.

*{from the channel of the river*} Or, *from the flood*; as Psal. 69.2,15. (for in this notion, it is nowhere else found) and it is deemed to import such a stream, as runs with strength and noise, *of the river*, to wit, Euphrates, chap. 8.7. whose several branches, do some of them, in heathen writers, bear their names from the word here used, as *Nahar-fares*, and *Nahar-malcha*; Pliny, l. 6. c. 26. Ammiane, l. 24. c. 3.

*{to the river of Egypt*} That is, to Nilus. See on chap. 23.3. Out of all parts of the land of Israel, whose limits these two were, Deut. 1.7. & 11.24. Josh. 1.4. & 13.3. as some; or out of all those countries that lie between Euphrates and Nilus, the utmost parts of Assyria, the one way toward the east, and the farthest parts of Egypt towards the west. See chap. 11.11,12. a place parallel to this, see also ver. 13.

*{and ye shall be gathered one by one, O ye children of Israel*} The term of *gathering* here used, as appears by the word of *beating* premised, is not taken from the gathering or gleaning of corn; for that is first gathered, and then beaten out, Ruth 2.17. but from the gathering of fruit, or berries, that are picked up from the ground one by one, after that they have either fallen of themselves, or been beaten down from the tree; whereby the prophet would either intimate the small number of the people, that having been formerly faithful, or being sincerely converted, should be preserved in those times of general calamity, and reserved for mercy, in regard of the whole nation, chap. 1.9. & 10.12,13. it being a note of some scarcity, where berries are picked up one by one, or signify an exact collection of them (the verb also being in a form of some emphasis) God picking them out, as it were, one by one, out of several places into which they had been dispersed; so expressed, to assure them of an entire relief, and return of all those that were to have a share in this mercy, to meet and partake together in the same; albeit they were never so far asunder one from another; or never so few of them in any one place, Deut. 30.3,4. Neh. 1.9. ch. 26.19. Jer. 3.14. Ezek. 39.25,28. Amos 9.9,10.

**V. 13.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown*} Heb. *with a great trumpet* (such an one, as may be heard far and near) *shall it be sounded*; that is, *the trumpet* (such an one) *shall be sounded*, as Amos 3.6. Cyrus his proclamation shall come forth, for the return of God's people out of all parts, where they remained in captivity, into their own country, 2 Chr. 36.22,23. Ezr. 1.1,2. an allusion to the *Jubilee-trumpet*, that was sounded in the year of release, wherein men were set free, and returned each one to his inheritance and possession again, Lev. 25.9,10. a type of the evangelical trumpet, whereby, under the Messiah, God's elect out of all parts, are called in out of their spiritual thraldom, under sin and Satan, to inherit a share in the kingdom of grace here, ch. 61.1,12. Luk. 4.18,19. Joh. 5.24,25. Act. 26.18. Rom. 10.18. as also of that celestial trumpet, whereby they shall at the last day be summoned to appear, that they may enter upon the full possession, and entire fruition of their eternal inheritance, both in body and soul, in the kingdom of glory hereafter, Mat. 24.31. & 25.34. Joh. 5.28,29. 1 Cor. 15.52. 1 Thes. 4.16.

*{and they shall come, that were ready to perish, in the land of Assyria,}* Whither the ten tribes had been carried captive, 2 King. 17.6.

*{ready to perish*} Heb. *perished*; as Deut. 26.5. Job 29.13. Ps. 119.176. so *destroyed*, for, *ready to be destroyed*, Ps. 137.8. or, *perished*, in no better case than as utterly perished, deemed no other, than as dead, ch. 26.19. Ezek. 37.11.

*{and the outcasts*} Ps. 147.2. ch. 16.3,4. Jer. 30.17. Ezek. 34.16. Mic. 4.6. Zeph. 3.19.

*{in the land of Egypt*} Whither they had many of them fled, Jer. 43.7. & 44.28. and many other had at sundry times also been led captive, Deut. 28.66. Hos. 8.13. Zach. 10.10. *Assyria* and *Egypt* seem mentioned, not as the only places, into which the people of God had been dispersed; but as Euphrates and Nilus, ver. 12. as two of the remotest places one from another, into which they had been sequestered; & this helps to confirm that which was before spoken of those two famous rivers was not intended to set out the boundaries of their own land: but to intimate the extent of their deportation and captivity, Lam. 1.4.

*{and shall worship the Lord, in the holy mountain at Jerusalem*} They shall again, at their return, renew and set up again the solemn service of God, that had been wholly intermitted (the temple, the place peculiarly assigned thereto, being demolished) during the time of their captivity.

*{and shall worship*} Or, *to worship*; *that they may worship*, as Josh. 24.9. Heb. *bow themselves*, that is, worship by *bowing themselves*, as Ps. 72.11.

*{in the holy mountain*} Mount Zion. See ch. 2.2. *mountain of holiness*, as Ezek. 20.40.

### CHAPTER 28

**V. 1.** *{Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim,}* This chapter contains a new sermon, or prophecy, consisting of two principal parts; the former, concerning Ephraim, or the ten tribes, ver. 1–4. the latter, concerning the people of Judah, and their adherents, ver. 5–29. He begins that concerning the ten tribes, with denunciation of a *wo* against them, for their pride and haughtiness; describing them, as men drunk with prosperity, and drowned in sensuality: see the like of them, Hos. 4.11. & 5.5. Amos 6.1,4,6.

*{Woe*} In way of commination; as Chap. 5.11. though some read it, by way of compellation; *O the crown*, &c. See Chap. 10.5.

*{to the crown of pride*} The proud king, or kingdom, Hos. 7.10. *crown*, for kingly state, or kingdom, as Jer. 13.18. Lam. 5.16.

*{pride*} So here, as Ps. 17.10. See on Chap. 12.5. & 26.10. *the crown of pride*, as, *the foot of pride*, that is, of proud persons, Ps. 36.12. though some render it, not the *haughty*, but the *lofty crown*; because for multitude and power it seemed to exceed that of the other two tribes.

*{to the drunkards*} Or, *of the drunkards*, Joel 1.5. ver. 3.

*{of Ephraim*} Israel, the ten tribes, whereof *Ephraim* the chief, Psal. 60.7. Hos. 13.1. See on ch. 7.2.

*{whose glorious beauty is a fading flower*} Heb. *and a fading flower the goodliness of bravery*, or *gallantry*; which being rendered according to our version, the copulative is put for the relative, as Chap. 4.6. & 17.2. But some render it, as rendering a reason of the *wo*; *for*, or *because* (as chap. 16.2.) *his glorious beauty is*, or shall be, *a fading flower*. But that comes after, ver. 3,4. Some, (to pass by the rest) carrying on the sentence, with reference still to the *wo*, and to him *whose goodly bravery* shall become *a fading flower*; that is, to Ephraim, whose kingdom and state, for all the flourish they now make, shall shortly like a fading flower, be soon, and suddenly blasted and blown away, by the coming of Salmaneser, whom God shall send in upon them, v. 2. Or, *and to the fading flower of his goodly*, or *brave gallantry*, see ver. 4.

*{glorious beauty*} Heb. *goodliness of bravery*, or *gallantry*. See on Ch. 4.2. and ver. 4. Some take it as an explication of the word *crown*.

*{a fading flower*} Or, *as a fading flower*; the note of similitude supplied, as Chap. 22.18. See the like expression, Ps. 103.15,16. ch. 40.6,7. Jam. 1.11. Some suppose here an allusion, both in this word, and that of *a crown*, to the garlands, or coronets, made of flowers, that they used to wear on their heads at their feasts: of which, see Atheneus, l. 15. and Wisdom, 2.8. See somewhat the like, Chap. 1.30.

*{which are on the head of the fat valleys*} Or, *to them that are*; or, as others, *which* (to wit, flower) *is, on the top of the most fat*, or *fertile vale*; and by *flower*, these latter understand the state of that kingdom, formerly flourishing, but now beginning to decay.

*{which are on the head*} That is, as many expound it, *that are the princes* or *rulers*, in that fat vale: and it is true, that the word *head*, is commonly used for a *ruler*, or *governor*, and *headship*, for *principality*, or *rule*, Psal. 18.43. & 60.7. Chap. 7.8. & 9.14,15. But the form of speech, here used will not admit it, for it should then be, *the head over the vale*, Psal. 110.6. *the heads over many countries*: not as our text has it; *on the head of the vale*: which I suppose, therefore to signify rather, *which are*, that is, dwell and abide *on the head*, that is, *on the top*, (as Exod. 17.10. Deut. 34.1.) *of the vale*: to wit, in the mountain situate above the vale; in the mountain of Samaria, Hos. 6.1. *the head*, or *top of the vale*: as, *the rock of the plain*, Jer. 21.13. Or, *on the head*, that is, *in the chief*, or principal part of that fat vale: *head* for *chief*; as Exod. 30.23. 2 Sam. 23.8,18. Psal. 137.6. Cant. 4.14. For as for that, which some have, that the word *head*, should here be given to that land, because it lay higher, and was more hilly than Judah's country, I can hardly subscribe to, doubting somewhat, in part, of the thing itself.

*{of the fat valleys*} Heb. *vale of fatness*: that is, an exceeding fat and fertile vale: *fatness*, for *richness* and rankness of soil, Gen. 27.28,29. & 45.18. and *the head of the vale of fatnesses*, for the prime, and chief, of that exceeding fat, or rich vale: as, *the horn of the son of fatness*, chap. 5.1. for, a chief and principal rich soil. What *vale* is here intended, interpreters agree not. Some suppose the main body of the land, to be meant which lay all as a vale beneath Mount Lebanon and was a very fertile soil, Gen. 49.25. Deut. 33.19. Others conceive the vale to be meant, that lay next to the mountain, on which Samaria, the head city of the kingdom, was situate, 1 King. 16.24. and this seems the most probable; for to the court, the place of the king's residence, and the chief places of the kingdom, where the abuses, here pointed at, did most abound, the prophet seems to have a special eye. Howbeit, some of the Rabbines understand by it, the vale of Cinnereth; whereof Deut. 3.17. Josh. 11.2. 1 King. 15.20. in the New Testament called Genesareth, Mar. 6.53. a rich vale, indeed, but no reason rendered, why it should be here meant, save because it yields pleasant fruits. For those that would draw in hither Gethsemane (which, yet questionless, had hence its name) a fertile valley, at the foot of Mount Olivet, near to Jerusalem, Mar. 26.36. stride too far out of the prophet's way, who is here dealing with Ephraim and Samaria, not with Juda or Jerusalem. And I should rather imagine, that the prophet might have some glance in the word of *fatness*, used also for ointments, Cant. 1.3. & 4.10. at their immoderate use thereof in their feastings, expressly taxed in them, Amos 6.6. than (as some of the Jewish commenters do) expound the text, as speaking thereof directly, while they render the words, *on whose heads is a valley of ointments*: that is, whose heads run down with ointments, as abundantly, as valleys do with water, Psal. 104.10.

*{that are overcome with wine*} Or, as some, *of those that are overcome with wine*, as having reference to *flower*, that is, state before-mentioned. I rather, *to those overcome with wine*, referring it to the *woe*, or to the *drunkards*, here further described, *over-mastered with wine*. Heb. *smitten*, as Judg. 5.26. Psal. 141.5. chap. 41.10. or, *beaten*, Prov. 23.35. or, *beaten down*; as 1 Sam. 14.16. or, *broken*, as Judg. 5.22. or, *broken down*; as Psal. 74.6. chap. 16.8. the word is very significant, and from it comes the word, that signifies *an hammer*, used in the story of Sisera, Judg. 4.23. and nowhere else; which the prophet might well have an eye unto; as if he had said, they are struck down, or laid along with wine, no more able to stir or execute aught, than Sisera was, when Jael with the hammer had driven the nail through his temples, and fastened his head to the ground; a fit resemblance of a man over-mastered with drink. See another no less pregnant expression, ver. 7.

**V. 2.** *{Behold the Lord hath a mighty and strong one, which as a tempest of hail, and a destroying storm, as a flood of mighty waters overflowing, shall cast down to the earth with the hand*} The *woe*, in a general term denounced, ver. 1. is here more particularly specified, by the instrument that God would use for the effecting of it, described, partly, by his might and power, and partly by the mischief that he should do among them; both, elegantly and pregnantly set forth to the life, by variety of similitudes heaped up together; to intimate an utter ruin and subversion of all with them.

*{Behold*} See chap. 10.33. & 24.1.

*{the Lord hath a mighty and strong one*} That is, as they conceive the Hebrew text to run, that thus render it; *a mighty and strong one is to the Lord*: a common form, as well in other languages, as in Hebrew, Gen. 44.19. 1 King. 17.12. Hos. 4.1. and the meaning then is, that such an one he has ready at his command, to do his pleasure upon Samaria. Yet some others make no entire sentence of it, and therefore omitting these supplies, both of the verb substantive in this branch, and of the pronoun relative in the next, read the words, *one mighty*, or, *a mighty one, and strong to the Lord*: that is, *exceeding strong*; as, *sinners to the Lord*, (for so the words are there) that is, *exceeding great sinners*, Gen. 13.13. or, *strong from the Lord*: that is, strong by strength received from God: as, Psal. 115.15. *blessed of God*, or *from God*, Ezr. 3.13. or, *from the noise*, or *voice*, ch. 22.5. *a day of perplexity from the Lord*: in all which places and others the like, is the same particle found, that is in this place. So in the Greek Hebraizing, Act. 7.20. of Moses, *comely to God*; either for *exceeding comely*, or, *comely*, by comeliness received *from God*; as Ezek. 16.14. and of the Apostolical ministry, 2 Cor. 4.4. *mighty to God*: that is, *mighty* by power received *from God*, 2 Cor. 4.7. and this mighty one, there is no doubt, but it was Salmaneser, the king of Assyria, and his forces; who in the fourth year of Ezekiah, overran the whole land of Israel, sat down before Samaria, and after three years siege took it, dissolved their kingdom and state, carried the natives away captive and in the room of them, peopled the country with strangers brought out of remote parts, 2 King. 17.5,6,24. & 18.9–11.

*{mighty and strong one*} Either king, or host, or both, words of equal force, used for amplification: as chap. 27.1. nor need we to put in here with the Jewish commenters either *day*, as some, or *wind*, as other of them do, being unnecessary supplies.

*{which*} The relative is oft wanting, Exod. 13.8. chap. 42.5. but according to the latter reading, either of them has no use at all here.

*{as a tempest of hail*} More violent than rain; that beats down, and breaks asunder, not the standing corn only, and such things, as grow on the surface of the ground, or the fruit of trees only; but even the bigger branches also, as well as the smaller sprigs, yea, men and beasts themselves, sometime too, Exod. 9.23–25. Hos. 10.11. So ch. 25.4. & 28.17. & 20.30. Ezek. 13.11.

*{a destroying storm*} Heb. *a storm of excision*, or, *destruction*, Deut. 32.24. Psal. 92.6. Hos. 13.9. So interpreters, generally; which yet a late learned author controls, affirming the word here used, to signify not *a storm*, but *a gate*, and would have it rendered, *in the gate excision*; and the meaning to be such a storm of hail, as shall beat down the gate, that is, destroy the state. But the reading he follows, is not so general as he would have it, as by collation of copies I have observed; and the Rabbines, that comment upon the place, taking no notice of any other reading, go the same received way that our interpreters unanimously take.

*{a flood of mighty waters overflowing*} The word rendered *flood*, is the same, that was translated *tempest*, before. Of it, see on ch. 4.6. and 25.4. in the former of which places, it seems taken as in that branch, in the latter, as in this. *of mighty waters*, or, *of many waters*, see on ch. 16.14. & 17.12. *overflowing*, as the waters of the sea, or of great rivers, are wont to do with much force, and in great abundance, when they have swollen above their sea-walls, or have broken through their banks, Job 30.24. Psal. 42.7. & 69.1. & 88.16,17. ch. 8.7. v. 17,18. ch. 59.19. Jer. 51.42,55.

*{shall cast down to the earth*} Some, *shall make to rest on the ground*: but that notion concerns another, though neighbor root. Heb. *hath* (in a prophetical phrase) *left*, or, *laid to*, or, *on the ground*: there seems a defect of the particle *it*, as chap. 21.3. & 26.1. the mighty one before-mentioned shall *lay it*, that is, the crown of Ephraim, with all their gallantry, *on the ground*, as Psal. 89.39,44. chap. 14.12,15. *to the ground*, for *on the ground*: as, *to the earth*, for *on the earth*, chap. 26.9. and so Amos 5.7. (the same phrase with this here would be rendered) *they lay justice on the ground*.

*{with the hand*} Or, *with an hand*; or, *by hand*: that is, as most of ours; easily; with no great ado, as with the bare hand only; or with the one hand, chap. 10.13. or, quickly, soon, speedily: (for he was not long about it) as we use to say, *out of hand*, Lam. 4.5. See v. 4. but I suppose rather, that *by hand*, here is, by force of hand, by main might: so the Jewish interpreters, deeming a defect of the epithet to be in the text; *with hand*, that is, *with a strong hand*: expressed, Exod. 3.19. Ezek. 20.33. Dan. 9.15. *hand*, for *a strong hand*; as, *name*, for a great *name*, Gen. 6.4. & 11.4. or, a good *name*, Prov. 22.1. Eccl. 7.1.

**V. 3.** *{The crown of pride, the drunkards of Ephraim, shall be trodden under feet*} They, and it shall not be laid along on the ground only, ch. 51.23. but even trampled upon under feet, Mal. 4.3.

*{The crown of pride, the drunkards*} Or, as some read it, *The crown of pride, and the drunkards*; a defect of the copulative: as chap. 27.4. Or, *The drunkards of Ephraim, with their crown of pride*; a defect of the preposition: as, Psal. 5.4. I suppose it may well be rendered, *The crown of pride*: that is, the haughty, or lofty crown, *of the drunkards of Ephraim, shall be trampled upon with feet* (so the Hebrew is, see chap. 26.6.) all the difficulty in this version is, that the word *crown*, is singular, and the verb answering it, plural: but it is observed, that in such syntax, as this here is, the noun, or verb sometime agrees in form, with the latter term, in sense with the former: so 1 Sam. 2.4. *the bow of the mighty ones were broken*, for *was broken*, Job 29.10. *the voice of the nobles were hid*, for *was hid*, Hag. 2.7. *the desire of all nations shall come*: the verb plural, as here; but the disagreement less here, than in some of them: for the verb agrees, though not in number, yet in gender, with the word *crown*. See v. 1. and we need not therefore, either with that late learned annotator, read the words, as by way of apposition, *the crown pride*, that is, *the crown and the pride*: or, with the Belgic edition, *the proud crowns*, which neither sounds nor suits so well here, as appears by comparing this with ver. 1.

*{under feet*} The crown is abased as low as may be, from *upon the head*, Psal. 21.3. Job 19.9. to lie *under the feet*, Psalm 110.1. to be trampled upon; as mire and dirt, and such things as are of meanest and vilest esteem, ch. 10.6. Mic. 7.10. Mar. 5.13.

**V. 4.** *{And the glorious beauty which is on the head of the fat valley, shall be a fading flower*} Heb. *And his*, (that is, Ephraim's) *goodly gallantry shall be as the flower of a fading plant*: *fading*, for a *fading plant*: as *standing*, chap. 47.5. for *standing corn*: and, *fading*, or, *falling*, for *fading*, or *falling fig*, as chap. 34.4. *fading*, or *shedding*, that sheds flower, or leaf, ch. 1.30.

*{and, as the hasty fruit before the summer*} Or, *or as*, &c. because a similitude diverse from the former, wanting here, as Job 6.6. All their pomp and state shall be as rathe ripe fruit, that is, as we use to say, soon ripe and soon rotten, and are not wont, therefore, to be reserved for store, but to be spent out of the way; or, that is hastily plucked, and greedily devoured; because longed for commonly, and earnestly desired, Jer. 24.2. Hos. 9.10. Mic. 7.1.

*{which when he that looketh upon it, seeth it, while it is yet in his hand, he eateth it up*} Or, *which when one espyeth, as soon as it is in his hand, he devoureth it*. Heb. *swalloweth it*, greedily devours it, Job 20.15. See ver. 2.

**V. 5.** *{In that day shall the Lord of Hosts be for a crown of glory, and for a diadem of beauty, unto the residue of his people*} The prophet having done with Ephraim, comes now to Judah; and having related what evils he would bring on the one, he begins now to tell, what good he would do for, and what honor confer upon the other.

*{In that day*} When this judgment shall be executed upon Ephraim, which was in the days of Ezekiah.

*{shall the Lord of Hosts be*} Of the title, see chap. 1. ver. 9.

*{for a crown of glory*} Or, *goodliness*; *a goodly crown*: as *an inheritance of goodliness*, for *a goodly inheritance*, Jer. 3.19. for it, or instead of it, he will grace and honor that state, as much, or more, than the goodliest or richest crown in the world, had they it to wear, could: see the like, Prov. 4.9. chap. 62.3. and this is here opposed to Ephraim's haughty crown, like a garland of fading flower: for this is *a crown of amarantum*, or *everlasting*, a flower so termed, and this crown so from it, 1 Pet. 5.6. *a crown that fadeth not*, 1 Pet. 1.4.

*{a diadem of beauty*} Or, *of gallantry*, Jer. 13.18. *a gallant diadem*; the same thing, in effect with the former: the word rendered *diadem*, is in this notion nowhere else found: See ver. 1.

*{unto the residue of his people*} Unto the kingdom of Judah, that remained still in their own land, and retained their wonted state with addition of much honor, under Ezekiah and Josiah, after that the ten tribes were dispersed, and their state dissolved.

**V. 6.** *{And for a spirit of judgment, to him that sitteth in judgment, and for strength, to them that turn the battle to the gate*} The means whereby God would make their state so honorable and illustrious, by endowing their rulers with wisdom, and their warriors with valor: these two being the two principal pillars of a state, chap. 3.1,2. and these two endowments, the principal requisites, and true ornaments in either, ch. 11.2.

*{a spirit of judgment*} An ability to judge aright, and discern of truth and falsehood, right and wrong, in those things that come before them: in regard whereof, Solomon calls the king's doom, *a divination*, Prov. 16.10. as proceeding from a divine inspiration: such *a spirit of discretion*, for civil affairs; as was that *gift of discretion*, for spiritual affairs, called *the discretion of spirits*: 1 Cor. 12.10. a sagacity more than ordinary, in discerning of soundness, and discovery of unsoundness in others.

*{to him that sitteth in judgment*} Heb. *upon judgment*: that is, *upon the throne*, or seat *of judgment*, Psal. 9.4. Prov. 20.8. *judgment*, for *the judgment seat*: as *royalty*, for *royal robes*, Esth. 5.1. those narrow the text overmuch, that restrain this (as some do) to Ezekiah: for though the word be singular, yet it is collectively taken; as Prov. 20.8. and includes others also, together with him, that judged under him, or were assistant to him in judgment.

*{for strength*} For that also is God's, and in his hand to give, 1 Chr. 29.11,12. 2 Chr. 20.6.

*{that turneth the battle to the gate*} The old Latin corrupts the sense of this text, rendering the words, *that return from war to the gate*, that is, *home*, which some apply to Ezekiah's return from his war against the Philistines, 2 King. 18.8. as do those also that render it, *that turn the war away from the gate*. For neither will the words of the text admit either of these interpretations; and the meaning seems much more emphatical; such, as not only defend their own country from the enemy, but beat him back, and pursue him to his own gates, chap. 22.7. and so indeed did Ezekiah, when he did not only beat the Philistines home to the gates of their strongest forts, and fenced cities, but entered them also, and possessed himself of them, 2 King. 18.8.

**V. 7.** *{But they also have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way*} The prophet having begun this prophecy concerning Judah, with a gracious promise of God's favor toward that state, both in the continuance, and the advancement of it, after the ruin of Ephraim; whereas it might have been justly feared, that the subversion of the one, being so near neighbors, might have proved a great impeachment; if not a downfall of the other; does now pass on to a grievous complaint against those of Judah, as not free, from those enormities; for which, this heavy calamity befell that people, and therefore unworthy of so great favor.

*{But*} Heb. *And*, as ch. 16.12.

*{they also*} Those of Judah, whom God vouchsafes these favors unto, and that have God's Word and worship still among them, which the other tribes had abandoned, that professed to be better, and had better means, both to make, and to keep them better; yet take the same evil courses with them, 2 Chr. 13.8,11. ch. 48.1,2. & 58.2. Jer. 3.10.

*{have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way*} Or, *err through wine, and stray through strong drink*: for the tense is the same in either verb, and the sound somewhat alike in the original. They are guilty of the same crime, that those of Ephraim were charged with, to wit, sensuality, and excess, ver. 1.

*{strong drink*} The word, in the original, is but one; it signifies such drink, as is apt to make *drunk*: and from it, comes the term *drunkard*, used ver. 1. See ch. 5.11.

*{the Priest, and the Prophet have erred through strong drink*} Or, *do err*: they that should give good example, and endeavor by reproof, and censure, to restrain and reform it in others, are in this kind themselves as faulty as others, ch. 56.22.

*{err*} Either sin, in the immoderate use, and abuse of the creature, Prov. 20.1. for every sin is *a straying* from the way of truth and right, chap. 53.6. Jam. 5.19. or, fail in the duties of their special places, either corrupted hereby, or disabled thereunto, Mic. 2.11. & 3.5.

*{they are swallowed up of wine*} They take it in so excessively, that it over-masters them; and they seem rather to be over head and ears (as we say) in it, than to have it in them: it deprives them so of all abilities, for the use of the powers and parts, either of body or mind, Prov. 20.21. Jer. 23.9. Hos. 4.11. that which we use to say, *drowned in drink*. See somewhat the like expression, ver. 1.

*{they err in vision, they stumble in judgment*} The former member, specially, respects the prophets: the latter, the priests. Being drunken sots, and wholly addicted to sensuality, they regard not what they teach, or prophesy, the one, so it tend to looseness and licentiousness, which the people were well pleased with, chap. 30.10,11. Jer. 5.31. Ezek. 13.19,20,22. Mic. 2.6,7,11. & 3.5. nor what sentence they pass, so they might have wherewith to maintain their excess, the other, Jer. 5.31.

*{vision*} Prophecy, or teaching, Prov. 29.18. chap. 1.1. Mic. 3.6.

*{stumble*} Or, *reel* rather, or, *stagger*, alluding to their drunkenness, and the usual manner of men in drink: the word is used in this notion, here only, and Jer. 10.4. of images, said to be fastened with nails to the wall, that they may not *move*, as it is there rendered, or *stir*, certainly, *stagger*, or *reel*, rather than *stumble*, and a word derived from it, Nah. 2.10. rendered, *the knees smite together*: but the word there is a noun, and it may seem to be rendered better *staggering of knees*: knees, sure, may more fitly be said to *stagger* than to *stumble*.

*{in judgment*} The particle *in*, is wanting here; as chap. 26.8. and oft elsewhere. Howbeit, some of the Hebrew critics take occasion, thereby, to render the text, *they cause judgment to stagger*, or, to go awry, to go the wrong way; but the most agree in the other sense, *they stagger*, themselves *in judgment*; either ignorantly, not knowing, through sottishness, what sentence to give; or, willfully declining to this side, or that side, as their corrupt affections, and sinister respects biased them.

*{judgment*} Or, *the judgment of God*: for there is another word of this stock, that signifies *judgment* simply, chap. 16.3. See ch. 6.13. & 19.24. & Jer. 2.31. where words of the same stamp are found: that judgment, which by God's appointment they were to give, Deut. 17.9. Mal. 2.7. and which is said to be *the judgment* not of man but of God, 2 Chr. 19.6,8,11. that which, as seriously considered, should exact the greater care and circumspection, in the due performance of it: so does much conduce to the aggravation of their sin, that carried themselves so wretchlessly and irreligiously therein, Psal. 59.1,2. & 82.1,2.

**V. 8.** *{For all tables are full of vomit, and filthiness*} The generality, and the excess, in the loathsome effect of it.

*{all tables*} That is, many, or most: all, in a manner; as chap. 56.10. & 64.6. Jer. 9.2. Phil. 2.23. or, *all their tables*. The tables of these men, and the places where they met. A defect of the pronoun; as ch. 13.22. Job 5.12.

*{of vomit, and filthiness*} Or, *ordure*; for so the word properly signifies, ch. 36.12. See ch. 4.4. and excess of drunkenness, that makes men purge both ways. See ch. 19.14. Jer. 25.27. & 48.26. Hab. 2.16. A defect of the copulative; as ch. 27.4.

*{so that there is no place clean*} Or, *free*. A defect of the epithet; as ch. 5.2. See the note there; and the like phrase, ch. 5.8. For that exposition, which the learned annotator, here holds out, of one of the Talmudic doctors, *without place*, that is, *without God*, whom, by that term they oft design; as if the meaning were, There is no talking of God, or his law, at their tables; is of the same stamp with many other of their ridiculous toys and dalliances with divine oracles, which yet without any intimation of the least disallowance, that learned author oft relates.

**V. 9.** *{Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine? them, that are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts*} Or, as some read the words, by way of interrogation; *Those that are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts?* Another shameful effect of this their sensuality, and excess; it had made them so sottish, that they were become altogether unteachable, uncapable of learning aught: insomuch, that a man might as soon teach a child, newly weaned, letters, as to make them to understand aught, concerning themselves, or their duty to God, or man, Jer. 4.22. Hos. 4.11.

*{shall he teach*} Or, *can any man teach?* for the verb seems to be taken potentially; as ch. 26.18. and indefinitely; as ver. 5. and so, *can any make to understand* in the next branch. Yet some render it, *should God teach?* to wit, by his prophets, 1 Cor. 2.14. But I suppose the prophet's intention, more general.

*{doctrine*} Heb. *hearing*; as ver. 19. So ch. 53.1.

*{weaned*} Newly, or, lately, *weaned*. So Ps. 131.2. as if he should say, Either such, or none. It being as difficult a matter to teach such children, as to teach such sottish, and self-willed people; as these are; yea, in some regard more difficult; because, there is some want of understanding in the one; but there is, besides that, a perverseness, also, of disposition in the other, Rom. 8.7. 2 Tim. 2.25.

*{breasts*} Heb. *teats*; as Lam. 4.3. Joel 2.16. So called, as some think, from a word signifying *moisture*, Num. 11.8. Ps. 32.4. in regard of the pleasant liquor, or milk, that they yield. From the Syriac form of it, had *Thaddeus* his surname, Mat. 10.3. and thence also comes our English word, *teat*.

**V. 10.** *{For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line, here a little, and there a little*} Or, *precept hath been upon precept*, &c. Thus they must be taught, or, thus they have been taught, as little children are wont to be, when they begin to learn their first rudiments, either of reading, or writing, to know letter after letter, and to draw line after line, in the fashioning of their letters, to have the same rules oft given them, and the same things oft told them; and yet for all this diligence used about them, and pains taken with them, they are never a whit the better, they continue still, as grossly ignorant, and as unreformed, as ever, 2 Tim. 3.7. Heb. 5.12.

*{precept upon precept*} Or, *rule upon rule*; or, *rule after rule*. It is a short word, says a Rabbine, nowhere else read, and argues a *short rule*; yet, by his leave, it is found, Hos. 5.11.

*{line upon line*} Or, *line after line*. The word signifies properly, *a cord*, or, *line*, chap. 49.13. Jer. 31.39. Ezek. 47.3. thence taken, and applied to *lines* drawn with a pen, in writing and painting. An allusion, says one of the Jewish masters, to such as teach children to write, inuring them first to frame the several parts of each letter apart, and then to join them together, *line to line*, to make up the letter; (not letter to letter; for they never join them) or that guide their hand from line to line, and so cause them to draw one line after another. Though some of them would have it taken from the mason's *line*; by which he teaches his novice, to lay one row of stones after another, for the making up of a wall. But the first seems the more likely. There is an elegant consonancy between this word and the former, which our English cannot express. And there is a reiteration of either branch, to imply a frequent inculcation of one and the same point, in the teaching of them, as with dull scholars, is wont to be done.

*{here a little, and there a little*} Heb. *a little there, a little there*, that is, a little of one thing, and a little of another; or, a little at one time, and a little at another. A defect of the copulative; as vers. 8. And thus says a Rabbine, are they fain to do, that teach *a sucker*, so they call *a novice*, or young scholar, such as has need yet of *milk*, as the apostle speaks, alluding, in likelihood, to that term, 1 Cor. 3.1,2. Heb. 6.12,13.

**V. 11.** *{For with stammering lips, and another tongue will he speak to this people*} Or, *hath he spoken*; or, *must one speak*; as before, ver. 10. This passage has more difficulty in it, than the former. Some suppose the former similitude to be still insisted upon, that God has dealt with them, or they were to be dealt with, in a very plain and familiar manner, as nurses, or parents, are wont to do with little ones that lisp, and clip words, and change letters, and use divers new terms, when they teach them to speak; and yet all this would do no good. Others conceive their sottishness to be a new way deciphered; as if the prophet should say, that they were grown to that height of stupidity and senselessness, that they no more understood, or regarded, or reaped any fruit from aught spoken unto them, though never so plainly, either by God in his word, or from God by his prophets, than as if it were delivered in some strange and barbarous language, in a tongue utterly unknown to them. And this way, most, both Jewish, and Christian commenters, go; yet, in regard of the apostle's quotation of it, 1 Cor. 14.21. seeming to look another way, some other interpreters, whom our version seems to have followed, understand it, as delivered by way commination, as if God, by the prophet threatened them, to take another course with them; and because they were grown so brutish, he would speak to them now, not, as to reasonable creatures, by words and speech, but as men are wont to speak to brute beasts, by blows and stripes; by bringing in upon them, people of a strange language, which they should not understand, to handle them the more cruelly, in regard that they should not well know how to sue to them for mercy; because they had refused to hear him speaking to them, in his word, and by his messengers, in their own language which they might have understood. See Deut. 28.49. Jer. 5.15. Ezek. 3.5. And some, again, admitting the same interpretation, as spoken by way of relation, what was already past, that in such manner and by such people, (though to little purpose) God had spoken to them heretofore. But I see not why the second, and most received sense, of the words, may not as well, as this last, agree with the scope of the apostle, which is to show, that speech, in a language not understood, is unuseful.
