*{stammering lips*} Heb. *mocks*, or, *scoffs of lip*; *lip*, for, *language*, as Gen. 11.1. *one lip*, for *one language*: and *a pure lip*, for *a pure language*, Zeph. 3.9. *mocks*, *scoff*, or *derision of lip*, or *language* by an hypallage, or transposition, for, *lip*, or, *language of mocks*, or, *derisions*; (as, *choice of valleys*, for, *valleys of choice*, chap. 22.7.) that is, as some, stammering, stuttering, or lisping language: because such language men are wont to use in mocking; and such kind of language is such subject to derision. Or, as others, strange language; which to those that understand it not, seems ridiculous; and they are wont therefore, to deride, and deem, as barbarous, Psal. 114.1. 1 Cor. 14.11. And this latter way, both the words following, carry it: and the Greek also, 1 Cor. 14.21. See ch. 33.19.

*{another tongue*} For, *a strange tongue*: so *other tongues*, for, *strange tongues*, Act. 2.4. 1 Cor. 14.21.

**V. 12.** *{To whom he said, This is the rest, wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing, yet they would not hear*} Or, *Because when he said unto them, This is the rest,—yet they would not hear*; or, *they would not hear*: *He said,—and they would not hear*; that is, *when he said—they would not hear*; as, Prov. 1.24. *I called and ye refused*; that is, *Ye refused, when I called*. See ch. 50.2. ver. 18. The words then, thus read; the prophet proceeds to show what should betide them; for this their brutish stupidity, and willful obstinacy, in refusing to hearken to God's gracious admonitions; and slighting his wholesome instructions, to their own confusion.

*{To whom he said*} Heb. *which he said unto them*: but the relative is oft used for the causative; as 1 King. 15.13. and so here, *Because he said to them*.

*{he said*} God, by his prophets, ch. 7.4. & 30.15.

*{This is the rest*} The only means, whereby rest and quietness may be either procured, or preserved, to wit, by hearkening to God's prophets, following the directions of his word, and relying upon him, and keeping close to him, 2 Chr. 14.2–7. & 15.4–19. & 16.7–9. Jer. 6.16. Mat. 11.28,29.

*{wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest*} According to this reading there should be a defect of the relative; Psal. 109.19. that may procure rest for those, that are tired out with grievous pressures, and calamities of the times. But the form of the verb, admits not this reading. And others, therefore, more rightly render the words, with supply of the relative, as spoken in way of admonition, or exhortation, *cause the weary to rest*; Take some course, that your poor afflicted, whether country or countrymen, rather, may have some ease of, and rest from, these grievous scourges, wherewith they have been so much wearied.

*{the weary*} To wit, people: a defect of the substantive; as chap. 40.19. & 50.4. or, as some, *the weary land*: but then it should be feminine; as ch. 32.2. whereas, it is masculine.

*{the refreshing*} The word is for signification, the same, in effect with the former, rendered *rest* also, Jer. 6.16. where found in another form: but in this, here, the more fitly to comply in sound with the former; *ease*, and *rest*; *refreshing*, not so properly, but as that is an effect of it. See ch. 30.15.

*{they would not hear*} It was their willful obstinacy, as well as their blockish stupidity, both arising from their sensuality, that hindered God's word from producing any good effect with them, Psal. 81.11. & 82.5. Jer. 6.16. & 44.16. Zach. 7.11. Luk. 8.14. & 21.34.

**V. 13.** *{But the word of God was unto them, precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, and there a little: that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken*} Heb. *And the word of God was*, or, *shall be*: which some render, as here, *But the word of God was*, *And*, for, *But*; as ch. 29.13. Some, *Though the word of God, were*: *And*, for, *Though*, as ch. 49.5. Though the word were in so plain, and familiar a way delivered unto them; as before, ver. 10. Howbeit, some others read, and render it, as in way of commination, *Therefore the word of God shall be unto you*; as, Amos 5.27. as if God threatened to punish their former stupidity, and obstinacy, with further blindness, as ch. 6.9,10. & 16. & 29.10–12.

*{that they might go, and fall backward, &c.*} This some refer to the judgment here denounced, as a dismal effect of it, by God therein intended; as chap. 6.10. Others refer it to their obstinacy, mentioned ver. 12. as an effect thereof, though not intended by them, yet flowing necessarily from it. Of which manner of speech, see on chap. 3.8. & Jer. 7.18. and of the words, chap. 8.15. & 42.22.

*{go, and fall backward*} Heb. *go, and stumble backward*: that is, *stumble*, and *fall backward as they go*. A defective speech: the like whereunto, see chap. 1.4. and the supply, Psal. 27.1. ch. 8.15. Jer. 46.6. & 50.32.

**V. 14.** *{Wherefore hear the word of the Lord, ye scornful men, that rule this people, which is at Jerusalem*} The word of commination seems hence to begin; directed unto the rulers, such of them as Shebna was, of whom see ch. 22.15. that scorned, and scoffed at the menaces of God's prophets, as supposing themselves to be sufficiently secured against all occurrents whatsoever, ver. 15. ch. 5.19. 2 Chr. 36.16. Jer. 5.12,13.

*{hear the word of the Lord*} What, not I, but he, by me, says to you especially; as ch. 1.10.

*{scornful men*} Heb. *men of scorn*; as Prov. 29.8. not scorned, but scorning, *scornful*. Such as Solomon there says, *bring a city*, or state, *into a snare*. A thing glanced at, vers. 13. though, in this place, it may seem to imply more specially, (that which yet with scornfulness is commonly joined) matter of mockage, and may peradventure, therefore, more fitly be rendered here, *men of mockage*, or, *mockers*; as 2 Pet. 2.3. for that seems the crime, here, specially charged upon them, vers. 15. and which they are advised to leave, ver. 22.

*{that rule this people*} Heb. *the rulers of this people*, or, *domineerers*, over them; as the word and phrase is used, ch. 52.5. that abuse the power you have, in regard of your places, to domineer, and lord it over my people, at your pleasure, chapter 26.13. 1 Pet. 5.3.

**V. 15.** *{Because ye have said, we have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement*} Because you deem yourselves as safe and secure, as if death and you were entered into a solemn league, either with other. And whatsoever, therefore, might betide the state, you were sure to escape.

*{ye have said*} Or, *ye say*. That is, think with yourselves, make account so; as Psal. 14.1. & 94.7. And yet it is not unlikely, that some such scoffing terms, as these, they had sometime also in their mouths; as we find somewhat the like in some Latin comics. See ch. 22.13.

*{made a covenant*} Heb. *cut a covenant*; as chap. 55.3. The ground of which form is taken, either from the nature and manner of solemn covenants, in which the conditions, whereupon the covenant is made, are wont to be precisely and exactly on either side determined, and as it were cut out; the like whereunto, see vers. 22. ch. 10.22,23. Dan. 9.24. Or, from certain rites, that were commonly used at the solemn contracting of such leagues and agreement, both among the people of God, and other nations. Of which, see Gen. 15.9,10. Psal. 50.5. and on Jer. 34.18.

*{with death*} That is, say some, with Sennacherib, the deadly enemy to our state, whom we mean to comply with. But this pulls out the pith of the prophet's speech, whose words show, that death itself is intended, which the grave follows, as an attendant on it, Hos. 13.14. Rev. 6.8.

*{with hell*} Or, *the grave*. See chap. 14.15.

*{are we at agreement*} Heb. *we have made provision*; as Exod. 18.21. *provide able men*. And so the word following, verse 18. is to be expounded, which being another form, from the same root, shows this to be a noun: and of the same signification, in effect with the former. The Jewish critics are much are much divided about it, and seem to look any way, rather than to the right reason of the term. The Chaldee renders it *peace*; and the reason thereof, says one of them, is, because when men make peace, they meet together, and look one another in the face, Gen. 32.10. 2 Sam. 14.32. 1 King. 20.33. like *light to light*; or, *sight to sight*, in Solomon's temple, 1 King. 7.4,5. And so they do also, when they meet to fight, 2 Chro. 25.17,21. Another would have it a participle, and to signify, *a Seer* or *watchman*; as if they should say, We have set one to watch death, well enough, from surprising of us; as Ezek. 33.2–5. But it is not *death* that is mentioned in this branch, but the *grave*. Another would have it, We have set *a bound*, or, *a limit* unto death, or the grave, that it shall not pass, to come so near to us, as to fasten upon us. Deriving it from a word, used, Ps. 107.20. which, in Chaldee, commonly bears that sense. Another, lastly, to let the rest pass, *We have made a complication*, that is, a confederacy; from a word signifying to be enwrapped, or entangled, as the strings of a root, Job 8.17. or the boughs of a tree, Dan. 4.11. or, branched horns of a beast, Dan. 8.5. But of this sense of the word, in any one of these places, can hardly any good proof be made. And I stick therefore to what was given at first.

*{when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us*} Or, *though the scourge*, or, *the bore, of a surrounding flood*, or, *river, pass through* the land, *it shall not come at us*. Though these things, that the prophets prate so much of, scourges, and land-floods, and we know not what storms, and inundations, and deluges, should come and overflow the whole land; yet they shall not touch us: we shall, for all that, be safe; we have shelter sufficient enough at hand, to secure us.

*{when*} Or, *though*, as chap. 12.1. Psal. 23.4. For they little thought in likelihood, that ever they would come.

*{the overflowing scourge*} The word here used, does commonly, signify *a whip*, or *a scourge*, Pro. 26.3. Nah. 3.2. howbeit, some of the Jewish critics, in regard of the term of *inundation* annexed to it, understand by it here, the *shock*, or *bore*, or fierce stream of a river overflowing his banks, running along through the whole level, as coming of a word, that signifies *to run*, or *pass speedily*, through a place, 2 Sam. 24.2. Job 1.7. Jer. 5.1. but it is not unlikely, that the prophet did of purpose use the word *scourge* here, though to express that which they would have it here to import; in relating the words of those scoffing mates, that in mockery used these terms, because they heard the prophets, in their menaces, making mention of an *inundation*, and a *scourge*, chap. 8.7,8. & 10.22,26. and it may therefore be well rendered, *the scourge of an overflowing*, or *surrounding* river, or flood; a defect of the subject: as *fading*, for *a fading* plant, v. 4. so *overflowing*, for an *overflowing* flood: as it is supplied, and expressed, ch. 30.28. & 66.12. Jer. 47.20. 2 Chr. 32.4. or, *an overflowing* storm: as the supply is, Ezek. 13.11,13. & 38.22. which comes home much to one: such storms of rain commonly causing also great land-floods, and the term is common to either, see chap. 25.4. beside that mention is made of *a storm* also, ver. 17.

*{pass through*} To wit the land. So Dan. 11.10,40.

*{it shall not come unto us*} Heb. *come us*, for *come at us*, the particle omitted, as Ps. 36.11. supplied Psal. 91.20.

*{for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves*} The ground of this their security, from whence they presumed and promised to themselves undoubted safety: a *lie*, (so it is in the Hebrew) and *falsehood*, both in effect the same, whereby some understand their idols, so termed, chap. 44.20. Jer. 10.14. Rom. 1.25. wherein many of them much confided, chap. 1.31. & 17.8. Others, their treachery, and dissembling, in compliance with the adverse party, whereby they made account to save themselves, whatsoever became of others. Others, their crafty shifts, and wily devices, which may well include the former, ch. 29.15,16. Others lastly (which is most likely), their strength raised, and wealth gotten by fraudulent and deceitful courses, Psal. 52.7. & 62.9,10. ch. 30.12. *lies* and *falsehood* for goods thereby gotten: as *the robbery*, and *the oppression*, or *fraud*, for the thing gotten by *robbery*, *oppression*, or *fraud*, Lev. 6.4. So, *the mammon of iniquity*, Luke 16.11.

*{refuge*} See chap. 25.4. Zeph. 1.9.

*{we have hid ourselves*} Or, *are we hid*; See ver. 17.

**V. 16.** *{Therefore thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner-stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste*} Their deep security amidst their sensuality, and willful obstinacy, and vain confidence of safety, notwithstanding God's menaces by his prophets, which they scoffed at, was before. Now God, by the prophet, proceeding to relate what a round and sharp course he meant to take with them for these evils, does first premise, for the stay of the minds of his faithful ones, amidst the ensuing distractions and disturbances of the times, what provision he had made for their security and indemnity, to wit, such a rock, for them, by faith to rest on, as should stay by them, stay them up, and support them, amidst all those storms that should threaten the state, and sweep away those unsure and fickle stays, that those profane wretches, so much, but most fondly relied on.

*{Behold*} See chap. 7.14. and verse 2.

*{I lay for a foundation*} Heb. *I am founding*, or, *I have founded*; as chap. 14.32. *the Lord hath founded Zion*, for it seems, that in this form, the participle is sometime the same with the first of the verb; as in that of Solomon, Eccles. 4.2. *I praised the dead*: and then we need not, either with some of the Jewish critics, and some of ours, following them, make it a noun, reading the words, *I the founder*; or, with other of them, make a further needless supply, rendering them, *I am he that hath founded*: or lastly, it may be an interchange of the person, the third for the first: as the like is deemed to be, chap. 29.14. in those words, *I add*. But however we read or render them, the meaning is apparent, that God beforehand had laid a sure ground for the faithful to build and rest themselves upon, in those tumultuous and troublesome times.

*{in Zion*} In Jerusalem, a type of the church, then to come, and the principal seat, both of God's people, and of his service, at that present, Psalm 65.1. & 76.2. chap. 2.2.

*{a stone*} A foundation stone, that is, Ezekias, say some of the Jewish doctors; and a type of this stone, it is granted, he might be: but other of them better, the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the only true and sure foundation stone, Rom. 9.33. & 10.11. 1 Cor. 3.11. Eph. 2.20. 1 Pet. 2.6,8. laid in God's purpose from all eternity, 1 Pet. 1.20. and for efficacy the same, to all the faithful in all ages, *yesterday, at this day, and for ever*, chap. 26.4. Mat. 16.18. Heb. 13.8. opposed here to the fickle stays, and vain fastnesses of wicked worldlings: as Prov. 18.10,11.

*{a tried stone*} Heb. *a stone of trial*; or, *of proof*, rather; as we use to say, *armor of proof*, and as *a sword of proof*, Ezek. 21.13. for that it seems to relate to, there, from v. 9. that is, as some, *a touchstone*; whereby men may, and shall be tried, whether sound and sincere, or no, ch. 8.14,15. Mat. 11.6. & 21.44,45. Luk. 2.34,35. Rom. 9.33. 1 Pet. 2.7,8. or rather a stone thoroughly tried and approved of, *a choice stone*, 1 Pet. 2.4,6. Yet some of the Rabbines would have it to import, *a stone of munition*, or *defense*; because it is very near to a term that signifies a *fort*, or *tower*; properly *a sentinel*, or *watchtower*, chap. 23.13. & 32.14. There is a place called (with very small difference from the word here used) *the stone of Bohan*, Josh. 15.6. which might peradventure here be alluded unto.

*{a precious corner-stone*} Heb. *a stone of the corner of preciousness*; *a corner*, for *a corner-stone*; for thence, the chief heads in a state are termed; as resembling *corner-stones*, *corners*, Judg. 20.2. 1 Sam. 14.38. the choicest and firmest stones, are made choice of for corner-stones, as well for the surer knitting of the walls together, as for the better bearing up, and for the beauty also, (Psal. 144.12.) of the building: in both which regards, the name of a corner-stone suits well to Christ, Psal. 116.21. Mat. 21.42. Act. 4.11. since, that he not only bears up the entire structure of his church, Mat. 16.18. 1 Cor. 3.11. Ephes. 2.20. but also joins and unites most closely and firmly together, both the two main walls of Jew and Gentile, and each living stone also, in either wall, one to another, Ephe. 2.14–22. & 4.15,16. 1 Pet. 2.4,5. and again, *a stone of preciousness*, for *most precious*, 1 Pet. 2.4,6. See chap. 54.11.

*{a sure foundation*} Heb. *a foundation founded*: that is, a firm and sure, a well-grounded foundation: as *a founded staff*, ch. 30.32. ch. 26.4. Matth. 7.24,25. Luk. 6.48.

*{he that believeth shall not make haste*} So the word properly signifies, Jud. 20.37. Now because men being out of their way, are wont to run to and fro, hastily and unadvisedly, this way, and that way; some therefore render it, *he shall not go astray*. But I suppose rather, it respects the manner of those, that being in danger, without surety, or certainty of any means, whereby to escape, try this way, and that way, but keep not constant to any; or despairing of safety, if they stay by it, make all the haste they can to quit the place they are in at present, though as uncertain of safety elsewhere, Psal. 55.7,8. Act. 27.30. or that expecting helps from abroad, though having assurance given of their timely approach, yet refuse to stay their coming, and out distrust of relief, are ready to yield upon any, the basest terms. The meaning then is, that those, who by faith rest themselves upon this rock, upon God in Christ, and his powerful protection, shall not in their straits and distresses, as men at their wit's end, run backward and forward, seeking by sinister courses, and any base shifts, to rid themselves out of danger, as the faithless Jews frequently did, refusing to rely upon God, chap. 30.1,5,15. & 31.1. Jer. 2.18,36. Hos. 5.13. & 7.11. & 12.1. but they shall with assurance of a good and timely issue, depend upon God, and with patience, quietly expect the performance of his gracious promises, as well for a seasonable deliverance, as for a powerful and providential support, until the time thereof do come, Psal. 62.1,2. & 112.7,8. & 121.1,2. 2 Chr. 14.11. & 16.8. & 20.12. ch. 8.17. & 10.20. & 30.18. Jer. 17.7. and it is not amiss observed by some of the Jewish doctors, that he says, the rather, *he shall not make haste*, because the prophecies and promises concerning either the exhibition of the Messiah then expected, or the deliverances of the faithful, were not presently effected; and God might seem, therefore, in man's fleshly conceit, to be slow and slack in his performances; against which temptation, they were to arm themselves with faith and patience, Hab. 2.3,4. Luk. 21.19. Heb. 10.36,37. Now what the prophet says, *he shall not make haste*, the apostle seems to render, *he shall not be abashed or confounded*, Rom. 9.33. Whence, some suppose, some alteration to be in the original, from what anciently it was. But, besides what might be, and is commonly answered, that the apostle oft, in citing Scripture, regards not the words but the matter; and herein both, well agree; (since that it is the manner of men, that are in such confusion, to be heady and hasty) the apostle, as he joins in the former part of that quotation, two places of this prophet together, chap. 8.14. & 28.16. so in the latter part, likewise, he might well have an eye to two other, this, and that, chap. 49.23. where it is said, *They that wait on me, shall not be confounded*, or *abashed*; a place parallel to this. The Chaldee here renders it, *He that believeth these things, shall not tremble*; or *shall not be moved, when trouble cometh*: rightly interpreting, says the learned annotator, the term here used, by that of *moving*. For so, says he, the Ethiopic word signifies in the active form, *to move*, Mat. 27.39. in the passive, *to be moved*, Mat. 11.6. The sense is good and sound, doubtless, but that proves not this to be the genuine notion of the Hebrew term here used, and that in an active form, though a neuter or standing sense.

**V. 17.** *{Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet*} Or, *And I will set out judgment by line, and justice by plummet*. Having provided sufficiently for my faithful and loyal ones security, I will proceed to an exact and precise way of justice, against these sensual, secure, and scornful wretches, and this is laid down by a metaphor, taken from the practice of masons and carpenters, who when they will have a thing done exactly and exquisitely, are wont to do it by line and level, so Amos 7.8. In which manner of speaking, may two things be intimated: First, a strict and severe proceeding against this brutish, profane, and malignant party, chap. 9.27. & 27.11. and secondly, a wary and cautelous carriage of this sad business, that though it fall heavy upon them; yet it does not so far extend itself, as to hurt, or endamage any of those whom he shall be pleased to exempt; as workmen, to this end, draw the line over timber to be squared, or stone to be hewed, that in cutting, they may keep precisely to it, and not cut an hair's breadth beyond it.

*{Judgment I will lay*} Heb. *set judgment*, for those scorners, v. 14. so ch. 34.5.

*{to the line*} Or, *by line*: as chap. 34.17. For, as for the particle here used, the prophet seems to have retained it, in reference to what was before, ver. 10. and we find it also so used, Job 35.2. chap. 32.1. *by line* here, as *by judgment* there: that is, according thereunto; so the rather it would be read, to remove an ambiguity, that it be not understood of some strict examination of the judgment and righteousness of others: the line is here meant, that workmen in building make use of, Job 38.5. chap. 44.13.

*{righteousness*} Or, *justice*: for that is the term we use most in matter of judicature: as when we say, *do a man justice*, and *do justice upon a man*.

*{to the plummet*} Or, *by level*, as before: the word signifies the weight that hangs at the line's end, to keep it straight and even, 2 King. 21.13. *judgment* and *justice* by *line* and *level*: nor neither *judgment* without *justice*, nor *justice* without *judgment*: as neither any use of the *line* in such case, without the *level*; no more than of the *level*, without the *line*: so that the meaning is, both jointly, by both; though by a rhetorical amplification, very familiar with this prophet, expressed by way of distribution: of which manner of speech, see on ch. 5.13. & 22.6.

*{and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place*} The effect of this strict proceeding of God with them; to wit, the utter abandoning of all their vain confidences.

*{the hail*} A storm of hail, Ezek. 13.11–15. See ver. 2.

*{sweep away*} As with a *besom*: the like whereunto, see 1 King. 14.10. ch. 14.24. Or, as others, *shovel away*, as with a shovel: and others again, *thrust out*, as with a fork: thus several expositors, according to their several conceits, concerning the signification of a word from this root, nowhere else found, deduced; whereof see on Jer. 52.18. But the forementioned learned annotator renders it, *shall burn up*, because the word in the Ethiopic tongue, signifies *to burn*, Mat. 3.12. & 13.40. and hail, besides that it has a burning or parching quality, is oft, accompanied, in storms, with fire, Exod. 9.24. Psal. 18.13.

*{the refuge of lies*} Heb. *of a lie*; as ver. 15. but termed so, here, not only in regard of the ground of it, as there; but in regard of the effect of it, *a lying refuge*: as if he should say, *Your refuge of lies shall prove a lying refuge*: a refuge that shall not perform what it promised, and what you presumed of it: it shall fail you then, when it should stand you in stead. So Jer. 7.4. & 27.15.

*{the waters*} The land-flood, ver. 15.

*{overflow the hiding place*} Shall surround your covert: of which, ver. 15. see ch. 16.4. & 32.2. a defect of the pronoun: as ch. 13.22. God's judgments shall discover the vanity of your shifts, and ferret you out of all your hiding holes, Jer. 7.21. & 16.16. Ezek. 7.19. & 17.11,14. and all your deep designs, and cunning projects, shall be as a shed of thatch built on the sand, that a shower of hail shall beat down, and the stream of the land-flood, sweep away with it, Mat. 7.27.

**V. 18.** *{And your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand*} You shall be destroyed, notwithstanding all the courses, whereby you suppose yourselves sufficiently secured against death.

*{Your covenant with death*} Of which, ver. 15.

*{disannulled*} Heb. *expiated*. See chap. 27.9. or, as some, *daubed over*; because the word is so used, Gen. 6.14. it shall be clean wiped away, as a writing blotted out, and a deed defaced and canceled; for so it is also, when sins are expiated with God, chap. 43.25. Col. 2.14.

*{agreement*} Heb. *vision*: as chap. 21.2. & 29.11. here rather, *provision*: as the verb it comes of, sometime signifies, *to provide*, Exod. 18.21. See ver. 15. the *security*, as we use the word, whereby you make account, that you have made *provision* sufficient, to secure yourselves from destruction.

*{with hell*} Or, *the grave*: as ver. 15.

*{shall not stand*} Shall be of no force to secure you: So chap. 7.7.

*{when the overflowing scourge shall pass through*} Or, *for the scourge of the overflowing* storm, or, flood, *shall pass through*, or, *over the land*, to wit, of Judah, chap. 8.7,8. and so did Sennacherib with his forces, ch. 36.1. see ver. 15.

*{then shall ye be trodden down by it*} Heb. *and ye shall be to it for a treading down*: as ch. 5.5. the scourge, or storm, that you now scoff at, and the bore of the flood, that you now make but a jest of, shall bear you down before it, with all your supports, and shall tread you down like dirt: see ch. 10.6. ver. 3. The words, entirely, may thus be rendered; *For the scourge of the surrounding* flood, or storm, *shall pass through the land, and ye shall be trodden down by it*: or, *For when the scourge shall pass through ye shall be trodden down by it*; as ver. 11.

**V. 19.** *{From the time that it goeth forth, it shall take you*} Heb. *From its passing through* (as Ezek. 5.17.) *it shall take you*: as 1 Sam. 18.30. *from their going forth*: that is, *when they went forth*: so here, *when it passeth through*; or, *As it passeth over, it shall take you*: it shall surprise you: as Ezek. 23.25. though you say, it shall not come at you, ver. 15. or, *it shall take you away*: it shall carry you away with it; as the word is used, 1 King. 14.26. Ezek. 22.25.

*{for morning by morning, shall it pass over, by day and by night*} Heb. *by morning, by morning*; as ch. 50.4. that is, as some interpreters, *very early in the morning*: as if he should say, it shall be upon you, ere you are up, it shall surprise you in your deepest security, when you least of all dream of it, as you lie sleeping in your beds: or, *morning after morning*; every morning, in a constant and continued course, it shall run over the land, again and again, day after day; and it shall pursue you incessantly, without intermission: it shall not suffer you to rest, day or night, Rev. 14.11. So the phrase is taken, Ezek. 46.13,14,15. and so, *by day, by day*, for constantly, continually; every day, Ps. 68.19. & 71.15. It shall break in with that violence, that nothing shall be able to stand before it; and it shall pass over so oft, that there shall be no escape from it. The Hebrew doctors, some of them, expound it, of Sennacherib's army marching night and day (see Jer. 6.5.) though not discovered until the morning, in which they entered upon Judea, ch. 10.28–31. but this is, as many other, one of their groundless surmises.

*{and it shall be a vexation, only to understand the report*} These words are diversely understood of interpreters: for some, by the word *report*, conceive to be meant, the wholesome doctrines, and serious admonitions, delivered by God's prophets to this people, as the word is taken chap. 53.1. and they render the words; *and it shall come to pass, that the commotion, or vexation, at least, shall make them to understand the word*, or, *the doctrine*, to wit, now delivered: they shall then, at least, to their woe and smart, understand and believe, by what they undergo, and endure, the truth of that, which they will not now apprehend: and this suits well with what went before, v. 9. But others, and so most of the Jewish commenters, by *report*, understand the fame and rumor of the enemy's approach: as chap. 37.7. Jer. 10.22. which alone should make them to tremble and quake for fear: see Ezek. 21.7. Hab. 3.16. and they render the text, *it shall be a quaking only*, or, *it shall make them quake, only, to hear the report of it*: either the report, alone, shall cast them into a fit of trembling; or, the report of it shall affright them only, but no way conduce to procure any means of escape; and the latter of these, do the Hebrew pauses seem to abet.

*{vexation*} So is the verb rendered, Hab. 2.7. *that shall vex thee*. But in other places, otherwise; as Est. 5.9. where it is said of Mordecai, that *he stood* bolt-upright, and *did not move*, or *stir*, to Haman; and Eccl. 12.3. where *the keepers of the house*, that is, the hands, or arms, as most conceive it, are said *to tremble*, or *shake*, in old age: from whence divers render the word, here, nowhere else found in this form, *a trembling*, or, *a quaking*; and some other, *a commotion*; understanding it of that combustion and confusion that should then be in the land. Yet some other, in regard that another word, in sound very near it, is constantly used for *a removal*, Deut. 28.25. 2 Chr. 29.8. Jer. 15.4. & 24.9. & 29.18. & 34.17. Ezek. 23.46. supposing this by transposition of a letter only, to be the same with that, render it indeed, *a commotion*, but understand thereby, *an amotion* rather, a deportation, or removal of them, by captivity, into Babylon. But one of the most curious Jewish critics, is of the mind, that those two words come from several roots. However it be, for the peculiar and proper notion of the word, certain it is: that both the terror that the rumor of the enemy's approach should strike into them, and his presence much more, together with the dismal effects of it, as well the commotions in it, as the removal of them out of it, would exceedingly dismay, and seal up unto them the truth of the things, which they formerly made so light of, Job 33.14. Ezek. 6.10.

**V. 20.** *{For the bed is short, that a man cannot stretch himself on it; and the covering is narrower, than that he can wrap himself in it*} Or, *For the bedstock is so short, that one cannot stretch out himself on it, and the coverlet too strait for one to wrap himself in*. The words seem to contain a proverbial kind of speech; the meaning whereof is that they should be in such straits and distresses, as all their wiles and shifts should not be able either to secure, or succor them in. A similitude borrowed from one that lies in little ease, by reason of the shortness of the bedstock he lies on, and with as little warmth, in regard of the scantness of the bedclothes that should cover him. And the prophet might, peradventure, have some glance at their beds, on which they were wont to lie strutting at pleasure, with their rich bed-furniture hanging down on either side at large. See Amos 6.4. Prov. 7.16. and the like allusion, ch. 14.11. They seem too strait, that would restrain it to Jerusalem; that before being as a large bed; whereon men might lie and stretch themselves at pleasure, should now be cut short, and straitened in her former liberty and plenty, ch. 29.2,3. and those too nice, that would have this passage meant of their affliction by night; as the next, of what, by day, they were to endure: Those too, wide from the prophet's purpose, that would have it to intimate, the small number of those that should be exempted from destruction; as if the covert of God's protection were said to be narrowed, and to reach no further than the city of Jerusalem only: and those no less, that would have it import a reclaiming of them from their idols, that they committed whoredom with: as implying that though the marriage-bed were large enough to hold man and wife; yet it was too strait, to take in an adulterer with them. See ch. 57.7,8.

*{the bed*} Or, *bedstock*, or whatsoever is laid under one to lie, and take rest on: as Ps. 139.8. alluded unto, Job 17.14. ch. 14.11. yet the word here used, is nowhere else found.

*{is short that a man cannot stretch himself on it*} Heb. *is short from stretching out one's self*, that is, *is so short, that one cannot stretch out himself on it*, or *in it*: Of the phrase, see on ch. 23.1. a defect of the pronoun, as ch. 26.13. for they seem not sufficiently to express the force, or observe aright the use of the word, that render the text, *the bedding is too short to hang over*: the word is nowhere else found, but one not much unlike it in the same notion with it, Amos 6.4,7.

*{the covering*} Of which see ch. 30.1. here in way of metaphor, or similitude; *the coverlet*, or such bedclothes, as are cast over a man to cover him, or to wrap himself in, for warmth, while he takes his rest, Exod. 22.27. 1 Sam. 18.13.

*{narrower than that he can wrap himself in it*} Heb. *is narrow in one's gathering up himself*: that is, when a man, because he cannot lie at full length, for the shortness of his bed, would fain gather up his body, that he might lie at more ease, the bedclothes prove too scanty then to cover him, and to afford him any shelter; they shall have nothing to accommodate them, or relieve them, either under them, or over them, from above, or from beneath. See ch. 24.17,18.

**V. 21.** *{For the Lord shall rise up, as in mount Perazim*} God shall come suddenly, and fiercely in upon them, as he did sometime upon their enemies; and deal with them, in another manner, than he is wont to do with his people.

*{rise up*} Or, *stand up*: he will rise, and stand up then, who now seems to sit still, and you deem will so ever do, Zeph. 1.12. See chap. 5.19.

*{as in mount Perazim*} Heb. *according to mount Perazim*: as he then did, when he there discomfited, and dispersed the Philistines' forces before David, whereof the place had its name, 2 Sam. 5.20. 1 Chr. 14.16. See the like phrase, ch. 10.26. & 13.19.

*{he shall be wroth, as in the valley of Gibeon*} *Be wroth*; as Prov. 29.9. or, *raise himself*: as cap. 14.9. thus, the rather, because it suits fitly with the former: *as in the valley of Gibeon*, Heb. *according to the valley of Gibeon*, as before: this some refer to the story of the discomfiture of the Amorites before Joshua, Josh. 10.10. where it is further related, that in the descent from thence to Bethoron, God slew many of them with hailstones from heaven, ver. 11. which sorts well with the storm of hail mentioned here, ver. 17. But others rather deem, that one, and the same story, is in either branch, after our prophet's usual manner, respected. For the same story that relates that discomfiture, and dispersion of the Philistines at mount Perazim, withal tells us; that upon the Philistines recollecting of themselves again, David, by God's direction, upon a sign given him, of God's setting out against them, set the second time upon them, put them to flight, and pursued them from Gibeon to Gezer, 2 Sam. 5.25. 1 Chr. 14.16. Howbeit, the prophet might have an eye to either.

*{that he may do his work, his strange work, and bring to pass his act, his strange act*} Heb. *to do his deed, his strange deed; and to work his work, his foreign work*: that is, to effect this heavy doom, and to inflict this dismal judgment, upon the main body of his own people grown now to such an height of extreme impiety and profaneness, ch. 10.6. called here, *a strange act*, and *a foreign work*: either because admirable and wonderful; as ch. 29.14. or, because unusual and dreadful; as Prov. 23.33. or, because *strange* with God, as being contrary to his disposition, of himself, inclining rather to mercy, than to wrath, ch. 27.4. Lam. 3.33. Ezek. 33.11. or *strange* to him, in regard of his people, fighting against those, ch. 29.2,3. Jer. 21.4,5. & 33.5. whom he was wont to protect, ch. 37.35. and to fight for, as at the times pointed to, in the words next before-going; and carrying himself as *a stranger*, Jer. 14.8. yea, as *an enemy*, Jer. 30.14. toward those, whom he had formerly been as tender of, as any the most affectionate parent, father, or mother is, or can be, of their dearest darling, Deut. 8.5. & 32.10,11. Psal. 103.13. ch. 49.14.

**V. 22.** *{Now therefore be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong*} The prophet here concludes his foregoing denunciations, with a serious admonition to those mockers and scoffers at the menaces of God's prophets, ver. 13,14. advising them to forbear, and give over, this their profane and irreligious practice; lest God tie them up the straiter for it, and lay the heavier things upon them, Lev. 26.23,24.

*{bands be made strong*} *Bands*, for afflictions and straits, Psal. 66.11. & 73.4. & 116.16. an allusion to such *bands*, as prisoners, and captives, are wont to be bound with, ch. 52.3. Jer. 30.8. the bands that God binds them with, will be too strong for them to break; and the more they now slight them, the straiter and stronger they are like to prove. See Jer. 28.10,11,13. though some suppose an allusion to those *bands*, that as sheaves of corn, so bundles of other trash also are wont to be bound up with, to make fuel of, or matter for the fire, Mat. 13.30. to which purpose, also, they expound somewhat, v. 26. but the prophet seems not to have arrived at that similitude from husbandry, as yet.

*{for I have heard from the Lord God of Hosts, a consumption even determined upon the whole earth*} I can assure you from God, that he is fully resolved, without further delay, to make an utter riddance of such of you, as so continue, through the whole land. See ch. 10.22,23.

**V. 23.** *{Give ye ear, and hear my voice; hearken, and hear my speech*} Or, *Attend, and hear, what I say*. Being to give them further assurance, that God would not always be menacing; but would at length inflict; and withal, to declare the equity and wisdom of God, in the manner of his proceedings, by an argument taken, from the usual practice of husbandmen, in the tilling of their ground, and in the disposing of their grain: he does by those terms thus reiterated, labor to rouse and stir them up, to a more serious consideration of what he was to deliver to them. So v. 14. See the like, ch. 32.9. Now the husbandman's prudent, and provident practice, and discreet carriage of his business, is observed and described here, 1. In the preparing of his ground, for receipt of seed, v. 24. 2. In the manner of casting in his seed, ver. 25. 3. In the course he takes for the beating out of his grain, ver. 27,28.

**V. 24.** *{Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?*} Or, *Will the plowman be all day* (that is, continually, as Psal. 44.22.) *plowing, or opening, and harrowing his land?* the disjunctive is wanting; as chap. 17.6. Psal. 94.16. The verb is, in a notion, of a continued act, or employment, as Joh. 2.20. *Forty and six years hath this Temple been built*; that is, so long has it been in building: and the term of continuance, belongs, as well to the latter branch, as to the former; as Ps. 44.15. ch. 58.13. The meaning is, as the husbandman is not always about any one work, but has his several times and seasons, for his several employments: he is not always plowing, or harrowing his ground; but when he has sufficiently opened it, and broken the clods, and leveled the surface of it, he casts in his seed: and when the crop is come to maturity, he thrusts in the sickle, and cuts down the corn, and after threshes out the grain; and has his time, as well for these, as for those foregoing employments: so the Lord has likewise his times and seasons, for his several works and dispensations, as well of judgment, as of mercy; and will not therefore always be admonishing, and menacing, by the ministry of his messengers, but will at length, proceed to execution, and make good his menaces upon those that continue obstinate, and slight the warnings that now are given them, Gen. 6.3. Ezek. 12.28. that which before the prophet warned them of, v. 22. implying, as some conceive also, in those words, that God's harvest time was now at hand, ch. 17.5. Ezek. 7.10,11. Joel 3.13. Rev. 14.13.

*{break the clods*} Whether by rake, or mallet, or harrow, for the word has no special notation, that may restrain it to any one particular. It came after plowing, Hos. 10.11. and was, it seems, done ordinarily with some instrument, not unlike our *harrow* drawn over the land, first plowed, by some beast, Job 39.10. Thence *a field* seems to have had its name in Hebrew, as properly signifying such an one, as is used for tillage, Jerem. 26.18. Micha 3.12.

**V. 25.** *{When he hath made plain the face thereof, doth he not cast abroad the fitches, and scatter the cumin, and cast in the principal wheat, and the appointed barley, and the rye in their place?*} He does not plow, and harrow his ground to no purpose; or spend his whole time, and tire out himself, in an endless course, about that one employment, or sit down and proceed no further, when he has so done; but when he has fitted his ground for the receipt of his seed, he then commits it to the ground, disposing of each sort of grain, in his several quarter, according to the nature of the seed, and the soil. That which the prophet illustrates, by a particular recension of some of the special sorts of grain, and seed, then most in use. Now if it be demanded, how this fits the prophet's purpose, to wit, to intimate that God will not be always admonishing and menacing; but will, at length, proceed to execution, since that, howsoever, the breaking up of the ground, and the breaking of the clods, may in the spiritual husbandry, 1 Cor. 3.9. not unfitly resemble the pains, that the spiritual husbandman, 2 Tim. 2.6. the minister of God, takes about the fitting of men's souls, for the receipt of the spiritual seed, Luk. 5.8,11. of God's word and grace, Jer. 4.4. Hos. 10.12,13. And that *threshing*, be in Scripture, an ordinary emblem of afflictions, and sufferings; Of which see chap. 25.10. Yet *the sowing of the seed*, may seem not so fit to represent God's execution of judgment; and is both in the places, above pointed to, and elsewhere also, commonly used another way. To this it may be answered, First, that the same similitude, is in Scripture, many times, diversely, yea, contrarily, made use of. Of which, see on chap. 27.12. & 64.6. & 66.14. Secondly, that it is sufficient, that it holds in the general, to wit, that as the husbandman is not always about one work, but having dispatched that which he has in hand, proceeds unto that, that in his course of employment, is next to be done: so God having for some competent space of time, taken pains, by way of persuasion, and premonition, with his people, does, in the next place, proceed to that which in the course of his just, and most prudent dispensation is next; to the execution of judgment, with those that will take no warning, but refuse to be reclaimed, and reformed, by the former, 2 Chr. 36.15–17. Thirdly, the sowing of seed, is not altogether unfit to resemble the execution of God's judgment, partly, in the scattering of it upon the ground, Levit. 26.33. Deut. 28.64. chap. 24.1. partly, in the throwing of it into the ground, and for a time, as it were, burying it there, Ps. 26.5,6. Ezek. 37.11,12.

*{when*} Heb. *if*, as ch. 4.4. Judg. 21.21.

*{he hath made plain*} By breaking of the clods, that made it uneven and unequal. The word in this form, and thus applied, is nowhere else found.

*{the face*} Or, *surface of it*; as chap. 27.6. Eccl. 11.1.

*{cast abroad*} Or, *disperse*. A word, which I find not anywhere else used of *sowing*, save here: but of *dispersion*, by way of captivity, and discomfiture, very frequently, Deut. 4.27. Psal. 18.14. & 144.6. chap. 24.1. & 41.16. Jer. 18.17. Ezek. 36.19. and not without some special ground, therefore, in likelihood, made use of here.

*{fitches*} The Hebrew word, here used, does not signify *fitches*, or, *tares*, no more than the Greek word, so rendered, Mat. 13.25. And there is another word rendered *fitches*, Ezek. 4.9. but the seed of a plant, somewhat like to our *cockle*, called from the blackness of it, by the Greeks, Μελάνθιον, by the Latins, *Nigella*, and by some, *Gith*, Pliny lib. 29. c. 17.

*{scatter*} Nor do I find this word, used elsewhere of sowing, but of *sprinkling* blood, or water, for expiation, oft, Exod. 24.6. Levit. 1.5. Num. 19.20. Ezek. 36.25. and of *scattering* fire over the city, as a symbol of God's wrath to be poured forth upon it, Ezek. 10.2. It suits therefore well here; and it sorts well with *sowing*, in which men are wont to lay their seed on heaps, greater or less, but to scatter it so, that it may light in a convenient distance asunder; that which seems alluded to in another term, Prov. 11.24. & Psalm 112.9. as the apostle explains it, 2 Cor. 9.9,10.16. applied also to warlike, and wrathful dispersions, Psalm 89.10. Joel 3.2.

*{cumin*} A seed, it seems, in much use with them: as well as with us; though of meaner reckoning. See Mat. 23.23.

*{the principal wheat*} So the most; from a term that has a notion of *principality*, and *prevalency*, Judg. 9.22. Hos. 12.4. Whence *Sarah*, Gen. 17.15,16. and *Israel*, Gen. 32.28. And the word so taken, implies a greater care, that the husbandman has in procuring the choice, for seed especially, of this more noble grain, than about those other of less esteem. Howbeit, some read it, *the wheat in a principal place*, as making choice of his chief ground, for his principal grain. And so there is a defect of the particle *in*, as v. 7. and of the subject, as vers. 4. Others, *in measure*; as a word near it signifies, the same with our English, Levit. 19.39. Ezek. 4.11. And so it should intimate his discretion, in proportioning the quantity of his grain, to the ground that is to bear it.

*{the appointed barley*} Or, as some, *the marked barley*. That is, say they, set apart for seed in a sack, with a mark set upon it, for choice grain. But some other render it, *the barley in its appointed place*, or, *the place marked out for it*: as alluding to certain marks set up in the fields, to show how far such and such grain, or seed should be sowed. The defect of the subject, as before: and this the rather, because the word, *barley*, is in the Hebrew a feminine; whereas the participle, here used, is masculine: the word is nowhere else found in Scripture. But the Rabbines use it, for *to design*: and a word thence derived, for *rows*, whether ridges, or trenches, designed for receipt of seed.

*{the rye*} So it is rendered, Exod. 9.32. Howbeit, the plural masculine of it, is after the old Latin, by ours, rendered, *fitches*, Ezek. 4.9.

*{in their place*} Heb. *in*, or, *within, its bounds*. For the particle, *in*, is, as before, wanting, and the pronoun is singular, and seems to belong to this last, being masculine; because the word *seed*, or *grain*, is such: and because the word signifies *a bound*, or *border*, some of the Jewish commenters would have the meaning to be, as if it were said, He will sow his wheat in the principal part, or the midst of his field; but the rye in the verge, or the edges, and borders of it, neither so good, ofttime, nor so safe. But that seems not so well to suit with the context. The intention of the prophet seems to be, to show the husbandman's discretion, in sowing his seed, neither confounding, and mingling his seed, of several sorts and kinds, one with another, Deut. 22.9. nor casting them into the same ground; but assigning unto each sort and kind, a several place; and that such, as is suitable thereunto. Thereby implying, also, that God though after admonitions and menaces, he proceed to a further matter, unto execution of judgment; yet he does that also, with much discretion, according to the divers dispositions of those with whom he has to deal. Of which also, more after, ver. 27,28.

**V. 26.** *{For his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him*} In these words, thus read, should a reason be rendered how it comes to pass, that the husbandman carries himself so discreetly, and prudently, in these his affairs, to wit, because God has endued him with wisdom, and discretion so to do, Job 55.11. as implying, that God would much more do all things, so, himself, who had taught the husbandman so to do. And this, no doubt, is intended throughout the whole passage. But yet there is another reading, that seems more agreeable, both to the words of the text, and to the course of the context: for thus the words lie in order, and run word for word. *And he beateth it out, according to that course, that his God teacheth him*. According to which reading, the prophet here passes from the husbandman's discretion in disposing of his seed, after he has fitted the ground for it, unto his discretion in threshing, and beating it out; propounded in general terms in this verse; together with an intimation, how, and from whom he learned so to do, but more particularly declared, in his divers dealing, with divers sorts of grain and seed, in regard of the divers nature, and quality of them, v. 27,28. And this exposition I find approved, and confirmed, by the late learned annotator.

*{For*} Heb. *And*. Which here need not be altered.

*{he doth instruct him*} So most, both Jewish, and ours, applying it to God. Yet some of either otherwise understanding it of the husbandman. Among these, one of ours renders the word, *He bindeth it up*; conceiving it to be meant of the husbandman's binding his crop up in sheaves and bundles, after it is cut, Mat. 13.30. But though the word *binding* come near to that of *chastising*, here used; yet they are divers; and it is this, not that, that we have here. Again, one of the Jewish doctors understands it of his *breaking* the clods, to make the ground level, ver. 25,26. And one of ours, (whom I suppose to come home to the genuine sense of the place, *he beateth it out*, to wit, in the threshing of it, to sever the seed, or grain, from the stalk, or straw. The word signifies, first, and properly *to beat*: And so would be rendered in some other places: as 1 King. 12.11. & 2 Chr. 10.11. *My Father did beat you with whips, but I will beat you with hooked scourges*. Or, as some of the Jewish critics, *with brambles*. See Judg. 8.7,16. Sure the term of *chastising* fits not there: for the complaint was not of any sharp penalties for misdemeanors; but of heavy taxes and burdens, laid on them, for the maintenance of his state. And so may it also be rendered, in divers speeches of Solomon, concerning the correcting of children, by beating them with the rod; as Prov. 19.18. & 29.17. and of the use of the rod, in this piece of husbandry, see ver. 27. which seems, also, to have an allusion, to that manner of chastising children with the rod.

*{to discretion*} Or, *according to that course*, for the article here is significant, Heb. *judgment*, as *according to judgment*, Job 32.2. ch. 32.1. Jer. 30.11. so for the phrase. But the Hebrew word *judgment*, is far larger than judiciary proceedings, and is used frequently, for any *course*, *custom*, *manner*, or *usage*, good or bad. So 1 Sam. 2.13. *the manner*, or *custom of the Priest was*: and, *This will be the course*, or *manner of the King*, 1 Sam. 8.11. so Judg. 13.13. *what shall be the manner of the child?* that is, what course is to be taken with him; and, 2 King. 2.7. *what was the manner of the man?* that is, what manner of man was he?

*{his God*} *That*, or *which, his God*: a defect of the relative, as ver. 12. *his God*; the husbandman's God, as well as the statesman's; and the peasant's, as well as the prince's: for they are all, alike, the work of his hands, Job 34.19. Prov. 22.2. & 29.13.

*{teacheth him*} God teaches the husbandman how to manage his ground, and to sow his seed, as well as the warrior how to handle his weapon, Psal. 18.34. & 144.1. or the ruler, how to sway the scepter, Prov. 8.14–16. ver. 6. chap. 32.15,16. One of the Rabbines tells us, that his father thus expounded this verse; *And he beateth*, or *breaks* (to wit, the clods) *to pieces, and his God raineth upon it*: or, *And when he hath by beating broken the clods, he expecteth what time his God will rain upon it*, to make his seed come up; having done his endeavor, he expects God's blessing upon his labors, without which, all would be frustrate, Psal. 65.9–13. Zach. 10.1. Jam. 5.5. alluded to, Hos. 10.12. a place not rightly read: this difference of version arises from the various use of the word, signifying primarily, *to cast*, Exod. 15.4. Prov. 26.18. then more especially, *to cast out* arrows, *to shoot*, 1 Chr. 10.3. 2 Chr. 26.15. *to cast forth*, or deliver doctrine, direction, or instruction, *to teach*, Deut. 17.7. Psal. 32.8. v. 9. and lastly, *to cast forth*, or pour down showers, *to rain*, or *to water*, Hos. 6.3. & 10.12. Prov. 11.25. hence also that ambiguity, ch. 30.28. But the text, plain and free, of itself, seems overmuch squeezed, to force, it to this sense.

**V. 27.** *{For the fitches are not threshed out with a threshing instrument: neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cumin: but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cumin with a rod*} What was spoken in general, v. 26. of the husbandman's cautious and discreet carriage, in the threshing and beating out of his seed and grain, is here further confirmed, by an enumeration of some of the forementioned particulars, and his various dealing with his several sorts of them. And his discretion, and caution, is in two things observed: First, in that he has gentler ways, for the beating out of the tenderer seeds, than those, that he uses about the harder grain. And secondly, that though he makes use of some harsher means, for the threshing out of the harder grain; yet neither does he keep it continually under the cart, or the hoof; (the means mostly then used) nor does he suffer it to be bruised, or beaten to pieces, as are the clods, v. 24. and so spoiled by either, v. 28. The intent of the prophet being to show that God has divers sorts of dealing, for divers sorts of delinquents, according to the nature and quality, either of the offender, or of the offense, ch. 27.7,8. and again, that even when he deals more roughly, than ordinary, with his own people, being refractory, he does it not with such rigor, as utterly to destroy them, Jer. 30.11.

*{the fitches*} Or, *gith*. See on ver. 25.

*{a threshing instrument*} Not any such, as we in these parts use; but a kind of *sled*, or *dray*, drawn on wheels, shod with iron, beset with spokes, or teeth, which they drew over the corn, to strike out the grain. Of it mention is again, ch. 41.15. And this was used, for the beating out of their bread-corn, v. 28. the harder sort of their grain, such, as was the wheat, barley, and rye, mentioned, v. 25.

*{neither is*} Heb. *and is*; the negative, wanting, is supplied from the former branch: as Deut. 33.6. Prov. 30.3. & 31.3. otherwise, the copulative must go for the disjunctive: *and* for *or*, as Gen. 2.5,6. Job 6.22,23. See v. 28.

*{the cart-wheel*} The wheels of such a cart, or dray.

*{turned about*} As it is used to be, in drawing over the corn: these seeds are too tender, to endure such rough usage; and therefore, instead of the *sled*, and the *wheel*, a *staff*, or *flail*, is used for the one, the less tender of the two; and a *rod*, or *twig*, for the beating out of the other, that cannot fadge so well with the flail: as in chastising of sturdy servants, a cane or a cudgel is sometime used; in correcting of a tender youngling, a twig, or a rod, which we use to say, *will break no bones*.

**V. 28.** *{Bread-corn is bruised*} Thus is the text generally rendered and read; save that some for *bruised*, read *ground*: for it must, say they, be *ground*, before it can become *bread*: and some, *though it be threshed*. But neither does the prophet here meddle with grinding; nor does the word signify *to thresh*: and being read, as it is here, affirmatively, this branch should run directly counter to the close of the verse; where the same word is used, and that withal denied, that according to the received reading, is here affirmed. I suppose, therefore, that the negative is here wanting, to be supplied from the verse next before, as it was there supplied, in the latter branch, from the former: so it is in many places of Scripture, Job 23.17. Psal. 9.18. & 91.5,6. where it is thrice supplied in two verses, from the first branch of the former verse. Thus then the text would run, *For the gith is not threshed with a dray; nor is the cart-wheel turned about upon the cumin—Nor is the bread-corn bruised*. Or, if that seem better, the disjunctive supplied will help it as well; and then the text may be thus rendered, *For the gith is not threshed with a dray; or is a cart-wheel turned about upon the cumin.—Or, is the bread-corn bruised*. And the defect of the disjunctive is no less frequent. See 1 Sam. 20.12. 2 King. 9.32. Job 6.6. & 8.11. & 11.7. & 13.9. ch. 17.6. & 38.14. The meaning then is, the harder grain, such as *bread* is usually made of, as wheat, barley, and rye, though the dray be drawn over it, and the iron-wheel bruise the straw and stalk of it, which the husbandman does not so much regard (See ch. 5.10.) and the beast be suffered to trample upon it: yet is all this carried so cautiously by him, that the grain is not mauled to pieces, or marred; which he further confirms in the words ensuing.

*{bread-corn*} Heb. *bread*: *bread*, for *corn*, whereof bread is made, Psal. 104.15. Eccl. 11.1. ch. 30.23. as *corn*, for *bread*, that is made of corn, Lam. 2.12. Zach. 9.17.

*{is bruised*} Or, *beaten to powder*: so the word properly signifies, Exod. 30.36. & 32.20. 2 King. 23.6. and so it is used affirmatively, where mention is made of the enemies of God's people, chap. 41.15. Mic. 4.13. but so is not the husbandman wont to do, in threshing out of his grain, that especially, which he intends to make *bread* of.

*{because he will not ever be threshing it*} Heb. *for* (as ver. 17.) *he will not, for ever threshing, thresh it*. One reason, why the grain is preserved from being bruised and battered; because the husbandman does not suffer either the sled to pass incessantly over it, or the beasts to trample overlong upon it; but when it is once beaten out of the husk, and beaten off from the straw, he then stays his hand, and leaves further threshing: Nor is the husbandman always threshing his corn; nor is God always chastising his people: it would break their hearts, if he should so do, Ps. 103.9. & 125.3. ch. 57.16. Lam. 3.31,32.

*{nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen*} Heb. *and break it*: where again, we have either a defect of the negative, necessarily requiring a supply thereof; or, the copulative put in the room of the disjunctive: as v. 27. The words may well be rendered, *nor shall his cart-wheel break it to pieces; nor shall his horsemen*, or *iron teeth*, any of them *grind it to powder*. A second reason, why the grain is not spoiled, because the husbandman is careful so to order the matter, that neither from the beasts' hooves, nor from the wheel of the cart, notwithstanding the iron spokes of it, the grain shall receive any such harm, as thereby to be made unuseful. So God, though he exercise his sometime, with harsh and heavy things, Ps. 60.2,3. & 66.11,12. c. 10.6. yet he attempers the affliction to their strength, Psalm 103.13,14. 1 Cor. 10.13. and so disposes things, in his most wise and holy providence, that they shall not, in, or by the same, perish, Ezek. 11.16. Luk. 21.16,18. Rom. 8.28. Some read the words *that his cart-wheel may not break it; nor his iron spokes, bruise it*: and then this is given only, as a reason, why he does not prolong his threshing. It comes much to one, whether way it be read.

*{break it*} The word is so rendered, Deut. 2.15. and might well so be also, Jer. 51.34. a defect of the pronoun: as ver. 20.

*{with the wheel of his cart*} Or, *his cart-wheel*; whereof, ver. 27.

*{nor bruise it*} Or, *beat it to powder*, as before: nor seems that to have place here; he will so deal with it afterward in grinding it at the mill, but in not threshing it on the floor; it would not fit with the matter thereby here resembled.

*{with his horsemen*} That is, as some, those that guide the sled which the horses draw; or, as others, the hooves of the beasts; either those that draw the dray, or that themselves tread out the corn, Mic. 4.14. for that manner of threshing was usual also in those parts; whence the law concerning the *not muzzling of the Ox, that trode out the corn*, Deut. 25.4. 1 Cor. 9.9. and so the old Latin. But the word, that signifies *an hoof*, though in sound somewhat like this; yet is of another form and mold, and rises from a diverse root. And the Hebrew critics tells us, that the word signifies those *iron spokes*, or *teeth*, that the cart-wheel was beset with; so called, because they resembled the rowels of horsemen's spurs; and they observe here a double syntax, that which our version follows; which being admitted, there is a defect of the instrumental particle; as ch. 17.5,9. and that which was before exhibited; which if we follow, the word must be taken distributively; because the noun is plural, the verb singular: as Job 12.7. Joel 1.20. Howbeit, the learned annotator would have the word rendered *horsemen*, to signify *horses*, both here, and elsewhere: as ch. 21.7,9. & 22.6. 1 Sam. 8.11. & 2 Sam. 1.6. none of which places, yet seem necessarily to evince that notion of the word.

**V. 29.** *{This also cometh forth from the Lord of Hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working*} The word, *This*, the most suppose to have reference to the discreet, and prudent carriage of the husbandman, in the threshing out of his grain, as proceeding from the same ground with the former, in the earing of his land, and disposing of his seed, thereby implying, that that God, who has taught him to use such discretion in matters of less moment, will much more carry himself most wisely and providently, in matters of greater weight; as well in the execution of judgment, upon obstinate wicked ones; as also, and that more specially, in the chastising of his children: so that, though he proceed in just severity in the punishing of the one; yet he will have an eye still unto the indemnity of the other. See the like argumentation, Psalm 94.10. Yet some other refer the word, to the devastation of the land of Judah, before menaced, v. 22. either by the Assyrian, or by the Chaldean forces, or both; as proceeding from an appointment of God, and the enemy therefore coming, as with a commission from him, ch. 10.6. Jer. 25.9. But the former seems to flow more naturally from the course of the context.

*{which is*} Or, *who is*, rather; because of a person, a defect of the relative: as v. 12,26.

*{is wonderful in counsel*} See chap. 9.6. Heb. *maketh counsel wonderful*: Or, *doth wonderfully in counsel*; but the former rather, that is, takes strange and wonderful courses, according to his secret counsels and purposes, both for the destruction of his enemies, and the protection of his people, chap. 25.1. as Psalm 31.21. *he hath made his kindness wonderful*: that is, he has done wonderfully out of his kindness, or does wonderfully kindly. See chap. 29.14.

*{and is excellent in working*} The copulative is wanting: as chap. 15.1. Heb. *magnifieth*, or *maketh great, wisdom*; or, *doth greatly*, or *magnificently in wisdom*; that is, does exceeding wisely: as Gen. 19.19. *thou hast magnified thy kindness*; that is, *done exceeding kindly*. I render the word here used, rather *wisdom*, than *working*, for which, I never find it used; or than *essence*, or *substance*, which it seems sometime to import, Job 30.22. or, *the thing itself*, as some other here: and Job 11.6. & Mic. 6.9. because whatsoever the word may, in those other places, signify, it seems not to suit so well here: But, for *wisdom*, or *true wisdom*, as some; or *sound wisdom*, as others render it: for *wisdom*, indeed, it is apparently taken, Job 12.16. compared with v. 13. Prov. 2.7. compared with v. 6. Prov. 3.21. where this, and *discretion*; and Prov. 8.14. where this, and *counsel* are linked together. In either branch there seems a defect, not so much of the preposition which our version suggests and supplies, as of the pronoun, expressed in those places pointed to; *his counsel, his wisdom*: the like defect, chapter 27.9. and oft elsewhere; and the common use of the phrase seems here to require it.
